### COLOR-1 — Reason in HSL, not hex
**Rule.** Express related colors in HSL so hue family and saturation/lightness progression are legible in the values themselves; unrelated hex codes are the tell of an ad-hoc palette.
**Grounding.**
- Refactoring UI: "Using hex or RGB, colors that have a lot in common visually look nothing alike in code... HSL fixes this by representing colors using attributes the human-eye intuitively perceives: hue, saturation, and lightness." (p.138) — the mechanism: HSL exposes the *generative relationship* between shades (shared H, tuned S/L), so a palette can be reasoned about and extended rather than eyeballed.
- Refactoring UI defines the axes: "Hue is a color's position on the color wheel... measured in degrees, where 0° is red, 120° is green, and 240° is blue" (pp.138–139); "Saturation is how colorful or vivid a color looks. 0% saturation is grey... 100% is vibrant" (p.139); "Lightness... measures how close a color is to black or to white" (p.140).
- Caveat, same source: "lightness in HSL is not the same than brightness in HSB... browsers only understand HSL, so if you're designing for the web, HSL should be your weapon of choice." (pp.140–141) — HSB values pasted from a design tool silently mean something else.
**Objective test.** For any set of ≥3 related palette colors: can a reviewer identify the shared hue family from the code alone? Hex triplets with no visible generative relationship (e.g. `#03369E / #507DD7 / #9FB9ED`) = the diagnostic failure HSL fixes; converted, the values must show one shared H and a monotonic S/L progression, such that a reviewer can derive a fourth consistent shade by inspection.
**✗ WRONG.** A donut chart's three blue segments defined as `#03369E`, `#507DD7`, `#9FB9ED` — three codes with no visible mathematical or perceptual relationship to anyone reading the CSS, despite all being "blue."
**✓ RIGHT.** The same segments as `hsl(220,95%,34%) / hsl(220,65%,61%) / hsl(220,69%,80%)` — shared hue 220 explicit, darkest→lightest progression legible directly in the values, a fourth consistent shade derivable by eye.
**Crop.** RU-06.
**Score — grounded ladder (0→10).**
- **0 — ✗** Related color sets (≥3 colors sharing a visual family) defined in hex/RGB with no perceptible mathematical relationship legible in the values (the `#03369E/#507DD7/#9FB9ED` case) *(source: Refactoring UI p.138)*.
- **3** — Mixed tokens: some families in HSL, most still raw hex/RGB, no clear system *(source: Refactoring UI pp.138–141)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** Every related family is defined in HSL in the tokens/CSS (hue/saturation/lightness legible per value) *(source: Refactoring UI p.138)*.
- **6** — + Within each family the H value is identical (±2°) across all shades, or a deviation is an explained deliberate rotation *(source: Refactoring UI pp.138–139)*.
- **7** — + L progresses monotonically reading each family's values top-to-bottom *(source: Refactoring UI p.140)*.
- **8** — + S varies as a recognizable curve rather than scattered values `[derived: Refactoring UI pp.139, 152]`.
- **9** — + No HSB-pasted values: every token verified as web HSL (an HSB triplet silently means something else) *(source: Refactoring UI pp.140–141)*.
- **10 — ✓** A fourth consistent shade is derivable by inspection alone — steps regular enough to interpolate, matching the `hsl(220,…)` exemplar *(source: Refactoring UI pp.138–141)*.

### COLOR-2 — A full color system, not 5 brand swatches
**Rule.** A real UI needs 8–10 greys, 5–10 shades of 1–2 primaries, and 5–10 shades per semantic family (success/warning/danger + accents), defined up front — preventing the near-identical-ad-hoc-shades drift.
**Grounding.**
- Refactoring UI: "You can't build anything with five hex codes. To build something real, you need a much more comprehensive set of colors to choose from." (p.143) — the five-swatch generator palette applied to a real chat product is the book's own garish failure case (p.142): every panel, alert, and hover state forced onto one of five flat values.
- On greys: "You'll need more greys than you think, too — three or four shades might sound like plenty but it won't be long before you wish you had something a little darker than shade #2 but a little lighter than shade #3. In practice, you want 8-10 shades to choose from." (p.144)
- On overall scope: "All in, it's not uncommon to need as many as ten different colors with 5-10 shades each for a complex UI." (p.147) — pre-defining the scale up front is what prevents scattered `lighten()/darken()` calls producing 35 near-identical blues.
**Objective test.** Token-file audit: distinct grey shades 8–10; shades per primary 5–10; semantic families (success/warning/danger at minimum) present with 5–10 shades each. A flat 5-hex palette with zero tonal variants fails outright; `lighten()/darken()` calls scattered in component code instead of predefined steps = drift flag.
**✗ WRONG.** A team-chat app's entire visual system built from exactly five color-generator hex codes with zero tonal variants — a yellow sidebar beside a red error banner, because those were the only yellow and red available.
**✓ RIGHT.** The same app on a defined system: grey scale for text/panels/borders, a blue primary scale for nav/active states, dedicated red/yellow/green scales reserved for destructive, warning, and positive states — every UI need (hover, border, tint, alert) draws an appropriately-toned predefined step.

- **6** — + Grey scale reaches 8–10 distinct shades *(source: Refactoring UI p.144)*.
- **7** — + Each primary (1–2 hues) has a defined 5–10-step scale *(source: Refactoring UI p.147)*.

### COLOR-3 — Restrained palette; accents earn attention
**Rule.** Near-neutral base plus a few high-contrast accents reserved for what matters; broad loud palettes fragment attention.
**Grounding.**
- About Face: "visual interfaces should strive to be minimal, such as simple geometric forms or a restricted color palette composed primarily of less-saturated or neutral colors balanced with a few high-contrast accent colors that emphasize important information." Too many colors is one of the book's named noise forms (p.423).

**Objective test.** Count distinct saturated accent colors doing emphasis work on one screen: a small fixed set (≤~3), each with a stable meaning, reserved for genuinely important information; any accent applied to a decorative element = fail.
**✗ WRONG.** Five saturated KPI-card accents with no shared meaning; the same accent color reused decoratively on dividers and illustrations.
**✓ RIGHT.** Neutral grey/white base; exactly one accent (e.g., red) meaning exactly "needs attention" (over budget, error), used nowhere else.

### COLOR-4 — Shade math: saturation compensates lightness; hue carries brightness
**Rule.** Raise saturation as lightness departs 50% or extreme shades wash out; hues carry inherent perceived brightness, so rotate ≤20–30° toward/away from yellow/cyan/magenta to lighten/darken feel while preserving intensity.
**Grounding.**
- Refactoring UI: "as a color gets closer to 0% or 100% lightness, the impact of saturation is weakened... if you don't want the lighter and darker shades of a given color to look washed out, you need to increase the saturation as the lightness gets further away from 50%." (p.152)
- On perceived brightness: "every hue has an inherent perceived brightness due to how the human eye perceives color... there are three separate local minimums (red, green, and blue) and three local maximums (yellow, cyan, and magenta)." (pp.153–154) — rotating hue toward a maximum lightens the *felt* brightness without draining intensity the way pure lightness adjustment does.
- On the rotation bound: "it works best in small doses. Don't rotate the hue more than 20-30° or it will look like a totally different color instead of just lighter or darker." (p.157) The book's own failure case: its yellow scale darkened by lightness alone goes muddy olive; rotated toward orange with rising saturation it goes rich brown (p.156).
**Objective test.** Plot S vs L across a 5–9-step shade scale of one hue: flat/constant S while L sweeps ~10–90% = washed-out extremes; S must visibly rise at both ends relative to the middle step. Hue-rotation lightening/darkening: |ΔH| between base and variant ≤30° (beyond that it reads as a different hue, not a shade).
**✗ WRONG.** A yellow→dark scale built by dropping lightness only, saturation held constant — the dark steps read as dull, muddy olive-green.
**✓ RIGHT.** The same scale rotating hue toward orange as lightness decreases while saturating at the dark end — warm, rich brown/amber darks that keep their intensity.

### COLOR-5 — Greys are rarely neutral

### COLOR-6 — Accessible contrast without ugliness
**Rule.** Meet 4.5:1 (3:1 large/bold text): flip the contrast — dark same-hue text on a light tint instead of white-on-saturated (which also sheds unearned visual weight) — or rotate the text hue brighter instead of washing toward white.
**Grounding.**

- Refactoring UI: "The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) recommend that normal text (under ~18px) has a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1, and that larger text has a contrast ratio of at least 3:1." (p.162) Its status-pill example: white-on-saturated measured 2.25:1 / 1.56:1 / 3.14:1 — all failing — flipped to dark-on-tint they hit 5.34–9.78:1 AND stop dominating the row (pp.163–164): the flip fixes accessibility and hierarchy in one move.
- Refactoring UI, dark panels: "one way to increase the contrast without getting closer to white is to rotate the hue towards a brighter color, like cyan, magenta, or yellow" (p.165) — its example moves `hsl(240,44%,89%)` → `hsl(188,100%,85%)`, 8.37:1 → 8.71:1, both AAA but the rotated one stays colorful.
- Universal Principles adds a reading-performance threshold: "Performance is optimal when contrast levels between text and background exceed 70 percent" (p.148), and warns that passing numbers can still fail: "High-contrast, inverse text can 'visually bleed' to the background and dramatically reduce legibility" (p.148, note 4).

Any failing colored pill/badge: try dark-on-light-tint of the same hue BEFORE white/black; failing colored-on-colored text: try a ≤30° rotation toward cyan/magenta/yellow (60°/180°/300°) before lightening. **✓ RIGHT.** Dark-green-on-pale-green, dark-amber-on-pale-amber pills — 5.34–9.78:1 (AA/AAA), and the softer pills sit correctly in the row's hierarchy.

### COLOR-7 — Never encode meaning in color alone
**Rule.** Every color-carried state/severity/category gets a second channel (icon, label, shape, weight); multi-category encodings prefer lightness steps of ONE hue over many hues.
**Grounding.**

### COLOR-8 — Color similarity is a grouping claim
**Rule.** Reusing one color across functionally unrelated elements asserts a relationship that doesn't exist; color is the strongest similarity signal and must be spent semantically.
**Grounding.**
- Universal Principles: "Similarity of color results in the strongest grouping effect; it is strongest when the number of colors is small, and is decreasingly effective as the number of colors increases... Similarity of shape is the weakest grouping strategy." (p.226) Guideline: "Use similarity to indicate relatedness among elements in a design... Use the fewest colors and simplest shapes possible for the strongest grouping effects." (p.226) — because color grouping is involuntary, a shared color IS a claim of relatedness whether intended or not.
- Designing Interfaces: "If you have a few things 'of a type' and you want viewers to see them as equally interesting alternatives, give them an identical (and distinctive) graphic treatment" (p.218) — the inverse binds too: identical treatment on non-alternatives claims a false equivalence, and different treatment on the same role implies (wrongly) different behavior.
**Objective test.** Map each accent color to its semantic role: one color → one role. A hue appearing on interactive AND decorative AND status elements = fail. >~6–7 hues encoding one categorical dimension = grouping degraded (UP's count threshold). Same-role controls across the app must share the same {color, shape, radius, size} tuple; any outlier not explained by a documented state = fail.
**✗ WRONG.** Brand blue on links, inert icons, a status chip, and a decorative divider — four unrelated roles claiming kinship.
**✓ RIGHT.** Blue = interactive, amber = warning, grey = inert — each color one job, each job one color.

### COLOR-9 — Text over imagery needs contrast normalization
**Rule.** A busy photo spans light and dark regions; no single text color survives — reduce the image's dynamics: overlay tint, lowered contrast + raised brightness, desaturate + multiply brand color, or a zero-offset large-blur text glow.

- Same source, the four worked techniques: semi-transparent overlay `background-color: hsla(0,0%,0%,.55)` (p.203); "Brightness: +40%, Contrast: -70%" (p.204); "Lower the image contrast... # Copy & Language

Words on the interface. Pillars: 2, 3.

### COPY-1 — Omit needless words; instructions must die
**Rule.** Cut instructional text, welcome blurbs, and promotional filler ruthlessly (halve, then halve again); the goal for instructions is elimination via self-evidence, with survivors at ≤1 short sentence. Applies to button labels, headers, hints, and status text alike.
**Grounding.**
- Krug's Third Law: "Get rid of half the words on each page, then get rid of half of what's left." (p.77). Mechanism — the payoff is triple: "It reduces the noise level of the page... makes the useful content more prominent... makes the pages shorter" (p.77); default stance: "start with the assumption that everything is visual noise (the 'presumed guilty until proven innocent' approach) and get rid of anything that's not making a real contribution." (p.62)
- Krug on instructions: "The main thing you need to know about instructions is that no one is going to read them—at least not until after repeated attempts at 'muddling through' have failed." (p.78); "Your objective should always be to eliminate instructions entirely by making everything self-explanatory, or as close to it as possible." (p.78). His worked rewrite cuts 103 words to 34 with zero loss (pp.78–79).
- Universal Principles: "Excess is noise." (p.224); mechanism — "every unnecessary data item, graphic, line, or symbol steals attention away from relevant elements." (p.224)
**Objective test.** Remove any sentence/paragraph and check whether task completion or comprehension changes — unchanged = it goes. A first audit pass must achieve ≥50% word-count reduction on instructional blocks without losing a fact the user needs; if it can't, the block wasn't audited hard enough. Remove ALL helper text from a control: if a first-time user still operates it correctly (labeling, placeholder convention, affordance), the instruction was unnecessary; any surviving instruction is ≤1 short sentence.
**✗ WRONG.** A settings page opens with "Welcome to your account settings page! Here you can manage all aspects of your account, including your profile, security, and notification preferences. Feel free to explore the options below…" — and the search box above it carries a paragraph explaining how to type keywords and click Search.
**✓ RIGHT.** The page opens directly with the "Profile / Security / Notifications" section headers and their controls; the search control is a box + magnifier + "Search", nothing else.
**Crop.** KR-08 (Krug Ch.5 "Before: 103 Words / After: 34 Words" figure, pp.78–79).

- **2** — filler paragraph gone, but ≥2 sentences in the block are removable by the deletion test (unchanged task completion/comprehension without them) *(Krug — deletion test, p.77)*.
- **4** — exactly 1 removable sentence remains; maximal-cut attempt still recovers 20–40% of the block's words *(Krug Third Law, p.77)*.

### COPY-2 — Write for scanning
**Rule.** Users scan and satisfice — design copy as billboard, not literature: front-loaded keywords, headings, bolded anchor fragments that alone carry the task-critical path.
**Grounding.**
- Krug: "We're thinking 'great literature' (or at least 'product brochure'), while the user's reality is much closer to 'billboard going by at 60 miles an hour.'" (p.39)

Instead, we scan (or skim) them, looking for words or phrases that catch our eye." (p.40). ### COPY-3 — Plain, active, precise — in the user's vocabulary
**Rule.** Simple language, active voice, audience-matched precision; task vocabulary, never system vocabulary (no raw statuses, codes, internal nouns) — and never over-simplified into imprecision.
**Grounding.**
- Universal Principles: "Readability is determined by factors such as word length, word commonality, sentence length, number of clauses in a sentence, and number of syllables in a sentence." (p.198); the explicit caution — "Simple language is preferred, but overly simple language obscures meaning." (p.198); and "do not write for the formula" — readability formulas are "primitive guides and should not outweigh all other considerations" (p.198).
- About Face (unified file model, Ch14): Save/Save As/Close dialogs "reflect the internal mechanisms of data entry, storage, and retrieval" (p.325); the fix "abolish[es] all user interface recognition of the two copies" (p.338), design principle "Save documents and settings automatically." (p.337). Mechanism — copy exposing the implementation model is excise: work serving the system's internal bookkeeping, not the user's goal (pp.283–285).
**Objective test.** Run the copy through a readability formula (the book cites Fry's Graph): the estimated grade level must MATCH the intended audience's reading level, not merely be minimized. Zero internal-concept leaks (temp filenames, status codes, table names, implementation nouns) outside debug surfaces. Each term is one the target user would themselves use for the thing.
**✗ WRONG.** "Oopsie, something went wonky!" in a developer API error; "Do you want to save changes to Untitled-4.tmp?" exposing the memory-vs-disk distinction the user never asked to think about.
**✓ RIGHT.** "Request failed: missing required field `apiKey`. See docs/auth."; silent autosave with rename-in-place — no save dialog at all.

**Rule.** Copy register (formal vs casual) is a personality axis applied consistently everywhere; error/alert tone is polite and never blaming; and when a clever/branded phrasing costs comprehension, the obvious word wins.

# Cross-Surface Consistency

Pillar 4 in full: every element fits the app it lands in — same rule-set, same behavior, same vocabulary — while staying crafted. Two layers: internal system consistency (the screen obeys its own small rule-set) and sibling consistency (the screen matches the rest of the app).

---

### XCON-1 — Same role, same treatment — everywhere
**Rule.** Elements with one semantic role (primary buttons, card headers, severity chips, selection states, the same OBJECT class on different canvases/media) look and behave identically across every surface; visual difference is correctly read as meaning difference.
**Grounding.**
- *Universal Principles* (p.56): "According to the principle of consistency, systems are more usable and learnable when similar parts are expressed in similar ways. Consistency enables people to efficiently transfer knowledge to new contexts, learn new things quickly, and focus attention on the relevant aspects of a task." Mechanism: sameness lets learning transfer, so attention frees for the task instead of re-decoding each surface; the book names four kinds — aesthetic, functional, internal, external.
- *Designing Interfaces* (p.218): "If you have a few things 'of a type' and you want viewers to see them as equally interesting alternatives, give them an identical (and distinctive) graphic treatment." Mechanism: shared styling is a functional claim — a different treatment tells users (correctly or not) that the thing behaves differently.
- *About Face* (Ch17, p.431): the design-language argument — ad hoc per-screen choices, even individually fine, never accumulate into a coherent product.
**Objective test.** Build a role×surface matrix: for each recurring role/object class, list every rendering and interaction model across screens and media. All members of a class share the same {color, shape, corner-radius, size, position-in-group, interaction model} tuple; any role with >1 treatment absent a documented state reason (disabled/hover/selected) = defect. The same object class behaving differently on two sibling surfaces is the highest-severity form. Count deviations — 0 = internally consistent.
**✗ WRONG.** Delete is a red trash icon top-right on one screen, a grey "X" text link bottom-of-card on another; annotations on one canvas open popovers on click while the sibling canvas uses differently-styled inline panels for the same annotation objects.
**✓ RIGHT.** One destructive treatment, one confirm pattern, one position rule product-wide; one annotation grammar identical on every canvas the object appears on; a genuinely different role (destructive delete vs primary confirm) gets its own deliberately distinct, consistent treatment.
**Crop.** UP-15 (Universal Principles p.57 — identical logo/color/typeface across locations); Designing Interfaces Fig. 4-13 (p.219).
**Score (0–10).**
> - **0** — a recurring pattern (delete action, status badge, primary button, same object class on different canvases) has a different color/icon/position per screen with no functional justification *(source: Universal Principles — Consistency p.56; Designing Interfaces — Gestalt Similarity Fig.4-13 p.218)*.
> - **2** — consistent within one section but breaks in 1-2 other areas of the product — a partial audit fail *(Universal Principles — Consistency p.56)*.
> - **3** — same-role controls mostly consistent but one unexplained outlier exists in a class of ≥4 same-role controls *(Designing Interfaces — Gestalt Similarity p.218)*.
> - **5 — THRESHOLD:** zero unjustified deviations found in a full instance audit of a given recurring pattern (same icon/color/position/wording everywhere it appears); every member of a same-action-class shares the {color, shape, corner-radius, size} tuple, any outlier a documented state (disabled/hover/selected) *(Universal Principles — Consistency p.56; Designing Interfaces — Gestalt Similarity p.218)*.
> - **6** — threshold met AND the same object class behaves identically (interaction model, not just look) on every sibling surface/canvas it appears on *[derived — extends the visual-match test both books define to the behavioral dimension the principle's own Rule names]*.
> - **7** — threshold met across MULTIPLE recurring role classes (≥3), not just one spot-checked pattern, including internal consistency across the design system's own building blocks *(Universal Principles — Consistency p.56)*.
> - **8** — + recurring actions (delete, confirm, close) hold the same position-in-group on every surface, zero deviations *(Universal Principles — Consistency "position" dimension p.56)*.
> - **9** — + genuinely distinct roles (destructive vs primary) each carry their OWN consistent, deliberately distinct treatment, used to signal the difference *(Designing Interfaces — Fig.4-13 "distinguishing one item via a deliberate accent" p.219)*.
> - **10** — all four kinds — aesthetic, functional, internal, external — verified consistent, including alignment with platform/external convention where relevant *(Universal Principles — Consistency p.56-57, the Bob Evans franchise-identity standard)*.
> Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — Universal Principles: high; Designing Interfaces (Gestalt Similarity): high.

### XCON-2 — A design language: few recurring visual words
**Rule.** A deliberate vocabulary — a corner radius, an accent, a card treatment, a type scale, a copy tone — recurs across screens and accumulates into a recognizable product feel; per-screen invention never adds up.
**Grounding.**
- *About Face* (Ch17, p.431): "Think of this design language as a 'vocabulary' of design elements such as shape, color, typography, and how these elements are composed and combined. They create the appropriate emotional tone and establish patterns that a person can recognize, understand, and, ideally, use to create positive associations with the brand." Mechanism: recognition and brand association come from composition of a small vocabulary, not from any single good screen.
- *Refactoring UI* (p.20, p.25): "Every design has some sort of personality... a lot of it is determined by a few solid, concrete factors" — typeface voice, color, border radius, copy tone are chosen once; on radius specifically: "Whatever you choose, it's important to stay consistent. Mixing square corners with rounded corners in the same interface almost always looks worse than sticking with one or the other." Mechanism: each axis telegraphs personality; independently-decided components send contradictory signals.
**Objective test.** A reviewer unfamiliar with the internal system names the product's 3–5 recurring visual words (radius, accent, card treatment, type scale, tone) after seeing 3 unrelated screens — and can predict a 4th screen's styling from them. Failure to name a consistent set = language missing. Secondary check: exactly one radius convention (square OR rounded) across the interface; mixed conventions = fail.
**✗ WRONG.** Screen A: 4px-radius flat cards; screen B: 16px-radius shadowed cards; screen C: square outlined cards — three personalities, no product.
**✓ RIGHT.** One radius, one elevation token, one accent for primary actions, one copy register — screen D's styling is guessable sight-unseen.
**Crop.** RU-32 (Refactoring UI pp.20–26 personality axes).
**Score (0–10).**
> - **0** — 3 unrelated screens each invent their own vocabulary (corner radius, card treatment) with zero overlap *(source: About Face — design language Ch.17 p.431)*.
> - **2** — only 1 of 3–5 vocabulary elements (radius, accent, card style, type scale, copy tone) is shared across screens; the rest vary *(About Face p.431)*.
> - **3** — 2 of 4 personality axes (typeface/color/radius/tone) are internally consistent, 2 are not *(Refactoring UI — Coherent personality pp.313-320)*.
> - **4** — 3 of 4 axes internally consistent, one still drifting (commonly copy tone, least visually obvious) *(Refactoring UI p.316)*.
> - **5 — THRESHOLD:** a reviewer unfamiliar with the system, shown 3 unrelated screens, names a consistent set of 3–5 recurring visual words *(About Face p.431 — the book's stated test)*.
> - **6** — exactly one radius convention (square OR rounded) across the interface *(Refactoring UI p.20 — "mixing square corners with rounded corners... almost always looks worse")*.
> - **7** — all 3–5 named words are consistent AND consistently applied across every screen sampled (not just the 3 tested), no screen the odd one out *(About Face p.431)*.
> - **8** — all four personality axes internally consistent across the product, and the chosen direction plausibly matches the stated brand goal *(Refactoring UI pp.313-320)*.
> - **9** — the reviewer correctly PREDICTS a 4th, unseen screen's styling in advance from the named words *(About Face p.431 — the ✓ prediction standard)*.
> - **10** — matches the ✓ state fully: one radius everywhere, one consistent copy register, color and typeface both deliberately chosen and consistently applied, reinforcing a single coherent personality end to end *(Refactoring UI pp.20-26, 313-320; About Face p.431)*.

**Weight.** med (2) — Refactoring UI: medium; About Face: med-high (leans high at whole-product scale — noted, majority med for a per-surface review).

### XCON-3 — Small-rule-set repetition is the designed-vs-assembled tell
**Rule.** "Designed" shows as repetition of a constrained set (spacing increments, palette, radii, type steps) across the WHOLE surface; one beautiful component beside a default-styled one reads assembled even when each passes alone.
**Grounding.**
- *Designing Interfaces* (pp.216–217): "Creating a design that is based on a grid... allows the designer to focus on the content, assured that the layout will have visual consistency and balance"; "Using a grid is a good way to ensure that the content will create a visually harmonious composition, and will aid in reducing the cognitive load of your viewer." Its spacing-audit framing (Ch.5 argument, p.493 area): values clustering on a repeated scale = designed; scattered ad hoc = assembled regardless of individual component quality — the mechanism for "designed vs assembled" is repetition of a constrained visual system, not any single nice element.
- *About Face* (Ch17, p.423): "Unnecessary variation is the enemy of a coherent, usable design. If the spacing between two sets of elements is nearly the same, make that spacing exactly the same... Every visual element and every difference in color, size, or other visual property should be there for a reason." Mechanism: near-identical-but-not-identical values read as unintentional sloppiness even when each instance looks acceptable alone.
- *Refactoring UI* (pp.70–74, also 28–32): "If you want a system to be truly useful, it needs to take into consideration the relative difference between adjacent values" (p.71); rule of thumb: "make sure no two values in your scale are ever closer than about 25%" (p.72). Mechanism: pre-defined scales exist precisely to force this repetition and kill imperceptible distinctions.
**Objective test.** Sample ≥10 padding/margin values, all radii, all type sizes, all colors per screen: each clusters on the defined scale (e.g. 4/8/16/24px); ad-hoc values (11/17/9px), adjacent scale steps differing by <25%, near-duplicate colors doing one job, or browser-default controls beside styled ones = assembled.
**✗ WRONG.** A custom toggle beside an unstyled default dropdown with improvised 11px/17px padding between them — each element acceptable, the surface a patchwork.
**✓ RIGHT.** Every control on the same spacing scale, radius, and palette — one deliberate system; the toggle and dropdown are visibly siblings.
**Crop.** DI-06 (Fig. 4-8 gridless vs gridded, pp.216–217), RU-03 (pp.70–74 spacing-scale bar chart).
**Score (0–10).**
> - **0** — major block edges scattered across many one-off x-coordinates (12/18/15/22px picked by eye), no discernible grid; adjacent scale values differ by <10% with no relationship between them *(source: Designing Interfaces — grid pp.216-217/52-59; Refactoring UI — non-linear scales pp.70-74/79-85)*.
> - **2** — a grid loosely followed for some elements but broken by ≥30% of blocks; some scale steps meet the 25% threshold, others (especially at the small end) don't *(Designing Interfaces pp.216-217; Refactoring UI p.72 "no two values... closer than about 25%")*.
> - **3** — a near-duplicate value serving one functional role exists (two non-identical values within 20% doing the same job) *(About Face p.423 — "unnecessary variation is the enemy of a coherent design")*.
> - **4** — a browser-default control renders beside a custom-styled one, but only in a secondary/low-traffic region *[derived — the principle's own ✗ patchwork case, scoped to severity by traffic]*.
> - **5 — THRESHOLD:** distinct major-block edge x-values on the page ≤4–6 (a real grid system in use); every adjacent spacing/type-scale step ≥~25% apart *(Designing Interfaces pp.216-217; Refactoring UI p.72)*.
> - **6** — both the radius set and the type-size set are each closed (every observed value is a member of one defined scale) *(Refactoring UI p.20/pp.313-320 — one radius convention; #9 scale-membership mechanism)*.
> - **7** — margins and gutters are visually distinct and consistently sized (e.g. one 8px-unit scale) across all page regions; the scale is deliberate and sufficiently dense (~10+ steps) *(Designing Interfaces pp.216-217; Refactoring UI p.72 "a deliberate, sufficiently-dense scale")*.
> - **8** — zero near-duplicate values for one job anywhere on the surface *(About Face p.423 — "make that spacing exactly the same")*.
> - **9** — no default/styled patchwork anywhere, even in secondary regions; grid holds across MULTIPLE pages in the product, not just one screen *(Designing Interfaces pp.216-217 — cross-page harmony)*.
> - **10** — matches the ✓ examples fully: one deliberate spacing/radius/palette system with zero one-off values, verified across ≥2 pages *(Refactoring UI pp.70-74; Designing Interfaces pp.216-219)*.
> Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — Designing Interfaces (grid; spacing-audit): high; Refactoring UI (scales): high; About Face (unnecessary variation): med — majority high, AF dissent noted.

### XCON-4 — Consistency without rigidity; diverge in the spirit
**Rule.** Obey standards and the product's own idioms unless a truly superior alternative exists; when diverging, honor the spirit of the pattern — and when clarity and consistency genuinely conflict, clarity wins, stated as an explicit tradeoff.
**Grounding.**
- *About Face* (Ch17, pp.430–431): "Obey standards unless there is a truly superior alternative"; "Consistency doesn't imply rigidity." The book's own case: PowerPoint forced into Word/Excel's menu structure "doesn't gain much... It also loses quite a bit in ease of use by conforming to an alien structure that diverges from the user's mental models" — yet PowerPoint rightly keeps its unique slide-sorter. Mechanism: blind conformity produces awkward interfaces; un-anchored novelty breaks learned expectations — the fix is judged divergence with a stated reason.
- *Don't Make Me Think* (p.56): "CLARITY TRUMPS CONSISTENCY. If you can make something significantly clearer by making it slightly inconsistent, choose in favor of clarity." Mechanism: consistency is valuable but subordinate — it exists to serve comprehension, not to override it.
- *Universal Principles* (p.56, note 1): quotes Emerson's "A foolish consistency is the hobgoblin of little minds" in the margin — the book's own caveat against consistency for its own sake.
**Objective test.** Every divergence from platform convention or the product's own established pattern carries a one-line written rationale naming the concrete advantage; divergences with none on file = fail. Clarity-vs-consistency conflicts resolve via an explicit stated "clarity gain X / consistency cost Y" — never silently defaulted to "match the system" or "break the system".
**✗ WRONG.** A one-off left-aligned checkbox where every sibling screen uses right-aligned toggles, no reason on file; a destructive "Delete all" button forced system-grey "for consistency".
**✓ RIGHT.** The established toggle everywhere, or a documented "toggle can't express Off/Auto/On → dropdown"; "Delete all" deliberately rendered red — a stated clarity-over-consistency call about risk.
**Crop.** none.
**Score (0–10).**
> - **0** — a control diverges from platform or the product's own established pattern for the same job with zero documented rationale; AND a clarity-critical signal (destructive action) is forced into system-wide consistency with no acknowledgment of the cost *(source: About Face — Consistency Ch.17 p.430-431; Don't Make Me Think — Clarity trumps consistency p.56, p.81-89)*.
> - **2** — a divergence exists with a rationale, but it doesn't cite a genuine functional advantage (just preference/deadline) *(About Face p.430-431)*.
> - **3** — a clarity-vs-consistency conflict wasn't noticed/considered at all — outcome may accidentally be fine, but no reasoning trail exists *(Don't Make Me Think p.56)*.
> - **4** — the conflict is noticed and a choice is made, but the tradeoff isn't stated/documented anywhere *(Don't Make Me Think p.56)*.
> - **5 — THRESHOLD:** every divergence from convention has a written one-line rationale citing a specific advantage *(About Face p.430-431 — the book's own bar)*.
> - **6** — the tradeoff is stated and the choice reasonably favors clarity where it matters, with only minor unexplained residue elsewhere *(Don't Make Me Think p.56)*.
> - **7** — no unjustified divergences AND at least one divergence is a clear case of "truly superior alternative" correctly applied *(About Face p.431 — dropdown replacing a toggle that can't express tri-state)*.
> - **8** — every destructive/high-risk action keeps a visually distinctive treatment even against system uniformity *[derived — converges Don't Make Me Think's "Delete all" case with About Face's "obey standards unless truly superior" caveat]*.
> - **9** — consistent with established convention everywhere it should be, with occasional, well-reasoned, clearly-labeled departures that don't fight the user's mental model *(About Face p.431 — PowerPoint's slide-sorter case)*.
> - **10** — every clarity-vs-consistency conflict is explicitly reasoned and resolved in clarity's favor where it counts, zero silent defaults either way *(Don't Make Me Think p.56 — the red "Delete all" ✓ case)*.
> Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** med (2) — About Face: med; Don't Make Me Think (clarity trumps consistency): med.

### XCON-5 — Almost-consistent is worse than clearly different (uncanny valley)
**Rule.** A component ALMOST matching the system — near-radius, near-color, familiar-but-tweaked — reads as more wrong than a clearly distinct one; fix by full consistency or deliberate, obvious difference, never "almost".
**Grounding.**
- *Universal Principles* (p.242): "When a form is very close but not identical to a healthy human—as with a mannequin or computer-generated renderings of people—the form tends to become distinctly unappealing." Contributing conditions listed directly: "Abnormally proportioned or positioned facial features, asymmetry of facial features, subtleties of eye movement, and unnatural skin complexions are all sufficient conditions to trigger uncanny valley effects." Mechanism (via the book's own consistency cross-link): small deviations in proportion or subtle properties are sufficient triggers — so a partially-applied design system is not "a little off", it reads BROKEN, more wrong than an obviously different treatment; the two stable states are identical or clearly distinct.
**Objective test.** Token-diff a new component against the system across every axis — spacing, color tokens, radius, type scale, motion curves: the result must be 100% match, or a deliberately distinct, documented, visibly different treatment. 1–2 near-miss properties (e.g. matched colors but a subtly different radius) = the uncanny zone, fail.
**✗ WRONG.** New feature buttons use the exact system colors and spacing but a subtly different radius and shadow — users can't say what's wrong, only that it feels broken.
**✓ RIGHT.** Radius and shadow matched exactly to the system tokens; or the feature visibly restyled as a distinct, labeled treatment nobody mistakes for the standard one.
**Crop.** UP-12 (Universal Principles p.242 uncanny-valley curve).
**Score (0–10).**

**Rule.** The visual system, spacing, and indicator logic established at nav level 1 persists into levels 2–3+ (where systems usually go ad hoc); and the product's own OUTPUT (formats, ordering, phrasing, layout) stays reliable and consistent while INPUT tolerance stays liberal.

# Data & Money Legibility

Numbers must tell a story a scanning eye can follow — especially derived money (totals, rollups, coverage, net). Pillars: 2, 3.

### DATA-1 — Preattentive encoding makes the important value findable in constant time
**Rule.** Hue, brightness, saturation, size, position/alignment, orientation, shape, texture are processed before conscious attention; a table of uniform values forces linear reading (search ∝ N) — encode the values that matter on one preattentive channel so they pop in O(1).
**Grounding.** Designing Interfaces: "Certain visual features operate preattentively: they convey information before the viewer pays conscious attention" (p.436). The book's demonstrated exercise — "find the blue objects" among many red ones: "it doesn't matter how many red objects there are; the amount of time it takes you to find the blue ones is constant!... Color operates at a primitive cognitive level" (p.436). The text contrast: "When dealing with text such as this, your 'search time' really is linear with the number of items. But what if we still use text, but make the target numbers physically larger than the others?... Now we're back to constant time again. Size is, in fact, another preattentive variable" (p.437). The eight variables are given as a reference grid (Fig. 9-5, p.438). Mechanism: constant-vs-linear search time is the measurable difference between "the numbers feel flat" and a display that reads itself — preattentive channels shift outlier-finding from serial reading to parallel perception.
**Objective test.** In a table/dashboard of ≥20 same-class values, estimate how search time for an outlier scales with row count: if the only differentiator is reading each value in turn (search ∝ N, linear), preattentive encoding is absent — fail. If the exceptional value is coded via one of the 8 variables (hue, brightness, saturation, size, position/alignment, orientation, shape, texture), search is effectively O(1) — pass. Exceptional values styled identically to routine ones = fail.
**✗ WRONG.** A 70-row financial table renders every value in the same 12px black type; the one threshold-breaching value is discoverable only by reading all 70 rows in sequence.
**✓ RIGHT.** Out-of-threshold values rendered in a visibly larger size and/or a distinct color — they pop instantly regardless of table length.
**Crop.** DI-01 (Fig. 9-1/9-2 constant-time color search p.436; Fig. 9-3/9-4 linear-vs-constant via size p.437; Fig. 9-5 eight-variable grid p.438).
**Score (0–10 ladder).**
> - **0** — outlier/exceptional value discoverable only by reading every row in sequence; search time ∝ N *(source: Designing Interfaces p.436-437, Fig. 9-1–9-4)*.
> - **3** — a preattentive cue is used but weakly (e.g. a barely-larger font, <1.3× size ratio) so search stays closer to linear than constant *(Designing Interfaces p.437, Fig. 9-3/9-4)*.
> - **5 — THRESHOLD:** every exceptional/threshold-breaching value is encoded on ≥1 of the 8 preattentive variables (hue, brightness, saturation, size, position/alignment, orientation, shape, texture) strongly enough that search is effectively O(1) *(Designing Interfaces p.436-438, Fig. 9-5)*.
> - **6** — as 5, and no exceptional value is styled identically to routine values (no coverage gaps) *(Designing Interfaces p.436)*.
> - **7** — the encoding is consistent/systemized across the whole table or dashboard — every outlier class gets its own reliable cue *(Designing Interfaces p.438)*.
> - **8** — as 7, and the pop encoding stays selective (routine values remain quiet, roughly ≤10% of visible values carry it) so the exceptional ones keep winning *(Designing Interfaces p.436-438, [derived] selectivity corollary)*.
> - **9** — multiple reinforcing preattentive channels used at once for critical values (e.g. size + color) *(Designing Interfaces p.437, Fig. 9-4 pattern)*.
> - **10** — the reinforced encoding is verified to "pop" at any table length, in a 3-second glance, regardless of row count *(Designing Interfaces p.436-438)*.

### DATA-2 — One headline number; supporters subordinate and grouped
**Rule.** A data-dense region needs one dominant "most important number" (size/weight/position) with supporting figures visually subordinate and grouped next to their meaning.
**Grounding.** Krug: "The more important something is, the more prominent it is... Things that are related logically are related visually" plus visual nesting (pp.55–56); the extract's #29 applies this doctrine directly to numeric content — if the reader must read every number to find the story, the region fails the same don't-make-me-think test as prose, because every unresolved "wait, which number matters?" moment fills the thought balloon Krug's First Law forbids (p.29). Refactoring UI: "The problem with this approach is that it makes it difficult to present the data with any sort of hierarchy; every piece of data is given equal emphasis" (p.48); in dense scan-heavy contexts (dashboards/specs) the LABEL may lead because the user hunts for it (p.51), elsewhere the datum stars while its label shrinks — the heart-rate card keeps "HEART RATE" small and light while "82 BPM" is large and bold (pp.48–52). Mechanism: hierarchy pre-processes the region so the eye lands on the story instead of reconstructing it.
**Objective test.** Identify the region's most task-important figure by task relevance: it must render at strictly greater size/weight/contrast than every other number in the region, and every supporting number sits under a heading or proximity cluster tying it to its meaning. If a reader must read every number to find "the story," fail. Additionally: ≥3 fields in the literal `Label: Value` pattern at equal weight = fail unless it is a spec table scanned BY label.
**✗ WRONG.** Revenue, Cost, Tax, Refunds, Net Profit — all 16px grey in one flat unlabeled row; the reader computes the hierarchy in their head.
**✓ RIGHT.** "Net Profit $42,300" at 28px bold; the four contributors smaller, grouped beneath with a visible how-we-got-here path.

### DATA-3 — Enforce comparisons; numbers without context are inert
**Rule.** Show related values, baselines, trends, before/after side by side; never force the user to remember and mentally reconstruct the comparison.
**Grounding.** About Face (Tufte's "enforce visual comparisons" grand principle applied): "You should provide a means for users to compare related variables and trends or to compare before-and-after scenarios. Comparison provides a context that makes the information more valuable and comprehensible to users" (p.426). The cited case: a multi-stock chart lets a viewer "see that Barclays Bank (BCS) and UBS are closely correlated to each other and only loosely correlate to the S&P 500" (Fig. 17-6 caption, p.426) — a judgment impossible from three separate single-line charts read in sequence. Mechanism: working memory cannot hold one chart while decoding another; co-presence is what makes correlation and good/bad judgments possible at all.
**Objective test.** Any standalone metric with zero comparator (prior period, target, peer, or trend) in the SAME view = flag. For related series, verify they render on one shared canvas/axis rather than in separate sequential views the user must page between.

### DATA-4 — Integrate; never dequantify; keep data honest
**Rule.** (a) Label in place — no separate legend round-trips; labels beat legends, legends beat axis-interpolation: pick the least indirection the density allows. (b) A gauge/bar/color supplements the numeral, never replaces it. (c) Show only data with quality/relevance/integrity — stale values never wear live-data authority.
**Grounding.** About Face: "Diagrams that require separate keys or legends to decode require additional cognitive processing by users and are less effective than diagrams with integrated legends and labels. Reading and deciphering diagram legends is yet another form of navigation-related excise" (p.427). On dequantifying: "you should not abandon the display of the numbers themselves. For example, in the Windows Disk Properties dialog, a pie chart is displayed to give users a rough idea of their free disk space, but the numbers of gigabytes free and used are also displayed in numeric form" (p.428). On honesty: "Don't show information simply because it's technically possible to do so... Unreliable or otherwise poor-quality information will damage the trust you must build with users" (p.427). Designing Interfaces on the indirection ladder: "Labels are easier to use. They communicate data values precisely and unambiguously (when placed correctly), and they're located in or beside the data point of interest — no going back and forth between the data point and a legend. The downside is that they clutter up a graphic when overused, so be careful" (p.445). Mechanism: each hop (mark → legend → meaning) is excise; a visual-only quantity forces estimation; stale data in live clothing spends trust.
**Objective test.** (a) Chart meaning fully decodable from on-mark/adjacent labels; more than 1 legend round-trip to identify one series = fail; ≤5–6 series → direct end-labels required; denser charts may use a legend but every entry must be unambiguously traceable to its mark (unique hue/shape pairing, no near-duplicate colors). (b) Any value rendered only as bar/ring/color with no adjacent numeral = fail. (c) Each displayed field maps to a consuming workflow/decision (zero-consumer fields flagged); possibly-stale values carry an "as of" marker; any value older than its own stated recency claim fails.
**✗ WRONG.** A 4-line chart identified only via a corner legend; a storage ring with no numbers; a cached "last login" rendered identically to real-time fields.
**✓ RIGHT.** Lines end-labeled in place; "184 GB of 256 GB (72%)" at the ring's center; "Last login: 3:14 PM (as of last night's sync)" on the cached field.
**Crop.** AF-08, UP-02.

### DATA-5 — Order is a legibility decision
**Rule.** A default sort can hide the story (alphabetical) or surface it (magnitude/severity/recency); choose deliberately and offer resort where the data holds multiple stories.
**Grounding.** Designing Interfaces' Texas cancer-data pair: sorted alphabetically, the data "doesn't lead you to ask interesting questions. It's not clear why Abilene, Alice, Amarillo, and Austin all seem to have similar numbers, for instance; it might just be chance" (p.441); resorted numerically, "the graph becomes much more interesting. Galveston is ranked first — why is that, when its neighbor, Houston, is further down the scale?" (pp.441–442). Mechanism: "Sorting and rearranging puts different data points next to each other, thus letting users make different kinds of comparisons" (p.442) — order determines which comparisons are physically adjacent, so the default sort silently chooses which questions the display can raise.
**Objective test.** Table/chart ≥10 rows with a primary quantitative metric: a sort control exists on at least that metric's column; arbitrary/alphabetical default order (where the data isn't alphabetically meaningful and a magnitude order would surface the finding) with no resort control = fail.
**✗ WRONG.** City metrics locked alphabetical with no sort control — extremes and outliers scattered invisibly through the list.
**✓ RIGHT.** Click-to-sort numeric ordering putting the outliers adjacent at top/bottom, surfacing the Galveston-class question instantly.
**Crop.** DI-04 (Fig. 9-7 alphabetical vs. Fig. 9-8 numeric, pp.441–442).
**Score (0–10 ladder).**
> - **0** — a ≥10-row quantitative table has a fixed, non-meaningful default order (e.g. alphabetical) and no sort control at all *(source: Designing Interfaces p.441, city-metrics-table ✗)*.
> - **3** — a sort control exists but only for a non-primary column, or is hidden/hard to discover *(Designing Interfaces p.441)*.
> - **5 — THRESHOLD:** a sort control exists for at least the numeric column of primary interest *(Designing Interfaces p.441-442)*.
> - **6** — the default order itself is chosen deliberately — magnitude/severity/recency to surface the finding, or alphabetical only where lookup-by-name IS the task *(Designing Interfaces p.441, "doesn't lead you to ask interesting questions")*.
> - **7** — sorting the primary metric puts the extremes/outliers adjacent at top/bottom within the first screenful (not split across pagination/grouping) *(Designing Interfaces p.441-442, Fig. 9-8, Galveston example)*.
> - **8** — multiple columns are sortable, with clear visual feedback on current sort direction/column *(Designing Interfaces p.442)*.
> - **9** — sorting surfaces genuine outliers/relationships immediately, and where the data holds multiple stories ≥2 columns are combinably sortable *(Designing Interfaces p.442, "lets users make different kinds of comparisons")*.
> - **10** — matches the ✓ click-to-sort case exactly: numeric ordering puts outliers adjacent at top/bottom, surfacing the Galveston-class question instantly, across every re-sortable dimension the data holds *(Designing Interfaces p.441-442, Fig. 9-7/9-8)*.

**Weight.** med (2) — Designing Interfaces: high specifically for exploratory data tables, low for short fixed lists → med overall.

### DATA-6 — Detail on demand keeps the overview clean; filters live and in context
**Rule.** Exact values/slices go behind hover/tap/selection (datatip, spotlight); permanently labeling everything is noise, NO route to precision equally fails. Search/filter over data is interactive, iterative, contextual, and combinable.
**Grounding.** Designing Interfaces: Datatips/Data Spotlight patterns (Ch.9) — spotlight dims all but the pointed-at slice. The four filter-quality criteria verbatim: "Highly interactive — They respond as quickly as possible... (Don't react to individual keystrokes if it significantly slows down the user's typing, however.) / Iterative — They let a user refine the search... / Contextual — They show results in context with surrounding data... / Complex — They go beyond simply switching entire data sets on and off, and allow the user to specify nuanced combinations of conditions" (pp.444–445). The ski-trail map case: "the screenshot on the left shows no highlighted trails; the one on the right switches on the trails rated black diamond with a single click" (p.444) — filters toggled live, in place. Mechanism: precision-on-demand resolves the label-clutter vs. no-precision dilemma; in-context filtering preserves the user's mental frame across refinements.
**Objective test.** Data-dense view: (a) a hover/tap/selection route to exact values exists; (b) permanent all-values labeling = noise flag; (c) filter UI scores 4/4 on the criteria — results update without degrading keystroke responsiveness, a result set can be progressively narrowed without restarting, matches shown in context of surrounding data (not a blank results page), and at least one AND/OR/negation combination of ≥2 conditions is supported. One-condition-at-a-time, context-discarding reloads, or keystroke-lagging filters are gaps.
**✗ WRONG.** A map labeling every point permanently; a search allowing price OR bedrooms but never both, each search reloading to a blank page, every keystroke stuttering the input.
**✓ RIGHT.** Clean overview + datatips on hover; multiple filter toggles narrowing the same view in place, instantly.
**Crop.** DI-11 (Fig. 9-10 ski-trail map, p.444).

### DATA-7 — Derived money must show its arithmetic [derived]
**Rule.** When one figure is computed from others (net payable from estimate − exclusions − deductible against coverage), the display makes the derivation traceable: a visible tally structure (operands → operations → result), grouped as one unit, ordered as the computation runs, the result as the headline. Peer-chip scatter forces the user to do the accounting in their head — displaced complexity.
**Grounding.** Derived, four-book convergence. About Face: "Comparison provides a context that makes the information more valuable and comprehensible" (p.426), legends-as-excise (p.427), and "you should not abandon the display of the numbers themselves" (p.428) — related money values must sit together, labeled in place, fully quantified. Laws of UX (Tesler): "If a million users each waste a minute a day dealing with complexity that an engineer could have eliminated in a week by making the software a little more complex, you are penalizing the user to make the engineer's job easier" (p.108, quoted from Saffer 2006; statement p.107, Gmail absorption example p.110) — arithmetic the system already performed must not be re-performed by the reader. Krug: every unresolved "how do these tally?" moment is the think-tax his First Law forbids (p.29), and data legibility is hierarchy + grouping: "Things that are related logically are related visually" (pp.55–56). Designing Interfaces: "When you put things close together, viewers associate them with one another... Grouped items look related. Conversely, isolation implies a distinction" (p.218) and "Sorting and rearranging puts different data points next to each other, thus letting users make different kinds of comparisons" (pp.441–442) — grouping and ordering ARE meaning. Convergence: no single book states the money-tally form, but comparison-enforcement + complexity-absorption + hierarchy/grouping + order-as-meaning jointly entail it.
**Objective test.** (a) Every displayed derived figure: its operands and operations are visible in one grouped unit, ordered as the computation runs, result terminal and dominant (headline weight per DATA-2). (b) Sum-reconciliation check: the visible components arithmetically reconcile to the stated total (compute it), or the discrepancy is explained inline — a total whose visible parts don't sum to it with no inline explanation = fail. (c) The related money values share one region (LAY-10), never scattered as equal-weight chips across the view.
**✗ WRONG.** 1,580 / 2,500 / 2,000 / 500 as four disconnected equal-weight chips in different corners — the user reverse-engineers the arithmetic and can't tell if the numbers even reconcile.
**✓ RIGHT.** A tally block: estimate 2,500 → covered cap 2,000 → − deductible 500 → **net payable 1,580**, each line labeled, the mismatch (500 excluded) stated inline; components sum to the headline.
**Crop.** AF-08 (comparison/integration anchor), DI-01 (headline pop).
**Score (0–10 ladder).** ([derived] — four-book convergence; no single book states the money-tally form directly)
> - **0** — the derived figure's operands/values render as disconnected equal-weight chips scattered across the view, with no visible tally structure — the reader must reverse-engineer the arithmetic *(source: [derived] from Krug p.29,55-56 flat-hierarchy failure; About Face p.426-428 comparison/integration; Designing Interfaces p.218,441-442 grouping/ordering-as-meaning)*.
> - **2** — some operands are shown but ≥1 is left implicit, AND/OR the visible components don't reconcile to the stated total with no inline explanation *(Laws of UX — Tesler p.107-110, unabsorbed complexity pushed onto the reader)*.
> - **5 — THRESHOLD:** every operand and operation of the derived figure is visible in one grouped tally structure, all related money values share one region, and the visible components arithmetically reconcile to the stated total (or a discrepancy is explained inline) *(Designing Interfaces p.218 "grouped items look related"; About Face p.428 "should not abandon the display of the numbers themselves")*.

> - **7** — the result is the terminal line rendered at strictly greater weight than its operands (headline weight per DATA-2), not a visual peer *(Krug p.55-56, "the more important something is, the more prominent it is")*.

### DATA-8 — Numeric formatting is a system
**Rule.** Right-align numeric columns (decimals stack); consistent precision, units, currency notation everywhere; related data may share one hierarchical cell to cut column count.
**Grounding.** Refactoring UI: "If you're designing a table that includes numbers, right-align them. When the decimal in a list of numbers is always in the same place, they're a lot easier to compare at a glance" (p.130). On columns: "if a column doesn't need to be sortable, there's no reason you can't combine it with a related column and introduce some interesting hierarchy" (p.244). Mechanism: a fixed decimal position turns magnitude comparison into a purely visual length/alignment read; merged hierarchical cells (name+role, amount+type) cut column count without losing data.
**Objective test.** `text-align: right` on all currency/quantity/percent columns (decimal points align vertically row to row); one precision and one unit/currency notation per column (mixed 2dp/0dp in one column = fail); any table where some columns hold naturally related atomic fields (amount+type, name+role) is a restructuring candidate — pair them into one hierarchical cell.
**✗ WRONG.** A left-aligned price column with mixed 2dp/0dp precision — decimals fall at inconsistent positions, comparison requires reading every value.
**✓ RIGHT.** Right-aligned, uniform precision, decimals stacked; "amount + type" merged as one two-line hierarchical cell.
**Crop.** RU-21, RU-11.
**Score (0–10 ladder).**
> - **0** — a numeric table column is left- or center-aligned (decimals don't line up), with mixed precision in ≥2 columns *(source: Refactoring UI p.130, "If you're designing a table that includes numbers, right-align them")*.

### DATA-9 — Redundant coding for critical distinctions
**Rule.** Status/severity/category that matters gets ≥2 channels (color + icon + text); a hue-only distinction is fragile and less legible for everyone.
**Grounding.** Designing Interfaces: "The shape of the scatter markers could encode yet a fourth variable, but in this case, shape is redundant with color hue. The redundant encoding helps a user visually separate the three data groups" (p.438, Fig. 9-6) — the grouping survives grayscale, print, and colorblindness. Universal Principles: "There are four kinds of redundancy: diverse, homogeneous, active, and passive... Diverse redundancy is resistant to a single cause of failure" (p.204). Mechanism: two independent channels mean loss of any one (colorblindness, grayscale, screenshot, glare) leaves the distinction intact. Full mechanics → COLOR-7.
**Objective test.** Grayscale-simulate every status/severity pair: still distinguishable, or fail. For any chart distinguishing ≥3 categorical series, count independent encoding channels per series — color alone = 1 = fail for distinctions that matter; ≥2 channels (hue + shape / hue + line-style / color + icon + label) = pass.
**✗ WRONG.** Red-vs-green severity dots only — identical in grayscale and to a colorblind reviewer.
**✓ RIGHT.** Color + icon + text label per status; grayscale-safe.
**Crop.** DI-10 (Fig. 9-6, pp.438–439).
**Score (0–10 ladder).**

> - **7** — the redundant channel is chosen for maximal legibility — high-contrast shapes/icons/line-styles, not near-identical glyphs *(Designing Interfaces p.438)*.

### DATA-10 — Small multiples: repeat one consistent chart, never rescale per panel
**Rule.** To show more dimensions than one plot holds, repeat a small identical chart across a labeled grid — identical size, axis scale, encoding; per-panel auto-scaling manufactures fake visual differences.
**Grounding.** Designing Interfaces: "Small Multiples are data-rich — they show a lot of information at one time, but in a comprehensible way. Every individual picture tells a story. But when you put them all together and demonstrate how each picture varies from one to the next, an even bigger story is told" (p.466), quoting Tufte: "Small multiple designs, multivariate and data bountiful, answer directly by visually enforcing comparisons of changes, of the differences among objects, of the scope of alternatives" (p.466). Craft requirement: "Each image should be similar to the others: the same size and/or shape, the same axis scaling (if you're using plots), and the same kind of content... Try to eliminate the visual differences that don't mean anything" (p.467); and "make sure the users understand which data dimension is varying across the multiples" (p.467). Mechanism: the grid IS the comparison — any per-panel variation in scale or encoding injects a visual difference that carries no data, corrupting every cross-panel read.
**Objective test.** Every panel shares one y-axis range, identical size, and one encoding — any panel independently auto-scaled or differently colored than its siblings = defect; row/column headers state which dimension varies across which grid axis, or fail.
**✗ WRONG.** 12 panels each auto-scaled — two panels with wildly different absolute ranges rendered visually identical.
**✓ RIGHT.** One fixed y-range and one styling across all 12, dimension labels on rows/columns; a taller bar is genuinely larger.
**Crop.** DI-12 (Fig. 9-26/9-27, pp.467–468).
**Score (0–10 ladder).**
> - **0** — panels in a small-multiples grid use inconsistent axis scales/encodings, manufacturing fake visual differences *(source: Designing Interfaces p.467, auto-scaled-12-panel ✗)*.
> - **3** — axis scales are consistent but panel sizing/styling varies slightly — not a fully clean repeated unit *(Designing Interfaces p.467)*.
> - **5 — THRESHOLD:** all panels share identical size, one shared axis scale, and one encoding *(Designing Interfaces p.466-467)*.
> - **6** — no visual difference across panels carries meaningless variation — decorative per-panel drift is eliminated *(Designing Interfaces p.467, "eliminate the visual differences that don't mean anything")*.
> - **7** — row/column headers state which data dimension varies across which grid axis *(Designing Interfaces p.467, "make sure the users understand which data dimension is varying")*.
> - **8** — as 7, and the labeling is unambiguous — no guessing which dimension varies on which axis *(Designing Interfaces p.467)*.
> - **9** — the grid demonstrably enforces comparison of changes/differences the way Tufte's small-multiples doctrine intends — the bigger story reads across panels at a glance *(Designing Interfaces p.466, quoting Tufte)*.
> - **10** — full Tufte-grade small multiples: consistent panels, clear axis labeling, AND an additional encoded dependent variable (e.g. color) layered on top without breaking comparability *(Designing Interfaces p.466-468, Fig. 9-26/9-27)*.
