### FEED-5 — Motion communicates spatial continuity, never decorates
**Rule.** Transitions show where things came from and where they went, preserving the mental map; ~300ms-class, visually continuous; rapid repeated inputs coalesce into ONE animation; emphasis-motion is rationed and respects reduced-motion, with nothing essential conveyed by motion alone.
**Grounding.**
- *About Face:* "Animated transitions help users create a strong mental model of how what is presented in one view is related to what was presented in the previous view" (Ch11, p.266); per Saffer, transitions should "Maintain context during transitions between views or object states" and "Create a virtual space that helps guide users from state to state" (p.267). Mechanism: motion's job is expressing relationships between objects across states — decoration that shows no before→after relationship does none of that work.
- *Designing Interfaces:* "when the shift from one state to another is visually continuous, it's not so bad... This helps keep the user oriented" (p.203); "Research shows that 300 milliseconds might be ideal for smooth scrolling," and for rapid repeats "combine them into one animated action. Otherwise, the user might sit there through several seconds' worth of animation as the punishment" (p.204). Mechanism: the animation serves orientation only up to the point it delays input — hence the fixed duration class and the coalescing rule.
- *Laws of UX:* motion "can trigger dizziness, nausea, headaches, or worse" for users with BPPV, labyrinthitis, epilepsy, and migraine sensitivities — "We must carefully consider when and how we use motion in our designs to ensure users with motion sensitivity aren't negatively affected" (p.102). Mechanism: emphasis-motion is an accessibility hazard class, so it needs a dampened `prefers-reduced-motion` branch and can never be the sole carrier of a state.
**Objective test.** (a) Spatial state changes (delete, collapse, view switch) render a continuous path from before-position to after-position, ≤~300ms; an instant cut with no positional relationship = fail. (b) 10 rapid repeated inputs coalesce into ONE animation to the final state; duration stacking linearly per input (10× down-arrow = 10 sequential animations) = fail. (c) Every emphasis animation has a `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` branch that disables or substantially dampens it (no parallax, no large-amplitude motion); no state is communicated by motion only.
**✗ WRONG.** A deleted row vanishing with the list snapping up; 10 down-arrows queuing 3 seconds of back-to-back scroll animation; a parallax hero ignoring the OS motion setting.
**✓ RIGHT.** The row collapses ~250ms while neighbors slide up to fill the space; rapid repeats coalesce into one scroll to the final position; reduced-motion swaps parallax for a static or minimal-fade treatment.
**Crop.** DI-14.
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — a spatial state change (delete, collapse, view switch) cuts instantly with the surrounding layout snapping, no transition *(source: About Face #15 "0", p.266; Designing Interfaces #3 "0", p.203)*.
- **2** — a transition exists but is a generic fade with no positional before→after relationship *(source: About Face #15 "3"; Designing Interfaces #3 "3")*.
- **3** — a continuous positional transition exists but exceeds ~300ms (delays input), or repeated rapid input stacks linearly (10 presses = 10× duration, "punishment") *(source: Designing Interfaces #3 "3", p.204)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** a continuous visual path from before-position to after-position renders ≤~300ms on every spatial state change *(source: About Face #15 "5-6"; Designing Interfaces #3 "5-6", p.204)*.
- **6** — + rapid repeated input coalesces into ONE animation to the final state rather than queuing serially *(source: Designing Interfaces #3 "7-8", p.204)*.
- **7** — + every emphasis-only animation has a `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` branch that disables or substantially dampens it (no parallax, no large-amplitude motion) *(source: Laws of UX #22 "5-6", p.102)*.
- **8** — + applied consistently across every similar state change and every animated element on the surface, not just one case *(source: About Face #15 "7-8"; Laws of UX #22 "7-8")*.
- **9** — + no state is communicated by motion alone — every motion-conveyed state also has a static cue (color/label/position) *(source: Laws of UX #22, p.102 mechanism)*.
- **10** — matches the ✓ macOS-dock/iOS-flick class: motion itself communicates where things came from/went, zero decorative excess, reduced-motion fully handled everywhere *(source: About Face #15 "9-10", Fig. 11-10; Designing Interfaces #3 "9-10", Fig. 3-62; Laws of UX #22 "9-10")*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** med (2) — AF #15 med, DI #3 med, LU #22 low-med; majority med (LU's low-med noted — its lens is the reduced-motion accessibility slice only).

### FEED-6 — Peaks and endings carry the verdict
**Rule.** Users judge a whole flow by its most intense moment and its ending, not the average; the completion/confirmation/recovery screens deserve craft at least equal to the middle, and negative peaks weigh heavier than positive ones — prevent them first.
**Grounding.** *Laws of UX:* "People judge an experience largely based on how they felt at its peak and at its end, rather than on the total sum or average of every moment of the experience" (p.65). Evidence: Kahneman's cold-water experiment — participants preferred repeating a LONGER, objectively-more-painful trial because it ended less painfully — and the colonoscopy studies, where patients with the objectively longer procedure that ended gently "rated their overall experience as less unpleasant" and "were more likely to return for subsequent procedures" (p.66). On the negative side: "We have a tendency as humans not only to register negative events more readily but also to dwell on these events" (p.74, same memory-bias family as peak-end, p.67). Mechanism: memory samples the peak and the end, not the integral — so a review that only averages severity mis-weights a single rage moment or a dead ending, and preventing negative peaks (e.g., inline validation) beats polishing the average.
**Objective test.** Audit two moments in isolation from the rest of the flow: (1) the single most emotionally intense step (error / wait / celebration) shows deliberate design investment — not a bare default browser/OS state; (2) the final screen contains more than a bare system-default "Success" toast — matching the flow's polish, summarizing what happened, offering the next action. Both yes = pass; and no severity-averaged review may outvote a failing peak or ending.
**✗ WRONG.** Five illustrated onboarding steps ending on a grey browser alert "Setup complete."
**✓ RIGHT.** A final screen at step-1-level polish with a personalized summary of what was set up and a clear next action.
**Crop.** none (studies are data-only); Fig. 6-1 (Spotify Wrapped, Laws of UX p.68) is the adjacent visual for a designed peak moment.
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — the flow's most intense moment AND its ending are both bare system defaults (e.g. a polished flow ending on a plain gray browser alert "Setup complete") *(source: Laws of UX #14 "0", pp.65–66)*.
- **2** — of the two moments, the one with investment is only above-default and generic (styled but no summary/next action for the ending, or partially-designed custom styling around a default control for the peak) *[derived — splits LU #14's "3" band by which moment carries the partial credit]*.
- **3** — one of the two moments (peak or ending) received deliberate design investment, but the other remains a bare default *(source: Laws of UX #14 "3", pp.65–66)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** BOTH the single most emotionally intense step (error/wait/celebration) AND the final screen show deliberate design investment beyond a bare default state *(source: Laws of UX #14 "5-6", pp.65–66)*.
- **7** — + the ending includes a personalized summary of what happened and a clear next action, not a generic success state *(source: Laws of UX #14 "7-8", pp.65–66)*.
- **8** — + foreseeable negative peaks are pre-empted before they occur (inline validation instead of submit-and-reject; a warned wait instead of a hang) rather than merely handled gracefully after the fact *(source: Laws of UX #15 "negativity bias", p.74; [derived] convergence with #14's peak framing)*.
- **9** — + the audit treats a failing peak or ending as failing the whole flow, regardless of the average of the other steps *(source: Laws of UX #14, p.65 mechanism — "peak and end, not the total sum or average")*.
- **10** — matches the ✓ redesigned-ending case: final screen matches the rest of the flow's polish, with a personalized summary and next action, negative peaks pre-empted, and the peak-weighted verdict applied throughout *(source: Laws of UX #14 "9-10", pp.65–68, Fig. 6-1)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — LU #14 high, LU #15 medium-high; majority high (a single moment can override the whole recalled verdict).

### FEED-7 — Interaction pliancy (micro-feedback)
**Rule.** Hover/pressed/active/selected states on every interactive element confirm "the system heard you" before any network response.
**Grounding.** *About Face:* "Part of a button's affordance is its visual pliancy, which indicates its pressability. When the user points to it and clicks the mouse button... the button control visually changes from raised to indented, indicating that it has been activated... Poorly designed applications and many websites contain buttons that don't animate when clicked or tapped. This is disconcerting for users, because it generates a mental question: 'Did that actually do something?'" (Ch21, p.591); "Rich visual feedback is the key to successful direct manipulation" (Ch13, p.315). Mechanism: the state change is a local, zero-latency acknowledgment that closes the gesture loop before any round-trip — without it every click ends in doubt (and often a second, duplicate click). Mechanics and the screenshot-diff test live in AFFORD-5.
**Objective test.** AFFORD-5's pseudo-state screenshot diff: capture each interactive element at idle / hover / active (pressed) / selected; zero pixel change across the states = fail. The acknowledgment must be local and immediate — rendered before (and independent of) any network response.
**✗ WRONG.** A styled div-button identical across all states; the only sign a click registered is the page changing 600ms later.
**✓ RIGHT.** Darken on hover, compress/ripple on press, distinct selected state — instant local confirmation before the server replies.
**Crop.** AF-03.
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — a custom control has identical CSS across idle/hover/active states — zero pixel difference on click *(source: About Face #22 "0", p.591)*.
- **2** — one state (hover XOR pressed) is implemented across elements; the other gives no feedback *(source: About Face #22 "3")*.
- **3** — pliancy exists but is tied to/delayed by the network response rather than rendering instantly and independently of it (the only sign a click registered is the page changing later) *(source: About Face #22, p.591 mechanism)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** idle, hover/focus, and pressed/active states are all visually distinguishable, rendering before any network round-trip *(source: About Face #22 "5-6", p.591)*.
- **6** — + a visible `:focus`/`:focus-visible` treatment exists on interactive elements for keyboard navigation *[derived — keyboard focus is the accessibility twin of the same "did that register" mechanism, About Face p.591]*.
- **7** — + selectable elements (tabs, rows, options) carry a persistent selected state clearly distinct at a glance from unselected siblings (not just detectable side-by-side) *(source: About Face #22 "7-8", mechanism extension)*.
- **9** — + the feedback is near-instant and rich (darkens/compresses/ripples) rather than a minimal single-property change *(source: About Face #22 "7-8"/"9-10", p.591)*.
- **10** — matches the ✓ case: rich, unambiguous pliancy on every imperative control; automated hover/active screenshot diffs show zero controls with no visual delta *(source: About Face #22 "9-10", p.591)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — AF #22 high ("did that do something?" is a universal failure mode; base-level trust signal).

# Forms & Controls

Input surfaces: field design, formats, defaults, hints, pickers. Pillars: 2, 3.

### FORM-1 — Fewest fields; absorb what the system can infer
**Rule.** Every added field taxes completion and decision quality; never ask for what the system already knows or can infer.
**Grounding.**
- Laws of UX (Postel, pp.55–56): "the first consideration is to be conservative in how much information you ask people to provide. The more fields you require users to fill out, the more cognitive energy and effort you're asking of them, which can lead to a deterioration in the quality of the decisions made (commonly referred to as decision fatigue...)" — each field spends a finite budget of attention, so surplus fields degrade the answers given to the necessary ones.
- Laws of UX (Tesler, p.107/p.108): "for any system there is a certain amount of complexity that cannot be reduced"; Tesler's own words: "If a million users each waste a minute a day dealing with complexity that an engineer could have eliminated in a week by making the software a little more complex, you are penalizing the user to make the engineer's job easier" — irreducible complexity must land somewhere, and the system is the cheaper place at scale.
- Laws of UX (p.110): Gmail's compose window "reduce[s] complexity by populating the 'from' line and suggesting the 'to' line based on prior emails" — "the complexity isn't entirely gone; it's just abstracted away to reduce the effort required of the user."
- Universal Principles (Performance Load, p.178): "If the performance load is high, performance time and errors increase, and the probability of successfully accomplishing the goal decreases." — recall-and-retype is the high-load form; recognition and prefill are the low-load form.
**Objective test.** (a) Every field maps to a stated downstream consumer of the data at submission time; a field with no consumer is removed. (b) Data the system already holds from the same session/account (billing address, prior contacts, account email) is never re-asked without prefill/"same as above" — script-auditable: does the shipping form pre-check "same as billing", or leave two blank address blocks? (c) Performance-load count: distinct values the user must recall from memory across the flow — target 0 (the system surfaces them, e.g. a dropdown of previously-used addresses).
**✗ WRONG.** A 9-field signup including a phone number nothing in the product uses; checkout presents billing and shipping as two fully-blank forms back to back with no "same as billing" checkbox.
**✓ RIGHT.** Email + password only; "My shipping information is the same as my billing information" pre-checked, collapsing the duplicate block; prior addresses offered as a one-click dropdown.
**Crop.** LU-19.
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — fields with no downstream consumer AND already-held data re-asked as blank fields *(source: Laws of UX — Tesler's Law "inherent complexity"; Postel's Law; Refactoring UI "minimize the number of fields")*.
- **2** — every field arguably has a consumer, but ≥2 held values re-asked blank + several values need memory recall *(Laws of UX — Tesler; Miller/recognition-over-recall)*.
- **4** — ≤1 blank re-ask of held data; prefill exists but inconsistent *(Refactoring UI — good defaults)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** no consumer-less field, no held data shown blank (all prefilled/defaulted) *(Universal Principles — Performance Load; Refactoring UI — good defaults)*.
- **6** — + ≤1 value still requires memory recall; rest via dropdown/autofill *(Laws of UX — recognition over recall)*.
- **7** — + zero recall load *(Designing Interfaces — autocompletion/pickers, Ch.10)*.
- **8** — + all genuinely-optional data marked optional, never required *(Designing Interfaces — Structured Format; required-field marking)*.
- **9** — + optional data deferred past the gating action *(Laws of UX — progressive disclosure; Designing Interfaces — Ch.10)*.
- **10** — + provably minimal set; no field a reviewer could remove/merge *(Refactoring UI — minimize fields; Krug — "omit needless words")*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — Laws of UX (Postel: high; Tesler: high) and Universal Principles (Performance Load: high) agree.

### FORM-2 — Forgiving vs structured format: pick by real-world variability
**Rule.** Variable-format data (names, dates across locales, places, phones) gets one forgiving field interpreted intelligently and echoed back canonically; genuinely fixed universal shapes (a 4-digit code) get segmented structured entry. Either misapplied creates friction.
**Grounding.**
- Designing Interfaces (Forgiving Format, pp.477–478): "Permit users to enter inputs in a variety of choices, formats, and syntax, and make the application interpret it intelligently... The user just wants to get something done, not think about 'correct' formats and complex UI" — the parsing burden belongs to software, not to the person with the goal.
- Designing Interfaces (p.481): Google Calendar accepts "Saturday 7/20", "20/7/2019", "7/20", all correctly parsed and "echoed back... in the appropriate format" — the canonical echo confirms interpretation without forcing canonical entry.
- Designing Interfaces (Structured Format, p.482): use only when "That format is familiar and well defined, and you don't expect any users to need to deviate from the format you expect... It's generally a bad idea to use this pattern for any data in which the preferred format might vary from user to user. Consider especially what might happen if your interface is used in other countries" — and structure pays off where it applies, since it is "easier for someone to double-check several short strings... than one long one".
**Objective test.** Classify each field's data by real-world format variability: legitimately varies across users/locales (names, regional dates, international phones) → one forgiving field is required; a segmented rigid field here = fail. Genuinely invariant (4-digit SMS code, 16-digit card number) → structured segments with auto-advance; a single free box here forfeits the transcription-error reduction short segments give. Forgiving fields echo the interpreted canonical value back.
**✗ WRONG.** Rigid First/Middle/Last boxes breaking single-name and compound-name cultures; one free box for a 16-digit card number.
**✓ RIGHT.** One "Full name" field the software doesn't segment; the 4-digit SMS code as 4 auto-advancing structured boxes.
**Crop.** DI-20.
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — a field whose real-world format legitimately varies (name, date, phone) is forced into rigid segmented boxes, OR a genuinely fixed-shape field (4-digit code) is left as one unstructured free box *(source: Designing Interfaces — Forgiving Format p.477–478; Structured Format p.482)*.
- **2** — correct pattern family used for most fields, but ≥2 fields remain misapplied (a rigid split or an unstructured fixed-shape field) *(Designing Interfaces p.477–482)*.
- **4** — ≤1 misapplied field remains; forgiving fields exist but don't echo the parsed value back *(Designing Interfaces p.481, Fig. 10-5 mechanism)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** every field's format matches its real-world variability — forgiving for variable data, structured for truly fixed/universal data — with zero misapplied instances *(Designing Interfaces p.477–478, 482)*.
- **6** — + structured fixed-shape fields use auto-advance segments *(Designing Interfaces Ch.10 structured-format pattern)*.
- **7** — + every forgiving field echoes the interpreted canonical value back to the user *(Designing Interfaces p.481, Google Calendar echo)*.
- **8** — + echo verified correct against ≥3 known real-world format variants (e.g. "Saturday 7/20", "20/7/2019", "7/20") *(Designing Interfaces p.481)*.
- **9** — + both patterns applied side by side with no visual inconsistency between them in the same form *(Designing Interfaces Fig. 10-6)*.
- **10** — + full Fig. 10-6 standard: un-segmented full-name forgiving field and 4-box auto-advancing SMS code both present and behaving correctly, zero misapplied fields anywhere on the surface *(Designing Interfaces p.477–482)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — Designing Interfaces: high ("direct international-usability failure" in either direction).

### FORM-3 — Liberal validation; never call valid-but-unusual input "wrong"
**Rule.** Accept and normalize input variance (hyphens, apostrophes, short names, non-US formats, spelled numbers where unambiguous); a blunt "invalid" for reasonable input is the software's rigidity blamed on the user.
**Grounding.**
- Laws of UX (Postel, p.56): "Strict formatting rules can also be an issue for addresses that don't conform to a standard country/region... It's also important to consider formatting differences that could break form validation if it's too restrictive, like including hyphenated names... telling someone their name is 'wrong' or 'not accepted' can do a lot of damage" — the liberal-input half of "be conservative in what you do, be liberal in what you accept from others" (RFC 793, quoted pp.53–54).
- About Face (p.644): "Instead of software rejecting input, it must work harder to understand and reconcile confusing input." Design principle: "Make errors impossible." — the book's worked example is parsing "nine" typed into a numeric field instead of rejecting it: the error class is eliminated by interpretation, not policed by dialogs.
**Objective test.** Per constrained field, run ≥5 known-valid edge-case strings (O'Brien-Smith, 2-letter surnames, hyphenated phones, non-US postcodes, either name ordering per locale): all accepted or normalized, zero rejections. Error-copy check: no validation message asserts the input is "wrong"/"invalid" without also stating the expected form. Trivially-correctable formatting (spaces, hyphens in a phone) is stripped, never bounced.
**✗ WRONG.** "Invalid name" on O'Brien-Smith; a 2-letter surname rejected outright; a blocking dialog for a phone typed with hyphens.
**✓ RIGHT.** Apostrophes/hyphens/short names accepted; non-digits silently stripped from the phone; "nine" parsed as 9.
**Crop.** none.
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — over-collects (fields with no stated downstream use) AND bluntly rejects valid-but-unusual input (e.g. "Invalid name" on O'Brien-Smith) with no stated expected format *(source: Laws of UX — Postel p.53–56; About Face p.644)*.
- **2** — field count reasonable, but validation still bluntly rejects 1–2 known-valid edge-case strings (hyphenated name, non-US postcode) without stating the expected format *(Laws of UX — Postel p.56)*.
- **4** — ≤1 rejection remains among ≥5 tested edge strings; error copy occasionally still silent on the expected format *[derived — interpolated between Laws of UX Postel's 3 and 5-6 bands]*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** passes the 3-part test — every field maps to a stated necessary use; ≥5 known-valid edge-case strings per constrained field (hyphens/apostrophes, non-US formats, locale name ordering) all accepted or normalized; no error message asserts "wrong"/"invalid" without also stating the expected format *(Laws of UX — Postel p.53–56)*.
- **6** — + trivially-correctable formatting (spaces, hyphens in a phone) is stripped silently in every constrained field, never bounced *(Laws of UX — Postel, liberal-input half of RFC 793)*.
- **7** — + unambiguous non-canonical input (e.g. "nine" typed into a numeric field) is interpreted and accepted with no confirm step *(About Face p.644 — "make errors impossible")*.
- **8** — + genuinely optional data is deferred past the gating action rather than gating the initial submission *(Laws of UX — Postel p.55–56)*.
- **9** — + zero rejections found across an expanded probe of ≥8 known-valid strings per field *(Laws of UX — Postel p.56, own extension)*.
- **10** — + matches the Face-ID standard: the system absorbs the input-format burden almost entirely (biometric auth, autofill, near-zero manual constrained entry) rather than merely tolerating a wide input range *(Laws of UX — Postel p.56)*.

### FORM-4 — Hints and prompts that survive typing
**Rule.** Fields whose content/format isn't obvious get a small hint OUTSIDE the empty control (≥2pt smaller than the label, never 1pt); placeholder prompts sit where the user types but never serve as the field's ONLY identity — a floating or static label persists after fill.
**Grounding.**
- Designing Interfaces (Input Hints, p.489): "If you visually separate the hint from the main label, users who know what to do can more or less ignore the hint, and stay focused on the label and control"; sizing: "consider using a font two points smaller than the label font. (A one-point difference will look more like a mistake than an intended font-size change.)"; and the external hint "leaves the control blank — the user is forced to consider the question and give an answer, and there is no chance the input field will be skipped over because it looks already filled in."
- Designing Interfaces (Input Prompt, p.494): "An Input Prompt sits right where the user will type, so it can't be ignored" — but it vanishes on focus, so identity needs a label; (p.495): "Floating labels move and change size but do not disappear on focus" — the vanishing-identity problem was "formerly a huge drawback of input prompts."

For any field identified by placeholder alone: after filling, can the user still tell what the field was without deleting their entry? No = fail; pass requires a floating label or an adjacent static label.
**✗ WRONG.** A hint at label size sitting inside the box (reads pre-filled, gets skipped); "Enter your phone number" as placeholder-only identity, unrecoverable once typed over.
**✓ RIGHT.** A small grey example two points under the label size, box visibly empty; "Phone number (optional)" floating up to a small persistent position on focus so the user "can still refer to it, and not need to remember it."

### FORM-5 — Good defaults; never default the consequential
**Rule.** Prefill probable values from context — but never pre-decide sensitive/consent/high-stakes fields, and set every default to the option doing the most good and least harm for the user, not the business.
**Grounding.**
- Designing Interfaces (p.520): prefill from prior session/account/context — and by name, never leave marketing-email checkboxes selected by default; an always-correct default gets mentally skipped, which is exactly why consequential fields must stay explicit.
- Universal Principles (Nudge, p.170): "People prefer the path of least resistance when making decisions. When the path of least resistance happens to lead to a generally favorable outcome everyone is happy." The pension case makes the mechanism concrete: "when the default option is to enroll employees automatically into a basic pension plan, savings rates increase dramatically... employees are free to join, change plans, or not join" — defaults steer outcomes at population scale while leaving choice free, so the default guideline is the option that "does the most good and least harm."
**Objective test.** Score every pre-selected option: does it serve the majority user's interest, or the vendor's? Consent/sensitive/financial-terms fields carry NO default — explicit choice required. Trivially inferable values (state from ZIP, same-as-billing) ARE defaulted; leaving them blank is the inverse failure.
**✗ WRONG.** A new-user privacy screen defaulting every data-sharing toggle ON; a pre-checked marketing opt-in; a blank state field beside a filled ZIP.
**✓ RIGHT.** Sharing defaults OFF with active opt-in; marketing unchecked; state auto-filled from ZIP and editable.

- **2** — some defaults favor the user, others favor the business, with no consistent policy *(Universal Principles — Nudge)*.
- **4** — every default favors the user except one consequential field (consent/financial-terms) still pre-decided *(Universal Principles — Nudge; Designing Interfaces p.520)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** every pre-selected default is verifiably the option that does the most good/least harm for the majority AND no consent/sensitive/financial-terms field carries a default *(Universal Principles — Nudge p.170; Designing Interfaces p.520)*.

- **7** — + every default remains changeable at the point of encounter, control visible on the same screen rather than buried in settings *(Universal Principles — Nudge, "free to join, change, or not join")*.

### FORM-6 — Graduated, criterion-specific feedback on constrained input
**Rule.** Constrained inputs (password rules, formats) show incremental real-time feedback naming WHICH rule is met/unmet — color-graded, per keystroke — never a binary verdict at submit.
**Grounding.**
- Designing Interfaces (p.497): "If your system is going to reject weak passwords, it's usually best to do it instantly, not after the user has submitted the registration form"; mechanism: "display a text and/or graphic label indicating a weak, medium, or strong password... Colors help: red for unacceptable, green or blue for good, and some other color (often yellow) in between" — and the conditional hint names the exact missing rule ("try adding a symbol... and letter", p.493).
- Laws of UX (negativity bias, p.74): "a single bad error/friction point can outweigh many good ones"; "Mailchimp avoids this potential pain point by providing real-time validation to ensure passwords are secure while also making the rules easy to follow" — the post-submit rejection is the negative peak users remember; per-keystroke feedback prevents it from ever occurring.
**Objective test.** Keystroke-timing check: feedback updates on every keystroke (or at latest blur) BEFORE any submit — an invalid value triggers a visible state change within one field interaction, no full-page submit required. The feedback names the specific unmet criterion (length, symbol, case), not a generic "invalid". A meter/message revealed only after a failed submit = fail regardless of how granular its criteria list is.
**✗ WRONG.** Silence until "Create Account", then a page reload with a red banner "Password does not meet requirements" — which rule failed is unstated.
**✓ RIGHT.** A live checklist ("One lowercase ✓ / One special character ✗ / 8 characters minimum ✗") updating per keystroke, strength bar shifting red→yellow→green.
**Crop.** LU-16, DI-05.
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — no feedback until Submit; a single generic "invalid" message names no specific unmet rule *(source: Designing Interfaces p.497; Laws of UX — negativity bias p.74)*.
- **2** — feedback appears on blur only (not per-keystroke), or names criteria only partially *(Designing Interfaces p.497; Laws of UX p.74)*.
- **4** — feedback live per-keystroke but only names some rules, the rest collapsed into a generic message; no graduated color state *[derived — interpolated between Designing Interfaces/Laws of UX 3 and 5-6 bands]*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** feedback updates on every keystroke (or at latest blur), before any submit, and names each specific unmet criterion (length/symbol/case) individually *(Designing Interfaces p.497, 493; Laws of UX p.74)*.
- **6** — + a graduated color-coded state (≥3 states, red→yellow→green) reinforces the text *(Designing Interfaces p.497)*.
- **7** — + zero post-submit reveal anywhere: no constrained field shows its rules for the first time after a failed submit *[derived — Laws of UX negativity-bias p.74 mechanism, made explicit]*.
- **8** — + the itemized checklist format applies consistently across every constrained field on the surface, not just password *[derived — Designing Interfaces p.497 pattern generalized product-wide]*.
- **9** — + the negative-peak state (post-submit rejection) is structurally impossible to encounter, given the live-feedback design *(Laws of UX — negativity bias p.74)*.
- **10** — + full Mailchimp/Yelp-grade meter: live per-keystroke itemized checklist plus graduated strength bar simultaneously, zero generic messaging anywhere *(Designing Interfaces Fig. 10-21; Laws of UX p.74)*.

**Weight.** high (3) — Designing Interfaces: high; Laws of UX (negativity bias): medium-high (noted) — majority high.

### FORM-7 — Control conventions carry semantics
**Rule.** Squares = independent toggles, circles = exclusive choice — never swapped for style; required-vs-optional marked by ONE consistent convention product-wide, marking the SMALLER set; autocompletion defaults to "no", never overrides typing, and drops repeatedly-rejected suggestions.
**Grounding.**
- About Face (pp.594–597): "Traditionally, check boxes are square. Users recognize visual objects by their shape, and the square check box is an important standard... Don't make check boxes diamond-shaped, and especially not round (which confuses them with the visual idiom employed by radio buttons), regardless of what your marketing department or visual designers say." Radios "are almost always round" for the same reason — shape IS the learned semantic signal.
- Designing Interfaces (pp.473–475): "Should you mark the required fields, or the optional ones? You will need to decide on a standard approach for all your forms" — three valid conventions, one of them "count how many required fields versus optional fields there are and then label only the smaller number"; authority cited: "Usability experts Nielsen/Norman Group says marking all required fields is still the most usable approach" (p.475).
- Designing Interfaces (p.505): "Always give the user a choice to take the completion or not take it; default to 'no'" — and stop offering completions the user has repeatedly rejected. [flagged in the extract as needing verbatim re-verification at p.505]
**Objective test.** (a) Classify each selection control by semantics: mutually-exclusive rendered round, independent rendered square; any inversion = fail. (b) Marking-the-smaller-set procedure: per form, count required vs optional fields; exactly one of the three conventions applies product-wide, on the minority set — asterisks on one form and nothing on the next = fail. (c) Autocomplete: typing straight through a suggestion never costs an extra deletion keystroke; a suggestion rejected ~3 times no longer appears.
**✗ WRONG.** Square checkboxes for a pick-one shipping method and round buttons for multi-select add-ons; a red asterisk on one signup form, nothing on the next; an autocomplete that overwrites what's typed.
**✓ RIGHT.** Round radios for pick-one, square checkboxes for add-ons; a uniform "(optional)" on the two minority optional fields; suggestions accepted only by explicit action, default "no".
**Crop.** AF-02.

- **0** — shape convention inverted (a mutually-exclusive group rendered as square checkboxes, or vice versa), OR no required/optional marking convention exists, or it's inconsistent across forms *(source: About Face p.594–597; Designing Interfaces p.473–475)*.

- **7** — + the convention/legend is explained once clearly near the form top (e.g. "* Required") *(Designing Interfaces p.475)*.

### FORM-8 — Pickers: compact trigger, well-designed panel; conventions are a floor
**Rule.** Heavy selection UI collapses behind a compact chooser, but the expanded panel obeys full layout/grouping/hierarchy law; subset-building from a large source shows source AND destination simultaneously; and the textbook rendering of a component (bare radio list, plain link-stack dropdown) is a default to challenge, not a law.
**Grounding.**
- Designing Interfaces (Ch.10, Drop-down Chooser + List Builder): the chooser hides a rich panel behind a compact trigger; the List Builder keeps source and destination visible together — a modal reopened per pick fails the visibility-of-both-sides need.
- Refactoring UI (pp.241–246): "Most people have a lot of preconceived notions about how certain components are supposed to look... It's just a floating box on the screen, you can do anything you want with it. Break it into sections, use multiple columns, add supporting text or colorful icons"; on tables: "if a column doesn't need to be sortable, there's no reason you can't combine it with a related column and introduce some interesting hierarchy" — the mechanism is that the component's semantic role, not its browser-default rendering, is the constraint.
**Objective test.** Popover/chooser panels pass the same audits as full screens (one primary action, grouped content, no cramped scroll-dump). Dropdown for a feature-rich nav: single-column plain-link stack with zero icons/subtext is the default to challenge (sectioned multi-column with icons+descriptions tested against it). Tier/plan pickers of ≤5 mutually-exclusive options: selectable-card treatment considered vs bare circle+label radios.

### FORM-9 — Progressive enhancement; custom-styled but honest controls
**Rule.** Core input works for every modality and capability level FIRST; richer interaction layers on where supported and never gates the baseline. Style browser defaults into the brand — without breaking learned control shapes.
**Grounding.**
- Laws of UX (p.58): progressive enhancement "emphasizes access to the basic content and functionality for all users, regardless of browser feature support, device features and capabilities, or internet connection speed. Additional style and interaction layers are progressively added" — explicitly contrasted with graceful degradation, which "focuses first on the more advanced software and hardware while providing a fallback": floor-up vs ceiling-down.
- Laws of UX (pp.58–59): the baseline search box "will be usable by everyone, including those using assistive technology such as screen readers. If voice recognition support is detected, a layer of functional enhancement is added."
- Refactoring UI (p.222): "Just using one of your brand colors for the selected states instead of the browser defaults is often enough to take something from feeling boring to feeling polished" — brand the state, keep the shape semantics (FORM-7).
**Objective test.** Disable JavaScript and advanced APIs (voice, geolocation) in a test pass: the core task (search, submit, read) still completes; only enhancement layers (mic icon, animations) may vanish — a disabled input pending a JS bundle = fail. Custom-styled controls keep square/round semantics and native accessibility (focus, keyboard, screen-reader roles) while carrying brand color.
**✗ WRONG.** A search input rendered disabled with "please enable JavaScript" until a bundle attaches; default browser-blue checkboxes in a purple-brand product — or worse, rebuilt divs losing keyboard access.
**✓ RIGHT.** A plain submittable HTML form that gains a mic icon on capability detection; brand-purple selected states inside standard square checkboxes.
**Crop.** none.

### FORM-10 — Repetition deserves a macro
**Rule.** A multi-step sequence repeated across many objects gets record-once/replay-many (nameable, saveable, parameterizable, batch-applicable); identical per-record click-liturgy is kinematic load the system should absorb — and fewer manual repetitions = fewer slips.
**Grounding.**
- Designing Interfaces (pp.425–426): "No one wants to perform the same set of repetitive interactive tasks over, and over, and over again! This is exactly what computers are supposed to be good at"; beyond speed, macros "reduce the possibility of finger slips, oversights, and similar mistakes" — each manual repetition is another exposure to error.
- Designing Interfaces (pp.426–427): "The macro itself could be played back literally... or, if it acts upon an object that can change from one invocation to another, you could allow the sequence to be parameterized... Macros should also be able to act on many things at once" — per Photoshop's Batch, "the user can quickly and automatically process very large numbers of files, saving huge amounts of manual effort."
- Universal Principles (Performance Load, p.178): "If the performance load is high, performance time and errors increase" — kinematic load counts discrete physical actions; a replay mechanism collapses N×steps to one invocation.
**Objective test.** A sequence performed identically on ≥5 objects in a session with no record/replay/batch route = a macro gap. If a mechanism exists, verify: (a) nameable and saveable for reuse across sessions; (b) parameterizable where the target varies per invocation; (c) batch-applicable to many objects in ONE invocation. Kinematic count: total clicks/keystrokes for the N-object task should approach the 1-object cost, not N× it.
**✗ WRONG.** The same 6-step edit applied manually to 200 records — 1,200 opportunities for a slip.
**✓ RIGHT.** Record once as a named, saved action; apply to all 200 via one batch command.
**Crop.** DI-19.

- **2** — a macro/record feature exists but must be replayed one object at a time, no batch application *(Designing Interfaces p.425–427)*.

- **5 — THRESHOLD:** a record-once/replay mechanism exists AND supports naming/saving for reuse across sessions *(Designing Interfaces p.425–427)*.
- **6** — + batch application to many targets in a single invocation *(Designing Interfaces — Photoshop Batch, Fig. 8-30)*.
- **7** — + the macro is parameterizable where the target varies per invocation, not just literal replay *(Designing Interfaces p.426–427)*.

### FORM-11 — Fill-in-the-blanks: self-explanatory, but a localization trap
**Rule.** Embedding controls as blanks in a prose sentence makes rules/conditions self-explanatory — but comprehension then depends on word order, so multilingual products need a per-language layout plan, not string swaps.

**Objective test.** For any sentence-embedded control in a product shipping in ≥2 languages: a documented per-target-language control-reorder plan exists (layout rebuilt per language's word order, translator-reviewed), or the pattern is swapped for conventional labeled fields. **✗ WRONG.** English mid-sentence blanks string-swapped into an SOV language — the localized rule-builder reads as broken nonsense.
**✓ RIGHT.** The rule-builder's layout rebuilt per language word order with translator involvement — or, where that cost is a nonstarter, labeled fields instead.

# Gestalt Grouping

How the eye infers structure before reading a single word. Pillars: 2, 3, 4.

---

### GEST-1 — Proximity: closeness IS relatedness
**Rule.** Elements near each other read as related; proximity is among the strongest grouping cues and generally overwhelms competing signals; labels sit directly on/beside what they describe.
**Grounding.**
- Universal Principles (p.196): "Proximity is one of the most powerful means of indicating relatedness in a design, and will generally overwhelm competing visual cues (e.g., similarity)." Guideline verbatim: "Ensure that labels and supporting information are near the elements that they describe, opting for direct labeling on graphs over legends or keys." Mechanism: grouping via proximity "reduces the complexity of designs and reinforces the relatedness of the elements. Conversely, a lack of proximity results in the perception of multiple, disparate chunks" — the trail-sign misparse (destination words split so they pair with the wrong neighbor) is the canonical failure (p.197).
- Designing Interfaces (p.218): "When you put things close together, viewers associate them with one another. This is the basis for a strong grouping of content and controls on a user interface (UI). Grouped items look related. Conversely, isolation implies a distinction." Mechanism: spatial distance is parsed as semantic distance before any label is read.
- Refactoring UI (p.99): "Whenever you're relying on spacing to connect a group of elements, always make sure there's more space around the group than there is within it — interfaces that are hard to understand always look worse." Mechanism: equal gaps make group membership ambiguous; the eye can't tell which neighbor an item belongs to.
**Objective test.** Label-to-referent distance strictly less than label-to-any-unrelated-element. For any stacked pair relying purely on spacing (no border/bg): within-group gap strictly SMALLER than between-group gap — the book's own fix uses 10px within vs 20px between (a 2:1 ratio minimum); equal gaps (20px/20px) fail. Metric form in SPACE-4.
**✗ WRONG.** A billing form where each field label sits exactly 20px below the previous field and 20px above its own field — every label equidistant from two fields, group membership unreadable; two words of one name separated so they misparse with a stranger between them.
**✓ RIGHT.** Label 4–8px above its own field, ≥24px from the previous group (≥2:1 around-vs-within); name-pairs set as adjacent phrases; graph labels placed directly on the data, no legend.
**Crop.** UP-03, DI-07, RU-05.
**Score — grounded ladder (0→10).** Score = highest rung whose condition AND every rung below it hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
- **0 — ✗:** any label measurably closer to a wrong element than to its own referent (trail-sign misparse), OR any spacing-only group with within-gap ≥ between-gap (the 20px/20px form) *(source: Universal Principles Proximity p.196–197; Refactoring UI p.99 / #13; Designing Interfaces #7 p.218)*.
- **2** — no outright misparse, but ≥2 labels equidistant/ambiguous between two referents, or a related pair (name pair, label+value) split by an intervening unrelated element with no rescue cue (container/connector) *(source: Universal Principles p.197; Designing Interfaces #7)*.
- **3** — gaps run in the right direction everywhere (within < between) but ≥1 group's ratio <1.5:1 — glance-ambiguous *(source: Designing Interfaces #7 "<1.5× ambiguous" rung; Refactoring UI #13 "1.2:1 still ambiguous")*.
- **4** — all spacing-only groups ≥1.5:1, but a legend/key is used where direct labeling was feasible, or ≤1 labeled pair remains equidistant *(source: Refactoring UI #13 ~1.5:1 threshold; Universal Principles p.196 direct-labeling guideline)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** every label strictly closer to its own referent than to any unrelated element; every spacing-only group within < between at ≥1.5:1; graphs/charts directly labeled (no feasible-legend fail) *(source: Universal Principles p.196; Refactoring UI #13 threshold)*.
- **6** — + every group reaches ≥2:1 between:within (label-to-field ~4–8px vs ≥24px between groups; the book's 10px-within/20px-between fix) *(source: Designing Interfaces #7 floor; Refactoring UI p.99 + #13 "clear ≥2:1")*.
- **7** — + the ratio holds consistently across every grouping type on the screen (labels/fields, list items, icon+count pairs) — zero one-off exceptions *(source: Designing Interfaces #7 7–8; Refactoring UI #13 7–8)*.
- **8** — + blur/squint pass: emergent clusters match the semantic groups exactly — none merge across groups or split within one *[derived: Universal Principles glance-test 9–10 + Refactoring UI squint-test convergence]*.
- **9** — + no related pair anywhere on the surface split or rescued only by a container; direct labeling on ALL data displays *(source: Universal Principles p.196)*.
- **10 — ✓:** proximity alone resolves relatedness with zero ambiguity site-wide (corrected trail-sign standard) AND is reinforced by a second Gestalt cue (similarity/subtle background) *(source: Designing Interfaces #7 9–10; Universal Principles Proximity 9–10)*.
**Weight.** high (3) — Universal Principles: high; Designing Interfaces #7: high.

### GEST-2 — Similarity: same look claims same meaning
**Rule.** Shared color/size/shape asserts functional sameness; color is the strongest similarity cue (degrading as color count grows; never alone — colorblindness), size next (usable for ranking), shape weakest (combine). The inverse binds: two treatments for one role imply a difference that doesn't exist.
**Grounding.**
- Universal Principles (p.226): "Similarity of color results in the strongest grouping effect; it is strongest when the number of colors is small, and is decreasingly effective as the number of colors increases... Similarity of shape is the weakest grouping strategy." Guideline: "Use similarity to indicate relatedness among elements in a design... Use the fewest colors and simplest shapes possible for the strongest grouping effects." Accessibility mechanism (p.226 n.2): "a significant portion of the population is color blind, limiting the strategy of using color alone."
- Designing Interfaces (p.218): "Items that are similar in shape, size, or color are perceived as related to one another. If you have a few things 'of a type' and you want viewers to see them as equally interesting alternatives, give them an identical (and distinctive) graphic treatment... Align these items very precisely with one another to create a visual line." Mechanism: identical treatment marks peers; precise alignment reinforces the group as one visual line.
**Objective test.** Per action class: all members share the {color, shape, radius, size} treatment tuple; unexplained outliers = fail. Hues encoding one category dimension: ≤~6–7 (grouping effect decreases as color count grows). Grayscale pass: convert the screen to grayscale — every group must still separate (no color-alone encoding).
**✗ WRONG.** One "Save" filled blue, another "Save" elsewhere a plain text link — same role, two treatments implying a phantom difference; 9 background hues as the sole status encoding, indistinguishable in grayscale.
**✓ RIGHT.** One primary-confirm treatment (same fill, radius, size) everywhere the role recurs; statuses encoded as color+icon+label so the grayscale pass still reads.
**Crop.** DI-07.
**Score — grounded ladder (0→10).** Score = highest rung whose condition AND every rung below it hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
- **0 — ✗:** one role carries two systematically different treatments (filled "Save" here, text-link "Save" there — phantom difference), OR a single categorical dimension is color-only with >6–7 hues and fails a grayscale check *(source: Universal Principles Similarity p.226 / scoring 0; Designing Interfaces #8 p.218)*.
- **2** — the false-sameness or false-difference is narrower: exactly one unexplained outlier in one same-role class, or exactly one collision between two different roles (primary/secondary/destructive sharing a tuple) *(source: Universal Principles p.226 — weakest-cue/collision mechanism)*.
- **3** — a secondary encoding exists for SOME but not all color-only states, or hue count is reduced but still >6 without support *(source: Universal Principles scoring 3)*.
- **4** — 2–3 unexplained tuple outliers remain in one same-role class, but no role-to-role collision *(source: Universal Principles p.226 similarity-strength gradient)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** every color-only distinction carries a second independent encoding (icon/shape/label); grayscale/colorblind test passes for at least the majority of states; hue count ≤7 *(source: Universal Principles scoring 5–6 / p.226 n.2 colorblindness)*.
- **6** — + every same-role control class is tuple-uniform (outliers only for documented states: disabled/hover/selected) and no role collisions anywhere *(source: Designing Interfaces #8 p.218 "identical graphic treatment")*.
- **7** — threshold met for ALL states (not just majority), and the primary encoding uses the fewest colors/simplest shapes needed *(source: Universal Principles scoring 7–8 "fewest colors, simplest shapes")*.
- **8** — + peer items presented as "equally interesting alternatives" are precisely aligned to one visual line *(source: Designing Interfaces #8 p.218 "align these items very precisely... to create a visual line")*.
- **9** — + zero unexplained tuple outliers anywhere on the surface, hue count ≤6 *(source: Universal Principles p.226 "strongest when the number of colors is small")*.
- **10 — ✓:** full redundant encoding (color + icon/shape + text) across every categorical distinction, verified to survive complete grayscale conversion with zero ambiguity, AND every same-role/peer-alignment case matches the tuple-uniform + precise-alignment standard *(source: Universal Principles scoring 9–10; Designing Interfaces #8 9–10)*.
**Weight.** high (3) — Designing Interfaces #8: high; Universal Principles: med (split noted; DI's "compounds across the product" rationale carries the majority of grounding here).

### GEST-3 — Uniform connectedness: containers and connectors override everything
**Rule.** A shared bounded region or connecting line groups harder than proximity or similarity — strong enough to CORRECT bad positioning, and strong enough to LIE (a border around unrelated things asserts a false group).
**Grounding.**
- Universal Principles (p.246): "Uniform connectedness will generally overpower the other Gestalt principles. In a design where uniform connectedness is at odds with proximity or similarity, the elements that are uniformly connected will appear more related than either the proximal or similar elements." Repair use stated directly: "This makes uniform connectedness especially useful when correcting poorly designed configurations that would otherwise be difficult to modify... a particular set of controls can be grouped by connecting them in a common region using paint or overlays." Mechanism: the boundary/connector carries the grouping regardless of position — the Windows Print dialog's bordered clusters are the worked example (p.247).
**Objective test.** Functionally-related controls that can't be repositioned: a common region (box/tint) or connecting line present, or violation. Inverse audit: enumerate every drawn container on the screen — each must enclose ONLY genuinely related elements; one unrelated occupant = a false-group fail.
**✗ WRONG.** A print dialog scatters copy-count, page-range, and orientation controls with no grouping box — the user can't tell which controls belong to "output range" vs "output format"; elsewhere a panel border wraps a search box plus an unrelated settings toggle, asserting kinship that doesn't exist.
**✓ RIGHT.** Printer / Print Range / Copies each in its own tinted common region — the boundary groups them even where repositioning is infeasible; every container audited to hold one function family only.
**Crop.** UP-04.
**Score — grounded ladder (0→10).** Score = highest rung whose condition AND every rung below it hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
- **0 — ✗:** functionally-related controls (fixed positions, interleaved) are scattered with no shared visual boundary, line, or region — a user cannot tell which controls belong to which function group (the scattered print-dialog) *(source: Universal Principles p.246–247 / scoring 0)*.
- **2** — a region exists for the majority of clusters but ≥2 false-group containers exist (a container holds ≥1 genuinely unrelated occupant), or one container mixes ≥2 function families *(source: Universal Principles p.246 "will overpower... elements uniformly connected will appear more related" — the same mechanism misused asserts false kinship)*.
- **3** — a boundary exists for some groups but not others, or the grouping regions overlap/are ambiguous *(source: Universal Principles scoring 3)*.
- **4** — all-but-one cluster is bounded, and exactly one container has one unrelated occupant *(source: Universal Principles p.246–247, same mechanism)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** each functional cluster that fixed positioning prevents from being disambiguated by proximity alone sits inside its own bordered/tinted region or is joined by a connecting line — the book's Print-dialog remedy applied; zero false-group containers *(source: Universal Principles p.246–247 scoring 5–6)*.
- **6** — + region boundaries are clean: no overlaps, no ambiguous nesting, no double-draw (border + border) *(source: Universal Principles p.247 "clean" remedy application)*.
- **7** — threshold met and the regions are visually clean with grouping legible at a glance across the whole surface *(source: Universal Principles scoring 7–8)*.
- **8** — + all common regions on the surface use one consistent mechanism (all tint, or all border) — or, if two mechanisms coexist, an observable role rationale distinguishes them (tint for input groups, border for the dialog frame) *[derived: Universal Principles p.246 mechanism consistency + Refactoring UI #33 "one mechanism per component" convergence]*.
- **9** — + a minority-bounded edge case is fully closed: 100% of disambiguation-needing clusters carry a region, zero exceptions *(source: Universal Principles p.246–247)*.
- **10 — ✓:** uniform connectedness deliberately used to override an otherwise poor/legacy layout that can't be repositioned — the book's stated best-use case, applied precisely, with zero false-group containers and one consistent mechanism site-wide *(source: Universal Principles p.246 "especially useful when correcting poorly designed configurations" / scoring 9–10)*.
**Weight.** med (2) — Universal Principles: med (sole scoring source).

### GEST-4 — Continuity and closure: the eye completes implied lines and shapes
**Rule.** Aligned edges form implied lines the eye follows and assumes relationships along; whitespace shapes into implied regions the brain closes — use both deliberately to build flow, and never let an accidental line lead the eye off the path.
**Grounding.**
- Designing Interfaces (p.219): "Our eyes will naturally follow the perceived lines and curves formed by the alignment of other elements." Closure (p.220): "The brain will naturally 'close' lines to create simple closed shapes such as rectangles and blobs of whitespace, even if they aren't explicitly drawn for us... None of these shapes are actually represented in the image but the eye completes the line in your brain." Mechanism (p.220): "Continuity and closure explain alignment. When you align things, you form a continuous line with their edges, and the users will follow that line and assume a relationship." The gaze-directed hero photo (p.221) is the applied case: directional imagery steers the eye through the layout's key elements.
**Objective test.** Trace the implied line formed by the primary elements' aligned edges: it terminates at the intended next action, not off-page or at decoration. Imagery with directional cues (gaze, motion) points INTO the content path, never off-frame. Alignment audit: shared edges among related elements form one continuous line (no small unexplained offsets breaking it).
**✗ WRONG.** A hero photo whose subject gazes off-frame, away from the headline and CTA — the implied line exits the page and takes attention with it.
**✓ RIGHT.** The subject's gaze aimed at the headline, with left-aligned edges carrying one continuous line from headline through body to the CTA.
**Crop.** DI-07.
**Score — grounded ladder (0→10).** Score = highest rung whose condition AND every rung below it hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
- **0 — ✗:** the implied line (gaze direction, aligned edges) runs off-page or dead-ends at a decorative element, pulling attention away from the conversion path — the off-frame hero photo *(source: Designing Interfaces p.220–221 / scoring 0)*.
- **2** — the line doesn't run off-page but ≥3 unexplained edge offsets break continuity among related elements, or a directional-imagery cue points off-frame away from the path *(source: Designing Interfaces p.219 "form a continuous line... assume a relationship" — breaks defeat the mechanism)*.
- **3** — an implied line exists but terminates at a neutral/empty area (doesn't point at wrong content but doesn't help either) *(source: Designing Interfaces scoring 3)*.
- **4** — 1–2 unexplained edge offsets remain, or an implied whitespace shape enclosing unrelated content (false-group closure) *(source: Designing Interfaces p.220 closure mechanism, misapplied)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** the traced line (via alignment or gaze) terminates at the intended next action (headline→CTA); no directional imagery points off-frame *(source: Designing Interfaces p.220–221 scoring 5–6)*.
- **6** — + zero unexplained edge breaks in the shared line among related elements *(source: Designing Interfaces p.219 continuity mechanism)*.
- **7** — multiple aligned elements (headline, subhead, CTA) reinforce ONE continuous line *(source: Designing Interfaces scoring 7–8)*.
- **8** — + closure (implied whitespace shapes) is used deliberately, not accidentally — every implied region corresponds to a real semantic group *(source: Designing Interfaces p.220 scoring 7–8)*.
- **9** — + any directional imagery present (gaze/motion) actively points at the headline/CTA/content path, reinforcing the alignment line *(source: Designing Interfaces p.221 gaze-directed hero example)*.
- **10 — ✓:** full subconscious-guidance chain as in the book's own worked example — gaze + alignment + whitespace all cooperate to route the eye through every important element in order, site-wide *(source: Designing Interfaces p.221 Fig. 4-16 / scoring 9–10)*.
**Weight.** med (2) — Designing Interfaces #9: med (sole scoring source; "diminishing returns without a real CTA to route toward").

### GEST-5 — Chunk via the cheapest sufficient cue
**Rule.** Prefer whitespace to dividers, dividers to boxes, boxes to color blocks — the lightest mechanism that makes grouping unambiguous; and don't reach for a border at all when a background shift or spacing already separates.
**Grounding.**
- Refactoring UI (p.238): "When you need to create separation between two elements, try to resist immediately reaching for a border... using too many of them can make your design feel busy and cluttered." (p.239): "Box shadows do a great job of outlining an element like a border would, but can be more subtle and accomplish the same goal without being as distracting." (p.240): "If you're already using different background colors in addition to a border, try removing the border; you might not need it" — and sometimes extra spacing alone suffices (p.241). Mechanism: each separator is ink competing with content; the lightest sufficient cue wins.
- Universal Principles (p.224): "Excess is noise" — "every unnecessary data item, graphic, line, or symbol steals attention away from relevant elements"; and chunking is memory-scoped (p.40): "The maximum number of chunks that can be efficiently processed by short-term memory is four, plus or minus one," with the explicit misapplication warning that for scan/reference tasks "chunking in this case would dramatically increase the scan time and effort, and yield no benefits."
- Laws of UX (pp.33–36): chunking cues = headings, dividers, whitespace bands; "What chunking does not do is dictate a specific limit on the number of items that can be shown at a given time or within a group" (p.36).
**Objective test.** Count borders per component: each border coexisting with a background-color difference = likely redundant — remove and verify the region still separates. Groups of ≥5 related items carry ≥1 grouping cue (heading / divider / ≥1.5× group gap vs item gap). Memory-bearing strings (phone, code inputs) chunk into 3–5 groups of 3–5 (4±1); scan/reference lists stay flat and dense.
**✗ WRONG.** A "Contacts" invite modal drawing hard 1px borders around its search box AND its list panel while the modal already sits on a distinct background — separation triple-encoded, result busy.
**✓ RIGHT.** Border swapped for a soft shadow (`0 5px 15px hsla(0,0%,0%,.15)`), or a slight row-background shift, or 6px more margin — ONE mechanism, calm result; the 24-toggle settings list split into labeled sections with 24px between, 12px within.
**Crop.** RU-31, UP-19, LU-04.
**Score — grounded ladder (0→10).** Score = highest rung whose condition AND every rung below it hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
- **0 — ✗:** ≥4 redundant borders coexist with a background-color difference between the same two elements (the over-bordered modal class), OR a memory-dependent artifact (phone, code) shows as one flat run of >9 undifferentiated characters with no grouping *(source: Refactoring UI p.238–240 / scoring 0; Universal Principles Chunking scoring 0)*.
- **2** — 2–3 redundant borders remain, or a minority of ≥5-item groups carry a grouping cue *(source: Refactoring UI scoring; Laws of UX #6 chunking-cue mechanism)*.
- **3** — one redundant border removed, others in the same component remain; or grouping applied but misapplied (wrong group sizes, or chunking imposed on a scan/search task where it hurts) *(source: Refactoring UI scoring 3; Universal Principles p.40/224 scoring 3 — explicit misapplication warning)*.
- **4** — exactly one double-encoded separation spot remains (border + bg + spacing on one boundary), all-but-one dense group has a cue *(source: Refactoring UI p.239–240 mechanism-count logic)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** obviously-redundant borders (co-occurring with a bg-color difference) removed everywhere; every ≥5-item related group carries ≥1 grouping cue (heading/divider/≥1.5× gap); memory-dependent content grouped into 3–5 chunks of 3–5 (4±1) and scan/reference lists left flat *(source: Refactoring UI p.240 scoring 5–6; Universal Principles p.40 scoring 5–6; Laws of UX pp.33–36)*.
- **6** — + every separation point carries exactly one mechanism (no double/triple-encoding anywhere) *(source: Refactoring UI p.238–241 "each separator is ink competing with content")*.
- **7** — threshold met AND a suitable alternative (box-shadow, bg difference, or extra spacing) is substituted wherever separation is still needed after border removal *(source: Refactoring UI scoring 7–8)*.
- **8** — + chunk boundaries match real-world convention (area code/exchange/line for phone numbers) rather than arbitrary splits *(source: Universal Principles scoring 7–8)*.
- **9** — + zero redundant borders anywhere on the surface, all dense groups cue-covered, no exceptions *(source: Refactoring UI p.240; Laws of UX p.36 "does not dictate a specific limit")*.
- **10 — ✓:** matches the book's auto-formatting standard — e.g. (555) 123-4567 — memory-vs-scan distinction correctly applied everywhere, ONE calm separation mechanism used consistently product-wide *(source: Universal Principles scoring 9–10; Refactoring UI scoring 9–10)*.
**Weight.** med (2) — Laws of UX #6: high; Universal Principles (Chunking): med; Refactoring UI #33: low-med. Majority/median = med; the split is noted (LU rates the chunking half high as a structural gate; RU rates the border half a polish check).

### GEST-6 — Grouped navigation beats flat lists
**Rule.** Many destinations/options → labeled clusters (fat menus, sectioned lists), never one undifferentiated run; well-chunked long lists stay scannable far past any count myth.
**Grounding.**
- Laws of UX (p.36), verbatim rebuttal: "design patterns such as navigation menus don't require people to memorize them — the choices available to them via the navigation menu are visible at all times... there's no usability gain provided by limiting these links to a specific number." Counter-example: Nike.com's primary nav "number[s] well beyond seven, yet it is still easy to scan the list thanks to clear categorization and the use of whitespace and vertical dividers to separate sub-groupings" (p.36). Mechanism: recognition of visible, categorized items replaces recall — the 7±2 memory limit doesn't apply to always-visible menus. Full myth-rebuttal in DENS-2.
**Objective test.** Nav/option sets ≥8 items: grouped under labeled headers with divider/whitespace separation between sub-groups; a flat unlabeled run fails regardless of count. A set trimmed to exactly 7 with no stated functional reason = a myth-driven-cut flag, not a pass.
**✗ WRONG.** A 40-link nav column, flat and unlabeled — or the same nav "fixed" by deleting links down to 7 with no grouping added.
**✓ RIGHT.** All 40 links kept, organized into labeled sections with whitespace/divider separation behind hover-reveal categories — nothing removed, everything scannable.
**Crop.** LU-05.
**Score — grounded ladder (0→10).** Score = highest rung whose condition AND every rung below it hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
- **0 — ✗:** one flat unlabeled run of ≥8 items with no grouping, OR evidence of a count-driven trim (items removed with no grouping added to compensate) *(source: Laws of UX p.36 scoring 0; #7 "cut to 7, per Miller's Law" review-note case)*.
- **2** — partial grouping only (some of the set still an undifferentiated run), or sub-group separation present but <1.5× the item gap with no divider *(source: Laws of UX p.36 chunking mechanism)*.
- **3** — grouped but ≥1 sub-group lacks a header, or a set sits at exactly 7 items with no stated functional reason (a myth-cut flag, per the book, not itself a fail but a warning sign) *(source: Laws of UX p.36 #7 "no usability gain... limiting to a specific number")*.
- **4** — headers exist but one catch-all ("Other"/"Misc") holds >25% of items — semantically thin grouping *(source: Laws of UX p.36 chunking-quality gradient)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** every nav/option set ≥8 items is organized under labeled headers with sub-group separation via divider/whitespace (≥1.5× item gap or explicit divider); no count-driven trims *(source: Laws of UX p.36 Nike.com case — "clear categorization and the use of whitespace and vertical dividers")*.
- **6** — + every header names a real category (no arbitrary equal-size chunking with no semantic basis) *(source: Laws of UX p.36 categorization mechanism)*.
- **7** — + the full destination set ships whole and grouped — no items removed to hit a count target *(source: Laws of UX p.36 Nike.com "well beyond seven, yet still easy to scan")*.
- **8** — + zero sub-groups lack a header, separation ratio holds consistently across every sub-group on the surface *[derived: Laws of UX #6 + #7 convergence — chunking quality and myth-immunity both fully realized]*.
- **9** — + no catch-all category anywhere, every group's size reflects a genuine semantic boundary, not an arbitrary split *(source: Laws of UX p.36)*.
- **10 — ✓:** matches the Nike-nav standard exactly — the full set (well beyond any arbitrary count) kept whole, organized into labeled sections with clear whitespace/divider separation, scannable at a glance *(source: Laws of UX p.36 scoring 9–10)*.
**Weight.** med (2) — Laws of UX #6 (chunking mechanism): high; Laws of UX #7 (magic-7 anti-pattern): low ("score primarily off whether the result is intact"). Averaged to med; split noted.

### GEST-7 — Orientation: verticals/horizontals read ordered; ≥30° pops out
**Rule.** Vertical/horizontal dominance reads as more ordered and is judged faster than diagonals; an element differing ≥30° in orientation pops out preattentively — usable to flag the one outlier, noisy if accidental; angular displays need ≥30° reference spacing.
**Grounding.**
- Universal Principles (p.176): "The oblique effect is the ability to more accurately perceive and judge line orientations that are close to vertical and horizontal, than line orientations that are oblique." Pop-out precision: "the target line is easily detected when it differs from the background lines by 30 degrees or more" (p.176). The clock example makes the threshold concrete (p.177): "Standard analog clocks are easily read because numbers are separated by 30-degree increments. However, the same time on a twenty-four hour clock is more difficult to read because numbers are separated by only 15 degrees." Mechanism: orientation discrimination is preattentive but coarse — differences under ~30° must be consciously compared, over ~30° they pop out for free.
**Objective test.** Dials/gauges/radial marks: reference spacing ≥30°, or intermediate ticks added to restore reference points. Any rotated label/tilted chip audited for signaling intent — rotation with no intent = accidental pop-out noise (it WILL draw the eye). At most one deliberately rotated outlier per view.
**✗ WRONG.** A 24-hour clock widget with numerals every 15° and no intermediate ticks; a card grid where one badge is decoratively tilted 20°, drawing first fixation for no reason.
**✓ RIGHT.** Radial ticks at every 30° (finer marks only as secondary ticks); rotation reserved for the single element meant to pop — the one flagged outlier in an otherwise vertical/horizontal layout.
**Crop.** UP-11.
**Score — grounded ladder (0→10).** Score = highest rung whose condition AND every rung below it hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
- **0 — ✗:** a dial/gauge/radial display requires angle judgment with reference marks spaced <30° and zero intermediate tick marks — the 24-hour-clock-at-15° case, users must interpolate *(source: Universal Principles p.176–177 / scoring 0)*.
- **2** — spacing is <30° with some anchor ticks added, but not at every increment needed to restore fast judgment; or ≥2 accidental rotations (labels/chips/badges tilted with no signaling intent) *(source: Universal Principles p.176 scoring 3; p.176 pop-out mechanism misapplied)*.
- **3** — marks spaced <30° with SOME added anchors but incomplete coverage *(source: Universal Principles scoring 3)*.
- **4** — exactly one accidental rotation remains, or one oblique section used structurally with no signaling purpose *(source: Universal Principles p.176 oblique-effect gradient)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** angular spacing ≥30° natively, OR (if <30°) tick marks added at 30° increments restoring the empirically-validated fast/accurate judgment threshold; zero accidental rotations *(source: Universal Principles p.176–177 scoring 5–6)*.
- **6** — + the layout's primary lines are vertical/horizontal (no oblique grid or tilted section without purpose) *(source: Universal Principles p.176 oblique effect — vertical/horizontal judged faster)*.
- **7** — threshold met and pop-out is also used deliberately for any element needing pre-attentive detection — at most one deliberately rotated element per view, and it marks the true outlier *(source: Universal Principles scoring 7–8)*.

# Hierarchy & Focal Order

One obvious entry point, a deliberate ranking for everything else. Hierarchy is the strongest "designed vs assembled" lever. Pillars: 1, 2, 3.

---

### HIER-1 — Not all elements are equal
**Rule.** Deliberately over-emphasize what matters most and de-emphasize everything else; visual prominence must MATCH informational importance.
**Grounding.**
- Refactoring UI: "Visual hierarchy refers to how important the elements in an interface appear in relation to one another, and it's the most effective tool you have for making something feel 'designed.'" (p.36) "When you deliberately de-emphasize secondary and tertiary information, and make an effort to highlight the elements that are most important, the result is immediately more pleasing, even though the color scheme, font choice, and layout haven't changed." (p.37)
- Designing Interfaces: "A good visual hierarchy gives instant clues about the following: The relative importance of screen elements / The relationships among them / What to do next" (p.210); demonstrated with bare rectangles: "the arrangement of the screen elements, the relative size, and proportion of the elements imply their importance" (p.210, Fig 4-1). Its four independent levers are size, position, density, and background contrast (pp.211–214): "Adding a shade or a background color will draw attention to a block of text... Contrast draws attention" (p.214).
- Don't Make Me Think: "Pages with a clear visual hierarchy have three traits: The more important something is, the more prominent it is... Things that are related logically are related visually... Things are 'nested' visually to show what's part of what." (pp.55–56) "A good visual hierarchy saves us work by preprocessing the page for us, organizing and prioritizing its contents in a way that we can grasp almost instantly." (p.58)
- About Face lists "Weak visual hierarchy" among its named forms of visual noise (Ch17, p.423).

Mechanism: hierarchy alone — independent of palette, typeface, or layout — is what reads as "designed"; without it the user "is reduced to the much slower process of scanning the page for revealing words and phrases" (Krug, p.58).
**Objective test.** (a) Rank every element by task/business importance (1=highest) and separately by visual weight (size × contrast × position); the two rankings' correlation must be strongly positive — any importance-1 element at visual-rank-3+ is a hierarchy defect. (b) Squint/blur test — reduce the screen to grayscale blobs (blur removes text legibility, keeps size/position/contrast): the single largest, highest-contrast, most isolated blob must be the primary content or CTA; if a decorative or secondary element (ad banner, footer, background image) wins, hierarchy is broken. (c) Count elements sharing the SAME font-weight+color+size combination that are semantically NOT equal in importance — target 0; a screen where ≥5 distinct data points all render at identical weight/size/color fails. (d) For any two elements intended to read as different importance, at least one of {size ratio ≥1.5×, distinct background/contrast treatment, denser grouping+isolation, top-left-quadrant position} must differ; equal on all four = indistinguishable to the squint test = fail.
**✗ WRONG.** An invoice screen renders "Amount Due" and the internal reference ID side by side in the same 14px grey; a full top nav, tab row, and every table cell share that same undifferentiated weight; the blur test lands on a bright ad banner instead of the balance. The eye has no entry point — it reads as a database dump.
**✓ RIGHT.** "Amount Due: $1,240.00" at 32px bold in the primary color inside a shaded summary panel; reference ID 12px grey beneath; secondary table columns in smaller grey type with gain/loss carrying the only accent. Same colors, same font, same structure — only the weighting changed — and the blur test lands on the amount first.

**Score — grounded ladder (0→10)**
- **0** — ≥5 semantically-unequal data points render at identical weight+size+color AND the blur/grayscale test is won by a decorative or secondary element (banner, footer, background image) — a database-dump read with no entry point *(source: Refactoring UI p.36–37; Designing Interfaces p.210 Fig 4-19; Don't Make Me Think pp.55–56)*.
