### HIER-2 — Weight/color before size as the emphasis lever
**Rule.** Size-only hierarchy yields oversized primary and illegible secondary text; use font-weight and color/contrast as the main levers.
**Grounding.** Refactoring UI: "Relying too much on font size to control your hierarchy is a mistake — it often leads to primary content that's too large, and secondary content that's too small." (p.38) The fix: "using font weight or color to do the same job... making a primary element bolder lets you use a more reasonable font size, and often does a better job at communicating its importance anyways" (pp.38–39). Mechanism: two weights (400/700) plus two greys give four distinguishable emphasis levels at moderate, legible sizes — the book's worked example replaces a 30/24/14px all-regular ladder with exactly that system.
**Objective test.** On a single card/component, compute the ratio of largest to smallest font-size in use. A ratio > ~2.1:1 (e.g. 30px vs 14px on one card) driven purely by size (all weights = 400) is flagged; weight/color should carry the differentiation instead, compressing the size ratio toward ~1.3–1.5:1. Companion check: a card using >2 font weights or >2 grey shades for text hierarchy has over-fragmented the system.

**✓ RIGHT.** Title drops to 24px but goes bold and dark; price stays moderate but bolds; supporting text uses two greys at readable 16–18px instead of shrinking. Two colors, two weights — dark+bold for primary, grey+regular for secondary/tertiary — replace the size gymnastics.

### HIER-3 — Emphasize by de-emphasizing
**Rule.** When an element won't "pop" however hard it's pushed, soften what competes with it instead.
**Grounding.** Refactoring UI: "instead of trying to further emphasize the element you want to draw attention to, figure out how you can de-emphasize the elements that are competing with it" (p.46). Mechanism: an accent-colored active nav item still loses against equally high-contrast siblings — the accent adds nothing while every competitor stays loud; softening the INACTIVE items is what finally makes the active one read as selected. Same move at panel scale: a sidebar drops its own background color and sits directly on the page background, letting the main panel read as primary "without adding anything to it" (p.47).
**Objective test.** For an active/selected state not reading as such: measure the text contrast ratio of the active item vs its siblings against the shared background. If active and inactive contrast ratios are within ~1.0 of each other (e.g. both near 7:1 on white), color alone cannot win — de-emphasize siblings until their contrast drops meaningfully below the active item's (e.g. active ~9:1, inactive ~3:1). Panel variant: two adjacent regions both carrying distinct background fills while one is meant to dominate = flag; remove the competitor's fill first.

### HIER-4 — Labels are a last resort
**Rule.** `Label: value` on every datum flattens hierarchy and reads as a database dump; drop the label where format/context communicates, fold it into the value as a phrase, or de-emphasize it — EXCEPT in dense scan-heavy views where the user hunts the label (then emphasize the label instead).
**Grounding.** Refactoring UI: "The problem with this approach is that it makes it difficult to present the data with any sort of hierarchy; every piece of data is given equal emphasis." (p.48) The escape hatches in order of preference: infer from format/context — "you don't need a label to make the connection that [Customer Support] is the department the person works in" (p.49); fold the label into the value — "12 left in stock" vs "In stock: 12" (p.49); or keep but visually de-emphasize the label so the data leads (p.51) — the heart-rate card shrinks/lightens "HEART RATE" while "82 BPM" stars. The exception is deliberate: in a spec/scan table the user is hunting FOR the label, so there the label is emphasized instead (p.51).
**Objective test.** Count literal `Label: Value` prefixes on one card/panel. If ≥3 fields use the equal-weight `Label: Value` pattern, each must take one of the three fixes (drop / fold-in / de-emphasize) — target 0 unresolved pairs — except in a technical-spec or scan-heavy table, where the label is deliberately emphasized instead.
**✗ WRONG.** A profile card reads "Name: … / Job Title: … / Email: … / Phone: …" — four labels, four values, all at the same weight, reading like a raw DB dump; an inventory card reads "In stock: 12".
**✓ RIGHT.** Labels dropped: name bold/dark, title in a supporting color, contact lines grey — the format alone (an @ sign, a phone pattern) identifies each; "In stock: 12" becomes "12 left in stock"; a metric card keeps but shrinks/lightens its label while the big bold value leads.

### HIER-5 — Visual hierarchy ≠ semantic hierarchy
**Rule.** An `<h1>` need not be visually huge; section titles often act as small supportive labels while the content stars — and the page's most prominent text must be the content identifier, not chrome.
**Grounding.** Refactoring UI: "A lot of the time, section titles act more like labels than headings — they are supportive content, they shouldn't be stealing all the attention... **Objective test.** For any page-section heading, measure its rendered font-size against the LARGEST font-size used in the content it introduces. ### HIER-6 — Balance weight and contrast (ink control)
**Rule.** Bold elements feel emphasized because they carry more "ink"; de-emphasize a heavy element by lowering contrast, not shrinking it; strengthen a faint thin element by widening it, not darkening it.
**Grounding.** Refactoring UI: "The reason bold text feels emphasized compared to regular text is that bold text covers more surface area — in the same amount of space, more pixels are used for text than for the background" (p.56) — measured concretely: a bold "A" covers ~90px² vs ~50px² for the same regular-weight glyph. Consequence for icons: "Unlike text, there's no way to change the 'weight' of an icon, so to create balance it needs to be de-emphasized in some other way. A simple and effective way to do this is to lower the contrast of the icon by giving it a softer color." (p.57) Borders escape the harsh/invisible dichotomy the same way in reverse: the book's fix keeps the soft color but widens 1px→2px rather than darkening (pp.58–59).
**Objective test.** Icon-beside-label: the icon's color-contrast ratio against the background must be LOWER than the adjacent label's when the label is the primary element. Border fixes: prefer widening (1px→2px) over darkening the HSL lightness by more than ~10 points in one step.
**✗ WRONG.** A sidebar nav uses solid near-black icons next to lighter nav-label text — the heavy icons out-compete the labels they support; a card border flips between too dark (harsh) and too light (nearly invisible), neither working.
**✓ RIGHT.** Icons lightened to grey while the labels keep the dark color — the text now reads as primary; the border stays at its soft color but widens to 2px, gaining presence without harshness.

### HIER-7 — Reserve distinctiveness for the one thing that matters (Von Restorff)
**Rule.** The one visually different item in a uniform set is the one noticed and remembered; spend difference on the single most important action/fact, and compensate mid-list burial with distinctiveness.
**Grounding.**
- Laws of UX: "When multiple similar objects are present, the one that differs from the rest is most likely to be remembered." (p.93, from von Restorff's 1933 isolation-paradigm study.) Its confirm-modal case: "placing a visual emphasis on the destructive action... not only will help guide users who want to delete their accounts to the correct option but also will help those who don't intend to delete their accounts avoid accidentally selecting this option," reinforced "for extra safety" by "a warning icon... in the header of the modal" (p.97).
- Universal Principles: "The von Restorff effect occurs when there is a difference in context (i.e., a stimulus is different from surrounding stimuli) or a difference in experience" (p.254). Serial-position twin: "items at the beginning and end are better recalled than the items in the middle" (p.220) — "being first on the ballot is estimated to be worth between 1 percent and 4 percent of the vote" (p.221); a critical mid-list item therefore needs isolation-effect compensation.

Mechanism: distinctiveness both attracts intenders to the right target and protects everyone else from mis-selection — one lever, two safety effects.
**Objective test.** (a) Confirm dialogs: destructive vs safe buttons must differ on ≥1 visual channel (color saturation, fill vs outline, icon presence); script check — identical computed `background-color` AND `font-weight` on both action buttons = fail. (b) Lists/menus of ≥7 items: the single most consequential item sits at position 1 or last, not positions 3 through (n−2); if it must sit mid-list, a von Restorff–style distinct treatment (danger block, distinct color) must compensate.
**✗ WRONG.** A "Delete Account?" modal renders "Cancel" and "Delete" as twin grey outline buttons, same size, same color; a 12-item settings menu buries "Permanently delete all data" at position 7, styled identically to the 11 routine options around it.

### HIER-8 — Emphasis overuse cancels itself
**Rule.** When many elements compete via bold/color/badges, none stands out — emphasis becomes noise, and over-styled elements start reading as ads.
**Grounding.**
- Universal Principles: "If everything is highlighted, then nothing is highlighted." (p.254)
- Laws of UX: "If too many elements are visually competing with each other, their power is diluted and they no longer stand out among the other elements." (p.104) It connects this to banner blindness — "the tendency for people to ignore elements that they perceive to be advertisements... a strong and robust phenomenon that's been documented across three decades" (p.96) — warning that "when visually differentiating content, we might inadvertently lead to it being mistaken for an ad" if it sits in a bright box in ad-like corner placement (p.96).
- Don't Make Me Think: "The truth is, everything can't be important. Shouting is usually the result of a failure to make tough decisions about which elements are really the most important and then create a visual hierarchy that guides users to them first." (p.62)

Mechanism: emphasis works only as a difference against a quiet baseline; each additional emphasized element consumes the baseline everyone else depends on — and past the ad-convention threshold, users reflexively filter the emphasized element out entirely.
**Objective test.** (a) More than ~2 unrelated elements at the SAME top emphasis level (same saturation/size treatment) on one screen = diluted. (b) Compute emphasized-element-count / total-visible-element-count; a ratio above ~15–20% is self-canceling (UP's threshold); Krug's coarser bound — more than ~30% of visible elements carrying any emphasis treatment — signals over-formatting. (c) Any important element isolated in a bordered box with a bright color block in ad-like corner placement = false-banner risk regardless of count.
**✗ WRONG.** Six saturated-orange badges ("New!", "Beta", "Hot", "Updated", "Limited", "Popular") scattered across unrelated cards; a dashboard where 9 of 12 stat tiles are bolded red because each owner independently decided their metric was "important" — nothing stands out anymore.
**✓ RIGHT.** One genuine callout keeps emphasis — the single tile representing an active incident renders in red — while the other tiles and cards return to the uniform neutral style, restoring the "different from the rest" contrast the effect depends on.
**Crop.** LU-18.
**Score — grounded ladder (0→10)**
- **0** — >4 unrelated elements share the same top emphasis level, or effectively every element carries an emphasis treatment — nothing stands out (the 6-orange-badges / 9-of-12-red-tiles state) *(source: Laws of UX p.104; Universal Principles p.254 "if everything is highlighted…"; Don't Make Me Think p.62)*.
- **2** — 3–4 competing top-emphasis elements, or ~50–70% of visible elements emphasized — the focal point diluted but not eliminated *(source: Laws of UX p.104; Don't Make Me Think p.62)*.
- **4** — emphasis ratio down to ~30–40% of visible elements — inside Krug's coarser over-formatting bound, borderline *(source: Don't Make Me Think p.62)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD** — ≤2 unrelated elements at the same top emphasis level AND emphasized/total ratio ≤~20% AND no important element isolated in a bright bordered box at ad-like corner placement *(source: Universal Principles p.254 dilution threshold; Laws of UX pp.96, 104 banner-blindness)*.
- **6** — emphasis ratio ≤~15% — the strict edge of the book's own dilution band *(source: Universal Principles p.254)*.
- **7** — + the emphasized element(s) verified to be the genuinely most user/business-relevant items on the screen — emphasis purposeful, not incidental *(source: Laws of UX p.104; Universal Principles p.254)*.

### HIER-9 — Weight choices to guide decisions
**Rule.** When many peer options must coexist, add explicit relative-importance signals (recommended/default/popular), never a flat unweighted list.
**Grounding.**
- Laws of UX: Netflix "found that its customers took an average of 18 minutes to find a show or movie" due to option overload, and introduced "Trending Now" and "Popular on Netflix" as ways "to provide more weight to specific options through the social proof that others have enjoyed them" (p.45).
- Universal Principles (Nudge): "People prefer the path of least resistance when making decisions. When the path of least resistance happens to lead to a generally favorable outcome everyone is happy." (p.170) The default must be the option that "does the most good and least harm" for the majority (p.170) — the pension-enrollment case shows a default flip alone changing savings rates "dramatically" while "employees are free to join, change plans, or not join."

Mechanism: weighting converts an O(n) evaluation of peers into a short ranked shortlist; the default/recommendation carries the majority down the least-resistance path without restricting anyone's options.
**Objective test.** A set of ≥10 peer options must carry ≥1 visually distinct priority marker (a "recommended"/"popular"/"trending" badge, ranking-by-popularity order, or a highlighted default) distinguishable from all siblings. Companion default-check: any pre-selected option must be the one doing the most good and least harm for the majority of users — not the one cheapest for the business.
**✗ WRONG.** 20 identically-styled options in arbitrary (release-date) order, zero weighting or recommendation signal anywhere; a settings screen whose every data-sharing toggle defaults ON for the business's benefit.
**✓ RIGHT.** A ranked "Popular" row plus a badge on the recommended pick, siblings staying quiet; defaults set to the user-favorable option with opt-in left fully open.
**Crop.** LU-09.
**Score — grounded ladder (0→10)**
- **0** — a set of ≥10 peer options carries zero weighting signal anywhere (arbitrary order, identical styling) and/or pre-selected defaults are set for business benefit (e.g. all data-sharing toggles ON) *(source: Laws of UX p.45, the 20-titles-release-order ✗; Universal Principles p.170 Nudge)*.

- **4** — one clearly visible weighting signal present, but pre-selected defaults not verifiably user-favorable *(source: Laws of UX p.45)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD** — ≥1 clearly visible priority marker (recommended/popular badge, popularity-rank order, or highlighted default) distinguishable from all siblings AND every pre-selected default is the option doing the most good/least harm for the majority *(source: Laws of UX p.45; Universal Principles p.170)*.

### HIER-10 — Attention devices match the product's tone
**Rule.** Draw attention via contrast proportionally to the app's declared personality; a calm tool must not use jarring devices, and a critical alert must not whisper.
**Grounding.**
- About Face: "The tools to draw attention involve the fundamentals of human perception and are all based on contrast: Contrast of size, color, motion, etc... The deservedly vilified blink tag from early days of the web is a prime example." (Ch17, p.422) "If your app is meant to be serene, yes, a klaxon will get the users attention, but will also break the promise that the app has made." (p.423)
- Don't Make Me Think supplies the inverse calibration: "if you're a designer and you think a visual cue is sticking out like a sore thumb, it probably means you need to make it twice as prominent." (p.109)

Mechanism: attention devices spend the product's tonal credibility — disproportion in either direction (jarring device in a calm product, whispered critical alert) breaks the experience promise or under-communicates real severity; and designers systematically over-estimate how loud their own cues read.
**Objective test.** Inventory every attention-drawing device (badge, animation, color flash, sound) and cross-check its intensity (motion amplitude, saturation, sound level) against the product's documented tone/brand keywords ("calm," "professional," "playful"); flag disproportion in EITHER direction — too jarring for the declared tone, or too subtle for a genuine safety/critical alert. Severity mapping check: a routine state and a critical state sharing the same device intensity = fail.
**✗ WRONG.** A meditation app branded "calm, serene" uses a bright red rapidly-blinking badge and a harsh alarm for a routine "time for your session" reminder; the same product renders a genuinely critical alert in quiet grey.
**✓ RIGHT.** Routine states stay quiet (a soft single-pulse and gentle chime at most); the one critical state gets a single strong multi-channel cue — proportional to real severity, and consistent with the product's stated tone everywhere else.
**Crop.** none (checklist principle).
**Score — grounded ladder (0→10)**
- **0** — a maximally jarring device (blink/klaxon-class: rapid blink, looping alarm, saturated flashing) fires for a routine state in a declared-calm product, and/or a genuine critical alert renders at quiet/routine intensity (grey whisper) *(source: About Face Ch17 pp.422–423, the blink tag and the klaxon-in-a-serene-app case)*.
- **2** — a device somewhat mismatched to the declared tone (slightly too energetic for a calm brand) but not maximally jarring *(source: About Face p.423)*.
- **4** — exactly one mismatched device remains; all others proportional to the documented tone keywords `[derived: About Face p.423]`.
- **5 — THRESHOLD** — every attention device's intensity (motion amplitude, saturation, sound level) matches the product's documented tone keywords — zero mismatches in either direction *(source: About Face pp.422–423)*.
- **6** — + routine and critical states use device intensities that differ on ≥1 channel — severity begins to map onto intensity *(source: About Face p.423)*.
- **7** — routine and critical differ on ≥2 channels (motion, color, sound), and no routine/frequent state uses any blink/alarm/flash-class device *(source: About Face pp.422–423)*.
- **8–9** — + every genuine safety/critical alert uses a strong multi-channel cue — never whispered; cue strength set knowing designers under-estimate needed prominence ("make it twice as prominent") *(source: About Face p.423; Don't Make Me Think p.109)*.
- **10** — attention precisely calibrated to tone AND importance everywhere: routine = soft single-pulse/gentle chime at most, the one critical state = a single strong multi-channel cue, distinguishable without breaking the brand promise *(source: About Face pp.422–423 ✓ calibration)*.

**Weight.** low (About Face rates it low-med: tone-dependent and only assessable when tone keywords are documented; rounded low).

### HIER-11 — Focal order and visual flow
**Rule.** Set up few strong focal points and implied lines so the eye reads the screen in the intended 1-2-3 order; the CTA sits at the end of the reading path, never before the content that motivates it.
**Grounding.**
- Designing Interfaces: "Focal points are the spots your eyes can't resist going to. You tend to follow them from strongest to weakest, and skillfully designed pages have only a few — too many focal points dilute the importance of each one" (p.221). "If you want viewers to read a site's story and value proposition, arrange the critical pieces of that narrative along a continuous line, and don't interrupt it with eye-catching extras" (p.222); "don't scatter controls all over the page — that just forces the user to work harder to find them" (p.222). Alignment builds the path: "When you align things, you form a continuous line with their edges, and the users will follow that line and assume a relationship" (p.220); the older Uber home page's hero — "the gaze of the young woman in the photo... is pointed to the headline, which uses implied lines to subconsciously guide the viewer's eye around the layout" (p.221).
- Don't Make Me Think: without hierarchy "we're reduced to the much slower process of scanning the page for revealing words and phrases" (p.58) — the flow either preprocesses the page or the user word-scans.

Mechanism: the eye moves focal-point-to-focal-point from strongest to weakest along implied lines; the designer either scripts that sequence so it ends at the intended action, or competing focal points fragment it and the narrative never completes.
**Objective test.** (a) Count distinct high-contrast/high-saturation focal points outside the intended reading path: >3 = flow defect. (b) Trace the implied line formed by aligned edges (and any photo subject's gaze direction) from the entry point: it must terminate at the intended next action, not run off-page or dead-end at a decorative element. (c) The CTA sits after the content that motivates it, at the natural reading-order endpoint — a CTA placed before or beside unread content is a flow failure. (d) One honest squint yields a stable 1-2-3 focal order; no discernible order = failed hierarchy.
**✗ WRONG.** A landing page has a saturated-red "Sale" badge, a bright yellow trust-seal, and an orange CTA all fighting simultaneously; the CTA sits above the value-proposition copy it depends on; the hero photo's subject gazes off-frame away from the headline, pulling the eye off the conversion path.
**✓ RIGHT.** One dominant accent is reserved for the CTA, placed immediately after the copy that motivates it; aligned edges and the hero subject's gaze form implied lines leading INTO the reading path, which terminates on the CTA.
**Crop.** DI-07, DI-08, DI-02.
**Score — grounded ladder (0→10)**
- **0** — >3 competing high-saturation focal points outside the intended path and/or the CTA placed before the copy that motivates it; the implied line runs off-page or dead-ends at a decorative element; no discernible squint order — the user is reduced to word-scanning *(source: Designing Interfaces pp.221–222, the multi-badge landing ✗; Don't Make Me Think p.58)*.
- **2** — focal-point count controlled (≤3) but reading order violated on one axis — the CTA still precedes or sits beside its motivating copy *(source: Designing Interfaces p.222)*.
- **3** — an implied line exists but terminates at a neutral/empty area — it doesn't mislead, but doesn't route either *(source: Designing Interfaces p.220)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD** — ≤3 strong focal points outside the intended reading path AND the primary CTA sits after the content that motivates it, at the natural reading-order endpoint *(source: Designing Interfaces pp.221–222)*.
- **6** — + the implied line formed by aligned edges (and any photo subject's gaze) traces from the entry point to the intended next action *(source: Designing Interfaces pp.220–221)*.
- **7** — + the single dominant accent color is reserved exclusively for the primary CTA — zero accent collisions with non-actions *(source: Designing Interfaces p.221 "only a few" focal points)*.
- **8** — ≤1 focal point outside the path AND one honest squint yields the same stable first–second–third order on repeat *(source: Designing Interfaces p.221; Don't Make Me Think p.58)*.
- **9** — multiple aligned elements (headline, subhead, CTA) reinforce ONE continuous uninterrupted line; closure/whitespace shapes used deliberately *(source: Designing Interfaces pp.220–222 "arrange the critical pieces… along a continuous line")*.

# Layout, Balance & Composition

The "imbalance / left-heavy / one region loud, another thin" failure family. Pillars: 1, 4.

### LAY-1 — Balance: visual weight distributed, not lopsided
**Rule.** A layout's visual weight (size, density, saturation) should feel counterbalanced across the composition; a heavy region beside a near-empty region of similar size, with no compositional intent, reads unfinished.
**Grounding.**
- Designing Interfaces (pp.211–214) treats size, position, density, and background contrast as four independent importance signals: "The size of the headlines and subheads give the viewer a clue about order and importance... a small strip of text at the bottom of the page says quietly, 'I'm just a footer'" (p.211); "Density refers to the amount of space between elements of the screen... The less-dense example will also be slightly more difficult to read and for the viewer to distinguish which elements are related to one another" (p.213); "Adding a shade or a background color will draw attention to a block of text and distinguish it from other text... Contrast draws attention" (p.214). Mechanism: because each lever signals importance on its own, an unbalanced distribution of those signals across regions is itself a message — the loud region claims importance the content may not merit.
- Designing Interfaces' critique of a real weather page makes imbalance reviewable: "How many focal points are there, and how do they compete with one another? Where do your eyes want to go first, and why? What does this page say is important?" (p.223, on Weather Underground's "jumbled visual hierarchy"). Mechanism: competing/lopsided focal weight dilutes every focal point.
- Universal Principles "Symmetry": "symmetric forms tend to be seen as figure images rather than ground images, which means they receive more attention and be better recalled than other elements; symmetric forms are simpler than asymmetric forms, which also gives them an advantage with regards to recognition and recall" (p.234). Mechanism: balance is processed pre-verbally as figure-simplicity — uncompensated asymmetric mass is why "unbalanced" registers before the viewer can say why.
**Objective test.** Split the screen into its major regions; score each for content density and salience (rough ink/area). A region carrying >~2× a similar-sized sibling's weight with no framing intent (no deliberate negative space around a focal point) = fail. Mirror-line overlay (UP p.234): every heavy element on one side needs an equivalent-weight counterpart or a deliberate counterpoint element per the Rule-of-Thirds counterpoint technique (UP p.208). Count strong focal points: >3 simultaneous high-contrast focal points outside the intended reading path = flow defect (DI p.221–222).
**✗ WRONG.** All content and controls piled into the left half of a work screen; the right rail holds two lonely chips; nothing about the composition intends the emptiness — the mirror-line overlay shows one side at several times the other's ink with no counterweight.
**✓ RIGHT.** List on the left, the selected item's full assessment filling the right, decision summary anchoring the bottom — each region loaded to its job, weights roughly countered across the centerline.
**Crop.** UP-16, KR-06; DI Fig. 4-2/4-4/4-5 (size/density/background levers, pp.211–214); DI Fig. 4-19 (jumbled hierarchy, p.223).
**Score — grounded ladder (0→10).**
- **0 — ✗** one loaded half beside a near-empty similar-sized half with no counterpoint element and no framing intent; the mirror-line overlay shows one side at several times the other's ink *(source: Universal Principles Symmetry p.234; Designing Interfaces size/density/background levers pp.211–214)*.
- **2** — ≥2 similar-sized region pairs where one carries >~2× the other's ink/area weight without framing intent *(source: Designing Interfaces density p.213; Universal Principles p.234)* `[derived: DI+UP — pair-count granularity]`.
- **3** — exactly one offending >~2× region pair remains; the rest of the composition is countered *(source: Designing Interfaces pp.211–214)* `[derived: DI+UP]`.
- **4** — no offending region pair, but ≥1 heavy element still sits uncompensated across the mirror line (no counterpart, no counterpoint element) *(source: Universal Principles Symmetry p.234; Rule-of-Thirds counterpoint p.208)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** no similar-sized region pair >~2× without framing intent AND every heavy element has an equivalent-weight counterpart or a deliberate counterpoint element under the mirror-line overlay *(source: Universal Principles pp.208, 234; Designing Interfaces pp.211–214)*.

### LAY-2 — Symmetry and deliberate asymmetry
**Rule.** Symmetric arrangements read as stable and are recognized/recalled better; use simple symmetry when clarity matters, and give intentional asymmetry a counterweight.
**Grounding.**
- Universal Principles: "Symmetry has long been associated with beauty, and is a property found in virtually all forms in nature." (p.234) And the functional payoff, not just the aesthetic one: "symmetric forms tend to be seen as figure images rather than ground images, which means they receive more attention and be better recalled than other elements; symmetric forms are simpler than asymmetric forms, which also gives them an advantage with regards to recognition and recall." (p.234) Mechanism: symmetry lowers perceptual complexity, so symmetric compositions win attention, recognition, and recall by default.
- The book gives three testable symmetry types — reflection (across a mirror line), rotation (around a shared center), translation (repetition across space) (pp.234–235) — turning "balanced" from a taste word into a classification.
**Objective test.** Classify which symmetry type the composition uses (reflection / rotation / translation). For reflection symmetry, overlay the layout's mirror line: does every element on one side have an equivalent-weight counterpart on the other, OR is there a stated counterpoint composition (LAY-3)? Neither = the literal, testable form of an "unbalanced" complaint — not a subjective call.
**✗ WRONG.** Dense imagery and content on one side of the centerline, near-empty space opposite, with no counterbalancing element and no design rationale (not a deliberate rule-of-thirds composition).

- **7** — + where asymmetry is intentional, the counterweight sits at the Rule-of-Thirds opposing intersection, not just anywhere light *(source: Universal Principles p.208, cross-referenced with LAY-3)*.

### LAY-3 — Rule of thirds — and its centering exception
**Rule.** Place the primary element on a thirds intersection for dynamic asymmetric balance — but center it when it is already dominant AND reinforced by surrounding space/elements.
**Grounding.**
- Universal Principles: "The rule of thirds is a technique derived from the use of early grid systems in composition... The primary element within a design is then positioned on an intersection of the grid. The asymmetry of the resulting composition is interesting to look at, and generally agreed to be aesthetic." (p.208) Mechanism: intersection placement produces asymmetric tension that reads as deliberate rather than accidental.
- The exception is explicit: "When the primary element is so strong as to imbalance the composition, consider centering the element rather than using the rule of thirds — especially when the strength of the primary element is reinforced by the surrounding elements or space." (p.208) The book's own Ali–Liston photo is centered correctly only because the surrounding ring ropes/crowd reinforce the fallen fighter's centrality (p.209). The counterpoint technique balances an off-center primary with a secondary element at the opposite intersection (p.208).
**Objective test.** Identify the single most visually/informationally dominant element: (a) already reinforced by symmetric surrounding space/elements → center it; (b) sitting in neutral/asymmetric space → place it on one of the 4 thirds intersections. A dominant element dead-center with NO reinforcing surrounding symmetry (neither condition satisfied) = candidate defect.
**✗ WRONG.** A dashboard's hero metric — a large number weakly reinforced by asymmetric whitespace — sits dead-center of a wide layout, leaving large, unbalanced empty margins on both sides with no compositional justification.
**✓ RIGHT.** The metric moved to a rule-of-thirds intersection, paired with a smaller supporting sparkline at the counterpoint intersection to balance the composition.
**Crop.** UP-08 (p.209 — Ali–Frazier photo, thirds grid overlay, vs Ali–Liston photo, correctly centered instead).
**Score — grounded ladder (0→10).**

- **2** — placed near but not on a thirds intersection (off by more than a gridline's width, within ~10% of frame), with no reinforcement and no counterpoint *(source: Universal Principles p.208)* `[derived: granularity within UP's 0/3 band]`.
- **3** — placed near but not on a rule-of-thirds intersection, with no counterpoint element to balance the composition *(source: Universal Principles p.208)*.
- **4** — placement OR counterpoint condition is met but not both, and orphaned unbalanced margins remain *(source: Universal Principles pp.208–209)* `[derived]`.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** the dominant element is either (a) centered because it's reinforced by symmetric surrounding space/elements, or (b) placed on a rule-of-thirds intersection when the surrounding space is neutral/asymmetric *(source: Universal Principles p.208)*.
- **6** — + no large unbalanced empty margins remain on either side of the placement *(source: Universal Principles p.209)*.
- **7** — threshold met and a counterpoint element balances the composition at the opposing intersection where appropriate *(source: Universal Principles p.208)*.
- **8** — + the counterpoint sits precisely at the opposing intersection and margins read symmetric *(source: Universal Principles p.208)* `[derived]`.
- **9** — the strategy choice (thirds vs. reinforced centering) is driven by genuine reinforcement analysis, not default habit *(source: Universal Principles pp.208–209)*.
- **10 — ✓** matches the book's own Ali–Frazier/Ali–Liston standard — the correct compositional strategy is chosen based on genuine reinforcement analysis, verified via grid overlay *(source: Universal Principles p.209)*.

### LAY-4 — Don't fill the width just because you have it
**Rule.** If a component's natural width is 400–600px, use that with a max-width; stretching to viewport width makes content harder to interpret, and no section is obliged to match a full-bleed sibling's width.
**Grounding.**
- Refactoring UI: "If you only need 600px, use 600px. Spreading things out or making things unnecessarily wide just makes an interface harder to interpret, while a little extra space around the edges never hurt anyone." (p.76) Mechanism: width beyond the content's natural measure adds scanning distance and visual looseness without adding information.
- On matching siblings: "Give each element just the space it needs — don't make something worse just to make it match something else." (p.78) Mechanism: consistency of width is not a design goal; per-element fitness is.
**Objective test.** Measure the component's content width vs. its container width: content complete and legible at 400–600px while the container stretches past ~1400px viewport width = over-widened; apply a max-width equal to the content's natural comfortable width. Line length stays in the 45–75-character band (TYPE-4). A card/form inside a full-width-nav page need not match the nav's width.
**✗ WRONG.** A checkout summary ("chair — $429.00, Subtotal, Taxes, Total") stretched across a 1200px+ viewport, a narrow column of right-aligned numbers and one input floating in vast empty gutters; a login card widened to match the nav.
**✓ RIGHT.** The summary capped at ~600px max-width with intentional margin; the login card a fixed, appropriately-sized card centered on the page background regardless of nav width.
**Crop.** RU-18 (pp.76–77 — checkout panel full-width ✗ vs capped ✓; login-card-not-matching-nav example).
**Score — grounded ladder (0→10).**
- **0 — ✗** a component whose content is legible at 400–600px is stretched to fill a >1400px viewport, leaving large empty gutters (the checkout-panel case) *(source: Refactoring UI p.76)*.
- **2** — a max-width exists but is ≥1.5× the content's natural width (e.g. 900px cap for 500px content) *(source: Refactoring UI p.76)* `[derived: granularity within RU's 0/3 band]`.
- **3** — some max-width applied but still noticeably wider than the content needs *(source: Refactoring UI p.76)*.
- **4** — cap roughly matches the natural width, but running text inside the component exceeds the 45–75-character line-length band *(source: Refactoring UI p.76, cross-referenced with TYPE-4)* `[derived]`.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** max-width roughly matches the content's natural width — line length holds within the 45–75-character band *(source: Refactoring UI p.76)*.
- **6** — + no fixed-purpose component (card/form) is widened solely to match a full-bleed sibling (nav/hero) *(source: Refactoring UI p.78)*.
- **7** — + the cap is applied consistently across at least half the same-class components on the surface *(source: Refactoring UI p.78)* `[derived]`.
- **8** — max-width correctly sized to content across ALL relevant components; a card correctly does NOT stretch to match a sibling full-width nav *(source: Refactoring UI p.78)*.
- **9** — + verified holding on a second screen/surface of the product *(source: Refactoring UI p.78)* `[derived]`.
- **10 — ✓** matches the book's ✓ examples precisely — checkout panel capped ~600px with intentional margin, login card staying fixed/centered regardless of a full-width nav beside it *(source: Refactoring UI pp.76–78)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition AND every rung below it hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight:** med (2) — RU rates #10 medium (sole scoring source).

### LAY-5 — Grids give consistency; fixed-purpose elements get fixed widths
**Rule.** Base layout on a repeated margin/gutter system so edges land on few shared coordinates — but never give a fixed-purpose element (sidebar, avatar, login card) a percentage just to stay "on the grid".
**Grounding.**
- Designing Interfaces: "Creating a design that is based on a grid... allows the designer to focus on the content, assured that the layout will have visual consistency and balance. Grids also help multiple designers work on separate but related layouts" (p.216); "Grids are composed of margins and gutters... Margins are the space around the content and gutters are the spaces between" (p.217); "Using a grid is a good way to ensure that the content will create a visually harmonious composition, and will aid in reducing the cognitive load of your viewer" (p.217). Mechanism: a small repeated coordinate set is cheaper to parse than many one-off alignments.
- Refactoring UI: "Don't be a slave to the grid — give your components the space they need and don't make any compromises until it's actually necessary." (p.90) The failure mode is explicit: "If you make the screen wider the sidebar gets wider too, taking up space that could've been put to better use by the main content area... if you make the screen narrower, the sidebar can shrink below its minimum reasonable width, causing awkward text wrapping or truncation." (p.86) Mechanism: percentage math ties a fixed-purpose element's size to an unrelated variable (viewport), and can even render a card WIDER at a medium breakpoint than a large one.
**Objective test.** (a) Count distinct x-coordinates of major block edges across the page: a gridded page uses a small repeated set (~≤4–6 distinct edge x-values); edges scattered at many one-off x-values = gridless. (b) For any %-width fixed-purpose element, resize the viewport across the full supported range and measure rendered width at both extremes: swing exceeding the element's comfortable min/max bounds (e.g. a sidebar going 200px→500px, or a card wider at medium than large) = switch to fixed width, with the sibling content area flexing.
**✗ WRONG.** Cards at 12/18/15/22px left margins placed by eye; a `width: 25%` sidebar 200px on a laptop (labels wrap/truncate) and 500px on an ultrawide (wasted column).
**✓ RIGHT.** All edges land on the 8px-grid gutter positions (3–4 shared x-coordinates); the sidebar fixed at 240px, main content flexing on its own internal grid; the login card at `max-width: 500px`.
**Crop.** DI-06 (Fig. 4-8 gridless vs gridded; Fig. 4-10/4-11 margins/gutters, pp.216–217), RU-04 (pp.85–90 sidebar and login-card sequences).
**Score — grounded ladder (0→10).**
- **0 — ✗** major block edges scattered across many one-off x-coordinates (margins picked by eye) AND any %-width fixed-purpose element balloons/shrinks well past its comfortable bounds *(source: Designing Interfaces p.216; Refactoring UI p.86)*.
- **2** — a grid is loosely followed for some elements but broken by ≥30% of blocks, and percentage sizing still swings, though within ~1.5× the comfortable range *(source: Designing Interfaces p.217; Refactoring UI p.86)* `[derived: DI+RU]`.
- **3** — a grid is discernible (distinct edge x-values ≤4–6) but ≥30% of blocks sit off it; %-width fixed-purpose element still swings past bounds *(source: Designing Interfaces p.217; Refactoring UI p.86)*.
- **4** — distinct edge x-values ≤4–6 AND the fixed-purpose element is switched to fixed-width/clamp, but the sibling content doesn't yet flex to compensate *(source: Designing Interfaces p.217; Refactoring UI p.90)* `[derived: DI+RU]`.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** distinct edge x-values across the page ≤4–6 (a real grid system in use) AND every fixed-purpose element has a fixed width or min/max clamp with sibling content flexing, no swing past comfortable bounds *(source: Designing Interfaces p.217; Refactoring UI pp.86–90)*.
- **6** — + margins and gutters derive from one repeated unit scale (e.g. 8px multiples) across all page regions *(source: Designing Interfaces p.217)*.
- **7** — + no breakpoint paradox anywhere (a card is never wider at a medium breakpoint than at a large one) *(source: Refactoring UI p.90)*.
- **8** — the unit-scale discipline AND the fixed-width discipline both hold across every relevant page region, not a spot-check *(source: Designing Interfaces p.217; Refactoring UI p.90)*.
- **9** — + verified across a second screen of the product ("multiple designers... related layouts") *(source: Designing Interfaces p.217)* `[derived]`.
- **10 — ✓** grid holds across MULTIPLE pages/screens in the product (cross-page harmony) AND fixed sidebar/card sizing never swings or reverses at any breakpoint *(source: Designing Interfaces p.217; Refactoring UI pp.86–90)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition AND every rung below it hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight:** high (3) — DI rates grids high ("structural foundation"); RU rates #11 medium (disagreement noted; RU's medium scopes only the responsive fixed-width half, DI's high covers the whole grid system).

### LAY-6 — Proportions don't scale linearly
**Rule.** Elements large at large sizes must shrink FASTER than small ones across breakpoints; em-derived headline ratios and linearly-scaled paddings produce components that feel "zoomed", not sized.
**Grounding.**
- Refactoring UI: "As a general rule, elements that are large on large screens need to shrink faster than elements that are already fairly small." (p.94) Mechanism: perceptual "right size" is context-dependent, not ratio-dependent — a ratio correct at one body size has no claim at another.
- On em-relative sizing: "There's nothing inherently wrong with using relative units like em, but don't be fooled into believing that relationships defined this way can remain static — 2.5em might be the perfect headline size on desktop but there's no guarantee that it'll be the right size on smaller screens." (p.92)
- Applied to component internals: "Let go of the idea that everything needs to scale proportionally — giving yourself the freedom to fine-tune things independently makes it a hell of a lot easier to design for multiple contexts." (p.95) — button families need disproportionate padding to genuinely feel larger/smaller.
**Objective test.** Compute the headline:body px ratio at desktop and at mobile: a constant ratio (e.g. always exactly 2.5×) across breakpoints = proportional-scaling flag; the ratio should compress at small sizes (from ~2.5× desktop toward ~1.5–1.7× mobile). Button-size families: padding growth must exceed font-size growth at the large end and shrink faster at the small end (e.g. 28px-font button at 15px/30px padding vs 12px-font button at 6px/8px).
**✗ WRONG.** A `2.5em` headline against an 18px desktop body renders 35px over the deliberately-reduced 14px mobile body — oversized; four button sizes at pure `em` padding (`0.75em 1em`) reading as one button zoomed.
**✓ RIGHT.** The mobile headline hand-set to 20–24px (≈1.5–1.7× the 14px body, independent of the desktop ratio); the large button given disproportionately more padding, the small disproportionately less, so each size genuinely feels its scale.
**Crop.** RU-19 (pp.92–95 — CoffeeKit headline pair; four-button linear vs disproportionate-padding strip).
**Score — grounded ladder (0→10).**
- **0 — ✗** a headline defined relative to body text keeps an identical ratio (e.g. always 2.5×) across desktop and mobile, becoming oversized once body text shrinks, OR a component's internal proportions scale purely linearly with font-size across sizes *(source: Refactoring UI p.92)*.
- **2** — the ratio compresses only slightly (toward ~2.2×), still measurably oversized *(source: Refactoring UI p.92)* `[derived: granularity within RU's 0/3 band]`.
- **3** — the ratio compresses somewhat at the small end but not enough (headline still noticeably oversized relative to the mobile body) *(source: Refactoring UI p.92)*.
- **4** — the ratio compresses close to the target range but the component size family is still linear at one end *(source: Refactoring UI pp.92, 95)* `[derived]`.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** the ratio meaningfully shrinks at the small end (from ~2.5× toward ~2×), and the size family shows disproportionate differentiation at at least one end *(source: Refactoring UI pp.92, 95)*.
- **6** — + the ratio compression trends further toward the ~1.5–1.7× mobile target *(source: Refactoring UI p.92)*.
- **7** — + the headline/component is genuinely hand-set per breakpoint/size rather than derived from a fixed ratio *(source: Refactoring UI p.95)*.
- **8** — + the size family is disproportionate at BOTH ends (padding grows faster than font-size at the large end AND shrinks faster at the small end) *(source: Refactoring UI p.95)*.
- **9** — + key sizes are explicit per-breakpoint values, not derived from a single ratio/em chain, verified across the full family *(source: Refactoring UI p.95)*.
- **10 — ✓** matches the book's ✓ examples — mobile headline hand-set to 20–24px (≈1.5–1.7× the 14px body, not 2.5×), button family with disproportionate hand-tuned padding across sizes *(source: Refactoring UI pp.92–95)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition AND every rung below it hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight:** med (2) — RU rates #12 medium (sole scoring source).

### LAY-7 — Structural skeleton, not one undifferentiated mass
**Rule.** A screen's informational load is carried by a real frame — distinct labeled zones with jobs and overflow rules — not one dense block (mass) nor thin chrome with no internal structure (shell, which breaks the first time content varies).
**Grounding.**
- Universal Principles "Structural Forms": "Mass structures consist of materials that are put together to form a solid structure... Frame structures consist of struts joined to form a framework. Their strength is a function of the strength of the elements and joints, and their organization... Shell structures consist of a thin material that wraps around to contain a volume." (p.232) Mechanism: frames take load through organized members; the other two forms carry load only incidentally.
- Shell's explicit weakness: "Shell structures are effective at resisting static forces that are applied in specific ways, but are poor at resisting dynamic forces... an egg effectively resists loads that are applied to its top and bottom, but collapses quickly when the loads are applied to its sides." (p.232) Applied analogically to information architecture: border-and-shadow "structure" with no internal zones resists only the exact content it was styled around — shell-brittle (pp.232–233).
**Objective test.** (a) Name each region's single job in one phrase; a region with no job, or one region doing all jobs, fails. (b) Stress test: inject an edge-case content length (very long AND very short) — a frame-structured layout degrades gracefully (defined zones and overflow rules absorb it); a shell layout (chrome with no internal skeleton) breaks.
**✗ WRONG.** A card whose only "structure" is a border and drop-shadow around free-flowing content — inserting one much-longer text value than the design was tested with destroys the layout, because there was never an internal frame holding the content.
**✓ RIGHT.** The card has a defined internal frame — header zone, body zone with explicit max-height + overflow behavior, footer zone — so content variance is absorbed by the frame's own rules, not by the border/shadow shell.
**Crop.** none (analogical; UP p.233 diagrams — Statue of Liberty iron frame, Icosa shelters, Geocell wall — optional).
**Score — grounded ladder (0→10).**
- **0 — ✗** a component's apparent structure is purely decorative chrome (border/shadow) with no internal skeleton — an edge-case content-length test breaks the layout entirely *(source: Universal Principles Structural Forms p.232)*.
- **2** — some internal structure exists but is only a partial frame, missing overflow rules for some zones *(source: Universal Principles p.232)* `[derived: granularity within UP's 0/3 band]`.
- **3** — some internal structure exists but doesn't hold under edge-case content (partial frame, missing overflow rules for some zones) *(source: Universal Principles p.232)*.
- **4** — most regions have nameable jobs, but ≥1 region is jobless or an overflow rule is missing *(source: Universal Principles p.232)* `[derived]`.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** the component has a defined internal frame (labeled zones, explicit overflow/max-height rules) that absorbs varying content length without breaking — passes the edge-case insertion test *(source: Universal Principles p.232)*.
- **6** — + every region's single job is stateable in one phrase, no jobless or duplicate regions *(source: Universal Principles p.232)*.
- **7** — + both a long AND a short/empty content stress test pass gracefully *(source: Universal Principles pp.232–233)*.
- **8** — threshold met across ALL components of this class in the product, not just the one audited instance *(source: Universal Principles p.232)*.
- **9** — + verified under the most extreme realistic content, per the Normal-Distribution 1st/99th-percentile standard *(source: Universal Principles pp.166, 232)* `[derived: cross-read with Normal Distribution]`.
- **10 — ✓** matches the book's own frame-structure standard (Eiffel's iron skeleton) — the internal organization is genuinely load-bearing, verified under the most extreme realistic content the book's Normal-Distribution 1st/99th-percentile standard would demand *(source: Universal Principles p.232)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition AND every rung below it hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight:** med (2) — UP rates Structural Forms med (sole scoring source).

### LAY-8 — Figure-ground: the focal object must read as foreground
**Rule.** The intended focal content must separate cleanly and stably from its background; ambiguous figure-ground alternates and confuses.
**Grounding.**
- Universal Principles: "When the figure and ground of a composition are clear, the relationship is stable; the figure element receives more attention and is better remembered than the ground. In unstable figure-ground relationships, the relationship is ambiguous and can be interpreted in different ways." (p.96) Mechanism: attention and memory both bind to whatever wins figure status — an element that fails to win it is functionally background.
- Concrete cue, verbatim: "Elements in the lower regions of a design are more likely to be perceived as figures, whereas elements in the upper regions are more likely to be perceived as ground." (p.96) The other listed cues: definite bounded shape vs shapeless background, nearer implied depth, ground continuing behind the figure. The book's resort-logo case is recalled better simply by moving the name below the horizon line (p.97).
**Objective test.** The focal element satisfies ≥2 of the 4 cues (bounded shape · nearer depth/z-index · lower-region placement · continuous ground behind, no hard seam). Failing all 4 = ambiguous figure-ground. Squint test: does the panel detach from the page, or merge with it?
**✗ WRONG.** A brand/title placed into the busy upper region of an illustration, above the horizon line, competing with the illustration's own weight for figure status; low-contrast cards melting into a similar-toned page.
**✓ RIGHT.** The title moved to the lower, quiet region of the composition — unambiguous figure, better recalled; cards separated from the page via a lightness shift or elevation (see DEPTH-3).
**Crop.** UP-10 (p.97 — Rubin vase; Dalmatian-in-noise; resort logo unstable-top vs stable-bottom placement).
**Score — grounded ladder (0→10).**
- **0 — ✗** the focal element satisfies none of the 4 cues (no bounded shape, no depth cue, sits in the upper/competing region, ground has a hard seam) — genuinely ambiguous figure-ground *(source: Universal Principles p.96)*.
- **2** — satisfies exactly 1 of the 4 cues, still likely to alternate/compete with the background for attention *(source: Universal Principles p.96)* `[derived: granularity within UP's 0/3 band]`.
- **3** — satisfies 1 of 4 cues, AND a competing non-focal element carries stronger figure cues elsewhere *(source: Universal Principles p.96)* `[derived]`.
- **4** — approaches but does not yet reach 2 of 4 cues, and under squint/blur the panel still merges with the background *(source: Universal Principles p.96)* `[derived]`.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** satisfies ≥2 of the 4 cues (bounded shape, nearer depth, lower-region placement, continuous ground) — the book's own test threshold *(source: Universal Principles p.96)*.
- **6** — + under the squint/blur test the focal panel detaches from the page *(source: Universal Principles p.96)*.
- **7** — + no non-focal element carries stronger figure cues than the intended focal element *(source: Universal Principles p.96)*.
- **8** — satisfies 3 of 4 cues, verified via a quick recall/attention check (the element is what a viewer names first) *(source: Universal Principles p.96)*.
- **9** — + the recall/attention check is cross-checked against having no competing figure anywhere on the surface *(source: Universal Principles p.96)* `[derived]`.
- **10 — ✓** all 4 cues satisfied — matches the book's own corrected resort-logo case (moved below the horizon, unambiguous figure, better-recalled) *(source: Universal Principles p.97)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition AND every rung below it hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight:** med (2) — UP rates Figure-Ground med (sole scoring source).

### LAY-9 — Content resiliency: design for the distribution, not the modal case
**Rule.** Layouts must survive real variance — 3× text expansion, RTL, user font scaling, extreme values — by reflowing/reprioritizing gracefully; review at the distribution's edges (1st–99th percentile), never just the average.
**Grounding.**
- Laws of UX: "English, a very compact language, contains words that can expand up to 300% when translated into a less compact language such as Italian" (p.61) — with the concrete 1:3 example "Views" vs "Visualizzazioni" (Fig. 5-5, p.62). Mechanism: any container sized to exact English strings is sized to one point of a wide distribution.
- Laws of UX on font scaling, the ✓ case: Amazon "accounts for the possibility of minimum font size customization by organizing the quick links below the search bar by importance and removing the links of lesser importance as the font size increases" (p.62) — priority-based degradation, not breakage.
- Universal Principles "Normal Distribution": "The probability that a person will match the average of their population group in two measures is approximately 7 percent; this falls to less than 1 percent for eight measures." (p.166) And the guideline: "Where possible, create designs that will accommodate 98 percent of the population; namely, the first to the 99th percentile." (p.166) Mechanism: variance between the average and the rest of the population IS the variance the design must accommodate — the average is not the preferred design parameter just because it is the most common.
**Objective test.** (a) Inject a string 3× the current English length into any container: no clipping, no sibling overlap, no page horizontal scroll. (b) Simulate max OS/browser text size: lower-priority items reflow, wrap, or hide — never overlap higher-priority content. (c) The test-fixture set explicitly includes 1st- and 99th-percentile lengths/values (very short and very long names, minimum and maximum realistic amounts, empty and maximal record counts) — a median-only fixture set has validated ~7% of reality on just 2 dimensions (UP p.166).
**✗ WRONG.** A fixed-width nav with 6 links sized to exact English labels truncating 3 of them mid-word in German (~1.3–2× expansion), no ellipsis or wrap handling; a form tested only with "John Smith"-length names and 4-digit amounts breaking on a hyphenated long name and a 7-figure value.
**✓ RIGHT.** The nav drops its lowest-priority 2 links into a "More" overflow menu once label width exceeds available space, whatever language triggered it; the test suite includes extreme-length names and amounts and the layout holds at both ends.
**Crop.** LU-14 (Figs. 5-5/5-6, pp.61–62), UP-07 (p.167 — percentile chart over the bell curve).
**Score — grounded ladder (0→10).**
- **0 — ✗** a fixed-width container clips/truncates mid-word with no ellipsis/wrap when text length triples (English→German/Italian expansion), or a max-font-size setting causes overlap; OR a test suite/design is validated only against "average"-length/value inputs *(source: Laws of UX pp.61–62; Universal Principles p.166)*.
- **2** — some overflow handling (ellipsis) exists but meaning is lost, and edge cases are considered on only one axis (length OR value, not both) *(source: Laws of UX p.62; Universal Principles p.166)* `[derived: LU+UP]`.
- **3** — some edge cases considered but not systematically (e.g. long names tested but not extreme amounts, or vice versa) *(source: Universal Principles p.166)*.
- **4** — the 3× string injection passes on one axis, but max-font-scale reflow is not yet priority-ordered *(source: Laws of UX pp.61–62)* `[derived]`.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** injecting a string 3× current English length causes no clipping, no sibling overlap, no forced horizontal scroll; at max font-size setting, lower-priority items reflow/wrap/hide rather than overlapping higher-priority content; fixtures span the 1st–99th percentile on at least one axis *(source: Laws of UX pp.61–62; Universal Principles p.166)*.
- **6** — + the degradation is graceful and priority-ordered (least-important content drops first) rather than uniform shrinking/scrambling *(source: Laws of UX p.62)*.
- **7** — + the fixture set includes 1st- AND 99th-percentile cases on BOTH length and value axes (very short/long names, min/max realistic amounts, empty/maximal counts) *(source: Universal Principles p.166)*.
- **8** — threshold met across MULTIPLE input dimensions simultaneously (length AND value AND count), not just one axis *(source: Universal Principles p.166)*.
- **9** — + the layout holds at the extremes across ≥2 dimensions simultaneously in the same render (e.g. longest name AND maximal value/count together) *(source: Universal Principles p.166)*.
- **10 — ✓** matches the book's own "accommodate 98% of the population" / Amazon standard — quick-links are organized by importance and progressively removed/collapsed as font size increases, verified across both translation-expansion AND font-scaling axes, holding from 1st to 99th percentile *(source: Laws of UX p.62; Universal Principles p.166)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition AND every rung below it hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight:** high (3) — UP rates Normal Distribution high; LU rates content resiliency medium (disagreement noted; LU's medium carries a single-locale-MVP caveat, UP's high is unconditional).

### LAY-10 — [derived] Region-contract test
**Rule.** A strong composition assigns each region a contract (WHAT lives here, at what disclosure depth) and the contracts partition the task — overview | selected-item detail | outcome/decision. Content in the wrong region is a composition defect even when each element is fine alone.
**Grounding (derived — no single book names it; three converge on it).**
- Designing Interfaces: "A good visual hierarchy gives instant clues about the following: The relative importance of screen elements / The relationships among them / What to do next" (p.210); position, density, and background are each independent importance signals (pp.211–214). Mechanism: if placement itself signals meaning, then a region is a semantic slot — content in the wrong slot broadcasts the wrong meaning.
- Universal Principles "Structural Forms": "Frame structures consist of struts joined to form a framework. Their strength is a function of the strength of the elements and joints, and their organization." (p.232) Mechanism: a layout's strength comes from organized members with defined jobs — regions are the struts, and an unassigned region carries no load.
- About Face, orchestration: "It is vital that all the elements in an interface work together coherently toward a single goal. When an application's communication with a person is well orchestrated, it becomes almost invisible." (Ch11, p.250) Mechanism: each screen paces the task — downstream content (detail, outcome) stays downstream, not crowded into the entry region.
- Convergence: all three imply the same reviewable artifact — placement is meaning (DI), regions are load-bearing members (UP), and the task's stages map onto the screen's zones (AF) — so every region must carry a stateable contract and the contracts must jointly cover the task.
**Objective test.** State each region's contract in one phrase; then check three flags: (1) an element violating its region's contract (full detail rendered inside the overview region; decision inputs scattered across regions); (2) a task output with no home region (the outcome figure floating in a corner chip); (3) two regions claiming the same contract, or a region with none. Any flag = composition defect, independent of element-level quality. # Navigation & Orientation

Where am I, what is this, where can I go. Pillars: 2, 3, 4.

---


### NAV-1 — Every screen answers the trunk-test questions at a glance
**Rule.** Any screen, reached from anywhere, instantly answers: what system is this (site ID)? what screen am I on (page name)? what are the main sections? what are my options here? where am I ("you are here")? how do I search? A home surface additionally answers what the thing IS and why be here.
**Grounding.**
- Krug, trunk test: "Imagine that you've been blindfolded and locked in the trunk of a car, then driven around for a while and dumped on a page somewhere deep in the bowels of a Web site. If the page is well designed, when your vision clears you should be able to answer these questions without hesitation: What site is this? (Site ID) What page am I on? (Page name) What are the major sections of this site? (Sections) What are my options at this level? (Local navigation) Where am I in the scheme of things? ('You are here' indicators) How can I search?" (pp.112–113). Mechanism — the test must run at a blur, not scrutiny: "the true test isn't whether you can figure it out given enough time and close scrutiny... you want to be relying solely on the overall appearance of things, not the details" (p.113).
- Krug, big picture: "The one thing you can't afford to lose in the shuffle—and the thing that most often gets lost—is conveying the big picture" (p.115); "You need to show the Home page to people from outside your organization... because the 'main point' is the one thing nobody inside the organization will notice is missing" (p.124). Mechanism: clarity has no internal champion, so insiders cannot grade it.
- Krug, self-evidence (first law): "It's the overriding principle—the ultimate tie breaker when deciding whether a design works or it doesn't" (p.29); the neighbor test — a cold viewer "could look at your Home page and say, 'Oh, it's a _____'" (p.29). Mechanism: each unresolved "what is this?" fills a thought balloon; small hesitations compound into fatigue and abandonment.
**Objective test.** Perform the book's procedure: screenshot a page reached mid-flow (not home), view it blurred/at arm's length, and time locating each of: Site ID, Page name, Sections, Local nav, "You are here" indicator, Search — each must be locatable in ≤2 seconds of blurred viewing; failing items are the defects. Home: a zero-context viewer, shown only the above-the-fold hero, states what the product does within 5 seconds — any hedge, guess, or "I'm not sure" = fail.
**✗ WRONG.** A deep settings pane showing only a back arrow and controls — no product identity, no title, no breadcrumb — so a user arriving via deep link cannot tell what product they're in; a homepage hero reading only "Reimagine what's possible" over an abstract gradient.
**✓ RIGHT.** The pane keeps the persistent header (logo + name), titles itself "Settings > Notifications," and highlights "Notifications" in the settings nav; the hero names the product category in plain words ("[Product] turns your meeting notes into action items automatically").
**Crop.** KR-04, KR-06.
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — zero trunk-test items locatable at a blur, AND a cold-viewer cannot state page identity even unblurred *(source: Krug #1 "0" p.29 self-evidence; Krug #11 "0" p.112–113 trunk test — the settings sub-page case)*.
- **1** — 1–2 trunk-test items locatable blurred; a lost user arriving mid-flow still can't orient *(Krug #11 "3")*.

### NAV-2 — Nav elements must earn their place
**Rule.** A wayfinding element belongs only if it answers "where am I / where can I go" better than its absence; more nav chrome than destinations is clutter.
**Grounding.** Designing Interfaces: "Breadcrumbs show each level of hierarchy leading to the current page, from the top of the application all the way down. In a sense, they show a single linear 'slice' of the overall map of the site or app... like a Progress Indicator, Breadcrumbs help a user to pinpoint where they are. This is especially handy if they've jumped abruptly to somewhere deep in the tree" (p.194). The pattern's own Use-When is the earn-your-place test: breadcrumbs matter "because global navigation alone isn't sufficient to show a 'You are here' signpost" when "the hierarchy is too deep or large" (p.194). Mechanism: each wayfinding pattern is justified by a condition (depth, abrupt entry) — absent the condition, the element is pure weight; DENS-3's subtraction audit applies to chrome.
**Objective test.** Count wayfinding affordances vs distinct reachable destinations/levels on the screen; remove-test each nav element — zero orientation loss = cut it. Conversely, any screen at ≥3 levels of navigational depth (or reached via search/filter/deep-link) must carry ≥1 wayfinding element resolving to a clickable ancestor chain — zero such elements on a ≥3-level-deep screen = fail (p.194–195).
**✗ WRONG.** A breadcrumb, a section tab bar, AND a sidebar all encoding the same two levels of a shallow app — three mechanisms doing one job; meanwhile a filter-reached detail page four levels deep shows only its own title.
**✓ RIGHT.** One mechanism per orientation job: the shallow app keeps only its tab bar; the deep detail page shows `Home / Settings / Notifications / Email` as clickable links.
**Crop.** DI-13.
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — a ≥3-level-deep (or search/filter-reached) screen has zero wayfinding element, AND/OR ≥2 redundant mechanisms encode the same levels (breadcrumb + tab bar + sidebar for two levels) *(source: Designing Interfaces #1 "0" p.194 — the settings sub-page ✗)*.

- **4** — breadcrumb/equivalent present + clickable at every ≥3-level-deep node, resolving to real ancestors, but the current level isn't visually distinguished from them; exactly one nav mechanism is still cuttable with zero orientation loss *(DI #1 "5–6" objective floor)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** breadcrumb/equivalent present + clickable at every qualifying deep screen, resolving to real ancestors; zero remaining nav elements survive the remove-test as redundant *(DI #1 "5–6")*.
- **6** — as 5 + breadcrumb is prominent, not buried *(DI #1 "7–8")*.
- **7** — as 6 + current level visually distinguished from clickable ancestors (non-link styling, weight/color difference) *(DI #1 "7–8")*.
- **8** — as 7 + breadcrumb is a first-class, prominent component integrated with search/filter state, so search-reached deep pages still show the full ancestor slice *(DI #1 "9–10")*.
- **10** — ✓ matches the B&H Photo standard: prominent, clickable, distinguished breadcrumb on every qualifying screen including search-reached ones, zero redundant mechanisms anywhere *(DI #1 "9–10")*.

### NAV-3 — Group destinations; structure choice
**Rule.** Many destinations → labeled clusters revealed progressively (fat menus/sections), never one flat run; overwhelming option sets get structuring facets. Mechanics in GEST-6, DENS-1/2; nudge framing (structured choices) in HIER-9.
**Grounding.**
- Laws of UX, progressive disclosure: "Progressive disclosure is an interaction design technique that displays only important actions or content by default, while making additional features or content easily accessible. The result is a more streamlined interface that helps to keep the user's attention focused by reducing clutter, confusion, and cognitive load" (p.116) — Stripe's hover-menus let users "quickly scan and find relevant information without needing to dig through a mountain of content" (p.116).
- Laws of UX, chunking mechanism: "What chunking does not do is dictate a specific limit on the number of items that can be shown at a given time or within a group" (p.36) — grouping cues, not item caps, make dense sets scannable (pp.36–37).
- Universal Principles, structured choices/nudge: "People prefer the path of least resistance when making decisions" (p.170); a long undifferentiated option list must be filterable/browsable by a structuring facet rather than presented flat (the book's Netflix Structured Choices example, p.170).
**Objective test.** GEST-6's grouped-run check; top-level visible items materially fewer than total reachable items (DENS-1) — sub-items reached via a single additional interaction (hover/expand), ≤~7 top-level categories visible by default; every group of ≥5 related items carries a visible grouping cue (heading, divider, or ≥1.5× inter-group spacing vs within-group); long option sets expose a structuring facet, not one flat list.
**✗ WRONG.** 40 sub-pages flatly listed in the main nav across every category simultaneously, no grouping, no hover-reveal.
**✓ RIGHT.** 6 labeled categories, sub-items revealed on hover/expand — same 40 destinations, now staged and chunked.
**Crop.** LU-05, LU-20.

- **0** — a primary nav/toolbar flatly lists all reachable items (e.g. 40 sub-pages) simultaneously with no grouping or hover-reveal, AND a dense region (≥5 related items) has zero grouping cue *(source: Laws of UX #26 "0" p.116; Laws of UX #6 "0" — "a genuine wall of controls")*.
- **2** — some grouping exists but top-level item count is still >10 always-visible with only partial deferral of sub-items; grouping cues inconsistent across sections *(Laws of UX #26 "3"; #6 "3")*.
- **4** — top-level exposes only ≤~7 categories by default, sub-items reached via one additional interaction, but ≥1 group cue is missing/weak, or a ≥15-item option set has only a search box, not a structuring facet *(Laws of UX #26 "5–6"; #6 "5–6"; Universal Principles Nudge "3")*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** ≤~7 top-level categories visible by default, deeper sub-items deferred via one interaction (hover/click-expand); every group of ≥5 related items carries a visible grouping cue (heading, divider, or ≥1.5× inter-group vs within-group spacing); any ≥15-item option set exposes a structuring facet *(Laws of UX #26 "5–6"; #6 "5–6"; Universal Principles Nudge "5–6")*.

- **7** — as 6 + grouping cues are consistent and labeled across the whole surface, reflecting genuine semantic categories, not arbitrary chunks *(Laws of UX #6 "7–8")*.

- **10** — ✓ matches the Stripe/Netflix standard: a small top-level set, hover reveals well-organized sub-menus, zero flat runs anywhere, structuring facets on every long list *(Laws of UX #26 "9–10"; #6 "9–10"; Universal Principles Nudge "9–10")*.

**Rule.** Global navigation recurs in the same place/style/item-set on every screen; ≤5 utilities; focused task flows (checkout/registration) are the stated exception. Full spec → XCON-7.

**✓ RIGHT.** The same 5 utility links, same logo position, same section list appear identically on every non-checkout page.

### NAV-5 — Location indicators must be unmissable
**Rule.** "You are here" needs ≥2 simultaneous visual distinctions (e.g., color AND bold AND fill) — designer instinct toward subtlety reliably fails hurried users; active tabs must visually connect to their content.
**Grounding.** Krug: "The most common failing of 'You are here' indicators is that they're too subtle. They need to stand out; if they don't, they lose their value as visual cues... One way to ensure that they stand out is to apply more than one visual distinction—for instance, a different color and bold text" (p.109). And the calibration maxim: "if you're a designer and you think a visual cue is sticking out like a sore thumb, it probably means you need to make it twice as prominent" (p.109). Mechanism: hurried, scanning users miss single-channel cues entirely — the designer's studio viewing conditions systematically overestimate salience; the tab-pop comparison shows the front-most affordance made or broken by contrast + connection to its panel.
**Objective test.** The current-location marker differs from the inactive baseline on ≥2 independent channels (of: color, weight, background fill, border, icon, size); a single-channel difference (e.g., only a slightly darker gray) = fail. Active tab must be visually continuous with its panel (shared fill/border, no separating line).
**✗ WRONG.** The active tab rendered 5% darker grey than inactive tabs — same weight, same size, no border.
**✓ RIGHT.** Bold text + colored underline + filled background — three simultaneous cues — with the tab fused to its content panel.
**Crop.** KR-01, KR-05.
