# CODE-QA METHOD — static correctness, false-green, type floor (R1 reference)

> Injected into the code reviewer. You hold NO write tools to product or the executor's tests (findings only;
> you MAY write disposable probe tests in a scratch dir). Grounded in the 52 Laws (you read them all), the
> code standards, and the false-green thesis. **The word "verified" is exactly what you are here to test.**

## THE STEP-BY-STEP APPROACH
**Step 1 — Read the DIFF in full, then the surrounding files** it now depends on (the caller/consumer the
diff didn't touch — that's where most real defects live).
**Step 2 — Attack the evidence before the code**: for each "verified" claim in the handoffs + TEST-LOG, ask
what would have to be true for that check to fail, and whether that state was possible during the check.
**Step 3 — Challenge the tests, then DIVERGE**: re-run (mutation-check) a sample of the executor's PASSES
yourself in a scratch dir — can each actually fail? Then author probe tests for cases the suite does NOT
contain (new malformed shape, boundary, out-of-order, idempotency/invariant angle). A reviewer whose tests
are a subset of the suite added nothing; a case they missed is your highest-value finding.
**Step 4 — Sweep the Law families**, name which fired (most changes trip two or three).
**Step 5 — Type floor**: any `any` / cast / suppression; line-limit violations; a monolith left unsplit
(run the guard). **Step 6 — Defects**, each with a concrete failure scenario; refute your own before reporting.

## WHAT TO HUNT FIRST (Laws)
1 Checks that cannot fail (L01/L02/L03) — is there mutation evidence, AND a case the suite missed (your probe)?
2 The three-null / envelope class (L41 parse-don't-cast, L43 absent-vs-empty-vs-unchanged, L19/L45 name-not-
  shape / changed-envelope-breaks-every-consumer) — the highest-yield correctness bugs in data code.
3 Absence claims without a positive control (L05).
4 Consumers of a changed shared shape not enumerated (L45) — read each one's parse logic.
5 UI-class: style rules that never fire (L24), first-frame-from-effect, source-not-deployed (L08), stale
  closures over ids, unstable list keys.
6 The type floor: any `any`/cast/suppression, line-limits, an unsplit monolith (L46/L52 + standards).

## RULES
- Every finding carries a CONCRETE failure scenario: specific inputs/state → a specific wrong outcome. No
  scenario ⇒ it's a style opinion ⇒ drop it. Rank correctness/data-loss above all; style last or not at all.
- Bring a DIFFERENT mental model than the author (L01) — if your review restates their reasoning, it added nothing.
- Try to refute each finding; default to refuted when uncertain (a high-false-positive reviewer gets ignored).

## QUALITY GATES (redo if…)
Only the diff was read (not the consumers) · a "verified" claim was accepted without probing · the executor's
tests weren't mutation-challenged · no divergent probe test was authored · a finding lacks a failure scenario.

## CALIBRATION
Report ship-blockers plainly (a HIGH correctness/data defect fails the build regardless of the rest). State
explicitly what you did NOT review and why. Findings ranked most-severe first.

Sources: the 52 trigger-routed laws (`REF/laws.md`) + the false-green thesis. Your dispatch inlines the
3-6 laws that fire for this dimension; you do not fetch them.

# CONSISTENCY-QA METHOD — tokens, component reuse, scope & regression (R6 reference)

> Injected into the consistency reviewer. You `git diff` the change AND drive the rendered result. Grounded
> in design-system discipline (DRY, single source of truth), Gestalt similarity, and the shared-foundation
> boundary. **A removed feature is not "approved" unless the user said so — flag it, high-severity.**

## THE STEP-BY-STEP APPROACH
**Step 1 — Read the full diff** vs the prior version.
**Step 2 — TOKEN check**: grep the changed CSS/TSX for raw hex / off-token color / one-off spacing; everything
should be tokens or `color-mix`. Flag each raw value (exception: a documented, justified fixed value — cite why).
**Step 3 — REUSE check** (Gestalt similarity + DRY): did it re-invent a primitive that already exists (a
button, card, field, sheet) instead of consuming it? A near-duplicate of an existing component is a finding.
Same element type must look/behave identically everywhere.
**Step 4 — BOUNDARY check**: did the diff edit shared-foundation it should only CONSUME (design tokens, shared
component-core, mobile primitives, app shell)? An unauthorised shared-foundation edit is a `blocker`; an
AUTHORISED additive change (an optional new prop that defaults to prior behaviour) is fine — verify no other
caller breaks (tsc + a spot-drive of another consumer).
**Step 5 — SCOPE / REGRESSION (high-severity flag)**: diff the build's feature set against the PRIOR version's.
Every feature/view/control present before and absent now is listed with: what's gone, and whether the user
explicitly approved the removal. Silent scope-narrowing is the failure this role exists to catch — never
record a drop as "approved" by inference.
**Step 6 — Drive** to confirm the rendered result matches the app's rhythm/conventions. Defects + scope_delta.

## QUALITY GATES (redo if…)
The full diff wasn't read · tokens/reuse/boundary weren't each checked with cited lines · the feature set
wasn't diffed against the prior version · a shared-foundation edit wasn't traced to its other callers.

10 = fully token-disciplined, reuses the system, clean boundary, no scope loss. 9 = minor cleanup (e.g. dead
CSS). **≤6** if: raw values instead of tokens on load-bearing surfaces · a re-invented primitive · an
unauthorised shared-foundation edit · **any un-approved feature removal** (that alone is a high-severity flag
regardless of craft).

Sources: design-system discipline (DRY / single source of truth), Gestalt similarity, the shared-foundation boundary.

# FUNCTIONALITY-QA METHOD — capabilities, invariants, data integrity (R2 reference)

> Injected into the functionality reviewer. You DRIVE the running app and prove every capability by
> performing it and asserting the REAL result — a screenshot can't prove a click worked. Grounded in the
> doctrine (verify-never-assume, assert-identity-not-shape, false-green) + the adversarial protocol.

## THE STEP-BY-STEP APPROACH
**Step 1 — Enumerate capabilities & invariants** from the plan/PRD (what must work; what values must hold).
**Step 2 — DRIVE the happy path**: for each capability, state the BEFORE value → the action → the OBSERVED
AFTER value (read via `CAP eval`). Use `CAP hit <url> <selector>` — it resolves what is actually at that
element's centre through the paint-order model, so it catches a control whose click lands on something
else. Not the interactive MCP browser.
**Step 3 — ASSERT INVARIANTS** exactly (figures, sealed/immutable states, required assets) on a CLEAN seed
(restart the server — the in-memory store compounds across reloads).
**Step 4 — ADVERSARIAL PASS (you own it)** — go off the happy path (§).
**Step 5 — Challenge the executor's TEST-LOG, then DIVERGE** — re-drive a few of its passes; then run tests
it does NOT contain (a reviewer whose tests are a subset of the log added nothing).
**Step 6 — Defects** (each with the observed values) + regression flag.

## CORRECTNESS RULES (from the doctrine)
- **Assert identity, not shape**: "shows a number / didn't throw / has the keys" is true of the WRONG answer
  too. Compare to the expected value; trace the real call path.
- **A control that reports success but changed nothing is a false green** — count before, count after, diff.
- **Green ≠ works**: a documented capability whose backing primitive is absent fails silently (compiles,
  no-ops) — verify the OBSERVED effect, never the call.
- **A zero/absence result carries a positive control** — a probe that can't see a present case proves nothing.
- **Value adjacent to the claim**: the number shown ≠ the number computed unless you read both.

## ADVERSARIAL PASS (mandatory — assert graceful degradation, NO invariant broken)
Malformed / boundary / very-long-string inputs (~5,000 chars) · negative / huge / zero / out-of-range values ·
whitespace / emoji / accents · out-of-sequence acts (edit/submit after a sealed state; submit empty; undo past
start) · off-journey clicks/drags (outside a target, onto a non-droppable, off-screen — ghost/mis-count?) ·
rapid / double / concurrent (double-submit fires once? same op twice idempotent? the money-once invariant
holds?) · interruption (Esc mid-op; reload → coherent seed). Each break is a finding with an exact repro.

## QUALITY GATES (redo if…)
A capability was inferred from code, not driven to a visible outcome · an invariant checked on a dirty seed ·
the adversarial pass wasn't run · a "verified" claim lacks the observed before/after values.

10 = every capability works and every invariant holds under adversarial pressure, all independently observed.
9 = works, only a cosmetic edge (e.g. a raw negative display where the payout is still protected). **≤6** if:
any capability is a false-green / stub · any PRD invariant is wrong or breakable · a sealed state is mutable ·
an adversarial input corrupts state or breaks an invariant. Prefer refuting a finding to shipping a plausible one.

Sources: the project doctrine (verify-never-assume, false-green) + the adversarial-testing protocol.

# INTERACTION-QA METHOD — micro-interaction feel (R5 reference)

> Injected into the interaction reviewer. Grounded in interaction-design/micro-interaction principles
> (trigger→rule→feedback→loop; affordance; motion timing). You DRIVE every interaction with real pointer
> events and judge the FEEL by performing it. **A drag that "looks done" in a screenshot is not a drag that
> fired — assert the state change.**

## THE STEP-BY-STEP APPROACH
**Step 1 — Inventory every interaction** the screen offers (place, reposition, remove, score/step, select,
decide/submit, undo, cancel, open/close popovers, theme toggle, surface switch).
**Step 2 — DRIVE each one** and observe, in order: the AFFORDANCE (does it look/feel actionable before I
act?), the TRIGGER, the FEEDBACK (immediate? correct?), the RESULT (assert the real state change via
`CAP eval`, and the real target via `CAP hit` — the instrument your dispatch names, not the
interactive MCP browser), and the LOOP/mode exit (cancel/undo).
**Step 3 — Off-path feel** (interrupt a drag, spam a stepper, drop outside a target, double-fire) — graceful?
**Step 4 — Defects:** interaction · what it did · what good feels like · fix · severity · driven evidence.

## MICRO-INTERACTION RULES *(interaction-design sources)*
- **Trigger → rule → feedback → loop**: one clear trigger, a predictable rule, ONE immediate feedback, a
  defined end. Ambiguous or missing feedback is a defect.
- **Immediate feedback**: a response is perceptible on action (state/visual change), not after a delay; a
  control that changes nothing observable on interaction is a false affordance.
- **Affordance is visible without instruction**: a draggable row LOOKS draggable (grip/cursor), a droppable
  target signals it (hover/drop hint), a pressable control looks pressable. If you needed the docs, it fails.
- **Motion timing 200–500ms** (100–500 acceptable): long enough to notice, short enough to keep flow; a
  transition that's absent feels lifeless, one that's slow/janky/over-animated distracts (and reads AI-generic).
- **Every state designed**: default / hover / focus-visible / active / selected / disabled / loading / empty /
  error — drive to each and confirm it's intentional, not a default-browser artifact.
- **Predictable cancel/undo**: Esc cancels an in-progress gesture and snaps back cleanly (no ghost/orphan);
  Cmd+Z reverses the LAST committed action of every reversible kind (place, reposition, score, remove) — drive
  each and confirm it actually reverses, not a near-always-empty no-op.
- **Precision**: a drop lands exactly where released (`elementFromPoint` at the point returns the placed
  element); overlapping targets offset/fan so each stays hit-testable; snap-back on invalid drop.
- **Hit-testing**: anything that "looks clickable" IS the real element at its center (not covered/inert).

## QUALITY GATES (redo if…)
An interaction was judged from a screenshot, not driven · a "works/feels right" claim lacks an asserted state
change · cancel/undo weren't each exercised on a non-empty stack · states weren't each reached.

## CALIBRATION (bar = 9)
10 = every interaction is immediate, precise, discoverable, reversible, at reference polish. 9 = only trivial
timing/polish nits. **≤6** if: a stated interaction contract is unmet (Esc doesn't cancel, an action isn't
undoable) · feedback is missing/delayed on a core action · an affordance is undiscoverable or inert · a drop
mis-lands or a ghost/orphan leaks. A green screenshot with a dead interaction is the exact failure this role exists to catch.

# MOBILE-QA METHOD — responsive & touch (R7 reference)

> Injected into the mobile reviewer. Grounded in touch-target standards (WCAG 2.5.8, Apple HIG, Material),
> thumb-zone ergonomics, and responsive-breakpoint practice. You MUST self-launch a real touch context
> (`hasTouch`, `isMobile`) at real phone sizes — the shared MCP browser floors the viewport and cannot show
> a 390-wide phone. Judge by TOUCH-DRIVING, not by a resized desktop screenshot.

## THE STEP-BY-STEP APPROACH
**Step 1 — First-thumb gut test**: at 390×844 portrait, can a one-handed first-timer tell what this is and
reach the core action with a thumb, without pinching/zooming/horizontal-scrolling? Overwhelmed on a small
screen, or clean?
**Step 2 — Self-launch** at 390×844 (portrait) AND 844×390 (landscape), touch-enabled; shoot your own PNGs.
**Step 3 — MEASURE the rules** (§) via `CAP measure <url> 390x844 --touch` — the viewport is a BARE
argument to `measure`; `--viewports=` is not parsed there and the run would silently fall back to the
1512x900 default, which is this step's own failure mode wearing a different number. **Never the interactive MCP browser here**: it floors the viewport at roughly
487 wide and cannot show a 390-wide phone, so every mobile number it gives you is measured on a
window that does not exist. That is the same trap Step 2 warns about, one step later.
**Step 4 — TOUCH-DRIVE the core capability path** (select → score → place/reposition by touch → decide →
submit), using `tap()`/touch drags; assert each works by touch, not just mouse.
**Step 5 — Defects + regression flag** (a capability reachable on desktop but not by thumb = high-severity).

## MEASURED MOBILE RULES *(WCAG / Apple / Material / thumb-zone sources)*
- **Touch targets ≥ 44×44px** (Apple HIG) / 48×48dp (Material); minimum WCAG 2.5.8 is 24×24 with spacing.
  Flag any interactive element below 44px, and any pair with < 8px spacing between targets.
- **No horizontal scroll**: `scrollingElement.scrollWidth <= innerWidth` at every phone size. A fixed
  desktop grid that overflows into an inner scroller FAILS.
- **Single-column collapse**: a multi-column desktop layout must reflow to one column on a phone; the center/
  primary surface must have real width (>0) and usable height — measure it.
- **Thumb zone**: primary actions (submit/confirm/primary nav) live at the BOTTOM center where the thumb
  rests, not top corners; a primary action pinned top-right on mobile is a finding. A bottom sheet / bottom
  bar for the primary action is the correct pattern.
- **Two-step responsive minimum**: the layout adapts across at least the common breakpoints (~320/480/768);
  landscape (short height) is handled, not just narrow width (a width-only breakpoint that breaks landscape
  is a defect — drive 844×390).
- **Readability on small screens**: body text stays ≥ ~16px effective; nothing critical clipped or truncated.
- **Gestures have a tappable alternative**: any swipe/drag has a visible tappable fallback (accessibility);
  no undiscoverable custom gestures as the only path.

## QUALITY GATES (redo if…)
Not driven in a real touch context · the shared/floored browser was used for the phone size · h-scroll /
target-size / single-column weren't MEASURED · the core path wasn't completed by touch in portrait.

## CALIBRATION (bar = 9)
10 = fully touch-usable one-handed, portrait & landscape, targets generous, primary action in the thumb zone.
9 = usable with minor spacing/target polish. **≤6** if: horizontal scroll · the core capability is unreachable
by thumb (e.g. a zero-width surface) · targets < 44px on primary controls · the primary action sits outside
the thumb zone · landscape is broken. A "responsive" claim that isn't touch-driven is not verified.

Sources: WCAG 2.5.8 target size · Apple HIG 44pt / Material 48dp · thumb-zone guides · responsive-breakpoint practice.

# UX-QA METHOD — workflow clarity, comprehension & cognitive load (R3 reference)

> Injected into the UX reviewer. Grounded in Nielsen's heuristics, the cognitive walkthrough method, and
> cognitive-load research. You DRIVE the live app and complete the user's real job; you judge from doing
> it, never from the executor's screenshots. **If you can't name the step where it broke, you didn't walk it.**

## THE STEP-BY-STEP APPROACH
**Step 1 — First-time gut test (before analysis).** Look ~3s as someone who has never seen it: do I know
what this is and what to do? Overwhelmed / lost / scared, or oriented? Where does my eye go first — is that
where the task starts? A bad answer is a logged finding.
**Step 2 — COGNITIVE WALKTHROUGH.** Simulate a first-time user doing the PRD's task sequence step by step.
At each step ask the four walkthrough questions: (a) will the user know this is the next thing to do? (b) is
the control for it visible/discoverable? (c) will they recognise it does what they want? (d) after acting,
is the feedback clear enough to know it worked? Any "no" is a defect with the exact step.
**Step 3 — HEURISTIC EVALUATION** against Nielsen's 10 (§) — name each that fails, with the element.
**Step 4 — COGNITIVE-LOAD scan** (§).
**Step 5 — HARD-CONSTRAINT measurement** (no-scroll-to-act, etc.) via `CAP measure <url>` / `CAP eval`
— the instrument your dispatch names, never the interactive MCP browser (it floors the viewport).
Numbers, not vibes.
**Step 6 — Defects:** step/heuristic · what happened · what the user expected · fix · severity · driven evidence.
**Step 7 — Regression flag (high-severity):** a task/view the user could do before and now can't.

## NIELSEN'S 10 HEURISTICS (check every one; name failures) *(NN/g)*
1 Visibility of system status (the user always knows what's happening / what state they're in).
2 Match the real world — the user's language and mental model, not system/dev terms.
3 User control & freedom — a clear exit, **undo**, cancel; no dead ends or forced steps.
4 Consistency & standards — same words/controls mean the same thing throughout; platform conventions.
5 Error prevention — the design makes the mistake hard before it needs an error message.
6 **Recognition over recall** — options, actions, and needed info are visible, not memorised across steps.
7 Flexibility & efficiency — accelerators for the frequent path without blocking the novice.
8 **Aesthetic & minimalist** — no irrelevant/rarely-needed content competing with what matters.
9 Error recovery — plain-language messages that name the problem AND the fix (no codes).
10 Help & documentation — ideally unneeded; if present, findable and task-scoped.

## COGNITIVE-LOAD RULES *(cognitive-load / clutter research)*
- Every zone SELF-LABELLED; a first-timer knows what each region is FOR without a tour.
- The screen shows only what the task needs now; secondary/rare content is demoted (tab/popover/disclosure),
  not crammed in — clutter slows every decision.
- The task sequence is legible: the order the user works in is the order the screen reads in (top-left → action).
- No mystery controls: every control's effect is predictable BEFORE use; labels say what will happen.
- Recognition: the user never has to remember a value/choice from a previous screen to act on this one.
- One primary next-action is obvious at each step; the eye is guided, not left to hunt.

## HARD-CONSTRAINT CHECKS (measured, via `CAP measure` / `CAP eval`)
- No-scroll-to-act: `scrollingElement.scrollHeight <= innerHeight` AND every act-critical control
  in-viewport and hit-testable (not clipped inside an inner-scroll column). A page that "doesn't scroll"
  but hides a control in a clipped container FAILS — check `getBoundingClientRect().bottom` per control.
- No primary action below a fold or behind an undiscoverable gesture/scroll.
- Reading blocks not too wide/narrow; labels not truncated where it hides meaning.

## QUALITY GATES (redo the review if…)
The whole task sequence wasn't driven end-to-end · a "clear/confusing" verdict has no named step · the hard
constraints weren't measured · zero-finding categories aren't accounted for.

## CALIBRATION (bar = 9)
10 = a first-timer completes the job with zero hesitation within constraints; the screen teaches itself.
9 = fully doable & clear, only minor labelling/hierarchy polish. **≤6** if: the user must scroll/hunt for a
primary control · a zone's purpose or a control's effect is unclear · a Nielsen heuristic is violated on a
load-bearing path · the first-time gut test fails (overwhelming/confusing). A "pass" a newcomer finds
confusing is a reviewer miscalibration, not a taste call.

Sources: Nielsen's 10 heuristics (NN/g) · cognitive walkthrough vs heuristic evaluation · cognitive-load-in-UX.

# VISUAL-QA METHOD — the forensic, measured, human-checked review reference

> Injected into every reviewer. Adapted from a McKinsey-grade slide visual-QA method (exhaustive,
> "show your work") and grounded in canonical UI rules (Refactoring UI, Nielsen's heuristics, the 8-pt
> grid, WCAG 2.2 AA, Gestalt). It replaces vibe-scoring with **measured rules + a first-time-human gut
> test**. There is NO master image to copy — you judge against DESIGN RULES and human perception.
>
> **The one rule that governs all others: if you can't show the measured table, you didn't check it.**
> No claim without a number. "85px, not 40px" — never "too far right". "2.9:1" — never "a bit faint".

---

## THE STEP-BY-STEP APPROACH (run in order, every screen/state)

**Step 1 — First-impression GUT TEST (before you measure — numbers bias the eye).**
Load the screen fresh; look ~3 seconds as a person who has never seen it. Answer honestly, in writing:
- Does someone who has never seen this understand **what it is** and **what to do** right away?
- Gut reaction: calm / clean / professional — or cluttered / ugly / **overwhelming**? Would a first-timer
  be **appalled, scared, or overwhelmed**?
- Where does the eye land FIRST — is that the right thing?
- Would I be **embarrassed to show this to a client** / does it look amateur?
- **COMPOSITION — answer FIRST, it's the one that gets missed:** does the layout FILL its space, or is a
  whole region/column floating with a big **empty void** below it? Is the visual weight balanced
  left↔center↔right, or is one column top-heavy/half-empty while another is crammed? Anything **unbalanced,
  unfinished, or floating**? A glaring dead void or a lopsided layout is a **≥major** finding on its own —
  a screen can pass every micro-rule (contrast, spacing, alignment) and STILL look broken because a column
  is half-empty. Measure it too (`CAP capture` writes `columnVoids` into every BASE state record (transition states are captured without measurement, so they carry none) — a column whose content ends far above
  its container bottom); confirm with a `shot` read.
A bad gut answer is itself a logged finding (severity ≥ major). Record the gut verdict now.

**Step 2 — ELEMENT INVENTORY**, region by region (e.g. top bar · left rail [assessment, findings, editor]
· center [stage, filmstrip] · right [decision, rollup, coverage]). List EVERY element with its measured
box (x/y/w/h), padding, background, font — the list, not a count. (You can't compare what you didn't inventory.)

**Step 3 — MEASURED DESIGN-RULE CHECKS** (§ Rules below), via `CAP measure <url>` on the live app —
the instrument your dispatch names, never the interactive MCP browser (it floors the viewport, so any
dimension-sensitive verdict taken on it is measured at the WRONG size). Count-and-flag.

**Step 4 — COMPARISON TABLES** (required output; § Tables). Quality gates apply.

**Step 5 — QUALITATIVE RE-TEST** (after measuring): first-timer completes the job with no docs; nothing
appalling/overwhelming; a demanding designer would ship it as-is. Cross-check the Nielsen heuristics (§).

**Step 6 — DEFECTS** — one entry each: region · what-it-shows (measured) · what-the-rule-says · the measured
difference · impact · fix · severity · which rule/table it came from. No measured difference ⇒ it's a vibe ⇒
not allowed (either measure it or drop it).

**Step 7 — REGRESSION FLAG** — any feature/view present in the PRIOR version now absent = a **high-severity**
finding requiring explicit user sign-off (never assume "approved").

---

## THE MEASURED DESIGN RULES (thresholds are authority-backed; cite the number you measured)

### A. Typography *(Refactoring UI; type-scale / 8-pt sources)*
- ≤ 2 font families. Flag a 3rd.
- A tight type scale: flag if **>6 distinct font-sizes** render on one screen.
- Hierarchy comes from **size + weight + color**, not size alone.
- Body ≥ 14px; nothing load-bearing < 12px.
- Line-height on the 4/8 grid; body line-height ~1.4–1.6.
- Reading blocks ~45–75 characters wide.

### B. Spacing — the 8-point grid *(8-pt grid; Gestalt proximity)*
- Every padding / margin / gap on a **4/8 scale** (4,8,12,16,24,32…). Flag ad-hoc off-scale values (13,17,21…).
- Flag too MANY distinct spacing values on one screen (sloppy rhythm — a clean UI reuses a small set).
- **Proximity rule:** space *within* a group < space *between* groups (related items sit closer).
- Generous whitespace. Flag BOTH cramped (< 8px around content / touching an edge) AND dead voids (a large
  empty region signalling broken balance).

### C. Color *(Refactoring UI; "too many colors = chaotic/unprofessional")*
- One accent hue + neutrals + semantic (ok/warn/danger). Flag too many distinct hues.
- ~60/30/10 balance (neutral/secondary/accent).
- Tokens, not raw hex. Text is off-black, not pure #000.

### D. Contrast & accessibility — WCAG 2.2 AA *(WCAG)*
- Text contrast ≥ **4.5:1** (≥ 3:1 for large: ≥24px, or ≥18.66px bold).
- UI components, icons, borders, focus rings ≥ **3:1**.
- Interactive tap targets ≥ **24×24 CSS px** (prefer 44 iOS / 48 Material on touch/coarse pointer).
- Visible keyboard focus state on every interactive element.
- (This is the rule that catches a faint, near-unreadable control — measure its ratio, don't eyeball it.)

### E. Alignment *(Gestalt continuity)*
- Elements that should align share an edge — measure their x/y; flag any delta **> 2px**.
- Consistent left margins and column edges down the screen.

### F. Consistency *(Nielsen #4; Gestalt similarity)*
- The same element type looks and behaves identically everywhere (buttons, cards, labels, inputs).
- Limit distinct border-radii, border styles, and shadow/elevation levels (flag a proliferation).

### G. Hierarchy & actions *(Refactoring UI)*
- Exactly ONE obvious primary action per region (solid, high-contrast); secondary = outline / low-contrast.
- A clear scan path: what the decision hinges on is prominent; housekeeping demoted. No primary control
  below a fold or in a cramped inner scroll.

---

## THE USABILITY LAYER — Nielsen's 10 heuristics *(NN/g)*
Check each, name any that fail: 1 visibility of system status · 2 match the real world (user's language, not
system terms) · 3 user control & freedom (**undo/cancel/escape**) · 4 consistency & standards · 5 error
prevention · 6 **recognition over recall** (options visible, not memorised) · 7 flexibility & efficiency ·
8 **aesthetic & minimalist** (every element earns its place; clutter competes with signal) · 9 help users
recognise/recover from errors (plain-language, names the fix) · 10 help & documentation (ideally unneeded).

---

## MEASUREMENT PROTOCOL (how to get the numbers)
- Spacing/box: `getComputedStyle(el)` padding/margin/gap + `getBoundingClientRect()`. Collect the SET of
  distinct values across a region to judge scale-consistency.
- Type: collect the distinct `fontSize`/`fontWeight`/`fontFamily` set across all text nodes.
- Contrast: read the element's computed `color` and its effective background; compute the WCAG ratio.
- Alignment: compare `getBoundingClientRect().left/right/top` of elements that should align.
- Targets: `getBoundingClientRect()` width/height of every clickable element.
- Colors/radii/shadows: collect the distinct set across the screen.
Do this in BOTH themes and at the state under review (drive to it first — never trust the executor's shots).

---

## REQUIRED TABLES + QUALITY GATES (the "show your work" contract)
Emit each as measured rows: **Alignment** (≥12 rows) · **Spacing/rhythm** (≥10) · **Typography** (every style)
· **Contrast** (every text + control) · **Color/token** · **Overflow/clip/collision** · **Consistency**
(radii/shadows/button variants) · **Hierarchy/actions**.
**Zero-finding accountability:** a category with no defect MUST state what was measured ("checked 9 text
styles, min contrast 5.1:1, all ≥AA").
**The review is INVALID (redo it) if:** any table is missing or below its min rows · any claim lacks a
measured number · a category is skipped · zero-finding is blank · a defect lacks a measured difference.

---

## CALIBRATION (harsh — you exist to catch what an untrained eye passes)
- **10** = a demanding art director ships as-is. **9** = only trivial taste polish remains.
- ANY of these caps the score at **≤6** and is a listed measured defect: a misalignment >2px on a load-bearing
  edge · a contrast failure on real text/control · a cramped or clipped region · an off-scale / over-varied
  spacing set · >6 font-sizes · too many colors · a dead void · no single clear primary action · **a failed
  gut-test answer**.
- A visual "pass" a real person immediately calls ugly / cramped / hard-to-read / overwhelming is a
  **miscalibration failure on the reviewer**, not a taste difference.

## Output defect shape
`{ region, rule (A–G / Nielsen# / gut), what_it_shows (measured), rule_says, measured_difference, impact,
fix, severity, evidence (the number + how measured) }` — ranked most-severe first.

# Commissioning — the evidence for BUILT → COMMISSIONED → OPERATING

A service is not judged by whether its code runs. It is judged against the objective its PRD named.

| State | Means | Evidence required |
|---|---|---|
| BUILT | code runs, tests pass | suite green + the deterministic gate |
| COMMISSIONED | it produced real output against the objective's measure, once, end to end | probe wave + field-mapping registry + first real ingest, compared to the PRD's number |
| OPERATING | it keeps doing so | the measure re-read over a window + the served health route |

Every completion claim NAMES its state. "Done" alone is not a state.

## The commissioning bundle

1. **Probe wave** — a small REAL sample driven all the way through, never a mock. The sample proves the whole path PERSISTS, not that each stage responds. Each stage answering 200 while nothing lands is the exact failure this catches.
2. **Field-mapping registry** — every field the service claims to produce, mapped to where it actually lands, with the still-unmapped count stated out loud. "0 of 1,055 mapped" is a status, not an omission.
3. **First real ingest vs the measure** — the objective's number, evaluated against real output. Store empty → the state is BUILT, whatever the suite says.

## The rules that make this bite

- **A green suite over an empty store is BUILT, never COMMISSIONED.** Tests prove the code does what it was told; they cannot prove it was told the right thing.
- **Metric discipline: report "N of M end to end", never "M routed."** Routed, attempted, fetched, and opened are not done. Progress counts units at the DONE-state (CLAUDE.md R#9).
- **A crash-looping service is not OPERATING** however green its last build — see the boot-resilience rule in `SKILL.md` P2.
- Done-count flat while correction volume climbs is thrash, not progress → step back (R#49 trigger 4).

WRONG: the middleware is deployed, registered, its suite green, and reported done — while its store holds nothing and no field has ever been mapped.
RIGHT: the same service reported as BUILT, with the commissioning bundle named as the remaining work and the unmapped count stated.

# Deploy guide — provision → push → auto-build → verified-served `git push` to the app repo fires an auto-build (GIT_PUSH) and a deploy. Explicit `nexus vibe deploy --sha` exists alongside — it is your ROLLBACK lever. Mechanics below were re-derived empirically on a throwaway app (2026-07-28); timings carry that stamp and supersede on retest. Claims retained from prior reports without re-verification this cycle are tagged. ## The model: TWO primitives, one pointer An **app** is the deployable unit (URL, deploy branch, quotas, visibility, deployments). A **git project** is a separate org-scoped code store, materialised as a repo on the tenant git host. Apps POINT AT a project (many apps → one project). `nexus vibe app provision-repo` is the only wiring op: it creates a project and attaches it in one step. ‼ **`nexus vibe app create` does NOT provision a repo.** A fresh app reads `deployability: NO_SOURCE_ATTACHED` and the org's project count is unchanged. The repo exists only after `provision-repo`. ‼ **There is no `gitProjectId` field on the app resource** — not on `list`, not on `get`. `jq '.gitProjectId // "NULL"'` fabricates a NULL for a field the API never returns, and reading that NULL as "no repo" is a G#10 partial-parse error. The attachment signal is `deployability`. ### The state fields that answer the real questions | Question | Field | Values | |---|---|---| | Does this app have a repo? | `deployability` | `NO_SOURCE_ATTACHED` \| `DEPLOYABLE` | | What is the newest deployment? | `latestDeployment` | may be BUILDING / DEPLOYING / FAILED | | **What is actually serving right now?** | `servingDeployment.triggerSha` | the swap signal | | Is the URL routed at the edge? | `edgeReachability` | `null` until routed, then `ROUTED` | ‼ All four live on **`app list`**, and **`app get` returns FEWER fields — none of them.** For deploy state use `app list` (or `deployments list`). This inverts the usual list-vs-get assumption and is the trap for anyone reaching for `app get` to inspect one app. Deployment statuses: `BUILDING` → `DEPLOYING` → `HEALTHY`; retired ones go `SUPERSEDED`. Blue/green is real (colors alternate BLUE → GREEN → BLUE). ### Two different git addresses for the same repo | Address | Shape | Use | |---|---|---| | `gitProject.gitRemoteUrl` | `http://10.0.x.y:23000/vibe/.git` | INTERNAL — what the build executor clones. Unroutable from your machine; the IP differs per materialisation. | | `git-credentials.cloneUrlBase` + repo name | `https://git./vibe/.git` | EXTERNAL — what YOU push to. | Pushing to `gitRemoteUrl` cannot work. `nexus vibe git-credentials --json` returns `{cloneUrlBase, username, forgejoOrg, gitHostName, pushToken}`. The `pushToken` is a LIVE SECRET: never echo it, and mask any `https://user:tok@` in captured output (`sed -E 's#https://[^@]*@#https://***@#g'`). 404 = the org has no dedicated git host; 409 = the host is still provisioning. ### The repo is SEEDED — a virgin first push is REJECTED Shortly after `provision-repo` the tenant commits `Initial commit` (author `vibe-platform`) containing `README.md`. A locally-init'd repo's first push therefore fails with `! [rejected] HEAD -> main (fetch first)`. **Clone the repo, or `git fetch origin && git rebase origin/main`, before the first push.** ## The lifecycle ### 0. Preconditions (once per org) ```bash nexus vibe cluster status --profile

# need Status HEALTHY + Git host HEALTHY nexus vibe git-project list --profile

--json | jq -r '.gitProjects[].name' ``` That name list is the **collision pre-check** (see the 409 branch). If your intended app name is already a project name, pick another NOW — it can never be freed. ### 1. Create the app (no repo yet) ```bash nexus vibe app create --description "" --profile

--json ``` `` must be a DNS label (lowercase letter first, then lowercase/digits/hyphens, ≤63) because it backs the subdomain. `publicUrl` and `deployBranch: main` are stamped server-side. Default visibility is **PRIVATE**. ### 2. Provision the repo, then PROVE the wiring ```bash nexus vibe app provision-repo --profile

--json # project lands PENDING nexus vibe app list --profile

--json \ | jq -r '.apps[]|select(.name=="")|.deployability' # want DEPLOYABLE ``` Measured: PENDING → READY in under 10s; the seed commit lands ~14s after provision. ‼ `--git-url` is settable **at provision time only** — no route changes it later, and no route deletes the project. Omit it to use the tenant's own git host (the normal path); pass it only when the build executor must clone an external remote. Getting this wrong is unrecoverable. ### 3. Wire the local repo to the EXTERNAL address, rebase onto the seed ```bash CREDS=$(nexus vibe git-credentials --profile

--json) USER=$(echo "$CREDS" | jq -r '.username'); TOK=$(echo "$CREDS" | jq -r '.pushToken') BASE=$(echo "$CREDS" | jq -r '.cloneUrlBase') git remote add origin "https://$USER:$TOK@${BASE#https://}.git" git fetch origin && git rebase origin/main ``` ### 4. Push — the push IS the deploy ``` git pull --rebase # ALWAYS first on a shared repo # rejected/rebased? a FOREIGN COMMIT exists → grep its CONTENT at HEAD before any claim about it: # git log --oneline -3 ; git show HEAD: | grep -c "" # never conclude clobbered/survived from file-copy reasoning (R#50(5)) git status --short # eyeball strays FIRST — shared scratchpads collect other processes' files && git add && git commit -m "" # never -A in a shared scratchpad git push # auto-build fires skills/shared/scripts/deploy_watch.sh [timeout-s] [poll-s] [profile] [appId] ``` Pass `appId` so the audit poll is scoped to YOUR app — an org-wide poll can be satisfied by a different app's deploy. Measured push→HEALTHY on a tiny zero-dep image: | Event | Δ from push | |---|---| | `DEPLOYMENT_TRIGGERED` (`triggerSource: GIT_PUSH`) | ~2s | | `BUILD_JOB_SUCCEEDED` (build itself 14–17s) | ~54s | | `DEPLOYMENT_HEALTHY` | **~66–90s** | ### 5. Verify SERVED — two independent signals ```bash # signal A — the platform's own swap field nexus vibe app list --profile

--json \ | jq -r '.apps[]|select(.name=="")|"\(.servingDeployment.triggerSha) \(.edgeReachability)"' # want: ROUTED # signal B — the served content marker, cache-busted, WITH the status code curl -s -o /tmp/b -w '%{http_code}\n' -m 20 "https://./?cb=$(date +%s)"; grep -c "" /tmp/b ``` Take BOTH. The skew runs in **both** directions (measured): once `latestDeployment` was DEPLOYING while `servingDeployment` still named the OLD sha (status led), and once the served content already carried the NEW env value while `servingDeployment` still named the old sha (content led). Neither signal alone is authoritative. Record the sha as LAST-KNOWN-GOOD once served. ### 5b. Smoke the ROUTE you changed, authenticated, against the real store Both signals above prove the right BYTES are being served. Neither proves the app WORKS. A data route can return 500 on every request while the shell renders perfectly, the sha matches and the marker greps clean — so a green §5 is not a licence for a "fixed / live / please reload" claim. Measured, on one dawn outage: two consecutive fixes were announced as live (*"Both screens should load again — please reload"*, then *"The fix is live… I believe they work now, and this time I have evidence rather than a hypothesis"*), and both were wrong. The owner sent five messages and three screenshots before the third fix found the real cause. The gate that passed in between drove the **offline twin** — `WAREHOUSE=local` — so it could not have failed. The same blindness had left one screen broken for DAYS before anyone noticed. So, before any completion word on a deploy that touched a schema, a query, a projection or a data adapter: ```bash # authenticate as the owner-supplied test user, then drive the ROUTE THAT CHANGED curl -s -c /tmp/j -X POST "https://./api/auth/login" \ -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"email":"","password":""}' -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' curl -s -b /tmp/j -o /tmp/r -w '%{http_code}\n' -m 20 "https://./" head -c 300 /tmp/r # a 200 carrying an error envelope is still a failure — READ the body ``` Rules that make it real: - **Drive the SERVED app, never the local twin or a fixture server.** If the harness can pass with the datastore unreachable, it is not this check. - **Drive the route that CHANGED**, plus any route that reads the same store. A shell that renders is not a screen that loads. - **Read the body, not just the status.** A 200 with `{"error":…}` is the failure this check exists to catch. - **A test credential is a build input.** If the owner has supplied one, it belongs in the deploy gate — asking them to reload and report back is making the owner your QA (R#20). - If no credential exists and the route needs auth, say so and ask for one. An unsmoked data route ships as `⚠ user-resolved` in the R#27 table, never as verified. ## ‼ Visibility gates the marker check — the failure that masquerades as swap lag **Apps are created PRIVATE, and a private app returns `401` to any plain HTTP client** even with a HEALTHY deployment and correct content: ``` {"error":"unauthorized","reason":"App '' is private. Present a valid session cookie or the app token."} ``` A content-marker grep therefore returns 0 hits **forever** on a flawless deploy. No timeout ever fixes this — the cause is authentication, not lag. So before treating a marker miss as a deploy problem, **read the HTTP status**: | Status | Meaning | Action | |---|---|---| | `401` / `403` | ACCESS, not deploy: the app is private, or the token is absent/stale | verify via `servingDeployment.triggerSha` + `edgeReachability`, or fetch with the app's edge token. Marker-by-curl only works on a PUBLIC app | | `200`, no marker | genuine swap lag, or wrong content shipped | keep polling; a 0-hit right after HEALTHY is NOT wrong-code evidence | | `503` | transient serving gap (also seen right after a visibility flip) | keep polling | | `404` | edge/routing layer, not your app | platform issue — escalate; don't debug the container | Visibility mechanics (measured) — `nexus vibe app visibility public|private --profile

`: - `private` → `public`: `edgeReachability` flips to `ROUTED` at once; the URL goes 401 → 200 + marker in ~11s. - `public` → `private`: a transient **503 window** (~10-20s) before settling to 401. --json ``` ‼ **There is no `--builder` flag.** `deploy` accepts only `--sha` and `--confirm-overage`; the request body is `{triggerSha, confirmOverage}`. Any "switch the builder to escape the immutable tag" advice is wrong — delete it on sight. Re-deploying an **already-built sha** is accepted (verified): it gets a new `versionNumber`, rebuilds, swaps, and the prior deployment goes `SUPERSEDED`; `triggerSource: CLI`, measured trigger→HEALTHY ~66s. The changing axis is the deployment version, not the image tag. Track the last-known-good sha at all times. Usage soft limit: over cap the deploy ASKS rather than refuses — non-interactively it exits non-zero and prints the exact `--confirm-overage` re-run. `--confirm-overage` does NOT bypass an admin suspension (still 403). ## Env vars ```bash nexus vibe env set NAME=VALUE [--scope ALL|PROD|STAGING] --profile

--json nexus vibe env list --profile

--json nexus vibe env rm --profile

--json ``` - `NAME` must be SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE; the value is everything after the first `=` (may contain `=`, may be empty). Upsert per (scope, NAME). - The **full app UUID** is required — a short id returns `400 Validation error: appId: Invalid UUID` (a clean validation error, not a 500). Resolve via `vibe app list`. - ‼ **New env vars are NOT seen by the running process** — force a redeploy (empty commit) and re-verify by BEHAVIOUR, not deploy status. - ‼ Values are stored and returned in **PLAINTEXT** by `env set`/`env list` to any org API key. They are config, not secrets-grade storage. And nothing in the repo, ever. ## Platform mechanics (measured) - The build job records `builder` as an **OUTPUT**, not an input you can set. A `Dockerfile` with `EXPOSE 3000` was honoured (`builder: DOCKERFILE`, `detectedPort: 3000`). Still bind `PORT` plus 3000 and 8080 simultaneously and keep the server booting without any successful external call: a defensive server costs nothing, and a boot crash converts a delivery failure into a crash-loop mystery ("allocation unhealthy" rollback storms are this). - Image tags are `-` and IMMUTABLE; the deployment `versionNumber` distinguishes re-deploys of the same sha. Two builds in the same second can collide at the registry — serialize. [tag format verified; registry collision retained, unverified this cycle] - The audit feed emits `DEPLOYMENT_TRIGGERED`, `BUILD_JOB_SUCCEEDED`, `DEPLOYMENT_BUILD_SUCCEEDED`, `DEPLOYMENT_HEALTHY`, `DEPLOYMENT_SUPERSEDED`. ‼ Only the first appears in `audit list --help`'s own `--type` enum, so filtering by terminal types is undocumented — poll unfiltered with `--app ` and match the event name. The FAILURE event names are **UNVERIFIED** (no failure was induced this cycle): never key a script solely on a guessed `DEPLOYMENT_FAILED`. - **Nothing can be deleted.** There is no delete, rename, or attach-existing route for apps or git projects; the only DELETE in the whole vibe surface is `env/`. Every app and project you create is permanent — name deliberately, and prefer reusing a scratch app over minting new ones. - Keep the repo SMALL: no data files (warehouse-first, archetypes.md), no secrets (env vars). - A swap KILLS in-memory async work and un-synced state — queued backfills and in-flight jobs die with the old container. Space bulk work away from swap windows, or write through per item so nothing lives only in memory. [retained, measured 2026-07] - Watches run in BACKGROUND `until` loops (R#29) — never chained into one long foreground compound (precheck+commit+push+watch): a foreground timeout kills the chain mid-flight and hides which step failed. - Per-app read APIs (`app get`, `deployments list/get`) can 500 for apps with pathological history while push/auto-build/audit still work → `nexus vibe audit list` is the fallback state tracker. [retained; all reads succeeded on a fresh app this cycle] ## The pre-build deploy gate (run at P2, on the EMPTY scaffold) Retires every deploy risk before a line of app code exists — roughly 3 minutes. Do this INSTEAD of discovering the deploy path late, which is where whole sessions go. ```bash P=; SLUG=; set -e nexus vibe cluster status --profile $P # G1 cluster + git host HEALTHY nexus vibe git-project list --profile $P --json | jq -r '.gitProjects[].name' | grep -qx "$SLUG" \ && { echo "ABORT: project name '$SLUG' is taken org-wide and can never be freed — pick another"; exit 1; } APP=$(nexus vibe app create "$SLUG" --profile $P --json | jq -r .id) # G2 nexus vibe app provision-repo "$APP" --profile $P --json # G3 until [ "$(nexus vibe app list --profile $P --json \ | jq -r --arg s "$SLUG" '.apps[]|select(.name==$s)|.deployability')" = DEPLOYABLE ]; do sleep 5; done git fetch origin && git rebase origin/main && git push origin HEAD:main # G4 smallest app + a marker until [ "$(nexus vibe app list --profile $P --json \ | jq -r --arg s "$SLUG" '.apps[]|select(.name==$s)|.servingDeployment.triggerSha')" \ = "$(git rev-parse HEAD)" ]; do sleep 10; done nexus vibe app visibility "$APP" public --profile $P # G5 decide + APPLY visibility until curl -s -m 20 "https://$SLUG./?cb=$(date +%s)" | grep -q ""; do sleep 10; done nexus vibe env set "$APP" SMOKE_PROBE=v1 --profile $P --json # G6 env round-trip git commit --allow-empty -m "redeploy: apply SMOKE_PROBE" && git push origin HEAD:main git rev-parse HEAD > docs/.last-known-good-sha # G7 ``` Passing G1–G7 proves: cluster healthy, name safe, repo wired, push→build→deploy works, the URL is reachable **as the intended audience**, env+redeploy works, and rollback has an anchor. ## Reporting the deploy The script's terminal token is the machine verdict: `DEPLOY_WATCH: SERVED | MARKER_MISS | ACCESS_BLOCKED | FAILED_EVENT | EVENT_TIMEOUT`. Report the served state in those terms — "marker confirmed at ``", "HEALTHY, marker pending — still polling", or "HEALTHY but the app is PRIVATE so the URL 401s — verified via `servingDeployment` instead". Never an implicit done, never "live" on a readiness event alone (R#20, R#27). A push with no watch driven after it is an under-driven loop, and the re-push gets hook-flagged. ## Diagnostics that earn their keep - Read the 409 message LITERALLY. `provision-repo`'s conflict names the real guard (a taken project NAME), while its own `--help` text calls it "app already has a git project" — believing the help sends you hunting the wrong thing for an hour. - Pushes failing oddly → SIZE-BISECT with a tiny probe commit first (isolates transport caps in one step). - "Everything up-to-date" while the remote ref never moved (`git ls-remote` disagrees with your push output) = a SPLIT-BRAIN ref — treat the repo as poisoned, escalate; re-pushing the same sha does nothing (a swallowed push needs a FRESH sha: amend). - A platform fix is verified with the EXACT previously-failing input class (not a token retry) — then every doc that recorded the old limit gets a dated correction (R#35 capability-change sweep). - Boot crash on "missing files" → the files may never have SHIPPED (delivery failure) — verify the artifact landed at HEAD/remote before adopting a framework-specific theory.

# DESIGN PRINCIPLES — master index

The reference library for the UI/UX review system, synthesized from six canons — About Face (AF), Don't Make Me Think (KR), Laws of UX (LU), Refactoring UI (RU), Designing Interfaces (DI), Universal Principles of Design (UP) — deduplicated by MERGING (all tells + all citations kept), never by dropping. Every principle meets PRINCIPLE-FORMAT: Rule · Grounding (verbatim quote + page + the book's mechanism) · Objective test · ✗ WRONG / ✓ RIGHT · Crop (see `CROPS.md`).

## The 4 pillars — every element is judged by all four
1. **Beautiful** — crafted, not plain. Beauty is load-bearing: it measurably changes perceived AND actual usability and signals competence (CRAFT-1/2). → `aesthetic-usability-and-craft.md`
2. **Clear about what it IS** — identity legible at a glance: element type, current state, and interactivity self-evident (AFFORD-2/3/4, NAV-1). → `action-model-and-affordances.md`, `navigation-and-orientation.md`
3. **Understandable about what it ACHIEVES** — purpose/effect obvious before use, consequences previewed, results traceable (AFFORD-7/9, DATA-7, ERR-5). → `action-model-and-affordances.md`, `data-and-money-legibility.md`, `errors-reversibility-undo.md`
4. **Consistent with the rest of the app** — obeys the product's own small rule-set everywhere; new work lands native while staying crafted (XCON-1…9). → `cross-surface-consistency.md`

## Deterministic vs judged (the split stays intact)
Measured tells stay measured — scriptable as-is: contrast ratios (≥4.5:1 / 3:1 large; ≥70% reading), target floors (≥44px both axes) and gaps (≥8px; 16px opposite-intent), scale membership + near-duplicate detection (≥25% steps; 0 near-dupes), measure 45–75ch, line-height bands, grayscale/colorblind simulations, one-solid-primary counts, label/landing token overlap, tab-row wrap, undo-granularity (N objects/1 step), latency-tier matching, overlay bounding-box intersection (DLG-7), `elementFromPoint`/pseudo-state screenshot diffs. Craft stays judged — balance, personality coherence, propositional density, calm-vs-aggressive, designed-vs-assembled — but every judgment cites a principle ID and a concrete tell (METH-1), runs cold before driving (METH-9), discounts its own delight (METH-2), and checks both poles of each axis (METH-10).

# Action Model & Affordances

What looks interactive, what each control promises, how actions are ranked and reached. Covers view-vs-edit, context menus, primary/secondary, honest affordances. Pillars: 2, 3, 4.

---

### AFFORD-1 — Mental-model alignment: match what users learned everywhere else
**Rule.** Users transfer expectations from every other product onto yours; deviate from convention only with a stated reason, stage large changes with opt-in/preview/revert, and keep even novel designs recognizable as their category.
**Grounding.**
- *Laws of UX* (Jakob's Law): "Users spend most of their time on other sites, and they prefer your site to work the same way as all the other sites they already know." (p.1) Mechanism: familiarity lets people apply an existing mental model — "what we think we know about a system" (p.3) — so zero effort goes to re-learning structure. Paired evidence: Snapchat's untested 2018 redesign "caused ad views and revenue to drop and led to the app's user count dramatically shrinking" (p.4), while YouTube's 2017 redesign of similar magnitude let users "preview the new design, gain some familiarity, submit feedback, and even revert to the old version" (p.5) — same change size, no backlash, because the transition was staged.
- *Universal Principles* (Mental Model): "People understand and interact with systems and environments based on mental representations developed from experience." (p.154) Mechanism: the ABS-brakes case — despite measurable benefits in controlled tests, "antilock brakes have not reduced the frequency or cost of accidents in real-world driving situations" (p.155) because drivers kept the old pump-the-brakes reflex. (MAYA): "The most advanced form of an object or environment that is still recognizable as something familiar will have the best prospects for commercial success." (p.162) — novelty wins only inside a recognizable category envelope for non-expert audiences.
- *Don't Make Me Think*: "Innovate when you know you have a better idea, but take advantage of conventions when you don't." (p.51) — a replacement must be self-evident with no learning curve, or add value worth the curve (p.47, 51). Search specifically must look like search: "a box, a button, and either the word 'Search' or the universally recognized magnifying glass icon. Don't make it hard for them—stick to the formula." (p.102) — no clever relabeling, no premature scope options.
- *About Face*: "Obey standards unless there is a truly superior alternative." (p.430) and "Consistency doesn't imply rigidity." (p.431) — diverge in the spirit, not the letter, of the established pattern.
**Objective test.** For any new/changed pattern: (a) does a platform convention or top-5-by-traffic competitor already use this pattern in this location — yes/no; (b) if no, a written rationale exists (not "we like it"); (c) a structural redesign of an existing product ships with an opt-in/preview/revert path for ≥1 release cycle. Any (a)+(b) double-no, or (c)-no on a structural change, fails. Pre-ship prediction test for model-violating behaviors: ask users to predict what the control will do BEFORE using it — most users predicting the OLD behavior = revert or add explicit onboarding/signifiers (UP p.155).
**✗ WRONG.** Settings search moved to a floating bottom-right icon with no rationale, shipped to 100% in one release; swipe-left silently remapped from delete to archive — trained users silently archive mail they meant to delete.
**✓ RIGHT.** Search stays in the top bar; the variant ships as an opt-in beta first; the remap either keeps the trained gesture or signposts the new mapping with a distinct color/icon during the gesture itself.
**Crop.** LU-01, UP-13, UP-24.
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — ≥2 double-no pattern mismatches (no convention/competitor match, no rationale) AND a structural redesign shipped to 100% with no opt-in/preview/revert *(source: Laws of UX — Jakob's Law p.1,4 Snapchat case; About Face p.430)*.
- **2** — exactly 1 double-no pattern with no rationale; redesigns, if any, still shipped with no staged path *(DMMT p.51)*.
- **4** — no double-no patterns remain, but a structural redesign (if present) ships with no staged disclosure at all *(LU p.4-5 contrast case)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** every new/changed pattern either matches a platform convention/top-5 competitor in that location, or carries a written specific rationale *(DMMT p.51; About Face p.430)*.
- **6** — + any structural redesign discloses the departure somewhere (release note, settings), even if only away from point of use *(LU p.5 YouTube case, partial)*.
- **7** — + structural redesigns ship with an opt-in/preview/revert path for ≥1 release cycle *(LU p.4-5, YouTube vs Snapchat)*.
- **8** — + trained-gesture/behavior remaps are signposted during the gesture itself (distinct color/icon/label) rather than only in a settings note *(UP — Mental Model p.155 mechanism)*.
- **9** — + core controls (search/cart/nav/home) render in fully canonical, recognizable form *(DMMT p.102)*.
- **10** — + a pre-ship prediction test on any model-violating behavior shows users correctly predicting the new behavior before use *(UP — ABS-brakes p.155; DMMT p.47,51)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — LU (Snapchat retention evidence) and UP (Mental Model) both rate high; DMMT rates conventions med (justified exceptions allowed), UP MAYA med — majority high, disagreement noted.

### AFFORD-2 — Clickable must look clickable; the affordance is honest both ways
**Rule.** Every interactive element carries a visible non-hover signal of interactivity (shape, fill, color, elevation), AND every element that looks interactive must actually respond — a false affordance is a broken contract in either direction.
**Grounding.**
- *Don't Make Me Think*: "Since a large part of what people are doing on the Web is looking for the next thing to click, it's important to make it easy to tell what's clickable... things like shape (buttons, tabs, etc.), location (in a menu bar, for instance), and formatting (color and underlining)." (p.59) Mechanism: scanning users hunt for click cues, and hover cannot carry them — cursor-hover "doesn't work on touch screens because they don't have a cursor" (p.59 fn.2).
- *About Face*: "When we render a button on the screen, we are making a contract with the user that that button will change visually when she pushes it... it is astonishing how many applications offer bait-and-switch manual affordances." (p.314) Underlying definition via Norman: affordance is "the perceived and actual properties of the thing, primarily those fundamental properties that determine just how the thing could possibly be used" (p.312) — flattening trends "threaten ease of use by removing these virtual manual affordances in the service of visual simplification" (p.313).
- *Universal Principles* (Mimicry): "When a design mimics the surface aspects of a familiar object, the design implies (by its familiar appearance) the way it will function." (p.156) Mechanism: a mismatched mimic (a folder that doesn't contain, a checkbox that acts like a button) breaks the implication its own surface made (pp.156–157).
**Objective test.** Two-direction census: (a) list everything interactive — each carries ≥1 non-hover visual differentiator from inert text/decoration (border, fill, consistent link color+underline, button shape, elevation); `elementFromPoint` at the visual target's centre returns the actual interactive control, not a decorative sibling. (b) List everything that LOOKS interactive (button/chip/pill/card styling, mimicked object icons) — each responds to click/tap and its behavior matches what the surface implies (a folder icon opens/contains); styled-but-inert or surface-mismatched elements are findings. Zero tolerance in either direction.
**✗ WRONG.** "View report" as plain body text identical to the paragraph around it; header status pills with borders and fills that invite clicks but do nothing; a folder icon that fires a flat "share" action.
**✓ RIGHT.** Actions carry the app's one clickable grammar (fill/border/link treatment); inert status renders as flat text; the folder icon opens its contents and a differently-shaped icon carries "share" — nothing lies in either direction.
**Crop.** KR-02, AF-12.
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — ≥2 interactive elements with zero non-hover visual differentiator from inert text, AND ≥2 styled-but-inert (clickable-looking, does nothing) elements *(source: DMMT p.59; About Face p.314)*.
- **2** — exactly 1 miss in EITHER census (an interactive element with no differentiator, or a styled-but-inert element) *(DMMT p.59; About Face p.314)*.
- **4** — both censuses clean at the surface level, but ≥1 mimicry mismatch exists (icon whose surface implies a behavior it doesn't perform) *(UP — Mimicry p.156-157)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** every interactive element carries ≥1 non-hover visual differentiator (border/fill/color+underline/shape/elevation) from inert text/decoration, AND zero styled-but-inert elements exist *(DMMT p.59; About Face p.314)*.
- **6** — + `elementFromPoint` at each visual target's centre returns the actual interactive control for all but ≤1 element (1 decorative-sibling hit tolerated) *(About Face p.312, actual-vs-perceived properties)*.
- **7** — + `elementFromPoint` hit-target integrity holds for every element, zero decorative-sibling hits *(About Face p.312)*.
- **8** — + every mimicked-object icon's behavior matches what its surface implies (folder opens/contains, trash deletes) *(UP — Mimicry p.156-157)*.
- **9** — + the differentiator used is consistent product-wide (one clickable grammar: e.g. always fill+border, never ad hoc per screen) *(About Face p.313, flattening-trend critique)*.
- **10** — + touch-only surfaces pass every check above without relying on any hover-only cue (fully non-hover-dependent affordance system) *(DMMT p.59 fn.2)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — DMMT #6 high ("one of the book's three central mechanisms"), AF #21 high (base discoverability gate); UP Mimicry med.

### AFFORD-3 — Element classes must be visually distinct
**Rule.** Buttons, headings, links, inputs, disabled items, and inert text must not share near-identical styling; each class differs from every other on ≥1 dimension.
**Grounding.**
- *Don't Make Me Think*: "For affordances to work, they need to be noticeable... by definition, affordances are the last thing you should hide." (p.187) And on the flat-design tradeoff that produces the failure: "Flat design has a tendency to take along with it not just the potentially distracting decoration but also the useful information that the more textured elements were conveying." (p.188) Mechanism: the borders/bevels/fills ARE information — the book's "I'M A HEADING / I'M A BUTTON / I'M NOT" ambiguity demo (pp.186–188) shows heading, button, and plain text collapsing into one indistinguishable grey when the cues are stripped.
**Objective test.** Enumerate the control classes present on the screen (button / heading / link / input / disabled / plain text). For each pair of classes, verify ≥1 styling dimension (fill, border, shadow, color, weight, opacity, underline) differs; two classes visually identical at rest = stripped affordance, fail. Script proxy: compare computed style tuples {background, border, font-weight, text-decoration, opacity} across class exemplars — identical tuples across different classes = flag.
**✗ WRONG.** Buttons, section headings, and disabled controls all render as plain grey text after a flat redesign — no border, fill, or weight difference among three different classes.
**✓ RIGHT.** Buttons filled+rounded; headings bold+larger; disabled at reduced opacity — three classes, three distinct treatments, distinguishable at a glance.
**Crop.** KR-03.
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — ≥2 pairs of control classes render with identical computed-style tuples {background, border, font-weight, text-decoration, opacity} — the "I'M A HEADING / I'M A BUTTON / I'M NOT" collapse *(source: DMMT p.186-188)*.
- **3** — exactly 1 pair identical *(DMMT p.187-188)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** every pair of control classes present (button/heading/link/input/disabled/plain text) differs on ≥1 styling dimension *(DMMT p.187)*.
- **6** — every pair differs, but ≥1 pair only on a single dimension (thin margin of distinction) *(DMMT p.188)*.
- **8** — every class pair differs on ≥2 styling dimensions *(DMMT p.187-188)*.
- **9** — + disabled controls are distinguishable from active ones only on close inspection (subtle shade), not yet a glance-level delta *(DMMT p.188, information-carrying texture)*.
- **10** — + disabled controls are distinguishable from active ones at a glance in a grayscale screenshot (clear opacity/fill delta, no color dependency) *(DMMT p.188)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — DMMT #7 high ("directly gates whether clickability is even possible").

### AFFORD-4 — Every control has two duties: enable action AND show current state
**Rule.** A first-time viewer must read any control's CURRENT setting from its rendering alone — not just what clicking would do.
**Grounding.**
- *About Face*: state-switching controls "fail to fulfill the second duty of every control—to inform users of their current state." (p.596) Mechanism: a control that only advertises its click-result forces trial interaction to discover state — the book extends the duty to "switches, checkboxes, radio groups, and any indicator" (p.596), with the standard iOS/Android switch (distinct on/off renderings, Fig. 21-9, p.598) as the passing form.
**Objective test.** Fresh screenshot of the control at rest, never interacted with: a reviewer must state its current value/status from that single frame. Failure = any control whose state is only learnable by operating it. Run per control class (toggles, checkboxes, segmented controls, mode buttons) across the screen; every miss is a finding.
**✗ WRONG.** A "Notifications" bell button with no on/off distinction — you tap to find out whether notifications were enabled.
**✓ RIGHT.** A switch with unambiguous states (filled + thumb-right = on; grey + thumb-left = off), instantly legible without interaction.
**Crop.** AF-02.
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — ≥2 stateful controls whose current value is unreadable from a single at-rest screenshot (state only learnable by operating them) *(source: About Face p.596)*.
- **2** — exactly 1 such control *(About Face p.596)*.
- **4** — every control's state is readable at rest, but on ≥1 control the two states differ on only a subtle single channel (e.g. faint color shift, no position change) *(About Face p.598, Fig.21-9 contrast)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** from a single at-rest screenshot, a fresh reviewer states the current value of every stateful control (toggle, checkbox, segmented control, mode button) *(About Face p.596)*.
- **7** — + every control's states differ on ≥2 visual channels (e.g. fill color + thumb position, matching the standard iOS/Android switch) *(About Face p.598)*.
- **8** — + in a region with ≥3 sibling stateful controls, mixed states are individually readable only by comparing rows *(About Face p.596, "any indicator")*.
- **10** — + in a region with ≥3 sibling stateful controls, mixed states are individually readable without row-to-row comparison (or fewer than 3 siblings exist) *(About Face p.596)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — AF #25 high (universal control-legibility gate).

### AFFORD-5 — State-switching toggles are ambiguous; pliancy feedback is mandatory
**Rule.** A single control flipping between opposite meanings (play/pause-style) reads as either current-state or click-result — two reasonable, contradictory readings; avoid the idiom or pair it with an independent state confirmation. Every imperative control shows visible idle/hover/pressed/active changes.
**Grounding.**
- *About Face* (state-switching): "there are two very reasonable and contradictory interpretations of the icons on the button. The control can serve as either a state indicator or a state-switching selection control, but not both." (pp.595–596) Mechanism: the real-estate saving "comes at the cost of considerable user confusion" — a music player passes only because audibly-playing audio independently confirms state.
- *About Face* (pliancy): "Poorly designed applications and many websites contain buttons that don't animate when clicked or tapped. This is disconcerting for users, because it generates a mental question: 'Did that actually do something?'" (p.591) And the governing principle: "Rich visual feedback is the key to successful direct manipulation." (p.315) — pliancy (visible pressability) is part of the button's affordance contract.
**Objective test.** (a) Single-icon toggles: an INDEPENDENT, always-visible confirmation of current state exists elsewhere (audible playback, a "Paused/Playing" status label, an advancing progress bar) — the icon as the ONLY state signal, showing the action-to-take, fails. (b) Pliancy: verify ≥3 distinguishable visual states (idle, hover/focus, pressed/active) per imperative control; automated check: programmatically trigger `:hover` and `:active`/`:focus` pseudo-states and diff screenshots against idle — any control with zero pixel difference across states fails.
**✗ WRONG.** A muted video's lone triangle icon (paused, or silently playing with a stuck icon?); a `<div>`-button with identical CSS across idle/hover/active that gives no confirmation the click registered.
**✓ RIGHT.** Icon plus an always-visible "Paused/Playing" label or advancing progress bar; the button darkens ~10% on hover and visibly compresses (or ripples) on press, confirming before any network response.
**Crop.** AF-03.
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — any control with zero pixel delta across idle/hover/active states (no pliancy at all) *(source: About Face p.591)*.
- **2** — controls show only 2 distinguishable states (hover-only or active-only), no zero-delta controls *(About Face p.591)*.
- **4** — every imperative control shows ≥3 distinguishable states (idle/hover/pressed), but feedback is response-gated (renders only after the server responds) on some controls *(About Face p.591, p.315)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** every imperative control shows ≥3 distinguishable states (idle, hover/focus, pressed/active) via programmatic pseudo-state diffing *(About Face p.591, p.315)*.
- **6** — + a single-icon state-switching toggle, if present, is paired with an independent state signal, even if tiny/low-contrast/intermittent *(About Face p.595-596)*.
- **7** — + pressed/active feedback renders synchronously (CSS state, before any network response) on every control *(About Face p.315, "rich visual feedback")*.
- **8** — + any single-icon state-switching toggle is paired with an always-visible, clearly legible independent state signal (audible playback, "Paused/Playing" label, advancing progress bar) — or no such toggle idiom is used at all *(About Face p.595-596)*.
- **10** — + one consistent feedback grammar (same darken/compress/ripple family) holds across all imperative controls *(About Face p.315)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — AF #22 pliancy high ("did that do something?" is a universal failure mode); AF #24 state-switching med-high (conditional on the idiom being present) — majority high, noted.

### AFFORD-6 — Targets: sized, separated, placed where the flow ends
**Rule.** Exceed the ~44px floor on the HIT AREA; separate adjacent interactive elements (≥8px; opposite-intent pairs ≥16px or a distinct zone); place terminal actions adjacent to the last input, in the reachable band on mobile; pin global controls to screen edges.
**Grounding.**
- *Laws of UX* (Fitts's Law): "The time to acquire a target is a function of the distance to and size of the target." (p.15) Size: the published minimums (Apple 44×44pt, Material 48×48dp, WCAG 44×44 CSS px, Table 2-1, p.18) are floors — "these recommendations are minimums... Designers should aim to exceed these target touch sizes whenever possible" (p.18); undersized targets damage felt usability even at zero errors: "small touch targets add to the perception that an interface is less usable, even if the user is able to avoid errors" (p.18).
- Spacing: fingertips run 16–20mm (MIT Touch Lab, p.19), so Google's guidance is quoted verbatim: "touch targets should be separated by 8dp [density-independent pixels] of space or more to ensure balanced information density and usability." (p.19) — LinkedIn's cramped accept/deny pair is the book's failure case (p.21).
- Placement: submit buttons belong "in close proximity to the last form input... the distance the user must travel from the last form input to the submission button is minimal" (p.21); on mobile, "people prefer to view and touch the center of the smartphone screen, and this is where accuracy is the highest" (p.19). Edges: "There is no need to worry about overshooting the target... The edges of the screen act as natural walls for the cursor" (p.23) — reserve edges/corners for frequent global controls (p.24).
**Objective test.** Scripted: `getBoundingClientRect()` width AND height ≥44 CSS px for every `<button>`/`role="button"`/`<a>`/`input[type=checkbox]` hit area (either axis failing = fail, even with a small glyph — pad the hit area). Gap between bounding boxes of adjacent interactive elements ≥8px; a destructive/irreversible action opposite a benign one requires ≥16px gap OR a visually/positionally distinct grouping (different row, different color zone). Submit within one field-height of the last input with no unrelated content between; one-hand primary actions in the lower ⅔ of the mobile viewport, never the top corner opposite the holding hand; global/frequent desktop controls flush to an edge (computed margin = 0 on ≥1 side), not floating with margin all round.
**✗ WRONG.** Mobile checkout's Submit pinned in the top app bar, 600px from the last field; a 20×20px delete icon whose glyph IS the tap target; accept/deny circles 4px apart in identical styling; a global "new" action floating 40px from every edge.
**✓ RIGHT.** Submit directly below the last field and sticky at the viewport bottom; the icon inside a 44×44 invisible hit area; accept filled-primary and deny ghost-styled on the opposite side with ≥8dp between; the action in an edge-flush bar you can throw the cursor at.
**Crop.** LU-11, LU-12, LU-03.
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — any primary or frequent action's hit area is <44 CSS px on either axis, OR any adjacent interactive pair sits <8px apart *(source: Laws of UX — Fitts's Law, Table 2-1 p.18; Google 8dp spacing p.19)*.
- **2** — all hit areas meet ≥44px, and all adjacent gaps ≥8px, but a destructive/benign opposite pair sits at bare 8px in identical styling *(LU p.19,21, LinkedIn case)*.
- **4** — 1–2 non-primary/non-frequent sub-44px targets remain (none primary), general spacing clean *(LU p.18)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** every `<button>`/`role="button"`/`<a>`/checkbox hit area is ≥44×44 CSS px (padding counts, glyph alone doesn't), AND all adjacent interactive bounding boxes are ≥8px apart *(LU p.18-19)*.
- **6** — + destructive/irreversible-vs-benign opposite pairs get ≥16px gap OR a visually/positionally distinct grouping *(LU p.19,21)*.
- **7** — + terminal action (submit/primary CTA) sits on the same screen as the last input, though requiring scroll or with intervening content *(LU p.21)*.
- **8** — + terminal action sits within one field-height of the last input with no unrelated content between; on mobile, in the lower ⅔ of the viewport *(LU p.19,21)*.
- **9** — + desktop global/frequent controls are flush to a screen edge (computed margin 0 on ≥1 side), except the single most frequent action which floats *(LU p.23-24)*. Touch-only surface = this rung by default (LU scopes edges to pointer UIs).
- **10** — + every desktop global/frequent control, without exception, is edge-flush *(LU p.23-24)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — LU rates size and spacing high (felt-usability damage even at zero errors; opposite-intent mis-taps); placement med, edges low-med — the load-bearing majority is high, noted.

### AFFORD-7 — Mapping: position and behavior reveal effect
**Rule.** A control's placement/direction should make its effect inferable without labels — layout mirrors layout, direction mirrors direction, color carries learned meaning; one control driving many unrelated effects needs a visible mode indicator or a split.
**Grounding.**
- *Universal Principles*: "Good mapping is primarily a function of similarity of layout, behavior, or meaning. When the layout of stovetop controls corresponds to the layout of burners, this is similarity of layout; when turning a steering wheel left turns the car left, this is similarity of behavior; when an emergency shut-off button is colored red, this is similarity of meaning." (p.152) On overloading: "Avoid using a single control for multiple functions whenever possible; it is difficult to achieve good mappings for a one control-multiple effect relationship." (p.152) Mechanism: the book literally scores its stove-knob layouts (p.153) by spatial correspondence — poor (one row for a 2×2 grid), improved (knobs grouped with burners), good (knobs laid out like the burners).
**Objective test.** Place the control layout and the effect layout side by side: a straight line/rotation should map one onto the other without a 90°+ twist or an axis substitution. Unlabeled controls whose target cannot be guessed from position alone = fail. Any single control with >1 unrelated effect requires a visible mode indicator or gets split into per-effect controls.
**✗ WRONG.** Four knobs in a horizontal row controlling a 2×2 burner grid — which knob drives which burner is trial and error.
**✓ RIGHT.** Knobs arranged in the same 2×2 spatial layout as their burners — front-left knob under front-left burner.
**Crop.** UP-05.
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — no spatial relationship between control layout and effect layout (e.g. a row of knobs for a 2×2 burner grid) AND ≥2 unlabeled controls require trial and error *(source: UP — Mapping p.152-153)*.
- **2** — controls grouped near their effects but not in matching spatial arrangement (UP's "improved" middle case) *(UP p.153)*.
- **4** — spatial layout correspondence achieved (straight translation/rotation, no 90°+ twist, no axis substitution), but ≥1 overloaded control exists with no mode indicator *(UP p.152)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** placing the control layout beside the effect layout, a straight translation/rotation maps one onto the other with no 90°+ twist and no axis substitution *(UP p.152-153, "good" stove case)*.
- **7** — + every unlabeled control's target is inferable from position/direction alone, save ≤1 exception *(UP p.152)*.
- **8** — + every unlabeled control's target is inferable from position/direction alone with zero exceptions *(UP p.152)*.
- **9** — + any control driving >1 unrelated effect carries a visible mode indicator, though displaced from the control itself *(UP p.152)*.
