- **10** — + no single control drives >1 unrelated effect, or any that does carries its mode indicator directly on/at the control *(UP p.152, "avoid a single control for multiple functions")*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — UP Mapping high.

### AFFORD-8 — Links navigate, buttons act
**Rule.** A text link only navigates; a mutation/send/delete/purchase is only triggered by a button-styled control — and never weaponize the size/weight disparity to steer users away from their intended choice.
**Grounding.**
- *About Face*: "Use links for navigation and buttons for action." (p.593) Mechanism: "Because most users have learned that links are a navigational idiom, they will be confused and disoriented if clicking a link results in the execution of an action (such as the launching of a dialog)." (p.593) On the manipulative variant — a big default button beside a small hyperlink for the disfavored choice: "it has been used too often to trick users into not noticing the link... the tactic can be seen as manipulative, potentially reducing the user's trust in the site and the brand." (p.593)
**Objective test.** Programmatically enumerate every `<a>`/link-styled element in a flow and inspect its handler: any firing a POST/mutation/delete/send rather than GET-style navigation = fail. Enumerate every button-styled element: any purely changing route with no side effect = should be a link. Choice pairs where one option is a large filled button and the rival a low-contrast text link, with no consequence asymmetry justifying the disparity = dark-pattern flag.
**✗ WRONG.** "Keep my plan" as a big blue button, "Cancel anyway" as a faint text link beside it — the disparity engineered to discourage the user's actual intent.
**✓ RIGHT.** Both choices as equally-weighted buttons ("Keep my plan" / "Cancel my plan"); only true navigation ("Learn about plans") styled as a link.
**Crop.** none.
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — ≥2 link-styled elements fire a POST/mutation/delete/send, OR a large filled button sits beside a low-contrast text link for the user's likely intent (dark-pattern shape) *(source: About Face p.593)*.
- **2** — exactly 1 link-styled element fires a mutation, or a disparity exists but the disfavored option is still a clearly visible button *(About Face p.593)*.
- **4** — no link fires a mutation, but ≥1 button-styled element purely changes route with no side effect *(About Face p.593)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** zero link-styled elements fire a mutation (POST/delete/send), and every choice pair of comparable consequence gets comparable visual weight *(About Face p.593)*.
- **7** — + zero button-styled elements purely change route with no side effect *(About Face p.593)*.
- **8** — + a single link treatment and a single button grammar hold product-wide, even if occasionally mixed non-manipulatively *(About Face p.593)*.
- **10** — + one consistent link/button grammar holds with no exceptions anywhere in the product *(About Face p.593)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — AF #23 high (dark-pattern risk and user trust).

### AFFORD-9 — Label actions specifically and minimally
**Rule.** Beyond a handful of universal glyphs, icon-only actions fail; and where the pending operation is knowable, the label states it ("Undo Typing", "Add [person] to Contacts") — specific, yet MINIMAL: verbose multi-clause labels are their own noise.
**Grounding.**
- *Laws of UX*: "there is no icon standardization body that regulates what icons can be used where... the same icon [can] represent different actions" (p.49) — the heart/star glyphs alone span favorite/like/bookmark/rate/featured; "when an interface has been simplified to the point of abstraction, it's no longer clear what actions are available" (p.48). Label anything beyond home/search/back/close/menu (p.49).
- *Designing Interfaces* (Smart Menu Items): "Menu items that say exactly what they're going to do make the UI self-explanatory. The user doesn't need to stop and figure out what object will be affected. They're also less likely to accidentally do something that they didn't intend to do, such as deleting 'Chapter 8' instead of 'Footnote 3.'" (p.402) On undo specifically, dynamic labels are "absolutely critical to usability here. They explain exactly what's going to happen, which reduces the cognitive burden" (p.421) — users have no mental model of the undo stack.
- *Don't Make Me Think*: "Get rid of half the words on each page, then get rid of half of what's left." (p.77) — the minimality bound: extra label words are scanning noise.
**Objective test.** Icon-only controls outside the universal 5-set {home, search, back, close, menu}: visible text label or a discoverable tooltip required — an invisible `aria-label` alone fails sighted discovery. Context-dependent verbs (undo/delete/redo/apply/add): the label names the specific object/operation where knowable ("Undo Typing", not "Undo"); bulk operations name their scope. Word budget: a label restating context the surface already gives (multi-clause) = trim to verb+object.
**✗ WRONG.** Eight unlabeled toolbar glyphs (share, duplicate, archive, flag, pin, mute, export, more); a bare "Undo" over a 17-record bulk change; "Remove this item from this photograph" as a button inside the item's own popover.
**✓ RIGHT.** Labeled icons or a labeled "More" menu; "Undo Bulk Tag (17)"; "Remove".
**Crop.** LU-06, DI-15.
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — ≥3 icon-only controls beyond {home, search, back, close, menu} have no visible label/tooltip *(source: Laws of UX p.48-49)*.
- **2** — 1–2 unlabeled non-universal icons remain *(LU p.49)*.
- **4** — all icons beyond the universal 5-set are labeled, but bare generic verbs are used on destructive/bulk/ambiguous targets (e.g. bare "Undo" over a bulk change) *(Designing Interfaces p.421)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** every icon-only control beyond {home, search, back, close, menu} has a visible text label or a discoverable tooltip (invisible `aria-label` alone fails) *(LU p.48-49)*.
- **7** — + context-dependent verbs (undo/delete/redo/apply/add) name their operation, though scope/target is sometimes omitted where knowable *(DI p.402,421)*.
- **8** — + context-dependent verbs name their specific object/operation where knowable, and bulk operations name their scope ("Undo Bulk Tag (17)") *(DI p.402,421)*.
- **9** — + labels hold this specificity without restating context the surface already gives, save 1–2 multi-clause exceptions *(DMMT p.77)*.
- **10** — + no label restates context the surface already gives; every label is a minimal verb+object *(DMMT p.77, "get rid of half the words")*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — LU #10 high (unlabeled icons silently block completion), DMMT word-economy high; DI Smart Menu Items med — majority high, noted. (The DMMT-minimality vs DI-specificity pull is resolved by the verb+object bound, not a scoring conflict.)

### AFFORD-10 — Action pyramid: exactly one primary, subordinate everything else
**Rule.** Every screen/dialog/popover with multiple actions gets exactly ONE visually dominant primary (solid, high-contrast, at the end of eye travel); secondaries render as outline/lower-contrast, tertiaries as links. Style by pyramid position, not semantic drama — destructive ≠ big-red-bold unless it IS the surface's primary act (usually only its confirmation step); safe/reversible actions take the easy slot, irreversible ones deliberately less grabbable.
**Grounding.**
- *Refactoring UI*: "Every action on a page sits somewhere in a pyramid of importance. Most pages only have one true primary action, a couple of less important secondary actions, and a few seldom used tertiary actions." (p.60) On destructive styling: "Being destructive or high severity doesn't automatically mean a button should be big, red, and bold. If a destructive action isn't the primary action on the page, it might be better to give it a secondary or tertiary button treatment. Combine this with a confirmation step where the destructive action actually is the primary action, and apply the big, red, bold styling there." (p.62)
- *Designing Interfaces* (Prominent Done Button): "A well-understood, obvious last step gives your users a sense of closure. There's no doubt that the transaction will be done when that button is clicked" (p.396); place it "at the end of the eye's travel through the visual layout of the screen" (p.396). The graded airline comparison diagnoses the twin-button failure: Southwest "uses the same button design for two buttons, so the user's attention is split. It's no longer a single call to action" (p.399), vs. JetBlue's single high-contrast, generously-spaced CTA rated most effective.
**Objective test.** Count solid high-contrast fills per view: exactly 1 = pass; 0 (no clear CTA) or ≥2 of equal weight (split attention) = fail. The primary shares no accent+size tuple with any other control on the surface. Destructive actions off the primary path render secondary/tertiary; the solid red treatment appears only in the confirmation step where deletion IS primary. CTA position = end of the natural reading path, after the content that motivates it.
**✗ WRONG.** "Delete Listing" (solid red) + "Edit" (solid blue) + "Publish" (solid green) on one card, three equally bold buttons competing; "Apply Promo" and "Place Order" twin-orange side by side.
**✓ RIGHT.** Publish solid; Edit outlined; Delete a quiet link — whose confirm modal then makes "Delete" the solid red primary, exactly where it has become the primary act.
**Crop.** RU-02, DI-03, LU-08.
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — ≥2 solid high-contrast fills of equal weight per view/dialog (split attention, twin-button failure), e.g. solid red beside the solid primary *(source: Refactoring UI p.60,62; Designing Interfaces p.399)*.
- **2** — 0 solid high-contrast fills present anywhere (no clear CTA) *(RU p.60)*.
- **4** — exactly 1 solid primary exists, but destructive actions off the primary path are still toned down only to outline (equal-weight, not tertiary) *(RU p.62)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** exactly 1 solid high-contrast fill exists per view/dialog/popover *(RU p.60)*.
- **6** — + only 2 tiers exist (everything non-primary gets one same secondary treatment, no tertiary link tier) *(RU p.60)*.
- **7** — + three distinct tiers present (solid primary, outline secondary, link tertiary), primary shares its accent+size tuple with nothing else *(RU p.60)*.
- **8** — + destructive actions off the primary path render secondary/tertiary, and solid-red appears only in the confirmation step where deletion IS primary *(RU p.62)*.
- **9** — + the primary CTA sits at the end of the natural reading path, though it may compete mid-page with unread content *(DI p.396,399)*.
- **10** — + the primary CTA sits after the content that motivates it, at the true end of eye travel through the layout *(DI p.396, JetBlue case)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — RU #7 high (error rate + task clarity) and DI #19 high (completion confidence on every committing screen); unanimous.

### AFFORD-11 — No redundant actions; leverage ambient idioms
**Rule.** Two controls doing overlapping jobs signal an undecided design; when a lighter idiom already provides an action (click-out/Esc dismisses a modeless surface, a selection implies scope), an explicit duplicate button is clutter.
**Grounding.**
- *About Face* (leverage): "the concept of *leverage*, which is where a single interface element is used for several related purposes" (p.424) — leverage reduces surface area without reducing function, the chapter's definition of visual efficiency. And per modeless-surface convention: "Do not use terminating button commands for modeless dialogs." (p.629) — modeless surfaces close via their own close idiom, never a duplicate button.
- *Designing Interfaces*: duplicate same-weight actions split attention — "the user's attention is split. It's no longer a single call to action." (p.399)
- *Universal Principles*: "Excess is noise." (p.224) — every unnecessary element steals attention from relevant ones.
**Objective test.** Per surface, list actions and their effects: any two with indistinguishable outcomes = one goes. Any explicit button duplicating an ambient dismissal/commit idiom already active on that surface (a light-dismiss popover carrying a "Close" button; an instant-apply control paired with an "Apply" button) = remove. Candidate merge check per AF p.424: two single-purpose controls occupying adjacent semantic territory (identity + configuration of the SAME object), mergeable without first-time ambiguity = a leverage opportunity finding.
**✗ WRONG.** A light-dismiss popover carrying a full-width "Close" button beside its one real action; an instant-apply slider with a dead "Apply" button.
**✓ RIGHT.** The popover holds only the real action; click-out/Esc closes it, as everywhere else in the product.
**Crop.** RU-02 (pyramid framing).
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — ≥2 pairs of controls with indistinguishable outcomes on the same surface *(source: About Face p.424; Universal Principles — Signal-to-Noise p.224)*.
- **2** — exactly 1 duplicate-outcome pair *(UP p.224)*.
- **4** — no duplicate-outcome pairs, but ≥2 explicit buttons duplicate an ambient dismissal/commit idiom already active on the surface (e.g. a light-dismiss popover with a full "Close" button) *(About Face p.629)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** per surface, no two controls have indistinguishable outcomes *(UP p.224)*.
- **7** — + at most 1 explicit button duplicates an ambient idiom (click-out/Esc dismissal, instant-apply control) *(About Face p.629)*.
- **8** — + zero explicit buttons duplicate an ambient idiom already active on the surface *(About Face p.629)*.
- **9** — + at most 1 un-merged pair of single-purpose controls occupying adjacent semantic territory (identity + configuration of the same object) remains, where merging is possible without first-time ambiguity *(About Face p.424, leverage)*.
- **10** — + no such un-merged leverage opportunity remains anywhere on the surface *(About Face p.424)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** med (2) — genuine cross-book disagreement: About Face rates leverage low-med ("an efficiency bonus; absence isn't a defect unless crowding co-fails") while Universal Principles' "Excess is noise" (Signal-to-Noise) is high; the majority-of-scope resolution weights duplicates as real defects (C1/C2 = 7 pts) and un-taken leverage lighter (C3 = 3 pts), landing the principle at med.

### AFFORD-12 — View and edit are distinct modes with distinct surfaces [derived]
**Rule.** A reading surface shows the clean composed view (identity · description · key values) with zero mutation chrome at rest; editing affordances are earned by an explicit gesture (an Edit action, a context menu, inline click-to-edit per convention). Permanent edit controls on every viewable item are simultaneously excise (DENS-7) and a clarity failure (is this a document or a form?).
**Grounding.** Derived; each contributing book supplies one pole of the synthesis:
- *About Face* (frequent edits stay inline, rare chrome is excise): "Put primary interactions in the primary window." (p.625) — the inline-rename case (Omnigraffle, p.339) makes frequent edits one gesture in place, not a dialog; while excise doctrine bans permanent chrome serving rare paths: "*Excise tasks*... don't contribute directly to reaching the goal, but instead represent extra work that satisfies either the needs of our tools or those of outside agents." (p.272)
- *Designing Interfaces* (Moo.com, progressive disclosure into edit): "a customer doesn't see the customization options until they click into the editable parts of the card" (p.224) — editing controls materialize only on the explicit gesture into the editable region.
- *Don't Make Me Think* (the mixed state is a comprehension tax): a screen must be "self-evident. Obvious. Self-explanatory." (p.29) — an object permanently wearing mutation chrome makes the viewer ask "is this a document or a form?", exactly the thought-balloon question mark Krug bans.
- Convergence: all three arrive at the same shape — the rest state is a clean readable document, the edit state is entered deliberately and exited back to the clean view; neither permanent chrome nor undiscoverable editing survives any of the three doctrines.
**Objective test.** Rest render of an object: mutation controls visible = flag (unless editing IS the surface's primary task). An explicit, discoverable route into edit exists (double meaning: no permanent chrome, AND no undiscoverable editing — DENS-8): click-into-region, Edit action, or context menu per platform convention. Post-edit, the object returns to the clean composed view. Frequency check (AF p.625): a task performed more than ~once per session must not require a modal round-trip.
**✗ WRONG.** Every item on a review canvas permanently wearing remove/update/move buttons; or the inverse — a display page with no route into editing at all, forcing a support ticket to fix a typo.
**✓ RIGHT.** Items render as clean documents; the context menu (or an Edit affordance on selection, or click-into-the-editable-region) opens mutation; done, the document view returns.
**Crop.** AF-10, DI-09.
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — items permanently wear full edit chrome (remove/update/move on each) AND no route into editing exists anywhere (display-only, a typo needs a support ticket) *(source [derived]: About Face p.272 excise; DMMT p.29 self-evidence — convergence of both poles failing)*.
- **2** — one control class leaks onto rest state (e.g. a delete icon on every row), no discoverable edit route beyond that *(About Face p.272, excise)*.
- **4** — zero mutation controls at rest, but the route into edit is unconventional/hidden (undiscoverable without trial) *(DI p.224, progressive disclosure)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** every viewable object renders at rest with zero mutation controls visible (unless editing IS the surface's primary task), and every editable object has an explicit conventional route in (Edit action, click-into-region, or context menu) *(About Face p.272,625; DI p.224)*.
- **7** — + tasks performed more than ~once per session require a modal, but it is single-field/prefilled rather than multi-step *(About Face p.625, frequency)*.
- **8** — + tasks performed more than ~once per session are editable in ≤1 gesture in place, no modal round-trip *(About Face p.625)*.
- **9** — + after committing/cancelling an edit, the object returns to the clean composed view, though minor lingering chrome may briefly persist *(DMMT p.29)*.
- **10** — + the object returns cleanly to the composed view with zero lingering edit chrome, on every edit *(DMMT p.29; DI p.224)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — [derived] no direct expert line; adjacent scored entries: AF #28 primary-window high, AF #17 excise high, DMMT #1 self-evidence high; DI progressive disclosure med — majority high.

### AFFORD-13 — Contextual actions live in contextual menus [derived]
**Rule.** Object-scoped actions (move/edit/remove/add-here) belong in an on-demand, object-anchored menu (right-click / long-press / kebab) following the platform's learned convention — not splattered on the object at rest, not buried in a distant toolbar. The menu itself obeys the pyramid and grouping (destructive separated), and touch surfaces get a visible-at-rest equivalent.
**Grounding.** Derived; component quotes:
- *About Face* (the object is its own action anchor): leverage — "a single interface element is used for several related purposes" (p.424) — applied at the file-row example: the row's own icon communicates content AND is the target for right-click/long-press actions, one element, two jobs.
- *Don't Make Me Think* (the touch equivalence bound): "No cursor = no hover = no clue." (p.187) — every hover/right-click behavior needs a visible-at-rest touch replacement (always-visible icons or a persistent "⋮" menu), never silently dropped.
- *Designing Interfaces* (rank inside the menu): "The important point is that you want to make the most important actions visible." (p.432) — the frequent/important actions stay visible or first, the long tail subordinates into the menu's lower groups.
- Convergence: an object-anchored on-demand menu is the one idiom that satisfies all three at once — zero rest-state chrome (excise-free), actions discoverable exactly where the object is (leverage + trained convention per AFFORD-1's desktop right-click expectation), and a touch-visible fallback.
**Objective test.** Desktop data-object UIs: right-click on an object yields its action menu (or a kebab is visibly anchored to it); per-object actions rendered at rest = DENS-7/AFFORD-12 flag. The menu groups related actions and separates destructive ones (a divider or terminal position — never "Delete" adjacent to "Rename" in one undifferentiated dump). On touch viewports, audit every hover/right-click behavior: each has a persistent "⋮"/always-visible equivalent, zero hover-only actions.
**✗ WRONG.** No context-menu model anywhere in a desktop record-management app — actions only via inline buttons on every row; or a context menu that is one unordered dump ending in "Delete" directly beside "Rename".
**✓ RIGHT.** Right-click (or kebab) on any object opens a grouped menu — edit/move first, destructive isolated at the bottom behind a divider; touch gets the always-visible kebab.
**Crop.** none (convention synthesis).
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — no context-menu model anywhere in a desktop data-object UI (actions only via inline per-row buttons or a distant toolbar) AND hover/right-click-only actions are silently dropped on touch *(source [derived]: About Face p.424 leverage; DMMT p.187 "no cursor = no clue")*.
- **2** — the menu exists for some object classes but not their siblings *(About Face p.424)*.
- **4** — a menu exists for every object class, but it is one unordered dump (no grouping, no destructive separation) *(DI p.432)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** on a desktop data-object UI, right-click (or a visibly anchored kebab) on any object yields its action menu *(About Face p.424)*.
- **7** — + the menu groups related actions, but "Delete" sits directly adjacent to "Rename" with no separation *(DI p.432)*.
- **8** — + the menu groups related actions and isolates destructive ones behind a divider or terminal position *(DI p.432)*.
- **9** — + every hover/right-click behavior has a touch equivalent, but it is undiscoverable (bare long-press, no visible cue) *(DMMT p.187)*.
- **10** — + every hover/right-click behavior has a persistent, visible-at-rest touch equivalent ("⋮"/always-visible icons) *(DMMT p.187)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** med (2) — [derived] no direct expert line; adjacent scored entries: DMMT #27 hover-compensation med, DI #26 smart-menu med, AF #3 leverage low-med — majority med.

### AFFORD-14 — Recognition over recall
**Rule.** Let users pick from visible/searchable sets rather than remember values, IDs, or syntax; a free-text field over a bounded value set is a recall trap.
**Grounding.**
- *Universal Principles* (Recognition Over Recall): "People are better at recognizing things they have previously experienced than recalling those things from memory. It is easier to recognize things than recall them because recognition tasks provide memory cues that facilitate searching through memory." (p.200) The canonical case: command lines "required recall memory for hundreds of commands," while the GUI "presents commands in menus, allows users to browse the possible options, and select from them" (p.200).
- *Universal Principles* (Performance Load): "The advent of the graphical user interface allowed users to browse sets of commands in menus, rather than recalling them from memory. This reduction in cognitive load dramatically reduced the mental effort required to use computers." (p.178) Mechanism: "If the performance load is high, performance time and errors increase, and the probability of successfully accomplishing the goal decreases." (p.178)
**Objective test.** For every input field, ask: are the valid values a bounded, enumerable set known to the system? If yes and the field renders as free text (forcing exact recall/retype where typos silently fail) = fail; render as searchable list/dropdown/type-ahead. Cognitive-load count: values the user must hold in memory across steps of a task — target: the system remembers/surfaces them (prior addresses, prior selections) instead of the user.
**✗ WRONG.** "Assign to" as a free-text username box — the agent must recall a teammate's exact handle; typos silently fail to match.
**✓ RIGHT.** A type-ahead dropdown of valid teammates — recognize in the list, never recall from memory.
**Crop.** UP-20.
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — ≥2 free-text recall traps (fields with a bounded, system-known value set rendered as free text; typos silently fail) *(source: UP — Recognition Over Recall p.200)*.
- **2** — exactly 1 free-text recall trap *(UP p.200)*.
- **4** — all bounded-set fields render as recognition UIs, but at least one is a long unsearchable dropdown *(UP p.200)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** every input field whose valid values are a bounded, system-known set renders as a searchable dropdown/autocomplete/type-ahead *(UP p.200)*.
- **7** — + matching is exact-prefix-only or slow/incomplete rather than forgiving *(UP p.200)*.
- **8** — + matching is fuzzy/type-ahead (mid-string, forgiving) with a browsable/complete list *(UP p.200)*.
- **9** — + values needed across steps of a task are partly remembered/surfaced by the system, though some still require blind re-entry of data the system holds *(UP — Performance Load p.178)*.
- **10** — + values needed across steps of a task are fully remembered/surfaced by the system (prefill, prior addresses, prior selections) — no cross-step recall burden anywhere *(UP p.178,200)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — UP rates both Recognition Over Recall and Performance Load high.

### AFFORD-15 — Escape hatch: always a visible way out
**Rule.** Every flow/overlay/wizard step keeps a clearly labeled exit to a known-safe place (cancel/back/home) above the fold; Home/reset stays exactly one click away from anywhere, always visible.
**Grounding.**
- *Designing Interfaces* (Escape Hatch / wayfinding, Ch.3): "Breadcrumbs show each level of hierarchy leading to the current page, from the top of the application all the way down... like a Progress Indicator, Breadcrumbs help a user to pinpoint where they are. This is especially handy if they've jumped abruptly to somewhere deep in the tree." (p.194) Mechanism: a deep or deep-linked state must expose a clickable ancestor chain — a nav element that doesn't answer "where am I / where can I go" is pure weight.
- *Don't Make Me Think*: "Having a Home button in sight at all times offers reassurance that no matter how lost I may get, I can always start over, like pressing a Reset button." (p.101) Mechanism: the reset path is a standing safety guarantee, not a navigation feature — its value is the reassurance of its constant visibility.
**Objective test.** From the deepest reachable screen: clicks to a known-good home/reset state = exactly 1, via an always-visible control (logo-as-link or explicit Home item) — not scrolled off, not inside an overflow menu. Every multi-step or destructive flow shows a cancel/back control above the fold on every step. Screens at ≥3 levels of navigational depth (or reachable via search/deep-link) expose a wayfinding element resolving to a clickable ancestor chain; 0 such elements = fail (DI p.194–195).
**✗ WRONG.** A decorative non-clickable logo and no Home link — browser Back is the only escape; a wizard whose middle steps have no visible Cancel.
**✓ RIGHT.** The logo links Home on every page, always visible; every wizard step carries a visible Cancel; a deep settings page shows `Home / Settings / Notifications / Email` as clickable links.
**Crop.** DI-13.
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — no functional Home path (decorative logo, browser Back only) AND ≥2 flow steps have no visible cancel/back control *(source: DMMT p.101; Designing Interfaces p.194)*.
- **2** — a Home path exists but takes >1 click or the control is intermittently hidden, or exactly 1 flow step is missing its exit *(DMMT p.101)*.
- **4** — Home is exactly 1 click away via an always-visible control, and every flow step has a cancel/back control, but no wayfinding element exists at navigation depth ≥3 *(DI p.194-195)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** from the deepest reachable screen, a known-good home/reset state is exactly 1 click away via an always-visible control (logo-as-link or explicit Home), AND every multi-step or destructive flow shows a clearly labeled cancel/back control above the fold on every step *(DMMT p.101)*.
- **7** — + screens at ≥3 navigation levels (or reachable via search/deep-link) show a static ancestor-chain text path, but ancestors aren't clickable *(DI p.194)*.
- **8** — + screens at ≥3 navigation levels expose a wayfinding element resolving to a fully clickable ancestor chain (or no screen reaches that depth) *(DI p.194-195)*.
- **9** — + exit controls are occasionally scrolled off before a sticky header engages, or buried on some screens, but never fully hidden *(DMMT p.101)*.
- **10** — + exit controls never scroll off-screen and never live inside an overflow menu, anywhere in the product *(DMMT p.101)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — genuine cross-book disagreement: DMMT #13 high ("hard, binary, easily-verified safety net", universal) vs DI #1 med (breadcrumbs conditional on depth ≥3). Resolved: the depth-conditional criterion self-neutralizes on shallow surfaces (C3); the universal exit guarantee dominates the rule's scope → high, disagreement noted.

# Aesthetic Usability & Craft

Why "beautiful" is a functional requirement, and what craft concretely is. Pillar 1's home doc.

---

### CRAFT-1 — Beauty is load-bearing (aesthetic-usability effect)
**Rule.** Attractive interfaces are perceived — and in measured tests, experienced — as more usable than equally-functional plain ones; the verdict forms in ~50ms and rarely revises; visual polish is a usability line item and a trust signal, never deferrable "cosmetics".
**Grounding.**
- Laws of UX: "Users often perceive aesthetically pleasing design as design that's more usable" (p.79). The origin study — Kurosu & Kashimura (Hitachi, 1995), 26 ATM layouts, 252 raters — found "apparent usability is less correlated with inherent ease of use than with apparent beauty" (p.81), an r=0.59 beauty↔perceived-ease correlation (Fig. 7-2, p.82). On timing: "people form an opinion about a website within 50 milliseconds of seeing it, and that visual appeal is a primary determining factor... the opinion formed during this brief period — the visceral response — rarely changes as users spend more time on the site" (p.84). Mechanism: the visceral first impression sets a lasting usability prior that the interaction itself barely updates.
- Universal Principles: "More usable but less-aesthetic designs may suffer a lack of acceptance that renders issues of usability moot... These perceptions bias subsequent interactions and are resistant to change" (p.20). Mechanism: aesthetics buy tolerance — users forgive an attractive design the same defects that sink a plain one.
- Designing Interfaces (Ch.5 framing, argument-level): the "designed vs assembled" signal is the *repetition of a constrained visual system* (a small set of spacing increments, limited palette, consistent radii) across the whole surface — its absence reads as thrown-together and undermines trust even when the logic is correct.
**Objective test.** (1) Treat visual-consistency defects (mixed icon families, off-scale spacing, default-styled components) as usability findings with severity, not a "polish later" list; a review gating on function while deferring aesthetics indefinitely violates the effect's evidence. (2) Instrument: have users rate perceived ease-of-use and attractiveness on SEPARATE scales pre-task; strong correlation (r > ~0.5) despite measured-equal task-completion times = the effect is active in your data and craft must be weighted accordingly. (3) Spacing/sizing audit: sample ≥10 padding/margin values across a screen — clustering on a small repeated scale (4/8/16/24px) = designed; scattered ad-hoc values (11px, 17px, 9px) = "assembled", regardless of how good any single component looks.
**✗ WRONG.** "It technically works, ship it — visuals are non-blocking" on a settings screen with 5 button styles, 3 icon families, and ad-hoc spacing values.
**✓ RIGHT.** The screen held until spacing, type, and icon-family unify onto one scale — the gap logged as a usability defect on the review checklist, not a nice-to-have.
**Crop.** LU-07 (Figs. 7-1/7-2, pp.81–82 — ATM layouts + beauty/usability scatterplot), UP-17 (p.21 — Nokia covers + TiVo screens).
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — an "assembled" screen (5+ button styles, uneven spacing, mixed icon families) is shipped as "done" purely because it functions, polish explicitly deferred *(source: Laws of UX p.79,84 — aesthetic-usability effect, ✗ settings-screen case; Universal Principles p.20 — "cosmetic, ship it, polish later")*.
- **2** — visual inconsistency reduced but ≥2 mismatched button styles/icon families or scattered off-scale spacing values remain uncorrected *(Laws of UX p.79 "3" tier)*.
- **4** — spacing mostly on-scale but ≥2 one-off values remain; component styling mostly unified but one style/icon-family mismatch persists *(Refactoring UI p.20,28 — personality/scale framing; Laws of UX threshold-adjacent)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** padding/margins cluster on one small repeated scale (4/8/16/24px-style), one button style-system and one icon family throughout, and every visual-consistency defect is logged with a severity on the usability checklist rather than deferred *(Laws of UX p.79–84 "5–6"; Universal Principles p.20–21)*.
- **6** — + zero browser-default-styled components sit beside custom-styled ones *(Laws of UX p.84 "5–6"/"7–8" unified-system framing)*.
- **7** — + the visual system (spacing, type, color) is demonstrably unified across the WHOLE screen with no mismatched components *(Laws of UX p.84 "7–8"; Universal Principles p.21)*.
- **8** — + the review protocol carries perceived-ease-of-use and perceived-attractiveness as two SEPARATE pre-task rating fields *(Universal Principles p.20 "7–8" spot-check exercise)*.
- **9** — + a measured beauty↔perceived-ease correlation (r > ~0.5) is confirmed active in your own data despite equal completion times *(Laws of UX p.81–82 — Kurosu & Kashimura r=0.59 study)*.
- **10** — ✓ matches the ATM-study/TiVo standard: consistent, refined, independently high-rated on both scales, and this was explicitly weighted into design prioritization *(Laws of UX p.81–84; Universal Principles p.21 — TiVo comparison standard)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight:** medium (2) — LU and UP both weight medium (perception effect layered on other principles); DI weights its spacing-audit form high (trust-signal umbrella) — majority medium, DI dissent noted.

### CRAFT-2 — Beauty masks defects; the reviewer discounts their own delight
**Rule.** Because attractive designs test as more usable even when functionally identical, polish hides real defects from users AND evaluators; verdicts must gate on measured task outcomes, with aesthetic reactions logged separately.
**Grounding.**
- Laws of UX: Sonderegger & Sauer (2010) — two functionally-identical phone prototypes, one attractive, one deliberately plain; the attractive one's appearance "had a positive effect on performance, leading to reduced task completion times for the attractive model" (p.90). The warning: "perceived aesthetic quality has the potential to mask usability issues to an extent. This effect applies even when the device isn't actually easier to use, and it could be problematic when it comes to usability tests, where identifying issues is critical" (pp.90–91); keep listening to what users say secondary to watching what they do (p.91). Mechanism: the halo contaminates both self-report and evaluator judgment, so only recorded task metrics stay trustworthy.
- Universal Principles (Performance vs Preference): measure both axes separately, in context; "Do not rely on reports of what people say they have done, will do, or are planning to do in the future" (p.180). Mechanism: preference and performance are independent measurements — one is never a proxy for the other.
**Objective test.** Review protocol: task success/time/error recorded in fields INDEPENDENT of any "looks good" field, and the task metric is the gating one; a go/no-go decision citing only aesthetic praise (or only a preference survey, with no completion-time/error data) = invalid. When performance and preference diverge, surface the tradeoff explicitly rather than collapsing it. Reviewer discipline: probe the prettiest screens hardest.
**✗ WRONG.** "Participants loved the new visual design, ship it" — zero completion-time or error-rate data recorded or reviewed.
**✓ RIGHT.** Completion time and error count per task are the primary pass/fail metric; delight and preference are secondary logged data, collected during (not after) the task.
**Crop.** LU-17 (Fig. 7-6, p.90 — the two identical-function phone prototypes), UP p.181 (QWERTY vs Dvorak performance/preference diagram).
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — the go/no-go decision cites only aesthetic praise/preference, zero completion-time or error-rate data recorded *(source: Laws of UX p.90 — Sonderegger & Sauer warning; Universal Principles p.180 — Performance-vs-Preference "0")*.
- **2** — some task metrics exist somewhere but aren't treated as the gating criterion; a positive aesthetic reaction can override a measured problem in the final call *(Laws of UX p.90 "3" tier)*.
- **4** — both axes recorded but co-mingled in one field, or preference is measured only post-hoc rather than during the task *(Universal Principles p.180 "3" tier)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** task success/time/error is recorded in fields structurally independent of any "looks good" field, and task success is the stated gating metric for the go/no-go decision *(Laws of UX p.90–91 "5–6"; Universal Principles p.180 "5–6")*.
- **6** — + preference/delight data is timestamped/collected DURING the task, not only after *(Universal Principles p.180 — "during, not just after")*.
- **7** — + the review process structurally separates evaluator/moderator subjective impressions from measured outcomes (distinct sections/fields) *(Laws of UX p.90–91 "7–8")*.
- **8** — + the most-polished screens carry at least as many scripted task cases as the plainest — the halo is probed hardest where it's most likely to hide defects *(Laws of UX p.91 — "watch what users do"; [derived] from the masking mechanism)*.
- **9** — + where performance and preference diverge, both numbers appear side by side in the decision record with an explicit, disclosed tradeoff call *(Universal Principles p.181 — QWERTY/Dvorak "9–10")*.
- **10** — ✓ completion time and error count are the primary, SOLE gating metric across every reviewed screen/flow; aesthetic reactions are logged only as secondary, non-gating data, consistently applied *(Laws of UX p.90–91 "9–10")*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface (no review/test artifact exists to audit — per LU, do not penalize the screen itself).
**Weight:** medium (2) — LU-18 medium (process discipline, audit-dependent), UP Performance-vs-Preference medium; unanimous.

### CRAFT-3 — Craft = one committed personality, applied everywhere
**Rule.** Typeface voice, color temperature, border-radius convention, and copy register all telegraph a personality; pick one deliberately and apply it on every axis — mixed conventions read as unresolved decisions. Calm/harmonious/non-aggressive is itself a personality that then governs every element (HIER-10).
**Grounding.** Refactoring UI: "Every design has some sort of personality. A banking site might try to communicate secure and professional, while a trendy new startup might have a design that feels fun and playful... a lot of it is determined by a few solid, concrete factors" — typeface class, color psychology, radius, language (p.20). On radius: "Whatever you choose, it's important to stay consistent. Mixing square corners with rounded corners in the same interface almost always looks worse than sticking with one or the other" (p.25). On copy: "Words are everywhere in a user interface, and choosing the right ones is just as (if not more) important than choosing the right color or typeface" (p.26). Mechanism: each axis independently signals a personality; when they disagree, the user reads indecision, not style.
**Objective test.** Four-axis personality audit: (1) exactly one typeface convention (serif vs rounded-sans vs neutral-sans) throughout; (2) primary color matching the intended feel (blue=safe, gold=premium, pink=playful) rather than contradicting the stated brand goal; (3) ONE radius convention (sharp/small/large) on ALL cards/buttons/inputs; (4) one copy register (formal vs casual) across every screen, never swinging mid-flow. Any axis mixing conventions = fail.
**✗ WRONG.** A 16px-radius hero card, a 0px pricing table, a 4px modal in one product; "Please provide a phone number" (formal) on one screen, "Sweet, thanks Steve!" (casual) on the next.
**✓ RIGHT.** Every card, button, and input commits to one radius value; the register is chosen once and applied through onboarding, confirmations, and errors alike.
**Crop.** RU-32 (p.20 personality pair; pp.24–25 three-way radius comparison; pp.25–26 copy-tone pair).
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — ≥2 of the 4 axes (typeface/color/radius/copy-tone) contradict across the product — e.g. ≥3 distinct border-radius conventions mixed, or copy swings formal/casual screen-to-screen with no consistent choice *(source: Refactoring UI p.20,25–26 — personality/radius/copy framing; RU-35 "0")*.
- **2** — 2 of the 4 axes are internally consistent, 2 are not *(RU-35 "3")*.
- **4** — 3 of 4 axes consistent, the 4th still drifting (commonly copy tone, least visually obvious) *(RU-35 "5–6" threshold-adjacent)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** 3 of the 4 axes (typeface/color/radius/tone) are internally consistent across the product *(Refactoring UI p.20,24–26; RU-35 "5–6")*.
- **6** — + the still-drifting 4th axis is scoped to one named role rather than mixed arbitrarily (e.g. a second typeface reserved for display-only) *(Refactoring UI p.20 — personality-factors framing; [derived])*.
- **7** — all four axes are internally consistent across the product *(RU-35 "7–8")*.
- **8** — + the chosen direction plausibly matches the stated brand goal (blue=safe, gold=premium, pink=playful) *(Refactoring UI p.20; RU-35 "7–8")*.
- **9** — + copy register sampled across ≥3 screens including a confirmation and an error is uniform throughout *(Refactoring UI p.26; RU-35 "Measure")*.
- **10** — ✓ one radius value everywhere, one consistent register across onboarding/confirmation/error, color and typeface both deliberately chosen and consistently applied end to end *(Refactoring UI p.20,24–26; RU-35 "9–10")*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight:** medium (2) — RU-35 medium (whole-product coherence, load-bearing across screens, invisible on one); sole scoring source.

### CRAFT-4 — Systems produce polish; open-ended tuning produces drift
**Rule.** Pre-commit to constrained scales (type, spacing, shadows, radii, opacity, palette) and pick FROM them by elimination (guess middle, compare neighbors, converge); design structure in greyscale first so spacing/contrast/size carry the hierarchy before color arrives; typefaces/shadows/icons come after layout settles.
**Grounding.** Refactoring UI: "Having millions of colors and thousands of fonts to choose from might sound nice in theory, but in practice it's usually a paralyzing curse... When you're designing without constraints, decision-making is torture because there's always going to be more than one right choice" (p.28). The elimination procedure: "start by taking a guess at which one will look best... Then try the values on either side... Chances are, two of those options will seem like obviously bad choices" (pp.30–31). On deferring detail: "it's important that you don't get hung up making low-level decisions about things like typefaces, shadows, icons... By designing in grayscale, you're forced to use spacing, contrast, and size to do all of the heavy lifting" (pp.12–13). Mechanism: a scale converts an unbounded aesthetic judgment into a small forced choice, so every decision is fast AND automatically consistent with every other.
**Objective test.** Before finalizing any low-level value: (1) a defined scale exists for that property — if not, defining one (e.g. 12/16/24/32px icon sizes) is the gap to close first; (2) the final value sits ON the scale — fractional/arbitrary values on no defined scale are the open-ended-tuning tell; (3) the pick followed guess-middle → compare-neighbors → converge, not pixel-by-pixel iteration; (4) color/typeface/icon decisions postdate a settled greyscale structure — premature detail-work is the failure mode.
**✗ WRONG.** Visible iteration between three near-identical blues (#338188 / #2F7DB3 / #2D78AD) no scale contains; full color, shadows, and icons applied to a flow whose spacing hierarchy is still unresolved.
**✓ RIGHT.** Icon size picked from 12/16/24/32 by one neighbor comparison; the flow nailed in greyscale/sketch form before any color enters.
**Crop.** RU-33 (p.28 three-blues paralysis; pp.30–31 elimination sequence; pp.12–13 greyscale mockup).
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — a low-level value is picked via open-ended, unconstrained tuning with no defined scale, evidenced by near-indistinguishable final candidates (the three-blues case); OR full color/shadow/icon detail is applied before the underlying layout/spacing/hierarchy is settled *(source: Refactoring UI p.28,12–13; RU-36 "0")*.
- **2** — a scale exists for some properties but not the one in question, or detail-work and layout-work happen concurrently rather than sequentially *(RU-36 "3")*.
- **4** — ≤1 of the four scales {type, spacing, radius/shadow, color} is missing; most sampled values on-scale but 1–2 off *(RU-36 threshold-adjacent; [derived] granularity)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** a defined scale exists for the property being decided *(Refactoring UI p.28; RU-36 "5–6")*.
- **6** — + all four scales (type, spacing, radius/shadow, palette) exist, and sampled rendered values sit mostly on-scale (≤2 off among ≥10 sampled) *(Refactoring UI p.28; RU-36 "5–6")*.
- **7** — + the elimination method (guess middle, compare adjacent options, converge) is visibly used, evidenced in candidate history *(Refactoring UI p.30–31; RU-36 "7–8")*.
- **8** — + low-fidelity/greyscale-first sequencing is followed on every flow — layout/spacing/hierarchy settled before color/shadow/icon detail *(Refactoring UI p.12–13; RU-36 "7–8")*.
- **9** — + all ≥10 sampled rendered values sit on their scale, zero near-identical off-scale variants coexisting *(Refactoring UI p.28; [derived] from the three-blues test)*.
- **10** — ✓ matches the 12/16/24/32px icon-scale case picked via guess-and-compare, and a full flow resolved entirely in greyscale/sketch form before any color/icon/shadow decision *(Refactoring UI p.30–31,12–13; RU-36 "9–10")*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight:** low (1) — RU-36 low (process principle; output overlaps the scale-system principles, scored mainly on process artifacts); sole scoring source.

### CRAFT-5 — Small supercharged touches separate designed from assembled
**Rule.** Icon lists instead of bullets, real pull-quote treatment, brand-colored controls, an accent border along one edge of a card/nav-item/alert, and quietly decorated backgrounds (solid panel, gradient ≤~30° hue apart, low-contrast pattern, a corner geometric) — cheap, generic upgrades that inject intent without illustration skill.
**Grounding.** Refactoring UI: "You don't always have to add new elements to a design to add flare — there are a lot of ways to liven up a page by 'supercharging' what's already there" (p.220); "Just using one of your brand colors for the selected states instead of the browser defaults is often enough to take something from feeling boring to feeling polished" (p.222); "It doesn't take any graphic design talent to add a colored rectangle to your UI, and it can go a long way towards making something feel more 'designed'" (p.226); gradients: "use two hues that are no more than about 30° apart" (p.229); patterns: "Keep the contrast between the background and the pattern pretty low to ensure readability" (p.230). Mechanism: each default left unstyled reads as an un-made decision; replacing it with a branded variant is the lowest-cost signal of intent available.
**Objective test.** Marketing/feature lists rendering default browser bullets = challenge; browser-default control accents (default blue checkboxes/radios) in a branded product = flag; gradient stops >30° hue apart = clash risk, fail; background patterns exceeding low contrast behind readable text = fail.
**✗ WRONG.** Plain grey bullets on a security-feature list a padlock icon could own; default-blue checkboxes in a purple-brand product; a flat undecorated pricing card.
**✓ RIGHT.** Padlock icons as bullets; checkboxes recolored brand-purple; a teal accent stripe on the card's top edge, or a two-stop gradient ≤30° hue apart instead of the flat fill.
**Crop.** RU-30 (p.220 bullet/icon pairs; p.222 checkbox pair; pp.224–226 accent-border series; pp.228–230 backgrounds).
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — a generic pattern is left fully default with a near-zero-effort upgrade available and unused: plain bullets on a thematically-ownable list, unstyled browser-default checkbox/radio accents clashing with the brand palette, or a flat undecorated card with zero visual interest *(source: Refactoring UI p.220,222,226; RU-37 "0")*.
- **2** — one technique applied inconsistently (icons on some list items but not others) *(RU-37 "3")*.
- **4** — at least one supercharge technique correctly applied, but others available in the same view are left default *(RU-37 "5–6" threshold-adjacent)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** at least one supercharge technique is correctly applied — icon list, brand-colored inputs, accent border, or subtle background decoration *(Refactoring UI p.220–230; RU-37 "5–6")*.
- **6** — + every thematically-ownable list renders purposeful icon glyphs, and checkboxes/radios/selected states all carry a brand color *(Refactoring UI p.220,222; RU-37 "7–8" partial)*.
- **7** — + multiple techniques applied consistently and tastefully across the surface *(RU-37 "7–8")*.
- **8** — + every gradient's two stops stay ≤~30° hue apart, and any repeating pattern stays low-contrast under readable text *(Refactoring UI p.229–230; RU-37 "7–8")*.
- **9** — + restraint held throughout: each element carries at most one decorative technique, none stacking ≥3 *([derived] from RU-37's "executed with restraint" framing; Refactoring UI p.220–230)*.
- **10** — ✓ matches padlock-icon bullets, brand-purple checkboxes, a teal accent stripe or ≤30°-hue-apart gradient, executed with restraint — nothing over-decorated or clashing *(Refactoring UI p.220–230; RU-37 "9–10")*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight:** low (1) — RU-37 low (pure polish layer, leveraged only once foundations score well); sole scoring source.

### CRAFT-6 — Rich elements reward attention (propositional density)
**Rule.** Strong design packs multiple layered meanings into few visible elements (PD = deep/surface propositions > 1); an element with nothing to say beyond its literal shape is flat — density of intent, not density of stuff.
**Grounding.** Universal Principles: "High propositional density is a key factor in making designs engaging and memorable... Objects and environments with high PD (PD > 1) are perceived to be more interesting and engaging than objects and environments with low PD (PD < 1)" (p.190). Formula verbatim: "PD ≈ Pd / Ps where PD is propositional density, Pd is the number of deep propositions, Ps is the number of surface propositions"; the book scores the Obama 2008 logo itself: "PD ≈ 10 / 3 = 3.33" (p.191). Mechanism: layered meanings reward repeated attention, so dense elements stay interesting where literal ones exhaust in one glance.
**Objective test.** For a focal element (logo, hero mark, key icon): enumerate surface propositions (directly perceivable features) and articulable deep propositions (meanings each feature carries), compute PD = Pd/Ps; PD ≤ 1 on a supposedly-designed focal element = redesign candidate.
**✗ WRONG.** A circle-plus-initial logo: 2 surface propositions, 1 deep, PD 0.5 — says nothing beyond itself.
**✓ RIGHT.** The circle doubling as a progress ring, the letterform cut to read as an arrow — Pd exceeds Ps, PD > 1.
**Crop.** UP-14 (p.191 — the worked logo scoring).
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — the focal element has PD ≤ 0.5 — more surface marks than meanings, says nothing beyond its literal content *(source: Universal Principles p.190–191 — Propositional Density "0")*.
- **2** — PD ≈ 1 and no enumeration of deep propositions has been performed — functional but unremarkable *(Universal Principles "3" tier)*.
- **4** — surface propositions enumerated but deep meanings not fully articulated for all of them; PD borderline at 1 *([derived] granularity between the "3" and "5–6" bands)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** PD > 1 — at least one surface element carries ≥2 independently articulable meanings, matching the book's Apple-logo baseline (PD≈2) *(Universal Principles p.190–191 "5–6")*.
- **6** — + every counted deep proposition is independently articulable in one sentence, not a stretch *(Universal Principles p.191 "7–8" framing)*.
- **7** — + PD is noticeably > 1 across multiple elements of the focal design, not just one *(Universal Principles p.191 "7–8")*.
- **8** — + ≥2 focal/brand elements each score PD > 1 (breadth, not a single lucky mark) *(Universal Principles p.191 "7–8"; [derived] breadth extension)*.
- **9** — + each counted deep proposition was verified by a naive viewer not shown the author's list, not merely author-asserted *(Universal Principles p.191 — "Measure": verifiable by asking a naive viewer)*.
- **10** — ✓ PD sits in the range of the book's Obama-logo case (≈3.33) — many deep propositions compressed into few surface marks, naive-viewer-verified *(Universal Principles p.190–191 "9–10")*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface (no focal designed element — logo, hero mark, key icon — present).
**Weight:** medium (2) — UP Propositional Density medium; sole scoring source.

### CRAFT-7 — Restraint is not plainness (wabi-sabi vs wabi-slobby)
**Rule.** Calm, spare, naturally-ordered simplicity is a legitimate refined aesthetic — but it must show evidence of CARE; emptiness that could plausibly result from not finishing the work is the named failure, not restraint.
**Grounding.** Universal Principles: wabi-sabi must not be construed as "an unkempt or disorganized aesthetic, a common mistaken association often referred to as wabi-slobby" (p.256); "A defining characteristic of wabi-sabi is that an object or environment appears respected and cared for... The aesthetic is not disordered, but rather naturally ordered — that is, ordered in the way that nature is ordered" (p.256). Mechanism: the viewer distinguishes restraint from neglect by evidence of care — a discernible design decision behind every apparent simplicity.
**Objective test.** For any design defended as "minimal/restrained": (1) every element's placement traceable to a specific compositional decision (consistent negative space, deliberate palette, considered material choice); (2) the could-this-just-be-unfinished test — if the same look could plausibly result from simply not finishing the work, it is wabi-slobby, fail.
**✗ WRONG.** Unstyled whitespace gaps and inconsistent spacing defended in review as "restrained, wabi-sabi" — the gaps are unfinished layout work, not composition.
**✓ RIGHT.** Deliberate, consistent negative space and a muted natural palette, visibly composed — restraint that is evidently cared for.
**Crop.** UP p.257 (Wabi Sabi House — asymmetric, unfinished materials, deliberately composed).
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — large unstyled/inconsistent whitespace or minimalism is defended as "restrained" but traceable to unfinished work with no discernible design decision behind it — wabi-slobby *(source: Universal Principles p.256 — Wabi-Sabi "0")*.
- **2** — some deliberate restraint is evident but inconsistently applied — a few elements clearly unfinished rather than intentionally spare *(Universal Principles p.256 "3")*.
- **4** — most placements traceable but ≥1 area indistinguishable from unfinished work; palette mostly defined with stray default values *([derived] granularity between "3" and "5–6")*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** the apparent simplicity is traceable to specific, statable compositional decisions — every element's placement has a rationale, passing the "could this just be unfinished?" test in the negative *(Universal Principles p.256–257 "5–6")*.
- **6** — + whitespace gaps repeat a consistent measure across the surface *(Universal Principles p.256; [derived] negative-space consistency check)*.
- **7** — + colors are drawn from a defined muted/natural palette, no stray default values *(Universal Principles p.256)*.
- **8** — + the restraint is consistent across the WHOLE surface, not just isolated areas *(Universal Principles p.256 "7–8")*.
- **9** — + finishing evidence is present everywhere (styled empty areas, considered alignment, complete states) — no part of the surface could plausibly result from stopping early *(Universal Principles p.256–257; [derived] extension of the "could-this-be-unfinished" test)*.
- **10** — ✓ matches the Wabi-Sabi-House standard: deliberate, cared-for simplicity/asymmetry with a muted natural palette, every placement traceable to intent *(Universal Principles p.256–257 "9–10")*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface (no area presented/defended as minimal-restrained).
**Weight:** low (1) — UP Wabi-Sabi low (thin direct screen-craft precedent, analogical test); sole scoring source.

### CRAFT-8 — Delight rides on a working core
**Rule.** Flourish, animation, and surprise are bonuses atop a learnable, effective core — never a substitute; a flourish counts as net-positive only after the core task's completion metrics are confirmed unharmed with it present.
**Grounding.** Krug: "Making your app delightful is a fine objective. Just don't focus so much attention on it that you forget to make it usable, too" (p.191). Delight is "hard to pin down", identified via words like "fun, surprising, impressive, captivating, clever, and even magical" (p.191) — explicitly secondary to the learnable/effective/efficient triad usability is defined around (p.190). Mechanism: delight is a multiplier on a working experience and worthless (or negative) applied to a broken one.
**Objective test.** Any animation/sound/flourish investment cited as a positive: the primary task's completion rate/time measured with the flourish present vs absent (or at minimum with it present); no completion data for the flourished version = the delight investment cannot yet be credited; measured regressions = cut it regardless of praise.
**✗ WRONG.** An 800ms particle burst on checkout, praised in feedback, completion never measured.
**✓ RIGHT.** The burst ships only after A/B shows no abandonment or latency-perception cost.
**Crop.** Krug Ch.10 (p.191 — SoundHound / Paper: delight married to genuine capability).
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — a flourish is cited as evidence the flow is "great" with zero completion-rate/drop-off measurement ever taken *(source: Krug p.191 — #26 "0", the 800ms particle-burst checkout case)*.
- **2** — flourish exists, anecdotal user praise is cited, but no measurement exists and the flow's core completion is otherwise unverified *(Krug p.191 #26 "3")*.
- **4** — core task completion is known only from BEFORE the flourish landed; the flourish itself has not yet been isolated for testing *(Krug #26 "5–6" threshold-adjacent; [derived])*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** the flourish exists; core task completion is separately known to be fine, but the flourish itself was never isolated/tested *(Krug p.191 #26 "5–6")*.
- **6** — + completion rate/time is measured WITH the flourish present, not just assumed carried over from the pre-flourish baseline *(Krug #26; [derived] from the "5–6"→"7–8" gap)*.
- **7** — + the flourish was tested against a no-flourish baseline (A/B or sequential); the result is roughly neutral or a minor positive *(Krug p.191 #26 "7–8")*.
- **8** — + the comparison shows no measured abandonment or latency-perception cost *(Krug #26 "7–8"/"9–10" boundary)*.
- **9** — + records show the core task was verified learnable/effective BEFORE the flourish was added, not concurrently *(Krug p.190–191 — learnable/effective/efficient triad; [derived] core-first sequencing)*.
- **10** — ✓ the flourish shipped only after A/B testing confirmed no increase in abandonment/perceived latency, with a stated willingness to cut it otherwise *(Krug p.191 #26 "9–10")*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface (no flourish/animation/surprise investment present — per Krug, most screens have none).
**Weight:** low (1) — Krug #26 low (narrow applicability, flourish surfaces only); sole scoring source.

### CRAFT-9 — Assets at their intended size; defensive containment
**Rule.** Never scale assets past their intended rendering size: small icons blown up 2–4× go chunky (wrap them in a colored container or redraw for the size); detailed assets shrunk to icon scale turn to mush (recapture smaller, crop a region, or draw a simplified version). User-supplied imagery gets fixed-aspect cover-cropping and a subtle inset shadow against background bleed — never intrinsic-size trust, never a clashing hard border.
**Grounding.** Refactoring UI: "icons that were drawn to be used at 16-24px are never going to look very professional when you blow them up to 3x or 4x their intended size. They lack detail, and always feel disproportionately 'chunky'" (pp.208–209); "If you take a full-size screenshot and shrink it by 70% to make it fit... The 16px font in your app becomes a 4px font in your screenshot" (p.210); a 128px logo shrunk to favicon size "all turns to mush" (pp.212–213); "Displaying user-uploaded images at their intrinsic aspect ratio can really throw off a layout" — center them in fixed containers with `background-size: cover` (pp.214–215); for background bleed, "try using a subtle inner box shadow... Borders will often clash with the colors in the image, while most people will barely even realize the shadow is there" (pp.216–217). Mechanism: every asset encodes a detail budget tuned to one rendering size; scaling in either direction breaks that budget, and user content never honored your layout's assumptions to begin with.
**Objective test.** (1) Icon rendered ≥2× its source design size (source viewBox/artboard vs rendered CSS width) = flag. (2) Screenshots: the smallest embedded text at rendered size must stay ≥~8px; below = illegible, flag. (3) Small icons derived by shrinking full-detail logos rather than purpose-drawn = inspect at true render size for merged detail. (4) Grids of user images: fixed-aspect cover containers, never intrinsic ratios. (5) Avatars near background-toned edges carry a low-opacity inset hairline (e.g. `inset 0 0 0 1px hsla(0,0%,0%,.1)`), not a hard colored border.
**✗ WRONG.** A 24px-designed megaphone stretched to 48px in a features row; a desktop screenshot shrunk 70% with its 16px UI font smeared to ~4px; a jagged mixed-ratio photo grid; pale avatars bleeding into a pale chat-list background.
**✓ RIGHT.** The small icon inside a 48px colored circle (or redrawn for 48px with thicker strokes); a device-sized capture or a cropped full-detail region; uniform cover-cropped tiles; avatar edges defined by an invisible-against-photos inset shadow.
**Crop.** RU-28, RU-29 (pp.208–213 scaling comparisons; pp.214–217 cover-crop grid + inset-shadow avatars).
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — a small-drawn icon (16–24px) is blown up 2–4× and looks chunky, OR a full-detail asset is shrunk to icon/favicon scale and turns to mush/illegible *(source: Refactoring UI p.208–213; RU-30 "0")*; OR user images render at intrinsic aspect ratio in a grid producing jagged heights, or a background-toned avatar bleeds with no containment *(Refactoring UI p.214–217; RU-31 "0")*.
- **2** — a scaling issue exists but is milder (~1.5× icon upscale, or screenshot text just-barely-illegible); OR a fixed image container exists but crops badly (stretches) or uses a hard, arbitrarily-colored border *(RU-30/RU-31 "3")*.
- **4** — the specific asset in question is within its intended range but the broader system has no rule preventing recurrence elsewhere; images use cover-crop but avatar-bleed is unaddressed *(RU-30/RU-31 "5–6" threshold-adjacent)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** no icon renders ≥2× its source-design size; the smallest embedded text in any scaled screenshot stays legible; images correctly use `background-size:cover`/`object-fit:cover` in fixed containers *(Refactoring UI p.208–215; RU-30/31 "5–6")*.
- **6** — + the smallest scaled-screenshot text renders ≥8px and no small icon shows merged detail at true render size *(Refactoring UI p.210,212–213; RU-30 "Measure")*.
- **7** — + the correct technique is applied for every size mismatch — a small icon in a larger container, or a purpose-drawn/simplified variant — never naive scaling *(Refactoring UI p.208–209; RU-30 "7–8")*.
- **8** — + a subtle inset box-shadow/inner border is applied on avatars/photos prone to background-bleed, never a hard colored border *(Refactoring UI p.216–217; RU-31 "7–8")*.
- **9** — + both techniques hold together consistently across every instance: a fixed-aspect cropped grid AND inset-shadow-contained avatars *(Refactoring UI p.214–217; RU-31 "7–8"/"9–10")*.
- **10** — ✓ matches the ✓ examples: icon-in-a-larger-circle or a purpose-redrawn 48px icon, a device-captured/cropped screenshot, a purpose-simplified favicon, a uniform cover-cropped grid, and clean `inset 0 0 0 1px hsla(0,0%,0%,.1)` avatar edges *(Refactoring UI p.208–217; RU-30/31 "9–10")*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface (no icons, screenshots, or user imagery).
**Weight:** medium (2) — RU-30 medium and RU-31 medium (both constituent sources); unanimous.

### CRAFT-10 — The self-audit question
**Rule.** Standing calibration: in front of strong work, ask "what did this designer do that I wouldn't have thought to do?" — and fold the move into the system.
**Grounding.** Refactoring UI closes on exactly this practice as the engine of continuous improvement (p.249), paired with its parting warning: "Don't let your existing beliefs hold back your designs — constraints are powerful but sometimes a bit of freedom is just what you need to take an interface to the next level" (p.246). Mechanism: taste grows by decomposing admired work into named, reusable moves — inspiration that stays un-decomposed never changes what you build.
**Objective test.** Process check: the team's review notes on admired references contain extracted, NAMED moves (not "looks nice"); each adopted move lands as a rule in the design system, not a one-off; a growing inspiration folder with zero extracted rules = the practice is not running.
**✗ WRONG.** Screenshot folders of "inspiration" never decomposed into usable rules.
**✓ RIGHT.** "They separate panels with background shifts, zero borders — adopt: border-last policy" filed into the system.
**Crop.** none.
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — inspiration is collected (screenshot folders) with zero extracted moves, nothing sourced into the design system *(source: Refactoring UI p.249 — the closing self-audit practice; [derived] — no per-book scoring entry exists for this practice; low-tier process-only convention shared with RU-36/LU-#30-class principles)*.
- **2** — some references are decomposed into named moves, others are left "looks nice"-only; extracted moves live only in notes, absent from the system *([derived], same convention)*.
- **4** — most references are decomposed but landing in the system is inconsistent; conflicting moves are discarded solely for violating existing rules, without adjudication *([derived])*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** every logged reference carries ≥1 extracted move named as a reusable rule, not just "looks nice" *(Refactoring UI p.249 — "ask what did this designer do... fold the move into the system"; [derived] threshold)*.
- **6** — + each adopted move is traceable to a written rule actually living in the design system, not just in notes *(Refactoring UI p.249; [derived])*.
- **7** — + at least one extracted move is dated within the current work cycle/project period — the practice is actively running, not historical only *([derived] cadence check)*.
- **8** — + at least one recorded case exists where an admired move led to REVISING or extending an existing system rule, per the book's own "don't let existing beliefs hold back your designs" caveat *(Refactoring UI p.246,249)*.
- **9** — + the practice runs on a standing cadence — recurring dated extractions across multiple work cycles, not a one-time burst *([derived] extension of the cadence check)*.
- **10** — ✓ matches the book's closing standard fully: every admired reference decomposed into named moves, every adopted move landing in the system, and the system itself demonstrably revised over time by what was learned *(Refactoring UI p.246,249; [derived] — synthesized since no per-book scoring entry exists for this closing practice)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface (no review-notes/design-system process artifact available to audit).
**Weight:** low (1) — no per-book scoring entry exists for the closing p.249 practice; derived low by the experts' shared convention that process-only, artifact-dependent principles sit in the low tier (RU-36, LU-#30 class).

# Color & Shade Systems

Pillars: 1, 4.

---

### COLOR-1 — Reason in HSL, not hex
**Rule.** Express related colors in HSL so hue family and saturation/lightness progression are legible in the values themselves; unrelated hex codes are the tell of an ad-hoc palette.
**Grounding.**
- Refactoring UI: "Using hex or RGB, colors that have a lot in common visually look nothing alike in code... HSL fixes this by representing colors using attributes the human-eye intuitively perceives: hue, saturation, and lightness." (p.138) — the mechanism: HSL exposes the *generative relationship* between shades (shared H, tuned S/L), so a palette can be reasoned about and extended rather than eyeballed.
- Refactoring UI defines the axes: "Hue is a color's position on the color wheel... measured in degrees, where 0° is red, 120° is green, and 240° is blue" (pp.138–139); "Saturation is how colorful or vivid a color looks. 0% saturation is grey... 100% is vibrant" (p.139); "Lightness... measures how close a color is to black or to white" (p.140).
- Caveat, same source: "lightness in HSL is not the same than brightness in HSB... browsers only understand HSL, so if you're designing for the web, HSL should be your weapon of choice." (pp.140–141) — HSB values pasted from a design tool silently mean something else.
**Objective test.** For any set of ≥3 related palette colors: can a reviewer identify the shared hue family from the code alone? Hex triplets with no visible generative relationship (e.g. `#03369E / #507DD7 / #9FB9ED`) = the diagnostic failure HSL fixes; converted, the values must show one shared H and a monotonic S/L progression, such that a reviewer can derive a fourth consistent shade by inspection.
**✗ WRONG.** A donut chart's three blue segments defined as `#03369E`, `#507DD7`, `#9FB9ED` — three codes with no visible mathematical or perceptual relationship to anyone reading the CSS, despite all being "blue."
**✓ RIGHT.** The same segments as `hsl(220,95%,34%) / hsl(220,65%,61%) / hsl(220,69%,80%)` — shared hue 220 explicit, darkest→lightest progression legible directly in the values, a fourth consistent shade derivable by eye.
**Crop.** RU-06.
**Score — grounded ladder (0→10).**
- **0 — ✗** Related color sets (≥3 colors sharing a visual family) defined in hex/RGB with no perceptible mathematical relationship legible in the values (the `#03369E/#507DD7/#9FB9ED` case) *(source: Refactoring UI p.138)*.
- **3** — Mixed tokens: some families in HSL, most still raw hex/RGB, no clear system *(source: Refactoring UI pp.138–141)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** Every related family is defined in HSL in the tokens/CSS (hue/saturation/lightness legible per value) *(source: Refactoring UI p.138)*.
- **6** — + Within each family the H value is identical (±2°) across all shades, or a deviation is an explained deliberate rotation *(source: Refactoring UI pp.138–139)*.
- **7** — + L progresses monotonically reading each family's values top-to-bottom *(source: Refactoring UI p.140)*.
- **8** — + S varies as a recognizable curve rather than scattered values `[derived: Refactoring UI pp.139, 152]`.
- **9** — + No HSB-pasted values: every token verified as web HSL (an HSB triplet silently means something else) *(source: Refactoring UI pp.140–141)*.
- **10 — ✓** A fourth consistent shade is derivable by inspection alone — steps regular enough to interpolate, matching the `hsl(220,…)` exemplar *(source: Refactoring UI pp.138–141)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition AND every rung below it hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** low (1) — per Refactoring UI's own weighting: an authoring/tooling practice that doesn't change the rendered pixel but predicts COLOR-2/4/5 quality.

### COLOR-2 — A full color system, not 5 brand swatches
**Rule.** A real UI needs 8–10 greys, 5–10 shades of 1–2 primaries, and 5–10 shades per semantic family (success/warning/danger + accents), defined up front — preventing the near-identical-ad-hoc-shades drift.
**Grounding.**
- Refactoring UI: "You can't build anything with five hex codes. To build something real, you need a much more comprehensive set of colors to choose from." (p.143) — the five-swatch generator palette applied to a real chat product is the book's own garish failure case (p.142): every panel, alert, and hover state forced onto one of five flat values.
- On greys: "You'll need more greys than you think, too — three or four shades might sound like plenty but it won't be long before you wish you had something a little darker than shade #2 but a little lighter than shade #3. In practice, you want 8-10 shades to choose from." (p.144)
- On overall scope: "All in, it's not uncommon to need as many as ten different colors with 5-10 shades each for a complex UI." (p.147) — pre-defining the scale up front is what prevents scattered `lighten()/darken()` calls producing 35 near-identical blues.
**Objective test.** Token-file audit: distinct grey shades 8–10; shades per primary 5–10; semantic families (success/warning/danger at minimum) present with 5–10 shades each. A flat 5-hex palette with zero tonal variants fails outright; `lighten()/darken()` calls scattered in component code instead of predefined steps = drift flag.
**✗ WRONG.** A team-chat app's entire visual system built from exactly five color-generator hex codes with zero tonal variants — a yellow sidebar beside a red error banner, because those were the only yellow and red available.
**✓ RIGHT.** The same app on a defined system: grey scale for text/panels/borders, a blue primary scale for nav/active states, dedicated red/yellow/green scales reserved for destructive, warning, and positive states — every UI need (hover, border, tint, alert) draws an appropriately-toned predefined step.
**Crop.** RU-22.
**Score — grounded ladder (0→10).**
- **0 — ✗** A flat ≤5-hex palette with zero tonal variants carries the whole UI ("you can't build anything with five hex codes") *(source: Refactoring UI pp.142–143)*.
- **3** — A few extra shades exist but only as scattered ad-hoc `lighten()`/`darken()` calls; no defined scale (the 35-near-identical-blues drift) *(source: Refactoring UI p.147)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** A defined token scale exists: ≥5 distinct grey shades plus a defined shade scale for at least one primary *(source: Refactoring UI pp.143–144)*.
- **6** — + Grey scale reaches 8–10 distinct shades *(source: Refactoring UI p.144)*.
- **7** — + Each primary (1–2 hues) has a defined 5–10-step scale *(source: Refactoring UI p.147)*.
- **8** — + Success, warning, AND danger each present with their own 5–10-step scales (no flat single-value semantic colors) *(source: Refactoring UI p.147)*.
- **9** — + Zero one-off computed shades in component code: every rendered color resolves to a predefined step *(source: Refactoring UI p.147)*.
- **10 — ✓** Every UI need (text, panel, border, hover, tint, badge, alert) draws an appropriately-toned predefined step; nothing forced onto a mismatched flat value *(source: Refactoring UI pp.142–147)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition AND every rung below it hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — foundational system governing every colored surface (Refactoring UI weight line).

### COLOR-3 — Restrained palette; accents earn attention
**Rule.** Near-neutral base plus a few high-contrast accents reserved for what matters; broad loud palettes fragment attention.
**Grounding.**
- About Face: "visual interfaces should strive to be minimal, such as simple geometric forms or a restricted color palette composed primarily of less-saturated or neutral colors balanced with a few high-contrast accent colors that emphasize important information." (Ch17, p.423) — the mechanism: visual efficiency means the eye finds what matters fast; broad palettes fragment attention across low-value elements. Too many colors is one of the book's named noise forms (p.423).
- Universal Principles: color similarity gives "the strongest grouping effect; it is strongest when the number of colors is small, and is decreasingly effective as the number of colors increases" (p.226) — every added accent dilutes the grouping/emphasis power of all the others.
**Objective test.** Count distinct saturated accent colors doing emphasis work on one screen: a small fixed set (≤~3), each with a stable meaning, reserved for genuinely important information; any accent applied to a decorative element = fail.
