**✗ WRONG.** Five saturated KPI-card accents with no shared meaning; the same accent color reused decoratively on dividers and illustrations.
**✓ RIGHT.** Neutral grey/white base; exactly one accent (e.g., red) meaning exactly "needs attention" (over budget, error), used nowhere else.
**Crop.** none.
**Score — grounded ladder (0→10).**
- **0 — ✗** ≥6 distinct saturated accent colors doing emphasis work, no shared/traceable meaning *(source: Universal Principles p.226; About Face Ch17 p.423)*.
- **3** — 4–5 accent colors, meanings inconsistent or mixed across appearances *(source: Universal Principles p.226)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** ≤3 accent colors, each with a traceable meaning; a near-neutral base is present *(source: About Face Ch17 p.423)*.
- **6** — + every accent maps to exactly one consistent meaning wherever it appears on the screen *(source: About Face Ch17 p.423)*.
- **7** — + zero saturated accents applied to decorative elements (dividers, illustrations, inert icons) *(source: About Face Ch17 p.423)*.
- **8** — + page base (backgrounds, panels, body text) is fully neutral/near-neutral; no large saturated field carries no meaning *(source: About Face Ch17 p.423)*.
- **9** — + accent count is down to 1–2, maximizing the grouping/emphasis effect *(source: Universal Principles p.226)*.
- **10 — ✓** Exactly one accent with exactly one meaning, used nowhere else; base pure neutral *(source: About Face Ch17 p.423; Universal Principles p.226)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition AND every rung below it hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — About Face's visual-efficiency weighting: directly gates scannability, a top-line craft signal.

### COLOR-4 — Shade math: saturation compensates lightness; hue carries brightness
**Rule.** Raise saturation as lightness departs 50% or extreme shades wash out; hues carry inherent perceived brightness, so rotate ≤20–30° toward/away from yellow/cyan/magenta to lighten/darken feel while preserving intensity.
**Grounding.**
- Refactoring UI: "as a color gets closer to 0% or 100% lightness, the impact of saturation is weakened... if you don't want the lighter and darker shades of a given color to look washed out, you need to increase the saturation as the lightness gets further away from 50%." (p.152)
- On perceived brightness: "every hue has an inherent perceived brightness due to how the human eye perceives color... there are three separate local minimums (red, green, and blue) and three local maximums (yellow, cyan, and magenta)." (pp.153–154) — rotating hue toward a maximum lightens the *felt* brightness without draining intensity the way pure lightness adjustment does.
- On the rotation bound: "it works best in small doses. Don't rotate the hue more than 20-30° or it will look like a totally different color instead of just lighter or darker." (p.157) The book's own failure case: its yellow scale darkened by lightness alone goes muddy olive; rotated toward orange with rising saturation it goes rich brown (p.156).
**Objective test.** Plot S vs L across a 5–9-step shade scale of one hue: flat/constant S while L sweeps ~10–90% = washed-out extremes; S must visibly rise at both ends relative to the middle step. Hue-rotation lightening/darkening: |ΔH| between base and variant ≤30° (beyond that it reads as a different hue, not a shade).
**✗ WRONG.** A yellow→dark scale built by dropping lightness only, saturation held constant — the dark steps read as dull, muddy olive-green.
**✓ RIGHT.** The same scale rotating hue toward orange as lightness decreases while saturating at the dark end — warm, rich brown/amber darks that keep their intensity.
**Crop.** RU-07.
**Score — grounded ladder (0→10).**
- **0 — ✗** S flat/constant while L sweeps across the scale; both extremes read washed out *(source: Refactoring UI p.152)*.
- **3** — S rises at only one end of the scale; the other extreme still washes out *(source: Refactoring UI p.152)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** S visibly rises at BOTH extreme steps relative to the mid step; no washed-out extreme in side-by-side comparison *(source: Refactoring UI p.152)*.
- **6** — + every hue-rotation lighten/darken variant stays within |ΔH| ≤30° of base where rotation is used *(source: Refactoring UI p.157)*.
- **7** — + rotation direction is correct: toward a perceived-brightness maximum (yellow/cyan/magenta) to lighten, away to darken *(source: Refactoring UI pp.153–154, 157)*.
- **8** — + no muddy-extreme symptom anywhere — wherever lightness-only darkening risked going muddy, rotation was used instead *(source: Refactoring UI p.156)*.
- **9** — + the S-vs-L curve reads as a deliberate shape across the whole scale, not scattered ad-hoc values `[derived: Refactoring UI pp.139, 152]`.
- **10 — ✓** Matches the book's exemplar: rich, intensity-preserving darks/lights via combined S-compensation and bounded hue rotation *(source: Refactoring UI pp.152–157)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition AND every rung below it hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** med (2) — a refinement on top of COLOR-2; matters once a full scale exists (Refactoring UI weight line).

### COLOR-5 — Greys are rarely neutral
**Rule.** Tint greys slightly warm or cool for deliberate temperature; 0%-saturation grey reads lifeless, and grey scales need the same extreme-end saturation correction.
**Grounding.**
- Refactoring UI: "By definition, true grey has a saturation of 0%... But in practice, a lot of the colors that we think of as grey are actually saturated quite heavily. This saturation is what makes some greys feel cool and other greys feel warm." (p.158) — temperature is a deliberate personality decision, not an accident of the token file.
- Same source, on keeping it consistent: "To maintain a consistent temperature, don't forget to increase the saturation for the lighter and darker shades. If you don't, those shades will look a bit washed out compared to the greys that are closer to 50% lightness." (p.160) Book worked values: cool ≈ hue 208, warm ≈ hue 40, S 12–21%.
**Objective test.** Inspect the grey token scale's HSL values: every step at S:0% on a product wanting a cool/warm feel = flag; tinted scales carry small non-zero S (book range 12–21% at hue ~208 cool or ~40 warm) with S rising — not flat — toward the lightest/darkest ends.
**✗ WRONG.** An invoicing dashboard's grey ramp built at flat 0% saturation throughout — personality-free, and the extreme shades visibly duller than the mid-tones.
**✓ RIGHT.** The same ramp rebuilt with a consistent slight blue tint (hue ~208, S 12–21%, rising at the ends) — a deliberate cool temperature, no washout at the extremes.
**Crop.** RU-23.
**Score — grounded ladder (0→10).**
- **0 — ✗** Every grey step at flat 0% saturation — personality-free and no temperature *(source: Refactoring UI p.158)*.
- **3** — Mixed: some steps at 0% saturation, some tinted; incoherent, no defined temperature *(source: Refactoring UI p.158)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** Every grey step carries non-zero saturation, drawn from one hue family *(source: Refactoring UI p.158)*.
- **6** — + hue is consistent across the whole ramp (cool ≈208 or warm ≈40; no mixing of warm and cool steps) *(source: Refactoring UI pp.158, 160)*.
- **7** — + saturation rises at the lightest/darkest steps relative to the mid step (book band 12–21% at mid) *(source: Refactoring UI p.160)*.
- **8** — + no washout: extreme shades hold the same temperature read as mid-tones in side-by-side comparison *(source: Refactoring UI p.160)*.
- **9** — + saturation values sit within the book-verified range for the chosen temperature (≈12–21% at hue ~208 cool or ~40 warm) `[derived: Refactoring UI p.160]`.
- **10 — ✓** A deliberate, consistent temperature scale with zero washout anywhere, matching the book's exemplar *(source: Refactoring UI pp.158–160)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition AND every rung below it hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** low (1) — Refactoring UI marks this low-med (polish-level, visible on close inspection); recorded low, single-expert call noted.

### COLOR-6 — Accessible contrast without ugliness
**Rule.** Meet 4.5:1 (3:1 large/bold text): flip the contrast — dark same-hue text on a light tint instead of white-on-saturated (which also sheds unearned visual weight) — or rotate the text hue brighter instead of washing toward white.
**Grounding.**
- Laws of UX states the WCAG floor verbatim: "the color contrast ratio between text and its background should be at least 4.5:1. For larger text (at least 18 pt) or bold text (at least 14 pt), the ratio is a bit more lenient at 3:1" (p.101, citing WCAG SC 1.4.3).
- Refactoring UI: "The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) recommend that normal text (under ~18px) has a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1, and that larger text has a contrast ratio of at least 3:1." (p.162) Its status-pill example: white-on-saturated measured 2.25:1 / 1.56:1 / 3.14:1 — all failing — flipped to dark-on-tint they hit 5.34–9.78:1 AND stop dominating the row (pp.163–164): the flip fixes accessibility and hierarchy in one move.
- Refactoring UI, dark panels: "one way to increase the contrast without getting closer to white is to rotate the hue towards a brighter color, like cyan, magenta, or yellow" (p.165) — its example moves `hsl(240,44%,89%)` → `hsl(188,100%,85%)`, 8.37:1 → 8.71:1, both AAA but the rotated one stays colorful.
- Universal Principles adds a reading-performance threshold: "Performance is optimal when contrast levels between text and background exceed 70 percent" (p.148), and warns that passing numbers can still fail: "High-contrast, inverse text can 'visually bleed' to the background and dramatically reduce legibility" (p.148, note 4).
**Objective test.** Compute contrast for every text/background pair against the size-appropriate floor: ≥4.5:1 normal text (<18px), ≥3:1 for ≥18pt or ≥14pt bold (AAA: 7:1 / 4.5:1); reading-heavy surfaces additionally ≥70% contrast. Any failing colored pill/badge: try dark-on-light-tint of the same hue BEFORE white/black; failing colored-on-colored text: try a ≤30° rotation toward cyan/magenta/yellow (60°/180°/300°) before lightening. Inverse body text at small sizes or on textured grounds = flag even when the ratio passes.
**✗ WRONG.** White text on saturated green/yellow/red status pills — 2.25:1, 1.56:1, 3.14:1, all failing AA — and the saturated pills out-shout their rows, becoming the focal point.
**✓ RIGHT.** Dark-green-on-pale-green, dark-amber-on-pale-amber pills — 5.34–9.78:1 (AA/AAA), and the softer pills sit correctly in the row's hierarchy.
**Crop.** RU-24.
**Score — grounded ladder (0→10).**
- **0 — ✗** ≥2 failing text/background pairs, or any failing pair on primary content *(source: Laws of UX p.101; Refactoring UI p.162)*.
- **3** — Exactly one failing pair, confined to a non-primary surface *(source: Laws of UX p.101)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** Every text/background pair meets the size-appropriate WCAG floor (≥4.5:1 normal <18px; ≥3:1 at ≥18pt or ≥14pt bold) *(source: Laws of UX p.101; Refactoring UI p.162)*.
- **6** — + wherever a fix was needed, it uses a hue-preserving technique (dark-on-same-hue-tint flip or ≤30° rotation) rather than crude white/black *(source: Refactoring UI pp.163–165)*.
- **7** — + no saturated pill/badge/status element out-shouts its row after the fix *(source: Refactoring UI pp.163–164)*.
- **8** — + reading-heavy surfaces exceed 70% contrast *(source: Universal Principles p.148)*.
- **9** — + no small-size inverse or high-contrast text visually bleeds into its background even where the ratio passes *(source: Universal Principles p.148, note 4)*.
- **10 — ✓** AAA-level contrast (≥7:1 / ≥4.5:1) achieved via hue-preserving technique everywhere, no bleed, correct row hierarchy *(source: Refactoring UI pp.162–165; Universal Principles p.148)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition AND every rung below it hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — unanimous: Refactoring UI, Laws of UX, and Universal Principles all mark this a hard accessibility floor with legal/inclusion stakes.

### COLOR-7 — Never encode meaning in color alone
**Rule.** Every color-carried state/severity/category gets a second channel (icon, label, shape, weight); multi-category encodings prefer lightness steps of ONE hue over many hues.
**Grounding.**
- Refactoring UI: "Always use color to support something that your design is already saying; never use it as the only means of communication." (p.168) Its chart fix: "It's much easier for someone who's colorblind to tell the difference between light and dark than it is for them to tell the difference between two distinct colors." (pp.167–168) — hence the donut rebuilt as a single-hue lightness progression.
- Laws of UX: "Relying solely on color to communicate visual contrast, signify interactive elements, or indicate visual feedback is problematic for individuals with color blindness or low vision. It's important to use additional visual cues such as strokes, patterns, and shape" (p.101).
- Designing Interfaces: "The shape of the scatter markers could encode yet a fourth variable, but in this case, shape is redundant with color hue. The redundant encoding helps a user visually separate the three data groups" (Fig 9-6, p.438) — redundant shape+hue survives grayscale/print.
- Universal Principles ("Redundancy"): "Diverse redundancy is the use of multiple elements of different types... resistant to a single cause of failure" (p.204); its Signal-to-Noise guidance says to "increase signal via redundant coding and highlighting" (p.224).
**Objective test.** Grayscale/deuteranopia-protanopia simulation: every state pair must remain distinguishable. Trend indicators: an icon/arrow present inside the colored element, still distinguishable under the same simulation. Charts with ≥3 categorical series: count independent channels per series — color alone = 1 = fail; ≥2 channels (hue + shape/line-style) = pass, or switch to one-hue lightness steps. If ≥2 series/segments merge under simulation, the encoding fails.
**✗ WRONG.** Green vs red trend pills with no arrows — identical under red-green simulation; a blue/green/orange donut whose green and orange merge under blue-yellow simulation.
**✓ RIGHT.** ↑/↓ arrows inside the pills so direction survives the loss of hue; the donut as light/medium/dark of one blue — the lightness contrast stays legible.
**Crop.** RU-25.
**Score — grounded ladder (0→10).**
- **0 — ✗** ≥2 state/severity/category pairs merge under grayscale or colorblind simulation, and no second channel exists anywhere *(source: Refactoring UI pp.167–168; Laws of UX p.101)*.
- **3** — Exactly one pair merges under simulation, or some states carry a second channel while others rely on color alone *(source: Laws of UX p.101; Universal Principles p.204)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** Every state/severity/category pair remains distinguishable under grayscale AND deuteranopia/protanopia simulation *(source: Refactoring UI pp.167–168)*.
- **6** — + every color-carried state also carries a second channel (icon/label/shape/weight) *(source: Laws of UX p.101; Universal Principles p.204)*.
- **7** — + charts with ≥3 categorical series use ≥2 independent channels per series, or single-hue lightness steps *(source: Refactoring UI pp.167–168; Designing Interfaces Fig 9-6 p.438)*.
- **8** — + the second channel is applied consistently across every series, not just some *(source: Designing Interfaces p.438)*.
- **9** — + each secondary cue is legible at its actual rendered size (distinct, high-contrast, not vestigial) *(source: Universal Principles p.224)*.
- **10 — ✓** Full redundant encoding everywhere, survives grayscale and both colorblind simulations, legible at rendered size *(source: Refactoring UI pp.167–168; Laws of UX p.101; Designing Interfaces p.438; Universal Principles pp.204, 224)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition AND every rung below it hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — unanimous: Refactoring UI, Laws of UX, Designing Interfaces, and Universal Principles (Redundancy) all weight this high (accessibility floor).

### COLOR-8 — Color similarity is a grouping claim
**Rule.** Reusing one color across functionally unrelated elements asserts a relationship that doesn't exist; color is the strongest similarity signal and must be spent semantically.
**Grounding.**
- Universal Principles: "Similarity of color results in the strongest grouping effect; it is strongest when the number of colors is small, and is decreasingly effective as the number of colors increases... Similarity of shape is the weakest grouping strategy." (p.226) Guideline: "Use similarity to indicate relatedness among elements in a design... Use the fewest colors and simplest shapes possible for the strongest grouping effects." (p.226) — because color grouping is involuntary, a shared color IS a claim of relatedness whether intended or not.
- Designing Interfaces: "If you have a few things 'of a type' and you want viewers to see them as equally interesting alternatives, give them an identical (and distinctive) graphic treatment" (p.218) — the inverse binds too: identical treatment on non-alternatives claims a false equivalence, and different treatment on the same role implies (wrongly) different behavior.
**Objective test.** Map each accent color to its semantic role: one color → one role. A hue appearing on interactive AND decorative AND status elements = fail. >~6–7 hues encoding one categorical dimension = grouping degraded (UP's count threshold). Same-role controls across the app must share the same {color, shape, radius, size} tuple; any outlier not explained by a documented state = fail.
**✗ WRONG.** Brand blue on links, inert icons, a status chip, and a decorative divider — four unrelated roles claiming kinship.
**✓ RIGHT.** Blue = interactive, amber = warning, grey = inert — each color one job, each job one color.
**Crop.** none.
**Score — grounded ladder (0→10).**
- **0 — ✗** Some hue spans interactive AND decorative AND status roles at once — false kinship across unrelated roles *(source: Universal Principles p.226; Designing Interfaces p.218)*.
- **3** — One hue spans two roles, or >7 hues encode a single categorical dimension *(source: Universal Principles p.226)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** Every accent hue maps to exactly one semantic role; ≤7 hues encode any single categorical dimension *(source: Universal Principles p.226)*.
- **6** — + same-role controls across the surface share the same {color, shape, radius, size} tuple, with at most one unexplained outlier *(source: Designing Interfaces p.218)*.
- **7** — + no identical distinctive treatment is shared by functionally non-equivalent elements *(source: Designing Interfaces p.218)*.
- **8** — + hue count per categorical dimension is down to ≤6 (fewest colors for strongest grouping) *(source: Universal Principles p.226)*.
- **9** — + zero same-role outliers anywhere across the surface *(source: Designing Interfaces p.218)*.
- **10 — ✓** One color, one role, one job everywhere; minimal hue count; no false kinship anywhere *(source: Universal Principles p.226; Designing Interfaces p.218)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition AND every rung below it hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** med (2) — Universal Principles weights Similarity med; sole expert weight line for this principle.

### COLOR-9 — Text over imagery needs contrast normalization
**Rule.** A busy photo spans light and dark regions; no single text color survives — reduce the image's dynamics: overlay tint, lowered contrast + raised brightness, desaturate + multiply brand color, or a zero-offset large-blur text glow.
**Grounding.**
- Refactoring UI: "White text might look great in the dark areas, but it gets lost in the light areas. Dark text looks great in the light areas, but gets lost in the dark areas... the problem isn't the text, it's the image... you need to reduce the dynamics in the image to make the contrast between the text and the background more consistent." (pp.202–203) — fix the background's luminance range, not the text.
- Same source, the four worked techniques: semi-transparent overlay `background-color: hsla(0,0%,0%,.55)` (p.203); "Brightness: +40%, Contrast: -70%" (p.204); "Lower the image contrast... Desaturate the image... Add a solid fill, using the 'multiply' blend mode" (p.205); text-shadow-as-glow `text-shadow: 0 0 50px hsla(0,0%,0%,.4)` to preserve more of the photo's dynamics (p.206).
**Objective test.** Sample pixel luminance directly behind the headline across its full width: a span crossing both very-light and very-dark regions with no correction = fail. Post-fix, re-sample: the luminance range behind the text must be narrow enough that ONE text color holds WCAG-legible contrast (size-appropriate floor per COLOR-6) end-to-end.
**✗ WRONG.** A white hero headline over an untreated office photo — legible where it crosses a dark jacket, invisible where it crosses a bright window.
**✓ RIGHT.** A 55%-black overlay (`hsla(0,0%,0%,.55)`) applied over the whole photo first — every part of the headline sits on a uniformly darkened ground, legible along its entire length.
**Crop.** RU-27.
**Score — grounded ladder (0→10).**
- **0 — ✗** Text is illegible over a whole region; no correction applied where text crosses mixed light/dark regions *(source: Refactoring UI pp.202–203)*.
- **3** — A correction exists but the sampled luminance range still stays too wide for consistent legibility *(source: Refactoring UI pp.203–206)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** Post-fix, the luminance range behind the text is narrow enough that ONE text color holds the size-appropriate WCAG floor (per COLOR-6) end-to-end *(source: Refactoring UI pp.202–203)*.
- **6** — + the fix is one of the book's named techniques: overlay tint, lowered contrast + raised brightness, desaturate + multiply, or a zero-offset large-blur glow *(source: Refactoring UI pp.203–206)*.
- **7** — + the fix holds along the text's entire width, with no more than one narrow crossing that was ever even at risk *(source: Refactoring UI pp.202–203)*.
- **8** — + the technique flattens no more than needed for legibility, retaining photo detail where the aesthetic calls for it *(source: Refactoring UI p.206)*.
- **9** — + no crossing anywhere on the surface is left unaddressed where text sits over mixed light/dark image regions *(source: Refactoring UI pp.202–203)*.
- **10 — ✓** Matches the book's exemplar: uniform legibility end-to-end achieved with minimal flattening (technique choice fits the aesthetic, e.g. glow over blanket overlay) *(source: Refactoring UI pp.202–206)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition AND every rung below it hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** med (2) — Refactoring UI: matters specifically for hero/marketing photography sections, not control-dense app UIs.

# Copy & Language

Words on the interface. Pillars: 2, 3.

---

### COPY-1 — Omit needless words; instructions must die
**Rule.** Cut instructional text, welcome blurbs, and promotional filler ruthlessly (halve, then halve again); the goal for instructions is elimination via self-evidence, with survivors at ≤1 short sentence. Applies to button labels, headers, hints, and status text alike.
**Grounding.**
- Krug's Third Law: "Get rid of half the words on each page, then get rid of half of what's left." (p.77). Mechanism — the payoff is triple: "It reduces the noise level of the page... makes the useful content more prominent... makes the pages shorter" (p.77); default stance: "start with the assumption that everything is visual noise (the 'presumed guilty until proven innocent' approach) and get rid of anything that's not making a real contribution." (p.62)
- Krug on instructions: "The main thing you need to know about instructions is that no one is going to read them—at least not until after repeated attempts at 'muddling through' have failed." (p.78); "Your objective should always be to eliminate instructions entirely by making everything self-explanatory, or as close to it as possible." (p.78). His worked rewrite cuts 103 words to 34 with zero loss (pp.78–79).
- Universal Principles: "Excess is noise." (p.224); mechanism — "every unnecessary data item, graphic, line, or symbol steals attention away from relevant elements." (p.224)
**Objective test.** Remove any sentence/paragraph and check whether task completion or comprehension changes — unchanged = it goes. A first audit pass must achieve ≥50% word-count reduction on instructional blocks without losing a fact the user needs; if it can't, the block wasn't audited hard enough. Remove ALL helper text from a control: if a first-time user still operates it correctly (labeling, placeholder convention, affordance), the instruction was unnecessary; any surviving instruction is ≤1 short sentence.
**✗ WRONG.** A settings page opens with "Welcome to your account settings page! Here you can manage all aspects of your account, including your profile, security, and notification preferences. Feel free to explore the options below…" — and the search box above it carries a paragraph explaining how to type keywords and click Search.
**✓ RIGHT.** The page opens directly with the "Profile / Security / Notifications" section headers and their controls; the search control is a box + magnifier + "Search", nothing else.
**Crop.** KR-08 (Krug Ch.5 "Before: 103 Words / After: 34 Words" figure, pp.78–79).
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — a full welcome-blurb/promotional paragraph precedes the actual content with zero functional information, AND a control requires a full instructional paragraph to operate *(source: Don't Make Me Think Krug Third Law p.77 + instructions p.78, "Welcome to your account settings page" case)*.
- **2** — filler paragraph gone, but ≥2 sentences in the block are removable by the deletion test (unchanged task completion/comprehension without them) *(Krug — deletion test, p.77)*.
- **4** — exactly 1 removable sentence remains; maximal-cut attempt still recovers 20–40% of the block's words *(Krug Third Law, p.77)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** 0 removable sentences; maximal-cut attempt recovers ≤20% further words; no control requires a full paragraph to operate *(Krug — "get rid of half... then half again" p.77; instructions p.78)*.
- **6** — + every control operable without its helper text, but ≥1 surviving instruction is multi-sentence *(Krug — instructions, p.78)*.
- **7** — + every surviving instruction ≤1 short sentence *(Krug — "eliminate instructions entirely... or as close to it as possible" p.78)*.
- **8** — + 0 instructional text of any kind; labeling/placeholder/affordance alone suffice (at most a one-word microcopy hint) *(Krug — instructions p.78)*.
- **9** — + 0 filler blocks of any size (no welcome text, self-promotion, or restated-page-purpose text) anywhere on the surface *(Krug — "presumed guilty until proven innocent" p.62; Universal Principles — Signal-to-Noise/Excess-is-noise p.224)*.
- **10** — zero removable words remain anywhere in the block; every word carries a fact the user needs, matching the 103→34-word rewrite *(Krug — worked rewrite pp.78–79; Universal Principles p.224)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — Krug (Third Law + instructions, both weighted high) and Universal Principles (Signal-to-Noise, high) agree.

### COPY-2 — Write for scanning
**Rule.** Users scan and satisfice — design copy as billboard, not literature: front-loaded keywords, headings, bolded anchor fragments that alone carry the task-critical path.
**Grounding.**
- Krug: "We're thinking 'great literature' (or at least 'product brochure'), while the user's reality is much closer to 'billboard going by at 60 miles an hour.'" (p.39)
- Krug: "One of the very few well-documented facts about Web use is that people tend to spend very little time reading most Web pages. Instead, we scan (or skim) them, looking for words or phrases that catch our eye." (p.40). Mechanism — users are "usually on a mission" and "know they don't need to read everything," so scanning, not reading, is how they find the relevant bits (p.40).
**Objective test.** Strip the page's body copy of everything except headings/bold/links: a reader following ONLY the emphasized fragments must still complete the primary task. An incomplete or misleading emphasized-only path = the copy relies on reading, not scanning — fail.
**✗ WRONG.** "No setup fee, cancel anytime" buried mid-paragraph under a generic "Details" heading, indistinguishable from surrounding prose.
**✓ RIGHT.** "No setup fee · cancel anytime" bolded directly under the price; the paragraph, if kept, only elaborates.
**Crop.** none.
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — the single most important fact (differentiator, price, CTA condition) is buried in unstyled prose with no scannable echo anywhere *(source: Don't Make Me Think Krug p.40, buried "no setup fee" case)*.
- **2** — some facts are scannable but the primary task-critical fact is not; the emphasized-only path is misleading or incomplete *(Krug — scanning behavior, p.40)*.
- **4** — the primary task-critical fact is emphasized and the task is completable from the emphasized-only path, but ≥2 secondary task-relevant facts (price condition, differentiator, CTA condition) still require reading unstyled prose *(Krug p.40)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** task completable from headings/bold/links alone; ≤1 secondary task-relevant fact has no heading/bold/link echo *(Krug — "billboard going by at 60 miles an hour" p.39)*.
- **6** — + 0 unechoed task-relevant facts remain; only nice-to-know detail requires reading prose *(Krug p.40)*.
- **7** — + all headings/links front-load their differentiating keyword in the first two words, with ≤1 exception *(Krug — scanning/keyword prominence, p.40)*.
- **8** — + zero front-loading exceptions across every heading/link on the surface *(Krug p.40)*.
- **9** — + body prose, where kept, is verified optional enrichment only — removing it changes nothing about task completion *(Krug — scanning vs. reading, p.40)*.
- **10** — matches the ✓ case exactly: bolded "No setup fee · cancel anytime" directly under price, prose (if any) purely elaborates *(Krug — billboard principle pp.39–40)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — Krug weights scanning high ("foundational... underlies almost every other principle").

### COPY-3 — Plain, active, precise — in the user's vocabulary
**Rule.** Simple language, active voice, audience-matched precision; task vocabulary, never system vocabulary (no raw statuses, codes, internal nouns) — and never over-simplified into imprecision.
**Grounding.**
- Universal Principles: "Readability is determined by factors such as word length, word commonality, sentence length, number of clauses in a sentence, and number of syllables in a sentence." (p.198); the explicit caution — "Simple language is preferred, but overly simple language obscures meaning." (p.198); and "do not write for the formula" — readability formulas are "primitive guides and should not outweigh all other considerations" (p.198).
- About Face (unified file model, Ch14): Save/Save As/Close dialogs "reflect the internal mechanisms of data entry, storage, and retrieval" (p.325); the fix "abolish[es] all user interface recognition of the two copies" (p.338), design principle "Save documents and settings automatically." (p.337). Mechanism — copy exposing the implementation model is excise: work serving the system's internal bookkeeping, not the user's goal (pp.283–285).
**Objective test.** Run the copy through a readability formula (the book cites Fry's Graph): the estimated grade level must MATCH the intended audience's reading level, not merely be minimized. Zero internal-concept leaks (temp filenames, status codes, table names, implementation nouns) outside debug surfaces. Each term is one the target user would themselves use for the thing.
**✗ WRONG.** "Oopsie, something went wonky!" in a developer API error; "Do you want to save changes to Untitled-4.tmp?" exposing the memory-vs-disk distinction the user never asked to think about.
**✓ RIGHT.** "Request failed: missing required field `apiKey`. See docs/auth."; silent autosave with rename-in-place — no save dialog at all.
**Crop.** none.
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — register mismatched to audience in a way that obscures meaning (childish for a technical audience, or jargon-heavy for a general one), AND a user-facing internal concept (temp filename, storage-model exposure) leaks with an equivalent user-goal phrasing available and unused *(source: Universal Principles p.198; About Face #19 p.… "save changes to Untitled-4.tmp" case)*.
- **2** — register roughly appropriate but inconsistent across copy, and ≥2 internal-concept leaks remain *(Universal Principles p.198; About Face #19)*.
- **4** — register mostly consistent, exactly 1 internal-concept leak remains after most have been translated to user-goal language *(About Face #19)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** estimated grade level (Fry's-graph style: sentence length + syllable count) matches the intended audience's reading level — not merely minimized — on the sampled passage; 0 internal-concept leaks outside true debug surfaces *(Universal Principles p.198; About Face #19)*.
- **6** — + the grade-level match holds across ≥2 sampled passages, each within the audience's level *(Universal Principles — Fry's-graph measure, p.198)*.
- **7** — + 0 passive-voice sentences in the sampled instructional/status copy *(Universal Principles — readability factors, p.198; [derived])*.
- **8** — + the underlying mechanism a leak would expose (save/sync state) is handled automatically rather than merely relabeled *(About Face #19)*.
- **9** — + 0 phrasings where simplification/cuteness removed a detail the user needs to act (no vague term where the audience's own precise term exists) *(Universal Principles — "overly simple language obscures meaning" p.198)*.
- **10** — matches the ✓ case: plain, active, fully precise for its technical audience with no meaning lost to simplification, and the internal mechanism fully absorbed (no exposing dialog at all) *(Universal Principles p.198; About Face #19, unified-file-model case)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** med (2) — Universal Principles weights Readability med; About Face weights the internal-model leak high only where save/sync/storage state is user-facing (conditional), noted; med carried as the general case.

### COPY-4 — Tone is a system axis; clarity beats cleverness
**Rule.** Copy register (formal vs casual) is a personality axis applied consistently everywhere; error/alert tone is polite and never blaming; and when a clever/branded phrasing costs comprehension, the obvious word wins.
**Grounding.**
- Refactoring UI: "Words are everywhere in a user interface, and choosing the right ones is just as (if not more) important than choosing the right color or typeface." (p.26); register is one of the concrete personality factors picked once and held with typeface, color, and radius (pp.20–26).
- About Face: "The error dialog must be unfailingly polite. It must never even hint that the user caused this problem, because that is simply not true from the user's perspective." (p.647). Mechanism — an error dialog is "the application's way of reporting on its failure to do its job" (p.647), so blame-language inverts reality.
- Krug: "It's a simple formula: a box, a button, and either the word 'Search' or the universally recognized magnifying glass icon. Don't make it hard for them—stick to the formula." (p.102); "use the word Search, not Find, Quick Find, Quick Search, or Keyword Search" (p.102). Mechanism — a label needing close inspection to justify itself fails the glance test (p.51).
**Objective test.** Register consistent across onboarding/confirmations/errors — no formal↔jokey swings between screens. Zero fault-attributing error phrasing (no "you entered," "invalid," "you must" — ERR-3 scan). Standard-function labels use the standard word (Search/Cart/Home); any deviation carries a written rationale (AFFORD-1).
**✗ WRONG.** "Please provide a phone number" on one screen, "Sweet, thanks!" on the next; a search control branded "Quick Find" with placeholder prose instructing the user to type a keyword.
**✓ RIGHT.** One register held throughout every screen and dialog; the search control says "Search" beside a magnifier, no instructional placeholder.
**Crop.** RU-32 (Refactoring UI pp.25–26, formal vs casual "Verify your identity" copy-tone pair).
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — copy alternates formal↔casual register screen-to-screen with no consistent choice, AND an error dialog blames the user with only a bare OK ("Invalid input. User must type xyz.") *(source: Refactoring UI #35 p.… + About Face p.647, "Invalid input" case)*.
- **2** — register consistent on ≥1 axis but still drifting on ≥2 of the 4 personality axes (typeface/color/radius/tone); error copy carries only 1 of the 3 required elements (no-fault language / scope-impact / actionable path) *(Refactoring UI #35; About Face #35)*.
- **4** — 1 register swing remains across ≥3 sampled screens (onboarding/confirmation/error); error copy carries 2 of 3 required elements *(Refactoring UI p.26; About Face p.647)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** 0 register swings across ≥3 sampled screens; every error/alert has 0 fault-attributing tokens ("you entered", "invalid", "you must") *(Refactoring UI — personality coherence, p.26; About Face p.647)*.
- **6** — + every standard-function control (Search, Cart, Home…) uses the standard word, or every deviation carries a written rationale *(Krug — search formula, p.102)*.
- **7** — + all 3 required error elements present (no-fault language, explicit scope/consequence, ≥1 actionable step beyond OK) *(About Face p.647)*.
- **8** — + 0 branded/clever phrasings fail the glance test (a fresh reviewer decodes every label's function on first read) *(Krug — glance test, p.51)*.
- **9** — + the chosen register direction plausibly matches the stated brand goal, verified across all 4 personality axes *(Refactoring UI #35, pp.20–26)*.
- **10** — matches the ✓ case: one register held throughout every screen and dialog, search says "Search" beside a magnifier with no instructional placeholder, and any unavoidable error offers a genuinely helpful default action inline *(Refactoring UI pp.25–26; Krug p.102; About Face p.647)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** med (2) — Refactoring UI (personality coherence) med and Krug (search formula) med form the majority; About Face weights error politeness high where an error dialog is unavoidable, noted.

### COPY-5 — Identity copy differentiates
**Rule.** Titles/taglines/section names that would read equally true on a competitor's product are generic filler; identity copy is clear, informative, roughly 6–8 words, and states a benefit only you can claim.
**Grounding.**
- Krug: "Good taglines are clear and informative and explain exactly what your site or your organization does... Good taglines are just long enough, but not too long. Six to eight words seem to be long enough to convey a full thought, but short enough to absorb easily... Good taglines convey differentiation and a clear benefit." (p.125). Mechanism — Nielsen's bar, cited by Krug: "a really good tagline is one that no one else in the world could use except you." (p.125)
- Krug's anti-pattern: "Bad taglines sound generic" (p.125), and mission-statement language like "XYZCorp offers world-class solutions in the burgeoning field of blah blah blah blah" (p.124) is explicitly mocked.
**Objective test.** Substitution test: paste the tagline onto a direct competitor's site — equally plausible there = fail. Word count in the 6–8 band; outside 4–12 words needs written justification.
**✗ WRONG.** Tagline: "World-class solutions for the modern enterprise." — sits unchanged on literally any competitor's homepage.
**✓ RIGHT.** Tagline: "Turn meeting notes into tracked action items — automatically." — names the specific mechanism and benefit a competitor without it couldn't honestly claim.
**Crop.** none.
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — tagline is fully generic/interchangeable with any competitor ("World-class solutions for the modern enterprise") — zero differentiation *(source: Don't Make Me Think Krug pp.124–125)*.
- **2** — tagline gestures at the category but names no specific mechanism or benefit; still swappable onto a competitor's page *(Krug p.125)*.
- **4** — tagline names the category and a vague benefit but not the specific mechanism; word count outside the 4–12 band with no written justification *(Krug p.125)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** substitution test fails — pasted onto a direct competitor's site, the tagline reads implausible there (claims a mechanism/benefit the competitor couldn't honestly state); word count within 4–12 words *(Krug p.125)*.
- **6** — + word count lands in the 6–8 word band *(Krug — "six to eight words" p.125)*.
- **7** — + a concrete noun/verb naming the product's actual mechanism appears (not an abstraction like "solutions"/"empower"/"world-class") *(Krug p.125)*.
- **8** — + the tagline states a clear benefit AND the concrete mechanism together, per Nielsen's bar as cited by Krug *(Krug p.125, Nielsen citation)*.
- **9** — + the substitution test fails decisively across every plausible direct competitor, not just the nearest one *([derived] — extension of Krug's substitution test, p.125)*.
- **10** — matches the ✓ case exactly: "Turn meeting notes into tracked action items — automatically" — names the specific mechanism and benefit a competitor without it couldn't honestly claim, 6–8 words *(Krug p.125)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** low (1) — Krug's own weight line: high leverage per-pixel, but a single small element relative to the whole page.

# Cross-Surface Consistency

Pillar 4 in full: every element fits the app it lands in — same rule-set, same behavior, same vocabulary — while staying crafted. Two layers: internal system consistency (the screen obeys its own small rule-set) and sibling consistency (the screen matches the rest of the app).

---

### XCON-1 — Same role, same treatment — everywhere
**Rule.** Elements with one semantic role (primary buttons, card headers, severity chips, selection states, the same OBJECT class on different canvases/media) look and behave identically across every surface; visual difference is correctly read as meaning difference.
**Grounding.**
- *Universal Principles* (p.56): "According to the principle of consistency, systems are more usable and learnable when similar parts are expressed in similar ways. Consistency enables people to efficiently transfer knowledge to new contexts, learn new things quickly, and focus attention on the relevant aspects of a task." Mechanism: sameness lets learning transfer, so attention frees for the task instead of re-decoding each surface; the book names four kinds — aesthetic, functional, internal, external.
- *Designing Interfaces* (p.218): "If you have a few things 'of a type' and you want viewers to see them as equally interesting alternatives, give them an identical (and distinctive) graphic treatment." Mechanism: shared styling is a functional claim — a different treatment tells users (correctly or not) that the thing behaves differently.
- *About Face* (Ch17, p.431): the design-language argument — ad hoc per-screen choices, even individually fine, never accumulate into a coherent product.
**Objective test.** Build a role×surface matrix: for each recurring role/object class, list every rendering and interaction model across screens and media. All members of a class share the same {color, shape, corner-radius, size, position-in-group, interaction model} tuple; any role with >1 treatment absent a documented state reason (disabled/hover/selected) = defect. The same object class behaving differently on two sibling surfaces is the highest-severity form. Count deviations — 0 = internally consistent.
**✗ WRONG.** Delete is a red trash icon top-right on one screen, a grey "X" text link bottom-of-card on another; annotations on one canvas open popovers on click while the sibling canvas uses differently-styled inline panels for the same annotation objects.
**✓ RIGHT.** One destructive treatment, one confirm pattern, one position rule product-wide; one annotation grammar identical on every canvas the object appears on; a genuinely different role (destructive delete vs primary confirm) gets its own deliberately distinct, consistent treatment.
**Crop.** UP-15 (Universal Principles p.57 — identical logo/color/typeface across locations); Designing Interfaces Fig. 4-13 (p.219).
**Score (0–10).**
> - **0** — a recurring pattern (delete action, status badge, primary button, same object class on different canvases) has a different color/icon/position per screen with no functional justification *(source: Universal Principles — Consistency p.56; Designing Interfaces — Gestalt Similarity Fig.4-13 p.218)*.
> - **2** — consistent within one section but breaks in 1-2 other areas of the product — a partial audit fail *(Universal Principles — Consistency p.56)*.
> - **3** — same-role controls mostly consistent but one unexplained outlier exists in a class of ≥4 same-role controls *(Designing Interfaces — Gestalt Similarity p.218)*.
> - **5 — THRESHOLD:** zero unjustified deviations found in a full instance audit of a given recurring pattern (same icon/color/position/wording everywhere it appears); every member of a same-action-class shares the {color, shape, corner-radius, size} tuple, any outlier a documented state (disabled/hover/selected) *(Universal Principles — Consistency p.56; Designing Interfaces — Gestalt Similarity p.218)*.
> - **6** — threshold met AND the same object class behaves identically (interaction model, not just look) on every sibling surface/canvas it appears on *[derived — extends the visual-match test both books define to the behavioral dimension the principle's own Rule names]*.
> - **7** — threshold met across MULTIPLE recurring role classes (≥3), not just one spot-checked pattern, including internal consistency across the design system's own building blocks *(Universal Principles — Consistency p.56)*.
> - **8** — + recurring actions (delete, confirm, close) hold the same position-in-group on every surface, zero deviations *(Universal Principles — Consistency "position" dimension p.56)*.
> - **9** — + genuinely distinct roles (destructive vs primary) each carry their OWN consistent, deliberately distinct treatment, used to signal the difference *(Designing Interfaces — Fig.4-13 "distinguishing one item via a deliberate accent" p.219)*.
> - **10** — all four kinds — aesthetic, functional, internal, external — verified consistent, including alignment with platform/external convention where relevant *(Universal Principles — Consistency p.56-57, the Bob Evans franchise-identity standard)*.
> Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — Universal Principles: high; Designing Interfaces (Gestalt Similarity): high.

### XCON-2 — A design language: few recurring visual words
**Rule.** A deliberate vocabulary — a corner radius, an accent, a card treatment, a type scale, a copy tone — recurs across screens and accumulates into a recognizable product feel; per-screen invention never adds up.
**Grounding.**
- *About Face* (Ch17, p.431): "Think of this design language as a 'vocabulary' of design elements such as shape, color, typography, and how these elements are composed and combined. They create the appropriate emotional tone and establish patterns that a person can recognize, understand, and, ideally, use to create positive associations with the brand." Mechanism: recognition and brand association come from composition of a small vocabulary, not from any single good screen.
- *Refactoring UI* (p.20, p.25): "Every design has some sort of personality... a lot of it is determined by a few solid, concrete factors" — typeface voice, color, border radius, copy tone are chosen once; on radius specifically: "Whatever you choose, it's important to stay consistent. Mixing square corners with rounded corners in the same interface almost always looks worse than sticking with one or the other." Mechanism: each axis telegraphs personality; independently-decided components send contradictory signals.
**Objective test.** A reviewer unfamiliar with the internal system names the product's 3–5 recurring visual words (radius, accent, card treatment, type scale, tone) after seeing 3 unrelated screens — and can predict a 4th screen's styling from them. Failure to name a consistent set = language missing. Secondary check: exactly one radius convention (square OR rounded) across the interface; mixed conventions = fail.
**✗ WRONG.** Screen A: 4px-radius flat cards; screen B: 16px-radius shadowed cards; screen C: square outlined cards — three personalities, no product.
**✓ RIGHT.** One radius, one elevation token, one accent for primary actions, one copy register — screen D's styling is guessable sight-unseen.
**Crop.** RU-32 (Refactoring UI pp.20–26 personality axes).
**Score (0–10).**
> - **0** — 3 unrelated screens each invent their own vocabulary (corner radius, card treatment) with zero overlap *(source: About Face — design language Ch.17 p.431)*.
> - **2** — only 1 of 3–5 vocabulary elements (radius, accent, card style, type scale, copy tone) is shared across screens; the rest vary *(About Face p.431)*.
> - **3** — 2 of 4 personality axes (typeface/color/radius/tone) are internally consistent, 2 are not *(Refactoring UI — Coherent personality pp.313-320)*.
> - **4** — 3 of 4 axes internally consistent, one still drifting (commonly copy tone, least visually obvious) *(Refactoring UI p.316)*.
> - **5 — THRESHOLD:** a reviewer unfamiliar with the system, shown 3 unrelated screens, names a consistent set of 3–5 recurring visual words *(About Face p.431 — the book's stated test)*.
> - **6** — exactly one radius convention (square OR rounded) across the interface *(Refactoring UI p.20 — "mixing square corners with rounded corners... almost always looks worse")*.
> - **7** — all 3–5 named words are consistent AND consistently applied across every screen sampled (not just the 3 tested), no screen the odd one out *(About Face p.431)*.
> - **8** — all four personality axes internally consistent across the product, and the chosen direction plausibly matches the stated brand goal *(Refactoring UI pp.313-320)*.
> - **9** — the reviewer correctly PREDICTS a 4th, unseen screen's styling in advance from the named words *(About Face p.431 — the ✓ prediction standard)*.
> - **10** — matches the ✓ state fully: one radius everywhere, one consistent copy register, color and typeface both deliberately chosen and consistently applied, reinforcing a single coherent personality end to end *(Refactoring UI pp.20-26, 313-320; About Face p.431)*.
> Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** med (2) — Refactoring UI: medium; About Face: med-high (leans high at whole-product scale — noted, majority med for a per-surface review).

### XCON-3 — Small-rule-set repetition is the designed-vs-assembled tell
**Rule.** "Designed" shows as repetition of a constrained set (spacing increments, palette, radii, type steps) across the WHOLE surface; one beautiful component beside a default-styled one reads assembled even when each passes alone.
**Grounding.**
- *Designing Interfaces* (pp.216–217): "Creating a design that is based on a grid... allows the designer to focus on the content, assured that the layout will have visual consistency and balance"; "Using a grid is a good way to ensure that the content will create a visually harmonious composition, and will aid in reducing the cognitive load of your viewer." Its spacing-audit framing (Ch.5 argument, p.493 area): values clustering on a repeated scale = designed; scattered ad hoc = assembled regardless of individual component quality — the mechanism for "designed vs assembled" is repetition of a constrained visual system, not any single nice element.
- *About Face* (Ch17, p.423): "Unnecessary variation is the enemy of a coherent, usable design. If the spacing between two sets of elements is nearly the same, make that spacing exactly the same... Every visual element and every difference in color, size, or other visual property should be there for a reason." Mechanism: near-identical-but-not-identical values read as unintentional sloppiness even when each instance looks acceptable alone.
- *Refactoring UI* (pp.70–74, also 28–32): "If you want a system to be truly useful, it needs to take into consideration the relative difference between adjacent values" (p.71); rule of thumb: "make sure no two values in your scale are ever closer than about 25%" (p.72). Mechanism: pre-defined scales exist precisely to force this repetition and kill imperceptible distinctions.
**Objective test.** Sample ≥10 padding/margin values, all radii, all type sizes, all colors per screen: each clusters on the defined scale (e.g. 4/8/16/24px); ad-hoc values (11/17/9px), adjacent scale steps differing by <25%, near-duplicate colors doing one job, or browser-default controls beside styled ones = assembled.
**✗ WRONG.** A custom toggle beside an unstyled default dropdown with improvised 11px/17px padding between them — each element acceptable, the surface a patchwork.
**✓ RIGHT.** Every control on the same spacing scale, radius, and palette — one deliberate system; the toggle and dropdown are visibly siblings.
**Crop.** DI-06 (Fig. 4-8 gridless vs gridded, pp.216–217), RU-03 (pp.70–74 spacing-scale bar chart).
**Score (0–10).**
> - **0** — major block edges scattered across many one-off x-coordinates (12/18/15/22px picked by eye), no discernible grid; adjacent scale values differ by <10% with no relationship between them *(source: Designing Interfaces — grid pp.216-217/52-59; Refactoring UI — non-linear scales pp.70-74/79-85)*.
> - **2** — a grid loosely followed for some elements but broken by ≥30% of blocks; some scale steps meet the 25% threshold, others (especially at the small end) don't *(Designing Interfaces pp.216-217; Refactoring UI p.72 "no two values... closer than about 25%")*.
> - **3** — a near-duplicate value serving one functional role exists (two non-identical values within 20% doing the same job) *(About Face p.423 — "unnecessary variation is the enemy of a coherent design")*.
> - **4** — a browser-default control renders beside a custom-styled one, but only in a secondary/low-traffic region *[derived — the principle's own ✗ patchwork case, scoped to severity by traffic]*.
> - **5 — THRESHOLD:** distinct major-block edge x-values on the page ≤4–6 (a real grid system in use); every adjacent spacing/type-scale step ≥~25% apart *(Designing Interfaces pp.216-217; Refactoring UI p.72)*.
> - **6** — both the radius set and the type-size set are each closed (every observed value is a member of one defined scale) *(Refactoring UI p.20/pp.313-320 — one radius convention; #9 scale-membership mechanism)*.
> - **7** — margins and gutters are visually distinct and consistently sized (e.g. one 8px-unit scale) across all page regions; the scale is deliberate and sufficiently dense (~10+ steps) *(Designing Interfaces pp.216-217; Refactoring UI p.72 "a deliberate, sufficiently-dense scale")*.
> - **8** — zero near-duplicate values for one job anywhere on the surface *(About Face p.423 — "make that spacing exactly the same")*.
> - **9** — no default/styled patchwork anywhere, even in secondary regions; grid holds across MULTIPLE pages in the product, not just one screen *(Designing Interfaces pp.216-217 — cross-page harmony)*.
> - **10** — matches the ✓ examples fully: one deliberate spacing/radius/palette system with zero one-off values, verified across ≥2 pages *(Refactoring UI pp.70-74; Designing Interfaces pp.216-219)*.
> Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — Designing Interfaces (grid; spacing-audit): high; Refactoring UI (scales): high; About Face (unnecessary variation): med — majority high, AF dissent noted.

### XCON-4 — Consistency without rigidity; diverge in the spirit
**Rule.** Obey standards and the product's own idioms unless a truly superior alternative exists; when diverging, honor the spirit of the pattern — and when clarity and consistency genuinely conflict, clarity wins, stated as an explicit tradeoff.
**Grounding.**
- *About Face* (Ch17, pp.430–431): "Obey standards unless there is a truly superior alternative"; "Consistency doesn't imply rigidity." The book's own case: PowerPoint forced into Word/Excel's menu structure "doesn't gain much... It also loses quite a bit in ease of use by conforming to an alien structure that diverges from the user's mental models" — yet PowerPoint rightly keeps its unique slide-sorter. Mechanism: blind conformity produces awkward interfaces; un-anchored novelty breaks learned expectations — the fix is judged divergence with a stated reason.
- *Don't Make Me Think* (p.56): "CLARITY TRUMPS CONSISTENCY. If you can make something significantly clearer by making it slightly inconsistent, choose in favor of clarity." Mechanism: consistency is valuable but subordinate — it exists to serve comprehension, not to override it.
- *Universal Principles* (p.56, note 1): quotes Emerson's "A foolish consistency is the hobgoblin of little minds" in the margin — the book's own caveat against consistency for its own sake.
**Objective test.** Every divergence from platform convention or the product's own established pattern carries a one-line written rationale naming the concrete advantage; divergences with none on file = fail. Clarity-vs-consistency conflicts resolve via an explicit stated "clarity gain X / consistency cost Y" — never silently defaulted to "match the system" or "break the system".
**✗ WRONG.** A one-off left-aligned checkbox where every sibling screen uses right-aligned toggles, no reason on file; a destructive "Delete all" button forced system-grey "for consistency".
**✓ RIGHT.** The established toggle everywhere, or a documented "toggle can't express Off/Auto/On → dropdown"; "Delete all" deliberately rendered red — a stated clarity-over-consistency call about risk.
**Crop.** none.
**Score (0–10).**
> - **0** — a control diverges from platform or the product's own established pattern for the same job with zero documented rationale; AND a clarity-critical signal (destructive action) is forced into system-wide consistency with no acknowledgment of the cost *(source: About Face — Consistency Ch.17 p.430-431; Don't Make Me Think — Clarity trumps consistency p.56, p.81-89)*.
> - **2** — a divergence exists with a rationale, but it doesn't cite a genuine functional advantage (just preference/deadline) *(About Face p.430-431)*.
> - **3** — a clarity-vs-consistency conflict wasn't noticed/considered at all — outcome may accidentally be fine, but no reasoning trail exists *(Don't Make Me Think p.56)*.
> - **4** — the conflict is noticed and a choice is made, but the tradeoff isn't stated/documented anywhere *(Don't Make Me Think p.56)*.
> - **5 — THRESHOLD:** every divergence from convention has a written one-line rationale citing a specific advantage *(About Face p.430-431 — the book's own bar)*.
> - **6** — the tradeoff is stated and the choice reasonably favors clarity where it matters, with only minor unexplained residue elsewhere *(Don't Make Me Think p.56)*.
> - **7** — no unjustified divergences AND at least one divergence is a clear case of "truly superior alternative" correctly applied *(About Face p.431 — dropdown replacing a toggle that can't express tri-state)*.
> - **8** — every destructive/high-risk action keeps a visually distinctive treatment even against system uniformity *[derived — converges Don't Make Me Think's "Delete all" case with About Face's "obey standards unless truly superior" caveat]*.
> - **9** — consistent with established convention everywhere it should be, with occasional, well-reasoned, clearly-labeled departures that don't fight the user's mental model *(About Face p.431 — PowerPoint's slide-sorter case)*.
> - **10** — every clarity-vs-consistency conflict is explicitly reasoned and resolved in clarity's favor where it counts, zero silent defaults either way *(Don't Make Me Think p.56 — the red "Delete all" ✓ case)*.
> Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** med (2) — About Face: med; Don't Make Me Think (clarity trumps consistency): med.

### XCON-5 — Almost-consistent is worse than clearly different (uncanny valley)
**Rule.** A component ALMOST matching the system — near-radius, near-color, familiar-but-tweaked — reads as more wrong than a clearly distinct one; fix by full consistency or deliberate, obvious difference, never "almost".
**Grounding.**
- *Universal Principles* (p.242): "When a form is very close but not identical to a healthy human—as with a mannequin or computer-generated renderings of people—the form tends to become distinctly unappealing." Contributing conditions listed directly: "Abnormally proportioned or positioned facial features, asymmetry of facial features, subtleties of eye movement, and unnatural skin complexions are all sufficient conditions to trigger uncanny valley effects." Mechanism (via the book's own consistency cross-link): small deviations in proportion or subtle properties are sufficient triggers — so a partially-applied design system is not "a little off", it reads BROKEN, more wrong than an obviously different treatment; the two stable states are identical or clearly distinct.
**Objective test.** Token-diff a new component against the system across every axis — spacing, color tokens, radius, type scale, motion curves: the result must be 100% match, or a deliberately distinct, documented, visibly different treatment. 1–2 near-miss properties (e.g. matched colors but a subtly different radius) = the uncanny zone, fail.
**✗ WRONG.** New feature buttons use the exact system colors and spacing but a subtly different radius and shadow — users can't say what's wrong, only that it feels broken.
**✓ RIGHT.** Radius and shadow matched exactly to the system tokens; or the feature visibly restyled as a distinct, labeled treatment nobody mistakes for the standard one.
**Crop.** UP-12 (Universal Principles p.242 uncanny-valley curve).
**Score (0–10).**
> - **0** — a component claims to match an existing design system but deviates on 1-2 properties (corner-radius, shadow) while matching everything else — reads as "broken," not intentional *(source: Universal Principles — Uncanny Valley p.242)*.
> - **2** — the deviation is reduced to a single subtle property but still triggers an "almost right" perception on close inspection *(Universal Principles p.242)*.
> - **3** — only a partial/spot-check audit exists, not a full token diff across all six axes *[derived — from the principle's own Measure: "audit every token... count partial/near-match deviations"]*.
> - **4** — a deliberately distinct component exists but is visibly different yet undocumented/unlabeled *[derived — from the principle's own ✓ case requiring a "clearly-marked" distinct treatment]*.
> - **5 — THRESHOLD:** the component is either 100% consistent with the system's tokens (spacing/color/type/motion) OR deliberately, visibly styled as a distinct treatment (e.g. clearly-marked beta) — never "almost the same" *(Universal Principles p.242)*.
> - **6** — a full side-by-side token audit is performed across ALL six axes {spacing, color, radius, type, shadow, motion}, not spot-checked *(Universal Principles p.242 — the book's own Measure)*.
> - **7** — threshold met and verified via that full audit, with recorded values per component on every axis *(Universal Principles p.242)*.
> - **8** — any deliberately distinct component differs on ≥2 axes at a clearly visible magnitude AND is documented/labeled as distinct *(Universal Principles p.242 — mechanism of the ✓ case)*.
> - **9** — zero "almost right" components found across a full audit of the surface *(Universal Principles p.242)*.
> - **10** — matches the book's own standard exactly: full consistency or an unmistakably distinct, intentional treatment, with zero "almost right" components found anywhere on the audited surface *(Universal Principles p.242)*.
> Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** med (2) — Universal Principles: med.

### XCON-6 — Interaction continuity: name-match and landing contracts
**Rule.** What you click matches where you land (link label ≈ destination heading); deep entries (notification, search, shared link) land on the specific target, never a generic top screen. Consistency includes behavior across time, not just style across space.
**Grounding.**
- *Don't Make Me Think* (p.106): "Every site makes an implicit social contract with its visitors: The name of the page will match the words I clicked to get there... Each time a site violates it, I'm forced to think, even if only for milliseconds, 'Why are those two things different?' And if there's a major discrepancy... my trust in the site—and the competence of the people who publish it—will be diminished." Mechanism: each mismatch is a micro-doubt tax that compounds into distrust.
- *Don't Make Me Think* (p.185): "Don't leave me standing at the front door. Another real nuisance: You tap on a link in an email or a social media site and instead of taking you to the article in question it takes you to the mobile Home page, leaving you to hunt for the thing yourself." Mechanism: a generic landing converts a completed navigation into a fresh search the user never asked for.
**Objective test.** Click-test every primary nav/CTA label against the destination H1/page title using string similarity: flag any pair with <70% token overlap that lacks an obviously-equivalent phrasing (Krug's own tolerated case: "Gifts for Him" → "Gifts for Men"). Separately, verify every external entry point (email link, push notification, shared URL, search-result link) resolves to the specific referenced content; any landing on Home/a generic feed instead = fail, zero tolerance.
**✗ WRONG.** Nav "Pricing" → H1 "Plans & Packages" with no echo of "Pricing" above the fold; a "Your order has shipped" notification opening the generic home feed, leaving the user to find the order.
**✓ RIGHT.** "Pricing" → "Pricing"; the notification opens that order's tracking detail screen directly.
**Crop.** none (prose-only, pp.106/185).
**Score (0–10).**
> - **0** — a nav label and its destination's H1 share no discernible relationship, with no visual echo anywhere above the fold; AND/OR an entry point lands on a generic home/feed, forcing the user to re-navigate manually *(source: Don't Make Me Think — name-match p.106, deep-link integrity p.185)*.
> - **2** — token overlap is <70% and the mismatch is not an obviously-equivalent reworking *(Don't Make Me Think p.106)*.
> - **3** — an entry point lands closer to the target (the right section) but not the specific item, still requiring extra navigation *(Don't Make Me Think p.185)*.
> - **4** — token overlap is borderline (~60–70%) or the relationship is inferable but requires a beat of thought *(Don't Make Me Think p.106)*.
> - **5 — THRESHOLD:** token overlap ≥70% (an accepted equivalent phrasing counts — "Gifts for Him" → "Gifts for Men"); an entry point lands on the correct content though it may drop context (right order, wrong tab) *(Don't Make Me Think p.106, p.185)*.
> - **6** — wherever label and H1 differ, the clicked word appears somewhere above the fold on the destination *(Don't Make Me Think p.106 — "implicit social contract")*.
> - **7** — every deep entry point lands on the exact referenced content with only cosmetic loss of context *(Don't Make Me Think p.185)*.
> - **8** — the same label leads to the same destination everywhere it appears, zero exceptions *[derived — the name-match contract applied product-wide per Don't Make Me Think p.106]*.
> - **9** — label and destination H1 match exactly or near-exactly with zero ambiguity across the primary nav *(Don't Make Me Think p.106 — the ✓ "Pricing"→"Pricing" case)*.
> - **10** — every external entry point (email link, push notification, shared URL, search result) lands precisely on the referenced content in full context, zero extra navigation required, anywhere on the product *(Don't Make Me Think p.185 — "Zero tolerance")*.
> Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — Don't Make Me Think: deep-link integrity high ("zero tolerance"), name-match med — split within the source noted; the zero-tolerance half carries the majority of the principle's points, so high.

### XCON-7 — Persistent chrome is a stability promise
**Rule.** Global navigation (site ID, sections, ≤5 utilities, search) appears in the same place, style, and item set on every screen (focused task flows — checkout, registration — excepted).
**Grounding.**
- *Don't Make Me Think* (p.97, p.101): "Persistent navigation should include the four elements you most need to have on hand" — Site ID, Sections, Utilities, Search — with the constraint: "the persistent navigation can accommodate only four or five Utilities—the ones users are likely to need most often. If you try to squeeze in more than that, they tend to get lost in the crowd." Mechanism: navigation that stays put on every page is what lets users stop re-orienting; crowding utilities destroys the very findability the chrome exists to provide.
**Objective test.** Diff the nav's item set, position, and styling across ≥5 representative pages (excluding declared checkout/registration exceptions): zero unexplained differences allowed; count of persistent utility items ≤5.
**✗ WRONG.** 8 utilities on the home page, 5 different ones on the product page, the logo migrating from left to center between sections.
**✓ RIGHT.** Identical nav — same items, same positions, same styling — on every non-checkout page; ≤5 utilities, the rest tucked behind an account/More entry.
**Crop.** KR-04 (Ch.6 persistent-navigation anatomy diagram, "XYZ Corp." Site ID / Utilities / Sections / Subsections, p.97 area).
**Score (0–10).**
> - **0** — nav item set, position, or styling changes substantially across pages with no declared exception (logo migrating, item count/set differing) *(source: Don't Make Me Think p.97, p.101)*.
> - **2** — nav is mostly stable but ≥2 unexplained differences exist across a 5-page sample *(Don't Make Me Think p.97, p.101)*.
> - **3** — more than 5 persistent utility items crowd the chrome *(Don't Make Me Think p.101 — "the persistent navigation can accommodate only four or five Utilities... more tends to get lost")*.
> - **4** — nav stable in position and core sections, but 1 unexplained utility-item or styling difference remains *(Don't Make Me Think p.97, p.101)*.
> - **5 — THRESHOLD:** utility items ≤5; nav stable in position and core sections across the sample *(Don't Make Me Think p.101)*.
> - **6** — all four required elements — Site ID, Sections, Utilities, Search — present in the chrome on every sampled page *(Don't Make Me Think p.97 — persistent-navigation anatomy)*.
> - **7** — nav identical across all sampled pages except declared exceptions (checkout/registration), utility count ≤5 *(Don't Make Me Think p.97, p.101)*.
> - **8** — chrome is dropped only on declared focused flows, which still retain the Site ID *[derived — from the principle's own exception framing]*.
> - **9** — zero unexplained differences across any sampled page, utility items clearly the most-needed ones *(Don't Make Me Think p.97, p.101)*.
> - **10** — matches the ✓ case exactly: identical nav — same items, positions, styling — on every non-checkout page, ≤5 utilities, the rest tucked behind an account/More entry *(Don't Make Me Think p.97, p.101)*.
> Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — Don't Make Me Think: high (page-diff measurable, high blast radius).

### XCON-8 — Depth doesn't decay; output stays conservative
**Rule.** The visual system, spacing, and indicator logic established at nav level 1 persists into levels 2–3+ (where systems usually go ad hoc); and the product's own OUTPUT (formats, ordering, phrasing, layout) stays reliable and consistent while INPUT tolerance stays liberal.
**Grounding.**
- *Don't Make Me Think* (p.104): "In so many sites, as soon as you get past the second level, the navigation breaks down and becomes ad hoc. The problem is so common that it's actually hard to find good examples of third-level navigation." Krug's cited reasons: designers run out of time on levels 1–2 and stakeholders under-invest — yet "the reality is that users usually end up spending as much time on lower-level pages as they do at the top." Mechanism: effort is allocated by org attention, but user exposure is flat across depth — so decay at depth hits users exactly as often as the polished top.
- *Laws of UX* (Postel, p.53–54): "Be conservative in what you do, be liberal in what you accept from others." Mechanism: the conservative half is an output-consistency mandate — the system's own emissions (formats, orderings, generated layouts) must be dependable precisely so that variability can be absorbed on the input side.
**Objective test.** Compare spacing unit, indicator style, and grouping logic at nav level 1 vs the deepest level: same tokens; any one-off pattern appearing only at depth = fail. Product outputs (dates, currency, orderings, generated layouts) byte-consistent across every surface that emits them — diff exported/rendered values across screens; >1 format for the same datum = fail.
**✗ WRONG.** Level-1 tabs with a clean active underline; level-3 an unstyled bullet list with no active state; export dates formatted three ways ("2026-07-24", "Jul 24", "24/07/26") across three screens.
**✓ RIGHT.** Level-3 reuses the level-1 treatment one indent deeper — same tokens, same active-state grammar; one date format everywhere the product emits one.
**Crop.** none.
**Score (0–10).**
> - **0** — the deepest level abandons the level-1 system entirely (unstyled bullet list, no active-state indicator at all); AND/OR product outputs (dates, currency, orderings) render in ≥3 different formats across the surfaces that emit them *(source: Don't Make Me Think — multi-level nav p.104; Laws of UX — Postel's Law p.53-54 "be conservative in what you do" [derived] extended to output-format consistency)*.
> - **2** — the deepest level uses some structure but a materially different visual language (different spacing unit, no active-state at all) *(Don't Make Me Think p.104)*.
> - **3** — exactly one emitted datum has two competing formats across surfaces *[derived — Postel's output-conservatism mechanism, p.53-54]*.
> - **4** — the deepest level has an active-state indicator and consistent spacing, but introduces ≥1 one-off pattern not used at level 1 *(Don't Make Me Think p.104)*.
> - **5 — THRESHOLD:** the deepest level matches level-1 tokens closely, with only minor cosmetic drift; exactly one format per emitted datum, product-wide *(Don't Make Me Think p.104; [derived] Postel's Law p.53-54)*.
> - **6** — the same active-state indicator grammar is present at every level, on the same channels as level 1 *(Don't Make Me Think p.104 — "same underline/bold treatment, one indent deeper")*.
> - **7** — exports/generated layouts diffed across emitting surfaces show the same structure with only minor styling drift *[derived — Postel's conservative-output mechanism applied to generated artifacts]*.
> - **8** — the deepest level uses identical design tokens (spacing, indicator style, grouping logic) as level 1, just nested deeper *(Don't Make Me Think p.104 — the book's own ✓ standard)*.
> - **9** — exports/generated layouts are byte/structure-identical across all emitting surfaces *[derived — strict form of Postel's conservative-output mandate, p.53-54]*.
> - **10** — matches the ✓ case fully: level-3 reuses the level-1 treatment one indent deeper with zero one-off patterns, and one format holds everywhere the product emits a given datum, verified across every level and every emitting surface *(Don't Make Me Think p.104; Laws of UX p.53-54 [derived])*.
> Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** med (2) — Don't Make Me Think (multi-level rigor): med; Laws of UX (Postel): high, but its high rating is grounded chiefly in the input/forms half, which lives in FORM-1/3 — majority med for the output/depth half here, split noted.

### XCON-9 — New-surface intake rule [derived]
**Rule.** Any NEW element/surface starts from the app's existing vocabulary — read the sibling screens first, reuse their tokens/components/behaviors, then craft within that envelope. "Crafted" and "native" are simultaneous: an improvement ignoring the household style is a pillar-4 regression even when beautiful in isolation; and an improvement applied to one surface without its siblings creates the divergence XCON-1 forbids.
**Grounding.**
- *About Face* (Ch17, pp.430–431): "Obey standards unless there is a truly superior alternative"; "Consistency doesn't imply rigidity" — the internal standard is the default envelope, divergence only in spirit and with a reason.
- *Designing Interfaces* (pp.216–218): grid + similarity — "the layout will have visual consistency and balance"; same-type things get "an identical (and distinctive) graphic treatment" — the repeated small rule-set IS what a new surface must be assembled from.
- *Universal Principles* (p.242): forms "very close but not identical" to the familiar turn "distinctly unappealing" — partial adoption of the house style lands the new surface in the uncanny zone, not the crafted zone.
- Convergence: no single book frames the intake procedure, but all three entail it — the existing vocabulary is the standard to obey (About Face), the rule-set to repeat (Designing Interfaces), and the thing you must match fully or diverge from visibly (Universal Principles).
**Objective test.** Before a new surface's first unit: the token/component inventory of ≥2 sibling screens is extracted and cited; the new surface's tokens diff clean against it (the XCON-5 100%-or-deliberately-distinct test); any improvement introduced (a better popover, a new chip style) is either propagated to all surfaces sharing the role in the same change or logged as an approved, written staged migration.
**✗ WRONG.** A new tab built in a visibly different idiom than its neighbors — new radius, new spacing, new control styles; a redesigned marker style shipped on one canvas while sibling canvases keep the old one, with no migration plan.
**✓ RIGHT.** The new tab assembled from the app's own components and tokens, with craft spent inside that envelope; the improved marker rolled out to every canvas in the same change, or its staged rollout explicitly approved and logged.
**Crop.** none (procedure).
**Score (0–10).** [derived — rungs built from this entry's own Objective test, converging the three books named in its Grounding]
