> - **0** — the new surface is built in a visibly different idiom than its neighbors (new radius, spacing, control styles), with no sibling inventory taken *[derived — About Face p.430 "obey standards" violated at the first step; Designing Interfaces grid/similarity absent, pp.216-218]*.
> - **2** — a token/component inventory exists from only one sibling screen, not the required ≥2 *[derived — from this entry's own Objective test]*.
> - **3** — ≥2 near-miss axes surface when the new surface is token-diffed against the inventory *(Universal Principles — Uncanny Valley p.242, applied to the new-surface case)*.
> - **4** — ≥1 newly-invented control duplicates a role an existing component already serves *(Designing Interfaces — Gestalt Similarity p.218)*.
> - **5 — THRESHOLD:** a token/component inventory of ≥2 sibling screens is extracted and cited before the new surface's first unit *[derived — from this entry's Objective test, converging About Face p.430-431, Designing Interfaces pp.216-218, Universal Principles p.242]*.
> - **6** — exactly one near-miss axis when the new surface is diffed against the inventory *(Universal Principles p.242)*.
> - **7** — every recurring role on the new surface uses the app's existing components *(Designing Interfaces p.218)*.
> - **8** — the new surface is a 100% token match against the inventory, or a deliberately distinct, documented treatment *(Universal Principles p.242 — the ✓ standard)*.
> - **9** — any improved treatment introduced (better popover, new chip style) is propagated to all surfaces sharing the role in the same change, or a written staged migration exists and is approved/logged *(About Face p.430-431 — "truly superior alternative" correctly applied and documented)*.
> - **10** — matches the ✓ case fully: the new surface is assembled entirely from the app's own components and tokens, craft spent inside that envelope, and any improvement is rolled out product-wide or explicitly staged/approved *[derived — convergence of About Face pp.430-431, Designing Interfaces pp.216-218, Universal Principles p.242]*.
> Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** med (2) — derived: constituents rate About Face (standards/rigidity) med, Universal Principles (uncanny) med, Designing Interfaces (similarity/grid) high — majority med.

## Scoring-conversion notes — cross-book observable-definition conflicts
1. **Near-duplicate threshold (XCON-3).** About Face's expert defines a near-duplicate as two non-identical values for one role within **20%** of each other; Refactoring UI's expert anchors the minimum legitimate separation of adjacent *scale steps* at **≥25%** (with <10% as the 0-band). The two thresholds measure different objects (role-duplicates vs scale-step spacing) and are kept on separate criteria (C3 vs C1/C2), but reviewers should note the 20–25% band is contested territory between the books.
2. **Weight splits (noted in the Weight lines).** XCON-2: About Face med-high vs Refactoring UI medium → med. XCON-3: About Face med vs Designing Interfaces/Refactoring UI high → high. XCON-6: name-match med vs deep-link high (same source book, two entries) → high. XCON-8: Krug med vs Postel high (Postel's high is grounded in the input half, filed under FORM-1/3) → med.
No other genuine observable-definition conflicts found: the books' tests for consistency, design language, uncanny near-match, nav diffing, and landing contracts are complementary rather than contradictory.

# Data & Money Legibility

Numbers must tell a story a scanning eye can follow — especially derived money (totals, rollups, coverage, net). Pillars: 2, 3.

---

### DATA-1 — Preattentive encoding makes the important value findable in constant time
**Rule.** Hue, brightness, saturation, size, position/alignment, orientation, shape, texture are processed before conscious attention; a table of uniform values forces linear reading (search ∝ N) — encode the values that matter on one preattentive channel so they pop in O(1).
**Grounding.** Designing Interfaces: "Certain visual features operate preattentively: they convey information before the viewer pays conscious attention" (p.436). The book's demonstrated exercise — "find the blue objects" among many red ones: "it doesn't matter how many red objects there are; the amount of time it takes you to find the blue ones is constant!... Color operates at a primitive cognitive level" (p.436). The text contrast: "When dealing with text such as this, your 'search time' really is linear with the number of items. But what if we still use text, but make the target numbers physically larger than the others?... Now we're back to constant time again. Size is, in fact, another preattentive variable" (p.437). The eight variables are given as a reference grid (Fig. 9-5, p.438). Mechanism: constant-vs-linear search time is the measurable difference between "the numbers feel flat" and a display that reads itself — preattentive channels shift outlier-finding from serial reading to parallel perception.
**Objective test.** In a table/dashboard of ≥20 same-class values, estimate how search time for an outlier scales with row count: if the only differentiator is reading each value in turn (search ∝ N, linear), preattentive encoding is absent — fail. If the exceptional value is coded via one of the 8 variables (hue, brightness, saturation, size, position/alignment, orientation, shape, texture), search is effectively O(1) — pass. Exceptional values styled identically to routine ones = fail.
**✗ WRONG.** A 70-row financial table renders every value in the same 12px black type; the one threshold-breaching value is discoverable only by reading all 70 rows in sequence.
**✓ RIGHT.** Out-of-threshold values rendered in a visibly larger size and/or a distinct color — they pop instantly regardless of table length.
**Crop.** DI-01 (Fig. 9-1/9-2 constant-time color search p.436; Fig. 9-3/9-4 linear-vs-constant via size p.437; Fig. 9-5 eight-variable grid p.438).
**Score (0–10 ladder).**
> - **0** — outlier/exceptional value discoverable only by reading every row in sequence; search time ∝ N *(source: Designing Interfaces p.436-437, Fig. 9-1–9-4)*.
> - **3** — a preattentive cue is used but weakly (e.g. a barely-larger font, <1.3× size ratio) so search stays closer to linear than constant *(Designing Interfaces p.437, Fig. 9-3/9-4)*.
> - **5 — THRESHOLD:** every exceptional/threshold-breaching value is encoded on ≥1 of the 8 preattentive variables (hue, brightness, saturation, size, position/alignment, orientation, shape, texture) strongly enough that search is effectively O(1) *(Designing Interfaces p.436-438, Fig. 9-5)*.
> - **6** — as 5, and no exceptional value is styled identically to routine values (no coverage gaps) *(Designing Interfaces p.436)*.
> - **7** — the encoding is consistent/systemized across the whole table or dashboard — every outlier class gets its own reliable cue *(Designing Interfaces p.438)*.
> - **8** — as 7, and the pop encoding stays selective (routine values remain quiet, roughly ≤10% of visible values carry it) so the exceptional ones keep winning *(Designing Interfaces p.436-438, [derived] selectivity corollary)*.
> - **9** — multiple reinforcing preattentive channels used at once for critical values (e.g. size + color) *(Designing Interfaces p.437, Fig. 9-4 pattern)*.
> - **10** — the reinforced encoding is verified to "pop" at any table length, in a 3-second glance, regardless of row count *(Designing Interfaces p.436-438)*.
> Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — Designing Interfaces marks it high for data-dense/dashboard surfaces.

### DATA-2 — One headline number; supporters subordinate and grouped
**Rule.** A data-dense region needs one dominant "most important number" (size/weight/position) with supporting figures visually subordinate and grouped next to their meaning.
**Grounding.** Krug: "The more important something is, the more prominent it is... Things that are related logically are related visually" plus visual nesting (pp.55–56); the extract's #29 applies this doctrine directly to numeric content — if the reader must read every number to find the story, the region fails the same don't-make-me-think test as prose, because every unresolved "wait, which number matters?" moment fills the thought balloon Krug's First Law forbids (p.29). Refactoring UI: "The problem with this approach is that it makes it difficult to present the data with any sort of hierarchy; every piece of data is given equal emphasis" (p.48); in dense scan-heavy contexts (dashboards/specs) the LABEL may lead because the user hunts for it (p.51), elsewhere the datum stars while its label shrinks — the heart-rate card keeps "HEART RATE" small and light while "82 BPM" is large and bold (pp.48–52). Mechanism: hierarchy pre-processes the region so the eye lands on the story instead of reconstructing it.
**Objective test.** Identify the region's most task-important figure by task relevance: it must render at strictly greater size/weight/contrast than every other number in the region, and every supporting number sits under a heading or proximity cluster tying it to its meaning. If a reader must read every number to find "the story," fail. Additionally: ≥3 fields in the literal `Label: Value` pattern at equal weight = fail unless it is a spec table scanned BY label.
**✗ WRONG.** Revenue, Cost, Tax, Refunds, Net Profit — all 16px grey in one flat unlabeled row; the reader computes the hierarchy in their head.
**✓ RIGHT.** "Net Profit $42,300" at 28px bold; the four contributors smaller, grouped beneath with a visible how-we-got-here path.
**Crop.** RU-01, RU-14.
**Score (0–10 ladder).**
> - **0** — all figures render at identical size/weight/contrast in a flat, unlabeled row; no headline figure exists *(source: Don't Make Me Think p.29,55-56, "flat Revenue/Cost/Tax/Refunds/Net-Profit row"; Refactoring UI p.48, "every piece of data given equal emphasis")*.
> - **2** — one figure is marginally larger but the difference is subtle enough to require a close look; grouping is absent *(Don't Make Me Think p.29)*.
> - **4** — ≥3 fields still run in literal equal-weight `Label: Value` form with no fix applied, even if a headline figure elsewhere is emerging *(Refactoring UI p.48-52, "Labels are a last resort")*.
> - **5 — THRESHOLD:** a headline figure clearly renders larger/bolder than every other number in the region on ≥1 of {size, weight, contrast}, AND no run of ≥3 fields sits in literal equal-weight `Label: Value` form (or the surface is a spec table scanned BY label — the sanctioned exception) *(Don't Make Me Think p.29; Refactoring UI p.48-52)*.
> - **6** — the headline figure wins on ≥2 of {size, weight, contrast} simultaneously, not just one *(Refactoring UI p.48-52, heart-rate card: "HEART RATE" small/light, "82 BPM" large/bold)*.
> - **7** — most supporting figures are grouped/labeled to show their relationship to the headline; one relationship remains unclear *(Don't Make Me Think p.29,55-56, "Things that are related logically are related visually")*.
> - **8** — every supporting number sits under a heading or inside a proximity cluster tying it to its meaning — zero floaters *(Don't Make Me Think p.55-56; Refactoring UI p.51, label-leads-in-scan-context exception correctly applied)*.
> - **9** — under a blur/3-second glance the eye lands on the headline figure first, with zero re-scanning needed *(Don't Make Me Think p.29, "First Law")*.
> - **10** — one figure unambiguously reads as "the story" via strictly greater size/weight/contrast, and every other figure is grouped/labeled to show how it contributes — matches the ✓ "Net Profit: $42,300" case *(Don't Make Me Think p.29,55-56; Refactoring UI p.48-52)*.
> Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — Krug's expert marks it high (frequent dashboard failure mode); Refactoring UI's hierarchy entry high; RU's label entry medium (minority).

### DATA-3 — Enforce comparisons; numbers without context are inert
**Rule.** Show related values, baselines, trends, before/after side by side; never force the user to remember and mentally reconstruct the comparison.
**Grounding.** About Face (Tufte's "enforce visual comparisons" grand principle applied): "You should provide a means for users to compare related variables and trends or to compare before-and-after scenarios. Comparison provides a context that makes the information more valuable and comprehensible to users" (p.426). The cited case: a multi-stock chart lets a viewer "see that Barclays Bank (BCS) and UBS are closely correlated to each other and only loosely correlate to the S&P 500" (Fig. 17-6 caption, p.426) — a judgment impossible from three separate single-line charts read in sequence. Mechanism: working memory cannot hold one chart while decoding another; co-presence is what makes correlation and good/bad judgments possible at all.
**Objective test.** Any standalone metric with zero comparator (prior period, target, peer, or trend) in the SAME view = flag. For related series, verify they render on one shared canvas/axis rather than in separate sequential views the user must page between.
**✗ WRONG.** "Revenue: $482K" alone — good or bad? The user opens another report to know.
**✓ RIGHT.** "$482K ▲12% vs last month" with a 6-month sparkline inline.
**Crop.** AF-08 (Fig. 17-6, Google Finance multi-stock comparison, p.426).
**Score (0–10 ladder).**
> - **0** — a metric/value stands alone with zero comparator (no baseline, trend, prior period, peer) rendered in-view *(source: About Face p.426, "Revenue: $482K," nothing else)*.
> - **3** — a comparator exists but requires navigation/memory (a link to "view history" rather than inline) *(About Face p.426)*.
> - **5 — THRESHOLD:** every displayed metric carries ≥1 comparator (baseline, trend, prior period, or peer) rendered in the SAME view, without navigation *(About Face p.426)*.
> - **6** — the comparator is directly relevant — matched time window/like-for-like peer or unit, not just any number nearby *(About Face p.426)*.
> - **7** — related series that could be compared render on one shared canvas/axis rather than in separate sequential views the user must page between *(About Face p.426, Fig. 17-6)*.
> - **8** — as 7, and the comparator is present for every metric in the region, not just the headline one *(About Face p.426, [derived] extending the single-metric threshold to full coverage)*.
> - **9** — multiple related series/variables render together such that a relationship becomes visible that wouldn't be from separate views *(About Face p.426, Fig. 17-6, Barclays/UBS/S&P correlation)*.
> - **10** — matches the ✓ tile exactly: an in-view trend delta (e.g. ▲12% vs last month) plus an inline sparkline, or the Google Finance multi-stock comparison standard *(About Face p.426)*.
> Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — About Face marks it high for any data/dashboard surface.

### DATA-4 — Integrate; never dequantify; keep data honest
**Rule.** (a) Label in place — no separate legend round-trips; labels beat legends, legends beat axis-interpolation: pick the least indirection the density allows. (b) A gauge/bar/color supplements the numeral, never replaces it. (c) Show only data with quality/relevance/integrity — stale values never wear live-data authority.
**Grounding.** About Face: "Diagrams that require separate keys or legends to decode require additional cognitive processing by users and are less effective than diagrams with integrated legends and labels. Reading and deciphering diagram legends is yet another form of navigation-related excise" (p.427). On dequantifying: "you should not abandon the display of the numbers themselves. For example, in the Windows Disk Properties dialog, a pie chart is displayed to give users a rough idea of their free disk space, but the numbers of gigabytes free and used are also displayed in numeric form" (p.428). On honesty: "Don't show information simply because it's technically possible to do so... Unreliable or otherwise poor-quality information will damage the trust you must build with users" (p.427). Designing Interfaces on the indirection ladder: "Labels are easier to use. They communicate data values precisely and unambiguously (when placed correctly), and they're located in or beside the data point of interest — no going back and forth between the data point and a legend. The downside is that they clutter up a graphic when overused, so be careful" (p.445). Mechanism: each hop (mark → legend → meaning) is excise; a visual-only quantity forces estimation; stale data in live clothing spends trust.
**Objective test.** (a) Chart meaning fully decodable from on-mark/adjacent labels; more than 1 legend round-trip to identify one series = fail; ≤5–6 series → direct end-labels required; denser charts may use a legend but every entry must be unambiguously traceable to its mark (unique hue/shape pairing, no near-duplicate colors). (b) Any value rendered only as bar/ring/color with no adjacent numeral = fail. (c) Each displayed field maps to a consuming workflow/decision (zero-consumer fields flagged); possibly-stale values carry an "as of" marker; any value older than its own stated recency claim fails.
**✗ WRONG.** A 4-line chart identified only via a corner legend; a storage ring with no numbers; a cached "last login" rendered identically to real-time fields.
**✓ RIGHT.** Lines end-labeled in place; "184 GB of 256 GB (72%)" at the ring's center; "Last login: 3:14 PM (as of last night's sync)" on the cached field.
**Crop.** AF-08, UP-02.
**Score (0–10 ladder).**
> - **0** — a chart with ≥3 series decodable ONLY via a distant legend requiring repeated eye travel, OR any bar/gauge/ring/color-intensity value shown with zero accompanying numeral, OR stale data rendered with the same visual authority as live data and no "as of" marker *(source: About Face p.427 legend-as-excise; About Face p.428 dequantify; About Face p.427 integrity; Designing Interfaces p.445 labels-vs-legends)*.
> - **3** — a legend exists but is partially redundant (some series color-coded near their data, others not), OR a gauge's numeral exists but is buried behind hover/a secondary screen, OR only 1-2 fields show the no-consumer/staleness problem *(About Face p.427-428)*.
> - **5 — THRESHOLD:** chart meaning is decodable from what's rendered on/adjacent to each element with at most one required legend glance (≤5–6 series directly end-labeled, or a denser chart's legend entries are unambiguously traceable via unique hue/shape pairing); every gauge/bar/ring value has an adjacent numeral; every displayed field has an identified consumer and any possibly-stale value carries an "as of" indicator *(About Face p.427-428; Designing Interfaces p.445)*.
> - **6** — as 5, and the numeral is prominent and co-located (legible at the same glance as the visual, not just "somewhere nearby") *(About Face p.428)*.
> - **7** — every series/element is directly labeled at or beside its data, zero separate legend box needed; stale values are visually de-emphasized relative to live ones (not just labeled) *(About Face p.427-428)*.
> - **8** — as 7, plus zero near-duplicate legend colors/shapes anywhere a legend is still used, and every field maps to a documented persona/workflow decision *(About Face p.427; Designing Interfaces p.445)*.
> - **9** — the number is integrated INTO the visual itself (e.g. printed at a ring's center), and all shown fields map to an actual decision/action a documented persona takes *(About Face p.428, "184 GB of 256 GB used (72%)")*.
> - **10** — full integration of text, graphics, data, input, and output in one display — no decode step exists anywhere, matching the ✓ integrated tally/gauge/freshness case in full *(About Face p.427-428, Fig. 17-7)*.
> Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — experts split 2–2 (About Face's integrate + don't-dequantify entries high; About Face's quality/integrity entry and Designing Interfaces' labels/legends entry medium); high chosen because the two high lines govern sub-rules (a) and (b), which carry 6 of the 10 points.

### DATA-5 — Order is a legibility decision
**Rule.** A default sort can hide the story (alphabetical) or surface it (magnitude/severity/recency); choose deliberately and offer resort where the data holds multiple stories.
**Grounding.** Designing Interfaces' Texas cancer-data pair: sorted alphabetically, the data "doesn't lead you to ask interesting questions. It's not clear why Abilene, Alice, Amarillo, and Austin all seem to have similar numbers, for instance; it might just be chance" (p.441); resorted numerically, "the graph becomes much more interesting. Galveston is ranked first — why is that, when its neighbor, Houston, is further down the scale?" (pp.441–442). Mechanism: "Sorting and rearranging puts different data points next to each other, thus letting users make different kinds of comparisons" (p.442) — order determines which comparisons are physically adjacent, so the default sort silently chooses which questions the display can raise.
**Objective test.** Table/chart ≥10 rows with a primary quantitative metric: a sort control exists on at least that metric's column; arbitrary/alphabetical default order (where the data isn't alphabetically meaningful and a magnitude order would surface the finding) with no resort control = fail.
**✗ WRONG.** City metrics locked alphabetical with no sort control — extremes and outliers scattered invisibly through the list.
**✓ RIGHT.** Click-to-sort numeric ordering putting the outliers adjacent at top/bottom, surfacing the Galveston-class question instantly.
**Crop.** DI-04 (Fig. 9-7 alphabetical vs. Fig. 9-8 numeric, pp.441–442).
**Score (0–10 ladder).**
> - **0** — a ≥10-row quantitative table has a fixed, non-meaningful default order (e.g. alphabetical) and no sort control at all *(source: Designing Interfaces p.441, city-metrics-table ✗)*.
> - **3** — a sort control exists but only for a non-primary column, or is hidden/hard to discover *(Designing Interfaces p.441)*.
> - **5 — THRESHOLD:** a sort control exists for at least the numeric column of primary interest *(Designing Interfaces p.441-442)*.
> - **6** — the default order itself is chosen deliberately — magnitude/severity/recency to surface the finding, or alphabetical only where lookup-by-name IS the task *(Designing Interfaces p.441, "doesn't lead you to ask interesting questions")*.
> - **7** — sorting the primary metric puts the extremes/outliers adjacent at top/bottom within the first screenful (not split across pagination/grouping) *(Designing Interfaces p.441-442, Fig. 9-8, Galveston example)*.
> - **8** — multiple columns are sortable, with clear visual feedback on current sort direction/column *(Designing Interfaces p.442)*.
> - **9** — sorting surfaces genuine outliers/relationships immediately, and where the data holds multiple stories ≥2 columns are combinably sortable *(Designing Interfaces p.442, "lets users make different kinds of comparisons")*.
> - **10** — matches the ✓ click-to-sort case exactly: numeric ordering puts outliers adjacent at top/bottom, surfacing the Galveston-class question instantly, across every re-sortable dimension the data holds *(Designing Interfaces p.441-442, Fig. 9-7/9-8)*.
> Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** med (2) — Designing Interfaces: high specifically for exploratory data tables, low for short fixed lists → med overall.

### DATA-6 — Detail on demand keeps the overview clean; filters live and in context
**Rule.** Exact values/slices go behind hover/tap/selection (datatip, spotlight); permanently labeling everything is noise, NO route to precision equally fails. Search/filter over data is interactive, iterative, contextual, and combinable.
**Grounding.** Designing Interfaces: Datatips/Data Spotlight patterns (Ch.9) — spotlight dims all but the pointed-at slice. The four filter-quality criteria verbatim: "Highly interactive — They respond as quickly as possible... (Don't react to individual keystrokes if it significantly slows down the user's typing, however.) / Iterative — They let a user refine the search... / Contextual — They show results in context with surrounding data... / Complex — They go beyond simply switching entire data sets on and off, and allow the user to specify nuanced combinations of conditions" (pp.444–445). The ski-trail map case: "the screenshot on the left shows no highlighted trails; the one on the right switches on the trails rated black diamond with a single click" (p.444) — filters toggled live, in place. Mechanism: precision-on-demand resolves the label-clutter vs. no-precision dilemma; in-context filtering preserves the user's mental frame across refinements.
**Objective test.** Data-dense view: (a) a hover/tap/selection route to exact values exists; (b) permanent all-values labeling = noise flag; (c) filter UI scores 4/4 on the criteria — results update without degrading keystroke responsiveness, a result set can be progressively narrowed without restarting, matches shown in context of surrounding data (not a blank results page), and at least one AND/OR/negation combination of ≥2 conditions is supported. One-condition-at-a-time, context-discarding reloads, or keystroke-lagging filters are gaps.
**✗ WRONG.** A map labeling every point permanently; a search allowing price OR bedrooms but never both, each search reloading to a blank page, every keystroke stuttering the input.
**✓ RIGHT.** Clean overview + datatips on hover; multiple filter toggles narrowing the same view in place, instantly.
**Crop.** DI-11 (Fig. 9-10 ski-trail map, p.444).
**Score (0–10 ladder).**
> - **0** — fails ≥3 of the 4 filter-quality items (interactive/iterative/contextual/complex) — single-condition-only filters, full page reload per search, stuttering keystrokes; AND/OR every point permanently labeled with no precision-on-demand route *(source: Designing Interfaces p.444-445, property-search ✗)*.
> - **3** — meets 1–2 of the 4 filter items (e.g. fast but not combinable, or combinable but not contextual); a precision route exists for some marks only *(Designing Interfaces p.444)*.
> - **5 — THRESHOLD:** meets 3 of the 4 filter-quality items; a hover/tap/selection route (datatip/spotlight) reveals exact values on every dense mark *(Designing Interfaces p.444-445)*.
> - **6** — no permanent all-values labeling remains — labels appear on demand or only on key values, leaving the overview clean *(Designing Interfaces Ch.9, datatip/spotlight pattern)*.
> - **7** — all 4 filter-quality items are met (interactive, iterative, contextual, complex) *(Designing Interfaces p.444-445)*.
> - **8** — as 7, and active filters are displayed and individually removable, not only clearable wholesale *(Designing Interfaces p.444-445, [derived] filter-state legibility corollary)*.
> - **9** — all 4 items met AND demonstrated live/instantly with zero perceptible lag even under combined multi-condition filters *(Designing Interfaces p.444, ski-trail map, Fig. 9-10)*.
> - **10** — matches the ✓ case exactly: a clean overview with datatips on hover, plus multiple filter toggles narrowing the same view in place, instantly, with legible removable filter state *(Designing Interfaces p.444, Fig. 9-10)*.
> Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — Designing Interfaces marks the filter criteria high for any search/filter-bearing product.

### DATA-7 — Derived money must show its arithmetic [derived]
**Rule.** When one figure is computed from others (net payable from estimate − exclusions − deductible against coverage), the display makes the derivation traceable: a visible tally structure (operands → operations → result), grouped as one unit, ordered as the computation runs, the result as the headline. Peer-chip scatter forces the user to do the accounting in their head — displaced complexity.
**Grounding.** Derived, four-book convergence. About Face: "Comparison provides a context that makes the information more valuable and comprehensible" (p.426), legends-as-excise (p.427), and "you should not abandon the display of the numbers themselves" (p.428) — related money values must sit together, labeled in place, fully quantified. Laws of UX (Tesler): "If a million users each waste a minute a day dealing with complexity that an engineer could have eliminated in a week by making the software a little more complex, you are penalizing the user to make the engineer's job easier" (p.108, quoted from Saffer 2006; statement p.107, Gmail absorption example p.110) — arithmetic the system already performed must not be re-performed by the reader. Krug: every unresolved "how do these tally?" moment is the think-tax his First Law forbids (p.29), and data legibility is hierarchy + grouping: "Things that are related logically are related visually" (pp.55–56). Designing Interfaces: "When you put things close together, viewers associate them with one another... Grouped items look related. Conversely, isolation implies a distinction" (p.218) and "Sorting and rearranging puts different data points next to each other, thus letting users make different kinds of comparisons" (pp.441–442) — grouping and ordering ARE meaning. Convergence: no single book states the money-tally form, but comparison-enforcement + complexity-absorption + hierarchy/grouping + order-as-meaning jointly entail it.
**Objective test.** (a) Every displayed derived figure: its operands and operations are visible in one grouped unit, ordered as the computation runs, result terminal and dominant (headline weight per DATA-2). (b) Sum-reconciliation check: the visible components arithmetically reconcile to the stated total (compute it), or the discrepancy is explained inline — a total whose visible parts don't sum to it with no inline explanation = fail. (c) The related money values share one region (LAY-10), never scattered as equal-weight chips across the view.
**✗ WRONG.** 1,580 / 2,500 / 2,000 / 500 as four disconnected equal-weight chips in different corners — the user reverse-engineers the arithmetic and can't tell if the numbers even reconcile.
**✓ RIGHT.** A tally block: estimate 2,500 → covered cap 2,000 → − deductible 500 → **net payable 1,580**, each line labeled, the mismatch (500 excluded) stated inline; components sum to the headline.
**Crop.** AF-08 (comparison/integration anchor), DI-01 (headline pop).
**Score (0–10 ladder).** ([derived] — four-book convergence; no single book states the money-tally form directly)
> - **0** — the derived figure's operands/values render as disconnected equal-weight chips scattered across the view, with no visible tally structure — the reader must reverse-engineer the arithmetic *(source: [derived] from Krug p.29,55-56 flat-hierarchy failure; About Face p.426-428 comparison/integration; Designing Interfaces p.218,441-442 grouping/ordering-as-meaning)*.
> - **2** — some operands are shown but ≥1 is left implicit, AND/OR the visible components don't reconcile to the stated total with no inline explanation *(Laws of UX — Tesler p.107-110, unabsorbed complexity pushed onto the reader)*.
> - **5 — THRESHOLD:** every operand and operation of the derived figure is visible in one grouped tally structure, all related money values share one region, and the visible components arithmetically reconcile to the stated total (or a discrepancy is explained inline) *(Designing Interfaces p.218 "grouped items look related"; About Face p.428 "should not abandon the display of the numbers themselves")*.
> - **6** — the tally lines run in the order the computation runs (inputs → adjustments → result terminal), not shuffled *(Designing Interfaces p.441-442, "order determines which comparisons are physically adjacent")*.
> - **7** — the result is the terminal line rendered at strictly greater weight than its operands (headline weight per DATA-2), not a visual peer *(Krug p.55-56, "the more important something is, the more prominent it is")*.
> - **8** — all related money values sit in exactly one grouped region with zero related figures sitting elsewhere on the view *(Designing Interfaces p.218)*.
> - **9** — the arithmetic is fully absorbed by the system and shown, not re-performed by the reader — the tally reads as pre-computed, per Tesler's complexity-conservation standard *(Laws of UX — Tesler p.107-110)*.
> - **10** — matches the ✓ tally block exactly: estimate → covered cap → deductible → net payable, each line labeled, mismatch stated inline, components sum to the headline, headline dominant *(About Face p.426,428; Krug p.29,55-56; Designing Interfaces p.218,441-442; Laws of UX — Tesler p.107-110)*.
> Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — the convergent sources score high (Laws of UX marks Tesler high; Krug marks the numbers-hierarchy doctrine high); derived money on data surfaces is the doc's title failure mode.

### DATA-8 — Numeric formatting is a system
**Rule.** Right-align numeric columns (decimals stack); consistent precision, units, currency notation everywhere; related data may share one hierarchical cell to cut column count.
**Grounding.** Refactoring UI: "If you're designing a table that includes numbers, right-align them. When the decimal in a list of numbers is always in the same place, they're a lot easier to compare at a glance" (p.130). On columns: "if a column doesn't need to be sortable, there's no reason you can't combine it with a related column and introduce some interesting hierarchy" (p.244). Mechanism: a fixed decimal position turns magnitude comparison into a purely visual length/alignment read; merged hierarchical cells (name+role, amount+type) cut column count without losing data.
**Objective test.** `text-align: right` on all currency/quantity/percent columns (decimal points align vertically row to row); one precision and one unit/currency notation per column (mixed 2dp/0dp in one column = fail); any table where some columns hold naturally related atomic fields (amount+type, name+role) is a restructuring candidate — pair them into one hierarchical cell.
**✗ WRONG.** A left-aligned price column with mixed 2dp/0dp precision — decimals fall at inconsistent positions, comparison requires reading every value.
**✓ RIGHT.** Right-aligned, uniform precision, decimals stacked; "amount + type" merged as one two-line hierarchical cell.
**Crop.** RU-21, RU-11.
**Score (0–10 ladder).**
> - **0** — a numeric table column is left- or center-aligned (decimals don't line up), with mixed precision in ≥2 columns *(source: Refactoring UI p.130, "If you're designing a table that includes numbers, right-align them")*.
> - **3** — some numeric columns are right-aligned but ≥1 remains left/center-aligned, or exactly one column mixes precisions (e.g. 2dp and 0dp) *(Refactoring UI p.130)*.
> - **5 — THRESHOLD:** every currency/quantity/percent column is right-aligned with decimals stacking vertically row to row, and one precision holds per column everywhere *(Refactoring UI p.130)*.
> - **6** — one unit/currency notation holds per column (symbol placement, thousands separators consistent) — no mixed notation within a column *(Refactoring UI p.130, [derived] notation-consistency corollary)*.
> - **7** — candidate hierarchical-cell pairs (naturally related atomic fields, e.g. amount+type, name+role) are identified and some are merged where the column needn't be sortable *(Refactoring UI p.244, "combine it with a related column and introduce some interesting hierarchy")*.
> - **8** — all obvious hierarchical-cell pairs are merged, cutting column count without losing data *(Refactoring UI p.244)*.
> - **9** — right-alignment, precision, and notation consistency hold across every table in the product, not just the one audited *(Refactoring UI p.130,244, [derived] product-wide extension)*.
> - **10** — matches the ✓ case exactly: right-aligned, uniform precision, decimals stacked, plus "amount + type" merged as one two-line hierarchical cell *(Refactoring UI p.130,244)*.
> Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** med (2) — both Refactoring UI source entries (alignment; grid/column restructuring) are marked medium.

### DATA-9 — Redundant coding for critical distinctions
**Rule.** Status/severity/category that matters gets ≥2 channels (color + icon + text); a hue-only distinction is fragile and less legible for everyone.
**Grounding.** Designing Interfaces: "The shape of the scatter markers could encode yet a fourth variable, but in this case, shape is redundant with color hue. The redundant encoding helps a user visually separate the three data groups" (p.438, Fig. 9-6) — the grouping survives grayscale, print, and colorblindness. Universal Principles: "There are four kinds of redundancy: diverse, homogeneous, active, and passive... Diverse redundancy is resistant to a single cause of failure" (p.204). Mechanism: two independent channels mean loss of any one (colorblindness, grayscale, screenshot, glare) leaves the distinction intact. Full mechanics → COLOR-7.
**Objective test.** Grayscale-simulate every status/severity pair: still distinguishable, or fail. For any chart distinguishing ≥3 categorical series, count independent encoding channels per series — color alone = 1 = fail for distinctions that matter; ≥2 channels (hue + shape / hue + line-style / color + icon + label) = pass.
**✗ WRONG.** Red-vs-green severity dots only — identical in grayscale and to a colorblind reviewer.
**✓ RIGHT.** Color + icon + text label per status; grayscale-safe.
**Crop.** DI-10 (Fig. 9-6, pp.438–439).
**Score (0–10 ladder).**
> - **0** — a critical value/state (or a ≥3-categorical-series chart) relies on hue alone; grayscale/colorblind simulation collapses it into indistinguishable marks *(source: Designing Interfaces p.438, single-channel scatter; Universal Principles p.204,233-238, "diverse redundancy is resistant to a single cause of failure")*.
> - **3** — a second channel exists but is inconsistently applied — some series/values get a distinct shape or icon, others share one *(Designing Interfaces p.438; Universal Principles p.233-238)*.
> - **5 — THRESHOLD:** every critical status/severity/category distinction is carried by ≥2 independent channels (hue+shape, hue+line-style, or color+icon+text), and grouping/distinction survives a grayscale check *(Designing Interfaces p.438, Fig. 9-6; Universal Principles p.233-238)*.
> - **6** — every ≥3-categorical-series chart specifically uses ≥2 channels per series, not just isolated status values *(Designing Interfaces p.438-439, Fig. 9-6)*.
> - **7** — the redundant channel is chosen for maximal legibility — high-contrast shapes/icons/line-styles, not near-identical glyphs *(Designing Interfaces p.438)*.
> - **8** — threshold met with ≥2 independent DIVERSE (not homogeneous) encodings for every critical value across the whole product, not just one screen *(Universal Principles p.204,233-238)*.
> - **9** — full multidimensional encoding as in the book's own reference case — position + hue + redundant shape all legible together, verified in both color and grayscale *(Designing Interfaces p.438, Fig. 9-6)*.
> - **10** — matches the book's own "Super Cow" diverse-redundancy standard — every genuinely critical path/value verified by simulating loss of each single channel, color+icon+text throughout *(Universal Principles p.204,233-238)*.
> Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — Designing Interfaces and Universal Principles both mark it high.

### DATA-10 — Small multiples: repeat one consistent chart, never rescale per panel
**Rule.** To show more dimensions than one plot holds, repeat a small identical chart across a labeled grid — identical size, axis scale, encoding; per-panel auto-scaling manufactures fake visual differences.
**Grounding.** Designing Interfaces: "Small Multiples are data-rich — they show a lot of information at one time, but in a comprehensible way. Every individual picture tells a story. But when you put them all together and demonstrate how each picture varies from one to the next, an even bigger story is told" (p.466), quoting Tufte: "Small multiple designs, multivariate and data bountiful, answer directly by visually enforcing comparisons of changes, of the differences among objects, of the scope of alternatives" (p.466). Craft requirement: "Each image should be similar to the others: the same size and/or shape, the same axis scaling (if you're using plots), and the same kind of content... Try to eliminate the visual differences that don't mean anything" (p.467); and "make sure the users understand which data dimension is varying across the multiples" (p.467). Mechanism: the grid IS the comparison — any per-panel variation in scale or encoding injects a visual difference that carries no data, corrupting every cross-panel read.
**Objective test.** Every panel shares one y-axis range, identical size, and one encoding — any panel independently auto-scaled or differently colored than its siblings = defect; row/column headers state which dimension varies across which grid axis, or fail.
**✗ WRONG.** 12 panels each auto-scaled — two panels with wildly different absolute ranges rendered visually identical.
**✓ RIGHT.** One fixed y-range and one styling across all 12, dimension labels on rows/columns; a taller bar is genuinely larger.
**Crop.** DI-12 (Fig. 9-26/9-27, pp.467–468).
**Score (0–10 ladder).**
> - **0** — panels in a small-multiples grid use inconsistent axis scales/encodings, manufacturing fake visual differences *(source: Designing Interfaces p.467, auto-scaled-12-panel ✗)*.
> - **3** — axis scales are consistent but panel sizing/styling varies slightly — not a fully clean repeated unit *(Designing Interfaces p.467)*.
> - **5 — THRESHOLD:** all panels share identical size, one shared axis scale, and one encoding *(Designing Interfaces p.466-467)*.
> - **6** — no visual difference across panels carries meaningless variation — decorative per-panel drift is eliminated *(Designing Interfaces p.467, "eliminate the visual differences that don't mean anything")*.
> - **7** — row/column headers state which data dimension varies across which grid axis *(Designing Interfaces p.467, "make sure the users understand which data dimension is varying")*.
> - **8** — as 7, and the labeling is unambiguous — no guessing which dimension varies on which axis *(Designing Interfaces p.467)*.
> - **9** — the grid demonstrably enforces comparison of changes/differences the way Tufte's small-multiples doctrine intends — the bigger story reads across panels at a glance *(Designing Interfaces p.466, quoting Tufte)*.
> - **10** — full Tufte-grade small multiples: consistent panels, clear axis labeling, AND an additional encoded dependent variable (e.g. color) layered on top without breaking comparability *(Designing Interfaces p.466-468, Fig. 9-26/9-27)*.
> Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** med (2) — Designing Interfaces marks it medium (applies only to multi-panel comparative dashboards).

# Density & Progressive Disclosure

The "clogged / crammed / everything up-front" failure family. Rest state shows the minimum the task needs; depth is earned by interaction. Pillars: 1, 3.

---

### DENS-1 — Progressive disclosure: reveal complexity on demand
**Rule.** Show only what the current step needs; put advanced/secondary/rare-path content behind an explicit interaction (expand, drill-down, hover/click reveal) — reachable, never amputated.
**Grounding.**
- Universal Principles (p.188): "Progressive disclosure involves separating information into multiple layers and only presenting layers that are necessary or relevant. It is primarily used to prevent information overload." / "Information presented to a person who is not interested or ready to process it is effectively noise." Mechanism — the book's own note demolishes the show-everything excuse: "A common mistake is to present all available information and options at once with the rationale that it reduces kinematic load. Since progressive disclosure affects only infrequently used elements... it will generally have minimal effect on kinematic load. Conversely, presenting everything at once will significantly increase cognitive load" (p.188, note 2).
- Laws of UX (p.116): "Progressive disclosure is an interaction design technique that displays only important actions or content by default, while making additional features or content easily accessible. The result is a more streamlined interface that helps to keep the user's attention focused by reducing clutter, confusion, and cognitive load." Mechanism — Stripe's hover-menus keep the surface scannable "without needing to dig through a mountain of content in the process" (p.116).
- Laws of UX, Hick's-law staging (pp.42–44): Google "simplifies the initial task of searching... and provides the ability to filter results only after you've begun your search" (p.44). Mechanism — the jam study: shoppers shown 24 varieties were "only one-tenth as likely to buy" than those shown 6, even though "the larger display captured more attention" (p.42) — more simultaneous choice raises engagement but collapses conversion.
- Designing Interfaces (p.224): "In some contexts, information is shown only after the user takes a specific action. Moo.com... uses this technique in its 'create a custom product' flow... a customer doesn't see the customization options until they click into the editable parts of the card." Mechanism — the trigger for revealing depth is the user entering the region that needs it.
- About Face (Ch11, p.250): "It is vital that all the elements in an interface work together coherently toward a single goal. When an application's communication with a person is well orchestrated, it becomes almost invisible." Mechanism — orchestration reveals work progressively; the chapter's harmonious-interaction strategies (pp.261–262) explicitly avoid front-loading every option.
**Objective test.** (a) A control whose use-frequency is <1 in 10 sessions rendered at the same visual weight (size/contrast) as an every-session control = violation (UP p.188). (b) A "More Choices"/"Fewer Choices"-style disclosure pair must exist for the second tier; clicking it must add ≥1 new field group in place, without navigation or lost state (UP p.189). (c) Decision-critical screens: initial-screen option count >8 equally-weighted with zero options deferred to a secondary interaction (dropdown, "more filters", step 2) = fail (LU Ch.4). (d) Count controls visible on initial load vs controls actually exercised by a majority of users completing the primary task — a large gap = disclosure failure (DI p.224). (e) Multi-step tasks: controls visible on the FIRST screen that are only relevant to step 3+ target 0 (AF Ch11). (f) Nav: DOM top-level-visible item count materially smaller than full reachable item count, sub-items one interaction away (LU p.116).
**✗ WRONG.** A filter panel renders 14 fields at once, ungrouped, though users only ever touch status+date; every annotation shows full metadata at rest; a "create invoice" screen shows tax, shipping, discounts AND recurring-billing config before a customer name is entered.
**✓ RIGHT.** Two fields + "More filters" revealing the other 12 in place without reload or lost state; the rest state shows identity + one key figure, selection reveals the full assessment; the invoice screen opens with customer + line items, everything else in expandable sections revealed once the core exists.
**Crop.** UP-01, LU-13, LU-20, DI-09.
**Score — grounded ladder (0→10).** Score = highest rung whose condition AND every rung below it hold.
- **0 — ✗:** no disclosure affordance for the second tier at all — every reachable control/option flatly rendered at first load, >8 equally-weighted options with zero deferral, ≥2 controls used <1 in 10 sessions at the same visual weight as every-session controls *(source: Universal Principles p.188 note 2; Laws of UX Hick's pp.42–44; Designing Interfaces p.224)*.
- **2** — a second-tier disclosure trigger exists but reveals via page navigation/reload or loses entered state (not in place) *(source: Universal Principles p.189 "More Choices/Fewer Choices" in-place requirement; Designing Interfaces PD band-3)*.
- **3** — in-place reveal works, but decision-critical first render still shows >8 equally-weighted options (only partial staging) *(source: Laws of UX Hick's pp.42–44, band 3)*.
- **4** — ≤8 equally-weighted initial options, but ≥3 controls serving only step 3+ sit on a multi-step first screen, or ≥2 sub-1/10-session controls remain at every-session weight *(source: About Face Ch11 orchestration p.250; Universal Principles p.188 test a)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** a "More"-type disclosure adds ≥1 field group in place with no navigation and no lost state; initial equally-weighted option count ≤8 with extras deferred to a secondary interaction; ≤2 leaked step-3+ controls; ≤1 rare control at full weight *(source: Universal Principles p.189; Laws of UX Hick's pp.42–44; About Face Ch11)*.
- **6** — + zero step-3+ controls on first screens of multi-step tasks AND zero <1/10-session controls rendered at every-session weight *(source: About Face Ch13-orchestration band 5–6, p.250; Universal Principles p.188)*.
- **7** — + nav: top-level always-visible item count materially smaller than the full reachable item count, sub-items one hover/expand interaction away *(source: Laws of UX p.116 Stripe; Designing Interfaces p.224)*.
- **8** — + the default first-render set is verified against actual/estimated use-frequency across the product, not just this screen *(source: Universal Principles Progressive Disclosure band 7–8, p.188)*.
- **9** — + the reveal interaction is low-friction (hover/inline, no full navigation) and revealed second-tier sets are themselves grouped and labeled, not one undifferentiated overflow *(source: Laws of UX #26 band 7–8 p.116; Laws of UX Hick's band 7–8)*.
- **10 — ✓ top-1%:** + layered disclosure with >2 tiers where warranted, state/position preserved across toggles, and a measured near-zero gap between controls shown at load and controls exercised by a majority of users on the primary task *(source: Universal Principles p.188–189 band 9–10; Designing Interfaces p.224 band 9–10; Laws of UX p.116 Stripe band 9–10)*.
N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — high in Universal Principles, Laws of UX (Hick's staging), and About Face (orchestration); Designing Interfaces and LU's nav-disclosure entry say med; majority high.

### DENS-2 — Chunk everything; walls of anything fail — and count-caps are a myth
**Rule.** Group related content/controls into labeled, scannable clusters via headings, dividers, whitespace; an unbroken block fails regardless of item count — and never trim a visible list to ~7 "because Miller".
**Grounding.**
- Laws of UX (p.36): "What chunking does not do is dictate a specific limit on the number of items that can be shown at a given time or within a group." And the direct rebuttal of the 7-cap: "design patterns such as navigation menus don't require people to memorize them — the choices available to them via the navigation menu are visible at all times... there's no usability gain provided by limiting these links to a specific number" (p.36). Mechanism — Miller "himself only used the expression 'the magical number seven' rhetorically and was surprised by its frequent misinterpretation" (p.30); Nike.com's primary nav "number[s] well beyond seven, yet it is still easy to scan the list thanks to clear categorization and the use of whitespace and vertical dividers to separate sub-groupings" (p.36).
- Universal Principles (p.40): "The maximum number of chunks that can be efficiently processed by short-term memory is four, plus or minus one." Mechanism — scope limit stated verbatim: "The limits specified by this principle deal specifically with tasks involving memory... Reference-related tasks consist primarily of scanning for a particular item; chunking in this case would dramatically increase the scan time and effort, and yield no benefits" (p.40).
**Objective test.** (a) Any parent containing ≥5 sibling interactive/text items with zero heading, zero divider/border, and uniform inter-item spacing (no group gap larger than item gap) fails — REGARDLESS of total item count (LU p.36; group gap should be ≥1.5× the within-group gap). (b) An option set trimmed to exactly ~7 with no stated functional reason (search relevance, business priority) and no accompanying grouping change = cargo-cult flag (LU p.36). (c) Memory-bearing strings (phone numbers, codes the user must retain after looking away) chunk into 3–5 groups of 3–5 (4±1); scan/search references (alphabetized lists) stay flat and dense (UP p.40).
**✗ WRONG.** A settings page lists 24 toggles in one flat vertical list at uniform 12px spacing, no headers, no dividers; a review note says "cut the nav to 7 per Miller" with items simply deleted and no grouping change.
**✓ RIGHT.** The 24 toggles in 5 labeled sections ("Notifications," "Privacy," "Display," …), 24px between sections and 12px within; the 11-item nav ships whole, organized into 3 labeled sub-groups with dividers — nothing removed, everything scannable.
**Crop.** LU-04, LU-05.
**Score — grounded ladder (0→10).** Score = highest rung whose condition AND every rung below it hold.
- **0 — ✗:** ≥2 parents containing ≥5 sibling interactive/text items with zero grouping cue — no heading, no divider, uniform spacing throughout (walls) *(source: Laws of UX p.36 Chunking band 0 — "24 toggles in one flat list")*.
- **2** — exactly one uncued dense parent remains; grouping elsewhere inconsistent (some sections headed, others not) *(source: Laws of UX p.36 Chunking band 3)*.
- **3** — every dense parent carries some cue but the inter-group gap is <1.5× the within-group gap — groups barely distinguishable from items *(source: Laws of UX p.36 Chunking band 3 gap clause)*.
- **4** — cues + ≥1.5× group gap present, but groups are unlabeled or are arbitrary chunks of 5–7 with no semantic basis *(source: Laws of UX p.36 band 7–8 inverse — semantic labeling absent)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** every parent with ≥5 sibling items carries ≥1 visible grouping cue (heading, divider, background band, or ≥1.5× inter-group vs intra-group spacing) — passes regardless of total item count *(source: Laws of UX p.36 Chunking band 5–6)*.
- **6** — + groups carry text labels naming genuine semantic categories *(source: Laws of UX p.36 band 7–8)*.
- **7** — + no option set trimmed to ~7 without a stated functional reason; large sets (>7) ship in full, organized into labeled sub-groups *(source: Laws of UX p.36 magic-7 anti-pattern bands 5–8; Miller p.30)*.
- **8** — + memory-bearing strings (codes, phone numbers the user must retain after looking away) chunk into 3–5 groups of 3–5 (4±1), AND scan/reference lists (alphabetized lookups) stay flat and unchunked *(source: Universal Principles p.40 Chunking band 5–6, memory-vs-scan scope)*.
- **9** — + memory-chunk boundaries match real-world convention (area code / exchange / line), not arbitrary splits *(source: Universal Principles p.40 band 7–8)*.
- **10 — ✓ top-1%:** labeled, well-spaced grouping holds across EVERY dense region of the product (reads as information architecture, not a list); full large sets ship whole per the Nike-nav case; the memory-vs-scan distinction correctly applied everywhere *(source: Laws of UX p.36 bands 9–10; Universal Principles p.40 band 9–10)*.
N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — Laws of UX rates chunking high (structural, script-auditable); Universal Principles rates its memory-scoped chunking med and LU rates the magic-7 anti-pattern low; the core grouping rule carries the entry, so high (disagreement noted).

### DENS-3 — Maximize signal-to-noise; every element earns its place
**Rule.** Remove anything whose deletion loses no information or function; Cooper's test: take things away until the design breaks, then put the last thing back.
**Grounding.**
- Universal Principles (p.224): "The goal of good design is to maximize signal and minimize noise, thereby producing a high signal-to-noise ratio." / "Excess is noise." Mechanism — "Minimizing noise means removing unnecessary elements, and minimizing the expression of necessary elements... every unnecessary data item, graphic, line, or symbol steals attention away from relevant elements."
- About Face (Ch17, p.424): "Take things away until the design breaks, and then put that last thing back in." Mechanism — framed via Saint-Exupéry ("Perfection is attained not when there is no longer anything to add, but when there is no longer anything to take away"); noise survives precisely because no one tested whether each element is load-bearing.
- About Face, named noise forms (Ch17, p.423): "Visual noise can take many forms: Ornate embellishment; 3D rendering that doesn't add information; Rule boxes and other visually 'heavy' elements to separate controls; Crowding of elements; Intense colors, textures, and contrast; Using too many colors; Weak visual hierarchy." And crowding is functional damage: "Cluttered interfaces attempt to provide an excess of functionality in a constrained space, resulting in controls that visually interfere with each other. Visually baroque, disorderly, or crowded screens increase the user's cognitive load" (p.423).
- Krug (p.62): "start with the assumption that everything is visual noise (the 'presumed guilty until proven innocent' approach) and get rid of anything that's not making a real contribution." Mechanism — the burden of proof sits on each element, not on the remover.
**Objective test.** (a) Per element (rule, box, icon, color swatch, label): remove it in a mockup — zero observable loss of capability or information = defect; target 0 removable-without-loss elements per screen; any survivor is cut or justified in writing (AF p.424). (b) Tick the named noise forms present per screen, citing the specific triggering element; ≥2 categories present = mandatory noise-reduction pass (AF p.423). (c) Charts/tables: every unbolded gridline or border duplicating an already-labeled data value is removable; audit non-data ink as a fraction of total ink (UP p.224). (d) Dense regions: any pair of adjacent controls whose hit-areas nearly touch/overlap or whose boundaries lack a consistent gutter = flagged; target 0 flagged pairs (AF p.423).
**✗ WRONG.** Bordered boxes around every field group + rules between every row + alternating tints — spacing already carried the grouping; a 3D-beveled pie chart with drop shadow and cross-hatch textures for categories color alone could distinguish.
**✓ RIGHT.** Spacing-only grouping (24px between groups, 8px within); the same data as a flat 2D donut with thin 1px separators and direct labels — identical story, far less ink.
**Crop.** UP-02, AF-13.
**Score — grounded ladder (0→10).** Score = highest rung whose condition AND every rung below it hold.
- **0 — ✗:** ≥2 elements removable in a mockup with zero observable loss (rule-boxes + tint + borders duplicating what spacing carries) AND ≥2 of the six named noise categories present *(source: About Face p.424 subtraction band 0; About Face p.423 named noise forms)*.
- **2** — 2–3 removable-with-zero-loss elements remain; only some redundant chrome trimmed *(source: About Face p.424 band 3)*.
- **3** — ≤1 removable element, but ≥2 named noise categories still ticked (the mandatory noise-reduction-pass threshold still breached) *(source: About Face p.423 band 3)*.
- **4** — exactly 1 noise category present, and redundant gridlines/borders duplicating already-labeled values remain *(source: About Face p.423 band 5–6; Universal Principles p.224 band 3)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** ≤1 removable-with-zero-loss element; ≤1 named noise category; zero adjacent-control pairs whose hit-areas nearly touch or lack a consistent gutter *(source: About Face p.424 band 5–6; About Face p.423 bands 5–6 [noise + clutter]; Universal Principles p.224)*.
- **6** — + zero removable elements — every survivor is load-bearing under the presumed-guilty burden of proof *(source: About Face p.424 band 7–8; Krug p.62)*.
- **7** — + zero of the six named noise categories (ornate embellishment, uninformative 3D, heavy rule boxes, crowding, intense colors/textures, too many colors) *(source: About Face p.423 band 7–8)*.
- **8** — + no gridline/border/decoration duplicating an already-labeled data value; remaining structural ink deliberately minimized in weight (thin, muted) *(source: Universal Principles p.224 band 7–8)*.
- **9** — + clean cluster/gutter discipline in the densest region — consistent gutters, related actions visually unitized, zero flagged pairs *(source: About Face p.423 clutter band 9–10)*.
- **10 — ✓ top-1%:** grouping/hierarchy carried entirely by spacing/type-weight alone; charts flat 2D with direct labels replacing decorated originals — identical story, markedly less ink; a reviewer cannot suggest a single further cut *(source: About Face p.424 band 9–10; Universal Principles p.224 band 9–10)*.
N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — unanimous: Universal Principles (signal-to-noise), About Face (subtraction test, named noise forms, clutter-as-functional-defect) all high.

### DENS-4 — Leverage: one element, several purposes
**Rule.** Prefer one element legitimately serving multiple related purposes over one control per purpose.
**Grounding.**
- About Face (Ch17, p.424): "Related to the drive for simplicity is the concept of *leverage*, which is where a single interface element is used for several related purposes. For example, in Microsoft Windows 8, an icon appears next to the window's title... This icon visually communicates the window's contents... and provides access to window configuration commands such as Minimize, Maximize, and Close." Mechanism — leverage reduces total surface area without reducing function, the chapter's very definition of visual efficiency: "The more useful work a visual element can accomplish while still retaining clarity, the better" (p.424).
- Universal Principles, propositional density (p.190): "High propositional density is a key factor in making designs engaging and memorable... Objects and environments with high PD (PD > 1) are perceived to be more interesting and engaging than objects and environments with low PD (PD < 1)." Mechanism — the same economy stated as a ratio: pack multiple deep propositions into few surface elements (PD ≈ Pd/Ps; the book scores the Obama 2008 logo at "PD ≈ 10 / 3 = 3.33", p.191).
**Objective test.** For each pair of adjacent single-purpose controls: (a) do they occupy overlapping semantic territory (identity + configuration of the SAME object)? (b) can one merged control's legend/icon still communicate both functions unambiguously to a first-time user? Both yes = an unmerged-leverage finding; ship the count of such pairs as a review metric (AF p.424). For a designed focal element (logo, hero icon): list surface vs deep propositions and compute PD = deep/surface; PD ≤ 1 = redesign candidate (UP p.190).
**✗ WRONG.** A file-browser row shows a purely decorative generic type icon AND a separate "…" button for that row's rename/move/delete actions.
**✓ RIGHT.** The row's icon shows the real content thumbnail (communicates content) AND anchors the row's context menu (provides the actions) — one element, two jobs, as in the Windows 8 title-bar icon.
**Crop.** AF-01.
**Score — grounded ladder (0→10).** Score = highest rung whose condition AND every rung below it hold.
- **0 — ✗:** ≥2 adjacent single-purpose control pairs pass both merge questions (overlapping semantic territory of the same object + a merged control would still be unambiguous) yet remain unmerged *(source: About Face p.424 leverage band 0 — decorative icon + separate "…" button)*.
- **2** — exactly 1 such unmerged pair; or leverage only partially realized (icon shows content but a separate button duplicates one of its functions) *(source: About Face p.424 band 3)*.
- **3** — a merged element exists but its second function is not visually communicated (undiscoverable to a first-time user) *(source: About Face p.424 band 3; p.424 "retaining clarity" clause)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** zero unmerged leverage-eligible pairs remain; controls stay single-purpose only where merging would create ambiguity *(source: About Face p.424 band 5–6)*.
- **6** — + every designed focal element (logo, hero icon) has PD ≥ 1 — at least as many articulable meanings as surface marks (vacuously satisfied if none exists) *(source: Universal Principles p.190 band 3, PD ≈ 1)*.
- **7** — + ≥1 element demonstrably serves ≥2 related purposes, both unambiguous to a first-time user (the Windows 8 title-bar-icon pattern) *(source: About Face p.424 band 7–8)*.
- **8** — + every designed focal element has PD > 1 (≥2 meanings on ≥1 surface element) *(source: Universal Principles p.190 band 5–6, Apple-logo tier)*.
- **9** — + leverage is the default posture: every eligible identity+configuration pair merged, each merge unambiguous *(source: About Face p.424 band 9–10)*.
- **10 — ✓ top-1%:** + focal-design PD in the ≈3+ range, each deep proposition independently articulable by a naive viewer *(source: Universal Principles p.190–191 band 9–10, Obama-logo PD ≈ 3.33)*.
N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** med (2) — Universal Principles rates propositional density med; About Face rates leverage low-med (an efficiency bonus, absence not a defect unless crowding also fails); majority med (noted).

### DENS-5 — Visibility without the kitchen sink
**Rule.** Status, available actions, and consequences must be apparent at a glance — but total exposure is visibility's own failure mode; survive complexity via hierarchical organization and context sensitivity (show what's relevant to the current state, dim/hide the rest).
**Grounding.**
- Universal Principles (p.250): "When it comes to the design of complex systems, the principle of visibility is perhaps the most important and most violated principle of design." The named failure mode: "kitchen-sink visibility... they try to make everything visible all of the time. This approach may seem desirable, but it actually makes the relevant information and controls more difficult to access due to an overload of information" (p.250). The stated remedy, verbatim: "Hierarchical organization and context sensitivity are good solutions for managing complexity while preserving visibility... Relevant controls and information for a particular context are made highly visible, and irrelevant controls (e.g., unavailable functions), are minimized or hidden" (p.250). Mechanism — both hiding everything and showing everything converge on the same outcome: "operators do not know" what state the system is in; Three Mile Island operators could not see true system state ("the water level in the primary loop is actually dropping" while every visible indicator said otherwise, p.251) and misdiagnosed fatally.
- About Face (Ch11): orchestration corollary — controls for a downstream step the user hasn't reached are clutter now, relevant later; reveal them at the step that needs them (pp.250, 261–262).
**Objective test.** (a) Current system status, available-vs-disabled actions, and confirmation of the last triggered action each answerable from the screen alone, without hovering, clicking, or asking, in ≤2 seconds (UP p.250). (b) Count controls rendered at full opacity/size: any disabled/context-irrelevant control rendered at the same opacity/weight as active ones (not dimmed, hidden, or nested) = kitchen-sink fail (UP p.250). (c) Controls relevant only to a downstream step visible before the user reaches it = orchestration fail, target 0 (AF Ch11).
**✗ WRONG.** A toolbar shows 40 icons at full color at all times regardless of selection, 30 of them inert until a specific object type is selected, with nothing distinguishing them; a Save button that looks identical before, during, and after saving — the user must reload to find out.
**✓ RIGHT.** The toolbar for a text object shows only text-relevant tools, others hidden or dimmed to ~30% and non-clickable until preconditions are met; Save becomes a spinner on click, then a checkmark + "Saved" on success or a red inline error on failure, returning to idle.
**Crop.** UP-09.
**Score — grounded ladder (0→10).** Score = highest rung whose condition AND every rung below it hold.
- **0 — ✗:** none of the three glance states (current status / available-vs-disabled / last-action confirmation) answerable from the screen, AND irrelevant controls indistinguishable from active ones at scale (the 40-icon toolbar) *(source: Universal Principles p.250 Visibility band 0 + Kitchen-Sink band 0)*.
- **2** — only one of the three glance states answerable, or dimming attempted but inconsistent ("hidden" controls still clickable — dead clicks) *(source: Universal Principles p.250 Visibility band 3; Kitchen-Sink band 3)*.
- **3** — two of the three glance states answerable from the screen alone in ≤2 seconds *(source: Universal Principles p.250 objective test)*.
- **4** — all three glance states answerable, but a minority of context-irrelevant controls remain at full opacity/size/weight *(source: Universal Principles p.250 Kitchen-Sink band 3)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** all three states answerable from the screen alone, without hover/click, in ≤2s AND every disabled/context-irrelevant control is dimmed, hidden, or nested — active controls alone at full weight *(source: Universal Principles p.250 Visibility + Kitchen-Sink bands 5–6, the stated context-sensitivity remedy)*.
- **6** — + ≤2 controls visible that are relevant only to a step the user hasn't reached *(source: About Face Ch11 orchestration band 3, p.250)*.
- **7** — + zero downstream-step controls leaked *(source: About Face Ch11 band 5–6, pp.261–262)*.
- **8** — + the surviving high-visibility set is itself compact (hierarchical organization, not just binary dim/hide) and the three-state answerability holds for every mutating action incl. edge outcomes (partial failure, timeout) *(source: Universal Principles p.250 Kitchen-Sink band 7–8 + Visibility band 7–8)*.
- **9** — + the visible-control count scales with context precisely (a text-object toolbar shows only text tools), verified across every object-type context *(source: Universal Principles p.250 Kitchen-Sink band 9–10)*.
- **10 — ✓ top-1%:** + the full state machine is visible at a glance (idle→loading→success/error→idle) with no ambiguous window, verified under simulated failure — the anti-Three-Mile-Island state *(source: Universal Principles pp.250–251 Visibility band 9–10)*.
N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — Universal Principles rates both Visibility and Kitchen-Sink Visibility high ("most important and most violated"); About Face's orchestration corollary is high; unanimous.

### DENS-6 — The tragedy of the commons clogs shared surfaces
**Rule.** Prime shared real estate degrades by accretion — each stakeholder's addition is locally rational while the clutter cost is diffused; a clogged screen is usually accreted, not designed, and prevention is standing governance.
**Grounding.**
- Krug (p.129): "It's a perfect example of the tragedy of the commons. The premise is simple: Any shared resource (a 'commons') will inevitably be destroyed by overuse... The problem is, the rewards and the costs of adding more things to the Home page aren't shared equally. The section that's being promoted gets a huge gain in traffic, while the overall loss in effectiveness of the Home page as it gets more cluttered is shared by all sections." Mechanism — asymmetric incentives: gain is concentrated on the promoter, cost diffused across everyone, so each addition is individually rational.
- Krug, governance corollary (p.130): "Preserving the Home page from promotional overload requires constant vigilance, since it usually happens gradually, with the slow, inexorable addition of just...one...more...thing. All the stakeholders need to be educated about the danger of overgrazing the Home page and offered other methods of driving traffic." Mechanism — the failure is a process failure, so a one-time redesign without a review-cadence rule will simply recur.
**Objective test.** (a) Count distinct stakeholder-championed CTAs competing for primary visual weight in the top fold: ≥3 CTAs of near-equal weight, each traceable to a different internal owner rather than one user-need hierarchy = commons-degraded (KR p.129). (b) Root-cause classification of a clogged surface: trace each competing element to its origin date/owner; elements added across ≥3 time periods by ≥2 owners with no single coordinating review = governance drift — a redesign without a review-cadence fix will recur (KR p.130).
**✗ WRONG.** A dashboard header carries five equally-sized promotional banners from five product teams rotating in a carousel, none clearly more important; a de-cluttering redesign ships with no add-review process — six months later the same clutter is back from four teams.
**✓ RIGHT.** One primary action tied to the user's top task; other promotions demoted to a low-weight secondary zone; the redesign ships alongside a standing rule — any new element needs single-design-owner sign-off and one existing element removed or demoted for each one added.
**Crop.** KR-06, KR-07.
**Score — grounded ladder (0→10).** Score = highest rung whose condition AND every rung below it hold.
- **0 — ✗:** ≥5 near-equal-weight promotional elements compete for primary attention, each traceable to a different internal owner, no hierarchy (the 5-banner carousel) *(source: Krug p.129 band 0)*.
- **2** — 3–4 competing near-equal-weight elements from different owners *(source: Krug p.129 band 3)*.
- **4** — exactly 2 near-equal competitors, but the governance-drift signature is present: competing elements trace to ≥3 time periods and ≥2 owners with no coordinating review *(source: Krug p.129 band 5–6; Krug p.130)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** ≤2 near-equal-weight competing elements AND no ≥3-period/≥2-owner accretion signature — the surface still reads as one hierarchy *(source: Krug p.129 band 5–6; Krug p.130)*.
- **7** — + exactly one primary CTA dominates the top fold, tied to the user's top task; other promotions sit in a visibly lower-weight zone (smaller, dimmer, or below the primary region) *(source: Krug p.129 band 7–8)*.
- **9** — + all other promotions demonstrably secondary/dismissible; every element traces to one user-need hierarchy rather than stakeholder ownership *(source: Krug p.129 band 9–10)*.
- **10 — ✓ top-1%:** + a documented standing add-review rule exists (single design-owner sign-off, one-in-one-out) and audit shows zero unauthorized accretion since *(source: Krug p.130 band 9–10)*.
N/A if no instances on the surface (single-owner, non-shared surfaces).
**Weight.** med (2) — Krug rates the commons diagnostic med (home-page/dashboard specific) and the governance corollary low (process, only scoreable when ownership history is knowable); majority med (noted).

### DENS-7 — Excise: separate goal-work from bookkeeping
**Rule.** Excise is work/chrome serving the software's own navigation/configuration/bookkeeping rather than the user's goal; classify every element and eliminate avoidable excise — but excise is CONTEXTUAL, so the fix for power-user controls is conditional reveal, not deletion; absorb the system's own complexity instead of displacing it.
**Grounding.**
- About Face (Ch12, p.272): "*Excise tasks*... don't contribute directly to reaching the goal, but instead represent extra work that satisfies either the needs of our tools or those of outside agents." Design principle: "Eliminate excise wherever possible" (p.273). Mechanism — users perform four types of work (cognitive, memory, visual, physical, p.271) and excise spends all four on the tool instead of the goal.
- About Face, contextuality (Ch12, p.285): "One man's (or persona's) goal-directed task may be another's excise task in a different context... For sovereign posture applications, however, the slightest excise becomes agonizing over time." Mechanism — the same control is goal-directed for one persona and clutter for another, so the remedy is conditional reveal, never blanket deletion.
- About Face, absorb bookkeeping (Ch14, pp.325–338): the unified file model replaces Save dialogs that "reflect the internal mechanisms of data entry, storage, and retrieval" (p.325): "In the unified model, we abolish all user interface recognition of the two copies, so the Save function disappears from the mainstream interface." Design principle: "Save documents and settings automatically" (p.337). Also: "No matter how cool your interface is, less of it would be better" (Ch11, p.250).
- Laws of UX, Tesler (pp.107–110): "for any system there is a certain amount of complexity that cannot be reduced" (p.107); Tesler quoted directly: "If a million users each waste a minute a day dealing with complexity that an engineer could have eliminated in a week by making the software a little more complex, you are penalizing the user to make the engineer's job easier" (p.108). Mechanism — Gmail "reduce[s] complexity by populating the 'from' line and suggesting the 'to' line based on prior emails" (p.110): the complexity is absorbed, not gone.
- Laws of UX, complexity bias (p.109): "When we find ourselves favoring a more complex solution, it's a good sign that we don't have enough information or that we need to better understand the underlying problem." Mechanism — elaborateness is mistaken for rigor, so gratuitous flows survive review.
**Objective test.** (a) Classify every visible element/step goal-directed vs excise; avoidable-excise count target 0 — only excise genuinely unavoidable given current technology remains (AF p.273). (b) Any field re-asking data the system already holds from the same session/account (billing address, prior contacts, account email) with no prefill/"same as above" = fail (LU p.112 pattern). (c) Internal-concept leaks in user copy (raw statuses, error codes, file mechanics, "sync"/"commit"/"flush", literal paths) target 0 outside debug surfaces (AF pp.325–338). (d) A control goal-directed for one persona and excise for another passes only if conditionally revealed — hidden by default, reachable in one explicit "Advanced"/expert step (AF p.285). (e) For each proposed extra step/field: a reviewer must articulate the specific NEW requirement it serves; "feels more thorough" = complexity-bias candidate (LU p.109).
**✗ WRONG.** Two fully blank address forms back-to-back with no "same as billing"; a note app asking "save changes to Untitled-4.tmp?" on every close; a 20-slider color-grading panel shown by default to every first-time user who only wants to trim a clip.
**✓ RIGHT.** "Same as billing" pre-checked, collapsing the duplicate block entirely; continuous silent autosave with no Save dialog at all; trim front-and-center, the grading panel behind an explicit "Advanced" tab a beginner never sees and a pro reaches in one click.
**Crop.** LU-19, AF-09.
