**Score — grounded ladder (0→10).** Score = highest rung whose condition AND every rung below it hold.
- **0 — ✗:** ≥6 avoidable excise steps in the audited flow (the 8-step phone-number-change state) and/or fully blank re-asks of data the system already holds this session/account *(source: About Face p.272 excise band 0; Laws of UX Tesler pp.107–110 band 0)*.
- **1** — 4–6 avoidable excise steps remain after the obvious ones are removed *(source: About Face p.272 band 3)*.
- **2** — 3–5 avoidable excise steps; some prefill exists but is incomplete or requires noticing an unobvious shortcut *(source: About Face p.272; Laws of UX Tesler band 3)*.
- **3** — ≤2 avoidable excise steps, but ≥2 internal-concept leaks (raw statuses, "sync"/"commit"/"flush", literal temp filenames) in user-facing copy *(source: About Face pp.325–338 absorb-bookkeeping band 0/3)*.
- **4** — ≤1 internal-concept leak, but a persona-split control (goal-directed for one persona, excise for another) is shown to all by default, or its reveal is buried for the persona who needs it *(source: About Face p.285 contextual-excise bands 0/3)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** only technology-unavoidable excise remains; no blank re-ask of held data (prefilled or defaulted "same as above"); zero internal-concept leaks outside debug surfaces; persona-split controls hidden by default and reachable in one explicit "Advanced" step *(source: About Face p.273 + pp.325–338 bands 5–6; About Face p.285 band 5–6; Laws of UX Tesler p.110 band 5–6)*.
- **6** — + the inference is opt-out, not opt-in: defaults pre-checked/pre-selected, collapsing redundant entry entirely *(source: Laws of UX Tesler band 7–8, "same as billing" pre-checked)*.
- **7** — + a reviewer can articulate the specific NEW requirement every extra step/field serves — no step justified only as "feels more thorough" *(source: Laws of UX complexity bias p.109 band 5–6)*.
- **8** — + goal-directed step count verified near the theoretical minimum for the task (counted, compared to a stripped-down redesign) *(source: About Face p.272 band 7–8)*.
- **9** — + the underlying mechanism is absorbed automatically (continuous silent autosave; the Save dialog gone from the mainstream interface), with the Advanced reveal sensibly placed and labeled *(source: About Face pp.325–337 bands 7–10; About Face p.285 band 7–8)*.
- **10 — ✓ top-1%:** the top task collapses to essentially one goal-directed action (8 steps → 1), and a simpler alternative was demonstrably attempted before the shipped complexity *(source: About Face p.272 band 9–10; Laws of UX p.109 band 9–10)*.
N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — About Face rates excise and absorb-bookkeeping high (contextual-excise med); Laws of UX rates Tesler high (complexity bias low-med); majority high.

### DENS-8 — The oversimplification ceiling (the opposite failure)
**Rule.** Reducing too far strips the cues that say what's possible: icon-only actions, hidden-gesture-only features, chrome so minimal nothing is discoverable — a screen can fail clarity by being TOO reduced.
**Grounding.**
- Laws of UX (p.48): "When an interface has been simplified to the point of abstraction, it's no longer clear what actions are available, what the next steps are, or where to find specific information." Mechanism — icon meaning is not universal: "there is no icon standardization body that regulates what icons can be used where... the same icon [can] represent different actions" (p.49) — the heart/star glyphs "typically indicate the ability to favorite, like, bookmark, or rate an item, but... may sometimes simply indicate a featured item" (p.49).
- Krug, the Clear-app case (pp.193–195): after a ten-screen tour and tutorial, users asked to "create a new list called 'Chicago trip' with three items in it... So far, no one has succeeded... And if you can't figure that out, you can't get to the Help screens. Catch-22." Mechanism — a novel interaction vocabulary that is neither inferable nor re-discoverable collapses learnability entirely, tour or no tour.
**Objective test.** (a) Every icon-only control beyond the universally-recognized set (home, search, back, close, hamburger-menu) carries a visible text label OR a hover/long-press tooltip discoverable without trial interaction — an accessible name only in `aria-label` (invisible to sighted users) does not count (LU p.49). (b) A novel-interaction feature must have a persistent visible affordance AND re-openable help; run the onboarding exactly once, then assign the single most common task with zero further help — if the team cannot state a measured first-attempt success rate, presume the principle failing (KR pp.193–195).
**✗ WRONG.** An 8-icon toolbar (share/duplicate/archive/flag/pin/mute/export/more) with zero labels or tooltips, relying purely on glyph recognition; folder-creation only via a two-finger gesture shown once in an onboarding animation, with no persistent control and no way to re-open the tutorial.
**✓ RIGHT.** Visible labels beside/below each icon, or the less-common actions collapsed into a labeled "More" menu; the gesture stays as a power-user shortcut while a persistent "+" button also creates folders and a "?" reopens the tutorial at any time.
**Crop.** LU-06.
**Score — grounded ladder (0→10).** Score = highest rung whose condition AND every rung below it hold.
- **0 — ✗:** ≥3 unlabeled non-universal icon-only controls (the 8-icon toolbar), or a novel gesture is the ONLY path to a core action with onboarding shown once and no way to re-open it (the Clear-app Catch-22) *(source: Laws of UX pp.48–49 band 0; Krug pp.193–195 band 0)*.
- **2** — 1–2 non-universal icons remain unlabeled, or the gesture remains the only path but the tutorial is at least re-openable *(source: Laws of UX p.49 band 3; Krug pp.193–195 band 3)*.
- **3** — every control is named, but ≥1 only in `aria-label` — invisible to sighted users *(source: Laws of UX p.49 band 5–6, visible-text clause)*.
- **4** — every icon named sighted-visibly, but the conventional path for a novel-gesture feature exists only buried/undiscoverable *(source: Krug pp.193–195 band 5–6)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** every icon-only control beyond the universal set (home, search, back, close, hamburger) carries a visible text label OR a hover/long-press tooltip discoverable without trial interaction; every novel-gesture feature also has a conventional path *(source: Laws of UX p.49 band 5–6; Krug pp.193–195 band 5–6)*.
- **6** — + the conventional control is persistent and visible (button/menu item); the gesture is an optional shortcut *(source: Krug pp.193–195 band 7–8)*.
- **7** — + less-common actions are organized into a labeled "More" menu rather than a flat unlabeled row *(source: Laws of UX p.49 band 7–8)*.
- **8** — + onboarding/tutorial content re-accessible at any time from the surface itself *(source: Krug pp.193–195 band 9–10, reopenable "?" clause)*.
- **9** — + a measured first-attempt success rate exists for the primary task after exactly one onboarding pass, and it is adequate *(source: Krug pp.193–195 objective test — "if the team cannot state a measured rate, presume failing")*.
- **10 — ✓ top-1%:** every icon carries a visible text label at all times (not hover-only) — no action anywhere in the product requires prior glyph-meaning knowledge *(source: Laws of UX p.49 band 9–10, X/Twitter-nav case)*.
N/A if no instances on the surface (no icon-only controls and no novel interactions).
**Weight.** high (3) — Laws of UX rates the abstraction ceiling high (unlabeled icons silently block completion); Krug rates learnability collapse high when novel interactions exist; unanimous.

### DENS-9 — Prioritize by frequency under space pressure
**Rule.** On constrained surfaces, frequent/urgent things go close at hand; rare things go a few taps deeper with a discoverable path — depth-based disclosure, never omission of the capability.
**Grounding.**
- Krug (p.183): "Things I want to use in a hurry or frequently should be close at hand. Everything else can be a few taps away, but there should be an obvious path to get to them." Mechanism — follows directly from "the tyranny of the itty-bitty living space" (p.183): a small screen cannot hold everything at rank one, so frequency, not omission, allocates the prime positions.
- Universal Principles, performance load (p.178): "If the performance load is high, performance time and errors increase, and the probability of successfully accomplishing the goal decreases." Mechanism — every extra tap on a frequent action is repeated kinematic load; depth belongs on rare actions where its cost is paid rarely.
**Objective test.** Classify each control on a constrained surface frequent vs rare (by actual usage data or stated task priority): frequent-use controls reachable in ≤1 tap from the default view; rare-use controls may sit 2+ taps deep but must retain a labeled, discoverable path — never removed outright (KR p.183). Kinematic audit: taps-to-complete for the top 1–3 tasks; a redesign reducing that count without adding memory burden is a net win (UP p.179).
**✗ WRONG.** "Create new task" sits 3 taps deep in a hamburger menu while a rarely-used "Export to CSV" occupies the main toolbar.
**✓ RIGHT.** Create is a persistent primary/floating action button on the main screen; Export moves into a labeled "More options" menu — still reachable, just not prime real estate.
**Crop.** none (prose principle).
**Score — grounded ladder (0→10).** Score = highest rung whose condition AND every rung below it hold.
- **0 — ✗:** a frequent-class action sits ≥3 taps deep while a rare-use action occupies prime real estate (Create buried, Export on the toolbar), or a rare capability is removed outright instead of deepened *(source: Krug p.183 band 0 + "never removed" clause)*.
- **2** — the frequent action is 2 taps deep; rare paths reachable but entry is unlabeled/icon-only *(source: Krug p.183 band 3)*.
- **4** — frequent actions reach ≤1 tap in some flows but not from the default view; no prime-slot inversion remains *(source: Krug p.183 band 5–6)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** every frequent-class control (by usage data or stated task priority) is reachable in ≤1 tap from the default view; rare controls sit deeper but retain a labeled, discoverable path *(source: Krug p.183 band 7–8; the doc's objective test)*.
- **6** — + rare actions live behind a clearly labeled "More options"-type path *(source: Krug p.183 band 9–10 clause)*.
- **7** — + taps-to-complete counted for the top 1–3 tasks; at most one removable step remains *(source: Universal Principles pp.178–179 kinematic audit)*.
- **8** — + no step removable without adding memory burden — kinematic minimum reached *(source: Universal Principles p.179)*.
- **9** — + the frequent action is a persistent 1-tap control (FAB/primary button) on the default view *(source: Krug p.183 band 9–10)*.
- **10 — ✓ top-1%:** + the frequent/rare classification is backed by actual usage data (not guessed priority) and the kinematic count is verified against a baseline product-wide *[derived: Krug p.183 measure + Universal Principles Performance Load band 7–8]*.
N/A if no instances on the surface (unconstrained surfaces with no space pressure).
**Weight.** med (2) — Krug rates frequency prioritization med (constrained/mobile-specific); Universal Principles rates performance load high; the direct-source book carries the entry, so med (split noted).

### DENS-10 — Layering: choose the disclosure structure by the data's relationship type
**Rule.** 2D layering (linear wizard, hierarchical tree, parallel, web) switches context; 3D layering (opaque popup vs transparent overlay) elaborates without switching context — match the type to the content's actual relationships.
**Grounding.**
- Universal Principles (p.146): "Layering involves organizing information into related groupings and then presenting or making available only certain groupings at any one time. Layering is primarily used to manage complexity, but can also be used to reinforce relationships in information." The 3D distinction, verbatim: "Opaque layers are useful when additional information about a particular item is desired without contexts (e.g., software pop-up windows). Transparent layers are useful when overlays of information combine to illustrate concepts or highlight relationships (e.g., weather maps)" (p.146). Mechanism — a hierarchical dataset forced into a flat linear presentation hides the relationship the data actually has: the layering type either reinforces or erases the structure (pp.146–147).
**Objective test.** Classify the content's actual relationship type and check the layering matches: sequential/story-shaped → linear layers (wizard, slideshow); superordinate/subordinate → hierarchical layers (nested/collapsible tree); organized by external correspondence → parallel layers; densely cross-linked → web layers. Flag any mismatch (org-chart data as one long scroll; flat content forced into a wizard). Elaboration that must keep the parent visible → transparent/dimmed overlay, not a full navigation (UP pp.146–147).
**✗ WRONG.** An org-chart-shaped dataset (clear superordinate/subordinate relationships) presented as one long flat scroll with no nesting — the hierarchy the data has is invisible; an in-place point-detail forced into a full page navigation that discards the parent context.
**✓ RIGHT.** The same data as a collapsible tree where each node's children reveal only on expand — the layering type matches the data's structure; point-detail in a dimming overlay that keeps the parent visible behind it.
**Crop.** UP-21.
**Score — grounded ladder (0→10).** Score = highest rung whose condition AND every rung below it hold.
- **0 — ✗:** clear relationship-type mismatch — content with an obvious structural relationship presented so the relationship is invisible (org-chart data as one long flat scroll) *(source: Universal Principles p.146 band 0)*.
- **2** — content is layered but with a poor-fit type (densely cross-linked content forced into strict linear steps, losing the links) *(source: Universal Principles p.146 band 3)*.
- **3** — the 2D type matches, but point-detail that needed its parent discards the parent context entirely via full navigation *(source: Universal Principles p.146, opaque-vs-transparent distinction)*.
- **4** — detail keeps only partial context (a pane replaces part of the overview); opaque/transparent uses mixed correct and incorrect *(source: Universal Principles p.146)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** the layering type used matches the content's actual relationship classification — sequential→linear, superordinate/subordinate→hierarchical/collapsible, external correspondence→parallel, densely cross-linked→web *(source: Universal Principles p.146 band 5–6)*.
- **6** — + opaque layers used for context-free item detail (popups) AND transparent layers used where information must combine with what is beneath (overlays/maps), each per its content *(source: Universal Principles p.146, verbatim opaque/transparent rule)*.
- **7** — + elaboration that must keep the parent visible uses a transparent/dimmed overlay or in-place expansion, never a context-discarding navigation *(source: Universal Principles pp.146–147)*.
- **8** — + layer transitions (expand/collapse, popup, overlay) preserve whatever context the content type requires — no state or orientation lost across a toggle *(source: Universal Principles p.146 band 7–8)*.
- **10 — ✓ top-1%:** + verified that the chosen layering type could not be swapped for another without degrading the content's actual structure (the genuinely-hierarchical dataset as a collapsible tree) *(source: Universal Principles pp.146–147 band 9–10)*.
N/A if no instances on the surface (no layered/disclosed content).
**Weight.** med (2) — Universal Principles (sole grounding book) rates Layering med.

### DENS-11 — [derived] Rest-state budget
**Rule.** Define what a surface's rest state is FOR (orient + select) and admit only elements serving that; everything else must justify itself as earned-by-interaction. A rest state already showing the deepest detail has no disclosure architecture at all.
**Grounding.** Derived — no single book states the composite; four converge on it:
- Universal Principles (p.188): "Information presented to a person who is not interested or ready to process it is effectively noise" — at rest, the user is not yet ready for depth, so resident detail is noise by definition.
- Universal Principles (p.250): kitchen-sink visibility "actually makes the relevant information and controls more difficult to access due to an overload of information" — total exposure defeats the very visibility it seeks.
- About Face (Ch11–12): orchestration reveals work progressively (p.250) and "*Excise tasks*... don't contribute directly to reaching the goal" (p.272) — rest-state chrome not serving orient-or-select is excise.
- Designing Interfaces (p.224): Moo.com — "a customer doesn't see the customization options until they click into the editable parts of the card" — depth is earned by entering the region that needs it.
- Refactoring UI (p.67/69) supplies the sanctioned exception: dense UIs ("dashboards needing max info-density") are "a deliberate exception, not a fallback default" — density must be chosen, not accreted.
Convergence: all four give the same two-state architecture — a lean rest state for orienting/selecting, and a distinct richer state entered by explicit interaction.
**Objective test.** (a) Compare the rest render and the post-selection render of the same object: if selection changes nothing meaningful (all detail already visible at rest), disclosure is absent — fail. (b) Enumerate the rest state's elements: each member maps to orient-or-select, or to an explicit, user-approved density exception (an info-max dashboard, RU p.69); unmapped elements are excise findings. (c) The detail state must be reachable by one explicit interaction and must not require navigation that discards the overview.
**✗ WRONG.** Every item on an overview canvas permanently displays its full metadata block; clicking an item adds only one more field — the two states are indistinguishable and the canvas reads as a wall.
**✓ RIGHT.** Items at rest show identity + one key value; selection populates a dedicated detail region with the full record — two visibly different states, depth earned by the click.
**Crop.** UP-01 (as the canonical two-state pair).
**Score — grounded ladder (0→10).** Score = highest rung whose condition AND every rung below it hold. (Derived principle — every rung synthesized; sources are the convergent seeds.)
- **0 — ✗:** rest render and post-selection render of the same object are indistinguishable — all detail already resident at rest, selection changes nothing meaningful; no disclosure architecture exists *[derived: Universal Principles p.188 ("noise" at rest) + Designing Interfaces p.224 (depth entered by action)]*.
- **2** — selection adds only marginal detail (≤1 additional field) — the two states nearly indistinguishable *[derived: Designing Interfaces p.224 + Universal Principles p.188]*.
- **3** — a distinct detail state exists, but ≥3 rest-state elements map to neither orient nor select (the canvas reads as a wall) *[derived: About Face p.272 excise + Universal Principles p.250 kitchen-sink]*.
- **4** — ≤2 unmapped rest elements, but the detail state needs multi-step reach or a navigation that discards the overview *[derived: Designing Interfaces p.224 + About Face Ch11 orchestration]*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** selection enters a visibly distinct, richer detail state reachable by ONE explicit interaction, without losing the overview *[derived: Designing Interfaces p.224 (Moo.com) + Universal Principles p.188 + About Face Ch11]*.
- **6** — + ≤1 rest-state element unmapped to orient-or-select *[derived: About Face pp.272–273 excise classification]*.
- **7** — + zero unmapped rest elements — every resident element serves orienting or selecting (the excise target of 0) *[derived: About Face p.273 "eliminate excise wherever possible"]*.
- **8** — + any info-max dense region present is a stated deliberate exception (dashboard class) — density chosen, never accreted *(source: Refactoring UI pp.67/69, the sanctioned exception)*.
- **10 — ✓ top-1%:** + the two-state architecture holds for every object class on the surface — rest = identity + one key value, selection = the full record in a dedicated detail region — with no accreted resident density anywhere *[derived: Universal Principles p.188 + p.250 + Designing Interfaces p.224 + About Face Ch11–12 convergence]*.
N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — derived principle; its seeds are all high (Universal Principles progressive disclosure p.188 and kitchen-sink visibility p.250, About Face excise/orchestration); Refactoring UI supplies only the exception clause.

# Depth, Shadow & Light

Pillars: 1, 4.

---

### DEPTH-1 — One consistent light source (raised vs inset grammar)
**Rule.** Light comes from above, everywhere in the UI: raised elements take a lighter top edge and a small dark shadow below; inset elements the exact inverse (lighter bottom lip, dark inner shadow at top). One light direction across the whole product sells the illusion.
**Grounding.** Refactoring UI: "Notice how the top edge of the panel is lighter? That's because it's angled towards the sky and receives more light... The only way those edges could possibly be oriented that way is if the panel itself is raised, so that's how our brains perceive it." (p.173). The inverse for the inset cabinet: "it's clear that the panels are inset because there's a shadow at the top indicating that the lip above is blocking the light, and the bottom edge is lighter, indicating that it's angled upward." (p.174). Mechanism: the brain infers 3D orientation from which edge catches light, so edge treatments — not literal texture — encode raised vs recessed; worked CSS build-ups at pp.176–178. Restraint clause: borrow real-world depth cues, no photo-realism (p.179).
**Objective test.** Raised element: top edge/border LIGHTER than its face (e.g. `inset 0 1px 0 hsl(224,84%,74%)`) AND a small dark drop-shadow BELOW only (e.g. `0 1px 3px hsla(0,0%,0%,.2)`) — not on all sides. Inset element: the reverse — lighter BOTTOM lip (e.g. `0 -2px 0 hsla(0,0%,100%,.15)`) + dark inset shadow at TOP (e.g. `inset 0 2px 2px hsla(0,0%,0%,.1)`). Any element mixing both conventions (light top AND light bottom, or shadows on four sides), or two components lit from different directions on one screen = fail.
**✗ WRONG.** A "Create Account" button with no edge treatment at all — flat color, no shadow — ambiguous whether it is pressable; one card on the screen lit from above while its sibling appears lit from the side.
**✓ RIGHT.** Buttons uniformly get a lighter top edge (`inset 0 1px 0 <lighter>`) plus a small below-shadow (`0 1px 3px`); a "Drag and drop to upload" well gets the inverse (`0 -2px 0 <light>` lip + `inset 0 2px 2px` top shadow) — a single sun over the whole interface.
**Crop.** RU-08 (p.173 blue-door raised panel; p.174 grey-cabinet inset panel; pp.176–178 button/well build-ups).
**Score — grounded ladder (0→10).**
- **0 — ✗ anchor:** no edge treatment on any raised/inset element (flat color, no shadow — pressability ambiguous), OR elements mix both conventions (light top AND light bottom, or shadows on all four sides) *(source: Refactoring UI #25 p.173–174 — the ✗ flat "Create Account" button + mixed-convention fail)*.
- **2** — edge treatments exist but ≥2 components on the same screen imply DIFFERENT light directions (one lit from above, a sibling from the side/below) *(source: Refactoring UI #25 p.173 "single light source rule")*.
- **3** — treatments exist and mostly agree on a direction, but ≥1 element is backwards for its intended depth (dark top / light bottom on a raised element) *(source: Refactoring UI #25 rung-3 — wrong-direction edge treatment)*.
- **4** — every treated element's direction is correct (raised: lighter top + dark shadow below only; inset: lighter bottom lip + dark inset top shadow), but ≥1 primary pressable control still carries zero cue *(source: Refactoring UI pp.173–178; Krug p.187 "affordances are the last thing you should hide")*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** correct light-top/dark-below for raised (inverse for inset) applied on every raised/inset element AND every pressable control carries ≥1 depth cue — even if the treatments are subtle/easy to miss *(source: Refactoring UI #25 rung 5–6)*.
- **6–7** — cues are clearly perceptible (edge highlight visible against the face at 100% zoom; shadow offset ≥1px) and consistent with one implied light direction across every component on the screen *(source: Refactoring UI #25 rung 7–8 — perceptible, correctly-directioned, consistent implied light source)*.
- **8** — + a box-shadow/border-value audit shows zero exceptions product-wide: all drop shadows positive-Y, all highlights top-edge (or exact inverse on inset), no four-side shadows anywhere *(source: Refactoring UI #25 Measure — inspect box-shadow/border values across the whole UI)*.
- **9** — + raised AND inset grammars both present where apt (buttons vs wells/inputs), each built with the paired two-part treatment (highlight + shadow), matching the p.176–178 build-ups *(source: Refactoring UI pp.176–178 button/well worked examples)*.
- **10 — ✓ anchor:** matches the ✓ button/well pair exactly — lighter top inset-highlight + small dark below-shadow for raised, lighter bottom lip + dark inset top shadow for recessed — one light direction across the entire product, with no photo-realism creep (real-world cues borrowed, not imitated) *(source: Refactoring UI #25 rung 9–10; restraint clause p.179)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition AND every rung below it hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** med (2) — per Refactoring UI's weight line (specific depth-cue technique; less relevant to purely flat designs, which route to DEPTH-3).

### DEPTH-2 — Shadow scale maps to intentional elevation
**Rule.** Define a fixed 4–5 step shadow scale: tight = barely raised (buttons), medium = floating (dropdowns), large diffuse = commanding (modals). Rich elevation combines TWO shadows — a soft offset cast + a tight dark ambient-occlusion shadow that fades as elevation rises.
**Grounding.** Refactoring UI: "Small shadows with a tight blur radius make an element feel only slightly raised off of the background, while larger shadows with a higher blur radius make an element feel much closer to the user... The closer something feels to the user, the more it will attract their focus." (p.180) — elevation is an attention lever, so it must map to intended prominence, not per-component whim. Two-part model: "The first shadow is larger and softer, with a considerable vertical offset and large blur radius. It simulates the shadow cast behind an object by a direct light source... The second shadow is tighter and darker, with less of a vertical offset and a smaller blur radius. It simulates the shadowed area underneath an object where even ambient light has a hard time reaching." (pp.186–187). Elevation tuning: "As an object gets further away from a surface, the small, dark shadow created by a lack of ambient light slowly disappears... make sure you make that shadow more subtle for shadows that represent a higher elevation." (pp.188–189).
**Objective test.** Token audit: ≥4 distinct steps with strictly increasing blur-radius + offset (e.g. `0 1px 3px` → `0 4px 6px` → `0 10px 24px` → `0 15px 35px`); buttons/small controls on the smallest step, dropdowns mid, modals largest. Two-part shadows: the ambient (second, tighter) shadow's opacity/size DECREASES as the direct shadow's elevation increases across the scale — a constant ambient value across all steps fails.
**✗ WRONG.** Buttons, dropdown menus, AND modal dialogs all sharing one identical `box-shadow: 0 4px 6px hsla(0,0%,0%,.1)` — a modal reads as "floaty" as a small button.
**✓ RIGHT.** A 5-step scale (`0 1px 3px` → `0 15px 35px`) assigned by prominence; a rich elevated card combines `0 4px 6px hsla(0,0%,0%,.7)` (direct) + `0 5px 15px hsla(0,0%,0%,.1)` (ambient), and at higher elevation steps the ambient component is reduced to near-invisible.
**Crop.** RU-09 (p.180 elevation diagram; pp.181–183 shadow tiers + 5-step scale bar; pp.186–189 two-shadow card + ambient-shrinks-with-height scale).
**Score — grounded ladder (0→10).**
- **0 — ✗ anchor:** one identical shadow value shared by every elevated element (buttons, dropdowns, modals alike) regardless of prominence — the single `0 4px 6px` everywhere *(source: Refactoring UI #26 p.180 — the ✗ shared-shadow case)*.
- **2** — exactly 2 distinct shadow values exist, assignment per-component whim (same element class lands on different steps, or a dropdown out-shadows a modal) *(source: Refactoring UI #26 rung-3 — some tiering but not matched to importance)*.
- **3** — 2–3 distinct steps with strictly increasing blur/offset, assignment mostly matching prominence but ≥1 inversion remains *(source: Refactoring UI #26 rung-3; p.180 elevation-as-attention mechanism)*.
- **4** — ≥4 distinct shadow tokens with strictly increasing blur-radius AND offset exist in the token file, but ≥1 element-to-step assignment inversion remains on screen *(source: Refactoring UI #26 Measure — audit the shadow-token scale for ≥4 strictly-increasing steps)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** ≥4-step strictly-increasing scale AND roughly-correct assignment (buttons/small controls smallest, dropdowns/popovers mid, modals largest — zero inversions), even if not fine-tuned *(source: Refactoring UI #26 rung 5–6, pp.181–183)*.
- **6** — + no per-component ad-hoc shadow values outside the token scale anywhere on the screen (every box-shadow resolves to one of the defined steps) *(source: Refactoring UI #26 "fixed set of shadows" system audit, pp.181–183)* `[derived: Refactoring UI #26 + #9-style token-audit form]`.
- **7** — + rich-elevation elements (cards/modals) combine the TWO-part shadow: a soft large-offset large-blur cast shadow + a tight dark low-offset ambient shadow *(source: Refactoring UI pp.186–187 two-shadow model)*.
- **8** — + the ambient component's opacity/size decreases across at least the adjacent steps where elevation rises (not constant scale-wide) *(source: Refactoring UI pp.188–189 — ambient shadow "slowly disappears" with height)*.
- **9** — full 4–5-step scale correctly assigned per element type AND ambient strictly decreases across every step, near-invisible at the top step *(source: Refactoring UI #26 rung 7–8; pp.188–189)*.
- **10 — ✓ anchor:** matches the ✓ examples — each element class on its correct step, the two-shadow "Agile Mornings"-class card technique executed, ambient tuned per elevation step across the whole scale *(source: Refactoring UI #26 rung 9–10, pp.186–189)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition AND every rung below it hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** med (2) — per Refactoring UI's weight line (system-level consistency check, shadows only).

### DEPTH-3 — Flat designs still need depth cues
**Rule.** Even without shadows: lighter-than-background reads raised, darker reads inset; hard-edged zero-blur offset shadows and cross-boundary overlaps create layering cheaply. "Flat" never excuses zero perceptible layering.
**Grounding.** Refactoring UI: "In general (especially with shades of the same color), lighter objects feel closer to us and darker objects feel further away. Make an element lighter than the background color to make it feel like it's raised off of the page, or darker than the background color if you want it to feel inset like a well." (p.191) — lightness alone carries the z-axis, so flat systems keep depth via color relations. Solid shadows: "Another way to communicate depth in a flat design is to use short, vertically offset shadows with no blur radius at all... It's a great way to make a card or button stand off the page a little bit without sacrificing that flat aesthetic." (p.192). Overlap: "instead of containing a card entirely within another element, offset it so it crosses the transition between two different backgrounds" (p.194); overlapping photos need "an 'invisible border' — one that matches the background color — so there's always a bit of a gap between images." (p.196).
**Objective test.** Flat-raised elements: background HSL lightness strictly HIGHER than the page background (not merely a different hue with no lightness relation); flat-inset: strictly lower. Solid shadows: blur-radius exactly `0` with a small positive vertical offset only (e.g. `0 3px 0`). Bridging cards: the card's bounding box (via negative margin, e.g. `margin-bottom: -60px`) actually crosses the boundary line between the two background colors, not fully contained in one section. Overlapping avatars/photos: each carries a border matching the page background (e.g. `border: 4px solid #FFFFFF`).
**✗ WRONG.** "It's flat design" excusing every panel and card flush against the page with zero lightness differentiation and zero shadow — one undifferentiated plane; touching same-tone avatar circles with no border merging into one blob.
**✓ RIGHT.** The login card lighter than the page (raised), the secondary panel beneath it darker (receded), no shadow at all; cart rows with a crisp `0 3px 0 hsl(220,7%,83%)` solid shadow; destination cards pulled up `-60px` to straddle the hero/page boundary; avatar circles with 4px background-colored borders.
**Crop.** RU-26 (p.190 flat social feed; p.191 lighter=raised/darker=receded; p.192 solid-shadow rows; pp.194–196 overlap + invisible-border pair).
**Score — grounded ladder (0→10).**
- **0 — ✗ anchor:** no lightness differentiation, no shadow, no overlap anywhere — every panel/card sits flush in one undifferentiated plane, justified by "it's flat design" *(source: Refactoring UI #27 p.190 — the ✗ undifferentiated flat layout)*.
- **2** — minimal lightness differentiation attempted but too subtle to register as raised/inset, OR a solid shadow is attempted with the wrong blur/offset, OR a bridging element sits entirely within one background color with no crossing offset *(source: Refactoring UI #27 rung-3; #28 rung-0/3)*.
- **3** — at least one flat depth technique (lightness, solid-shadow, or overlap) is correctly executed on SOME containers, but ≥1 panel/card still sits flush with zero perceptible cue *(source: Refactoring UI #27 pp.190–192)*.
- **4** — the primary technique in use meets its individual threshold on most containers, but ≥1 violation remains somewhere on the surface: a wrong-direction lightness relation, a non-zero-blur "solid" shadow, an uncrossed boundary, or an unbordered overlapping avatar *(source: Refactoring UI #27 rung-3–5; #28 rung-3)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** every flat-raised element's background lightness is strictly HIGHER than the page background and every flat-inset strictly LOWER, AND every panel/card carries ≥1 depth cue (lightness delta, zero-blur solid shadow, or cross-boundary overlap) — no flush undifferentiated container remains *(source: Refactoring UI #27 rung 5–6 p.191; #28 rung 5–6 p.194)*.
- **6–7** — the cues in use are clearly perceptible (not subtle) and consistently applied product-wide; solid shadows where used are exactly zero-blur with a small positive vertical offset; overlaps where used measurably cross the background boundary *(source: Refactoring UI #27 rung 7–8 p.192; #28 rung 7–8 p.194)*.
- **8** — overlapping avatars/photos consistently carry background-matching borders preventing edge-clash, AND bridging cards produce a clear, deliberate straddle of the boundary rather than a barely-visible one *(source: Refactoring UI #28 rung 7–8 p.196)*.
- **9** — all applicable techniques (lightness, solid-shadow, overlap) are combined where each is apt, each independently meeting its rung-8 bar with zero exceptions across the surface *(source: Refactoring UI #27+#28 rung 9–10)* `[derived: Refactoring UI #27 + #28 combined]`.
- **10 — ✓ anchor:** matches the ✓ examples exactly — the login card lighter/raised against a darker secondary panel via lightness alone with no shadow; cart rows with a crisp zero-blur `0 3px 0` solid shadow; destination cards at `margin-bottom:-60px` visibly straddling the hero/page boundary; avatar circles with a clean 4px background-matching border *(source: Refactoring UI #27 rung 9–10 p.191–192; #28 rung 9–10 p.194–196)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition AND every rung below it hold. N/A if no instances on the surface (e.g. the product uses a realistic shadow system instead — per Refactoring UI, apply whichever depth technique is present).
**Weight.** med (2) — experts mark both source techniques low-med (RU #27, #28); rounded to med here since this entry merges both, noted.

### DEPTH-4 — Depth cues are information; strip only with a replacement, add only where apt
**Rule.** Bevels/shadows/borders historically encode "pressable / typeable / in front" — flattening that removes the cue without another signal removes information; conversely, heavy metaphor/skeuomorphism that adds no functional information is noise, and the interface must never bend to preserve a metaphor's logic.
**Grounding.** Krug: "Flat design has a tendency to take along with it not just the potentially distracting decoration but also the useful information that the more textured elements were conveying." (p.188); "For affordances to work, they need to be noticeable... by definition, affordances are the last thing you should hide." (p.187) — the texture WAS the signal of what is clickable. About Face: "Never bend your interface to fit a metaphor." (p.304) — the Magic Cap system forced users to "go down the hallway and into the game room to play Solitaire" purely to obey its metaphor (p.303); "3D rendering that doesn't add information" is a named visual-noise form (p.423). The book's own dated-mechanism caveat yields the surviving general rule: signal interactivity by SOME visual means, whatever the era's style (flattening trends "threaten ease of use by removing these virtual manual affordances").
**Objective test.** For each control class on the screen (button / input / disabled item / plain text), ≥1 styling dimension (fill, border, shadow, color, weight) differs from every OTHER class — two classes visually identical = affordance stripped (KR p.187 test; see AFFORD-3). For each skeuomorphic/metaphoric element: count steps to use it vs a plain non-metaphoric equivalent — MORE steps, or a physical rendering that informs nothing = metaphor cost; also count navigational paths gated behind maintaining the metaphor's internal consistency.
**✗ WRONG.** A flat redesign leaving buttons, section headings, and disabled items all as plain gray text with no fill/border/weight difference; a note app rendering a 3D wooden desk whose drawers add two drag gestures to every note retrieval.
**✓ RIGHT.** Flat but differentiated — solid fill for buttons, weight for headings, reduced opacity for disabled; the same notes as a plain searchable flat list, retrieval one tap away.
**Crop.** KR-03 ("I'M A HEADING / I'M A BUTTON" flat-ambiguity example, pp.186–188), AF-11 (Fig. 13-1 Magic Cap, p.303).
**Score — grounded ladder (0→10).**
- **0 — ✗ anchor:** ≥2 pairs of control classes on the screen are visually identical — buttons, headings, and disabled items all render as plain gray text with no distinguishing dimension at all *(source: Don't Make Me Think #7 p.187–188 — the flat-redesign case)*.
- **2** — exactly one pair of control classes is visually identical (the rest collapse into sameness), OR a core task is gated behind metaphor navigation (the Magic Cap hallway class) *(source: DMMT #7 rung-3 p.187; About Face p.303–304 Magic Cap)*.
- **3** — every control class has ≥1 differing dimension but distinctions are subtle enough a fast scan could still misclassify (e.g. disabled vs. active look too similar), AND/OR a metaphoric element constrains a feature's design without adding extra steps *(source: DMMT #7 rung 5–6 p.187; About Face p.304 rung-3)*.
- **4** — control classes are confidently distinguishable at a glance (1–2 dimensions each), but ≥1 flattened element that lost a legacy cue (bevel/border/shadow) carries no replacement signal at all, OR task-path elements are still wrapped in non-informative 3D/texture noise *(source: DMMT #7 rung 7–8 p.187; About Face #5 p.423 needless-3D category)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** every control class differs from every other class on ≥1 styling dimension AND every flattened element that lost a legacy cue carries a replacement signal (fill, weight, opacity, color) AND no metaphoric element costs more steps than a plain non-metaphoric equivalent *(source: DMMT #7 rung 5–6; About Face p.304 rung 5–6 "meets the book's test")*.
- **6–7** — differentiation uses a multi-dimensional treatment (fill+corner vs. bold+size vs. muted opacity) confidently readable at a glance product-wide; any lightweight metaphor present is genuinely apt (diegetic) and never bends function to fit it *(source: DMMT #7 rung 9–10 p.187–188; About Face p.304 rung 7–8)*.
- **8** — zero non-informative 3D/texture rendering anywhere on the surface, even decorative uses outside the task path *(source: About Face #5 p.423 rung 7–8 — "0 categories present")*.
- **9** — every control class carries a distinct, multi-dimensional treatment with zero ambiguity anywhere AND zero navigational path is gated behind any metaphor's internal consistency *(source: DMMT #7 rung 9–10; About Face p.304 rung 9–10)* `[derived: DMMT #7 + About Face p.304 combined]`.
- **10 — ✓ anchor:** matches the ✓ examples — flat but clearly differentiated (solid fill for buttons, weight for headings, reduced opacity for disabled) AND the notes rendered as a plain searchable flat list, retrieval one tap away, with zero non-informative 3D/texture anywhere *(source: DMMT #7 rung 9–10 p.187–188; About Face p.304 rung 9–10; About Face #5 rung 9–10)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition AND every rung below it hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — experts disagree: Krug marks the affordance-stripping test high ("directly gates whether clickability is even possible"); About Face marks metaphor restraint med (rare in modern flat UI). Majority-of-substance goes to the affordance half, which carries 6 of this entry's 10 points — noted.

### DEPTH-5 — Overlays sit above — and must look like it
**Rule.** Anything floating (popover, menu, tooltip, dialog) must read unambiguously as the top layer: an elevation step from the shadow scale, a scrim/dim where modal, a crisp boundary from the content beneath.
**Grounding.** Refactoring UI: "larger shadows with a higher blur radius make an element feel much closer to the user... The closer something feels to the user, the more it will attract their focus." (p.180) — modal-class elements take the largest, most diffuse shadow because elevation signals attention priority (pp.180–184). Universal Principles, figure-ground: "When the figure and ground of a composition are clear, the relationship is stable; the figure element receives more attention and is better remembered than the ground. In unstable figure-ground relationships, the relationship is ambiguous and can be interpreted in different ways." (p.96) — an overlay whose layer status is ambiguous alternates figure/ground and confuses. Designing Interfaces' spotlight approach foregrounds by receding the rest: dim everything except the pointed-at content (Data Spotlight, Ch.9).
**Objective test.** Every overlay carries the TOP elevation token of the shadow scale (or a scrim/dim where modal) — never a card-level shadow; two simultaneously-open floating surfaces never share ambiguous equal elevation (z-order + shadow step differ, or only one is open at a time); the overlay's boundary remains legible against every page region it can appear over (figure-ground stable per UP p.96 cues: bounded shape, nearer implied depth, ground continuing behind it).
**✗ WRONG.** A popover with the same card-level `0 4px 6px` shadow as the content beneath, visually merging into the page; two panels at equal elevation fighting for front-most.
**✓ RIGHT.** The popover at the top shadow step (`0 15px 35px`-class) with the page dimmed behind it when modal; only one floating layer at a time, or clearly distinct elevation steps.
**Crop.** RU-09. Occlusion/collision rules → dialogs-popovers-overlays.md DLG-7.
**Score — grounded ladder (0→10).**
- **0 — ✗ anchor:** ≥1 overlay shares the same shadow value as content cards beneath it — no elevation differentiation, it merges into the page *(source: Refactoring UI p.180 elevation-as-attention mechanism — the ✗ popover-merges case)*.
- **2** — the overlay is elevated above cards but sits on a mid-scale shadow step rather than the top one, AND/OR no modal in the product carries a scrim *(source: Refactoring UI p.180–184; the ✗ two-panels-equal-elevation case)*.
- **3** — some overlays reach a distinguishable elevation, but ≥1 floating surface still ties/collides with another at equal elevation + z-order *(source: Universal Principles p.96 unstable figure-ground pattern; the ✗ equal-elevation collision)*.
- **4** — every modal dims/scrims the page behind it and overlays sit visibly above cards, but the TOP shadow-scale step is not consistently used (a mid-scale step still appears on some overlays) *(source: Refactoring UI p.180–184 scale-assignment logic)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** every floating surface (popover/menu/tooltip/dialog) carries the TOP elevation token of the scale (or a scrim where modal) AND no two floating surfaces are ever simultaneously open at the same z-order + shadow step *(source: Refactoring UI p.180 rung 5–6; DEPTH-5 objective test)*.
- **6–7** — + the overlay's boundary satisfies ≥2 of the figure-ground cues (bounded shape, nearer implied depth, ground continuing behind it) over most page regions it can appear on *(source: Universal Principles p.96 rung 5–6 — "the book's own test threshold")*.
- **8** — + the boundary satisfies all 3 figure-ground cues over EVERY region the overlay can appear on, verified via a quick recall/attention check (the overlay is what a viewer names first) *(source: Universal Principles p.96 rung 7–8)*.
- **9** — every modal scrims consistently, zero equal-elevation collisions occur anywhere, the top elevation token is applied product-wide, and the figure-ground boundary is fully stable across all 3 cues everywhere *(source: Refactoring UI p.180–184 + Universal Principles p.96 rung 9–10)* `[derived: Refactoring UI + Universal Principles combined]`.
- **10 — ✓ anchor:** matches the ✓ examples exactly — the popover sits at the top shadow step with the page dimmed behind it when modal, only one floating layer is open at a time (or clearly distinct elevation steps when more than one is), and the boundary stays legible with a fully stable figure-ground relationship over every region it can cover *(source: Refactoring UI p.180–184 rung 9–10; Universal Principles p.96 rung 9–10)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition AND every rung below it hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** med (2) — Refactoring UI's shadow-scale weight line and Universal Principles' figure-ground weight line both med; no disagreement.

# Dialogs, Popovers & Overlays

Secondary surfaces: when to use them, how they behave, and what they must never do. Pillars: 2, 3, 4.

---

### DLG-1 — Primary interactions live in the primary surface
**Rule.** Dialogs/modals are supporting rooms for the confusing, dangerous, or rare — never the main stage; frequent everyday tasks live inline in the main view.
**Grounding.**
- *About Face* (p.625): "Put primary interactions in the primary window." And: "If a user is the chef, and the application is the kitchen, a dialog is the pantry. The pantry plays a secondary role, as should dialogs. They are supporting actors rather than lead players." Also: "Dialogs are appropriate for functions that are out of the main interaction flow." (p.625)
  - Mechanism: "It is very difficult to create fluid interactions if you force users through a maze of pop-up dialogs" — every modal detour breaks the flow state the main surface exists to sustain; the pantry metaphor assigns dialogs a structurally secondary role.
- *About Face* (p.339): the Omnigraffle inline-rename example (Fig. 14-5) replaces a Properties dialog for a frequent task — the positive form of "primary interactions in the primary window."
  - Mechanism: the harmonious-interaction list (p.251) — "Keep necessary tools close at hand" — and "it is better to make the user ask explicitly for configuration one time in ten than it is to make the user reject the configuration interface nine times in ten" (pp.263–264): frequency decides where an interaction lives.
**Objective test.** For each task a persona performs more than ~once per session, count whether completing it requires opening a modal dialog: any such HIGH-frequency task gated behind a modal = flag; a genuinely rare/dangerous/confusing task gated behind a modal = pass. Target: 0 more-than-once-per-session tasks requiring a modal.
**✗ WRONG.** Renaming a record — a task users do many times a day — requires opening a modal Properties dialog, clicking into a text field inside it, and clicking OK to close it.
**✓ RIGHT.** Clicking the record's name in its normal location makes it editable in place; typing and committing happens inline, no dialog involved for this frequent action.
**Crop.** AF-10 (Fig. 14-5, Omnigraffle inline rename, p.339 — positive; Fig. 21-30, stacked-tabs Options dialog, p.638 — the over-reliance-on-dialogs negative).
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — a high-frequency task (done more than once per session) requires opening a modal dialog demanding several settings every single time, with no inline path at all *(source: About Face p.625, p.339, p.251, pp.263-264; scoring #28 rung 0)*.
- **2** — the task is inline for the common case, but a fairly common variant still opens a dialog *(About Face p.625; scoring #28 rung 3)*.
- **4** — inline editing exists for the frequent case but with no visible affordance (hover cue/pencil) — must be known to be found *(About Face p.339, Fig.14-5 mechanism)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** no high-frequency task is gated behind a modal; only genuinely rare/dangerous/confusing tasks use dialogs *(About Face p.625; scoring #28 rung 5-6 — the book's stated target)*.
- **6** — + each frequently-edited value is editable in place with a visible affordance *(About Face p.339 mechanism — discoverability of the inline path)*.
- **8** — + common variants of frequent tasks also complete inline, not just the trivial case *(About Face pp.263-264 — "ask explicitly one time in ten" frequency principle, applied to variant coverage)*.
- **10** — frequent tasks are fully inline with zero dialog involvement for the task class, as in the Omnigraffle inline rename *(About Face p.339, Fig.14-5; scoring #28 rung 9-10)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — per About Face's weight line (directly measures interaction friction for the most common flows).

### DLG-2 — One dialog, one coherent subject, one specific title
**Rule.** A dialog organizes controls/info about ONE object or ONE function; every section shares a statable reason for being together; the title is the function's verb ("Export Report") or the object's name ("Jane Doe — Details"), never a generic noun alone.
**Grounding.**
- *About Face* (p.626): "Dialogs are appropriate for organizing controls and information about a single domain object or application function."
  - Mechanism: the negative case study is the defunct Word Options dialog cramming 10 unrelated tabs (Security, Spelling & Grammar, Track Changes, User Information…) with "little connection among the 12 panes" (p.639) — no single subject means the user can never predict what lives inside.
- *About Face* (p.627): "Use verbs in function dialog title bars" / "Use object names in property dialog title bars." "When you request the Properties dialog for a directory named Backup, the title bar says Backup Properties."
  - Mechanism: the title is the user's only pre-reading cue about scope — a verb names the action being configured, an object name tells them WHICH thing they are editing without reading the body.
**Objective test.** Per dialog tab/section: write one sentence connecting it to the dialog's stated single subject — no coherent one-sentence rationale possible = extract that section into its own dialog. Titles: (a) function dialogs contain the action's verb; (b) property dialogs contain the specific object's name/identifier; a bare generic noun ("Settings"/"Details"/"Properties" alone) when specificity is available = fail.
**✗ WRONG.** One "Options" dialog holding Spelling, Printer Settings, and Account tabs — three subjects with no statable common reason; an export dialog titled simply "Settings"; a customer record's dialog titled "Details" with no name.
**✓ RIGHT.** A song-properties dialog whose tabs (Info, Sorting, Lyrics, Artwork) are all facets of the ONE song; "Export Report"; "Jane Doe — Customer Details".
**Crop.** AF-14 (Fig. 21-29, iTunes tabbed song-properties dialog, p.637 — positive; Fig. 21-30, Word Options dialog, p.638 — negative).
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — a dialog crams unrelated subjects into one container with no coherent one-sentence rationale connecting ≥2 sections, AND its title (function or property) is a bare generic noun *(source: About Face p.626, p.639 Word-Options case; p.627; scoring #29 rung 0, #30 rung 0)*.
- **2** — one of the two dialog title classes (function/property) is titled correctly, the other isn't, in the same product *(About Face p.627; scoring #30 rung 3)*.
- **4** — every tab/section has a statable one-sentence rationale connecting it to the dialog's single subject, but titling is still inconsistent across the product *(About Face p.626; scoring #29 rungs 3→5-6 blended with #30 rung 3)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** every section has a coherent one-sentence rationale AND function dialogs are titled with the performing verb, property dialogs with the specific object's name *(About Face p.626, p.627; scoring #29 rung 5-6, #30 rung 5-6 — both objective-test floors)*.
- **7** — threshold met, consistently across every dialog in the product (not just a sample) *(About Face p.627; scoring #30 rung 7-8)*.
- **8** — + the dialog's scope is narrow enough that removing any one section would clearly break the why-together logic (tight cohesion, not just defensible) *(About Face p.626; scoring #29 rung 7-8)*.
- **10** — every tab is a distinct facet of the exact same domain object, titles fully specific throughout — the iTunes Song Properties state (Info/Sorting/Lyrics/Artwork) *(About Face p.626-627, Fig.21-29; scoring #29 rung 9-10)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** med (2) — About Face weights subject-coherence med and titles low-med; med carries the majority.

### DLG-3 — Modal vs modeless conventions are strict
**Rule.** Modal → terminating buttons (OK/Cancel) at the bottom, no title-bar close (ambiguous cancel-vs-commit). Modeless (popover, panel, light-dismiss) → NO terminating command buttons; closes via its own close idiom. Terminating labels never change dynamically.
**Grounding.**
- *About Face* (p.629): "Modal dialogs must include one or more terminating commands, usually in the form of large pushbuttons at the bottom of the dialog." "Do not use terminating button commands for modeless dialogs."
  - Mechanism: the two types must be visually AND behaviorally distinguishable — a terminating button on a modeless surface implies a commit/discard semantics that surface doesn't have.
- *About Face* (p.629): "Modal dialogs should not use Close controls in their title bars, not only to help differentiate them from their modeless brethren, but because the function executed by the close control may be unclear to users."
  - Mechanism: an X on a modal is ambiguous — does it cancel or commit? Only explicit terminating buttons carry unambiguous meaning.
- *About Face* (p.629): "One particular modal dialog variation to avoid is the use of terminating buttons that change from Cancel to Apply, or from Cancel to Close... These labels should never change." Design principle: "Don't dynamically change the labels of terminating buttons."
  - Mechanism: a returning user who paused mid-task clicks what they remember as "Cancel" and instead commits — the dynamic label betrays them.
**Objective test.** Modals: (1) ≥1 bottom terminating pushbutton; (2) no independent title-bar X; (3) script a UI test asserting each terminating button's accessible label is EQUAL before and after any state-changing interaction inside the dialog. Modeless surfaces: zero terminating command buttons (a "Close" on a light-dismiss popover doubles as an AFFORD-11 redundancy); close only via the surface's own close idiom (click-out/Esc/window control).
**✗ WRONG.** A button reading "Cancel" until the user makes an edit, then silently relabeling to "Apply"; a light-dismiss popover with a full-width Close button.
**✓ RIGHT.** A static Cancel (dismiss without saving) plus a separate, always-present static OK/Apply — neither label ever changes; the popover holds only its real action and closes on click-out/Esc.
**Crop.** AF-05 (Fig. 21-32, Vista cascading dialogs, p.640 — adjacent evidence of the breakdown).
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — a terminating button's label dynamically changes (Cancel→Apply) based on interaction state *(source: About Face p.629 "these labels should never change"; scoring #31 rung 0)*.
- **2** — labels are static, but a modal either lacks a terminating button OR carries a title-bar close control (one of the two structural requirements missing) *(About Face p.629; scoring #31 rung 3)*.
- **4** — modals meet the terminating-button + no-title-bar-close requirements, but a modeless surface still carries a terminating command button (e.g. a full-width Close) *(About Face p.629 "do not use terminating button commands for modeless dialogs")*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** modal dialogs have ≥1 static terminating pushbutton, no title-bar close, and modeless dialogs have no terminating buttons (close via window control/click-out/Esc only) *(About Face p.629; scoring #31 rung 5-6 — meets all three checks)*.
- **7** — same, verified via an automated pre/post state-change label-equality test across every modal in the product *(About Face p.629; scoring #31 rung 7-8)*.
- **9** — full, product-wide discipline: every modal unambiguously modal (static OK/Cancel, no X), every modeless panel unambiguously modeless, zero dynamic-label instances anywhere *(About Face p.629; scoring #31 rung 9-10)*.
- **10** — as 9, plus every modeless surface's close idiom is independently confirmed reachable without any command button in every sampled instance *(About Face p.629 mechanism — modal/modeless must be visually AND behaviorally distinguishable)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — About Face's weight line reads med-high (a correctness/trust issue risking real data loss); rounded up, noted.

### DLG-4 — Popover payloads obey full layout law
**Rule.** A compact trigger doesn't excuse a disorganized panel: the expanded popover passes the same hierarchy/grouping/action-pyramid audits as any screen — one primary at most, quiet secondaries, grouped content, no oversized equal-weight button stacks, no cramped scroll-dump.
**Grounding.**
- *Refactoring UI* (pp.241–243): "It's just a floating box on the screen, you can do anything you want with it. Break it into sections, use multiple columns, add supporting text or colorful icons — do something fun with it!" And: "just because we've been conditioned to believe that there's only one way to design a particular component, doesn't mean it's true."
  - Mechanism: the book's worked redesign turns a plain 9-link single-column dropdown into a two-column icon+description mega-menu with a visually separated docs/API section — the panel is a full design surface, not a degenerate list.
- *Designing Interfaces* (Ch.10, "Drop-down Chooser"): collapse rich pickers behind a compact closed state, but the expanded panel itself is a designed surface with the same grouping and hierarchy obligations as any other.
  - Mechanism: the closed state buys screen economy; the open state re-enters normal layout law — nothing about being summoned exempts it.
- Convergence: AFFORD-10's action pyramid (≤1 solid primary, quiet secondaries) binds INSIDE the panel exactly as on a page.
**Objective test.** Run the screen-level audits on the expanded panel: (1) exactly ≤1 solid/primary-weight action; (2) intra-group spacing < inter-group spacing (grouping is measurable); (3) payload navigable within the panel's rendered size — no unstructured ≥50-item scroll-dump; (4) for feature-rich menus, count columns and icon/subtext presence — a single-column plain-link list with zero differentiators is the default to challenge.
**✗ WRONG.** A popover stacking two full-width equal-weight buttons over an ungrouped 30-option dump the user must scroll blindly.
**✓ RIGHT.** A sectioned panel — content grouped with visible section boundaries, one quiet action row with a single emphasized action, destructive action isolated.
**Crop.** RU-11 (pp.241–243, dropdown-to-mega-menu redesign series).
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — the panel holds ≥2 equal-weight prominent actions (e.g., two full-width filled buttons stacked) over an ungrouped flat dump, AND — if feature-rich (≥6 heterogeneous items) — defaults to a single-column plain-link list with zero differentiators *(source: Refactoring UI pp.241-243; scoring RU#… richness rung 0; AFFORD-10 pyramid)*.
- **2** — a partial richness attempt exists (e.g. icons added but still single-column) OR grouping is present but ≥1 boundary is ambiguous (intra- and inter-group spacing equal) *(Refactoring UI pp.241-243; scoring richness rung 3)*.
- **4** — the payload is navigable within the panel's rendered size (no unstructured ≥50-item blind scroll) and holds ≤1 solid/primary-weight action, but section boundaries still aren't crisply visible *(Refactoring UI pp.241-243 — floating-box-as-design-surface mechanism; Designing Interfaces Ch.10)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** ≤1 solid/primary-weight action; intra-group spacing measurably < inter-group spacing with visible section boundaries; no scroll-dump *(Refactoring UI pp.241-243; Designing Interfaces Ch.10 — the panel re-enters normal layout law on open)*.
- **7** — threshold met, plus for feature-rich menus (≥6 heterogeneous items) columns and/or icons+subtext and/or separated sections are used *(Refactoring UI pp.241-243, dropdown-to-mega-menu redesign)*.
- **8** — + any destructive action in the panel is visually separated from routine actions *(convergence: AFFORD-10 pyramid applied inside the panel)*.
- **10** — the full mega-menu redesign state: two-column icon+description layout with a visually separated docs/API-equivalent section, single primary action, destructive isolation, zero scroll-dump *(Refactoring UI pp.241-243, worked redesign)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** med (2) — blend, noted: Refactoring UI weights the richer-treatment opportunity low (polish), but the panel's hierarchy/grouping obligations inherit the high-weight screen-level audits (AFFORD-10 pyramid); med splits the difference.

### DLG-5 — Idioms have practical limits: never stack tabs
**Rule.** Tabs that wrap to a second row — or reflow when clicked — are a broken idiom; five or six tabs is fine, more means restructuring (split dialogs, sidebar), not squeezing.
**Grounding.**
- *About Face* (pp.638–639): "All interaction idioms have practical limits." Design principle: "Don't stack tabs." "Five or six tabs is fine, fifty is not."
  - Mechanism: the worked failure is Word's 10-tab Options dialog "stacked two deep... when she clicks a tab in the back row, the entire row of tabs moves forward, pushing the other two rows to the back... it's disconcerting to click a tab and then have it move out from under the mouse" (p.638) — the idiom breaks the moment the control the user just clicked relocates itself.
**Objective test.** Render the tab bar at the minimum supported viewport width and assert its rendered height equals exactly one tab-row height (no wrap); additionally assert that clicking any tab causes zero repositioning of other tabs. Count check: tab count exceeding what fits one row at target width = fail.
**✗ WRONG.** A properties dialog with 12 tabs wrapping into 2 rows at standard window width, back-row tabs visibly repositioning on click.
**✓ RIGHT.** The same functionality split into two well-titled dialogs (e.g., "Formatting Options" and "Security Options"), each ≤6 tabs, single-row always, no reflow ever.
**Crop.** AF-04 (Fig. 21-30, Word's stacked-tabs Options dialog, p.638 — the canonical negative).
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — the tab bar's tab count causes wrapping to ≥2 rows, AND clicking a back-row tab repositions the whole tab bar *(source: About Face pp.638-639, Word's stacked-tabs Options dialog; scoring #32 rung 0)*.
- **3** — tabs wrap to 2 rows but clicking doesn't reposition rows (partial mitigation) *(About Face p.638; scoring #32 rung 3)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** tab count fits a single row at the target viewport width with no wrapping (rendered height equals exactly one tab-row height) *(About Face pp.638-639; scoring #32 rung 5-6)*.
- **7** — threshold met, plus clicking any tab causes zero repositioning of other tabs (confirmed, not merely absent because it never wraps) *(About Face p.638 mechanism)*.
- **8** — threshold + no-reposition met, with headroom — tab count comfortably ≤6, the book's "five or six is fine" ceiling *(About Face p.639 "Five or six tabs is fine, fifty is not"; scoring #32 rung 7-8)*.
- **10** — functionality is cleanly split into separate, well-titled dialogs/screens so no single tab bar ever approaches the wrap limit *(About Face p.639, split into "Formatting Options"/"Security Options"; scoring #32 rung 9-10)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** med (2) — per About Face's weight line (a specific, easily-automated structural check; N/A where no tabbed panels exist).

### DLG-6 — Cascading dialogs signal structural failure
**Rule.** A modal opening another modal with its own OK/Cancel makes termination scope ambiguous (what does THIS Cancel cancel?); treat any need for it as a sign the interaction framework needs restructuring.
**Grounding.**
- *About Face* (pp.639–640): "Cascading dialogs are a diabolical idiom whereby controls, usually pushbuttons, in one dialog summon another dialog in a hierarchical pile... What is the scope of each Cancel? What are we OKing?"
  - Mechanism: each nested terminating pair multiplies ambiguity — the user at the innermost level cannot know whether Cancel discards just that dialog or the whole chain.
- *About Face* (p.641): "If you find your application requiring cascading dialogs for anything other than really obscure stuff that your users generally won't need, you should take another look at your interaction framework. It may have structural problems that could be remedied using tabbed dialogs, sidebars, or even toolbars."
  - Mechanism: the need to nest is diagnostic — the fix is restructuring the framework, never a third layer.
**Objective test.** Trace every dialog-launch path in the product: flag any path where a modal, while open, launches a SECOND modal with its own independent OK/Cancel pair; count nesting-depth-≥2 occurrences; target 0 outside truly obscure, rarely-touched configuration.
**✗ WRONG.** Settings → sub-dialog → sub-sub-dialog (e.g., Region and Language → Text Services → Add Input Language), three Cancel buttons of unknowable scope.
**✓ RIGHT.** The whole flow redesigned as ONE dialog with an inline searchable list and a direct Add button that appends to a list in the same view — no nesting at all.
**Crop.** AF-05 (Fig. 21-32, Windows Vista cascading dialogs, p.640).
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — a modal dialog, while open, launches a second modal with its OWN independent OK/Cancel — nesting depth ≥2 — on a mainline path *(source: About Face pp.639-640, Region and Language → Text Services → Add Input Language; scoring #33 rung 0)*.
- **2** — nested modals exist but are confined to genuinely obscure, rarely-touched configuration *(About Face p.641 "obscure stuff your users generally won't need"; scoring #33 rung 3)*.
- **4** — no nested modals with independent terminating pairs, but a mostly single-surface design still uses one child picker as a leftover pattern (even though it carries no OK/Cancel of its own) *(About Face p.641 mechanism)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** at no moment are two OK/Cancel pairs with different scopes simultaneously on screen; no depth-≥2 nesting anywhere *(About Face pp.639-640; scoring #33 — the "what is the scope of each Cancel" test resolved)*.
- **7** — no nested modals anywhere; any multi-facet configuration uses tabs/sidebars instead *(About Face p.641; scoring #33 rung 7-8)*.
- **9** — the entire flow is redesigned as a single dialog with inline searchable list and direct Add, no nested dialog needed at all *(About Face p.641, language-selection flow collapsed to one view; scoring #33 rung 9-10)*.
- **10** — as 9, verified across every dialog-launch path traced in the product with zero exceptions found *(About Face pp.639-641, full trace discipline)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — per About Face's weight line (high wherever multi-step configuration exists; N/A for single-dialog products).

### DLG-7 — An overlay must never occlude its own subject [derived]
**Rule.** A detail surface opened FROM an object (annotation popover, finding card, datatip) exists to elaborate that object — covering the object, its anchor, or a sibling annotation destroys the very context that justified the overlay. Position dynamically (flip/shift to the free side), keep the anchor visible and visually connected, dim competitors rather than covering them, and guarantee non-collision between simultaneously-pinned overlays.
**Grounding.** Derived — no book states the collision rule; owner feedback named it, and three sources entail it:
- *Designing Interfaces* (p.439): "A good visualization should permit a user to focus on a point of interest, while simultaneously showing enough stuff around that point of interest to give the user a sense of where it is in the big picture."
  - Mechanism: "focus plus context" — the elaboration is only intelligible while its surroundings stay visible; an overlay covering its own anchor deletes the context half of the mantra. The book's Ch.9 spotlight technique dims competing content rather than covering it.
- *About Face* (pp.266–267): "Animated transitions help users create a strong mental model of how what is presented in one view is related to what was presented in the previous view"; transitions should "Maintain context during transitions between views or object states."
  - Mechanism: an overlay is a view change — it must preserve the mental map of where things are, which fails the instant the subject it describes disappears beneath it.
- *Universal Principles* (p.146, "Layering"): "Transparent layers are useful when overlays of information combine to illustrate concepts or highlight relationships"; opaque layers suit information wanted "without contexts."
  - Mechanism: an elaborating overlay is by definition a WITH-context layer — choosing occluding (opaque, covering) behavior for it is a layering-type mismatch.
- Convergence: all three books require the elaborated object and its neighborhood to remain visible while the elaboration shows; simultaneous overlays occluding each other or their anchors violates every one of them at once.
**Objective test.** Scripted: open the detail for EVERY object instance (including edge-of-canvas and dense clusters): (a) the clicked anchor's bounding box remains ≥~80% visible; (b) the overlay's box intersects no sibling annotation/marker; (c) an anchor connection (pointer, highlight) is rendered; (d) with N pinned overlays, pairwise intersection = 0 or later ones reflow.
**✗ WRONG.** Clicking an annotated item opens a card that lands on top of the annotation it describes; two open cards overlapping each other so neither is fully readable.
**✓ RIGHT.** The card flips to the free side of its anchor, the anchor stays highlighted and visibly connected, competing content dims rather than being covered, and additional pinned cards reflow so no two intersect.
**Crop.** DI-11 (in-context elaboration), UP-21 (p.147, opaque vs. transparent layering diagram).
**Score (0–10).** [derived — rungs built from this principle's own Objective test, cross-read against the three entailing books' own band language]
- **0** — the default overlay placement covers its own anchor, with no dynamic repositioning attempted *(source: Designing Interfaces p.439 focus-plus-context — the context half is deleted; About Face pp.266-267 — the view-change loses the mental map; [derived] convergence)*.
- **2** — anchor visibility holds for typical placements, but ≥1 edge-of-canvas or dense-cluster case covers its anchor below ~80% *(Designing Interfaces p.439; [derived])*.
- **4** — anchor stays ≥80% visible in every tested case (including edge/dense clusters), but the overlay's box still intersects a sibling annotation/marker in at least one placement *(Universal Principles p.146 Layering — opaque/with-context mismatch; [derived])*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** clicked anchor's bounding box remains ≥~80% visible AND the overlay intersects no sibling annotation/marker, across every tested instance *(Designing Interfaces p.439; Universal Principles p.146; [derived] — both entailing sources' own objective-test floor)*.
- **7** — threshold met, plus a visible pointer/highlight connects the overlay to its anchor in every case *(About Face pp.266-267 — transitions must "maintain context"; [derived])*.
- **9** — threshold + anchor connection met, plus with N overlays pinned simultaneously, pairwise intersection = 0 except exactly one remaining intersecting pair after reflow *(Universal Principles p.146 — transparent/with-context layering; [derived])*.
- **10** — full non-collision: with N overlays pinned, pairwise intersection = 0 (later ones reflow), competing content dims rather than being covered, anchor connected and ≥80% visible in every case *(all three sources converge; [derived])*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** med (2) — derived (no book weight line); the entailing sources both carry med (Designing Interfaces' Focus-plus-Context, Universal Principles' Layering).

### DLG-8 — Escape and safety in every overlay
**Rule.** Every overlay/flow step keeps a visible way out and never traps; operations launched from it stay cancelable; deep states keep their wayfinding (breadcrumb/progress map) so the user knows where the overlay sits in the whole.
**Grounding.**
- *Designing Interfaces* (Ch.3, Escape Hatch; p.194): "Breadcrumbs show each level of hierarchy leading to the current page... they show a single linear 'slice' of the overall map of the site or app... Breadcrumbs help a user to pinpoint where they are. This is especially handy if they've jumped abruptly to somewhere deep in the tree."
  - Mechanism: "global navigation alone isn't sufficient to show a 'You are here' signpost" when "the hierarchy is too deep or large" (p.194) — a deep or jumped-into overlay state needs its own clickable ancestor slice.
- *Designing Interfaces* (pp.415–416, Cancelability): "The ability for software users to cancel a task or process in the UI at any time is an important usability standard. It relates to 'user control and freedom.'" "When the user clicks or presses the Cancel button, cancel the operation immediately. If you wait too long — for more than a second or two — the user might doubt whether the cancel actually worked."
  - Mechanism: an overlay that launches work but offers no immediate-effect cancel converts a secondary surface into a trap the user must wait out.
- *Krug* (p.101): Home one click away — the whole-app form of the same guarantee: from anywhere, one visible action returns the user to safe ground.
**Objective test.** (1) Cancel/back/close visible above the fold in every overlay/wizard step — 0 steps without one. (2) Any operation running >2s or blocking interaction has a Cancel adjacent to its progress indicator that takes effect within ≤2 seconds with a visible confirming status change (per ERR-6). (3) Any overlay state reachable at ≥3 levels of depth (or via deep-link/search) carries a clickable ancestor chain — 0 wayfinding elements on such a state = fail.
**✗ WRONG.** A wizard step with no cancel or back, so the only exit is completing the flow; a deep-linked settings pane showing only its own title with no path up; a 10-second operation launched from a modal with no cancel at all.
**✓ RIGHT.** Every step shows a visible Cancel; `Home / Settings / Notifications / Email` renders as clickable links each jumping to that level; the in-flight operation shows a Cancel beside its progress bar that halts it instantly.
**Crop.** DI-13 (Fig. 3-55/3-57 breadcrumbs, pp.194–197; Fig. 8-24/8-25 cancelability, pp.416–417).
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — a wizard/overlay step has no cancel or back control at all (the only exit is completing the flow), OR an operation >2s launched from an overlay has no Cancel/Stop control at all *(source: Designing Interfaces pp.415-416 Cancelability rung 0, p.194 Escape Hatch rung 0; scoring #22 rung 0, #1 rung 0)*.
- **2** — a Cancel control exists on the operation but takes noticeably >2s to take visible effect, or leaves ambiguous side effects; deep states show wayfinding text but it isn't clickable *(Designing Interfaces p.416; scoring #22 rung 3, #1 rung — degraded wayfinding)*.
- **4** — a Cancel/back/close control is visible above the fold in every step, and the ≥3-level-deep state has SOME clickable ancestor chain, but at least one link doesn't resolve to its real ancestor *(Designing Interfaces p.194 mechanism; Krug p.101)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** Cancel/back/close visible above the fold in every overlay/wizard step; every operation >2s has a Cancel adjacent to its progress indicator halting within ≤2s with a visible confirming status change; every ≥3-level-deep or deep-linked state carries a clickable, correctly-resolving ancestor chain; zero trap states *(Designing Interfaces pp.194, 415-416; Krug p.101; scoring #22 rung 5-6, #1 rung 5-6 — both objective-test floors)*.
- **7** — threshold met, plus multiple concurrent cancelable operations each expose an unambiguous, specifically-labeled per-operation cancel *(Designing Interfaces p.416; scoring #22 rung 7-8)*.
- **9** — threshold + concurrent-cancel met, plus the breadcrumb/ancestor chain is a prominent, first-class component (not buried) integrated with search/filter state *(Designing Interfaces p.194, Fig.3-57; scoring #1 rung 9-10)*.
- **10** — full discipline: instant zero-side-effect cancellation demonstrated across all concurrent operations (per Google Play/Adobe CC), first-class integrated wayfinding, and zero trap states anywhere in the product *(Designing Interfaces pp.194, 416-417, Fig.8-24/25; Krug p.101)*.
