Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — majority: Designing Interfaces' Cancelability high + Krug's home-one-click high, vs. Designing Interfaces' breadcrumbs med (noted).

# Empty States & Onboarding

Pillars: 1, 3.

---

### EMPTY-1 — The zero state is a first impression, designed with equal care
**Rule.** A bare "no items" message on a feature the user just entered is a dead end; the empty state gets an icon/illustration, encouraging copy, and one prominent CTA driving the very next action — and content-dependent chrome is hidden until content exists (TABLE-6).
**Grounding.** Refactoring UI: "Empty states are a user's first interaction with a new product or feature. Use them as an opportunity to be interesting and exciting — don't settle for plain and boring." (p.236) The failure scene is drawn concretely: after spending "a ton of time crafting the perfect realistic sample data... an excited user clicks the new item in the nav" only to see a bare "No contacts found." (pp.234–235) On dead supporting UI: "If you're working on something that has a bunch of supporting UI like tabs or filters, consider hiding that stuff entirely. There's no point in presenting a bunch of actions that don't do anything until the user has created some content." (p.236) Mechanism: the zero state is the moment of maximum motivation and minimum content — designing it as an afterthought converts an excited first click into a letdown, while dead filter/sort/search controls advertise actions that cannot do anything yet.
**Objective test.** Render every list/table/dashboard view with zero data and inspect what appears. Fail = a bare text string ("No X found") with no icon/illustration and no CTA button, OR a fully-rendered filter bar / sort control / search input still visible above the empty body (dead chrome with nothing to act on). Pass = an icon or illustration + encouraging copy + one prominent CTA to create the first item, with all content-dependent controls (filter/sort/search tabs) hidden until content exists.
**✗ WRONG.** A messaging app's new "Contacts" feature, when empty, shows only a centered grey "No contacts found." text string — no icon, no button, no next step; a discount-codes admin panel, when empty, still renders its full "All / Active / Scheduled / Expired" filter tab bar and a search box above the blank body.
**✓ RIGHT.** The empty Contacts screen shows a friendly illustration, the line "Add a new contact and start messaging," and a prominent "+ Add contact" button; the empty discounts panel hides tabs and search entirely, showing a large "Create a discount code" headline, supporting copy, and a single prominent CTA.
**Crop.** RU-10 (pp.234–236: bare vs illustrated-CTA "Contacts" pair; dead-filter-chrome vs hidden-chrome discounts panel).
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — a zero-data view shows a bare text string ("No X found") with no icon/illustration and no CTA *(source: Refactoring UI p.234–236, principle 32)*.
- **2** — a bare string, but at least a link-styled/generic CTA now exists ("Learn more") *(RU p.236)*.
- **3** — an icon or illustration exists, or a CTA exists, but not both; dead filter/search/sort chrome still renders above the empty body *(RU p.236, principle 32)*.
- **4** — icon/illustration AND a CTA both present, but the CTA is generic ("Learn more") rather than naming the first-item action *(RU p.236)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** icon/illustration + encouraging copy + a CTA naming the create-first-item action are all present — objective-test met — but content-dependent chrome (filter/sort/search/tabs) is still shown despite nothing to filter/sort/search *(RU p.236, principle 32)*.
- **6** — as 5, AND the CTA is the single most visually prominent control in the view (largest filled/primary-styled element), but dead chrome is still visible *(RU p.236)*.
- **8** — full pass on one view: illustration + copy + prominent, correctly-labeled CTA, AND all content-dependent chrome hidden until content exists *(RU p.236, ✓ Contacts/discounts examples)*.
- **9** — the full pass (rung 8) holds across every empty-capable list/table/dashboard view on the surface, not just one *(RU p.234–236, principle 32 — "first interaction with a new product or feature")*.
- **10** — matches the ✓ examples exactly across every view: illustration + exact next-action copy + single prominent CTA, chrome fully hidden, with zero views regressing to a bare string *(RU p.234–236, ✓ Contacts + discounts pair)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** med (2) — Refactoring UI: high-value first-impression moment, but scoped to views that can be empty, not universal.

### EMPTY-2 — Users act first, read never: help lives in the flow
**Rule.** Nobody reads instructions before acting; guidance is embedded in context — sensible empty states, inline hints, tooltips at the point of need — never relegated to external docs or a one-shot tutorial that can't be re-found.
**Grounding.** Laws of UX (Paradox of the Active User): "Users never read software manuals but instead start using the software immediately." (p.115, quoting Carroll & Rosson 1987, IBM User Interface Institute) Mechanism: "we must remember to not build products and services for an idealized, rational user... we can account for this paradox by making guidance accessible throughout the product experience... no matter what path they choose to take (e.g., tooltips with helpful information)" (p.115). Krug (instructions must die): "The main thing you need to know about instructions is that no one is going to read them—at least not until after repeated attempts at 'muddling through' have failed." (p.78) "Your objective should always be to eliminate instructions entirely by making everything self-explanatory, or as close to it as possible." (p.78) Krug's novel-gesture case (Clear app): after a ten-screen tour plus tutorial, first-time users asked to "create a new list called 'Chicago trip' with three items in it... So far, no one has succeeded... And if you can't figure that out, you can't get to the Help screens. Catch-22." (pp.193–195) Mechanism: a one-shot tour is memory-bound guidance for users who act, not read — without a persistent affordance and re-openable help, the interaction vocabulary is unrecoverable under real task pressure.
**Objective test.** (1) For each nontrivial control/feature: in-context guidance (tooltip, inline hint, contextual empty-state copy) is reachable WITHOUT navigating away from the current screen — hovering/focusing the control or viewing its empty state surfaces guidance inline, zero navigation. (2) Remove all instructional/helper text: if a first-time user can still operate the control via labeling, placeholder convention, or affordance alone, the instruction was excise; anything surviving is ≤1 short sentence. (3) Novel-interaction features: a persistent visible affordance for the primary task AND a way to re-open the tutorial/help exist; give a first-time user the stated onboarding exactly once, then assign the most common primary task with zero further help — a team that cannot state the measured first-attempt success rate is presumptively failing.
**✗ WRONG.** A complex filter-builder has no inline hint — its only explanation lives on a Help Center page three clicks away; a note-taking app's only way to create a folder is a two-finger swipe shown once in an onboarding animation, with no persistent icon and no way to re-open the tutorial.
**✓ RIGHT.** The filter-builder shows a first-hover tooltip explaining its syntax and one example filter directly in its empty state; the gesture survives as a power-user shortcut beside a persistent visible "+" button, and a "?" icon reopens the tour at any time.
**Crop.** KR-08.
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — a nontrivial/complex control has no inline hint at all; its only explanation lives on a separate help page reached via multiple clicks *(source: Laws of UX — Paradox of the Active User p.115; Krug "Instructions must die" p.78)*. If a novel gesture is ALSO the only path to a core action with no persistent control and no re-openable tutorial, score 0 regardless of other rungs *(Krug pp.193–195, Clear-app Catch-22)*.
- **2** — inline guidance exists for some entry points only, or requires an explicit "?" click rather than hover/focus/empty-state *(Laws of UX p.115)*; a required instruction is still full-paragraph-length *(Krug p.78)*.
- **4** — in-context guidance (tooltip/inline hint/empty-state copy) is reachable for every nontrivial control WITHOUT navigating away — zero-navigation met — but any surviving instruction is still multi-sentence *(Laws of UX p.115; Krug p.78)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** zero-navigation guidance covers every nontrivial control, AND any surviving instructional text is ≤1 short sentence, control mostly self-evident without it *(Laws of UX p.115; Krug p.78, "instruction ≤1 sentence" band)*.
- **6** — as 5, AND a novel gesture (if any) has at least a re-openable tutorial, even without a persistent conventional control *(Laws of UX — Learnability collapses #25 p.pp.193-195 band 3)*.
- **7** — as 5, AND ≥1 guidance instance includes a concrete working example (not just abstract description) *(Laws of UX p.115, "7-8" band)*.
- **8** — no instructional text remains anywhere beyond one-word microcopy (e.g. placeholder "Search"); affordance/labeling/convention alone suffice *(Krug p.78, "7–8" band)*; AND, if a novel gesture is used for a core action, a persistent visible conventional control now exists alongside it *(Laws of UX — Learnability collapse, "novel gesture + persistent button" pass)*.
- **9** — as 8, AND the flow's first-attempt success is verified: a first-time user given the stated onboarding exactly once completes the most common primary task unaided, OR re-opens help at most once *(Laws of UX #25 band 7-8; rule's stated onboarding-once test)*.
- **10** — matches the ✓ filter-builder case exactly: zero instructional text anywhere, a working example live in the UI, gesture (if any) is a pure optional shortcut beside a persistent "+"-style control and a re-openable "?" tutorial, and a measured first-attempt success rate is stated and passing *(Laws of UX p.115 band 9-10; Krug p.78 band 9-10; Laws of UX #25 band 9-10)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — majority: Krug "instructions must die" high, Krug learnability-collapse high (when novel interactions present); Laws of UX rates the active-user paradox medium (noted disagreement).

### EMPTY-3 — Give complexity a familiar way in (Rosetta Stone)
**Rule.** Introduce novel/complex surfaces through a key of already-understood elements — an unmistakably familiar example/template first — revealing complexity in stages where each solved stage scaffolds the next.
**Grounding.** Universal Principles (Rosetta Stone): "The Rosetta stone illustrates the power of embedding elements of common understanding in messages to ensure that their meaning can be unlocked by a receiver who may not understand the language of transmission." (p.206) The two-step method is given directly: "First, identify and embed an element of common understanding, or a key, that the receiver will understand... It is critical to make the key identifiable as a key... Second, construct the message to be revealed in stages, with each stage acting as a supporting key for subsequent stages." (p.206) Mechanism: crossword-puzzle logic — each solved stage supplies the vocabulary the next stage needs, so a first-time user always has a familiar referent to decode the unfamiliar against.
**Objective test.** For an onboarding flow or complex-form introduction: (1) the first step contains an unambiguously familiar anchor for the target audience (a recognizable icon, a known concept, a pre-filled recognizable template, a solved example) BEFORE any abstract/unfamiliar step; (2) complexity is revealed in stages where each solved stage scaffolds the next — stage-removal test: delete stage 1 and check whether stage 2 becomes unsolvable/confusing without it (yes = the scaffold was real, pass); (3) a flow opening directly on its most abstract step = fail.
**✗ WRONG.** A complex configuration wizard opens directly on its most abstract, unfamiliar step ("define your data schema") with no prior familiar anchor for a first-time user to orient from.
**✓ RIGHT.** The wizard opens on a fully pre-filled, familiar "Customer list" template the user can inspect and modify; that familiar example becomes the key that scaffolds the abstract schema step that follows.
**Crop.** none (concept spread; book anchor: p.207 Pioneer plaque + Rosetta Disk).
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — the flow opens directly on its most abstract/unfamiliar step, with no familiar anchor anywhere in the flow *(source: Universal Principles — Rosetta Stone p.206–207, band 0)*.
- **2** — a familiar anchor exists somewhere in the flow, but the first step is already abstract/unfamiliar (anchor mis-sequenced) *(UP p.206, band 3)*.
- **3** — the anchor is now first, but it is buried or unlabeled — a first-time user cannot tell it is the thing to decode against *(UP p.206, "key must be identifiable" requirement + band 3)*.
- **4** — the full complexity lands on one screen at once even though a familiar anchor opens it (no staged reveal yet) *(UP p.206, "revealed in stages" requirement unmet)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** the flow opens with an unambiguously familiar, explicitly-labeled anchor (a recognizable example/template, inspectable/modifiable) before any abstract step, AND complexity is revealed across sequential stages *(UP p.206, band 5–6)*.
- **6** — as 5, AND at least the first stage-to-stage transition passes the removal test — deleting stage 1 makes stage 2 meaningfully harder *(UP p.206, stage-removal test)*.
- **8** — every later stage, not just the first, becomes unsolvable/confusing when its predecessor is hypothetically removed — the full scaffold chain verified *(UP p.206, band 7–8, "verified by literally removing the first stage")*.
- **10** — matches the book's crossword-puzzle-logic standard exactly: a fully scaffolded, stage-by-stage reveal where every solved layer is indispensable to the next, anchor unmistakably familiar and explicitly presented as the key *(UP p.206–207, band 9–10)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** med (2) — Universal Principles rates Rosetta Stone medium.

### EMPTY-4 — Flows borrow story structure
**Rule.** Guided flows carry six elements: setting (orient up front), characters (name the actors/roles), plot (visible cause-effect between steps), invisibility (chrome recedes), mood (one deliberate tone), movement (no dead stalls) — elements are rarely subtractable without damage.
**Grounding.** Universal Principles (Storytelling): "Good storytelling experiences generally require certain fundamental elements. While additional elements can be added to further augment the quality of a story or storytelling experience, they can rarely be subtracted without detriment." (p.230) Two elements defined verbatim: "Invisibility—The awareness of the storyteller fades as the audience focuses on a good story. When engaged in a good movie or book, the existence of the medium is forgotten." / "Movement—In a good story, the sequence and flow of events is clear and interesting. The storyline doesn't stall." (p.230) Mechanism: the six elements are load-bearing, not decorative — the book's worked example annotates the Civil Rights Memorial against all six (p.231), and any missing element is a felt detriment, which is why the audit runs element-by-element rather than by overall impression.
**Objective test.** Audit a wizard/onboarding flow against all six, per the book's worked example: Setting — does the flow establish context up front? Characters — are the actors/roles named? Plot — is each step's "because" visible (cause-effect sequence, not just a list — "now that we know X, let's set Y")? Invisibility — does the chrome recede, or does it visually compete with content? Mood — one deliberate, consistent tone? Movement — continuous transitions, no dead stalls or loading voids? Each absent element is a documented gap.
**✗ WRONG.** An eight-step onboarding wizard of disconnected forms: no sense of why each step follows the last (no plot), no acknowledgment of who is involved (no characters), and progress bars/borders that visually compete with the content (no invisibility).
**✓ RIGHT.** The same eight steps re-framed with a visible thread — "Step 3 of 8: now that we know your team size, let's set up permissions for them" (explicit plot causality) — chrome receded to a minimal progress indicator, and continuous motion between steps instead of jarring reloads.
**Crop.** UP-22.
**Score (0–10).** Run the 6-element story audit (setting/characters/plot/invisibility/mood/movement) on the flow; count elements identifiably present, per rung's added qualifier.
- **0** — 0–1 of the 6 elements present: no causal plot (disconnected steps), no named characters/roles, chrome visually competes with content *(source: Universal Principles — Storytelling p.230–231, band 0)*.
- **2** — 2 of 6 elements present, others clearly absent or weak *(UP p.230, band 3, low end)*.
- **3** — 3 of 6 elements present, others clearly absent or weak *(UP p.230, band 3)*.
- **4** — 4 of 6 elements present, but at least one of the two omissions is plot or invisibility (the elements the rule treats as load-bearing: visible cause-effect, chrome recession) *([derived] — UP p.230 band 5–6 floor + rule's own emphasis on plot/invisibility as annotated in the book's worked example)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** at least 4 of the 6 elements are identifiably present in the flow *(UP p.230, band 5–6)*.
- **6** — 5 of 6 elements present, but the still-missing element is not yet remedied *(UP p.230, band 7–8 floor)*.
- **8** — 5 of 6 elements present, AND the flow's chrome genuinely recedes with progress feeling continuous — no dead stalls *(UP p.230, band 7–8)*.
- **9** — all 6 elements present, but at least one is only weakly/inconsistently expressed across steps (e.g. mood held in copy but not visuals) *([derived] — UP p.230 band 9–10 requires independent verifiability of each element, treated as the gate between 8 and 10)*.
- **10** — all 6 elements present and each independently verifiable in the flow, matching the book's own Civil-Rights-Memorial standard *(UP p.230–231, band 9–10)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** low (1) — Universal Principles rates Storytelling low.

# Errors, Reversibility & Undo

Prevention beats handling; reversibility beats confirmation. Pillars: 3.

---

### ERR-1 — Make errors impossible before making them polite
**Rule.** Most "errors" are the software's own rigidity (rejecting reasonable, out-of-sequence, or trivially-correctable input); the first-order fix is a design where the error can't happen — the error dialog is a last resort, never a normal pattern.
**Grounding.**
- *About Face:* "Probably no user interface idiom is more annoying—or more historically misused—than the error dialog." (p.641) "Most error dialogs stop the proceedings with idiocy." (p.643) "Instead of software rejecting input, it must work harder to understand and reconcile confusing input." (p.644) Design principle: "Make errors impossible." (p.644) Mechanism: the error is a symptom of the app's brittleness, not the user's failure — the worked case is rejecting "nine" typed into a numeric field instead of parsing it (p.644, ref p.327); redesign the input handling and the whole error class disappears.
- *Designing Interfaces:* "Permit users to enter inputs in a variety of choices, formats, and syntax, and make the application interpret it intelligently... The user just wants to get something done, not think about 'correct' formats and complex UI" (pp.477–478, Forgiving Format). Mechanism: the preventive input patterns (Forgiving Format, Good Defaults, structured entry, Ch.10) exist precisely to design the error away rather than announce it.
**Objective test.** Classify each shipped error dialog's trigger: (a) input the system could reasonably auto-correct or infer (number-words, typo'd formats, out-of-sequence-but-recoverable entry) → must be eliminated via smarter input handling — count category-(a) dialogs remaining, target 0; (b) genuinely invalid/dangerous/unrecoverable → may remain, held to ERR-3's copy checklist.
**✗ WRONG.** A form rejects a phone number typed as "555-123-4567" with a blocking dialog demanding digits only — the hyphens are trivially strippable, so the dialog exists only because the parser is lazy.
**✓ RIGHT.** The field silently strips non-digit formatting characters and accepts the input; no error dialog exists for that class of format variant.
**Crop.** AF-06.
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — ≥3 shipped error dialogs fire on category-(a) triggers (input the system could auto-correct/infer: number-words, strippable formatting, out-of-sequence-but-recoverable) *(source: About Face p.644 "make errors impossible"; scoring #34 band-0)*.
- **2** — 1–2 category-(a) dialogs remain *(source: About Face p.644, scoring #34 band-3)*.
- **3** — 0 category-(a) dialogs remain among currently-shipped ones, but ≥1 sampled canonical-format field (phone/date/amount) rejects a common format variant *(source: Designing Interfaces pp.477–478, Forgiving Format)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** 0 category-(a) dialogs remain AND every sampled canonical-format field accepts ≥2 common variants (hyphens/spaces/leading words/casing) without an error surface *(source: About Face p.644, scoring #34 band-5/6; Designing Interfaces pp.477–478)*.
- **6** — + no remaining dialog fires on arguably-recoverable input (all genuinely category-(b): invalid/dangerous/unrecoverable) *(source: About Face p.644)*.
- **7** — + remaining unavoidable errors are rare/deep in the flow, none within the first field interaction of a fresh session's primary flow *(source: About Face p.644, scoring #34 band-7/8)*.
- **9** — + input handling actively reconciles ambiguity (auto-strips/infers) rather than merely avoiding rejection — no dialog fires for that class at all *(source: About Face p.644, ✓ hyphens-silently-stripped case; scoring #34 band-9/10)*.
- **10** — provably zero avoidable-error surface product-wide, verified by testing every canonical-format field with ≥3 variants each, all accepted *[derived — About Face p.644 + Designing Interfaces pp.477–478 convergence]*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — About Face weights this high (top-line frustration signal, design-maturity measure).

### ERR-2 — Validate inline, co-located, as-you-go — modeless feedback over interruption
**Rule.** Validation appears next to the offending field, on the same screen, progressively as the user moves — never a dismissed-to-fix modal, never a separate error page, never submit-only. More broadly: state the user needs (validity, unsaved changes, an impending consequence) surfaces as a persistent glanceable inline cue BEFORE commitment.
**Grounding.**
- *About Face:* "Provide modeless feedback to help users avoid mistakes." (p.653) The spell-check squiggle is the canon: "As you type, red wavy underlines identify words that the application doesn't recognize... you don't have to change anything, and you are not interrupted by dialogs or other forms of modal idiocy." (p.331) The print-clipping dialog is the counter-case: "This dialog provides too little help too late. What if the application could display the printable region right in the main interface as dotted guides?" (p.653) Mechanism: continuous non-blocking cues let the user correct on their own schedule, before commitment, instead of being stopped after it.
- *Laws of UX (negativity bias):* "Mailchimp avoids this potential pain point by providing real-time validation to ensure passwords are secure while also making the rules easy to follow" (p.74). Mechanism: the post-submit rejection is the negative peak that dominates memory of the whole experience; per-keystroke validation prevents the peak from ever occurring.
- *Designing Interfaces:* co-located error messages let the user read the message and make the form corrections easily (Ch.10 Error Messages). Mechanism: message-to-field distance is correction cost.
**Objective test.** (a) An invalid value triggers a visible state change within one field interaction (keystroke/blur), pre-submit — no submit-and-reject cycle required. (b) No error is shown in a modal that must be dismissed to see the field, nor on a separate page requiring Back. (c) Each state-info class (validity, unsaved changes, out-of-range consequence) has a persistent inline cue — flag any class delivered exclusively via an interrupting dialog.
**✗ WRONG.** A password field silent until "Create Account" is clicked, then a full-page reload with a top banner listing errors far from their fields; clipping announced only after Print is pressed.
**✓ RIGHT.** A live checklist ("One special character ✗ / 8 characters minimum ✗") updating on every keystroke at the field; a dotted printable-area guide always visible in the preview canvas.
**Crop.** LU-16, AF-09, AF-17.
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — feedback only after a full submit-and-reject cycle (page reload, top banner far from field) *(source: Laws of UX p.74, #15 band-0; About Face p.653, print-clipping "too little too late")*.
- **2** — inline feedback exists but only on blur/after leaving the field, or covers only some of the field's constraints *(source: Laws of UX p.74, #15 band-3)*.
- **3** — a persistent inline cue exists but is subtle/easy to miss, and an interrupting dialog still also fires redundantly *(source: About Face p.653, scoring #37 band-3)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** an invalid value triggers a visible state change within one field interaction (keystroke/blur), pre-submit; no modal-dismiss or separate page required to see the field; message co-located with it *(source: Laws of UX p.74, #15 band-5/6; About Face p.653, scoring #37 band-5/6; Designing Interfaces Ch.10, co-located error messages)*.
- **6** — + itemized per-requirement pass/fail checklist, not a single binary valid/invalid toggle *(source: Laws of UX p.74, #15 band-7/8)*.
- **7** — + the cue is actionable in place (click/right-click fix, no navigation) *(source: About Face p.653, scoring #37 band-7/8)*.
- **8** — + every state-info class present (validity, unsaved changes, out-of-range/impending consequence) has a persistent glanceable inline cue; none delivered exclusively via an interrupting dialog *[derived — About Face p.653 mechanism generalized across state-info classes]*.
- **10** — continuous audit-as-you-go feedback across all classes — live per-keystroke checklist + always-visible preview guide — zero interrupting dialogs anywhere for this class of info *(source: About Face pp.331,653, scoring #37 band-9/10; Laws of UX p.74, #15 band-9/10)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — About Face: high; Laws of UX: medium-high (majority high; LU's med-high noted).

### ERR-3 — Error copy: polite, illuminating, forward-moving
**Rule.** A necessary error never implies the user failed, states the real scope/impact, and offers at least one concrete way forward — never a bare OK that dumps the problem back.
**Grounding.**
- *About Face:* "The error dialog must be unfailingly polite. It must never even hint that the user caused this problem, because that is simply not true from the user's perspective... It needs to make clear the scope of the problem, what the alternatives are, what the application will do as a default, and what information was lost, if any." (p.647) "It is wrong for the application to dump the problem in the user's lap and wash its hands of the matter. It should offer to implement at least one suggested solution right there within the error message." (p.648) "An error may not be your application's fault, but it is its responsibility." (p.330) Mechanism: the dialog is the application reporting on ITS failure to do its job — the copy must carry the application's accountability, not deflect it.
- *Universal Principles ("Readability"):* "Readability is determined by factors such as word length, word commonality, sentence length..." and "Simple language is preferred, but overly simple language obscures meaning." (p.198) Mechanism: error copy must match the audience's reading level — plain but precise.
**Objective test.** Per remaining dialog, ALL three parts of the checklist: (1) zero fault-attributing language ("you entered", "invalid", "you must"); (2) explicit what-happened + consequence/scope statement; (3) ≥1 actionable option beyond a bare OK (retry, alternative, auto-fix applied). Any part missing = fail.
**✗ WRONG.** "Invalid input. User must type xyz." + a single OK button — blames the user, illuminates nothing, offers no path forward.
**✓ RIGHT.** "Couldn't save over the network — the connection was lost. A copy will be saved to your desktop and synced back automatically when the connection returns." with Save-as… and OK — real cause, consequence, and a concrete implemented solution.
**Crop.** AF-06.
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — remaining error dialogs carry 0 of the 3 required elements (no-fault language, scope/consequence statement, actionable path) — blames the user, illuminates nothing, offers only bare OK *(source: About Face p.647, scoring #35 band-0)*.
- **2** — 1 of the 3 required elements present *(source: About Face p.647, scoring #35 band-3)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** 2 of the 3 required elements present *(source: About Face pp.647–648, scoring #35 band-5/6)*.
- **7** — all 3 present: zero fault-attributing language, explicit what-happened + scope/consequence, ≥1 actionable option beyond bare OK *(source: About Face p.648, scoring #35 band-7/8)*.
- **8** — + sampled error copy's estimated reading level matches the product's stated audience — plain but precise, no meaning lost *(source: Universal Principles p.198, Readability)*.
- **9** — + ≥1 dialog offers a default solution implemented inline (auto-retry plan, "Save as…" executed from the dialog itself) *(source: About Face p.648, scoring #35 band-9/10)*.
- **10** — every remaining dialog product-wide meets all 5 criteria with zero exceptions *[derived — About Face pp.647–648 + Universal Principles p.198, full-product extension]*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — About Face: high (fallback-quality gate for ERR-1's remainder); Universal Principles rates Readability med (noted, subordinate criterion only).

### ERR-4 — Do, don't ask: reversibility replaces routine confirmation
**Rule.** Replace routine confirmations and success alerts with confident action + undo. Habitual confirmations train click-through (crying wolf), so the one that matters gets dismissed by rote; success alerts announcing an explicitly-requested action interrupt for nothing.
**Grounding.**
- *About Face:* "Do; don't ask." / "Make all actions reversible." (p.652) "For confirmation dialogs to work, they must appear only when the user will almost definitely click the No or Cancel button. They should never appear when the user is likely to click the Yes or OK button. Seen from this perspective, they look rather pointless, don't they?" (p.652) "Like the fable of the boy who cried wolf, the confirmation box won't work if it cries too many times when there is no danger." (p.652) On alerts: "The rationale for alerts is to keep users informed. This is a great objective, but it need not come at the expense of smooth interaction flow." (p.649) "Never use transitory dialogs as error messages, alerts, or confirmations." (p.636) Mechanism: habituation — a dialog answered the same way every time stops being read, so it protects nothing while taxing everything; undo protects without asking.
- *Designing Interfaces:* "Don't underestimate the positive feelings that come from giving people the ability to play around safely with your interface... because they understand how to preview, initiate, cancel and reverse actions." (p.432) Mechanism: safe exploration is the payoff of reversibility — confidence replaces interrogation.
**Objective test.** Per confirmation: measure/estimate the affirmative click-through rate; if ≥~90% of users click Yes/OK (a common + reversible action), remove it in favor of undo. Per success alert: if the action was (a) explicitly user-requested AND (b) already visually confirmed by the resulting state change, the alert is redundant — remove.
**✗ WRONG.** "Move to Recycle Bin?" fires on every delete of a trivially-restorable file; a "Saved successfully" modal requires dismissal after the user pressed Save.
**✓ RIGHT.** Instant delete, item visibly gone from the list (the state change IS the confirmation), plus a dismissible "Deleted report.pdf — Undo" toast for a few seconds.
**Crop.** AF-07.
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — a common, easily-reversible action (delete-to-trash) triggers an "Are you sure?" confirmation every single time *(source: About Face p.652, scoring #36 band-0)*.
- **2** — the confirmation is present but only for a subset of reversible actions (inconsistent) *(source: About Face p.652, scoring #36 band-3)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** no confirmation fires for actions where the historical/estimated affirmative-click rate would be ≥~90% — those actions are reversible via Undo instead *(source: About Face p.652, scoring #36 band-5/6)*.
- **7** — + redundant success alerts (announcing an already-visually-confirmed, explicitly user-requested action) are also removed *(source: About Face pp.649,652, scoring #36 band-7/8)*.
- **8** — + the state change is visible at the action point (item gone from the list, value updated in place) without opening another view *[derived — About Face p.652 mechanism; Designing Interfaces p.432, safe exploration]*.
- **9** — + every reversible destructive action that fires without confirmation has a working undo path (toast/menu/shortcut) verified to actually restore state *(source: About Face p.652; Designing Interfaces p.432)*.
- **10** — confident, immediate action + a lightweight dismissible Undo toast applied product-wide — zero cry-wolf confirmations, zero redundant success alerts anywhere *(source: About Face p.652, scoring #36 band-9/10)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — About Face: high (top interruption-fatigue source).

### ERR-5 — Deliberate friction ONLY for the genuinely irreversible/high-stakes — with preview
**Rule.** Truly irreversible/external/high-stakes acts (submit a final decision, permanent delete, send, pay) get a perceptible commitment step: a realistic preview of the outcome BEFORE the commit, a non-routine confirmation, visible acknowledgment. Zero-ceremony completion of a grave act reads careless; too-instant completion even undermines trust.
**Grounding.**
- *Designing Interfaces ("Preview"):* "Render a lightweight sample of the effects of a command, or the likely outcomes of an action... proactively rendered before the user has even submitted the action." (p.404) "By showing the user a summary or visual description of what's about to happen, you give them a chance to back out or correct any mistakes." (p.405) Mechanism: previews prevent errors at the only moment prevention is free — before commitment.
- *Laws of UX:* "A too-fast response time can result in mistrust if it doesn't align with the user's expectations... Purposefully adding a delay to a process can actually increase its perceived value and instill a sense of trust." (pp.127–128) A confirmation modal "can be enough friction to activate the effortful and evaluative mental process known as System 2 thinking... and thus decrease the likelihood of mistakes or errors." (p.128) Mechanism: friction here is functional — it switches the user from automatic to evaluative processing exactly where a mistake is unrecoverable.
**Objective test.** Every irreversible action: (a) an outcome preview (what/scope/N-affected) visible before the commit control is pressed — a text-only restatement with no visual/data preview fails the bar for visually-unpredictable actions; (b) ≥1 explicit confirmation step (modal, re-type-to-confirm, paced review) between trigger and effect — the action must NOT complete on a single tap with zero intervening confirmation UI; (c) a visible completion acknowledgment after.
**✗ WRONG.** "Delete account" firing silently and permanently on one tap; a bulk send with a bare "Are you sure?" and no recipient count or content preview.
**✓ RIGHT.** "This will notify 412 recipients — preview below" with the rendered message → type-to-confirm → a visible sent state.
**Crop.** DI-16, LU-21.
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — no outcome preview exists AND the irreversible action completes on a single tap with zero confirmation UI *(source: Designing Interfaces p.404, scoring #20 band-0; Laws of UX p.127, #29 band-0)*.
- **2** — a "confirm" dialog exists but only restates the request in text, with no visual/data rendering of the outcome; or the confirmation is trivially dismissible (single "OK", no re-type/pause) *(source: Designing Interfaces p.404, scoring #20 band-3; Laws of UX p.128, #29 band-3)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** a realistic rendering of the outcome (thumbnail/sample/summary reflecting real data, incl. scope such as N-affected/recipient count) is visible before the commit control fires, AND every irreversible/high-stakes action requires ≥1 explicit confirmation step (modal, re-type-to-confirm, paced review) between trigger and effect *(source: Designing Interfaces pp.404–405, scoring #20 band-5/6; Laws of UX p.128, #29 band-5/6)*.
- **7** — + the confirmation step specifically engages evaluation (educates/informs what will happen) rather than a bare "are you sure?" *(source: Laws of UX p.128, #29 band-7/8)*.
- **8** — + the preview updates live as inputs change, not a one-shot static render *(source: Designing Interfaces p.405, scoring #20 band-7/8)*.
- **9** — + a visible completion acknowledgment (sent/deleted/paid indicator) confirms the act completed *[derived — Designing Interfaces p.404 mechanism, post-commit extension]*.
- **10** — full live-configurator-grade preview + paced, educational confirmation + completion acknowledgment, matching both books' top cases *(source: Designing Interfaces p.405, scoring #20 band-9/10; Laws of UX p.128, #29 band-9/10)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — Designing Interfaces: high for irreversible/costly actions; Laws of UX: high (unanimous).

### ERR-6 — Multilevel undo at the user's granularity; in-flight cancel
**Rule.** Editing surfaces carry stack-based undo (≥10–12 levels) over every state-changing operation, recorded at the grain the USER thinks in (one bulk gesture = one undo step); a browsable, reapplicable history compounds the trust; and any operation >~2s (or modal-blocking) has a cancel that takes effect within ~2s, per-operation, with no lingering side effects.
**Grounding.**
- *Designing Interfaces (Multilevel Undo):* "The ability to reverse a long sequence of operations step by step lets users feel that the interface is safe to explore... This is true for users of all levels of skill, not just beginners." (p.418) "The stack should be at least 10 to 12 items long to be the most useful." (p.420) — "Users are seldom able to make effective use of more than a dozen levels." (Constantine & Lockwood, quoted p.420) Granularity: "if one action is done en masse to 17 objects, record it as one action, not 17." (p.422) Undoable set = text entry, transactions, canvas edits, layout, file ops, creation/deletion, cut/copy/paste; navigation, selection, cursor and scroll position stay OFF the stack (p.419). Mechanism: undo granularity must mirror the user's mental unit of work, or reversal itself becomes an error-prone chore.
- *Designing Interfaces (Command History):* "Lists of commands — oldest to newest — tend to work well" (p.423); Photoshop's History "allows the user to selectively turn actions on or off or rearrange their sequence" (p.424) — a browsable, reapplicable record, distinct from the stack.
- *Designing Interfaces (Cancelability):* cancel "relates to 'user control and freedom,' one of the top 10 usability heuristics" (Nielsen, p.415). "When the user clicks or presses the Cancel button, cancel the operation immediately. If you wait too long — for more than a second or two — the user might doubt whether the cancel actually worked." (p.416) Concurrent operations each expose their own cancel ("the Cancel button's label or tool tip can state exactly what is being canceled," p.416). Mechanism: a cancel that lags destroys the very trust it exists to provide.
**Objective test.** (a) One-undo-reverts-N check: perform a bulk edit on N objects in one gesture, press Undo ONCE — all N revert, not 1. (b) Stack depth ≥10–12 distinct actions retrievable; no navigation/selection/scroll noise in the stack. (c) Every >2s or modal-blocking operation shows a per-operation cancel adjacent to its progress indicator; pressing it halts within ≤2s with a visible confirming status change and no lingering side effects. (d) History (where present) lists oldest→newest and records en-masse operations as one entry.
**✗ WRONG.** Undo reverting 1 of 17 tagged records, forcing 17 presses to reverse one gesture; a 10s report spinner with no cancel at all.
**✓ RIGHT.** One Undo reverts the whole batch; an X sits beside the progress bar and stops the operation instantly with a "Canceled" status.
**Crop.** DI-17, DI-18.
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — no undo stack, or a bulk edit on N objects only reverts 1 on Undo (N presses required); AND/OR an operation >2s or modal-blocking has no Cancel/Stop control at all *(source: Designing Interfaces pp.418–420, scoring #23 band-0; pp.415–416, scoring #22 band-0)*.
- **2** — undo exists but granularity is wrong (navigation/selection/scroll pollute the stack, or depth <5); Cancel exists but takes noticeably >2s to take effect or leaves ambiguous side effects *(source: Designing Interfaces pp.419–420, scoring #23 band-3; p.416, scoring #22 band-3)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** undo stack ≥10–12 levels deep, a bulk gesture on N objects reverts as exactly 1 entry, navigation/selection excluded from the stack; a Cancel control is present adjacent to the loading indicator and halts the operation within ≤2s with a visible confirming status change *(source: Designing Interfaces p.420, scoring #23 band-5/6; p.416, scoring #22 band-5/6)*.
- **7** — + every book-listed reversible-operation class (text entry, DB transactions, canvas edits, layout, file ops, create/delete, cut/copy/paste) is actually covered *(source: Designing Interfaces p.419, scoring #23 band-7/8)*.
- **8** — + multiple concurrent operations each expose an unambiguous, specifically-labeled per-operation cancel *(source: Designing Interfaces p.416, scoring #22 band-7/8)*.
- **9** — + a history/log (where present) lists actions oldest→newest and records bulk operations as one entry *(source: Designing Interfaces pp.423–424, scoring #24 band-5/6)*.
- **10** — instant, zero-side-effect cancellation across all concurrent operations with clear per-item labeling + dynamically-labeled undo entries + fully manipulable/searchable history *(source: Designing Interfaces p.416, scoring #22 band-9/10; p.420, scoring #23 band-9/10; pp.423–424, scoring #24 band-7/10)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — Designing Interfaces: Multilevel Undo high, Cancelability high, Command History med (majority high; history med noted, carried as a single upper rung).

### ERR-7 — Audit, don't edit: surface what the system changed
**Rule.** Auto-corrections/normalizations leave a visible marker distinguishing system-changed content from user-entered, reachable by a targeted undo; silent modification erodes trust in what the record contains. Corollary: save work automatically and put things where users can find them.
**Grounding.**
- *About Face:* "Audit, don't edit." (p.330) Spell-check marks and lets the user decide (p.331); AutoCorrect is the counter-case: "it silently changes words it thinks are misspelled... the corrections leave no obvious audit trail, so the user often doesn't realize that what he typed has been changed. It would be better if Word could provide some kind of mark that indicates it has made a correction on the off chance that it has miscorrected something." (p.332) Mechanism: without an audit trail the user can no longer trust that the record contains what they entered — every silent fix is also a potential silent corruption.
- *About Face (unified file model corollary):* "Save documents and settings automatically." (p.337) "Put files where users can find them." (p.340) The Save/Save As/Close dialogs "reflect the internal mechanisms of data entry, storage, and retrieval" (p.325); "In the unified model, we abolish all user interface recognition of the two copies, so the Save function disappears from the mainstream interface." (p.338) Mechanism: manual save is bookkeeping excise — absorb it, and the lost-work error class disappears with it.
**Objective test.** Any auto-modification: a visible marker distinct from user-typed content (underline, highlight, inline badge) + a single-action revert of just that change — flag any silent modification with zero marker and zero targeted undo path. Data-entry surfaces: no manual-save excise; work persists continuously (kill the app mid-edit → reopen → the edit is there).
**✗ WRONG.** Smart-formatting silently "correcting" a correctly-typed technical acronym into a common word, with no trace and no way to see or revert just that change.
**✓ RIGHT.** The changed word briefly highlighted with a one-click revert, spell-check-style; the app auto-saves continuously and has no Save-changes dialog at all.
**Crop.** AF-09.
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — an auto-correction silently modifies user input with zero visible marker and zero targeted undo path *(source: About Face p.332, scoring #40 band-0)*.
- **2** — a marker exists but is very hard to notice (extremely subtle, momentary) and no dedicated undo path exists *(source: About Face p.332, scoring #40 band-3)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** system-modified content carries a distinct visible marker AND is reachable via an undo/history mechanism that reverts just that correction *(source: About Face p.332, scoring #40 band-5/6)*.
- **7** — + the marker is persistent enough to be noticed even if the user isn't watching at the moment of correction (not just a flash) *(source: About Face p.332, scoring #40 band-7/8)*.
- **8** — + work persists continuously with no manual-save excise (kill the app mid-edit, reopen: the edit is there) *(source: About Face p.337, "save documents and settings automatically")*.
- **9** — + zero manual-save bookkeeping surfaces or internal-storage leaks in user-facing copy (Save-changes dialogs, temp filenames, sync/commit terms) *(source: About Face pp.338,340, unified file model; "put files where users can find them")*.
- **10** — full audit-not-edit discipline mirrored consistently across all auto-correct features, one click/keystroke to revert every system change, plus the save/storage model fully absorbed product-wide *(source: About Face p.332, scoring #40 band-9/10; pp.337–338)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — About Face: audit-don't-edit med-high, absorb-bookkeeping/unified-file high (majority high; the med-high noted).

### ERR-8 — Graceful degradation: the weakest link is designed, and critical signals are redundant
**Rule.** Under space/data/failure stress, the design CHOOSES what fails: a designated low-value element degrades first so the critical content survives (per-row failure boundaries, priority-based truncation); critical information travels on ≥2 independent channels so one channel's loss doesn't lose the fact.
**Grounding.**
- *Universal Principles ("Weakest Link"):* "the weakest element in a system can be used to protect other more important elements, essentially making the weakest link one of the most important elements in the system." (p.262) Two variants: "it can fail and passively minimize damage, or it can fail and activate additional systems that actively minimize damage" (p.262) — the fuse (passive) vs. the sprinkler's fusible link (active). Mechanism: failure is inevitable under stress; designating WHERE it lands converts breakage into protection.
- *Universal Principles ("Redundancy"):* "Diverse redundancy is the use of multiple elements of different types... Diverse redundancy is resistant to a single cause of failure." (p.204) Mechanism: two independent channels can't be killed by one cause; a color-only or single-route signal can.
- *Laws of UX (content resiliency):* Amazon "organiz[es] the quick links below the search bar by importance and remov[es] the links of lesser importance as the font size increases" (p.62) — priority-based truncation under font growth. Mechanism: degradation by design (lowest-priority element folds first), not breakage wherever the layout happens to snap.
**Objective test.** Simulate the failure/stress condition and verify only the designated weak element absorbs it: one malformed row in an N-row import is skipped + logged, never aborting the batch; at maximum text-size/3× string expansion, lower-priority links fold into overflow while higher-priority content never clips or overlaps. Critical status: strip any one channel (color → grayscale; icon → text-only; primary route removed) — the fact must still be readable via a second independent encoding/route (see COLOR-7/DATA-9).
**✗ WRONG.** One malformed row crashing a 10,000-row import with a single opaque error; text expansion shattering the header layout at whatever element happened to overflow.
**✓ RIGHT.** Per-row boundaries skip and flag the bad row while 9,999 import; the header sheds its lowest-priority links into a "More" menu, in any language, at any text size.
**Crop.** none (mechanism principle).
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — one malformed unit crashes/aborts the whole batch (no per-unit boundary) AND a critical value relies on a single encoding channel with no backup *(source: Universal Principles p.262, Weakest Link band-0; p.204, Redundancy band-0)*.
- **2** — a failure boundary exists but is too coarse (fails a chunk, not just the offending unit) or trips spuriously under normal conditions; a second encoding exists for some critical values but not all *(source: Universal Principles p.262, Weakest Link band-3; p.204, Redundancy band-3)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** a deliberately-designated weak point fails first and absorbs the failure condition (per-unit skip/log), protecting the rest of the system; every critical value/state has ≥2 independent encodings *(source: Universal Principles p.262, Weakest Link band-5/6; p.204, Redundancy band-5/6)*.
- **7** — + verified that only the designated cheap/easy-to-replace element fails under simulated stress, everything else confirmed unaffected; ≥2 diverse (not homogeneous) encodings cover every critical value *(source: Universal Principles p.262, Weakest Link band-7/8; p.204, Redundancy band-7/8)*.
- **8** — + at 3× string expansion / max text-size, lowest-priority content folds/collapses first (overflow menu, drop) with zero clipping/overlap of higher-priority content *(source: Laws of UX p.62, content resiliency/priority-based truncation)*.
- **10** — crumple-zone standard met (designated element absorbs damage, rest verified unaffected) + diverse "Super Cow" redundancy applied to every critical path, verified by simulating loss of each channel *(source: Universal Principles p.262, Weakest Link band-9/10; p.204, Redundancy band-9/10)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** med (2) — experts disagree: Universal Principles rates Redundancy high but Weakest Link low; Laws of UX rates content resiliency medium. No majority; median med taken, disagreement noted.

# Feedback, Status & Motion

The system tells you it heard you, what it's doing, and where things went. Pillars: 3.

---

### FEED-1 — Feedback scales to measured duration
**Rule.** Match feedback intensity to latency: <0.1s feels live, nothing extra; up to ~1s a subtle cue; 1–10s a visible animated progress indicator (real proportion when computable, not a stateless spinner); >10s explicit status + time estimate + background option + cancel.
**Grounding.**
- *About Face:* "If the response takes longer than a tenth of a second but less than a second, you will need to provide one subtle visual cue that the command was received... If the response takes longer than that up to ten seconds, you'll need to let the user know about the small delay and provide some visual cue that the process is running" (Ch17, p.422). Its Ch11 companion gives the same buckets with the escalation: "Up to about 10 seconds... Providing a progress bar is critical here... After about 10 seconds, you will lose your users' attention... processes that take this long should be conducted offline or in the background... A cancel mechanism is critical" (Ch11, pp.265–266). Mechanism: the feedback tier is set by the MEASURED latency bucket, not by taste — under-feedback reads as a hang, over-feedback as noise.
- *Designing Interfaces:* "Longer than a one-second delay in response, the user is likely to think the UI is not working... spinners or loading indicators are mandatory if you want users to know that your software is indeed working" (pp.409–410, citing Nielsen/Norman). Mechanism: a stateless spinner "does not communicate a changing state," so where progress is computable the book requires the meter form — "tell the user: What's currently going on / What proportion of the operation is complete / How much time remains / How to stop it" (pp.409–410).
- *Laws of UX:* "a 100 ms response feels instantaneous... Once the delay extends past 1,000 ms (1 second), people begin thinking about other things" (p.120); "When wait times must extend beyond the maximum of ten seconds, progress bars are still helpful but should be augmented with an estimation of the time remaining" (p.126). Mechanism: <400ms keeps the human-computer pace matched so "neither has to wait on the other" (p.119) — flow breaks are a productivity cost, not just annoyance.
**Objective test.** Measure actual operation latency; bucket it against the four thresholds (≤0.1s / ≤1s / ≤10s / >10s) and check the implemented feedback matches the tier: nothing extra / one subtle cue / visible animated progress indicator / explicit status + time-remaining + cancel + background option. Interactive feedback (press → visible response) within 400ms at p95 (RUM or synthetic timing). Fails: >1s with no indicator; a stateless spinner where byte/step counts exist (known-progress operation); >10s with no time estimate, no cancel, or no background path.
**✗ WRONG.** A 25s report generation behind a static spinner, no estimate, no cancel; a 45s upload with known byte counts showing a generic circle.
**✓ RIGHT.** "Generating — about 20s left" with a filling bar, Cancel, and dismiss-and-notify; the upload showing percent and bytes processed vs. total.
**Crop.** AF-15, LU-21; also Fig. 21-27 (Chrome tab-embedded progress, About Face p.634), Fig. 10-5 (Apple "About a minute remaining", Laws of UX p.126), Fig. 8-24 (Google Play install with prominent cancel X, Designing Interfaces p.416).
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — any operation >1s runs with no indicator at all (UI reads as frozen) *(source: About Face #38 "0"; Designing Interfaces #21 "0"; Laws of UX #27 "0")*.
- **1** — an indicator appears but is mismatched by ≥2 tiers from what the measured latency requires (e.g. only shown past 10s, nothing below) *[derived — interpolates the AF 4-tier table's missing middle]*.
- **2** — a determinate operation (known byte/step count) hides its computable progress behind a stateless spinner *(source: Designing Interfaces #21 "3")*.
- **3** — the feedback tier is exactly one step short of what the measured latency requires (e.g. a progress bar but no cancel button on a 15s operation) *(source: About Face #38 "3", p.343)*.
- **4** — interactive acknowledgment (press→first visible response) lands >400ms but ≤1s at p95 *(source: Laws of UX p.119–120)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** every operation's implemented feedback matches its measured latency bucket per the 4-tier table (nothing extra / one subtle cue / visible animated progress / full explicit status), AND interactive acknowledgment ≤400ms at p95 *(source: About Face #38 "5-6", Ch17 p.422 + Ch11 pp.265–266; Designing Interfaces #21 "5-6"; Laws of UX p.119–120, p.126)*.
- **6** — + every determinate operation shows real proportion (percent, bytes-of-total, step x/y) instead of a stateless spinner *(source: Designing Interfaces #21 "5-6"/"7-8", pp.409–410)*.
- **7** — + every >1s tier shows an accurate, updating time estimate (not a static guess) *(source: About Face #38 "7-8")*.
- **8** — + every operation measured >10s shows a time estimate AND a cancel control AND a background/dismiss path, all three together *(source: About Face Ch11 pp.265–266; Laws of UX p.126)*.
- **9** — + the match holds consistently across every operation of that latency class on the surface, not just one instance *[derived — convergence of AF/DI/LU across surfaces]*.
- **10** — full top-tier match everywhere: progress bar, live time-remaining, cancel, and background-continue, as in Fig. 21-27 (Chrome's tab-embedded progress) *(source: About Face #38 "9-10", p.634)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — LU #27 high, AF #38 high, DI #21 high; unanimous.

### FEED-2 — Waits: engaged, transparent, progressing
**Rule.** An unavoidable wait shows all three at once: something moving (idleness aversion), what stage is happening (operational transparency), and advancement toward the goal (goal gradient) — never a silent ambiguous pause.
**Grounding.** *Laws of UX*, on Uber's Express POOL redesign addressing "three concepts related to wait time: idleness aversion, operational transparency, and the goal gradient effect... Uber customers are presented with an animation that helps to keep them not only informed but also entertained (idleness aversion). The app provides an estimated time of arrival and information on how arrival times are calculated (operational transparency). It clearly explains each step of the process so customers feel that they are continuously making progress toward their goal" (p.69). Mechanism: "By focusing on people's perceptions of time and waiting, Uber was able to reduce its post-request cancellation rate" (p.69) — the triad manages perceived time when actual time can't shrink, and the measured payoff is fewer abandonments.
**Objective test.** Any wait state exceeding ~2s shows simultaneously (a) an animated/moving element (not a static frozen frame), (b) a text description of the current stage ("Finding your driver" / "Confirming payment"), and (c) an indication of advancement (step indicator, percentage, or sequential status change). Any of the three missing = fail.
**✗ WRONG.** A ride-booking screen shows only a static "Please wait…" label with no animation, no ETA, and no step description for the full duration of the search.
**✓ RIGHT.** A pulsing map pin + "Finding nearby drivers — usually under 2 min" + a status update to "Driver found, 4 min away" once matched.
**Crop.** LU-15; Fig. 6-2 (Uber ride-request sequence, Laws of UX p.69).
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — a wait state >2s shows only a static "Please wait…" with no animation, no ETA, no step description *(source: Laws of UX #16 "0", p.69)*.
- **2** — exactly one of the three elements (motion / stage text / advancement) is present *(source: Laws of UX #16 "3", lower half)*.
- **3** — two of the three elements are present *(source: Laws of UX #16 "3", upper half)*.
- **4** — all three elements exist on the surface but never appear on the same screen state at once (sequential/separate screens rather than simultaneous) *[derived — the rule's own simultaneity requirement, consistent with the Uber example's single-screen composition]*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** all three — (a) an animated/moving element, (b) stage-description text, (c) an incremental-progress signal — are simultaneously present for any wait >2s *(source: Laws of UX #16 "5-6", p.69)*.
- **6** — + the progress/advancement signal updates meaningfully at least once during a longer wait, not a single static message the whole time *(source: Laws of UX #16 "7-8")*.
- **8** — + the stage text names the SPECIFIC current operation ("Finding your driver" / "Confirming payment"), not a generic "Loading…" *(source: Laws of UX #16, p.69)*.
- **10** — matches the ✓ Uber case: animated pin + explicit ETA/how-it's-calculated + sequential status updates ("Finding drivers" → "Driver found, 4 min away"), all three woven together and updating as the wait progresses *(source: Laws of UX #16 "9-10", p.69, Fig. 6-2)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — sole expert line (LU #16) is medium-high, rounded up on its own rationale (tied to a measured business outcome, cleanly observable in any wait state); noted as a between-band call.

### FEED-3 — Optimistic UI for near-certain actions
**Rule.** High-success low-risk actions (like, comment, toggle) show the success state within one frame of the gesture, before the server responds, with a defined rollback on rare failure.
**Grounding.** *Laws of UX:* "It works by optimistically providing feedback that an action was successful while it is being processed, as opposed to providing feedback only once the action has been completed. For example, Instagram displays comments on photos before they are actually posted... it immediately provides visual feedback that assumes the comment will be successfully posted, and only displays an error afterward in the event that the action isn't successful" (p.126). Mechanism: because such actions almost always succeed, paying the round-trip latency on every action to guard against a rare failure inverts the odds — the app "seems faster than it actually is" while the error path still covers the exception.
**Objective test.** For a near-always-successful, low-risk action: client-side state updates synchronously with the user gesture — within one animation frame, before the network response resolves (no spinner for the round-trip) — AND a defined rollback + error path exists that visibly reverts the optimistic state on failure. Either half missing = fail.
**✗ WRONG.** Tapping "like" shows a loading spinner on the heart icon for the full 200–800ms network round-trip before filling in.
**✓ RIGHT.** The heart fills instantly on tap; if the background request later fails, the icon reverts and a small error toast appears.
**Crop.** LU-21; Fig. 10-6 (Instagram comment shown as "Posting…" pre-confirmation, Laws of UX p.127).
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — a high-stakes/irreversible action fires optimistically before confirmation, OR a near-always-successful low-risk action blocks visual feedback for the full network round-trip *(source: Laws of UX #28 "0", p.126; scoping guard `[derived]` — convergence with LU #29 "deliberate friction can build trust")*.
- **2** — no high-stakes misapplication, but optimistic treatment is inconsistent across low-risk actions of similar risk profile *(source: Laws of UX #28 "3", p.126)*.
- **3** — consistently optimistic across qualifying actions, but no rollback/error path is defined for failure *(source: Laws of UX #28 "3", p.126)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** client-side state updates to the success state within one animation frame of the gesture, before the network response resolves, AND a defined rollback/error path exists if the request later fails *(source: Laws of UX #28 "5-6", p.126)*.
- **7** — + the rollback is graceful and clearly communicated (a toast, a visible revert animation) rather than a silent or jarring state flip *(source: Laws of UX #28 "7-8", p.126)*.
- **9** — + applied to every qualifying near-certain action on the surface — none left blocking on the round-trip path *[derived — convergence of the "9-10" "applied consistently" clause with the scoping requirement]*.
- **10** — matches the ✓ Instagram comment-posting case: apparent success is instant, rollback/error handling is present and unobtrusive, applied consistently to every appropriate low-risk action, with zero high-stakes leakage *(source: Laws of UX #28 "9-10", p.126–127, Fig. 10-6)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** med (2) — LU #28 medium (real perceived-speed win, narrowly scoped; misapplication is a defect).

### FEED-4 — Skeletons preserve layout; loading never jumps
**Rule.** Loading states reserve the final layout's geometry (skeleton placeholders), replaced progressively — never a blank screen, never a content pop that shifts what was visible.
**Grounding.** *Laws of UX:* where true speed isn't achievable, engineer perceived speed — "skeleton screens, blur-up image loading, animated loaders" (pp.119–126, Doherty Threshold chapter); past 1,000ms "people begin thinking about other things" (p.120), so the loading interval must look like the destination, not like absence. Mechanism: a skeleton that holds the loaded content's bounding boxes gives the eye a stable frame to parse early and prevents the re-orientation cost of content shifting under an already-reading user (Instagram skeleton screen, Fig. 10-2, p.123).
**Objective test.** The loading DOM reserves the same bounding-box dimensions as the loaded content — cumulative layout shift ≈ 0 as placeholders are replaced. Blank-white intervals >~1s = fail; a content pop that displaces anything already visible = fail.
**✗ WRONG.** A feed shows a completely blank white screen for 2.5s, then all content pops in at once, shifting everything that was already visible.
**✓ RIGHT.** Grey placeholder blocks matching each item's final geometry (avatar circle, two text lines, image rectangle), progressively replaced as data arrives — zero layout shift.
**Crop.** LU-10; Fig. 10-2 (Instagram skeleton screen, Laws of UX p.123).
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — a completely blank white screen persists for the loading interval, then all content pops in at once, shifting anything already visible *(source: Laws of UX #27 "0", pp.119–126)*.
- **2** — a loading indicator (spinner) exists but doesn't match the final layout's geometry; visible layout shift (CLS >0.25) once content arrives *(source: Laws of UX #27 "3")*.
- **4** — interactive response is fast for typical requests OR a skeleton is shown, but a blank-white interval of 1–2.5s still occurs on at least one surface, or the shift reduction is only partial (CLS 0.1–0.25) *[derived — splits LU #27's "5-6" band against its own CLS/blank-interval measure]*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** interactive response completes within ~400ms typical OR a skeleton/placeholder matching the final layout's bounding-box dimensions is shown (no blank white screen, CLS ≈ 0/<0.1) *(source: Laws of UX #27 "5-6", pp.119–126)*.
- **6** — + placeholders are replaced progressively per-item/region as data arrives, rather than a single all-at-once swap *(source: Laws of UX #27, Instagram skeleton mechanism, p.123, Fig. 10-2)*.
- **8** — + the fast-or-skeleton, zero-CLS pattern is applied consistently across every async/loading surface in the product, including the >10s dual indicator (time estimate + progress) where relevant *(source: Laws of UX #27 "7-8")*.
- **10** — matches the ✓ Instagram/Apple cases: skeleton precisely mirrors the content's structure (avatar circle, text lines, image rectangle at final positions) with zero CLS, applied everywhere relevant in the product *(source: Laws of UX #27 "9-10", p.123–126)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — LU #27 high (measurable, business-outcome-linked perceived-speed engineering).

### FEED-5 — Motion communicates spatial continuity, never decorates
**Rule.** Transitions show where things came from and where they went, preserving the mental map; ~300ms-class, visually continuous; rapid repeated inputs coalesce into ONE animation; emphasis-motion is rationed and respects reduced-motion, with nothing essential conveyed by motion alone.
**Grounding.**
- *About Face:* "Animated transitions help users create a strong mental model of how what is presented in one view is related to what was presented in the previous view" (Ch11, p.266); per Saffer, transitions should "Maintain context during transitions between views or object states" and "Create a virtual space that helps guide users from state to state" (p.267). Mechanism: motion's job is expressing relationships between objects across states — decoration that shows no before→after relationship does none of that work.
- *Designing Interfaces:* "when the shift from one state to another is visually continuous, it's not so bad... This helps keep the user oriented" (p.203); "Research shows that 300 milliseconds might be ideal for smooth scrolling," and for rapid repeats "combine them into one animated action. Otherwise, the user might sit there through several seconds' worth of animation as the punishment" (p.204). Mechanism: the animation serves orientation only up to the point it delays input — hence the fixed duration class and the coalescing rule.
- *Laws of UX:* motion "can trigger dizziness, nausea, headaches, or worse" for users with BPPV, labyrinthitis, epilepsy, and migraine sensitivities — "We must carefully consider when and how we use motion in our designs to ensure users with motion sensitivity aren't negatively affected" (p.102). Mechanism: emphasis-motion is an accessibility hazard class, so it needs a dampened `prefers-reduced-motion` branch and can never be the sole carrier of a state.
**Objective test.** (a) Spatial state changes (delete, collapse, view switch) render a continuous path from before-position to after-position, ≤~300ms; an instant cut with no positional relationship = fail. (b) 10 rapid repeated inputs coalesce into ONE animation to the final state; duration stacking linearly per input (10× down-arrow = 10 sequential animations) = fail. (c) Every emphasis animation has a `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` branch that disables or substantially dampens it (no parallax, no large-amplitude motion); no state is communicated by motion only.
**✗ WRONG.** A deleted row vanishing with the list snapping up; 10 down-arrows queuing 3 seconds of back-to-back scroll animation; a parallax hero ignoring the OS motion setting.
**✓ RIGHT.** The row collapses ~250ms while neighbors slide up to fill the space; rapid repeats coalesce into one scroll to the final position; reduced-motion swaps parallax for a static or minimal-fade treatment.
**Crop.** DI-14.
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — a spatial state change (delete, collapse, view switch) cuts instantly with the surrounding layout snapping, no transition *(source: About Face #15 "0", p.266; Designing Interfaces #3 "0", p.203)*.
- **2** — a transition exists but is a generic fade with no positional before→after relationship *(source: About Face #15 "3"; Designing Interfaces #3 "3")*.
- **3** — a continuous positional transition exists but exceeds ~300ms (delays input), or repeated rapid input stacks linearly (10 presses = 10× duration, "punishment") *(source: Designing Interfaces #3 "3", p.204)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** a continuous visual path from before-position to after-position renders ≤~300ms on every spatial state change *(source: About Face #15 "5-6"; Designing Interfaces #3 "5-6", p.204)*.
- **6** — + rapid repeated input coalesces into ONE animation to the final state rather than queuing serially *(source: Designing Interfaces #3 "7-8", p.204)*.
- **7** — + every emphasis-only animation has a `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` branch that disables or substantially dampens it (no parallax, no large-amplitude motion) *(source: Laws of UX #22 "5-6", p.102)*.
- **8** — + applied consistently across every similar state change and every animated element on the surface, not just one case *(source: About Face #15 "7-8"; Laws of UX #22 "7-8")*.
- **9** — + no state is communicated by motion alone — every motion-conveyed state also has a static cue (color/label/position) *(source: Laws of UX #22, p.102 mechanism)*.
- **10** — matches the ✓ macOS-dock/iOS-flick class: motion itself communicates where things came from/went, zero decorative excess, reduced-motion fully handled everywhere *(source: About Face #15 "9-10", Fig. 11-10; Designing Interfaces #3 "9-10", Fig. 3-62; Laws of UX #22 "9-10")*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** med (2) — AF #15 med, DI #3 med, LU #22 low-med; majority med (LU's low-med noted — its lens is the reduced-motion accessibility slice only).

### FEED-6 — Peaks and endings carry the verdict
**Rule.** Users judge a whole flow by its most intense moment and its ending, not the average; the completion/confirmation/recovery screens deserve craft at least equal to the middle, and negative peaks weigh heavier than positive ones — prevent them first.
**Grounding.** *Laws of UX:* "People judge an experience largely based on how they felt at its peak and at its end, rather than on the total sum or average of every moment of the experience" (p.65). Evidence: Kahneman's cold-water experiment — participants preferred repeating a LONGER, objectively-more-painful trial because it ended less painfully — and the colonoscopy studies, where patients with the objectively longer procedure that ended gently "rated their overall experience as less unpleasant" and "were more likely to return for subsequent procedures" (p.66). On the negative side: "We have a tendency as humans not only to register negative events more readily but also to dwell on these events" (p.74, same memory-bias family as peak-end, p.67). Mechanism: memory samples the peak and the end, not the integral — so a review that only averages severity mis-weights a single rage moment or a dead ending, and preventing negative peaks (e.g., inline validation) beats polishing the average.
**Objective test.** Audit two moments in isolation from the rest of the flow: (1) the single most emotionally intense step (error / wait / celebration) shows deliberate design investment — not a bare default browser/OS state; (2) the final screen contains more than a bare system-default "Success" toast — matching the flow's polish, summarizing what happened, offering the next action. Both yes = pass; and no severity-averaged review may outvote a failing peak or ending.
**✗ WRONG.** Five illustrated onboarding steps ending on a grey browser alert "Setup complete."
**✓ RIGHT.** A final screen at step-1-level polish with a personalized summary of what was set up and a clear next action.
**Crop.** none (studies are data-only); Fig. 6-1 (Spotify Wrapped, Laws of UX p.68) is the adjacent visual for a designed peak moment.
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — the flow's most intense moment AND its ending are both bare system defaults (e.g. a polished flow ending on a plain gray browser alert "Setup complete") *(source: Laws of UX #14 "0", pp.65–66)*.
- **2** — of the two moments, the one with investment is only above-default and generic (styled but no summary/next action for the ending, or partially-designed custom styling around a default control for the peak) *[derived — splits LU #14's "3" band by which moment carries the partial credit]*.
- **3** — one of the two moments (peak or ending) received deliberate design investment, but the other remains a bare default *(source: Laws of UX #14 "3", pp.65–66)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** BOTH the single most emotionally intense step (error/wait/celebration) AND the final screen show deliberate design investment beyond a bare default state *(source: Laws of UX #14 "5-6", pp.65–66)*.
- **7** — + the ending includes a personalized summary of what happened and a clear next action, not a generic success state *(source: Laws of UX #14 "7-8", pp.65–66)*.
- **8** — + foreseeable negative peaks are pre-empted before they occur (inline validation instead of submit-and-reject; a warned wait instead of a hang) rather than merely handled gracefully after the fact *(source: Laws of UX #15 "negativity bias", p.74; [derived] convergence with #14's peak framing)*.
- **9** — + the audit treats a failing peak or ending as failing the whole flow, regardless of the average of the other steps *(source: Laws of UX #14, p.65 mechanism — "peak and end, not the total sum or average")*.
- **10** — matches the ✓ redesigned-ending case: final screen matches the rest of the flow's polish, with a personalized summary and next action, negative peaks pre-empted, and the peak-weighted verdict applied throughout *(source: Laws of UX #14 "9-10", pp.65–68, Fig. 6-1)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — LU #14 high, LU #15 medium-high; majority high (a single moment can override the whole recalled verdict).

### FEED-7 — Interaction pliancy (micro-feedback)
**Rule.** Hover/pressed/active/selected states on every interactive element confirm "the system heard you" before any network response.
**Grounding.** *About Face:* "Part of a button's affordance is its visual pliancy, which indicates its pressability. When the user points to it and clicks the mouse button... the button control visually changes from raised to indented, indicating that it has been activated... Poorly designed applications and many websites contain buttons that don't animate when clicked or tapped. This is disconcerting for users, because it generates a mental question: 'Did that actually do something?'" (Ch21, p.591); "Rich visual feedback is the key to successful direct manipulation" (Ch13, p.315). Mechanism: the state change is a local, zero-latency acknowledgment that closes the gesture loop before any round-trip — without it every click ends in doubt (and often a second, duplicate click). Mechanics and the screenshot-diff test live in AFFORD-5.
**Objective test.** AFFORD-5's pseudo-state screenshot diff: capture each interactive element at idle / hover / active (pressed) / selected; zero pixel change across the states = fail. The acknowledgment must be local and immediate — rendered before (and independent of) any network response.
**✗ WRONG.** A styled div-button identical across all states; the only sign a click registered is the page changing 600ms later.
**✓ RIGHT.** Darken on hover, compress/ripple on press, distinct selected state — instant local confirmation before the server replies.
**Crop.** AF-03.
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — a custom control has identical CSS across idle/hover/active states — zero pixel difference on click *(source: About Face #22 "0", p.591)*.
- **2** — one state (hover XOR pressed) is implemented across elements; the other gives no feedback *(source: About Face #22 "3")*.
