**Objective test.** The current-location marker differs from the inactive baseline on ≥2 independent channels (of: color, weight, background fill, border, icon, size); a single-channel difference (e.g., only a slightly darker gray) = fail. Active tab must be visually continuous with its panel (shared fill/border, no separating line).
**✗ WRONG.** The active tab rendered 5% darker grey than inactive tabs — same weight, same size, no border.
**✓ RIGHT.** Bold text + colored underline + filled background — three simultaneous cues — with the tab fused to its content panel.
**Crop.** KR-01, KR-05.
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — no distinguishable current-location indicator exists at all (active and inactive items render identically) *(source: Krug #15 "0")*.
- **2** — exactly 1 weak channel differs (e.g. ~5% darker gray) — the subtle-failure case Krug names explicitly *(Krug #15 "3")*.
- **4** — 1 clear channel differs (a distinct color OR bold, alone), identifiable only at full resolution, not survivable at a blur *(Krug #15 "5–6" — single-channel)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** ≥2 independent channels differ (e.g. color + bold, or underline + fill), and the active item is identifiable in a blurred screenshot *(Krug #15 "7–8"; calibration maxim p.109)*.
- **6** — as 5 + the active tab (where a tab construct exists) is visually continuous with its content panel — shared fill/border, no separating line; where no tab/panel construct exists, the indicator adjoins the content it governs *(Krug p.109 tab-pop mechanism)*.
- **8** — as 6 + the same active-state treatment is used consistently at every nav level/surface *(Krug #15 "9–10" mechanism — consistency implied by "unmissable at a glance" everywhere)*.
- **10** — ✓ ≥3 simultaneous channels distinguish the active item (bold + colored underline + filled background), fused to its content panel, unmissable at a glance across every surface *(Krug #15 "9–10")*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** med (2) — Krug #15: med (a specific instance of the broader hierarchy principle); sole source.


### NAV-6 — Name-match and deep-link contracts
**Rule.** Clicked label ≈ destination heading; deep entries land on the specific target. Full spec → XCON-6.
**Grounding.** Krug, name-match: "Every site makes an implicit social contract with its visitors: The name of the page will match the words I clicked to get there... Each time a site violates it, I'm forced to think, even if only for milliseconds, 'Why are those two things different?' And if there's a major discrepancy... my trust in the site—and the competence of the people who publish it—will be diminished" (p.106). Krug, deep-link integrity: "Don't leave me standing at the front door. Another real nuisance: You tap on a link in an email or a social media site and instead of taking you to the article in question it takes you to the mobile Home page, leaving you to hunt for the thing yourself" (p.185). Mechanism: both are broken promises — the mismatch or the dumped landing forces the user to re-derive what the system promised to deliver.
**Objective test.** XCON-6's token-overlap and entry-point checks: click-test every primary nav/CTA label against the destination's H1/page title — flag any pair with <70% token overlap lacking an obviously-equivalent reason (Krug's tolerated case: "Gifts for Him" → "Gifts for Men," p.106). For every external entry point (email link, push notification, shared URL, search result), the resulting screen must be the specific referenced content — any entry landing on Home/generic feed instead of its target = fail, zero tolerance.
**✗ WRONG.** A nav link "Pricing" opens a page headed "Plans & Packages" with no echo of "Pricing" above the fold; a "Your order has shipped" notification opens the app's generic home feed.
**✓ RIGHT.** "Pricing" leads to an H1 reading "Pricing"; the shipping notification opens that order's tracking detail screen.
**Crop.** none.
**Score (0–10).** Deep-link's zero-tolerance framing caps the score: any entry point landing on a generic Home/feed holds the ladder at rung 0–1 regardless of name-match quality.
- **0** — any external entry point (email link, notification, shared URL, search result) lands on a generic Home/feed instead of the referenced content, OR a nav/CTA label and its destination H1 share no discernible relationship with no echo anywhere above the fold *(source: Krug #28 "0" p.185 — shipping-notification-to-home-feed; Krug #14 "0" p.106 — "Pricing"→"Plans & Packages")*.
- **2** — deep-link entry lands closer to the target (right section) but not the specific item; name-match overlap is <70% with no equivalence *(Krug #28 "3"; #14 "3")*.
- **4** — deep-link lands on the correct content but drops context (e.g. right order, wrong tab); name-match overlap is borderline ~60–70% *(Krug #28 "5–6"; #14 "5–6")*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** deep-link lands on the exact referenced content with only cosmetic context loss; name-match overlap is ≥70% or an obviously-equivalent phrasing ("Gifts for Him"→"Gifts for Men"); clicked words echoed somewhere on the destination *(Krug #28 "7–8"; #14 "7–8")*.
- **7** — as 5 + the echo is above the fold, and deep-linked context (item + sub-state/tab) both arrive correct *(Krug #14 mechanism p.106; #28 "9–10" context clause)*.
- **10** — ✓ every deep-link entry point lands precisely on the referenced content in full context with zero extra navigation, AND label/H1 match exactly or near-exactly *(Krug #28 "9–10" — direct-to-order-tracking; #14 "9–10" — "Pricing"→"Pricing")*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — split source: Krug #14 name-match med vs Krug #28 deep-link high ("zero tolerance", binary); deep-link's zero-tolerance framing carries the majority of the principle's risk — noted, resolved high.

### NAV-7 — Depth doesn't decay
**Rule.** Level-2/3+ navigation keeps level-1's visual system, spacing, and indicator logic — the ad-hoc decay zone is where users actually spend their time. Full spec → XCON-8.
**Grounding.** Krug: "In so many sites, as soon as you get past the second level, the navigation breaks down and becomes ad hoc. The problem is so common that it's actually hard to find good examples of third-level navigation" (p.104). Mechanism: designers run out of time on levels 1–2 and stakeholders under-invest because "it's not primary... it's not even secondary" — yet "the reality is that users usually end up spending as much time on lower-level pages as they do at the top" (p.104), so the neglected zone carries the real traffic.
**Objective test.** Token diff level 1 vs deepest level: compare the nav's spacing unit, indicator style, and grouping logic at level 1 against level 3 (or deepest available) — they must resolve to the same design tokens; any level introducing a one-off pattern not used elsewhere in the nav system fails.
**✗ WRONG.** Level-1 nav is a clean horizontal tab bar with a consistent "you are here" underline; by level 3, sub-items are an unstyled bullet list with no active-state indicator at all.
**✓ RIGHT.** Level-3 sub-items use the same active-state underline/bold treatment and spacing rhythm as level 1, just nested one indent deeper.
**Crop.** none.
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — deepest level abandons the level-1 system entirely — unstyled bullet list, no active-state indicator at all *(source: Krug #16 "0" p.104 — the level-3-bullet-list case)*.
- **2** — deepest level uses some structure but a materially different visual language (different spacing unit, no active-state at all) *(Krug #16 "3")*.
- **4** — deepest level has an active-state indicator and consistent spacing, but introduces ≥1 one-off pattern not used at level 1, and/or sub-items are grouped by ad-hoc logic *(Krug #16 "5–6")*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** deepest level matches level-1 tokens (spacing unit, indicator style) with only minor cosmetic drift; grouping logic at depth matches level 1 *(Krug #16 "7–8")*.
- **7** — as 5 + zero one-off patterns anywhere in the nav system below level 1 *(Krug #16 mechanism — no materially different visual language, p.104)*.
- **10** — ✓ deepest level uses identical design tokens (spacing, indicator style, grouping logic) as level 1, just nested one indent deeper *(Krug #16 "9–10")*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface (fewer than 3 nav levels).
**Weight.** med (2) — Krug #16: med ("only applicable to ≥3 nav levels"); sole source.

### NAV-8 — Linear flows carry a progress map
**Rule.** Any ≥3-step linear flow (wizard, checkout) shows total steps, current position, and completed steps as navigable (future steps disabled until unlocked); a bare page-count suffices only where navigation isn't the point.
**Grounding.** Designing Interfaces, "Progress Indicator": "Progress Indicators indicate to a user how far they've come through a series of steps — and, more important, how far they have yet to go before the process is finished. Knowing this helps them decide whether to continue, estimate how long it will take, and stay oriented" (p.189). They also "serve as navigational devices," letting a user "go back to a previously completed step... by clicking that step in the map of steps" (p.189). Boundary cases: the National Geographic Kids slideshow's "simple page count... The user cannot use it to actually move through the sequence" (p.190) is valid only when navigation isn't the point; transactional flows gate the future — B&H Photo's checkout "steps are disabled when the user hasn't completed the required earlier step" (p.193). Mechanism: knowing remaining effort is what lets users decide to continue at all — an unmapped flow forces a blind commitment.
**Objective test.** ≥3-step flows expose (a) total step count, (b) current position, (c) completed steps as clickable/navigable; absence of (a) or (b) = fail; transactional flows (checkout, application) must also supply (c) and disable not-yet-reachable steps.
**✗ WRONG.** A 5-screen onboarding wizard with no step count or position indication at all — the user cannot estimate remaining effort or return to a prior step.
**✓ RIGHT.** "1 Shipping — 2 Payment — 3 Review": current step highlighted, completed steps clickable back, future steps visibly disabled until unlocked.
**Crop.** DI-13.
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — a ≥3-step flow shows no count, no position at all *(source: Designing Interfaces #2 "0" p.189 — the onboarding-wizard ✗)*.
- **3** — shows a bare page count ("3 of 5") with no navigability — acceptable ONLY per the book's own carve-out when navigation isn't the point (narrative/slideshow); a transactional flow (checkout, application) at this level still fails, since completed-step navigability is required for that class *(DI #2 "3")*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** total steps + current position exposed; for transactional flows, completed steps are clickable and future/disabled steps are clearly inert (B&H Photo pattern) *(DI #2 "5–6")*.
- **7** — as 5 + disabled-state and labels make clear WHY a step is unreachable (dependency, not just greyed), and steps carry names (Shipping/Payment/Review), not bare numbers *(DI #2 "7–8")*.
- **10** — ✓ full back-and-forth progress map (Mini Cooper configurator pattern) — freely navigable in both directions, current step highlighted, no dead ends *(DI #2 "9–10")*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface (no ≥3-step linear flow).
**Weight.** high (3) — Designing Interfaces #2: "high for checkout/application flows; low for narrative/slideshow flows" — conditional weight noted; scored surfaces with only narrative flows are usually N/A here, so the transactional high governs.

### NAV-9 — Focus plus context on drill-down
**Rule.** Zooming/drilling retains an echo of the whole — an overview inset with a viewport rectangle, a breadcrumb, dimmed-but-visible surroundings — so precision never costs bearings; a detail view with no position indicator and no one-action return is orphaned.
**Grounding.** Designing Interfaces: "There's a famous mantra in the information visualization field: 'Focus plus context.' A good visualization should permit a user to focus on a point of interest, while simultaneously showing enough stuff around that point of interest to give the user a sense of where it is in the big picture" (p.439). The concrete mechanism: "Sometimes an overview next to a detail view can help the user stay oriented. A small view of the whole graphic can be shown with an indicator rectangle showing the visible 'viewport'" (p.440); breadcrumbs are "a single linear 'slice' of the overall map" (p.194). Universal Principles, layering: "Layering involves organizing information into related groupings and then presenting or making available only certain groupings at any one time. Layering is primarily used to manage complexity, but can also be used to reinforce relationships in information" (p.146) — drill-down is a layer switch, and the layer type must match the data's relationship structure (hierarchical data → nested/collapsible layers, not a flat cut).
**Objective test.** After any drill/zoom action, the interface still exposes (a) an indicator of the zoomed region's position within the whole (inset, viewport rectangle, breadcrumb, dimmed surroundings), or (b) a one-action path back to the prior overview; neither = fail (orphaned drill-down). Layer-type check: hierarchical data presented without nesting/collapse (or sequential data without a linear map) is a layering-type mismatch.
**✗ WRONG.** Clicking a data point on a dense scatter plot navigates to a full-screen detail with no back button, no breadcrumb, and no mini-map showing where that point sat in the original plot.
**✓ RIGHT.** The detail keeps a small inset of the full plot with the selected point highlighted — or a one-click "back to overview" affordance — per the overview-plus-viewport-rectangle technique.
**Crop.** DI-13.
**Score (0–10).**
- **0** — a drill-down/zoom navigates away with no indicator of position-in-whole and no one-click return, AND/OR content with a clear structural relationship (hierarchical/sequential) is presented in a mismatched layering type (a hierarchy forced flat) *(source: Designing Interfaces #14 "0" p.439–440 — full-screen-detail-with-no-way-back; Universal Principles Layering "0")*.
- **2** — a return path exists (browser-back/generic escape) but no position-in-whole indicator is ever shown; layering type is a poor fit, losing some structure *(DI #14 "3"; Universal Principles Layering "3")*.
- **4** — either (a) a position indicator (mini-map/viewport rectangle/breadcrumb) OR (b) a one-action path back is present, not both; the drilled item is unmarked within any context indicator that does exist *(DI #14 "5–6")*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** both (a) a position-in-whole indicator and (b) a one-action return control are present; the layering type used matches the content's actual relationship type (hierarchical → nested/collapsible; sequential → linear map) *(DI #14 "7–8"; Universal Principles Layering "5–6")*.
- **7** — as 5 + the drilled item is highlighted within the context indicator (selected point marked in the inset/breadcrumb leaf), and layer transitions (expand/collapse, popup, overlay) are smooth without losing context *(DI #14 mechanism; Universal Principles Layering "7–8")*.
- **10** — ✓ a live overview-plus-viewport inset stays visible DURING the detail view (not just reachable via a button) with the focus marked, matching the layering type a reviewer couldn't swap without degrading the content's structure *(DI #14 "9–10"; Universal Principles Layering "9–10")*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface (no drill-down/zoom interaction).
**Weight.** med (2) — Designing Interfaces #14 med and Universal Principles Layering med; unanimous.

# Performance & Speed

The surface is fast where it claims to be, measured — not felt — and it never regresses
silently. FEED-* judges how an app FEELS while slow; this category judges whether it IS slow,
with numbers. Pillars: 3.

Method notes for the seat: drive the LIVE app at the latency-floor fixture (a zero-latency
fixture certifies a screen that exists on no real machine). Measure cold and warm separately —
a mean is the number that hides the cold path. Read the PRD `Perf-budget:` line and
`docs/PERF.md` before scoring; a surface with no budget line scores against the FEED-1
latency tiers instead and files that absence as a PERF-1 defect. When a read is slow, bound
the FLOOR before judging the query: a no-op probe (`SELECT 1`-class) over the same path
separates the channel's constant cost from the query's work, and STATE the dataset's actual
size — multi-second reads over megabyte-scale data indict the channel or architecture, never
the query; classify against `../performance-playbook.md` (the diagnosis ladder + lever map)
and file channel findings as ARCHITECTURE rows, not query defects. A confirmed perf storm on
a surface HOLDS craft redesign of that surface (file it as a sequencing note): redesigning a
screen whose real problem is that it hammers the backend is thrown-away work.

---

### PERF-1 — A budget exists and every route is measured against it
**Grounding.** Measured build practice: a declared-but-unread budget preceded a day of user-reported slowness (5 complaints, every one the first measurement of its route); FEED-1's latency tiers (About Face Ch17/Ch11 · Laws of UX, Doherty) all presume a MEASURED number exists to tier against.
**Rule.** The PRD carries a machine-readable `Perf-budget:` line, and every primary route's
interactive latency has a MEASURED number (cold and warm) compared against it this round.
**Objective test.** `docs/PRD.md` contains `Perf-budget:`; `docs/PERF.md` (or this seat's own
drive) holds dated cold/warm numbers per primary route; each number is within its budget
component.
**✗ WRONG.** A budget declared at P0 that no artifact ever measures against; "feels fine"
as the only evidence.
**✓ RIGHT.** "Route /list: 320ms warm / 1.4s cold vs budget 500/2000 — pass" recorded this round.
**Score (0–10).** 0 — no budget line and no measurements anywhere. 2 — a budget exists but
nothing was measured against it this round. 4 — measurements exist but warm-only (the cold
path is unmeasured). **5 — THRESHOLD:** every primary route measured cold AND warm this round
against an explicit budget, overruns named. 7 — + measured at the latency-floor fixture with
the fixture named in the evidence. 9 — + the per-route numbers are tracked across rounds
(movement visible). 10 — + zero overruns, all routes, both paths.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A never — an app with no routes is
not under review.
**Weight.** high (3) — the category's anchor: an unmeasured budget is the measured root of
day-long user-reported slowness.

### PERF-2 — Cold and warm are separated, and the cold path is owned
**Grounding.** Measured instrument lesson: a blended mean hid a 2.3s cold path behind an 80ms warm one, and the slowness recurred every morning until the two were measured apart.
**Rule.** First-load and after-idle latency are measured apart from warm-path latency, and
the cold path has a named owner-strategy (warming, projection, skeleton-to-content budget) —
not an accident the user discovers.
**Objective test.** Evidence distinguishes cold from warm per route; the cold number has a
strategy attached where it exceeds the interactive tier.
**✗ WRONG.** "Average 400ms" over a 2.3s cold / 80ms warm distribution; slowness that
reappears every morning because only the warm path was ever measured.
**✓ RIGHT.** "Cold 1.9s (projection warms at boot, skeleton holds layout), warm 0.08s."
**Score (0–10).** 0 — one blended number per route. 3 — cold/warm separated on some routes.
**5 — THRESHOLD:** separated on every primary route. 7 — + every out-of-tier cold number
carries its named strategy. 10 — + the strategy is asserted by a journey (e.g. skeleton
present at the cold rung, content within budget).
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if the app has no primary route that reads server data.
**Weight.** med (2).

### PERF-3 — Request efficiency: no waterfalls, no refetch storms
**Grounding.** The measured recurrence mechanism of a real build: 15 requests refired on tab return and an N-line write firing N refetches — each fast read multiplied into felt slowness; R3 (frontend-architecture §6) states the parallel-reads half.
**Rule.** Independent reads go out together (R3); returning to a visited surface refires only
what changed; writes BATCH their invalidations (one user action dirties its tags ONCE — never
once per line of a loop); the same data is not fetched by parallel bespoke paths beside the
app's data layer.
**Objective test.** Count requests on route entry, on RETURN to a visited route, and after a
multi-line write; independent reads are parallel; the return count covers only invalidated
reads; one N-line submit produces one refetch per dirtied tag; grep finds no raw-fetch hook
duplicating a cached read.
**✗ WRONG.** 15 requests refired on returning to an already-visited tab, 12 of them identical
per-band reads a cache already held; an N-line delivery firing N refetches because invalidation
runs per mutation inside the write loop; a code comment claiming the cache dedupes while a
bespoke hook bypasses it.
**✓ RIGHT.** Return to a visited surface refires 0–2 invalidated reads; every server read
goes through the one data layer.
**Score (0–10).** 0 — sequential waterfalls on primary routes. 2 — parallel entry reads but
full refetch storms on return. 4 — return refires bounded but bespoke fetch paths exist beside
the data layer. **5 — THRESHOLD:** parallel entry + bounded return + one data layer, on the
primary routes. 7 — + measured request counts in evidence per route. 10 — + the counts are
journey-asserted so a regression goes red.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no surface reads server data.
**Weight.** high (3) — the measured recurrence mechanism of the mined build.

### PERF-4 — Payload discipline: the served bundle is within budget
**Grounding.** The served bundle is what ships (the dev server proves nothing about it — gates-and-ledger L08 class); an unmeasured served artifact grows silently.
**Rule.** The served production bundle's size is measured against the budget; removals state
the bundle delta; a dependency added for one feature is visible in the delta.
**Objective test.** `guard.sh perf` (layer 5) green on bundle size; "removed" claims carry
before → after bytes.
**✗ WRONG.** A "removed" feature whose dependency still ships; bundle growth nobody noticed
because nothing measures the served artifact.
**✓ RIGHT.** "Bundle 412KB → 388KB after retiring the chart lib" in the round's evidence.
**Score (0–10).** 0 — bundle never measured. **5 — THRESHOLD:** measured this round against
the budget, delta stated when it moved. 8 — + gate-enforced (layer 5 red on overrun). 10 — +
per-route code-split budgets where routes differ materially.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if the app ships no client bundle (API-only archetype).
**Weight.** med (2).

### PERF-5 — No silent regression: speed work stays fixed
**Grounding.** The check-ratchet doctrine (gates-and-ledger) applied to latency: every class that got a structural re-check stopped recurring; the measured failure was "fixed" speed complaints recurring next morning with no number re-measured.
**Rule.** A route that was measured fast stays measured: a closed speed issue re-measures its
number at wave close (the check-ratchet applies to latency exactly as to defects); a speed
complaint closed without a re-measured number is open.
**Objective test.** Each previously-recorded route number re-measured this round; any regression
surfaced as a REGRESSION (outranks new work per the ISSUE-LEDGER rule); no speed-tagged ledger
row closed without a number.
**✗ WRONG.** "Fixed the slowness" with no number; the same complaint recurring next morning
with nothing having re-measured the route.
**✓ RIGHT.** "Route /board 6.1s → 4.1s (round 3) → 3.9s (round 4)" tracked in the ledger.
**Score (0–10).** 0 — speed issues closed without numbers. 3 — numbers at close but never
re-measured after. **5 — THRESHOLD:** every speed-tagged row closes with a number AND prior
numbers re-measured at wave close. 8 — + regressions auto-surface via the ratchet
(`guard.sh perf` history). 10 — + cross-round movement visible per route in one place.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A only on a first round with no prior numbers recorded.
**Weight.** high (3) — recurrence is the user-visible failure ("again ages to load").

# Review Method & Calibration

How the assessor judges — the stance, the biases to correct, the severity model. Meta-doc: the assessor's stance, biases to correct, and severity model.

---

### METH-1 — Falsifiable verdicts, not taste
**Rule.** "People would(n't) like X" is unresolvable; a valid finding names a specific element, its context, and a principle — and a strong review verdict reads like a good design principle: opinionated, tradeoff-bearing, resolving to a checkable rule, never a truism.
**Grounding.** Krug: all users are unique, use is idiosyncratic — the productive question is whether THIS element, worded this way, in this context, works for likely users; "there's really only one way to answer that kind of question: testing" (p.139); debates move "into the realm of what works or doesn't work" (p.139). Laws of UX Ch.11: good design principles "aren't truisms… direct, clear, and actionable" (p.135); the worked frame ties a principle ("clarity over abundance of choice") to a named law (Hick's) and a numeric rule ("≤3 items at a time") (pp.136–137).
**Objective test.** Every finding parses as: element + context + principle ID + mechanism + checkable fix. Any argument phrased as a global preference claim with no instance and no test = invalid and struck.
**✗ WRONG.** "I don't think users like carousels" vetoing a specific design; "make it more intuitive" as a recommendation.
**✓ RIGHT.** "This carousel shows no next-arrow in the mobile viewport (AFFORD-2) — test whether slides 2–3 are ever discovered; fix: visible arrows + peek."
**Crop.** LU-22.

### METH-2 — Discount your own delight; probe pretty screens hardest
**Rule.** The aesthetic-usability effect inflates evaluator leniency exactly where defects hide; separate "looks resolved" from "is resolved" by exercising the interaction, and gate verdicts on task outcomes, never on the reviewer's visceral reaction.
**Grounding.** Laws of UX: functionally-identical prototypes — the attractive one even completed faster; polish "can mask usability issues… problematic when it comes to usability tests, where identifying issues is critical" (pp.90–91); watch what users do over what they say (p.91).
**Objective test.** Review protocol records task exercise results independently of aesthetic impressions; the task result gates. Reviewer rule: the most polished surface receives at least as much interaction probing as the roughest.
**✗ WRONG.** A beautiful screen waved through on sight; verdict citing only visual praise.
**✓ RIGHT.** The beautiful screen's flows driven end-to-end; its two real defects found behind the polish.
**Crop.** LU-07, LU-17.

### METH-3 — Fresh-eyes proxy: the structured cold-viewer pass
**Rule.** Without live users, substitute the mechanical cold-viewer battery — trunk test at a blur (NAV-1), squint for focal order (HIER-1/11), self-evidence ("would a first-timer stop and think?"), name-match click-test (XCON-6) — never a general impression.
**Grounding.** Krug: the trunk test is a literal procedure — blur, time the six answers (pp.112–113); self-evidence is the tie-breaker law (p.29); insiders cannot judge the big picture — show it cold (p.124); before any verdict on an ambiguous element, run the structured pass, not opinion (p.139 application).
**Objective test.** Each screen's review artifact contains the battery's outputs (trunk-test timings, squint focal order, name-match diffs); a verdict without them is incomplete. Every hesitation the reviewer personally feels is recorded AS a finding, not smoothed over.
**✗ WRONG.** "This nav feels a bit confusing."
**✓ RIGHT.** "Trunk test: site ID + page name <2s; you-are-here MISSING — the active tab has no state styling (NAV-5)."
**Crop.** KR-04.

### METH-4 — Severity follows consequence; performance ≠ preference
**Rule.** Don't flag "not maximally optimal" — weigh the shortfall's consequence tier: reversible/cosmetic shortfalls are legitimate satisficing; anything touching money, decisions, state truth, or irreversibility is never "good enough". And never collapse the two axes: what performs and what is preferred must both be measured, separately.
**Grounding.** Universal Principles: "The best design decision is not always the optimal design decision" (p.210) — with the explicit boundary: caution "when the consequences of a suboptimal solution can have serious consequences" (p.210); people "are poor at discriminating between features they like, and features that actually enhance their performance" (p.180) — the keyboard-layout case wins on performance and loses on preference; never accept self-report as a performance proxy (p.180).
**Objective test.** Each finding carries a consequence tier: (a) reversible/cosmetic → satisficing allowed, severity low; (b) irreversible/high-stakes → no satisficing, severity floor high. Decisions citing preference data alone (or performance alone) where both exist = flagged incomplete.
**✗ WRONG.** Twenty nits on an admin page's sort default at the same severity as an ambiguous net-payable figure; "90% prefer it" green-lighting with no completion data.
**✓ RIGHT.** The sort default noted-and-passed; the money ambiguity S1; both axes measured and the tradeoff surfaced.
**Crop.** UP-23, UP-18.

### METH-5 — Diagnose the mechanism, not the symptom
**Rule.** Name the root cause in canon vocabulary: "clogged" = kitchen-sink visibility + disclosure failure + commons accretion; "flat numbers" = missing preattentive encoding; "feels off" = unnecessary variation / ambiguous spacing; "amateurish" = weight-distribution/figure-ground failure. Symptom → mechanism → principle → fix direction, every time.
**Grounding.** Universal Principles hands the vocabulary: kitchen-sink visibility (p.250), isolation-effect dilution (p.254); Designing Interfaces the mechanism for illegible data: linear-vs-constant search time (pp.436–437); Krug the process cause of clutter: commons accretion (p.129); About Face the named noise checklist (p.423) — six specific tells replacing "looks busy".
**Objective test.** Each finding's mechanism field is one of the canon's named mechanisms (or explicitly novel); "busy/cluttered/off" with no mechanism = incomplete finding.
**✗ WRONG.** "This screen is too busy."
**✓ RIGHT.** "Rest state exposes step-3 controls (orchestration, DENS-5) + 6 same-level badges (HIER-8 dilution): kitchen-sink + emphasis-inflation — cut to one badge, defer step-3."
**Crop.** UP-09.

### METH-6 — Test the distribution's edges
**Rule.** Review with 1st- and 99th-percentile content — very long strings, extreme values, many items, zero items, rare states — the median demo case validates almost nothing.
**Grounding.** Universal Principles: matching the average on two measures ≈ 7% of people, under 1% on eight; accommodate the 1st–99th percentile (p.166). Laws of UX: 3× translation expansion and max font scaling as standard probes (pp.61–62).
**Objective test.** The review's fixture list explicitly includes: longest plausible names/descriptions, min/max realistic amounts, 0 items (EMPTY-1), maximal item counts, rare states. A review that only saw the happy median = incomplete.
**✗ WRONG.** Every screenshot showing 4-digit amounts and short names.
**✓ RIGHT.** The pass includes a 7-figure claim, a hyphenated 30-char name, an empty queue, and a 200-item list.
**Crop.** UP-07.

### METH-7 — Trace defects to tradeoffs; recommend with costs
**Rule.** Serious failures usually come from a real constraint resolved against the user, not from ignorance; a complete finding names the constraint that likely produced it and weighs the user's cost against the business benefit in the fix.
**Grounding.** Krug: "many — if not most — serious usability problems are the result of a poor decision about a tradeoff" (p.183); the mobile-pagination case is diagnosed exactly this way — ad impressions traded against read-completion, under-weighting the user (pp.180–183).
**Objective test.** Defect write-ups on systemic issues include: the producing constraint (revenue, performance, CMS, deadline) + an explicit user-cost vs business-benefit statement; absent = incomplete.
**✗ WRONG.** "Pagination is bad."
**✓ RIGHT.** "8 page-loads per article trades impression count against completion friction (8× waits); the tradeoff under-weights completion — recommend single-scroll with inline units."
**Crop.** KR-09.

### METH-8 — The subtraction audit
**Rule.** For any suspect region, run the removal test element by element: delete until something breaks, restore only the last removal; whatever never got restored was noise.
**Grounding.** About Face: "Take things away until the design breaks, and then put that last thing back in" (p.424) — noise survives precisely because nobody tested load-bearing-ness. Krug's presumed-guilty framing (p.62) is the same audit as a default stance.
**Objective test.** Per element: removable with zero user-observable loss = defect; the region's write-up lists which elements failed.
**✗ WRONG.** Judging "looks busy" without identifying which elements carry nothing.
**✓ RIGHT.** "Removable with zero loss: the row rules (spacing already groups), the duplicate status text, the decorative divider — three cuts."
**Crop.** AF-13.

### METH-9 — Shots first, then drive
**Rule.** Read ALL static shots and form the full composition/craft/consistency verdict FIRST (perception forms from stills; most such defects are visible at rest), THEN drive the app to confirm and extend into what only interaction reveals: input models, disclosure behavior, collisions, pliancy, undo, latency states.
**Grounding.** Laws of UX: the visual verdict forms in ~50ms from a still and resists revision (p.84) — the static layer is real and assessable alone. About Face: orchestration/flow properties (transitions, feedback, modality) exist only in motion (Ch11). Designing Interfaces: interaction patterns (cancel, undo granularity, validation timing) are runtime facts (Ch8/10). The split assigns each defect class its observable layer.
**Objective test.** The review artifact has two dated phases: a static verdict complete before first interaction (composition, hierarchy, craft, consistency matrix), then an interaction pass appending runtime findings — never a single blended impression; static findings are not revised by charm discovered while driving (METH-2).
**✗ WRONG.** Driving the app first, then rationalizing the layout as "fine once you know it".
**✓ RIGHT.** The static verdict banked cold, then interaction findings appended with repro steps.
**Crop.** none (protocol).

### METH-10 — Both failure directions, always
**Rule.** Every axis has two poles and both are failures: crammed AND over-reduced (DENS-1 vs DENS-8); too loud AND too subtle (HIER-8 vs NAV-5); no ceremony AND nagging ceremony (ERR-5 vs ERR-4); over-decorated AND wabi-slobby (CRAFT-5 vs CRAFT-7); rigid conformity AND unanchored novelty (XCON-4). Check each axis in both directions before passing it.
**Grounding.** The two-pole structure is explicit in the sources: Universal Principles gives visibility BOTH failure modes (hidden state AND kitchen-sink, p.250) and names wabi-slobby (p.256); Laws of UX pairs Hick's-reduction with the abstraction ceiling (pp.39–50); About Face pairs confirmation-nagging with zero-safety (pp.648–652); Krug pairs under- and over-formatting (p.62).
**Objective test.** The review checklist runs each axis as a PAIR; a pass on one pole without the other's check = incomplete axis.
**✗ WRONG.** Certifying "not cluttered" while icon-only minimalism leaves actions undiscoverable.
**✓ RIGHT.** "Density: rest state lean (pass); discoverability: 3 unlabeled icon actions (DENS-8 fail)."
**Crop.** none (protocol).

# Spacing Systems

Whitespace as structure. Pillars: 1, 4.

---

### SPACE-1 — Start with too much whitespace, then remove
**Rule.** Give elements more room than feels necessary, then pull back; the habitual inverse (add margin until it stops looking bad) yields only the minimum room needed to not look broken. Deliberately dense views are a conscious exception, never a fallback.
**Grounding.**
- Refactoring UI: "White space should be removed, not added... The problem with [adding minimum breathing room] is that elements are only given the minimum amount of breathing room necessary to not look actively bad. To make something actually look great, you usually need more white space." (p.67) Mechanism: the add-until-ok habit optimizes for "not broken," never for great — the stopping condition itself is wrong.
- Refactoring UI: "what might seem like 'a little too much' when focused on an individual element ends up being closer to 'just enough' in the context of a complete UI." (p.69) Mechanism: per-element judgment systematically underestimates the spacing the whole composition needs.
- Sanctioned exception: a hockey "Game Summary" dashboard deliberately keeps stats and box-score rows tightly packed because info-density is the explicit goal there (p.69) — density by stated intent, not by drift.
**Objective test.** The book's own diagnostic: reduce a panel's padding 20–30% — no visible harm = it was never generously spaced. Inverse probe: DOUBLE the current padding — if the doubled version still looks acceptable rather than absurdly empty, the original was under-spaced.
**✗ WRONG.** A "50 customer reviews" card gives its rating bars, headline, and "Write a review" button only the minimum padding needed to avoid touching the card's edge — every element sits at the bare edge of "not broken."
**✓ RIGHT.** The identical card, same content, same colors — just substantially more internal padding around the rating list and more gap before the CTA section — reads as calmer and more premium with zero content change. (A stats dashboard stays tight by stated intent.)
**Crop.** RU-17 (p.66–69 — tight/loose reviews-card pair; the deliberately-dense dashboard exception).
**Score — grounded ladder (0→10).**
- **0** — ≥2 regions where content sits at bare "just not touching" distance (<8px) from its container edge — the add-until-not-broken stopping condition everywhere *(source: Refactoring UI p.67 — ✗ review card, "minimum amount of breathing room necessary to not look actively bad")*.
- **2** — ≤1 bare-edge region, but doubling the padding of all 3 sampled containers still looks acceptable — the whole surface is under-spaced by the book's own diagnostic *(source: Refactoring UI p.67 doubling diagnostic)*.
- **4** — doubling looks clearly over-empty on 1–2 of 3 sampled containers; the rest remain under-spaced *(source: Refactoring UI p.67–69)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** doubling looks clearly over-empty on all 3 sampled containers AND a 20–30% padding reduction on a representative panel produces visible harm (grouping/calm degrades) — the originals were genuinely generous *(source: Refactoring UI p.67–69 — reduction + doubling probes)*.
- **6** — + zero content elements at bare-edge (<8px) distance anywhere on the surface *(source: Refactoring UI p.67)*.
- **7** — + every tightly-packed region is an explicit info-density context (dashboard/box score/data table); no density by drift *(source: Refactoring UI p.69 — hockey Game Summary exception, density by stated intent)*.
- **8** — + gaps before section boundaries/CTA blocks measurably larger than intra-section gaps — per-element generosity carried up to composition level *(source: Refactoring UI p.69 "'a little too much'… closer to 'just enough' in the context of a complete UI"; p.96–99 group-spacing floors)* `[derived: Refactoring UI pp.69+96–99]`.
- **10** — composition reads calmer/premium at a squint with zero content change vs a denser variant; every density exception is by stated intent, never as an excuse *(source: Refactoring UI p.66–69 — ✓ "50 customer reviews" card)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — RU#8: whitespace discipline is load-bearing across nearly every other principle's legibility.

### SPACE-2 — Non-linear scales for spacing, sizing, type
**Rule.** Use a constrained scale where adjacent steps differ ≥~25%, tight at the small end and geometric at the large end; hand-rounded values, never fractional modular-scale artifacts.
**Grounding.**
- Refactoring UI: "If you want a system to be truly useful, it needs to take into consideration the relative difference between adjacent values." (p.71) Mechanism: perception is relative — "Jumping from 12px to 16px is an increase of 33%! But... increasing the width of a card from 500px to 520px is only a difference of 4%, which is eight times less significant." (p.71)
- Refactoring UI rule of thumb: "make sure no two values in your scale are ever closer than about 25%." (p.72)
- Refactoring UI on type: a modular ratio scale "end[s] up with lots of sizes that don't land right on the pixel, like 31.25px, 39.063px, 48.828px" and "you usually need more sizes" than a clean ratio provides (p.104) — hence hand-crafted rounded scales for interface work.
**Objective test.** For every adjacent scale pair compute (v₂−v₁)/v₁ ≥ ~25%. Type scale: every value a whole (non-fractional) pixel — any `.xxx`px value is an unrounded modular artifact. Screen audit: sample ≥10 padding/margin values — clustering on a small repeated set = designed; scattered ad hoc values = assembled (DI p.493 spacing-audit test).
**✗ WRONG.** A hotel card with paddings of 26/24/12/15/21/25/13/22px — adjacent values like 24px/26px differ by under 10%, an imperceptible, wasted distinction; a 4:5-ratio type scale from a 16px base emitting 12.8, 25, 31.25, 39.06px.
**✓ RIGHT.** A 16px-base spacing scale — 4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32, 48, 64, 96, 128… — every step ≥25% (4→8 = 100%, 512→640 = 25%); a hand-set 12/14/16/18/20/24/30/36/48/60/72px type scale, every value a round pixel, steps widening as sizes grow.
**Crop.** RU-03 (p.70–74 — arbitrary-pixel hotel card vs the 16px-multiple scale bar chart; p.99–107 — the 10-font-size listing card vs the hand-crafted 12–72px scale).
**Score — grounded ladder (0→10).**
- **0** — ≥3 adjacent scale pairs differ by under ~25% (imperceptible distinctions) AND ≥2 fractional-px (`.xxx`px) values in use *(source: Refactoring UI p.71–72 — "no two values... closer than about 25%"; p.104 — "31.25px, 39.063px, 48.828px" modular artifacts)*.
- **2** — 1–2 adjacent pairs under 25%, or values scattered ad hoc with no repeated set *(source: Refactoring UI p.72; Designing Interfaces p.493 spacing-audit test)*.
- **4** — all in-use pairs ≥~25%, but 1 fractional-px value remains or the sampled values cluster imperfectly *(source: Refactoring UI p.71–72)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** all adjacent in-use pairs ≥~25% AND zero fractional-px values AND ≥10 sampled padding/margin values cluster on a small repeated set (≤8 distinct) *(source: Refactoring UI p.72, p.104; Designing Interfaces p.493)*.
- **6** — + no improvised off-scale value observed anywhere (the scale has enough steps for real usage) *(source: Refactoring UI p.104 — "you usually need more sizes")*.
- **8** — + steps are non-linear: tight at the small end, absolute increments widening at the large end (e.g. 4→8 vs 96→128) *(source: Refactoring UI p.71 — the 33%-vs-4% relative-perception mechanism)*.
- **10** — full hand-rounded geometric scale matching the book's ✓ example — every step ≥25%, every value a round pixel, progression widens with size *(source: Refactoring UI p.70–74, p.99–107 — 16px-multiple spacing bar chart + 12–72px type scale)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — RU#9: a foundational system decision governing consistency across the entire product (DI#33's spacing-audit umbrella concurs, high).

### SPACE-3 — Make nearly-identical values exactly identical
**Rule.** If two spacings/sizes/colors are almost the same, make them the same; every difference must have an articulable reason or be removed.
**Grounding.**
- About Face: "Unnecessary variation is the enemy of a coherent, usable design. If the spacing between two sets of elements is nearly the same, make that spacing exactly the same. If two typefaces are nearly the same size, adjust them to be the same size. Every visual element and every difference in color, size, or other visual property should be there for a reason. If you can't articulate a good reason why it's there, get rid of it." (Ch17, p.423)
- Mechanism: near-identical-but-not-identical values read to the eye as unintentional sloppiness even when each instance looks acceptable in isolation — the mismatch itself signals "not designed," independent of the individual values.
**Objective test.** Measure every value serving one functional purpose on a screen (all section gaps, all body text sizes): count distinct values within 20% of each other that are not byte-for-byte identical — target 0 near-duplicates; differences are either exact or categorically distinct (16 vs 32, not 16 vs 15).
**✗ WRONG.** Card A has 16px internal padding, Card B (same component, different screen) has 15px, Card C has 18px — each hand-tuned in isolation, none of the differences serving any purpose.
**✓ RIGHT.** One padding token (16px) everywhere the card pattern appears; a card that genuinely needs more room (e.g. one containing a chart) takes a distinctly different token (32px), not an incidental nudge.
**Crop.** none (measurement discipline, not a rendered example).
**Score — grounded ladder (0→10).**
- **0** — ≥2 near-duplicate pairs (values within 20% of each other, not byte-identical) serving the same functional purpose AND ≥2 deviating instances of the same component pattern *(source: About Face Ch17, p.423 — "Unnecessary variation is the enemy of a coherent, usable design")*.
- **2** — exactly 1 near-duplicate pair, or exactly 1 deviating instance of an otherwise-reused pattern *(source: About Face p.423)*.
- **4** — 0 near-duplicate pairs, but some remaining differences are not yet categorically distinct (e.g. 16 vs 20, not clearly a different token) *(source: About Face p.423)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** 0 near-duplicate pairs measured AND the same component pattern uses a byte-identical value everywhere it appears *(source: About Face p.423 — "make that spacing exactly the same")*.
- **7** — + every intentional difference is categorically distinct (16 vs 32, a different token — never an incidental nudge like 16 vs 15/18) *(source: About Face p.423)*.
- **10** — + every surviving distinct value maps to an identifiable functional reason (e.g. a chart-bearing card takes a distinctly different token than a plain card), matching the book's ✓ example *(source: About Face p.423 — "If you can't articulate a good reason why it's there, get rid of it")*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** med (2) — AF#2: a hygiene/craft signal that compounds visual-noise perception but rarely blocks task completion alone.

### SPACE-4 — Space within a group < space between groups
**Rule.** With no border/background separating groups, equal spacing above and below an element makes its membership ambiguous; intra-group space must be strictly smaller than inter-group space — labels/inputs, list items, headings, icon rows alike.
**Grounding.**
- Refactoring UI: "Whenever you're relying on spacing to connect a group of elements, always make sure there's more space around the group than there is within it — interfaces that are hard to understand always look worse." (p.99) Its fixes use ~2:1 ratios: 20px between / 10px within a label-field pair; 36px between bullets / 24px within; 6px icon-to-count / 36px to the next group (pp.96–99).
- Designing Interfaces: "Grouped items look related. Conversely, isolation implies a distinction" (p.218) — the same floor from Gestalt: intra-group gap strictly smaller, a ≥2× ratio defensible (label-to-field 4px, group-to-group ≥24px).
- Universal Principles: proximity "is one of the most powerful means of indicating relatedness in a design, and will generally overwhelm competing visual cues (e.g., similarity)." (p.196) Mechanism: get spacing wrong and the misparse wins regardless of styling — a lack of proximity produces "the perception of multiple, disparate chunks."
**Objective test.** Measure gap-above vs gap-within any spacing-grouped pair: within < between strictly, target ~2:1; equal gaps (20px/20px) fail. Label-to-referent distance < label-to-any-unrelated-element distance.
**✗ WRONG.** A billing form gives 20px above AND below "Street address" — the label floats equidistant between two fields, ambiguous which it names; list bullets spaced exactly at the wrapped-line height, so item boundaries vanish.
**✓ RIGHT.** 20px above the label, 10px to its own input; 24px within a bullet item, 36px between items; 6px icon-to-count, 36px to the next icon group.
**Crop.** RU-05 (p.96–99 — form/list/icon-row triad), UP-03 (p.197 — the Big Bend Trail sign misread vs corrected grouping).
**Score — grounded ladder (0→10).**
- **0** — ≥2 spacing-grouped pairs (label/field, list items, heading/paragraph, icon/count) with equal or inverted gap-within vs gap-between *(source: Refactoring UI p.99 — "always make sure there's more space around the group than there is within it"; Designing Interfaces p.218; Universal Principles p.196)*.
- **2** — exactly 1 equal/inverted pair, or any measured group's between:within ratio under 1.5:1 (visually ambiguous) *(source: Refactoring UI p.96–99)*.
- **4** — within < between strictly on every group, but the ratio is under 2:1 on at least one *(source: Refactoring UI p.96–99 — its own fixes run ~2:1)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** within < between strictly on every measured group AND the ratio is ≥2:1 everywhere *(source: Refactoring UI p.96–99 — 20px/10px label-field, 36px/24px bullets, 36px/6px icon groups)*.
- **7** — + every label is measurably closer to its own referent than to any unrelated element *(source: Universal Principles p.196 — "ensure that labels... are near the elements that they describe")*.
- **10** — + inter-item gap exceeds the intra-item wrapped-line gap in every list, so boundaries never vanish, matching the book's ✓ triad *(source: Universal Principles p.197 — Big Bend Trail sign misread vs corrected grouping; Refactoring UI p.96–99)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — majority: DI#7 high (foundational for any control-dense screen) + UP-Proximity high, vs RU#13 med (noted: RU treats it as a narrow micro-pattern).

### SPACE-5 — Whitespace is the grouping mechanism, not decoration
**Rule.** Proximity/whitespace signals structure before any label is read; use space first, and where repositioning is impossible, a shared container corrects the grouping (see GEST-3).
**Grounding.**
- Designing Interfaces: "When you put things close together, viewers associate them with one another. This is the basis for a strong grouping of content and controls on a user interface (UI). Grouped items look related. Conversely, isolation implies a distinction" (p.218). Mechanism: grouping is perceived pre-attentively from position alone — structure is read before a single label is.
- Universal Principles guideline, verbatim: "Ensure that labels and supporting information are near the elements that they describe, opting for direct labeling on graphs over legends or keys." (p.196) Mechanism: grouping via proximity "reduces the complexity of designs and reinforces the relatedness of the elements."
- Universal Principles (Uniform Connectedness): "a particular set of controls can be grouped by connecting them in a common region using paint or overlays" (p.246) — the sanctioned fallback when elements cannot be repositioned.
**Objective test.** For each control: its nearest neighbor by measured distance must be its own label/group. Any control equidistant-or-closer to an unrelated element = misgrouping. Direct labels on data displays; a legend forcing back-and-forth lookup fails where direct labeling fits.
**✗ WRONG.** A form field whose label sits 20px above it while the next question's label sits only 16px below — the field visually reads as belonging to the wrong label.
**✓ RIGHT.** Label-to-field 4–8px; group-to-group ≥24px; the grouping legible at a squint, before any text is read.
**Crop.** DI-07 (Fig. 4-12, p.218 — grouped controls vs isolated groups outlined in red).
**Score — grounded ladder (0→10).**
- **0** — ≥2 controls whose nearest neighbor by measured distance is NOT their own label/group *(source: Designing Interfaces p.218 — "Grouped items look related. Conversely, isolation implies a distinction")*.
- **2** — exactly 1 misgrouped control, or group boundaries merge/misparse when the surface is blurred *(source: Designing Interfaces p.218)*.
- **4** — every control's nearest neighbor is its own group, but squint legibility still fails (boundaries not perceptible from position alone) *(source: Designing Interfaces Fig.4-12, p.218)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** every control's nearest neighbor is its own label/group AND group boundaries are perceptible from position alone under blur, before any text is read *(source: Designing Interfaces p.218; Universal Principles p.196 — grouping "reduces complexity... reinforces relatedness")*.
- **7** — + data displays use direct labels wherever they fit, with no forced legend/key lookup *(source: Universal Principles p.196 — "opting for direct labeling on graphs over legends or keys")*.
- **10** — + every set that cannot be repositioned is corrected via a shared container/background, so no misgrouped set is left with neither proximity nor a common region *(source: Universal Principles p.246 — Uniform Connectedness, "grouped by connecting them in a common region using paint or overlays")*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — DI#7 high + UP-Proximity high (proximity "will generally overwhelm competing visual cues"); no dissent.

### SPACE-6 — Interactive targets: size and separation floors
**Rule.** Targets meet and exceed the ~44px class floor on BOTH axes (the hit area, not the glyph); adjacent interactive elements get ≥8px separation, and opposite-intent pairs (accept/deny, save/delete) get ≥16px or a distinct grouping.
**Grounding.**
- Laws of UX (Fitts): "The time to acquire a target is a function of the distance to and size of the target." (p.15) And: "small touch targets add to the perception that an interface is less usable, even if the user is able to avoid errors when attempting to select a target" (p.18) — size damages FELT usability even at zero errors. Published minimums (Table 2-1, p.18: Apple 44×44pt, Material 48×48dp, WCAG 44px, NN/g 1×1cm) are floors: "Designers should aim to exceed these target touch sizes whenever possible" (p.18).
- Laws of UX on separation: "the average adult human's fingertips are 16–20 mm in diameter" (p.19), so overlap onto neighbors is inevitable; Google's guidance quoted verbatim: "touch targets should be separated by 8dp... of space or more" (p.19). The book's own failure case is LinkedIn's accept/deny sitting "so close together that users must make a significant effort to focus on selecting the action they wish to perform without accidentally selecting the other" (p.21); Apple CarPlay's "ample space between interactive elements" is the fix (p.22).
- About Face: "Cluttered interfaces attempt to provide an excess of functionality in a constrained space, resulting in controls that visually interfere with each other." (Ch17, p.423) Mechanism: crowding is a functional defect — it raises error rate and cognitive load, not merely "looks bad."
**Objective test.** Scripted: `getBoundingClientRect()` width AND height ≥44 for every interactive node (`<button>`/`<a>`/`role="button"`/checkbox); either axis failing = fail. Edge-gap (not center distance) between adjacent interactive bounding boxes ≥8px; destructive-vs-benign adjacent pairs ≥16px OR different row/zone + different visual treatment. Per screen, count control pairs whose hit areas nearly touch or whose boundaries lack a consistent gutter — target 0.
**✗ WRONG.** A 20×20px delete icon that IS the tap target inside a 44px row; ✕/✓ circles 4px apart, same size and fill, on a mobile request card.
**✓ RIGHT.** The 20px glyph inside a 44×44 transparent hit area; accept as a filled primary, deny as a ghost button at the opposite side, 8dp+ of edge gap — spacing AND contrast both signal "don't chain-tap."
**Crop.** LU-02 (Fig. 2-2/Table 2-1, pp.18–20 — touch-accuracy heat map + minimums table), LU-03 (Fig. 2-5 vs 2-6, p.22 — LinkedIn cramped vs CarPlay spaced).
**Score — grounded ladder (0→10).**
- **0** — any primary/frequent action's hit area fails the ≥44px floor on either axis (`getBoundingClientRect()`), or ≥3 interactive nodes fail *(source: Laws of UX p.18 — Table 2-1, Apple 44×44pt/Material 48×48dp/WCAG 44px floors)*.
- **2** — 1–2 non-primary, edge-case controls fail the 44px floor, or ≥2 adjacent interactive pairs have closest-edge gap under 8px *(source: Laws of UX p.18–19)*.
- **4** — all interactive nodes pass the 44px floor on both axes, but a small glyph (<44px) IS the tap target somewhere *(source: Laws of UX p.18)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** all interactive nodes measure ≥44px on both axes AND every adjacent-pair edge gap is ≥8px *(source: Laws of UX p.18 floor table; p.19 — Google's "touch targets should be separated by 8dp... or more")*.
- **7** — + every destructive/irreversible-vs-benign adjacent pair has ≥16px edge gap OR sits in a different row/zone with distinct visual treatment *(source: Laws of UX p.21–22 — LinkedIn accept/deny cramped-failure vs Apple CarPlay "ample space" fix)*.
- **8** — + every small glyph is wrapped in an invisible padded hit area rather than being the tap target itself *(source: Laws of UX p.18–19 — fingertip/target-size mechanism)*.
- **10** — + high-frequency or error-costly actions (primary CTA, submit, delete) measure visibly above the floor, ≥48px on both axes *(source: Laws of UX p.18 — "Designers should aim to exceed these target touch sizes whenever possible")*.
Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — LU#2 high (undersized targets damage felt usability even at zero errors) + LU#3 high (mis-taps on opposite-intent actions are high-cost) + AF#6 high (crowding ties directly to error rate); unanimous.

# Tables & Lists

Pillars: 2, 3.

---

### TABLE-1 — Rows scannable, differentiated, never horizontally scrolled
**Rule.** Long text-only lists need per-row visual differentiators (icons/thumbnails/previews); a text list must never require horizontal scrolling to read an item (spreadsheet-class tables with frozen headers are the sanctioned exception).
**Grounding.**
- About Face: "A list control filled with line after line of text unrelieved by visual symbols is a dry desert indeed." (p.602) — icons in listviews are what make rows differentiable at scanning speed.
- About Face design principle, verbatim: "Distinguish important text items in lists with graphic icons." (p.603)
- About Face on horizontal scroll: "When a text list is scrolled horizontally, it hides from view one or more of the first letters of every single [item]" (p.606) — the first letters are exactly what scanning keys on, so scrolling destroys legibility and continuity; "Text should only be scrolled horizontally in large tables such as spreadsheets, where locked row and column headers can provide context for each column." (p.606)
- Mechanism: users scan lists by shape and leading characters, not by reading; a differentiator per row and intact item-starts are what keep the scan possible.
**Objective test.** (a) Any list of ≥10 similar text items: ≥1 visual differentiator (icon, thumbnail, color chip, avatar) per row; a pure-text list with zero differentiators fails. (b) Any text list/column that is not a spreadsheet-class table with frozen row/column headers: reading a single item's full text must never require horizontal scroll — wrap, or truncate with ellipsis + full value on hover, instead; any h-scroll to read = fail.
**✗ WRONG.** A file manager shows 200 files as bare filename text in one narrow column — no type icons, long names cut off behind a horizontal scrollbar, so identifying a file means scrolling every row.
**✓ RIGHT.** Each row carries a small file-type icon before the name; the name column wraps or ellipsizes with the full name on hover — every row identifiable without a single horizontal scroll.
**Crop.** AF-16.
**Score (0–10).**
> - **0** — a qualifying list (≥10 similar text items) is pure undifferentiated text AND requires horizontal scroll to read a single item fully *(source: About Face #27 "0"; p.606 first-letters-hidden mechanism)*.
> - **2** — either the missing-differentiator problem or the horizontal-scroll problem is present, not both *(About Face #27 "3")*.
> - **4** — differentiators exist per row, no h-scroll needed, but differentiators are generic/identical on every row (decoration, not information) *(About Face p.603 "distinguish... with graphic icons," partially met)*.
> - **5 — THRESHOLD:** a visual differentiator (icon/thumbnail/avatar/chip) exists per row on every qualifying list, AND no text-list item requires horizontal scroll to read fully (spreadsheet-class frozen-header tables exempt) *(About Face #27 "5-6"; p.602, p.606)*.
> - **6** — + overflow values are recoverable in place (wrap, or ellipsis with hover/tap full value) rather than hard-clipped *(About Face p.606 mechanism, [derived] extension)*.
> - **8** — + differentiators convey real per-row information (file-type-specific icons, status-specific chips), not generic bullets *(About Face #27 "7-8")*.
> - **10** — full craft: informative differentiator per row + wrap/ellipsis-with-hover on every column + zero horizontal scroll anywhere *(About Face #27 "9-10")*.
> Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold.
**Weight.** med (2) — About Face: med.

### TABLE-2 — Default order tells the story (or hides it)
**Rule.** Choose the default sort for meaning (severity/magnitude/recency); offer resort for the data's other stories.
**Grounding.**
- Designing Interfaces, the alphabetical failure: sorted alphabetically, the Texas cancer-mortality data "doesn't lead you to ask interesting questions. It's not clear why Abilene, Alice, Amarillo, and Austin all seem to have similar numbers, for instance; it might just be chance" (p.441).
- The numeric fix: "the graph becomes much more interesting. Galveston is ranked first — why is that, when its neighbor, Houston, is further down the scale?... Sometimes, just rearranging an information graphic can reveal unexpected relationships" (pp.441–442).
- Mechanism, verbatim: "Sorting and rearranging puts different data points next to each other, thus letting users make different kinds of comparisons" (p.442) — order is a legibility decision, and a bad default actively buries the finding.
- Full system treatment → DATA-5.
**Objective test.** For any table/chart of ≥10 rows presenting a quantitative metric: (a) a sort control exists for at least the numeric column of primary interest — its absence = fail; (b) the default order is meaningful (severity/magnitude/recency); an arbitrary default (alphabetical/insertion order where a meaningful order exists) = fail.
**✗ WRONG.** A findings table lists issues in insertion order while a severity column sits unsortable — the one critical finding lands at row 14, indistinguishable in position from trivia.
**✓ RIGHT.** Default severity-descending, the outlier at row 1; one click on any column header re-sorts to expose the data's other stories.
**Crop.** DI-04.
**Score (0–10).**
> - **0** — a ≥10-row quantitative table has a fixed, non-meaningful default order (alphabetical/insertion) AND no sort control at all *(source: Designing Interfaces #15 "0"; p.441 alphabetical-failure example)*.
> - **2** — a sort control exists but only for a non-primary column, or only via a hidden/overflow menu *(Designing Interfaces #15 "3")*.
> - **4** — a sort control exists on the primary numeric column but the default order is still arbitrary and buries the outlier *(Designing Interfaces p.441-442, partial)*.
> - **5 — THRESHOLD:** a sort control exists for at least the numeric column of primary interest *(Designing Interfaces #15 "5-6")*.
> - **6** — + the default order is meaningful (severity/magnitude/recency-keyed), even if the outlier isn't yet in the top rows *(Designing Interfaces p.442 "sorting... reveal unexpected relationships")*.
> - **7** — + the currently sorted column is visibly indicated (arrow/highlight), direction not yet shown *([derived] — feedback extension of the book's sort mechanism)*.
> - **8** — multiple columns are user-sortable with clear visual feedback on both sorted column AND direction *(Designing Interfaces #15 "7-8")*.
> - **9** — + the default order's most consequential row sits in the top 3, matching the Galveston-outlier standard *(Designing Interfaces p.441-442 Fig. 9-8 example)*.
> - **10** — sorting surfaces genuine outliers/relationships immediately and multiple sort dimensions are combinable *(Designing Interfaces #15 "9-10")*.
> Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold.
**Weight.** med (2) — Designing Interfaces: med (high for exploratory data tables, low for short fixed-order lists).

### TABLE-3 — Position effects: start and end are prime slots
**Rule.** First and last items get disproportionate recall and pick-rate; critical actions/rows never sit buried mid-sequence without compensating distinctiveness.
**Grounding.**
- Universal Principles, verbatim: "Serial position effects occur when people try to recall items from a list; items at the beginning and end are better recalled than the items in the middle." (p.220)
- The measured real-world stake: "being first on the ballot is estimated to be worth between 1 percent and 4 percent of the vote" (p.221) — tied explicitly to the 2000 Florida "butterfly ballot": position alone moves choices, before any content is read.
- Compensation mechanism: a mid-list item can only carry importance via isolation-effect distinctiveness — "If everything is highlighted, then nothing is highlighted." (p.254)
**Objective test.** For any list/menu/form of ≥7 items: identify the single most consequential item (default choice, primary CTA, critical/destructive action); it sits at position 1 or the last position, not positions 3 through (n−2). If it must be mid-list, verify a distinct visual treatment (color block, weight, separation) carries it — mid-list AND styled like siblings = fail.
**✗ WRONG.** A 12-item settings menu buries "Permanently delete all data" at position 7, visually identical in weight to the 11 routine options around it.
**✓ RIGHT.** The destructive option moves to the end of the list (recency-favored, matching the danger-convention slot) — or stays mid-list only inside a visually distinct danger-red block.
**Crop.** UP-06.
**Score (0–10).**
> - **0** — in a list/menu/form of ≥7 items, the single most consequential item (default choice, primary CTA, critical/destructive action) sits in the dead-middle positions with no distinctiveness treatment *(source: Universal Principles "Serial Position Effects" "0"; p.220)*.
> - **2** — the item sits near but not at an end (position 2 or n−1), still with no compensating treatment *(Universal Principles "Serial Position Effects" "3")*.
> - **4** — the item sits at position 1 or the final position, but emphasis ratio across the list exceeds ~35% (nothing else stands out, diluting the win) *(Universal Principles "Von Restorff" "0-3", cross-checked)*.
> - **5 — THRESHOLD:** the item sits at position 1 or the final position, OR (if mid-list) carries a von-Restorff-style distinctive treatment compensating for position *(Universal Principles "Serial Position Effects" "5-6"; p.221 ballot-position stake)*.
> - **6** — + emphasized-element ratio across the qualifying list is at or below ~20%, so the compensating treatment actually reads as distinct *(Universal Principles "Von Restorff" "5-6"; p.254 "if everything is highlighted, nothing is")*.
> - **8** — threshold met, placement additionally matches convention (danger options at the end, primary defaults first) for the item's actual semantics *(Universal Principles "Serial Position Effects" "7-8")*.
> - **10** — position AND (where relevant) isolation treatment both correctly applied, no consequential item anywhere left unmarked mid-list, emphasis ratio never dilutes the signal *(Universal Principles "Serial Position Effects" "9-10" + "Von Restorff" "9-10")*.
> Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold.
**Weight.** med (2) — Universal Principles: med.

### TABLE-4 — Cells can group; columns aren't sacred
**Rule.** Related data (name+role, amount+type) can share one visually-hierarchical cell, cutting column count and adding scannability; one-datum-per-column is habit, not law — reserve separate columns for what must sort independently.
**Grounding.**
- Refactoring UI, verbatim: "Tables don't have to work this way, though — if a column doesn't need to be sortable, there's no reason you can't combine it with a related column and introduce some interesting hierarchy." (p.244)
- The book's own demonstration: a 6-flat-column policy-holder table (Name/Role/Policy/Policy Type/Location/Status) drops to 4 richer columns by merging Name+Role and Policy-amount+Policy-type into two-line hierarchical cells (p.244).
- Broader mechanism: "It's just a floating box on the screen, you can do anything you want with it" (pp.241–243) — inherited component conventions are conditioning, not constraints; sortability is the only real reason a datum needs its own column.
**Objective test.** Count columns holding naturally-paired fields (name+role, amount+type, city+state): any pair that is not independently sorted or filtered is a merge candidate into a two-line hierarchical cell (primary field prominent, secondary field smaller/lighter). A table where every such non-sortable pair still occupies separate flat equal-weight columns = fail.
**✗ WRONG.** Name / Role / Amount / Type / Location / Status as six flat equal columns — none of Role, Type independently sortable, every cell the same visual weight, nothing scannable.
**✓ RIGHT.** "Name over role" and "amount over type" merged into two-line cells — four columns, primary values prominent, secondary values smaller and lighter: hierarchy built into the table itself.
**Crop.** RU-11.
**Score (0–10).**
> - **0** — every table column holds exactly one atomic field despite clearly-related pairs (name+role, amount+type, city+state), none independently sorted or filtered *(source: Refactoring UI #34 "0"; p.244 6-column ✗)*.
> - **2** — a partial attempt exists (1 of several related-column pairs merged) *(Refactoring UI #34 "3")*.
> - **4** — ≥1 pair merged into a shared cell, but fields sit on two lines of equal size/weight (stacked, not hierarchical) *(Refactoring UI #34 "5-6", partial — hierarchy not yet built)*.
> - **5 — THRESHOLD:** no non-sortable, naturally-paired field sits in a separate flat equal-weight column (all such pairs merged, or none exist) *(Refactoring UI p.244 "if a column doesn't need to be sortable... combine it")*.
> - **6** — + merged cells render the primary field prominent and the secondary field smaller AND lighter (≥2 visual channels differ) *(Refactoring UI #34 "5-6"; p.244 own demonstration: 6 columns → 4)*.
> - **8** — richer, purpose-fit merged-hierarchy treatment applied consistently across every qualifying pair in the table *(Refactoring UI #34 "7-8")*.
> - **9** — + every field that is independently sorted or filtered still keeps its own column (no sort/filter target buried inside a merge) *([derived] — sortability carve-out from p.244's own "if a column doesn't need to be sortable" clause)*.
> - **10** — matches the book's own worked example exactly: naturally-paired fields merged into two-line hierarchical cells, sortable fields left standalone, column count reduced with zero information loss *(Refactoring UI #34 "9-10"; p.244)*.
> Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold.
**Weight.** low (1) — Refactoring UI: low (delight/polish opportunity, rarely the primary usability defect).

### TABLE-5 — Numeric columns: right-aligned, uniform precision/units
**Rule.** Right-align numbers so decimals stack for at-a-glance comparison; one precision and one unit notation per column.
**Grounding.**
- Refactoring UI, verbatim: "If you're designing a table that includes numbers, right-align them. When the decimal in a list of numbers is always in the same place, they're a lot easier to compare at a glance." (p.130)
- Mechanism: magnitude comparison is done visually by digit position — decimals stacked in one vertical line let the eye read magnitude from length alone; left-aligned or mixed-precision figures scatter the decimal point so every comparison becomes a re-read.
- Uniform precision/units is the same mechanism extended: a column mixing 2dp and 0dp (or "€" and "EUR") breaks the digit-position alignment the right-align just bought. System framing → DATA-8.
**Objective test.** (a) `text-align: right` (or equivalent) on every currency/quantity/percentage column — a left-aligned numeric column = fail. (b) One decimal precision per column: mixed precisions (2dp and 0dp in the same column) = fail. (c) One unit notation per column; verify decimal points fall at a single horizontal position down the column.
**✗ WRONG.** A price column left-aligned, mixing "1,200" with "89.50" and "€14" — decimal points at three different horizontal positions, magnitudes unreadable at a glance.
**✓ RIGHT.** Prices right-aligned at uniform 2dp with one currency notation — every decimal in one vertical line, magnitude readable from row length alone.
**Crop.** RU-21.
**Score (0–10).**
> - **0** — a numeric table column is left-aligned (decimals don't line up) *(source: Refactoring UI #17 "0"; p.130 "right-align them")*.
> - **2** — column is right-aligned but mixes ≥2 decimal precisions (e.g. 2dp with 0dp) in the same column *(Refactoring UI p.130 mechanism, [derived] extension — mixed precision breaks the same digit-position alignment)*.
> - **4** — right-aligned, single precision, but mixes unit notations ("€" and "EUR") within the column *([derived] — same alignment mechanism, unit axis)*.
> - **5 — THRESHOLD:** every currency/quantity/percentage column is right-aligned, with one decimal precision and one unit notation throughout *(Refactoring UI #17 "5-6"; p.130)*.
> - **7** — threshold met consistently across all relevant screens/tables in the surface, not just one instance *(Refactoring UI #17 "7-8")*.
> - **8** — + decimal points (or implied decimal position for integers) verified to fall at a single horizontal position down the column (tabular figures) *(Refactoring UI p.130 "decimal... always in the same place")*.
> - **10** — matches the ✓ example exactly: fully right-aligned table, uniform precision/notation, decimals stacked in one vertical line, magnitude readable from row length alone *(Refactoring UI #17 "9-10"; p.130)*.
> Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold.
**Weight.** med (2) — Refactoring UI: medium.

### TABLE-6 — List chrome only when there's something to act on
**Rule.** Filter bars, sort controls, and search boxes over an empty (or trivially small) list are dead chrome; hide content-dependent controls until content exists.
**Grounding.**
- Refactoring UI, verbatim: "If you're working on something that has a bunch of supporting UI like tabs or filters, consider hiding that stuff entirely. There's no point in presenting a bunch of actions that don't do anything until the user has created some content." (p.236)
- The book's own demonstration: the discounts panel hides its All/Active/Scheduled/Expired filter tabs when no discount exists, leaving headline + CTA (p.236).
- Mechanism: "Empty states are a user's first interaction with a new product or feature" (p.236) — dead controls in that first frame add choice-noise, imply complexity, and compete with the one action that matters (creating the first item).
**Objective test.** Render every list view with zero data: any visible filter bar, sort control, tab row, or search box above the empty body = fail. The empty render shows only a headline, encouraging copy, and the create/primary CTA. (Same check at trivially-small counts: a filter set with fewer items than filter options is dead chrome.)
**✗ WRONG.** A full All/Active/Scheduled/Expired tab bar plus a search box rendered above "No discount codes yet" — six controls, none of which can do anything.
**✓ RIGHT.** Chrome hidden at zero data; a headline, one line of encouraging copy, and a single "Create discount" CTA — the tabs and search appear with the first record.
**Crop.** RU-10.
**Score (0–10).**
> - **0** — full content-dependent chrome (filter tabs, sort, search) renders over every zero-data view, with no icon/copy/CTA — a bare status string at best *(source: Refactoring UI p.236 "no point in presenting a bunch of actions that don't do anything")*.
> - **2** — chrome is hidden in ≥1 empty view but still rendered in ≥1 other empty view (inconsistent) *([derived] — partial application of the book's own pattern)*.
> - **4** — chrome hidden at zero data throughout, but the empty render shows only one or two of {headline, encouraging copy, CTA} *(Refactoring UI p.236, partial)*.
> - **5 — THRESHOLD:** no filter bar, sort control, tab row, or search box is visible above any empty list body *(Refactoring UI p.236 discounts-panel demonstration)*.
> - **6** — + the empty render shows all three of: a headline, encouraging copy, and a single create/primary CTA *(Refactoring UI p.236 "Empty states are a user's first interaction")*.
> - **8** — full pass — illustration, copy, prominent CTA, AND dead chrome hidden until content exists, across every list view on the surface *(Refactoring UI #32 "7-8")*.
> - **9** — + no filter/tab set has more options than the items it filters at trivially-small counts *(Refactoring UI p.236 mechanism, [derived] extension to the small-count case)*.
> - **10** — matches the ✓ examples exactly: Contacts-style illustration + encouraging copy + prominent CTA, filter tabs/search fully hidden until the first record exists *(Refactoring UI #32 "9-10"; p.236)*.
> Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold.
**Weight.** med (2) — Refactoring UI: medium.

### TABLE-7 — Selection is a first-class state [derived]
**Rule.** In master-detail patterns the selected row/item is unmistakably marked (≥2 simultaneous cues, never one subtle shade) and its selection visibly drives the detail region — the list item and its detail read as one connected unit.
**Grounding.** Derived — three books each supply one leg:
