- Krug (cue strength): "The most common failing of 'You are here' indicators is that they're too subtle... One way to ensure that they stand out is to apply more than one visual distinction—for instance, a different color and bold text." (p.109) And: "if you're a designer and you think a visual cue is sticking out like a sore thumb, it probably means you need to make it twice as prominent." (p.109)
- Universal Principles (binding to the detail region): "Uniform connectedness will generally overpower the other Gestalt principles... the elements that are uniformly connected will appear more related than either the proximal or similar elements." (p.246) — a shared region/accent binds row and pane harder than adjacency can.
- About Face (state as a control's duty): "The problem with these controls is that they fail to fulfill the second duty of every control—to inform users of their current state." (p.596) — a selectable row is a control; its rendering must announce that it IS the selection.
- Convergence: a selected master row is simultaneously a "you are here" marker (needs doubled cues), a state-bearing control (must show its state at rest), and one half of a connected unit with the detail it drives (needs uniform connectedness) — the master-detail application is the synthesis of all three.
**Objective test.** (a) The selected item carries ≥2 independent visual cues vs siblings (of: fill, border/edge, weight, icon, size) — a single-channel difference such as a slightly darker shade = fail. (b) A visible connection (shared accent color, aligned/continuous edge, pointer) ties the selected row to the detail pane. (c) Changing selection visibly repopulates the detail region within FEED-1's response budget. (d) A fresh screenshot at rest suffices to state which item is selected.
**✗ WRONG.** The active claim row rendered 5% darker grey — same weight, no edge, nothing tying it to the right-hand panel; a screenshot cannot say which claim the detail pane shows.
**✓ RIGHT.** Filled row + accent left edge + bold title (three cues), the same accent color heading the detail pane it drives — row and pane read cold as one unit.
**Crop.** KR-05.
**Score (0–10).** [derived — rungs synthesized from Krug #15, Universal Principles "Uniform Connectedness", About Face #25]
> - **0** — no distinguishable selected state exists at all (active and inactive rows render identically), AND nothing connects row to detail pane *(source: Krug #15 "0"; About Face #25 "0")*.
> - **2** — exactly 1 weak channel differs (a slight shade difference only) — the subtle-failure case named explicitly — and the row-detail tie rests on adjacency/layout alone *(Krug #15 "3"; Universal Principles "Uniform Connectedness" "3")*.
> - **4** — exactly 1 clear channel differs (e.g. a distinct fill only), state is technically readable at rest, but no shared visual device ties row to detail *(Krug #15 "5-6" partial; About Face #25 "5-6")*.
> - **5 — THRESHOLD:** the selected item carries ≥2 independent visual cues vs siblings (of: fill, border/edge, weight, icon, size), AND a visible device (shared accent color, aligned/continuous edge, pointer) ties the selected row to the detail pane *(Krug #15 "7-8" for cue count; Universal Principles "Uniform Connectedness" "5-6" for the tie; About Face p.596 "duty... to inform users of their current state")*.
> - **7** — + changing selection visibly repopulates the detail region within FEED-1's response budget *([derived] — About Face's control-state duty extended to the live update)*.
> - **8** — threshold met and the grouping/connection region is visually clean (no double-boundaries, no crowding), legible at a glance *(Universal Principles "Uniform Connectedness" "7-8")*.
> - **9** — ≥3 simultaneous channels distinguish the active/selected item (per Krug's own "unmissable" standard) *(Krug #15 "9-10")*.
> - **10** — a fresh static screenshot at rest suffices to state which item is selected, cues + connection + live-update all matching the ✓ case (filled row + accent edge + bold title, same accent heading the detail pane) *(Krug #15 "9-10"; Universal Principles "Uniform Connectedness" "9-10"; About Face #25 "9-10")*.
> Score = highest rung whose condition + all below hold.
**Weight.** med (2) — majority of contributing books: Krug (#15): med; Universal Principles (Uniform Connectedness): med.

# Typography Systems

Pillars: 1, 4.

---

### TYPE-1 — Constrained type system: few faces, a real scale
**Rule.** 1–2 typefaces at a small set of hand-tuned, whole-pixel sizes with meaningful steps; never a per-instance size zoo.
**Grounding.**
- About Face (Ch17, p.423): "Typography should not vary widely in an interface: Typically one or two typefaces, specified to just a few sizes, is sufficient for most applications." Mechanism: visual efficiency means the eye finds what matters fast; many typefaces fragment attention across low-value elements.
- About Face (Ch17, p.423): "If two typefaces are nearly the same size, adjust them to be the same size. Every visual element and every difference in color, size, or other visual property should be there for a reason." Mechanism: near-identical-but-not-identical values read as unintentional sloppiness — the mismatch itself signals "not designed."
- Refactoring UI (p.71–72): "If you want a system to be truly useful, it needs to take into consideration the relative difference between adjacent values" — "make sure no two values in your scale are ever closer than about 25%." Mechanism: at the small end a couple of pixels is a 33% jump; at the large end 20px is only 4% — linear scales waste decision time and breed inconsistency.
- Refactoring UI (p.104): a modular (ratio-based) type scale "end[s] up with lots of sizes that don't land right on the pixel, like 31.25px, 39.063px, 48.828px" and "you usually need more sizes" than a clean ratio provides. Mechanism: hand-crafted rounded scales beat mathematically "pure" ones for interface work.
**Objective test.** Count active typefaces per screen: ≤2. Count distinct type sizes: ≤~5–6 on a dense screen. Every size a whole (non-fractional) pixel on the defined scale — any `.xxx`px value is an unrounded modular-scale artifact. For the scale itself, compute `(value[n+1] − value[n]) / value[n]` for every adjacent pair: each step ≥ ~25%. Two sizes nearly-but-not-exactly equal = SPACE-3 violation (make them identical or meaningfully different).
**✗ WRONG.** A furniture-listing card using 10 different font sizes; a dashboard mixing a serif headline font, a rounded sans for buttons, monospace numbers, and a script "tip of the day" widget; a 4:5-ratio modular scale from 16px yielding 12.8, 20, 25, 31.25, 39.06px — fractional and inconsistently spaced.
**✓ RIGHT.** One family, 3 weights, a hand-crafted 12/14/16/18/20/24/30/36/48/60/72px scale — every value a round pixel, every step comfortably above 25%.
**Crop.** RU-03 (p.99–107 — the too-many-font-sizes furniture card ✗ vs the 10-step hand-crafted 12–72px scale ✓).
**Score — grounded ladder (0→10).**
- **0 — ✗:** ≥4 active typefaces on the screen, OR ≥9 distinct rendered type sizes, OR ≥2 fractional (`.xxx`px) sizes from an unrounded modular scale *(source: About Face Ch17 p.423 "one or two typefaces… a few sizes"; Refactoring UI p.104 fractional-scale artifact)*.
- **2** — exactly 3 typefaces, or 7–8 distinct sizes, or ≥2 adjacent scale steps under ~25% *(source: About Face p.423; Refactoring UI p.71–72 "no two values… closer than about 25%")*.
- **4** — ≤2 typefaces and ≤6 sizes, but exactly one residual defect: one fractional value, one sub-25% step, or one nearly-equal-but-not-identical size pair (<10% apart) *(source: Refactoring UI p.71–72, p.104; About Face p.423 "adjust them to be the same size")*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** ≤2 typefaces, ≤6 distinct rendered sizes, every size a whole pixel, every adjacent step ≥ ~25%, zero near-duplicate (<10% apart, non-identical) pairs *(source: About Face p.423; Refactoring UI p.71–72, p.104)*.
- **6** — + every rendered size drawn from ONE defined scale, not ad-hoc values that happen to comply *(source: Refactoring UI p.71–72 — a "system… truly useful")*.
- **7** — + the scale is hand-crafted and rounded: tight steps at the small end, widening toward the large end, zero fractional values anywhere in the defined scale *(source: Refactoring UI p.104)*.
- **8** — + weight/size differences each traceable to a reason — no two treatments differing without a role distinction (verify: pick any two differing text styles, name the role each encodes) *(source: About Face p.423 "every difference… should be there for a reason")*.
- **9** — + the defined scale is sufficiently dense for real use (~8–10 type steps) and visibly reused across the whole surface with no off-scale one-offs *[derived: Refactoring UI p.104 ✓ 12–72px scale + p.71–72]*.
- **10 — ✓:** one family, ~3 weights, a 12–72px-class hand-crafted whole-pixel scale, every step comfortably >25%, zero unjustified variation anywhere on the surface *(source: Refactoring UI p.104 ✓ example; About Face p.423)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition AND every rung below it hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — both experts high (Refactoring UI: "foundational system decision governing consistency across the entire product"; About Face: "directly gates scannability; a top-line craft signal").

### TYPE-2 — Line-height: proportional to measure, inverse to size
**Rule.** Longer lines need MORE leading (the eye must re-find the next line); larger text needs LESS (headlines near 1.0, body ~1.5); no universal value.
**Grounding.**
- Refactoring UI (p.125): "Line-height and font size are inversely proportional — use a taller line-height for small text and a shorter line-height for large text." Mechanism: a 1.5 line-height great for body copy is absurd for a large headline, which needs closer to 1.
- Refactoring UI (p.123): "The further your eyes have to jump horizontally to read the next line, the easier it is to lose your place. That means that your line-height and paragraph width should be proportional — narrow content can use a shorter line-height like 1.5, but wide content might need a line-height as tall as 2." Mechanism: leading exists to let the eye reliably relocate the next line after the horizontal return sweep.
- Universal Principles (p.148): leading (baseline-to-baseline) = type size + 1 to 4pt for standard text. Mechanism: a documented optimal band, not taste.
**Objective test.** (1) Measure > ~75ch → line-height ≥ 1.75–2, not the default 1.5. (2) Headline ≥ 30px → line-height ~1.0–1.1; body-value leading (1.5) on a 40px headline = fail. (3) Standard body text: leading within size + 1–4pt. Visual check: gaps between headline lines look tighter than gaps between body-paragraph lines, never looser.
**✗ WRONG.** A long-form paragraph set ~120 characters wide at line-height 1.25 — readers lose their place, re-reading or skipping lines. A two-line headline at line-height 1.5 (the same value as its body text) with gaping vertical space between its lines.
**✓ RIGHT.** The wide paragraph raised to 1.75, giving the eye enough vertical separation to track lines. The headline dropped to 1.0, reading as one cohesive block over a separately tuned, airier body paragraph.
**Crop.** RU-21 (p.123 — 1.25 ✗ vs 1.75 ✓ at the same wide measure; p.125 — headline at 1.5 ✗ vs 1 ✓).
**Score — grounded ladder (0→10).**
- **0 — ✗:** any wide block (>~75ch) at line-height ≤ 1.3, OR any headline ≥ 30px at body-value leading (~1.5) *(source: Refactoring UI p.123 "1.25" wide-measure fail; p.125 headline-at-1.5 fail)*.
- **2** — ≥2 wide-measure blocks below 1.75, or ≥2 headlines at body-value leading *(source: Refactoring UI p.123, p.125)*.
- **4** — exactly one residual defect: one wide block below 1.75 while others comply, OR one headline at body-value leading, OR body leading more than 1pt outside the size+1–4pt band *(source: Refactoring UI p.123, p.125; Universal Principles p.148)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** every body block > ~75ch has line-height ≥ 1.75, every headline ≥ 30px has line-height ≤ ~1.2, and standard body leading sits within size + 1–4pt *(source: Refactoring UI p.123, p.125; Universal Principles p.148)*.
- **6** — + wherever a multi-line headline sits near body copy, its inter-line gaps read visibly tighter than the body's *(source: Refactoring UI p.125 mechanism)*.
- **7** — + body leading holds precisely within the size+1–4pt band across ALL body text on the surface, not only a spot-checked sample *[derived: Universal Principles p.148]*.
- **8** — + every leading value is chosen proportionally to its own measure/size pairing (no reused value copy-pasted across a differently-measured block) *(source: Refactoring UI p.123 "leading and paragraph width should be proportional")*.
- **9** — + the same measure-to-leading mapping is reused consistently site-wide — no one-off leading values *[derived: Refactoring UI p.123, p.125]*.
- **10 — ✓:** wide blocks at 1.75–2, headlines at ~1.0–1.1, body leading in the UP band everywhere, headline gaps visibly tighter than adjacent body gaps, zero exceptions on the surface *(source: Refactoring UI p.123, p.125; Universal Principles p.148)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition AND every rung below it hold. N/A if no instances on the surface (e.g. no multi-line text).
**Weight.** med (2) — Refactoring UI: medium ("readability-critical where there's real body copy; less relevant to control-dense screens"); Universal Principles rates the umbrella Legibility entry high, but its high weight is carried by TYPE-5; noted.

### TYPE-3 — Alignment follows reading and data type
**Rule.** Left-align long-form text (centering only for ≤2–3-line independent blocks — or shorten the copy); right-align numeric columns so decimals stack; justified text requires hyphenation; baseline-align mixed sizes on one line, never center-align them.
**Grounding.**
- Refactoring UI (p.128–129): "text should be aligned to match the direction of the language it's written in... if something is longer than two or three lines, it will almost always look better left-aligned." Mechanism: ragged centered wrap lines read as awkward once a block runs long.
- Refactoring UI (p.130): "If you're designing a table that includes numbers, right-align them. When the decimal in a list of numbers is always in the same place, they're a lot easier to compare at a glance." Mechanism: stacked decimals turn comparison into a purely spatial scan.
- Refactoring UI (p.130–131): justified text "can create a lot of awkward gaps between words... whenever you justify text, you should also enable hyphenation." Mechanism: without word-breaks, lines forced to fill the measure stretch inter-word spaces.
- Refactoring UI (p.119–120): "align mixed font sizes by their baseline... you're taking advantage of an alignment reference that your eyes already perceive." When text is close together "the awkward alignment becomes more obvious." Mechanism: eyes expect different sizes to share a baseline, not a center — center-alignment reads subtly off at tight spacing.
**Objective test.** (1) Centered block > 3 lines = fail — shorten the copy or left-align. (2) `text-align` on currency/quantity/percent columns must be `right`. (3) `text-align: justify` without `hyphens: auto` = automatic fail. (4) Rows mixing font sizes: `align-items: baseline`, not `center`; manually, the smaller text's base sits on the large text's baseline (ignoring descenders), not floating mid-height.
**✗ WRONG.** One centered feature blurb running long and ragged beside short siblings; a stock table left-aligning Price/Chg/Mkt Cap so decimals wander; a justified paragraph with stretched word-gaps and no hyphenation; a card header vertically centering a large title against small "Refresh · See all" links, the links floating slightly high.
**✓ RIGHT.** Copy shortened to match its siblings (or the block left-aligned); numeric columns right-aligned with every decimal stacked; `hyphens: auto` added to the justified text; the header switched to `align-items: baseline` — same content, visibly resolved.
**Crop.** RU-20, RU-21 (p.118–120 "Who to follow" center- vs baseline-aligned; p.130 stock table; p.130–131 justification pair).
**Score — grounded ladder (0→10).**
- **0 — ✗:** ≥2 violations among {centered long-form block >3 lines, numeric column left/center-aligned, justified block without hyphenation, mixed-size row center-aligned} *(source: Refactoring UI p.128–131, p.119–120)*.
- **2** — exactly 1 violation among the four checks *(source: Refactoring UI p.128–131, p.119–120)*.
- **4** — zero violations, but at least one numeric column's decimals aren't fully stacked (inconsistent decimal precision) or one baseline-aligned row is off by a few px *(source: Refactoring UI p.130, p.119–120)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** zero centered blocks >3 lines, every numeric column right-aligned with decimals stacked, every justified block has hyphenation enabled, every mixed-size row baseline-aligned *(source: Refactoring UI p.128–131, p.119–120)*.
- **6** — + centering (≤3 lines) reserved only for genuinely independent short content, never sitting beside longer siblings *(source: Refactoring UI p.128–129)*.
- **7** — + all numeric columns share consistent decimal precision so the stack is exact, not merely aligned *[derived: Refactoring UI p.130]*.
- **8** — + baseline alignment of mixed sizes verified across the WHOLE surface, not spot-checked on one row *(source: Refactoring UI p.119–120)*.
- **9** — + reading-direction alignment (LTR/RTL) consistently honored with zero exceptions *(source: Refactoring UI p.128–129)*.
- **10 — ✓:** all four checks pass everywhere, centering reserved for short independent blocks only, decimals stacked exactly, baseline alignment universal *(source: Refactoring UI p.128–131, p.119–120)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition AND every rung below it hold. N/A if no instances on the surface.
**Weight.** med (2) — Refactoring UI splits this across two entries: alignment-direction/numeric/justify medium, baseline-alignment low ("narrow, automatable"); the broader medium entry governs; noted.

### TYPE-4 — Measure: keep line length in a readable band
**Rule.** Paragraphs at ~45–75 characters per line (fastest reading 35–55 per UP); cap paragraph width independently even inside wider containers — mixed widths in one section beat forced uniformity.
**Grounding.**
- Refactoring UI (p.114): "make your paragraphs wide enough to fit between 45 and 75 characters per line. The easiest way to do this on the web is using em units... A width of 20-35em will get you in the right ballpark." Mechanism: outside the band, the return sweep loses the line (too wide) or the rhythm chops (too narrow).
- Refactoring UI (p.116): "It might seem counterintuitive at first to use different widths in the same content area, but the result almost always looks more polished." Mechanism: a paragraph sharing a section with a wider component still takes its own max-width.
- Universal Principles (p.148): a line length "of 3 to 5 inches (8 cm to 13 cm)... resulting in a maximum of about 10 to 12 words per line, or 35 to 55 characters per line" reads fastest. Mechanism: the empirical reading-performance optimum sits narrower than the aesthetic ceiling.
**Objective test.** Count characters on a representative rendered full line: outside 45–75 = fail (~120ch is the book's flagged example); 35–55 is the reading-speed optimum for long-form. Width set in em: ~20–35em (typically ~34em). A paragraph inheriting full container width beside a wider element (icon row, image grid) instead of its own independent `max-width` = flag.
**✗ WRONG.** A hero section sets its intro paragraph to `max-width: none`, stretching it past 100 characters to match the three-column icon row beneath — needlessly wide next to short wrapped icon labels.
**✓ RIGHT.** The paragraph gets its own `max-width: 34em`, centered above the wider row, landing in the 45–75ch band even though the container is wider.
**Crop.** RU-20 (p.114 — the ~120ch Moby-Dick paragraph flagged too wide; p.115–116 — `max-width: none` ✗ vs `34em` ✓).
**Score — grounded ladder (0→10).**
- **0 — ✗:** any paragraph's representative rendered line < 35ch or > 90ch *(source: Refactoring UI p.114 — the ~120ch flagged example)*.
- **2** — ≥2 paragraphs at 76–90ch (near-miss), or ≥2 paragraphs inheriting full container width beside a wider sibling with no independent cap *(source: Refactoring UI p.114, p.116)*.
- **4** — one residual defect: exactly one paragraph at 76–90ch, OR one paragraph lacking its own `max-width` beside a wider element, OR width capped in fixed px rather than em/ch *(source: Refactoring UI p.114–116)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** every paragraph's representative line sits at 45–75ch, width capped in em (~20–35em) or equivalent, every paragraph in a mixed-width section carries its own `max-width` *(source: Refactoring UI p.114–116)*.
- **6** — + on surfaces whose primary job is sustained reading, the measure sits within the 35–55ch reading-speed optimum *(source: Universal Principles p.148)*.
- **7** — + the width-capping mechanism is applied consistently (same em/ch-based logic reused across paragraphs, not case-by-case) *[derived: Refactoring UI p.114–116]*.
- **8** — + band compliance verified against the actual RENDERED output across breakpoints, not just the authored CSS value *[derived]*.
- **9** — + paragraph widths are intentionally varied by component type (body paragraph vs caption vs list item) rather than forced to one uniform width *(source: Refactoring UI p.116)*.
- **10 — ✓:** full band+mechanism compliance everywhere, UP optimum met wherever reading is the primary job, mixed-width independence total, zero exceptions *(source: Refactoring UI p.114–116; Universal Principles p.148)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition AND every rung below it hold. N/A if no paragraph text on the surface.
**Weight.** med (2) — Refactoring UI: medium ("core readability metric wherever there's paragraph copy"); Universal Principles' high applies to the composite Legibility bundle (carried by TYPE-5); noted.

### TYPE-5 — Legibility floors are objective
**Rule.** Data-bearing text takes adequate size, real contrast, flat backgrounds, and correct leading; undersized or low-contrast type on working surfaces harms comprehension regardless of elegance.
**Grounding.**
- Universal Principles (p.148): "For printed text, standard 9- to 12-point type is considered optimal." / "Performance is optimal when contrast levels between text and background exceed 70 percent." Mechanism: these are measured reading-performance thresholds, not stylistic preferences.
- Universal Principles (p.148, note 4): "High-contrast, inverse text can 'visually bleed' to the background and dramatically reduce legibility." Mechanism: passing the numeric contrast threshold does not guarantee legibility — rendering context (inverse text, textured grounds) can still defeat it.
- Universal Principles (p.148): leading = type size + 1 to 4pt; background a flat, non-patterned fill. Designing Interfaces Ch.5 (pp.260–279) treats typography/readability floors as objective craft prerequisites — the repetition of a constrained visual system, not any single nice element, is what reads as designed.
**Objective test.** Body/data size ≥ 9pt-equivalent (larger for low-res/senior audiences) and ≥ the platform floor. Contrast ≥ 70% for long-form reading performance (in addition to COLOR-6's WCAG check — the two are separate thresholds). Background behind text: flat, non-patterned. Leading within size + 1–4pt. Secondary/muted text still passes the floors. Measure against the app's OWN scale for consistency.
**✗ WRONG.** 11px grey-on-grey metadata carrying decision-relevant values; white body copy over a subtly textured gradient at ~110 characters per line — the contrast number passes while texture and measure independently degrade legibility.
**✓ RIGHT.** Data text on-scale and on-contrast over a flat fill, column constrained to ~60–65 characters; texture reserved for non-text regions.
**Crop.** none (measured checks; UP p.149 comparison grid available — serif vs sans, justified vs ragged, monospaced vs proportional).
**Score — grounded ladder (0→10).**
- **0 — ✗:** ≥2 violations combined across {size floor, contrast floor, flat ground, leading floor, on-scale sizing} *(source: Universal Principles p.148)*.
- **2** — exactly 1 violation among the five checks *(source: Universal Principles p.148)*.
- **4** — zero violations, but the passing values sit right at the floor with no margin (e.g. exactly 9pt-equivalent, exactly 70% contrast) — fragile compliance *[derived: Universal Principles p.148 "optimal" band]*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** zero violations across all five checks — size ≥9pt-equivalent and ≥ platform floor (incl. muted/secondary text), contrast ≥70%, flat non-patterned ground, leading within size+1–4pt, every size on the app's own scale *(source: Universal Principles p.148)*.
- **6** — + size and contrast sit comfortably ABOVE the floor, not merely passing at the edge *[derived: Universal Principles p.148 note 4]*.
- **7** — + inverse/high-contrast text checked for visual "bleed" against textured or bright grounds even where the numeric contrast value passes *(source: Universal Principles p.148, note 4)*.
- **8** — + secondary/muted text independently re-verified against every floor, never assumed exempt *(source: Universal Principles p.148)*.
- **9** — + all five floors verified across the FULL surface, not a sampled subset *[derived]*.
- **10 — ✓:** all floors cleared with margin everywhere, zero bleed risk, muted text included, universal on-scale sizing, zero exceptions *(source: Universal Principles p.148)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition AND every rung below it hold. N/A if no data-bearing text on the surface.
**Weight.** high (3) — Universal Principles: high (measured reading-performance thresholds; Legibility is the umbrella entry, whose composite high weight lands here).

### TYPE-6 — Link styling budget
**Rule.** In link-dense contexts, not every link takes the loud treatment: primary content links carry weight/darker color; genuinely ancillary links may reveal affordance on hover only — balanced against AFFORD-2 (something must still signal interactivity where discovery matters, and hover doesn't exist on touch).
**Grounding.**
- Refactoring UI (p.126): standard blue/underlined styling matters in prose, "but when you're designing an interface where almost everything is a link, using a treatment designed to make links 'pop' in paragraph text can be really overbearing." Mechanism: link emphasis is proportional to link density — when everything shouts, nothing is emphasized.
- Refactoring UI (p.127): "emphasize most links in a more subtle way, like by just using a heavier font weight or darker color... Some links might not even need to be emphasized by default at all... consider adding an underline or changing the color only on hover." Mechanism: a demotion ladder — weight/darkening for primary, hover-only for secondary.
- Don't Make Me Think (p.187): "No cursor = no hover = no clue... many useful interface features that depended on hover are no longer available." Mechanism: any hover-only affordance silently disappears on touch and needs a visible-at-rest or tap equivalent.
**Objective test.** Count link-styled elements in one view: >4 elements all in the traditional blue/underline treatment = overload — demote per the ladder (primary → weight/darker color; secondary → hover-only). Audit every hover-only link: on touch surfaces it must remain discoverable via position/context, an always-visible cue, or a tap equivalent — any hover-only behavior with no touch equivalent fails.
**✗ WRONG.** A video-thumbnail grid rendering every title in blue underline — four cards, four blue titles, all shouting equally though none is more clickable than the others.
**✓ RIGHT.** Titles as plain dark, slightly bold text — still clearly each card's click target by position; a rare credit-line link carries no distinction at rest and underlines on hover, with an always-visible treatment on touch viewports.
**Crop.** RU-21 (p.126–127 — all-blue grid ✗ vs weight-only titles ✓ vs hover-only secondary link).
**Score — grounded ladder (0→10).**
- **0 — ✗:** >6 loud (blue/underline) link elements in one view, OR ≥2 hover-only links with no touch equivalent *(source: Refactoring UI p.126–127; Don't Make Me Think p.187)*.
- **2** — 5–6 loud-link elements in one view, or links demoted but into one uniform treatment with no primary/secondary grading *(source: Refactoring UI p.126–127)*.
- **4** — ≤4 loud links (count threshold met) but exactly one hover-only link lacks a touch equivalent, or the demotion ladder shows only a single tier *(source: Refactoring UI p.127; Don't Make Me Think p.187)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** ≤4 loud-treatment link elements per view, two distinct demotion tiers present (primary = weight/darker color, ancillary = hover-only/rest-quiet), every hover-only link has a touch equivalent, every primary link recognizable at rest *(source: Refactoring UI p.126–127; Don't Make Me Think p.187)*.
- **6** — + ancillary links are consistently hover-only/rest-quiet across the WHOLE surface, not just the audited view *[derived]*.
- **7** — + touch equivalents verified via actual tap-target behavior, not merely assumed present *(source: Don't Make Me Think p.187)*.
- **8** — + the primary/secondary tiering rule is documented as a reusable pattern, not decided ad hoc per screen *[derived]*.
- **9** — + link density itself is minimized where feasible (fewer, better-targeted links) rather than relying on demoted styling alone *[derived: Refactoring UI p.126 mechanism]*.
- **10 — ✓:** link-dense views never overload with the loud treatment, the demotion ladder applies consistently, zero touch-discoverability regressions anywhere *(source: Refactoring UI p.126–127; Don't Make Me Think p.187)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition AND every rung below it hold. N/A if the view is not link-dense (≤4 links total).
**Weight.** med (2) — Don't Make Me Think: med (no-hover compensation, "critical when a touch surface ships"); Refactoring UI: low-med ("matters specifically in link-dense contexts"); majority med, noted.

### TYPE-7 — Readability is about language, not rendering
**Rule.** User-facing prose is simple, active-voice, jargon-light — matched to the audience's level, without over-simplifying away precision.
**Grounding.**
- Universal Principles (p.198): "Readability is determined by factors such as word length, word commonality, sentence length, number of clauses in a sentence, and number of syllables in a sentence." Mechanism: readability is a property of the language itself, distinct from legibility (rendering clarity).
- Universal Principles (p.198): "Simple language is preferred, but overly simple language obscures meaning." And: "do not write for the formula" — readability formulas are "primitive guides and should not outweigh all other considerations." Mechanism: the target is a MATCH to the audience's level, not a minimum — dumbing down technical copy destroys the precision its audience needs.
**Objective test.** Run the copy through a readability formula (the book cites Fry's Graph: average sentence count and syllable count per 100-word sample) and compare the estimated grade level against the intended audience's reading level — pass = match, not "as low as possible." Technical audiences get precise technical copy; consumer surfaces get plain prose. See copy-and-language.md.
**✗ WRONG.** A developer-facing API error reading "Oopsie! Something went a lil wonky, sorry!" — a childish register that obscures the technical meaning the developer needs.
**✓ RIGHT.** "Request failed: missing required field `apiKey`. See docs/auth for setup." — plain, active-voice, AND precise for its actual audience.
**Crop.** none (UP p.199 — Fry's Readability Graph, college-level vs 4th-grade passages on the same content).
**Score — grounded ladder (0→10).**
- **0 — ✗:** estimated grade level of a 100-word sample more than ±2 grades from the intended audience (either direction), OR any system/error message in childish or filler register in place of the actionable fact *(source: Universal Principles p.198; example p.129-style "Oopsie, went a lil wonky")*.
- **2** — grade level within ±2 grades but not ±1, or <60% of sampled sentences active-voice *(source: Universal Principles p.198)*.
- **4** — one residual defect: grade level within ±1 but active voice only 60–79%, or exactly one register mismatch *(source: Universal Principles p.198)*.
- **5 — THRESHOLD:** grade level within ±1 of the intended audience, ≥80% active voice in the sampled passage, zero register mismatches, no childish/filler system messages *(source: Universal Principles p.198)*.
- **6** — + technical precision is preserved for technical audiences even where sentence structure is simplified — no meaning lost to the simplification *(source: Universal Principles p.198 "do not write for the formula")*.
- **7** — + the readability-formula check is run on multiple samples across the surface, not one passage *[derived]*.
- **8** — + register stays consistent across ALL user-facing prose classes (errors, empty states, tooltips), not just primary copy *[derived]*.
- **9** — + the match is corroborated by actual audience feedback/testing, not the formula alone *(source: Universal Principles p.198 — formulas are "primitive guides")*.
- **10 — ✓:** grade-level match precise and audience-verified, near-100% active voice, zero register mismatches, technical precision retained, consistent across the whole surface *(source: Universal Principles p.198)*.
Score = highest rung whose condition AND every rung below it hold. N/A if the surface carries no user-facing prose.
**Weight.** med (2) — Universal Principles: med (formulas are "primitive guides"; the target is a match, not a minimum).

# The design lock — board format, `docs/DESIGN.md` schema, re-pick protocol

> Gate: run at P0.5, for any app with a human-facing surface, BEFORE the first build pixel. This is
> the only phase whose mechanics previously had no reference home — the gate existed in SKILL.md and
> the HOW did not exist anywhere.

A quality adjective is not a spec. "Award-winning", "beautiful", "premium", "clean" describe a
feeling the user has about a result they have not seen yet. The lock converts that into something a
builder can execute and a reviewer can judge against: **a direction the user PICKED, from rendered
options, written down.**

---

## 1. The direction boards

**2-3 boards. Each is one REAL screen of THIS app, in the app's own nouns.** Not a swatch page, not a
mood board, not a component gallery — a screen the user would recognise, rendered three ways.

Each board carries, visibly:

| Token set | Shown as |
|---|---|
| palette | the actual surfaces/text/accent in use on the screen, not chips in a row |
| type | the real hierarchy — page title, section, body, meta — at real sizes |
| density | the real row/card rhythm at the real content volume |
| motion posture | stated in a line ("restrained: state changes only" / "expressive: entrance + transition") — boards are static, so this is a written commitment |
| one composed view | the whole screen, assembled |

**Static HTML, self-contained, served.** AUQ labels cannot carry pixels — so serve the set locally or
publish it, LINK it, and make the AUQ options the direction NAMES pointing at the rendered set. An
AUQ that asks the user to pick between adjectives has skipped this gate.

**Anti-references are named on the board:** what this direction is deliberately NOT. A direction with
no anti-reference is a preference, not a direction.

**The owner's taste is extracted BEFORE boards render** — one exchange, three questions: products or
surfaces they admire (references) · what this must never feel like (THEIR anti-references, not the
board's) · the visual register in their own words. Boards are judged against the owner's taste;
boards authored purely from the author's taste re-derive the owner's by rejection (measured: across a
six-round session no taste artifact ever existed — sibling briefs of the same writer class were
written, this one never was — and every round re-learned the owner's preferences from wholesale
rejections). The answers land in `docs/DESIGN.md` under `## Taste` (references · the owner's
anti-references · the register, in their words); the board-level `## Anti-references` draws from it.

**AT LEAST ONE DIRECTION IS DRAWN BLIND, and the board says which one.** A blind direction comes from
a lane given ONLY the objective, the data model and the token set — it never sees the other boards,
the current app, or a donor. Without it, 2-3 directions authored in one head are three angles on the
same first idea, and the user picks a winner from a field that was never wide.

**This is REQUIRED at the lock precisely because the lock fans out furthest.** `design-round.md` §3
already requires a blind lane for a PER-SURFACE round; the app-level lock had no such rule, which is
backwards — every screen in the build is judged against this pick, so it is the one design decision
where anchoring is most expensive and was least guarded. Caught by a build that flagged its own gap:
having produced three good boards, it wrote *"all three directions came from me, so none was drawn by
someone who hadn't seen the others"*, declared the picked shape settled, and committed to a blind
option only for the LATER per-surface rounds — the cheap decisions, not the expensive one.

**Waiver, stated in the plan, never assumed:** when the shape is genuinely not in question (a
re-skin inside a fixed IA, a one-screen addition to a locked app), the blind lane is waived — the
same carve-out and the same "the dispatcher states which case it is" rule as `design-round.md` §3.
And "at least one" never means "all": an all-blind set has no informed alternative, which is the
same incompleteness inverted.
✗ three boards from one author, all seeing each other → the pick looks like a choice and is a
preference between three drafts of one instinct.
✓ two informed, one blind, the board naming which is which → the user picks from a real field.

### Where the boards come from
- `Skill(frontend-design)` when the plugin is present.
- Absent → `ux-canon.md` is the floor for BOARD RENDERING. (At P3 build time the canon is ALWAYS read WITH the lock — the canon is the floor under whichever direction was picked, never a substitute; see the gate in the craft profiles.)
- The org starter ships board scaffolds (`starter-guide.md`).
- **A fork or donor's look is NEVER the default.** De-branding a donor is not a direction — it is the
  donor's direction with the logo removed.
- **Client-brand gate:** when the app is FOR a named client, their LIVE design language (their site,
  their product, brand canon in general-context) is read BEFORE boards render. A scraped hex value is
  not a design language. Their light/dark posture is the default posture. Read the THEME — the
  stylesheet's own tokens (primary/accent variables, radius, typeface, grounds) — not a homepage
  colour scrape: a hex-frequency count once concluded green-primary/dark-plausible for a client whose
  theme was slate-primary/light ("the design is too far from [the client] itself" — first board round
  lost); the six-minute theme read that followed held for the entire engagement.

---

## 2. `docs/DESIGN.md` — the committed lock

The user picks; you commit the lock **before any build pixel**. Schema:

```markdown
# Design lock — <app>
Picked: <direction name>, <date>, by <who>

## Machine-readable axes
colorScheme: light | dark | both
density:     compact | regular | comfortable
motion:      none | restrained | expressive

## Tokens
<the chosen palette / type scale / spacing step / radius / elevation, as real values>

## Board snapshot
<path or URL to the board that was picked, as rendered at pick time>

## Anti-references
- <what this is deliberately not>

## Taste (extracted from the owner before boards rendered)
references: <products/surfaces the owner admires>
anti_references: <what the owner said this must never feel like>
register: <the owner's own words for the visual register>

## Pick provenance (per surface — the per-surface round, design-round.md)
picked: <direction-name>          # the chosen alternative
alternatives: <n>                 # genuinely-different directions offered (n>=2; a 1 is not a slate)
axis: <layout|interaction|density|decision>   # the named axis they differed on
blind_lane: yes|no                # did >=1 alternative come from a lane that never saw the current screen
boards: <path-or-url>             # the rendered set the owner picked from
owner_reasoning: <one line>       # the owner's own arbitration, captured (often a synthesis)
```

A `docs/DESIGN.md` with tokens but no `alternatives:`/`picked:` provenance is an ASSUMED or INHERITED
lock, not a pick — the DESIGNLOCK gate's tightening (once this convention is written by a real build)
reads exactly these lines. The per-surface round + its lane (`app-redesigner`) → `design-round.md`.

### Why the axes are machine-readable
Because a lock a human honours and a guard cannot read is a lock that drifts silently. The three
binary-ish axes are named values the static guard greps against the code:

- `colorScheme: light` + a `prefers-color-scheme` boot in the source = **RED at the introducing
  commit**, not at user discovery. Measured: a lock saying "Light mode only" and a dark-mode boot were
  born in the *same commit*, and every capture ran the compliant path for hours, so the violated axis
  was structurally unobservable.
- `motion: none|restrained` + a decorative animation = RED.
- `density` sets the row-rhythm the spacing checks assert against.

### The capture consequence
**When the lock names a MODE, the capture set includes ONE opposite-mode shot.** A suite that can only
render the compliant path cannot fail on the violated axis — it will report green forever.

---

## 3. The lock is the visual authority

P3 reads it before the first unit of EACH surface. A reviewer judges AGAINST it: a dimension the lock
deliberately inverts scores **BY-DESIGN** with an intent-execution number, never a generic-rung fail.
The lock wins unless re-picked.

---

## 4. Re-pick protocol

A re-pick is a **NEW lock commit** — boards, pick, `docs/DESIGN.md`, dated. Not an edit in place, and
not an accumulation of taste notes.

- **Design drift without a re-pick is the redesign-wave class.** If the built surface no longer
  matches the lock, that is either a defect (fix the surface) or a re-pick (run the gate again). It is
  never "the design evolved".
- A seat that believes the locked intent actively harms the job files ONE `contract_challenges` row.
  Cue surfaces a re-pick AUQ. The challenge is a SIGN-OFF item, never a fix-loop row.
- The previous lock is not deleted — it is superseded, dated, so a later reviewer can tell a
  deliberate reversal from a drift.

# The per-surface design round — objective → alternatives → owner picks (inception AND redesign)

> Gate: run BEFORE the first build pixel of any human-facing surface, AND again at every redesign of
> one. This is a DIFFERENT grain from the app-level design lock (`design-lock.md`): the lock picks the
> app's visual LANGUAGE once (palette, type, density, motion); THIS round picks the SHAPE of each
> screen — its layout, what it foregrounds, its primary interaction — inside that locked language.

## Why this exists
A surface built with no proposed alternatives is a surface the owner first sees as a finished thing he
never chose. His first design feedback then arrives as a rejection, and every later round descends from
an unarbitrated first shape. The round makes the owner PICK the direction of each screen from RENDERED
options, before any build pixel.

## Improvement and redesign are NOT the same work — route first
- **Incremental improvement** (the review loop — SKILL.md crew ENGINE): the surface's SHAPE is settled;
  reviewers and the executor raise it — density, hierarchy, states, craft. It KEEPS the screen.
- **Redesign** (this round): the surface's shape itself is wrong or rejected — it is RE-CONCEIVED from
  the objective, not polished. A redesign is a different process from an improvement pass: it runs on
  the HIGHEST available model, it produces genuinely-different alternatives, and it CAPTURES the owner's
  own reasoning as he picks.

**Routing (which mechanism):**
- A clear owner rejection of a SPECIFIC surface — "I really don't like this screen", "this is not
  usable", "none of this landed", "make it drastically different" — is a REDESIGN trigger for THAT
  surface. It is never answered by another improvement round (polishing a shape the owner rejected is
  the measured failure class).
- A whole-app verdict — "it feels assembled", "make the whole app award-winning", a council
  structural finding — routes to the whole-app design director (`agents/app-design-director.md`): ONE
  cohesive direction across all views, not per-surface alternatives.
- A scoped craft complaint on a shape the owner accepts — "this is too dense", "the header is weak" —
  is the improvement loop.
- **A SETTLED-PARADIGM redesign — the shape is approved, the EXECUTION is rejected.** "This screen is
  already the right idea, it is just built badly", or an owner whose words fix the frame ("we keep the
  desktop true, just need a good mobile view ON TOP"). This is a redesign, so it is not the improvement
  loop — but the shape is NOT in question, so condition 3's blind lane is **waived** (or capped at one
  clearly-labelled probe the owner can ignore). Run INFORMED lanes with the settled paradigm frozen in
  the brief, stated as a constraint the lane may not re-open.
  **Measured, and it is the expensive one:** a round dispatched two surfaces as ALL-BLIND against a
  paradigm the owner had already approved. Six boards came back and every one was rejected — *"all
  absolute garbage and not thought for the experience of a professional"* — and the owner then wrote
  the corrective spec himself. Cue's own verdict that night: *"the round was the wrong exercise.
  Réserve is already a table — I sent three lanes to reinvent its shape when the shape was never the
  problem."* It recurred hours later at lane level: a mobile lane re-authored the phone's JOB
  ("stated and defended, not inherited") after the owner had fixed the frame, and had to be rebuilt.
  Blind is the anti-anchoring lane; when there is nothing wrong to anchor to, blind is not neutral —
  it is uninformed.
- Unsure which? Ask, in one line (R#6). Reading a redesign as a polish is the expensive mistake, and
  reading a settled-paradigm rebuild as a shape question is the same mistake pointed the other way.

## The round — per surface, eight conditions
No surface is built or re-designed until ALL hold:
1. **Objective, owner-approved.** What THIS screen must let the user do or decide. Cue (or the
   architect) DRAFTS the row from the PRD's core loop; the OWNER approves it before any lane fans out
   (a `docs/SUBSCREEN-OBJECTIVES.md` row, drafted at P0.5/P3 for the surfaces of this wave). The
   objective table is the thing that needs the owner's eye first. The row carries the JOB-SHAPE:
   WHO reads this surface and what they DO on it (scan/compare · decide · monitor · explore — Dim 8's
   questions) plus its primary interactions. A scan-and-compare job is a table before it is a concept;
   generate concepts only after the job-shape says the surface needs one. Measured: five concepts for
   a scan-and-compare screen were rejected wholesale ("they are all bad… ideally it should be just a
   nice table"); the job AND the reader ("think sales person") both came from the owner AFTER
   generation — both were askable before it.
2. **N genuinely-different alternatives on a NAMED axis** — what is dominant, what is hidden, what the
   primary action is, or what the screen fundamentally IS. Three variants of one idea is a false
   choice, not a slate; every lane kills its own weakest option before showing anything. Range comes
   from differing on a DIMENSION, never on section order — three boards that are the same page
   reordered are one idea wearing three names (measured verdict: "quite meh… still very bland"; the
   re-brief that fixed it: pick one thing per direction and let it DOMINATE).
3. **A BLIND lane — REQUIRED.** At least one alternative comes from a lane given ONLY the objective, the
   data model, the design system, and the user's real context — NEVER the current screen, a screenshot,
   the components, or another lane's file. A lane handed the current surface ANCHORS: every
   "alternative" becomes the current screen with better spacing. A round with no blind alternative is
   incomplete — **unless the routing block above classed this as a SETTLED-PARADIGM redesign, where the
   blind lane is waived: the shape is not the question.** The dispatcher states which case it is, in the
   dispatch. And "required" never means "only": a round that is ALL blind has no informed alternative
   either, which is the same incompleteness inverted — the written shape is ~2 informed to 1 blind.
   **The blind guarantee is the DISPATCHER's discipline first:** Cue never puts the current
   screen — a shot, the components, a sibling lane's file — into a blind `app-redesigner` brief; the
   agent's own ignore-and-report self-check is the second line, not the first. (This is an
   instruction-level guarantee today, not a structural gate — a leaked shot silently defeats the
   anti-anchoring, so the dispatch is where it is held.)
4. **Populated, plural, REAL data — not the schema.** Every lane designs against real, loaded, plural
   data. A lane given an empty or schema-only fixture designs an empty-state screen; a missing derived
   field makes a surface that never renders its loaded state.
5. **Mobile-primary, NAMED.** The viewports are not symmetric — name the primary (do not ask for
   "responsive"). Each board is designed for the primary viewport and adapted to the secondary, with
   the trade stated.
6. **Inside the lock, plus ONE licensed amendment.** Alternatives stay inside the app design lock;
   each lane MAY propose exactly one lock amendment with its cost stated, and MAY name any data that
   must exist for its design to work. Withholding these produces compliant-but-unchanged designs.
7. **Rendered at both viewports, labeled what each is WORSE at.** Alternatives are RENDERED as real
   screens on real data, not described — the owner compares pixels, not prose. Each carries what it
   trades away. This binds APPROVALS too: a direction is never put to the owner as a written document —
   two prose-approved directions in one measured session both died on first sight of the screen ("I
   approved a direction that reads well on paper and poorly on screen"; "a document is not a design").
   A written direction is a plan FOR a board, not a thing to approve.
7b. **DELIVERED as ONE served page the owner can open — and CUE owns that page.** The lanes render
   and write their boards; assembling them is never a lane's job (lanes die mid-report: both lanes of
   one measured round died on a network error before writing their notes). The page:
   **one URL · every alternative inline** (a live `<iframe>` per alternative at the primary viewport,
   so drivable boards stay drivable) **· a jump menu** to move between them **· generated FROM DISK**
   so it cannot drift from what exists (`REF/scripts/build-alternatives-index.mjs`).
   A per-alternative index of LINKS is the failure shape, not the deliverable — "a separate menu you
   have to click upon" is the owner's own verdict on it.
   **The URL is PROBED BEFORE IT IS SENT — the exact address, root first, then every board.** Probing a
   neighbouring path and announcing the root is the measured defect: it happened twice, 46 hours apart,
   cost 6h49m and 2m54s of dead link, and each fix took ~100 seconds. An announcement whose URL was not
   itself probed in the same turn is not a delivery.
8. **The owner PICKS before any build/executor lane fires,** and the pick is recorded in
   `docs/DESIGN.md` (`## Pick provenance`, `design-lock.md`) — the chosen direction, the alternatives
   count, the axis, the boards, whether a blind lane ran, and the owner's own reasoning.

## The dispatch brief contract — what every design-lane brief carries
The dispatcher's half of the lane's own stop-list (`agents/app-redesigner.md`, Critical decisions 1/1b).
Before ANY design lane fires, the brief carries:
- the SETTLED data model, owner-confirmed — never a dispatcher-derived model: a domain model invented
  at dispatch fanned into six alternatives and was withdrawn by the owner in five corrections, the
  entire first build discarded (the fan-out commit self-check applied to design briefs);
- the SURFACE CONTRACT — six categories, each settled or explicitly delegated with a default: metric
  semantics (inclusion rule + aggregate derivation for every displayed number) · object identity rules
  (real logos vs glyphs; colour exceptions) · interaction contract (hover / click / second-click) ·
  audience matrix · density tolerance · domain formula semantics;
- the TASTE/JOB ANCHOR — the job-shape from condition 1, plus any direction the owner has named
  closest (see the taste-anchor rule below);
- ONE checkpoint line — "report after the first alternative; corrections may be in flight" — because
  a running lane receives nothing mid-turn; only the brief can carry a steer.
An in-session A/B settles the stakes: the brief carrying all of this ran zero-rework; the brief
without it cost a discarded build plus four correction rounds. Settling a category costs a sentence;
leaving it costs a round.

## The redesign lane shape (highest available model)
A per-surface redesign fans TWO kinds of `app-redesigner` lane (the dedicated agent) on the top model:
- **Informed lane(s)** (`app-redesigner`, mode=informed) — see the current screenshots at both
  viewports → ~2 alternatives.
- **Blind lane** (`app-redesigner`, mode=blind) — never opens the app, a screenshot, the components, or
  an informed lane's file → 1 alternative. It designs what it would build if nothing had been built.
Net ~3 alternatives per surface. Each lane renders its alternatives (real screens, real data, both
viewports) and returns them for the owner to pick; `app-redesigner` proposes, never builds the final
surface (the executor does, after the pick), never scores. The blind lane's value is evidenced:
independent directors that both saw the running app reliably converge on "the current app, with a
better mechanism behind it" — looking first is what produces polish disguised as a redesign.

## The taste anchor — iterate the named-closest before a novelty wave
When the owner has named a CLOSEST ("X is the best, but bland"), the next wave ITERATES X by default —
density/refinement variants on X's skeleton, at most 1-2 deliberately wild tails. An explicit novelty
ask ("give me 5-10 innovative ones") does not silently override the anchor NOR get silently obeyed:
it gets a one-line fork — "innovative set, push the closest, or both?" — before the wave fires.
Measured: an 8-direction novelty wave shipped while the owner's anchor ("the dossier is probably the
best… still very bland") had been on record for two hours; the set was rejected wholesale ("they are
all shit") and the accepted design was the owner's own composition of the anchor with one rejected
direction's density. The anchor was the design input; the wave optimised past it.
An anchored iteration wave is NOT condition 2's slate — the owner has already picked the IDEA; the
wave varies its EXECUTION (density, refinement) and the 1-2 wild tails carry the cross-idea range.
The dispatch states which round type it is: an open slate (condition 2 governs) or an anchored
iteration (this rule governs).

## At inception there is no current screen — the split changes
The informed/blind split is a REDESIGN construct: it exists to keep one lane from anchoring on an
EXISTING surface. At the FIRST design of a surface nothing is built yet, so there is nothing to anchor
to. There, every `app-redesigner` lane runs from the objective + data model + design system alone
(effectively all-blind), and the alternatives differ only on the NAMED axis (condition 2) — the "blind
lane REQUIRED" rule is satisfied by construction. The ONE exception that makes a lane "informed" at
inception is a real REFERENCE the owner named (a reference app, a sibling surface already picked) — an
informed lane may see THAT, never a not-yet-existing current screen. So: inception = N objective-driven
lanes on distinct axes (+ optionally one reference-informed); redesign = informed(current) + a REQUIRED
blind. The dispatch states which case it is.

## Capturing the owner's thinking
Given real options, the owner's arbitration is frequently a synthesis neither alternative proposed
(e.g. "the timeline INSIDE the grid"). That reasoning IS design input — capture it verbatim into the
pick record and the executor brief. Recording only "he picked B" discards the most valuable output of
the round. And a synthesis is a direction that was NEVER RENDERED — sending it to the executor on
prose alone is exactly what condition 7 forbids for every other direction. Render the mix as ONE
confirming board (the parents' named elements composed, real data, primary viewport) and get the
owner's one-look confirm before the executor builds; a board costs minutes, a built surface on a
mis-translated synthesis costs a round.

## Screens are SEEN, not read (the review-with-owner contract)
- Every alternative and every built surface is put to the owner as a RENDER — real screens, real
  populated data, both viewports — so he judges pixels, not a description.
- A capture is EVIDENCE, never proof: a probe can report clean and be wrong. Drive it; do not trust a
  filename.
- A verdict invitation is valid only for a surface SERVING THE WORK: before asking the owner to judge,
  prove the served page contains the change (content marker / version check — a server that reads its
  config at boot serves the pre-pass build after the files change). Measured: an owner graded "I still
  see no logo" against a build that did not contain the wired logo — part of a wholesale rejection
  passed on phantom state, and the trust cost outlived the fix.
- The FELT properties — reactivity, perceived speed — are invisible to `tsc`, unit tests, and
  screenshots. Only the owner operating the surface finds them. A human-facing surface is not done on a
  green render; it is done when the owner has seen it rendered on real data at both viewports
  (`feature-manifest-format.md` — the owner-render-review stamp; R#27 render-evidence).

## A design verdict is only as good as its instrument
A grading fleet, a review pass, or a capture pipeline is an INSTRUMENT, and a verdict is valid only if
the instrument was proven able to catch the failure class it rules on. Five rules, each paid for:
- **One-card reference test at pilot.** Before grading a fleet's worth of output, render ONE unit
  side-by-side with the real running app and compare. An absolute rubric has no contrast signal for a
  UNIFORM failure: 137 cards were graded "good" across two waves while the brand font 404'd on every
  sheet — the rubric named tokens, not typography, so every card looked like every other card.
- **Destination-parity render at first upload.** Capture the way the DESTINATION renders (one shared
  document, real host restrictions), not only the way the local pipeline does: a dark-mode root-flip
  leak poisoned 41 cards in the destination pane and was structurally invisible to solo-capture
  grading. Same family as R#24's user-env parity.
- **Probe a muted warning's claim before dismissing it.** A warning class marked "informational — no
  action" embeds a factual claim; verify it once before relying on it. "The families load at runtime"
  was checkable with one curl, was false, and the probe ran 2h43m after the user's eye caught it.
- **Sheet-backing audit at every re-key.** A re-key (config/taxonomy/contract change) is a CONTRACT
  event demanding fresh verdicts, never a clerical one. The grade-trust rule: a verdict whose note
  claims "pixels match the previously graded state" is UNVERIFIED unless a fresh capture backs it on
  disk — audit backing (mtime vs re-key time) per unit before any bulk re-affirm. Measured: 137
  verdicts re-written with fresh sheets for 45; ≥3 units were provably non-compiling when marked
  "good"; an independent QA lane caught it by grepping the note pattern.
- **Calibrate "good" with the owner on 3 samples** before a fleet grades at scale — the fleet's
  absolute bar and the owner's bar are different instruments until proven aligned ("still a lot of
  issues" arrived after 137/137 "good").

## Binds at inception AND at every redesign
The round is owed at the FIRST design of a surface and again at every structural redesign of it. A
redesign that dispatches an executor/reorg lane with no fresh per-surface pick is the silent-rework
class. A donor/inherited look is NOT a pick — inheriting a lock by fiat means the owner's first sight
of the design is a look he never chose.

## Arbitration load
The owner arbitrating N surfaces × ~3 alternatives × 2 viewports is real load — sequence it (the two
core-loop screens first), one wave at a time, rather than dumping every surface's slate at once.
