# Desktop shell — a hosted app installed as a real Mac app

Fires when the user asks for a **real desktop app** of something that already exists (or is being built) as a hosted web app: "a Mac app", "an .app", "give me the .dmg", "install it on her machine", "make it into an Electron app".

!! Read this BEFORE the shell repo exists. Every trap below either fails the BUILD or ships an app that looks broken, and each one has been paid for once already. !!

## 1. The decision

The default answer is a **SHELL**: one Electron main process that opens ONE window on the hosted origin and adds what a browser tab cannot. It is **not** a second build of the app, and it holds **no** credential and **no** server.

- The hosted app stays the single source: every screen, fix and feature arrives from the server, so a change reaches the desktop app with **no rebuild and no reinstall**. A second copy of the interface is a second thing to keep in step.
- The server's secrets (warehouse keys, service accounts) stay on the server. The shell is a browser — it signs in as the user does, over HTTPS, with a cookie. Bundling the backend puts warehouse write access on somebody's laptop.

| Signal | Answer |
|---|---|
| Hosted app exists, the work is online, the user wants it installed | SHELL — this doc |
| Must work with no network, or local files are its primary job | NOT a shell — a real desktop build with its own PRD |
| The user only wants an icon in the Dock | say so: Safari's **File → Add to Dock** gives a Dock icon and its own window for free, and it is the honest first answer — an installer nobody needed is a cost you added |
| Windows or Linux users too | the shape holds; nothing below is measured there — cost that platform separately |

**The runtime: Electron is what is measured here.** A system-WebView wrapper (Tauri and the like) ships a far smaller binary and is a legitimate candidate — but nothing in this document is measured against it, and every §5 packaging step and the §4 bridge would have to be re-proved on that stack. Treat it as a probe with its own cost, never as a drop-in.

**A shell earns its install only by what a tab cannot do.** Name that list in the PRD before building; an empty list means the honest answer is a bookmark. The measured list: the session persists (sign in once) · exports land through a real save dialog and are revealed in Finder · one window, one instance, its own Dock icon and badge · OS notifications when the window is not in front · a readable screen when the network is down.

## 2. The feature floor

A shell missing any row reads as broken, and most of these are invisible until somebody tries.

| Feature | Why it exists | The failure when missing |
|---|---|---|
| An application menu | macOS gives a window no Cmd-C/V/Q/W without one | copy and paste silently dead — the most common defect in shells |
| A hand-built Window menu carrying `role:"close"` | `role:"windowMenu"` carries Minimise, Zoom and Bring-All-to-Front, never Close, and a shell has no File menu | Cmd-W bound to nothing — the first shortcut a Mac user reaches for |
| `app.setName()` at load time | macOS takes the first menu title from the bundle name, and an unpackaged run carries Electron's own Info.plist | the menu bar says "Electron" |
| Single-instance lock + an `activate` handler | two windows on one session | the user reads stale data in one of them |
| Window bounds persisted to a JSON file in `userData` | four numbers, and no dependency to keep updated forever | the window re-opens wrong every launch |
| `titleBarStyle:"hiddenInset"` + a measured top strip (30px, padding not margin — margin collapses into the header's own) | the traffic lights are drawn OVER the page | the app's own logo sits under the close button |
| A drag region on the app's HEADER only — negative margin up, padding back | a drag region swallows clicks, and an opt-out list can never be complete because it must name every element that will ever exist | every overlay stops responding; its close button does nothing |
| Navigation lock: `will-navigate` + `setWindowOpenHandler`, off-origin → `shell.openExternal` | a shell that follows any link is an unlabelled browser with no address bar | the worst possible place to land on a phishing page |
| `did-fail-load` → a local offline page (ignore `errorCode -3`, an ordinary aborted load) | the default is a blank white frame | reads as a broken app; the user goes to find someone |
| `will-download` → `shell.showItemInFolder` | one of the few things the tab cannot do | exports vanish into Downloads |
| `contextIsolation:true` · `nodeIntegration:false` · `sandbox:true` · **no preload** | otherwise the remote page runs with Node in reach | any script the page loads can read and write the filesystem |
| `window-all-closed` does NOT quit on darwin | notifications need a live process | closing the window kills the banners |
| `minWidth` BELOW the web app's responsive breakpoint | a window that cannot be dragged under the breakpoint can never show the phone layout | the mobile layout exists only on a phone (measured: 1060 then 960 both wrong against a 760px breakpoint; 380 correct) |

## 3. Notifications — what Electron does not give you

- **The banner is raised by the SHELL, not by the page.** The main process calls `new Notification(...)` itself, so the hosted app needs no web-push setup, no service worker and no browser Notification permission, and nothing has to be bridged INTO the page. The page's only job is to state a number (§4). Assuming the opposite — that wrapping a site somehow confers notifications, or that the page must ask — is the usual wrong turn.
- **There is no permission API.** `Notification` carries exactly one static, `isSupported`; `systemPreferences` has nothing for notifications. **Showing a notification IS the request.**
- **The app cannot read the answer.** Never claim notifications are on. Ship a Help-menu "test a notification" (fire one and look — the only honest answer) plus a link to `x-apple.systempreferences:com.apple.preference.notifications`.
- **macOS asks once, ever**, and remembers per bundle id — deleting and reinstalling does NOT re-ask. So ask deliberately on first launch, and write the "asked" flag BEFORE the notification fires: killed between the two, a second prompt on the next launch reads as a bug.
- ✗ a custom dialog in front of the system prompt, explaining what the app will notify about → the owner's verdict: *"it doesn't work like a normal app"*, it reads as fishy. No Mac app asks you to approve a dialog in order to be shown a dialog. ✓ let macOS ask in its own words, on first launch.
- **Fire on a RISE, not on a count.** Re-notifying every poll for the same overdue item is how a person turns notifications off for an app and never turns them back on. The badge tracks the COUNT (how much is waiting); the banner tracks the RISE (something just happened).
- **Clear the badge at zero** with `setBadge("")` — a Dock badge reading "0" is a red dot that means nothing is wrong, which is the one thing a red dot must never mean.
- Clicking a banner restores the window AND routes to the screen the notification is about; a banner that only raises the app leaves the user hunting for the thing it was about.
- One `console.log` per raised banner is diagnostics, not noise: a notification that does not appear was either never raised or suppressed by macOS, and from outside the process those two look identical.

## 4. The bridge — what the WEB app publishes

The shell has no preload and no bridge; that is what `sandbox: true` is for. The page states its own numbers on a plain DOM attribute, and the shell reads them the way any script would (`executeJavaScript` runs in the page's own world, and nothing privileged crosses in either direction).

- Page: `document.documentElement.dataset.notifUnread = String(n)` and, when there is one, `dataset.notifTop = JSON.stringify({title, body, route})` — the headline rides along so the banner can say something other than "3 notifications".
- Shell: polls that attribute (60s), badges the count, banners on a rise, routes on click.
- `undefined` is NOT `0`. Signed out, still loading, or a user with no bell must never read as an all-clear.

Both halves are small: the publisher is a ~10-line helper in the web app's notification component; the reader is `watchNotifications()` in `desktop-shell/main.js`.

## 5. Packaging for macOS with no Developer ID

The common case: the org has no Apple Developer ID and no Windows certificate, and the app is for a named colleague on a Mac.

1. `electron-builder`, `identity: null`, `type: "distribution"`, one `dmg` target, arch `universal`.
2. ‼ **Without an afterPack hook the app ships signed as "Electron".** Measured on the built artifact: `Identifier=Electron` / `flags=0x20002(adhoc,linker-signed)` — `linker-signed` means nothing ever signed the BUNDLE, only the linker signed the binary at build time. Info.plist carries your appId while the code signature says Electron, so everything that keys off the signature (the keychain, the notification subsystem, Gatekeeper's own records) sees a generic Electron app, and two Electron apps on the same Mac share that identity.
3. The hook ad-hoc signs with the real identifier: `xattr -cr <app>` then `codesign --force --deep --sign - --identifier <appId> <app>`.
   - **`xattr -cr` is not optional.** `codesign` refuses a bundle carrying extended attributes — *"resource fork, Finder information, or similar detritus not allowed"* — and it FAILS the build rather than warning.
   - **Sign the merged bundle only.** The hook fires three times for a universal build (arm64, x64, then the merged result), and signing the first two breaks the third: `lipo` requires every non-binary file byte-identical across the packs, and a signature writes a different `_CodeSignature/CodeResources` into each. Guard on `context.appOutDir.endsWith("mac-universal")`. The measured failure reads *"Expected all non-binary files to have identical SHAs … CodeResources did not"*.
   - **Read the signature back, from the right stream.** `codesign -dv --verbose=2` writes to **stderr**; a read-back that only captures stdout sees nothing and fails a correct build. Throw when `Identifier=<appId>` is absent — a codesign that "succeeded" and left the old identifier in place is exactly the state the hook exists to end.
4. **Ad-hoc buys a correct identity, not trust.** Gatekeeper still asks on first open, so the install note must say so in plain words (right-click → Open, once).
5. **Icon:** electron-builder needs `build/icon.png` at exactly 1024×1024. Render the source SVG at 1024 and assert the dimensions before building — a wrong size fails late.
6. Ship the DMG **with** a plain-language install note in the user's own language (§7).

## 6. Verification before the DMG leaves

Verify the app **inside the DMG**, never the build folder:

- mount the DMG, extract `Contents/Resources/app.asar` (`npx asar extract`), and diff its `src/main.js` against `git show HEAD:src/main.js` → must be IDENTICAL;
- grep the extracted `main.js` for one token per shipped feature (menu, single instance, badge, navigation lock…) AND for the token of every regression you fixed — those must be `0`;
- `codesign -dv --verbose=2` on the mounted app → `Identifier=<appId>`;
- `hdiutil verify` plus a checksum;
- behaviour needing two polls to demonstrate (the banner fires on a rise) gets an env override in the SHIPPED code, floored to a sane minimum and absent from every real run.

R#27: the Coverage Table's units are §2's rows; the E2E row is the user opening the installed app on their own machine and saying what they saw.

## 7. The artifacts — copy them, do not re-author (R#41)

`desktop-shell/` beside this file:

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| `main.js` | the whole shell, annotated with the WHY of every trap in §2–§4 |
| `afterPack.js` | the ad-hoc signing hook of §5 |
| `package.json` | build config: universal dmg, `identity: null`, icon, afterPack wiring |
| `offline.html` | the only screen shipped inside the binary; retries by itself, names what is safe |
| `INSTALL-note.md` | the note that ships WITH the DMG: install · the first-open Gatekeeper step · notifications · sign-in · what it adds over the browser |

Tokens to replace, everywhere: `<APP_ORIGIN>` · `<PRODUCT_NAME>` · `<APP_ID>` (reverse-DNS) · `<PKG_NAME>` · `<ORG>` · `<APP_BACKGROUND>` (the app's own paper colour, so a cold start does not flash white then repaint) · `<HEADER_SELECTOR>` (the app's top bar — the ONLY drag region) · `<NOTIFY_MS_ENV>` · `<BREAKPOINT>` (set `minWidth` below it). Menu labels and every user-facing string go in the **user's** language, never English by default.

## 8. Not covered here — state it, never invent it

Developer-ID signing and notarisation (impossible without the paid Apple Developer Program — do not spend time on it) · a system-WebView runtime (Tauri) · auto-update (`electron-updater`; a shell that loads the live origin already updates its CONTENT on every launch — only the shell binary would need a reinstall) · Windows and Linux packaging · notifications surviving a full Cmd-Q (that needs a login item plus a background agent, which is a bigger thing to install on somebody's machine) · App Store distribution.

# Dev loop — local serving, restart ritual, iteration

## Name the serving surface FIRST
Three surfaces can serve "the app": a static file server on the working master (no backend, fixture fallbacks) · the local node server (backend, possibly BOOT-CACHED bundle) · prod. Journeys and "done" claims run against the SHIPPED DEFAULT config — a component green in a gallery/harness while the default config never mounts it is ❌ untested (the measured "I don't see anything new on the UI" class; R#27 blind spot). Before debugging ANY "it works here, breaks there": which URL, which copy, which data snapshot? Version skew between surfaces mimics environment bugs (a JS throw on the NEW code reads as "localhost can't scroll but prod can"). The named surface is also the USER'S WINDOW: share the localhost/served URL proactively during long phases and re-share at each wave boundary (R#9 build heartbeat) — the serving surface exists for them, not only for your debugging.

## The preview-surface contract (fleet builds)
Scope: the app's own preview instance AND any other surface served FOR the owner to look at — a design
board set, an alternatives page, a report. A board set served ad-hoc on a scratch port from a lane
output dir is preview-class: it gets the same owner, the same pre-announcement check, the same rules.
The user's preview is a DELIVERABLE with an OWNER, not a side effect of serving:
- **One owner lane** keeps it alive AND current-to-last-merge — a content-marker check runs before ANY announcement referencing it (R#20); "look at the preview" with a dead/stale preview is the measured "I DO NOT SEE ANY IMPROVEMENT" class.
- **Excluded from every fleet kill-scope** (fleet-resources.md): no cleanup sweep, port reclaim, or suite run ever takes it down; verification traffic drives ISOLATED instances, never the preview.
- **Seeded to showcase:** the preview runs a demo config exercising every shipped capability — an empty-state preview under-sells the build and invites "where is X?".
- **Reachable BEFORE any unattended stretch:** reactivity + perceived speed are FELT — invisible to `tsc`, unit tests, and screenshots; only a human (or a driven journey) OPERATING the app finds them. A human-facing app that will build unattended needs a reachable preview + a real login IN PLACE before the stretch starts, not after — otherwise felt defects (blanking, stutter, dead controls) bake in across the whole run before anyone can see them.
- **Announcements are reviewer-first:** URL + what-to-click + what-changed since last time — never a bare "pushed". The capture set always includes the USER'S default click path (their entry route, their first action), not only the feature-under-test.

## One writer per shared store (local dev vs hosted)

A local dev instance pointed at the SAME shared store as the hosted app (warehouse tables, remote state) is a SECOND WRITER — and a stale local boot-restore can sync empty/old state OVER live data: the record the user just added simply disappears. Rules:
- Dev instances run READ-ONLY against shared state by default (an env flag the server honors, e.g. `<APP>_READONLY_SYNC=1`); writes are enabled deliberately, per session — never ambient.
- Sync WRITE-THROUGH per item on change, never a whole-state snapshot push (one stale snapshot clobbers everything at once).
- Boot-restore MERGES with post-boot mutations; an EMPTY restored value never overwrites a non-empty live one without an explicit repair path.
- Append-only history for shared state (the `app_state` pattern, SKILL P1) is what makes a clobber RECOVERABLE — a latest-only table loses the data outright.
- At deploy/swap time re-check the rule: kill or read-only the local instance FIRST — the hosted reboot re-restores shared state including anything local wrote.

## The restart ritual (one block, never partial)
A boot-cached server + env-var secrets + port fallbacks make partial restarts lie. ALWAYS:
```
pkill -f "node server.js"            # ALL instances — a zombie on the fallback port serves stale code
export <EVERY_SECRET>=...            # enumerate ALL of them (a partial re-export half-breaks: UI fine, API 500)
PORT=<pinned> nohup node server.js >/tmp/app.log 2>&1 &
curl -s localhost:<port>/ | grep -c "<fresh-content-marker>"    # served BYTES, not the file on disk
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" localhost:<port>/<api-route>   # one API route too
```
If the server reads its bundle ONCE at module load (e.g. `let INDEX = renderIndex()` at startup), `cp` alone changes NOTHING served — only a restart does; confirm by curl-ing a marker of the NEW code before any browser probe. Skipping any step reproduces a measured failure (keyless 500 / zombie port / stale page → a full test pass against old code).

## The iteration loop (per fix/feature round)
1. REPRODUCE the user's exact state live (their composition, their click path) — in the browser, before touching code.
2. Patch the SMALLEST span via string-replace with `assert count==1` (a drifted anchor aborts instead of mis-patching).
   - A rename/refactor touching anything that FEEDS displayed numbers ends with a FIGURE-DIFF GUARD: capture every displayed figure before, re-render, diff byte-identical after — a rename that silently moves a derived number ships a wrong figure under green tests.
   - A half-applied multi-file edit (script died midway, cwd drifted between calls) is NEVER reasoned back into place: reset to the last verified-green commit and re-apply once with absolute paths. Half-applied state is exactly where a quiet corruption gets rationalised into place.
3. Behavioral verify (evaluate + screenshot) — for scroll/layout claims, move the USER'S scroller (set scrollTop, assert it sticks); programmatic scrolls pass where wheel-scrolling is broken.
4. Restart ritual → commit (message = user-visible defect + mechanism) → push → deploy watch.
Status the user on a CADENCE — each wave boundary + each long silent stretch (R#9 build heartbeat: a watchable surface, not a changelog) — never only reactively; "before they ask twice" is the floor, and a queued complaint is a work item, not an interruption.
Every push: precheck green BEFORE it (never after a failure report); a checkpoint commit BEFORE each destructive rework wave (R#50(4)); and the rework DIFFS against the manifest's feature inventory (R#50(6)) — a rewrite silently dropping a shipped element is the regression class users catch.

## Cache + served-version discipline (from v1)

Stale browser cache mimics regressions: the user reports a fixed bug or a vanished feature while hosted provably serves the new code. From v1:
- `Cache-Control: no-cache` on the HTML + version-query asset links (`app.js?v=<version>`) so every swap invalidates.
- A version endpoint (healthz carrying semver/sha) + a visible served-version indicator, plus an in-app watcher that nudges "new version available — refresh".
- First stale-looking report → verify the SERVED version first (curl the marker/version), then instruct a hard refresh — never patch code against a stale report.
- A SECOND same-class stale report = a mechanism gap (missing headers/watcher), not a second explanation (R#33 mechanism-hunt).

## Async-run surfaces (design against "running forever")

Every in-app surface tracking an async run (pipeline, background job, long search):
- Explicit TERMINAL **and** STALLED states in the UI — "running" with no progress is a display-bug class to design against, not an edge case.
- Server-side stale detection: a non-terminal run older than the measured pipeline envelope flips to failed/interrupted with a human-readable reason — the UI never inherits an eternal "running".
- Poll the SPECIFIC execution by id — never enumerate a recent-executions list that parallel child runs flood (the children hide the parent).
- Poll budgets derive from MEASURED latency: a fixed short deadline strands legitimately long runs as stale "running".
- Timeout + non-2xx throw on EVERY orchestration fetch (one hung request must not freeze the run's state machine); boot-restore MERGES and never clobbers a mid-flight run; ghost runs get a cleanup path.

A "live/updated" claim is CONTENT-verified: screenshot/read AFTER the served content marker confirms — a mid-load frame or a HEALTHY event is not served state (R#20 server-response variant; watch mechanics → `deploy-guide.md`).

**The fleet driver arms on the FIRST lane death, not the Nth (R#29).** A 500/529/ENOTFOUND wave is Anthropic-infra, not a build defect — the persistent Monitor/driver that retries dead lanes on backoff is armed the moment the first lane dies, so the user never becomes the retry loop (measured: the user typed "Can you try again" four times across 86 minutes because the driver — which existed — armed 4 hours late). **A WAVE BOUNDARY (a lane done / a round opening or closing / a limit wave) triggers an EXHAUSTIVE roster reconciliation from the DURABLE feed** (not recall): every dispatched-not-completed lane is woken, replaced, or retired WITH A REASON; the BUILD-MODE roster is the survivable source, so a multi-session build never loses its dispatch count (measured: 22 lanes fired, 0 recorded, because the tally lived only in a session feed that reset).

## Screenshots (review + evidence)
Landing dirs (probed 2026-07, superseding the earlier "relative paths vanish" note): a bare relative filename lands in the PROJECT ROOT (the MCP's cwd) — real but repo-littering; the MCP's own artifacts land in `<project>/.playwright-mcp/`. ## 1. VERIFY, NEVER ASSUME

**Never report a pass you did not observe.**

- A check that has never failed is not a check. Before trusting any new test or guard,
  **break the thing it protects and watch it go red on that exact case**, then restore.
  If it cannot be made to fail, it is decoration — say so or delete it.
- **Assert identity, not shape.** "It returned a function", "it didn't throw", "the keys
  are right" are all true of the *wrong* answer. Compare to the expected value, or assert
  *which* collaborator was used.
- **A zero result is a claim about your probe, not about the world.** Before believing
  "not found" / "no matches" / "no rows", carry a **positive control** — something you
  know is present. If the control comes back empty, the probe is broken and the zero
  means nothing.
- **An error is not an answer.** Fallbacks (`||`, `2>/dev/null`, a default value) turn a
  failure into a confident wrong result. Confirm your check actually ran.
- **"I could not read it" ≠ "it is not set."** Two different sentences. Never merge them.
- A tool reporting success is not success — verify the artifact it claims to have made.
- A dashboard, a status field, or a cached value showing X is not X being true right now.
- **Source is intent; the built artifact is what shipped.** When the question is "what do
  users get", inspect what is deployed, not the repository.
- When documentation and observed behaviour disagree, **reality wins** — then write down
  what reality did.

**Always say which:** *"I verified X by doing Y"* or *"I did not verify this."* Never
present an assumption as a finding. If you were wrong or broke something, say so plainly
and fix it. An honest "unverified" is worth more than a confident guess and is never
penalised.

## 2. MOMENTUM

Decisions over questions. Reverse on **evidence**, not by asking.

Answer it yourself when the choice is reversible, when an existing rule settles it, or
when you can verify it — by reading the code, running the command, checking the type.
Most "should I…?" questions are answerable. Answer, state the decision in one line, proceed.

**Stop and ask only when** the action is irreversible *and* genuinely ambiguous, touches
production/money/customer data, or requires an authority you do not have. Then: drive the
work to the last safe step, present one recommendation with a one-line reason, and hand over.

**Understand before you edit.** Trace the root cause; do not patch the symptom. Read the
closest existing equivalent end-to-end before writing a new variant of it — the pattern,
the traps, and the reason for both are already in there.

## 3. SCOPE

Do the task that was asked. Do all of it.

- **Touch it, fix it.** A file you edit leaves your hands clean: no dead code, no `any`,
  no suppression comments, no TODO. If a proper fix is genuinely too large for this pass,
  say so explicitly and file it — never leave a marker and move on.
- **Before you write any code, climb three rungs and stop at the first that holds.**
  (a) Is it already in THIS repo — a helper, a pattern, a few files over? Reuse it.
  (b) Does the standard library or the platform do it natively — `<input type="date">`
  over a hand-built picker, CSS over JS, a built-in over a hand-rolled? Use the native
  thing. (c) Can it be one line? Make it one line. Never add a dependency for what a few
  lines cover; between two options the same size, take the one correct on edge cases.
  This shortens the SOLUTION, never the reading — and it never cuts: validation at trust
  boundaries, error handling, the three data states, accessibility, or anything
  explicitly asked for. (Raced A/B before adoption: 2×2 lanes on a frozen fixture —
  ladder arms shipped fewer lines with every state and every guard intact.)
- **Do not silently widen or narrow scope.** Finishing less than asked is not your call;
  say what you left out and why. Doing more than asked is equally a defect.
- **No bulk find-and-replace across many files.** A scripted rename cannot see context and
  will mangle strings, comments and near-matches. Edit deliberately, or split the work.
- Finish or don't start. "Partially migrated" is a state that costs more than either end.

### Server-side shape

Route-independent on purpose: this block travels INLINE in every executor dispatch, so the layering
rules reach whoever writes server code even when no backend lane was spawned. The measured failure
is exactly that — the layering half never entered a build because its only carrier was an agent
file nobody dispatched.

- **Domain entities and value objects hold the rules.** A rule that lives only in a route handler
  is a rule the next caller does not get.
- **Use cases orchestrate and do no I/O.** No framework types, no request objects, no direct
  adapter imports. Importing an adapter into a use case means the design is wrong, not the import.
- **One method per port, named `execute`, with an adapter behind it.** A port with five methods is
  a class wearing a port's name.
- **Return `Result<T, E>`, and capture the REAL error before mapping.** Logging the generic status
  throws away the one field that names the cause.
- **Tenant scope comes from the authenticated context.** Never from a request body, never from a
  module constant. ✗ `const CENTRE_ID = "…"` interpolated into SQL — the measured instance, and it
  is a data-leak shape, not a style preference. ✓ the scope arrives with the caller's identity.
- **Validate at the boundary with the shared schema; never cast.** A cast is a validation you
  decided not to write.

✗ a 250-line route handler doing parsing, business rules, persistence and formatting — the measured
instance, and it was the application layer by accident. WhyWrong: nothing in it can be called from
a second entry point, tested without HTTP, or reviewed for the rule it actually encodes.
✓ handler parses and delegates · use case decides · port persists — each testable alone.

## 4. HARD BOUNDARIES

- **Never print, log, commit, or echo a secret value.** Read one credential into a
  variable; never dump a whole credential store. Name credentials by *path* and *scope*,
  never by value. If a value does land somewhere persistent, say so immediately and treat
  it as burned — it must be rotated, not just deleted.
- **Request the narrowest permission that does the job**, and justify each one in a line.
  A scope you cannot justify in one line is a scope you do not need.
- **Never bypass a safety mechanism** — no skipping hooks, no disabling a failing check, no
  force-push over someone's work. If a guard fires on you, it is either right (fix the code)
  or it is a bug in the guard (fix the guard, and add a case so the next run catches it).
- **Never delete or overwrite something you did not create** without surfacing it first.
  Before any destructive action, inventory the full footprint and confirm ownership in
  *every* place ownership could live — a negative in the obvious place is not proof.
- **Build-then-swap on anything live.** Create the new resource, move the pointer, delete
  the old one last. Delete-then-create is an outage.
- Production writes require explicit approval. Non-production writes are fine — show
  before and after.

## 5. THE RECORD

A fact discovered once and written nowhere is a fact that will be paid for again.

Before you finish, ask: **what do I know now that was not written down 20 minutes ago?**
If the answer is anything at all, record it — a durable fact, a trap, a command that works,
a command that does not and why, a question you opened, a question you closed.

Write **mechanism, not status.** "The build is green" is stale within the hour. "This
build ignores changes under `packages/` because of a path filter" is true next quarter.
Correct anything you find wrong in the record, in place — a record people stop trusting is
worse than none.

## 6. REPORTING

Lead with the outcome, then the evidence. State plainly: what you did, **what you verified
and how**, what is still open, what needs a decision from someone else. No preamble, no
filler, no restating the request. Match the reader — assume an engineer.

## 7. DEFINITION OF DONE

1. It works **and you observed it working** — name the specific evidence.
2. Every check you added has been made to fail on purpose at least once.
3. What you learned is written where the next agent will find it.
4. You reported: done, verified how, still open, needs a human.

If #2 or #3 did not happen, you are not done.

## The handoff schema

Every handoff between crew roles is this structure. It is the only thing that crosses a
role boundary — an agent must not read another agent's reasoning transcript, only its
handoff. The orchestrator rejects a handoff missing `verified` (with a `how` for each
claim) or `unverified` — empty `unverified` is allowed; absent is not.

```yaml
from: <role>
to: <role>
task: "<one-line task>"

# What is now true, that the receiver can rely on
delivered:
  - path: <file>
    exports: [<symbols>]
    note: "<the invariant the artifact enforces>"

# What the receiver must do
required:
  - "<obligation, stated as a testable sentence>"

# What the sender verified, and how — never a bare claim
verified:
  - claim: "<the property>"
    how: "<the observation: what was driven/parsed/mutated and what was asserted>"

# What the sender did NOT verify — as important as the above
unverified:
  - "<the gap, named honestly>"

# Where the receiver will get hurt
traps:
  - "<law id>: <the concrete trap in this codebase>"

# Which laws the receiver must load (3-6, from laws.md's router)
laws: [<ids>]
```

**The two fields people delete first are the two that carry the value.** `verified` with
its `how` is what stops the receiver re-proving work or trusting work that was never
proven. `unverified` is what stops a gap being laundered into a fact by the next hop.

# Edge identity — who the platform says is calling

!! Read BEFORE the first server route, the first "who is the user" branch, and any line of sign-in code. The platform has already authenticated the caller by the time a request reaches the app — an app that builds a login is re-implementing a control that already ran, and building a SECOND, weaker one. !!

The policy half — PRIVATE vs PUBLIC, the `vibe_app` × `group` × `viewer` grant, the dashboard step — is `archetypes.md` "Boundary notes". This file is the RUNTIME half: what arrives on the wire, and what may be trusted about it.

## The three headers

Every request that reaches the app carries all three. Traefik's ForwardAuth middleware calls the edge authorizer first; the authorizer answers 200 with these headers, and Traefik copies them onto the upstream request.

| Header | Carries |
|---|---|
| `X-Vibe-User-Id` | the stable Nexus user id — **the key app-side data attaches to**. Empty string when there is no person |
| `X-Vibe-User-Email` | the signed-in user's email, for display. Empty string when there is no person. **Never a join key** — email changes, the id does not |
| `X-Vibe-Auth-Via` | which credential got the caller in: `session` · `app-token` · `public`. Exactly these three strings |

The app reads them. That is the whole integration — no SDK, no callback to the platform, no token exchange, no user list to sync.

## What arrives, per path

| Caller | `X-Vibe-Auth-Via` | `X-Vibe-User-Id` | `X-Vibe-User-Email` |
|---|---|---|---|
| a person signed in with Nexus | `session` | the user id | their email (may be empty) |
| a machine presenting the app's edge token (`X-Vibe-App-Token`) — registered agent tools | `app-token` | **empty** | **empty** |
| anyone at all, on a PUBLIC app | `public` | **empty** | **empty** |

A PUBLIC app is not "signed in as nobody" — it is **not authenticated at all**, and the edge says so in `X-Vibe-Auth-Via` rather than by omitting a header.

## The app owns no identity

- ✗ a `users` table, a `passwords`/`credentials` column, a session store, an OAuth client, a "log in" screen, an invite flow
- ✓ app-side rows keyed on `X-Vibe-User-Id` — preferences, assignments, drafts, audit rows

Membership ("may this person open this app at all") is decided by the platform before the request exists. **Roles beyond that are NOT in the headers** — nothing carries owner-vs-editor-vs-viewer today. An app that genuinely needs admin-vs-member derives it app-side from its own table keyed on the user id, and says so in the PRD; it still never authenticates anyone.

## ‼ Trust boundary — the middleware is the control, not the header

The headers are trustworthy for exactly one reason: **the authorizer writes all three on every allow, and Traefik overwrites whatever the client sent.** A caller who sets `X-Vibe-User-Id: someone-else` has it replaced before the app sees it. Three consequences, and each one is a hole if missed.

**1. Presence is not identity.** All three headers always arrive, so `if (req.headers['x-vibe-user-id'])` is not a signed-in check — on a PUBLIC app it reads an empty string, and on some servers an empty header still tests as present. Branch on `X-Vibe-Auth-Via === 'session'`, or on a NON-EMPTY id. Never on the header existing.

```
✗  const userId = req.headers['x-vibe-user-id'];        // "" on public + app-token
   if (userId) { /* treats "" as anonymous only by luck of the runtime */ }

✓  const via = req.headers['x-vibe-auth-via'];
   const userId = req.headers['x-vibe-user-id'] || null;
   const person = via === 'session' && userId ? { userId, email: ... } : null;
```

**2. Only these three names are overwritten.** The middleware copies exactly the names it lists, and the list and the writer are the same constants. **An `X-Vibe-*` name the app invents is not in that list, so it is passed straight through from the client — a client-controlled string wearing a platform prefix.** Do not read a header the platform does not write, and do not add one to carry a role.

**3. Off the edge, the headers are whatever the caller typed.** Local dev, a direct container port, a health checker, any second ingress — nothing overwrites them there, because the overwrite is the middleware's, not the app's. So the deployed app must be reachable ONLY through the edge, and a local dev server must treat the headers as a fixture it supplies to itself, never as evidence. A dev-mode impersonation switch is fine; shipping one that a deployed build can reach is the hole.

## Reserved paths — `/.vibe/*` never reaches the app

The edge intercepts these on the app's own host and answers them itself, before the access decision. A route the app defines here is dead code that never receives a request:

| Path | Is |
|---|---|
| `/.vibe/callback` | where a minted assertion is handed back and turned into the `vibe_session` cookie |
| `/.vibe/edge-probe` | the platform's routing-reachability probe; deliberately answered non-2xx |

Do not serve, proxy, or rewrite anything under `/.vibe/`. Do not read, set, or clear the `vibe_session` cookie — it is the edge's credential, verified before the app is reached, and an app that touches it can only break a session it cannot mint.

## Sign-in needs no app code

A browser with no valid session, navigating to a PRIVATE app, is redirected by the edge to the console's sign-in, authorized there against the org's real grants, and returned to the URL it asked for with the cookie set. **The app is not in that loop and renders no part of it.** There is no sign-in button to build, no redirect to construct, no return URL to thread through the app.

What the app SHOULD render is the signed-in state it now has for free: "signed in as `X-Vibe-User-Email`".

## Failing this contract

App-side auth exists only as the recorded FALLBACK on a PUBLIC app, taking the owner's quoted go (`Access:` in the PRD) — and public still means AUTHENTICATED, never open. Reaching for a login screen without that recorded decline is the failure this file exists to prevent: it ships a second credential for the same person, a password store the org never asked for, and a user list that drifts from the org's real membership the day someone leaves.

Access ladder + the grant's dashboard step → `archetypes.md` "Boundary notes". The PRD's `Access:` line → `prd-template.md`.

# Feature-manifest format (the parse contract)

The repo's feature/test contract at `docs/feature-manifest.md` — the SAME
convention the starter seeds and SKILL.md defines (one row per feature, written
the wave it ships). This file is the machine-parse companion: the deploy gate
(DG1) and the dropped-features tripwire (MAN1) parse EXACTLY this shape; a
non-standard table is invisible to both (they stay silent, never guess).

| Feature | Primitive | How to exercise | VISIBLE outcome | Last verified |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| grid-view | wf_9f2… | open /records, click Grid | rows render with data | 2026-07-22 local |
| csv-export | mock | Records → Export | file downloads | 2026-07-21 local |
| legacy-import | removed | — | — | retired PR #61, superseded by csv-export |

Parse contract (what the hooks read):

- **Feature** (col 1) = the stable key. Never rename a shipped row; retire it.
  The key also names the feature's journey in `journeys/run.mjs`.
- **Primitive** (col 2) = the backing Nexus resource id; `mock` while stubbed;
  **`removed`** when a feature is DELIBERATELY retired (keep the row, set the
  cell). DG1 flags an empty/`?`/`TBD` Primitive not marked mock (unwired
  feature — a UI capability with no primitive is ❌ untested, R#27 app twin).
- **How to exercise** (col 3) = the exact click path.
- **VISIBLE outcome** (col 4) = what a human sees that proves it ("the API
  returns 200" is not visible — under-specified).
- **Last verified** (col 5) = PER-ROW provenance stamped by the journey runner: the
  exact journey/probe + date + local/hosted. A blanket backfill (one string pasted
  down the column) is fabrication — a row's stamp changes only when ITS journey ran.
- **Reactivity (data surfaces)** = a feature that reads or edits server data MUST assert
  its applicable R1/R4 predicate (`frontend-architecture.md` §6) in its VISIBLE-outcome +
  journey ("rows stay visible while the filter reloads" / "the create shows without a
  manual refresh"). A data-surface row with no reactivity assertion is `❌ untested`
  (R#27 app twin) — the same class DG1 flags for an empty Primitive.
- **Performance (data surfaces)** = a data-surface feature also asserts its measured-latency
  outcome (R7, `frontend-architecture.md` §6) in its journey — driven at the latency-floor
  fixture, cold and warm, against the PRD `Perf-budget:` line. A data-surface row with no perf
  assertion is `❌ untested`, the same class as a missing reactivity assertion.
- **Owner-render-review (human-facing surfaces)** = a surface feature is not done until the
  OWNER has seen it RENDERED at both viewports on real populated data (the pick's viewports).
  Its `Last verified` stamp names the owner-render-review (date + both-viewport shots on real
  data), not only a journey pass — a green journey proves the path runs, not that the owner saw
  the surface. Felt properties (reactivity, perceived speed) are invisible to
  `tsc`/units/screenshots; only the owner operating it finds them (`design-round.md` "Screens are
  SEEN, not read"; R#27 render-evidence). A human-facing surface row with no owner-render-review
  is `❌ untested`.

MAN1 (dropped-features tripwire): at `git push` it compares the pushed manifest
(`git show @{upstream}:docs/feature-manifest.md`, fallback origin/main) against

# FLEET RESOURCES — concurrency, ports, kills, merges

> LOAD WHEN: running more than one lane/agent against the same machine or repo (build fleet,
> reviewer council, assessor sweep). Every rule here is a paid-for incident class: an
> oversubscribed machine poisons VERDICTS (a reviewer scoring a starved server files false
> defects), a broad kill takes out a sibling's server, a shared mutable store contaminates
> every later screenshot.

---

## Concurrency + machine-health (no cap — health-gated)

- **There is NO seat cap.** A wave runs EVERY seat its roster declares (review wave = ALL 7
  reviewers + ALL 21 assessors — the user's standing call), and as many lanes as the work
  needs, provided (i) no lane duplicates another's assignment (no double work — disjoint
  contracts, one writer per artifact) and (ii) the harness concurrency ceiling in
  settings.json is high enough (currently 100 concurrent / 1000 per session — raise it
  there if a topology ever needs more; never silently trim the roster instead).
- **Machine health is a VERDICT-VALIDITY signal, not a cap.** Before verdict-bearing work
  (a shoot, a review drive, a timing measurement) a lane checks load; any verdict taken
  while the machine was starved (load spike, server deaths, killed renders) is
  AUTO-RE-REVIEWED, never trusted — the measured incident class is poisoned verdicts, and
  re-review is cheaper than one wrong score. Log the health check + any re-review verdict
  swap in the lane's own output (countable).
- **Budget before a big wave:** check load/free memory, then fire the FULL roster anyway —
  stagger STARTS (not the roster) if load is already hot, and prefer more machines/worktrees
  over fewer seats. API-side stall under many lanes = throttle signal: pace, never trim.
- **EXECUTION lanes fan out to the DAG's level WIDTH** (SKILL "The dependency DAG +
  scheduler"): launch every ready lane, AS MANY AS POSSIBLE, health-gated — never a count cap.
  The speed lever is a WIDER DAG (partition into the finest clean disjoint slices); quality is
  held REGARDLESS of width by the DAG invariants (disjoint `owns` + a standalone acceptance +
  spine-rooted). The port/kill/worktree/quiesced-merge rules in THIS file ARE the inter-lane
  conflict-avoidance foundation and bind every execution lane — parallel execution keeps them
  all, it does not loosen them.

## Model policy per lane

A lane's model is a DECIDED parameter, not an inheritance default. Silent inheritance spent it
wrong in both directions on one build: a cheap mechanical lane ran on the most expensive tier while
a judging seat ran on a cheap one, which is the worst possible allocation of the same budget.

"Judgment" is NOT one tier — GENERATIVE/taste judgment and RECALL judgment split, because the measured
best allocation differs (a bake-off finding, not a preference):

| Lane class | Tier | Why |
|---|---|---|
| GENERATIVE / TASTE judgment — architect · taste · design-director · redesigner | the TOP tier available (a taste-specialised model where the account has one — e.g. Fable-class — preferred for architect · taste · redesigner) | vision and taste, not recall; a wrong direction costs a whole wave, and the QA recall rule below does not apply to a role that PROPOSES (the per-surface `app-redesigner` proposes alternatives, so it rides TOP, never the RECALL/EXECUTION tiers) |
| RECALL judgment — reviewer · assessor | one or two tiers BELOW the top (recall-first) | MEASURED best catch-rate on confirmed defects at the lowest cost (blind bake-off); its over-calls are a cheap, filterable class — never read raw scores as quality (the most LENIENT config scores highest) |
| EXECUTION — executor · contracts · backend · tests · migrations · release | one or two tiers BELOW the top | throughput work against a written contract; the contract, not the model, is what makes it correct. A lane that SELF-VERIFIES against a contract stays below-top; only a step with NO judgment content (captures/renames/port sweeps) drops to the CHEAPEST tier |
| VERIFICATION — tester · journey-verifier | one or two tiers below | driving and asserting a stated outcome is mechanical; the cast persona carries the judgment |
| code dimension, 2nd pass | + ONE independent TOP-tier pass | the one dimension where a second model surfaced real unique defects |

**Verify-gate + revisit:** never trust a lone high-thinking PASS on a MUST-invariant — cross-check via a
reviewer that drives the adversarial surface; any reviewer `critical` gets an independent main-loop
re-drive BEFORE it drives a fix (the over-call class is real; the gate is minutes). Premium tier capped →
main loop as fallback-critic. Revisit assignments by BLIND bake-off (catch-rate on confirmed defects),
never by vibe.

**Check before you rely on it, in this order:**
1. **What exists** — read the tiers actually available to THIS account; never hardcode a name from
   memory, and never assume last month's top tier is still the top tier.
2. **That it has usage** — a tier at its limit is not available. Confirm before committing a wave
   to it, because discovering it mid-wave costs the wave, not the dispatch.
3. **That it fires** — one throwaway dispatch on the chosen tier before a 27-seat wave rides on it.

Name the model per lane in the dispatch (hook MODEL1 nudges when it is absent) and record the
per-lane mapping in the BUILD-MODE card's `Lanes + models` row, so the wave's cost is legible
before it runs rather than after.

## Ports + binaries

- **Unique port per instance, derived + verified free** — never hardcoded (fleet agents
  collide on fixed ports):
  ```bash
  PORT=$(( 4400 + (RANDOM % 400) ))
  while lsof -i :$PORT >/dev/null 2>&1; do PORT=$(( 4400 + (RANDOM % 400) )); done
  ```
- **Uniquely-named server binary per instance** (`cp server/server.mjs server/exec-$PORT.mjs`)
  so a pattern-kill on the shared name cannot take you down — and so YOUR kill can name
  exactly you.
- Keep per-band conventions when many lanes run (e.g. executors 4400-4499, reviewers
  4500-4599) so a port in a log identifies its owner.

## Kills — self-scoped, never broad

- **Never `pkill -f` a shared pattern** (`pkill -f server.mjs` killed every sibling's
  server). Kill by YOUR unique binary name or the recorded PID only.
- **The user preview surface is EXCLUDED from every fleet kill-scope** — it is a
  deliverable with its own owner (`dev-loop.md` "## The preview-surface contract (fleet builds)"); a cleanup sweep
  that takes down the preview is the incident, not hygiene.
- Before any kill: `lsof -i :$PORT` / `ps` the exact target; a kill is a destructive
  command — issue it alone (R#5).

## Isolated seeded instances

- **One shared mutable server across N mutating reviewers = cross-contamination.** A
  reviewer that drives a state-changing action (decides a record, seals an entity) changes
  what every LATER reviewer sees — their screenshots show the mutated state and their
  verdicts are about the wrong baseline.
- Rule: **every mutating reviewer gets its OWN served instance** (own port, own in-memory
  store — restart re-seeds). Read-only reviewers may share. If a shared store was mutated
  mid-round, the round's later verdicts are re-reviewed, not trusted.
- Checks that assert transitions carry the both-poles guard anyway (scripts/
  guard-fix-authoring.md) so a pre-mutated store cannot false-fail them.

## Suite locks

- Two agents running the same test/journey suite against one instance interleave state.
  A lockfile per suite+instance (`/tmp/<suite>-<port>.lock` — create atomically, wait or
  pick another instance if held, remove in a trap) — the lock protocol exists because a
  suite once killed a sibling's run mid-flight.

## Worktrees, fork-base protection, merges

- **Lane isolation default = a git worktree** per lane. Where a worktree cannot be created,
  the fallback is an rsync COPY with `node_modules` symlinked (fast, disk-cheap):
  `rsync -a --exclude node_modules <repo>/ <copy>/ && ln -s <repo>/node_modules <copy>/node_modules`.
- **Fork-base protection:** land the executor's in-flight fixes BEFORE forking copies for
  parallel work — a copy forked mid-fix carries the broken base and every lane re-meets the
  same defect.
- **SNAPSHOT-READY quiesced merges:** merge from a lane only at a declared quiescent point
  (the lane stopped, its gate green, its worktree committed) — never from a lane mid-edit.
- **Foundation broadcasts are scoped cherry-picks, never wholesale syncs:** a broadcast
  that copies the foundation over lanes clobbers co-owned files mid-flight. Cherry-pick the
  named files only, and run a **post-sync line-count diff** on every touched file — a file
  that shrank unexpectedly is a clobber caught before it ships. Merge diff sanity includes
  the **doc-mass-deletion tripwire**: a merge deleting doc/spec content it did not set out
  to touch is held for review, not landed.

## Journey/verification targets

- **`JOURNEY_URL` (or any verification target) NEVER defaults to the live preview** — a
  journey run against the user's preview instance mutates the surface the user is watching.
  Verification drives an isolated instance; the preview is refreshed by MERGES, not by test
  traffic.

# Incident forensics — eight priors (read FIRST when something breaks)

Each prior replaces a measured misdiagnosis. Order of hypotheses, not conclusions.

1. **Error text is a POINTER, not a cause.** "No key provided to sign" meant an EMPTY ENV VAR upstream of the signer. Trace the input of the failing call before believing its message.
2. **Boot crash on missing files = DELIVERY failure first.** Files may never have shipped (push swallowed, parts missing) — verify the artifact at the remote/HEAD before adopting a framework-specific theory (the plausible Dockerfile story cost a detour).
3. **"HEALTHY but 404" = the edge/routing layer.** A healthy allocation that's unreachable is not an app bug — don't debug the container.
4. **A surprising E2E count = DATA hypothesis before code.** Check iteration count → resolved inputs → the FIXTURE itself (a dead test entity masquerades as a pipeline bug).
5. **Localhost/prod divergence = diff the SERVED versions first.** Version skew mimics environment bugs; only after versions match, debug the code.
6. **"Can't scroll / frozen" = console FIRST.** A JS throw mid-render presents as a layout/scroll complaint; read the exceptions before suspecting CSS.
7. **A funnel/pipeline question = ONE provenance query first.** With `discovered_via`-class provenance and per-drop `reason` columns in the store (archetypes.md data-layer defaults), "why is X empty / where did my rows go" resolves in a single warehouse query — read provenance before instrumenting or theorizing. No provenance columns = the store is under-designed; fix that before debugging through it.
8. **Work vanished with no error = check the swap window.** In-memory queues/backfills die with the old container at a deploy swap (deploy-guide "Platform mechanics") — re-run from the store; then space bulk work away from swaps or write through per item.

## Silent-failure catalogue (working backend, dead UI)

Hunt these classes per wave — each yields a spinner-forever or stuck state over a perfectly healthy backend:

| Class | Tell |
|---|---|
| Response-field mismatch | UI reads `resp.text`, route returns `{rewritten}` — spinner forever, backend fine |
| Nested envelope | UI reads flat, route returns `{data:{credentials:[…]}}` — "connecting…" stuck after success |
| Bare-array result | UI expects an object envelope, endpoint returns `[…]` — first-parse crash |
| Undefined CSS var | a `var(--x)` referenced but never defined — transparent/invisible panel |
| Route/regex key mismatch | ids with `:` or unusual chars break a route pattern — 404 on real records only |
| Required-but-hidden form element | an empty `required` field blocks submit with no visible error |

Probe the RESPONSE SHAPE per endpoint at first wiring (`jq keys` / log the raw body) — sibling endpoints legitimately differ; the same probe-first rule that governs CLI commands governs the app's own routes (CLAUDE.md "API Envelopes").

# FRONTEND ARCHITECTURE — where state lives, when a component splits, how CSS layers, the a11y floor

> LOAD WHEN: writing or reviewing any user-facing view. `ux-canon.md` governs how a surface LOOKS
> and READS (IA, type scale, measure, component inventory). This file governs how it is BUILT.
> Read both before the first unit of a surface; a compaction voids the read.

Every rule below is a paid-for defect class, measured on shipped code. Where a number appears, it
was counted.

---

## 1. State placement — four homes, one test

Most frontend tangle is state in the wrong home. Ask one question before adding any state:

> **The Blast Test: who else needs to know this changed?**

| Who needs it | Home | Shape |
|---|---|---|
| One element, dies with it | local `useState` inside that element | anything |
| One view's children | ONE state object in the view, passed down | a single `{}` + a reducer-ish updater, not 10 sibling `useState`s |
| Two sibling views | the route/page shell above both | lift once, never sync two copies |
| The whole app, or it survives navigation | the app store / URL / server | URL for anything a user could bookmark or a colleague could be sent |

**Server data is not state — it is a cache.** Anything fetched has three visible conditions
(loading, error, empty) and a fourth invisible one (stale). A view that renders only the success
condition is unfinished, not minimal.

WRONG: ten `useState` calls at the top of a view, mutated from six handlers — every handler must
now remember which four to update together. WhyWrong: the invariant lives in the developer's head,
so the first missed pair is a silent inconsistency the type system cannot see.
RIGHT: one state object for the view plus derived values computed at render — the invariant is a
single assignment, and an impossible combination is unrepresentable.

WRONG: `const [saving, setSaving] = useState(false)` plus `const [error, setError] = useState()`
plus `const [data, setData] = useState()` for one fetch. WhyWrong: three booleans encode eight
states, five of which are nonsense (saving AND error AND data).
RIGHT: one `status: 'idle' | 'loading' | 'ready' | 'error'` discriminated union carrying its
payload — the nonsense states cannot be written.

### 1a. The client data layer — a NAMED library, never-blank, shared cache, tag invalidation

Server reads go through a **NAMED server-state library** (RTK Query / TanStack Query), never a per-page
hand-rolled fetch (a bespoke loader gets the hard parts — races — right and the easy-to-notice parts —
blanking, dedup, invalidation — wrong, and it fans out into every surface that copies it). The layer's
scope is bounded by ENFORCEABILITY — freeze exactly what a type, a static check, or a journey can
verify; leave the rest to review/taste. **Four enforceable roots:**

1. **The typed store SHAPE** as a contract type — TypeScript compile-enforces every consumer; a
   component physically cannot build against a different shape.
2. **Unidirectional data-flow + mutation discipline** — components read via selectors, mutate only via
   actions/dispatch (static check: no direct store write; no shared server-value in a component's own
   `useState`).
3. **The selector/subscription pattern** — a reusable read template every surface instantiates; shared
   data is read through it, never re-fetched or duplicated per component.
4. **A reactivity ACCEPTANCE JOURNEY** — "a value change propagates live to every view that shows it".

**Three mechanics, each an unwritable-defect rule:**
- **Cache-then-revalidate (never-blank):** a read keeps its last value visible while a refetch is in
  flight — a loading state is NEVER rendered OVER data already on screen (a `ready` status wins over
  `fetching` once data exists). Closes: a refetch blanking the surface to a spinner on every
  dependency change or write.
- **One cache entry per key (shared cache):** a value two surfaces read is ONE entry; both react to one
  write. Never two independent fetches of the same server value. Closes: the same value fetched
  independently by N surfaces → drift.
- **Tag invalidation:** a write names the tags it dirties; every query whose tags intersect revalidates
  through its stored fetcher — no per-call-site reload. Closes: a hand-wired reload racing derived UI
  state and wiping it before paint.

## 2. When a component splits — five triggers, none of them "it feels long"

Line count is the last trigger, not the first. Split when ANY of these fire:

| Trigger | The signal | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| **Two reasons to change** | design touches one half, logic the other | every edit risks the unrelated half |
| **A named thing appears** | you write a comment like `// the day cell` | the comment is the component's name asking to exist |
| **Hook cluster** | ≥6 hooks in one function body | the body is now several behaviours sharing a scope by accident |
| **Prop drilling ≥2 levels** | a prop passed through a component that ignores it | the middle layer knows a secret it does not use |
| **Line limits** | component >200 lines, module >120 | the mechanical backstop (`guard.sh structural`) |

**The Extraction Test:** can you name the piece in 1-3 words WITHOUT using "and", "wrapper", or
"section"? If yes, it is a component. If the only honest name is "the middle bit", the seam is
wrong — find the real one.

WRONG (measured): a 428-line view function running 10 hooks before its first extracted child; 18
hook calls in the file. WhyWrong: nothing in it can be tested, reused, or re-rendered independently,
and every future change lands in one 428-line diff surface.
RIGHT: the view keeps orchestration and one state object; the day cell, the controls row, and the
legend are components with their own props — each nameable in two words.

**Exclusion — do NOT split when:** the piece is used once, has no state, and is under ~30 lines of
markup. Splitting that produces indirection with no reader benefit. A file with three small,
clearly-named local components is better than three files.

---

## 2a. The frontend seam ladder — where a unit becomes a FILE somebody can own

§2 answers a CRAFT question: when does this component deserve to be its own thing? This answers an
OWNERSHIP question: **what shape must the tree have so N units are N artifacts N lanes can own?**
They are different questions with different answers, and a build that only asks the first one arrives
at fan-out with eight units and four files (`REF/plan-format.md`, Step 4b — the ceiling is a property
of the TREE).

Descend these rungs IN ORDER, and stop the moment ownable-artifacts ≥ units. Each rung names its
directory, because a rung with no naming convention produces a tree nobody can predict
(`plan-format.md` Step 5b.3).

| # | Split at | Lives at | What one lane then owns |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **the route / screen** | `routes/<route>/` (flat tree: `<route>.html`) | a whole screen, top to bottom |
| 2 | **the view shell vs its named children** | `routes/<route>/index.*` + `routes/<route>/<Child>.*` | the shell keeps orchestration and the ONE state object; each named child is a file |
| 3 | **the shared component** (used by ≥2 routes) | `components/<Name>/` | the component, for every consumer at once |
| 4 | **the CSS layer** (§3) | `styles/tokens.*` · `primitives.*` · `<component>.*` · `responsive.*` | one layer, and NOTHING reaches across layers |
| 5 | **the data shape vs its fixtures** | `data/` (shape) · `fixtures/<lane>.json` (additive) | a fixture per lane, appended by ADDING a file |
| 6 | **the acceptance suite** | `journeys/<lane>.py`, globbed by a ROOT-OWNED runner | its own journeys, with its own allocated id range |

**Rung 2 is the one that raises the ceiling most cheaply**, and it is the one most often skipped
because §2's craft triggers do not fire on it: a 300-line screen with three obviously-named regions
passes every craft test as one file, and is a hard ceiling of ONE lane. Measured: a wave of 8 units
over 4 files merged broken (7 conflicts, suite 18/64, seams 1/15); the identical cut after the root
split ONE screen into its components merged clean with seams intact.

**A VIEWPORT IS A SURFACE BUT NOT AN ARTIFACT, and that resolves a real collision in the doctrine.**
`plan-format.md` counts desktop and mobile of one screen as TWO surfaces (they are two renders with
two sets of failures), while Step 4b caps lanes at ownable artifacts. When both viewports live in one
file behind media queries, those two rules point opposite ways. The resolution is rung 4, and it is
exactly two options:
- descend to rung 4 so the responsive layer is its own file, and the mobile lane owns it; **or**
- keep both viewports in ONE lane and write the `unsplittable_reason`.

Two lanes on one unsplit file is not the third option — it is the measured failure above.

**The split is the ROOT'S commit, before fan-out.** A lane that restructures its own file mid-wave
changes what every sibling diffs against. If rung 2 or 3 is needed, it lands in the root's tree and is
merged before lane one starts.

**The floor: §2's exclusion still binds.** A piece used once, holding no state, under ~30 lines of
markup does NOT become a file just to raise the lane count. If the tree bottoms out before
artifacts ≥ units, the remaining units merge into lanes that carry a written reason. Fan-out width is
never bought by inventing indirection.

## 3. The CSS layering contract — four layers, in this order

| Layer | What lives here | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 1 TOKENS | the design lock's values, and nothing else | `--dao-ink`, `--space-2`, `--radius-cta` |
| 2 PRIMITIVES | element-level defaults | `button`, `input`, `table` base |
| 3 COMPONENTS | one block per named component, in the component's own order | `.daoDay`, `.daoBanner` |
| 4 STATE + RESPONSIVE | modifiers and breakpoints, adjacent to their component AND last in the cascade for it | `.daoDay[data-state="unavailable"]`, the `≤760px` block |

**"Adjacent" is an AUTHORING rule; "last" is a CORRECTNESS rule. They are not alternatives, and
reading them as alternatives is how a mobile layout silently loses.** Adjacency says where a rule
LIVES — with the component it styles, so one file holds one component's whole story and one lane
owns it (§2a rung 4). Cascade order says which rule WINS — a breakpoint block of equal specificity
loses to any later rule that touches the same property, so within its own file the responsive block
comes last, and a per-route responsive stylesheet is linked last for that route. A media query
authored beside its component and then overridden by a later rule is not a layout bug you can see
in the source; the CSS is exactly what you wrote and the phone still renders the desktop layout.
✗ reading these as a fork and picking one → either the rule drifts away from its component, or it
sits beside it and quietly loses.
✓ both: it lives with its component, and nothing of equal specificity follows it.

Rules that keep the layers honest:
- **Every value in layer 3+ is a token reference.** A raw hex or px in a component block is a token
  that was never named — name it in layer 1 or use the existing one.
- **No `!important`.** It means two rules disagree about ownership; fix the ownership. (Measured
  counter-example worth keeping: an 860-line stylesheet with 47 section comments and ZERO
  `!important` — layering discipline is achievable at that size.)
- **Inline `style={{}}` only for genuinely computed values** (a measured width, a transform from a
  drag). A static inline style is a component rule in the wrong layer. (Measured: 23 inline-style
  sites across 6 pages — each one invisible to the stylesheet and to every later theme change.)
- **State is an ATTRIBUTE, not a class name.** `data-state="unavailable"` over `.is-unavailable`:
  the attribute is readable in the DOM, assertable in a test, and cannot silently coexist with a
  contradictory sibling class.

**The Grep Test:** grep the stylesheet for a hex value. If any appear outside layer 1, the token
layer is not the source of truth yet.

## 4. The a11y floor — mechanical, not aspirational

Six checks. All are automatable; none require a screen-reader session to catch.

| # | Floor | How it is checked |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Every interactive element is a real control (`button`, `a[href]`, `input`) or has `role` + `tabindex` + key handlers | grep for `onClick` on `div`/`span` → each must justify itself |
| 2 | Every control has an accessible name | axe-core / `getByRole` in the journey suite; a name that only exists visually fails |
| 3 | State is announced, not only coloured | a toggle carries `aria-pressed`; a current nav item carries `aria-current`; a live region announces async results |
| 4 | Focus is visible and never trapped | keyboard walk of the primary journey: every stop visible, no dead end |
| 5 | Colour is never the only signal | text or icon accompanies every colour-coded state |
| 6 | Text meets contrast at its real rendered size | contrast run on the captured screenshot, not on the token table |

Measured baseline this floor was written against: 21 `role=`, 8 `aria-label`, **1** `aria-pressed`,
**1** `aria-current` across a whole app whose core interaction is a four-state toggle grid. Checks
1-2 were largely met; checks 3-5 were the gap — the app's central control announced nothing.

WRONG: a shift cell that turns terracotta when selected, with `aria-label` naming the shift only.
WhyWrong: the label describes the cell, not its state, so a non-visual user cannot tell selected
from empty — and the measured defect went further: the label said one thing while the stored value
said another.
RIGHT: `<button aria-pressed={state==='available'} aria-label="Monday morning, available">` — state
lives in the attribute the platform already announces, and the label matches the stored value.

**ANTI-RATIONALISATION — do NOT relabel an a11y gap as:**
- "internal tool, no external users" — the floor is six mechanical checks, not a compliance program;
  they cost minutes and they also make every journey test assertable.
- "the design doesn't have a focus style" — a design without a focus style is an incomplete design;
  take it back to the lock, do not ship a keyboard dead end.
- "we'll add labels at the end" — labels added after the fact describe the markup that exists
  rather than the state that matters, which is how check 3 gets missed.

## 5. What "done" means for a view

Before a view is reported done, all six hold:
1. The state has ONE home per the Blast Test, and loading/error/empty conditions render; server reads go through the §1a client data layer (never-blank), and the surface's applicable R1–R7 predicates (§6) are asserted in the journey — not by inspection.
2. No split trigger is outstanding, or the outstanding one is named in the report with its reason.
3. `guard.sh structural` is green for the view's files (or its red rows are named as accepted debt).
4. The six a11y floor checks pass, evidenced by the journey suite (not by inspection).
5. The stylesheet touches only its own component layer, with every value token-referenced.
6. The view's measured latency (cold AND warm, at the latency-floor fixture) is within the PRD `Perf-budget:` line, or the overrun is named in the report with its cause.

---

## 6. Reactivity acceptance predicates — per data surface, driven journey assertions

A data surface asserts its applicable predicates in the journey suite; a data surface with NONE is
`❌ untested` (R#27 app twin), the same class as a UI feature with no primitive. These replace the
unfalsifiable "loading/empty/error triad" todo (which ships as blank regions because a prose todo with
no assertion cannot fail).

| # | Predicate | The assertion the journey drives | Rung |
|---|---|---|---|
| R1 | never-blank-what-was-shown | a filter/tab/nav/post-write refetch keeps prior rows visible (dimmed/busy) while new ones arrive | **2** — nav + filter axes driven by `guard.sh reactivity`; the post-write axis is rung 3 |
| R2 | first paint is content-shaped, not a word | a shared skeleton at the app's latency profile — assert `scrollHeight > innerHeight` at the latency rungs | **2** for the word-gate half (`guard.sh structural` statically, `guard.sh reactivity` on the served app); rung 3 for "content-shaped" |
| R3 | independent reads go out together | one parallel round of requests, not N sequential | **3** — the waterfall is RECORDED into `docs/REACTIVITY.md`, never verdicted |
| R4 | a control's effect is visible on the control | type in a filter → rows change or the control says why (no inert control) | **2** for a tagged `[data-surface-filter]`; rung 3 for anything untagged |
| R5 | in-progress input survives navigation | typed-but-unsaved values persist across a tab tap, a route change, and a failed write | **2** for the tagged filter across a route change; rung 3 for form fields and the failed-write axis |
| R6 | one search idiom app-wide | substring + accent/case-insensitive everywhere a thing is picked | **2** — case and accent folding driven per surface, plus a cross-surface agreement arm |
| R7 | measured speed within budget | the journey drives at the latency-floor fixture and measures route-read latency COLD and WARM separately against the PRD `Perf-budget:` line (a mean hides the cold path); returning to a visited surface refires only what changed — a full refetch storm on return is a fail even when each read is fast | **2** — `guard.sh perf` + the `PERFEV` check; warm gated, cold recorded |

### 6a. What the gate decides, and what it deliberately does not

The rung column is the honest one. `gates-and-ledger.md` says a gate that passes when the defect is
present is worse than none, so every arm this gate cannot decide is printed as its own `NOT-DRIVEN`
row rather than folded into a green.

**Two attributes arm it**, the `[data-mustsee]` precedent — the build tags, the gate drives what is
tagged, and ZERO tagged is a RED rather than a pass:

- `[data-surface]` — a data surface's content root (R1, R2)
- `[data-surface-filter]` — that surface's filter/search input (R1-filter, R4, R5, R6)

**And one machine row arms it**, the `Perf-budget:` precedent — in `docs/PRD.md`, naming which
predicates each surface carries. No row = reasoned GREEN, printed:

    Reactivity: /#/o/companies R1,R2,R4,R5,R6 · /#/o/deals R1,R2

**R3 is recorded, never gated.** The gate counts the non-asset requests a route load fires and how
many started after another had already finished, and writes that chain into the evidence. It does not
verdict it: nothing in a browser distinguishes a legitimately DEPENDENT chain (read the config, then
read the rows it names) from a serial waterfall, and a version driven by an author's declaration of
independence passes by under-declaring. Read the chain; there is no verdict to read.

**R2's "content-shaped" half is not decided either.** The word-gate half is — a loading state whose
whole rendered text is `Loading…` is the defect verbatim, catchable in the source and on the served
app. But "content-shaped" has no app-independent test: every candidate either invents a threshold or
contradicts the layer-3 no-scroll assertion, which requires the SETTLED page to fit the viewport and
so forbids the `scrollHeight > innerHeight` this table asks for. That half stays a review obligation.

**The residual hole in R4/R5/R6 is under-tagging.** A control the build never tagged is invisible
here. Zero tagged on a route that declares the predicate is a RED, which forces the first tag; it
does not force the last one.

Move it toward rung 1. | Rung | Mechanism | Failure rate | Cost | |---|---|---|---| | **1. Impossible** | Types, scoped tools, an API that cannot express the mistake | ~0 | high, once | | **2. Hoped** | "The agent knows better" | high | pay on incident | Rung 3 fails **silently and unevenly** — a prompt rule holds on turn 4 and slips on turn 40 under context pressure, and nothing marks the difference. **The rule: any rule that is violated twice becomes a gate.** Not a stronger prompt — a deterministic check in the guard suite. A third violation is a decision you made. (Executed live: the engine-entry rule was violated twice → BLD2 is now rung 2 — a DENY on zero-crew push/deploy with no `docs/BUILD-MODE.md` card, the card being its artifact.) **Instrument it:** a gate that never fires is either unnecessary or broken — check its self-test before concluding unnecessary (a scanner pointed at nothing has a perfect record). Never route around it, and never add a SILENT bypass — an invisible escape hatch is a rung-3 prompt wearing a costume. A deliberate override is allowed only when it is EXPLICIT, VISIBLE and LOGGED (the shipped form: re-issue the SAME command with `NEXUS_GATE_ACK=1` / `NEXUS_SOLO_ACK=1`), so every use is countable evidence about the gate. - **State-aware checks:** a check whose precondition is absent by design (the feature is behind a not-yet-built state, the record is sealed, the route is not seeded) returns a **reasoned GREEN** — it prints *why* it did not run, never a silent pass.
