The served bundle is what ships (L08); the dev server proves nothing about it. 3. **`guard.sh scroll`** — headless no-scroll assertion at the spec viewports, PLUS the `[data-mustsee]` visibility gate: every act-critical element (the primary action, the money total, the thing the user came for) is in-viewport AND hit-testable. Zero tagged elements is a RED, not a pass — tagging `data-mustsee` on act-critical elements is a build deliverable. 4. **`guard.sh fix`** — the per-app deterministic fix-gate (`guard-fix.mjs`, authored per `scripts/guard-fix-authoring.md`): one driven check per fixed defect, each asserting the *visible outcome* of the fix on the served app. 5. **`guard.sh perf`** — the measured-speed gate (the bundle-size budget SKILL.md P3 promises lives HERE): served-bundle size and route-read latency — cold AND warm, at the latency-floor fixture — measured against the PRD's `Perf-budget:` line, and the result written to `docs/PERF.md` (date · numbers · pass/fail per budget component; the evidence artifact the PERFEV check reads). No `Perf-budget:` line in the PRD = reasoned GREEN (prints why); a budget component exceeded = RED. 6. **`guard.sh reactivity`** — the driven R1–R6 gate (`frontend-architecture.md` §6): it reads the PRD's `Reactivity:` row, drives each declared surface in a real browser, and writes `docs/REACTIVITY.md` (per-predicate verdicts; the evidence artifact the REACTEV check reads). No `Reactivity:` row = reasoned GREEN (prints why). A predicate the gate cannot decide — R3's waterfall, R2's "content-shaped" half, the post-write and untagged-control axes — is printed as its own `RECORDED` or `NOT-DRIVEN` row and never counted as a pass. R7 is layer 5's job, not this one's. 7. **`guard.sh divergence`** — the serving-copy gate vs the PRD's `Read-path:` row: for every read surface declared as a `projection` (a SECOND COPY of a client-owned source of truth), the declared `divergence` check must exist and pass; `divergence none`, a missing check, or a failing one is RED. `divergence none` is legal ONLY for the modes that keep no copy (`direct`, `connector`). No `Read-path:` row = reasoned GREEN (prints why). Writes `docs/DIVERGENCE.md`. Detail: `performance-playbook.md` (the diagnosis ladder that picks the read path) and `prd-template.md`'s Data-architecture row (where the pick is recorded). This layer was previously documented only inside those two files, so an executor reading THIS doc — the one SKILL.md names as the guard suite's owner — never learned it existed; a projection could ship with `divergence none` while every layer here stayed green. Exit 0 = all green. Any RED = the build is NOT done — no completion word, no handoff. **Wave-close verification reads the TREE, never lane self-reports.** In one measured wave a lane reported a destructive write it never made while a sibling made one silently — a self-report is wrong in both directions. The wave-close check is `git status` + the diff; and before any corrective broadcast that could touch tracked files, run the git-recoverability check on the files at risk (tracked → an overwrite is reversible; untracked → protect first). --- ## The check-ratchet **Every fixed defect gains a permanent driven check the same round it is fixed.** The executor closes an issue → the orchestrator (or the executor, in the same pass) adds the check to the fix-gate → the gate re-tests it every subsequent round automatically. Push items under the gate aggressively: a subjective `visual` item can silently regress; a gated one cannot. The ratchet only tightens — a check, once added, is never removed while its feature exists (retiring a feature retires its checks in the same change, stated in the ledger). --- ## ISSUE-LEDGER — the single cross-round source of truth One file per build (`ISSUE-LEDGER.md` in the repo or the orchestration workspace). Every issue ever found gets a **STABLE id**. Each round, the orchestrator MATCHES every incoming finding to an existing id or mints a new one — then compares states: - An id that was `fixed` and reappears is a **REGRESSION** — surfaced explicitly, and it **outranks new work** (the loop is not making progress if greens are silently going red). - The executor receives THIS WHOLE FILE each round: `fixed` rows are **DO NOT REGRESS** obligations; `open`/`regressed` rows are the work. - Per-round reviewer dumps (`/tmp//*.json`) are *inputs* to the ledger, never the memory itself. ### Format ```markdown # ISSUE-LEDGER — (single source of truth across ALL rounds) Status: open · in-progress · fixed · regressed · dropped · floor · by-design · challenge · out-of-scope `check`: the fix-gate id that mechanically re-tests it (or `visual`/`manual`/`—`). ## In-scope issues | id | severity | issue | check | status | history (round: state) | fix / evidence | |----|----------|-------|-------|--------|------------------------|----------------| | I1 | blocker | not enforced at the source () | | fixed | r1:fixed · r2:verified | guard at source, handler-level. DO NOT REGRESS | | I2 | high | clipped at | | open | r2:found | | ## Out-of-scope (separate owners — the full-viewport review keeps surfacing these) | id | issue | owner | |----|-------|-------| | O1 | | | ## Adversarial floor (a top-1%-or-FAIL stance NEVER clears these — sign-off, not a fix loop) F1 · F2 <…> ## Round-N close-out ``` ### The row vocabulary, precisely - **severity** — blocker/critical · high · medium · low. A `critical` from a reviewer only enters as `open` after the verify-gate re-drive confirms it (see the skill's model policy). - **check** — the deterministic gate id once one exists; `visual`/`manual` marks the regression-vulnerable rows (candidates for the ratchet); `—` for verdicting rows. - **history** — append-only `rN:state` chain. The history IS the whack-a-mole detector. - **DO NOT REGRESS** — written into the fix/evidence cell of every verified-fixed row; the executor re-reads it every round. ### Adversarial floor + out-of-scope + the judgment layer Row classes that exist so the STOP CONDITION can be honest: - **Floor rows (F#)** — systemic craft gaps a maximum-severity reviewing stance will ALWAYS raise (the palette is ordinary, the hierarchy is flat). They never converge to zero by iteration; clearing them is a redesign decision, not a fix loop. Naming them keeps the loop from chasing them forever. **Before a finding lands as a floor row, check it against the CONTRACT BLOCK — a "gap" the design lock mandates is `by-design`, not floor.** - **By-design rows (B#)** — generic-canon findings the design contract deliberately overrides (locked monochrome vs hue-variety, locked sparseness vs density). NOT defects, never in the fix loop, never counted against convergence; kept so the next reviewer wave doesn't re-find them (matched like any stable id). An intent EXECUTED badly is a normal defect row, not by-design. - **Contract-challenge rows (CH#)** — a seat's case that the locked intent harms the JOB itself (canon · contract · concrete job impact). Routed to the user as a re-pick question; `resolved: lock-stands | re-picked` is the only close. Sign-off items, never fix-loop rows; a re-pick converts them into a NEW design-lock commit + a plan delta. - **Out-of-scope rows (O#)** — real defects owned by another surface (the app shell, the design tokens, a vendored component). Tracked so they are not silently lost; never counted against this build's convergence. ### STOP CONDITION The loop stops when: **no in-scope `open`/`regressed` row at critical/HIGH severity remains, no `challenge` row unresolved, and the full deterministic gate is GREEN with zero regressions on an independently re-run clean build.** Residual = floor rows + by-design rows + resolved challenges + out-of-scope rows = sign-off items presented to the user, not loop work. (Full convergence criteria incl. the per-lens score bars: `SKILL.md` "## The crew ENGINE — plan → contracts → build → review → converge (runs inside P3↔P5)".) --- ## Anti-patterns | Anti-pattern | Why it fails | Do instead | |---|---|---| | Fresh issue list per round | The same defect gets re-found, re-argued, re-fixed; regressions invisible | One ledger, stable ids, history chain | | LLM summarizes reviewer output into the ledger | Detail dropped, hedges stripped, severities drift | Deterministic collate (`collate.mjs --ledger docs/ISSUE-LEDGER.md --round ` — it MINTS the ids and flips a re-found `fixed` row to `regressed`; Cue owns only the closure columns) | | Fix verified only by the fixer's screenshot | L01 — the check inherits the blind spot | Ratchet a driven check into the fix-gate | | Bypass flag "for this one push" | The gate is now a suggestion; the next agent inherits the flag | Fix the code or fix the gate + self-test | | Chasing floor rows in the fix loop | They never clear; the loop never terminates | Mark F#, surface at sign-off | | Deleting a regressed row's history | The whack-a-mole evidence is the history | Append `rN:regressed`, escalate priority |

# Lane contract — the delegation pre-flight (R#50(5) operational form)

> Lifecycle around this pre-flight (spawn → report-before-idle → verify-stopped → quiesced merge → teardown+tombstone → liveness/reset recovery) → `../SKILL.md` "Lane lifecycle" (the crew ENGINE). This file owns the pre-flight decision itself.

!! Emit this table BEFORE spawning ANY build/craft lane (any workstream — app, deck, doc pipeline; the C2 hook nudges it on fan-out). The dividing law: **contract-checkability.** PLUMBING (adapters, data, endpoints, exports, mappings, verification) has a machine-checkable spec; CRAFT (visual identity, copy voice, the first unit of any surface) does not — its only judge is the user, and integration serialises "parallel" craft anyway. !!

## Pre-flight table (one row per unit considered for delegation)

| Unit | Work type (CRAFT / PLUMBING / VERIFICATION) | Contract written? (the checkable spec) | **INPUTS pre-provisioned** (fork point · doctrine · specs/boards · fixtures · shared harness) | Self-verification harness (assertions · typecheck · journey) | Output/writeback path (FILLED — a `<placeholder>` is empty) | Delivery mode | Integration + review owner | Model / effort (explicit) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

**Gate rules:**
- A CRAFT row routes to the ONE persistent `app-executor` (the engine's craft instance — re-awoken per round, never a sibling); the main loop's craft duty is JUDGMENT of each first unit (R#50(5)), never relaying the executor's self-assessment. **Craft JUDGEMENT = 1, not craft PRODUCTION.** One judge holds taste for one surface; the ✗ form is N ad-hoc lanes all deciding what "good" means (parallelism goes BELOW the one judge, never BESIDE it). It is NOT a cap on how many INDEPENDENT units are produced at once: **N alternatives, or N surfaces, are N disjoint lanes even though the work is visual** — they merely have to converge on one judge. Measured: the rule as previously worded ("craft concurrency = 1") was read three independent times as "never spawn a second design lane", and a request for six alternatives plus "several surfaces — build them properly" ran as ONE lane each time. The units were independent; only the taste call was not. A craft unit built by the main loop instead takes the disclosed, card-quoted solo go (SKILL entry gate).
- A PLUMBING row spawns ONLY when Contract + Self-verification are both filled. The proven template: a resident worker on a WRITTEN wire-contract brief, self-verifying with an assertion suite it runs itself, useful across phases. The anti-pattern: N design lanes delivering artifacts a human must hand-merge.
- VERIFICATION rows are delegate-safe (verification ≠ craft): a read-only journey/assert lane (the `journey-verifier` agent) that writes verdicts to `docs/COVERAGE.md`; the main loop spot-checks one result before relaying green.
- **Delivery mode DEFAULT = `isolation:"worktree"`** (the harness gives the lane its own git worktree; auto-cleaned if unchanged) — it removes the out-of-repo APPLY.md integration tax. Out-of-repo artifact delivery is the FALLBACK when a worktree is unavailable, priced as integration work. A shared repo takes exactly ONE writer (R#50(1)).
- **INPUTS are provisioned BY THE SPAWNER, never hunted by the lane.** The worktree is created AT the briefed fork point already carrying the lane doctrine, the spec/design boards it builds against, its fixtures, and the shared test harness. A `<not provisioned>` cell means the lane spends its first minutes finding its own inputs — measured at a 24.3 min mean spawn-to-first-source-write, with the SAME repair performed independently by all three lanes of one wave: *"my worktree is one commit behind the stated fork point, and the doctrine file is not here."* Provisioning converts a variable cost every lane pays into a fixed cost the spawner pays once. It closes two further failure modes: a lane building from PROSE because the real board is not in its tree (one measured 25-min rebuild when the board arrived mid-run), and a mid-run file drop into a running lane's worktree, which no lane can distinguish from its own work.
- **Model/effort is EXPLICIT per lane** — an ad-hoc lane silently inherits the expensive session model. Mechanical/plumbing lanes name a cheap model + modest effort; the session model is reserved for judgment lanes (architecture, adversarial verify, synthesis). A lane brief is a DATA PACKET (atoms/values/paths + the contract), never a step-by-step mechanism.
- **Task-record hygiene:** one record = ONE owner; a lane reports completion to its owner and never re-opens/reassigns a record it doesn't own — crossed "reopened assignment" echoes are transport noise the owner reconciles (R#9).
- **Lane artifact names — the harness vetoes four prefixes.** Claude Code ≥ 2.1.220 refuses a SUBAGENT `Write` whose basename matches `/^(REPORT|SUMMARY|FINDINGS|ANALYSIS).*\.md$/i`, with "Subagents should return findings as text…" (predicate read from the shipped binary, 2026-08-06; measured live twice in one week — a consolidation lane's `report-1-*.md`, an app lane's `REPORT.md`, each discovered only as a mid-flight tool error inside the lane). So a brief NEVER names a lane-written `.md` whose basename starts with one of those four words. Canonical names: `dossier-<topic>.md` · `entry-N-<slug>.md` · `HANDOFF.md` · `COVERAGE.md`. Directory names are free (`consolidation-reports/` is fine; `…/report-1.md` inside it is not). A Bash-written file bypasses the veto — an EMERGENCY hatch for a name that cannot move, never the default: it leans on a loophole the vendor may close. The `LANE-MD` hook enforces this at dispatch: a banned name pointing at a NONEXISTENT file (necessarily a write target) is denied with the rename in the message; one pointing at an existing file (probably a read-reference) warns.

## Kit-first briefs + fleet sequencing (front-end/component lanes)

Measured in one 87-lane build: lanes obey briefs exactly (41/41 opened the motion canon when a brief named its path) — so every rule here is about what the BRIEF carries, and each one's absence was paid for once.

- **The kit read order rides every craft brief, BY PATH** — the resolved `@agent-nexus/apps-ui` root's `AGENTS.md` → `docs/INDEX.md`/`catalog.json` → `docs/CHOOSING.md` → `docs/MOTION.md`. Never hand-assemble a per-lane read list, never re-inline what the canon states (the same ~600-char token map re-inlined into 22 briefs = 13KB of drift surface; the kit's front door reached 1 of 87 briefs while every failure traced to brief content).
- **A named precedent is acquired at SOURCE before it is briefed.** A repo/file the owner names is opened and cited file+line in the brief; a deployed site or compiled bundle is a pointer, never the spec (six lanes briefed off a minified bundle while the source repo sat on local disk → wholesale rejection: "the lane have been lazy" — and the lane had reproduced the thin brief faithfully).
- **Fidelity-contract shape for port/build briefs:** the spec file IS the contract — enumerate EVERY feature/state/micro-interaction FIRST, then implement; an allowed-deviation allowlist (tokens for colors, host props for demo data, the shared motion vocabulary for local keyframes); `spec_checklist_count: N` in the return JSON; a silently dropped feature is a defect, and the brief STATES the reason the rule exists. (The two waves with sub-1,300-char briefs were the two the owner rejected wholesale; the fidelity-contract wave drew zero per-component rejections.)
- **A brief's VERIFY command is proven able to fail before it ships.** A filtered grep over an erroring command returns empty and reads as pass (61/87 briefs carried a tsc verify while tsc could not run at all; count `'error TS'`, never `grep -c '^src/'`).
- **Engine-before-instances.** Before N lanes touch one shared mechanic (drag, FLIP/reflow, anchored overlay, reduced-motion, token reads), ONE lane lands the shared primitive and the consumer briefs name it by path; a lane that finds a defect in shared code it does not own REPORTS and PAUSES on that mechanic — never forks (a 73-min lane forked three components off the shared engine it couldn't fix; 6 of 13 landed engines ended with zero consumers while the same mechanics were re-implemented 3–12×). For multi-lane UI work, schedule the estate-wide CONVERGENCE audit (computed-style variance: radii, shadows, type ramp, spacing, timings) as a planned wave — style variance is "the predictable cost of 30 parallel lanes making local calls", not a surprise.
- **A producing lane's done includes its preview wiring.** A component lands rendered on the shared preview/showcase surface in the SAME lane; built-but-invisible reads as not done ("all built, all invisible to you" took two owner interventions to surface).
- **Liveness is read from the lane's own record** (transcript/task state), never from output-file presence — an artifact appears at the END of the work, and a roster tool that under-reports is an instrument to distrust (a false `ls` probe spawned 7 duplicate lanes and one lost-update race). Re-awake the original lane with named gaps (SendMessage); respawn only after a resume provably fails.
- **A shared instrument defect is fixed once, centrally, and its workaround broadcast** into the contract every lane reads — three lanes independently rediscovered the same capture bug; a discovering lane's repro scripts and ruled-out hypotheses ride the fixing lane's brief.

✗ a redesign panic fans out 4 design lanes + 4 build lanes on the session model; a safety rule forces out-of-repo APPLY.md delivery; every output hand-merges through the main loop while the user rejects the look twice — the parallelism bought integration debt. → ✓ the pre-flight: the visual direction is CRAFT (main loop, one direction at a time against the design lock); the adapter is PLUMBING (wire contract + "123 assertions green" + worktree + named cheap model); the journey run is VERIFICATION (journey-verifier → COVERAGE.md).

## The partition is an ARTIFACT, not a decision you remember

**Before the first lane of a fan-out is dispatched, the partition is WRITTEN to `docs/lane-dag.json`** — one row per lane: `id`, `owns` (exclusive globs), `depends_on`, `surfaces`, `unsplittable_reason`; plus top-level `units` (the unit count BEFORE any merging), `digest` and `root_files`. Full schema → `plan-format.md`. **`units` is what makes under-decomposition visible:** every other field describes the lanes that exist, so a partition that quietly merged eight units into four lanes looks identical to one that only ever had four. Deciding the width has its own procedure — `plan-format.md` "HOW TO DECOMPOSE" Step 4b, "Raising the ceiling" (count units, count ownable files, split the tree until they match) and the per-stack seam ladders it gates into. This is not app-build ceremony; it is what makes the partition checkable at all:

- **A partition held only in the dispatcher's head cannot be wrong, because nothing can read it.** Two registered checks (`FANOUT-ROOTS`, `PARTITION-VALID`) exist to catch a cyclic, overlapping, unclosed or fat partition, and both have produced ZERO rows in the estate's entire history — not because partitions were always sound, but because the file they read was never written by anything.
- **`surfaces` is the row that matters here.** One user-facing surface per lane; a lane claiming two needs a non-empty `unsplittable_reason`. Desktop and mobile of one screen are TWO surfaces. Countable, so it is arithmetic rather than a judgement call.
- **It costs one Write.** The dispatcher already decided the partition to write the briefs; serialising it is the difference between a decision and an auditable one.

✗ six alternatives and "several surfaces — build them properly" dispatched as ONE lane, no partition file, nothing able to notice → the wave runs at the speed of its fattest lane and the cause is invisible afterwards. → ✓ the partition written first, one lane per surface, `surfaces` filled on every row — and if the honest answer is one lane, that is a row with a reason, not an absent file.

## Target quiescence (pre-flight row for any MEASURING lane)

A lane whose verdict depends on a target's state records the target's HEAD and newest mtime AT
DISPATCH, and re-checks both AT CONSUME. A foreign writer between the two stamps invalidates the
measurement: re-run it, or scope the verdict to the stamped sha and say so.

```bash
git -C <target> log -1 --format=%h     # stamp at dispatch, compare at consume
git -C <target> status --short | head
```

Two commands, seconds each. Measured cost of skipping them: a doctrine probe ran 29 minutes against
a repo another session rebuilt twice underneath it, and the collision surfaced only in that lane's
own disclosure 31 minutes later — by which time its verdict had already been read as fact.

## Ruling size

A ruling to a lane is ≤~1,200 chars: the decision, the reason in one line, the next contracted item.
Context the lane already has is not re-sent; a spec longer than that belongs in a file the lane READS
(path in the message), never in the message body. Measured: a 2,752-char average across 108 messages
on a single serial path — an essay per message, where a file pointer costs the lane one Read and the
orchestrator nothing.

## Typed output per lane class (collate rejects an unknown shape)

A lane's final message is a machine-read object, not prose. `collate.mjs` normalises two shapes and
REJECTS anything else rather than silently scoring it `?` — a council file that collated to
`| ? | — | — |` contributed zero rows to a round nobody noticed was short.

| Lane class | REQUIRED keys |
|---|---|
| reviewer | `dimension` · `score` · `verdict` · `defects[]{severity, element, defect, corrected_target, evidence}` |
| assessor | `category` · `category_score` · `summary` · `dimensions[]{id, name, weight, score, reasoning, evidence, climb}` |
| tester | `persona` · `goals[]` · `verdict` (BROKEN-FOR-ME / CONFUSING / SLOW-ENOUGH-TO-QUIT / WORKS-BUT-WRONG / FINE / DELIGHTFUL) · `captures[]` |
| journey-verifier | `journeys[]{id, target (LOCAL/HOSTED), visible_outcome, verdict, evidence}` |
| tests | `checks[]{name, target, mutation_evidence}` · `unit_test_log` |
| taste | `changes[]{element, before, after, why}` · `gate_rerun` |
| every class | `docs_briefed[]` · `docs_read[]` (SKILL.md "Orchestrator card (Cue)", the read-completion bullet) · `code_organisation` where the lane wrote code |

`severity` values come from the vocabulary `blocker|critical|high|major|medium|moderate|low|minor|
trivial`. A value outside it sorts as `low` and slips under the critical/HIGH stop condition, so
collate rejects it by name.

# Family A — Evidence & Verification

*The false-green class. If you only enforce one family, enforce this one.*

### L01 — A check inherits the blind spot that wrote it
**Trigger:** writing a test or guard for code you also wrote.
**Mechanism:** the check encodes the same mental model as the code. If the model is wrong,
both are wrong *and they agree*. Agreement then reads as confirmation.
**Check:** break the guarded behaviour, watch the check fail **on that exact case**, restore.
A check never seen red is decoration.
**Seen:** a policy derived from a written description of the code; the detector built to
catch it scanned directories that generate nothing and reported success.

### L02 — A passing test may be asserting nothing
**Trigger:** a green test is your evidence that a fix works.
**Mechanism:** tests that assert shape (`typeof === "function"`, "no throw", "has these keys")
are satisfied by the wrong answer as readily as the right one.
**Check:** mutation-test it — revert the fix, run the test, require red, restore. Restore from
a copy, not from version control, if the change is uncommitted.

### L03 — Unit-test the reachable path
**Trigger:** testing a function by constructing its input by hand.
**Mechanism:** hand-fed input can be a shape production never produces. The function is
correct on data that never arrives; the real caller passes something else.
**Check:** trace one real call path from entry point to the function. If you cannot, the test
proves the function works in isolation and nothing about the system.

### L04 — A search proves presence, never placement
**Trigger:** confirming something exists / is wired up by searching for it.
**Mechanism:** text found is text found — in a comment, a fixture, a different field, your own
notes from ten minutes ago.
**Check:** match structure, not substrings — the import statement, the registration call, the
field you actually mean. Then read the surrounding context to confirm it is that field.

### L05 — A failed probe reports zero
**Trigger:** concluding anything from an empty result.
**Mechanism:** a broken probe and a true negative are the same output. Unquoted globs, wrong
case, wrong directory, a wrapper whose exit code masks the tool's.
**Check:** carry a **positive control** — a term you know is present. Control empty ⇒ probe
broken ⇒ the zero is meaningless. Echo the real exit code when a wrapper is involved.

### L06 — An idempotent write is not a permission probe
**Trigger:** testing whether you have write access by writing.
**Mechanism:** many systems short-circuit a no-op write *before* the permission check and
return success. You learn nothing about your rights.
**Check:** probe with a value-changing write, then revert. Or read the permission directly.

### L07 — A still-running collector is not a measurement
**Trigger:** reading counts or output from a process you started.
**Mechanism:** a growing file, a partial stream, a paging API mid-walk — all yield a number
that is real, current, and wrong.
**Check:** confirm the process **exited**, with its status, before treating output as a result.

### L08 — Source is not deployed
**Trigger:** answering "do users have X?" / "how bad is the blast radius?"
**Mechanism:** the repository is intent. The built artifact is what shipped. Build-time
inlined values exist only in the artifact — and an unset variable often builds to empty
string, so the code path exists and fails at use rather than being absent.
**Check:** inspect the deployed artifact — the served bundle, the running image, the live
config. Carry a positive control (L05).

### L09 — Deploy history is not a deploy trigger
**Trigger:** concluding a change will ship automatically.
**Mechanism:** an all-green history proves past deploys succeeded. It says nothing about
whether *this* path fires one. Path filters, empty trigger lists, and manual-only workflows
are all invisible in history.
**Check:** read the trigger definition, then confirm a run actually fired after your merge.

### L10 — An index added is not an index used
**Trigger:** adding an index, or claiming a query is now fast.
**Mechanism:** the planner decides. An `OR` across two columns cannot use either single-column
index; a leading-wildcard match cannot use a b-tree; a type mismatch silently disqualifies one.
Some ORMs never index foreign keys automatically. And a name-only check counts invalid or
partially-built indexes as present.
**Check:** run the actual query and read the plan. The index name must appear in it.

### L11 — A green deploy is not a live rollout
**Trigger:** testing immediately after a deploy goes green.
**Mechanism:** green means the *deployment* was accepted. Rolling replacement takes minutes;
old instances serve throughout, and their shutdown noise looks exactly like new-version errors.
**Check:** wait for rollout completion and confirm the running version, then test. Errors during
the window are suspects, not evidence.

### L12 — A 200 from an async trigger says nothing about the work
**Trigger:** an integration that fires a job and reports the HTTP result.
**Mechanism:** the response acknowledges receipt. The actual work happens later, elsewhere, and
its failure never travels back up the call.
**Check:** assert on the downstream artifact or a status the job writes — never on the trigger's
status code.

### L13 — A tool reporting success is not success
**Trigger:** any generator, migrator, sync, or bulk operation that prints a summary.
**Mechanism:** "0 errors" frequently means "did nothing" — wrong filter, empty match set, silent
skip. Exit code 0 is compatible with a complete no-op.
**Check:** verify the artifact changed. Count before, count after, diff.

### L14 — "I could not read it" is not "it is not set"
**Trigger:** concluding a value is missing, empty, or unconfigured.
**Mechanism:** a blank read and an absent value are indistinguishable at the call site — but a
transient failure, a wrong scope, or a wrong region produces the first while the second is false.
**Check:** retry, then read through a second independent path before concluding absence.

### L15 — Specs live outside the type gate
**Trigger:** trusting that "it compiles" covers the test suite.
**Mechanism:** test files are commonly excluded from the type check, and many test runners strip
types rather than checking them. Broken specs pass local pre-commit and land red on CI —
or worse, land green and assert nothing.
**Check:** type-check tests explicitly, in CI, as its own step.

### L16 — Widening a minted credential does not widen the minted ones
**Trigger:** editing the constant/template that issues tokens, keys, or grants.
**Mechanism:** already-issued credentials carry the *old* shape forever. The fix is real, and
every existing holder is still broken.
**Check:** ship a reconcile on a path every existing holder traverses, and make it union the new
permissions onto the old — never replace.

### L17 — A comment asserting an unverified property is a defect
**Trigger:** writing a comment, commit message, or doc line claiming behaviour.
**Mechanism:** prose is unexecuted and unowned. It is trusted like a test and maintained like
nothing. A comment saying "this is idempotent" outlives the day it stopped being true.
**Check:** if the property matters, encode it as a test and delete the prose. If it does not
matter, delete the prose. Never assert in prose what you have not executed.

---

# Family B — Diagnosis

### L18 — Diagnose the mechanism, not the ticket
**Trigger:** a bug report that names a cause.
**Mechanism:** reports are written from symptoms. The named culprit is a guess by someone
further from the code than you, and it will steer you into an adjacent, innocent subsystem.
**Check:** reproduce, then trace the mechanism against the live system before writing code.
Re-file if the report is wrong.

### L19 — Check the envelope, not the contents
**Trigger:** every data check comes back clean and the consumer still breaks.
**Mechanism:** the bug is the field *name*, the wrapper, the casing, or the serialisation —
not the value. Renaming conventions often apply in both directions and cancel out locally
while breaking across the boundary.
**Check:** capture the actual payload at the boundary, both directions, and compare key names
byte-for-byte with what the consumer reads.

### L20 — Verify the request fired before blaming the server
**Trigger:** "the button does nothing."
**Mechanism:** a swallowed handler, an unconfirmed dialog, a disabled control, a client-side
validation return — all produce a UI that does nothing and a server that is innocent.
**Check:** read the network log first. No request ⇒ the bug is in front of you.

### L21 — Count surfaces, not gates
**Trigger:** "is this behind the flag?" / "who can reach this?"
**Mechanism:** the flag is one gate. The question is how many *surfaces* reach the behaviour —
a second route, an admin path, a webhook, a CLI, a cached client. Auditing the gate you know
about proves nothing about the ones you don't.
**Check:** enumerate every entry point that reaches the code, then check the gate on each.

### L22 — A permission error names no scope on purpose
**Trigger:** a 403 saying "check your permissions/scopes."
**Mechanism:** the message is deliberately non-specific — telling you which scope is missing
is an information leak. So you cannot tell a missing scope from a disabled feature from a
wrong tenant.
**Check:** drive the same operation through a *different* identity type (a session instead of a
token, an admin instead of a user). What changes discriminates the cause.

### L23 — An admin bypass hides the bug
**Trigger:** a failure only non-privileged users hit.
**Mechanism:** privileged users often take a different code path — an unfiltered query, a
skipped policy layer. Testing as an admin exercises code the reporter never runs.
**Check:** reproduce with the *least* privileged identity that should work. Always.

### L24 — Read rule order before rule content
**Trigger:** debugging any ordered rule engine — firewalls, routers, middleware, policies, CSS.
**Mechanism:** a terminating rule above your rule means yours never evaluates. Reading your
rule's content will convince you it is correct, because it is — and it never runs.
**Check:** read the ordered list first, find the first rule that matches and terminates, and
confirm yours is above it.

### L25 — Live state is not code state
**Trigger:** assuming the repository describes the running system.
**Mechanism:** hand-patched config, manual console edits, and hotfixes applied under pressure
are invisible in code. The next automated apply silently reverts them.
**Check:** read live configuration from the running system. When you hand-patch, file the code
fix in the same hour or it will be undone by the next deploy.

### L26 — Read the closest sibling end-to-end first
**Trigger:** building a new variant of something that already exists.
**Mechanism:** the existing one encodes traps you have not met, in code you will not think to
look for — registration sites, ordering constraints, cleanup paths.
**Check:** read one complete existing implementation, entry point to persistence, before writing
a line. Then list what your variant must differ in, and treat everything else as copy.

---

# Family C — Destructive & Irreversible

### L27 — Inventory the full footprint before teardown
**Trigger:** any destroy, drop, prune, or cleanup.
**Mechanism:** state files, registries, and consoles each show a *partial* view. Acting on one
leaves orphans that still bill, still resolve, still serve.
**Check:** enumerate live resources *and* declared state *and* every region/account/namespace
they could live in. Reconcile the lists before deleting anything.

### L28 — Ownership must be checked in every scope
**Trigger:** deleting or reclaiming something you did not just create.
**Mechanism:** "not found here" is a fact about where you looked. Ownership hides in another
tenant, another region, a soft-deleted row, a different account.
**Check:** enumerate every place ownership can live and get a negative from each. One negative
is not proof.

### L29 — Never probe a deny by doing it
**Trigger:** verifying a new restriction actually blocks something.
**Mechanism:** permission changes propagate asynchronously. Inside the window the destructive
action **succeeds** — and does the damage — while the policy is already correct.
**Check:** use the platform's simulate/dry-run/evaluate endpoint. If none exists, test on a
disposable resource, never the real one.

### L30 — Build then swap; never delete then create
**Trigger:** replacing anything live — a resource, a volume, a DNS record, a key.
**Mechanism:** delete-then-create is an outage by construction, and the two halves can deadlock:
the create needs the resource free, the release needs the old holder present. No single pass
satisfies both.
**Check:** create the replacement, verify it serves, move the pointer, delete the old one last.

### L31 — "Gone" is not unrecoverable
**Trigger:** treating data as lost, or acting *because* a record is gone.
**Mechanism:** deletions are rarely total. Backups, replicas, mirrors, audit logs, caches,
downstream copies, and object versions routinely survive the delete you are looking at.
**Check:** enumerate the survivors before concluding loss — and before taking an irreversible
action justified by the absence.

### L32 — A negated condition over a multi-value set matches nothing
**Trigger:** writing "deny everyone except these N" in any policy language.
**Mechanism:** a not-like/not-equals condition against a *list* is evaluated per value and
OR-ed. Principal A is not-B, so the deny fires on A too. The rule denies everyone — including
the ability to fix the rule.
**Check:** one condition operator per exception, AND-ed. Test with an allowed principal before
attaching. Confirm a break-glass identity exists.

### L33 — Retiring a role means stopping reads, not deleting it
**Trigger:** removing a permission, role, enum value, or feature.
**Mechanism:** deleting the definition breaks every holder immediately and irreversibly.
Removing the *reads* is reversible and has the same effect.
**Check:** remove every read path, deploy, observe zero usage over a full cycle, then decide
whether deletion is worth any risk at all. Usually it is not.

---

# Family D — Concurrency & Distributed Correctness

### L34 — Per-instance cursors replay
**Trigger:** any incremental job with a cursor, in an environment with more than one instance.
**Mechanism:** an in-memory cursor plus a rotating leader means each elected instance resumes
from *its own* stale position. Cumulative metrics multiply; side effects repeat.
**Check:** the cursor lives in shared storage. Advance it, then emit. Never the reverse.

### L35 — A timestamp watermark skips late-visible rows forever
**Trigger:** paging by `created_at` or any clock-derived cursor.
**Mechanism:** in transactional databases the timestamp is typically assigned at transaction
*start*. A long transaction commits a row whose timestamp is already behind your cursor — it
becomes visible after you passed it, and is never seen again.
**Check:** add a settle lag (exclude the most recent window), or page by a monotonic commit
sequence instead of a clock.

### L36 — Write the ledger before you emit
**Trigger:** any idempotency record paired with a side effect.
**Mechanism:** emit-then-record fails *open*: a crash between the two means the retry emits
again, forever. Record-then-emit fails *closed*: at worst one event is missed, and a missed
event is a bug you can find.
**Check:** persist the idempotency key first, in the same transaction if possible. Order matters
more than the retry policy.

### L37 — A table's name is not its contract
**Trigger:** skipping a lock because the table "is append-only" / "is a log" / "is history".
**Mechanism:** names describe intent at creation. Grep the writers: there is usually an update
path added later by someone who also believed the name.
**Check:** enumerate every writer before relying on any concurrency property. The writers are
the contract.

### L38 — A batched backfill must converge
**Trigger:** writing a loop that processes rows until a guard column is set.
**Mechanism:** if the guard is set from a source that can itself be null, the row stays
unqualified, is re-selected, and the loop runs forever — at full load, in production.
**Check:** the guard column must be written from a guaranteed-non-null source, and the loop must
assert the remaining count strictly decreases each pass.

### L39 — Swallowed background errors are a silent-failure factory
**Trigger:** fire-and-forget work — `void asyncFn()`, event callbacks, listeners, crons.
**Mechanism:** an unhandled rejection either kills the process or vanishes. Either way nobody
learns the work did not happen, and the absence of an error reads as success.
**Check:** every background path catches, logs at error level, **and** writes a queryable status
somewhere a human or a test can read. An alerting sink alone is not a status.

### L40 — A producer must chunk to the consumer's cap
**Trigger:** sending a batch to an endpoint with an array-size limit.
**Mechanism:** an over-limit batch is rejected whole, retried whole, and rejected again. The
queue never drains and the failure looks like a network problem.
**Check:** the producer's chunk size is derived from the consumer's declared cap, in code, with
a test that fails if the cap shrinks.

---

# Family E — Types & Contracts

### L41 — Parse at boundaries; never cast
**Trigger:** data arriving from a database JSON column, an HTTP body, a queue, a file.
**Mechanism:** a cast is a compile-time assertion about runtime data. It cannot fail, so
malformed data flows inward and detonates far from its origin.
**Check:** validate with a schema at the boundary. Use a non-throwing parse with an explicit
fallback where existing data may predate the schema — crashing on legacy rows is worse than
a documented default.

### L42 — Coercion accepts garbage silently
**Trigger:** any lenient coercion of external input — dates, numbers, booleans.
**Mechanism:** permissive coercion maps `0`, `false`, and `""` to real values — commonly the
epoch for dates. "Everything since the beginning of time" is a valid-looking filter that
selects the entire table.
**Check:** reject wrong-typed input *before* coercion, or narrow the accepted input type.

### L43 — A nullable structured column has three nulls
**Trigger:** writing to a nullable JSON/JSONB column, or reusing a create-mapper for updates.
**Mechanism:** SQL `NULL`, the JSON value `null`, and "leave unchanged" are three distinct
states. A mapper that folds null to undefined is safe on create and silently turns every
"clear this field" into a no-op on update.
**Check:** map the three states explicitly. Test the clear path — it is the one that breaks.

### L44 — Runtime parsing activates dormant constraints
**Trigger:** migrating a type-only path to one that validates at runtime.
**Mechanism:** over-strict constraints written years ago never ran. Turn on validation and they
all fire at once, on production data, at the call site — not at the schema.
**Check:** run the new validator against a sample of real production data before shipping. Fix
the contract, not the call sites.

### L45 — Changing an envelope breaks every consumer, not just yours
**Trigger:** altering a shared response shape, wrapper, or error contract.
**Mechanism:** consumers you did not write are parsing the old shape. Some already handle both;
some fail loudly; the dangerous ones fail silently by reading `undefined`.
**Check:** enumerate every consumer of the *path*, not of the module you are editing. Read each
one's parse logic before deciding it is affected — or unaffected.

### L46 — Trace the type to its origin
**Trigger:** a type error you are about to silence with a cast, a widening, or a suppression.
**Mechanism:** the error is where the contradiction surfaced, not where it was created. Patching
the surface makes the next occurrence appear somewhere less obvious.
**Check:** find where the type is first defined and why it disagrees here. Fix it there. When
many errors appear at once, fix the first one and re-run — most of the rest are cascades.

---

# Family F — Craft & Collaboration

### L47 — Analyse before coding
**Trigger:** the fix looks obvious.
**Mechanism:** the obvious fix addresses the symptom you were shown. The system-level cause
produces four more symptoms you have not been shown yet.
**Check:** state the root cause in one sentence before editing. If you cannot, you are not ready
to edit.

### L48 — Never bulk-script a rename
**Trigger:** "replace X with Y across the codebase."
**Mechanism:** a text substitution cannot see scope. It hits strings, comments, unrelated
substrings, and generated files, and the damage is uniform enough to look intentional.
**Check:** enumerate the sites first, edit deliberately (or split across agents), and let the
compiler find what you missed. Where a codemod is genuinely warranted, review its diff in full.

### L49 — Prompt language does not bind a subagent
**Trigger:** delegating with instructions like "read-only", "do not commit", "just analyse".
**Mechanism:** an agent holding write tools can write. Instructions are a preference; the
toolset is the boundary. This is not a compliance failure — it is a design error.
**Check:** constrain the *tools* you grant. Then verify after the fact what changed.

### L50 — If a procedure exists, invoke it
**Trigger:** about to hand-roll a flow that already has a documented procedure.
**Mechanism:** a reconstructed procedure reproduces the steps someone remembered and omits the
guards they added after being burned. Partial compliance looks identical to compliance.
**Check:** invoke the procedure. If it is wrong, fix the procedure — do not route around it.

### L51 — Status rots; mechanism does not
**Trigger:** writing anything durable — a doc, a memory, a comment, a runbook.
**Mechanism:** "the migration is done", "this is on staging", "the flag is on" are all false
within weeks and become actively misleading, because they are still stated with confidence.
**Check:** record *how the thing works* and *how to check its state*. Route status to the place
that tracks status.

### L52 — Touch it, fix it
**Trigger:** editing a file that contains pre-existing rot.
**Mechanism:** codebases do not get cleaned by cleanup projects; they get cleaned by every edit
leaving its file better. Deferred cleanup is never scheduled.
**Check:** the file you touched leaves your hands compliant — no suppressions, no dead code, no
TODOs. If the full fix is genuinely too large, say so explicitly and file it; never leave a
marker in the code.

# Building software with parallel AI agents — what we measured, and what actually works **A standalone field report.** Everything you need is in this file: the setup, the architecture, every hypothesis, how it was tested, what the numbers were, and which of our own conclusions we had to retract. No other document is required. **Who this is for:** anyone orchestrating multiple AI coding agents on one codebase and trying to decide how to split the work. **Status of the evidence:** two full experiments, 23 agents, ~40 agent-hours, one real application. Small-N throughout. Every number below is measured from git commit timestamps or from running the code, never from an agent's self-report. Where a finding is weak, it says so. --- # PART 1 — THE SETUP You need this to interpret anything below. ## The actors | term | what it is | |---|---| | **Orchestrator** | The top-level agent. Holds the plan, writes the briefs, dispatches, merges. Has full conversation history. | | **Lane** | An autonomous coding subagent. Own context window, own git worktree, own browser. **Cannot see other lanes. Cannot talk to them. Reports once, at the end.** | | **Root** | A lane that runs FIRST and alone, producing the shared foundation everything else builds on. | | **Seam lane** | A lane that writes cross-surface tests instead of features. Explained in Part 2. | **The critical constraint:** lanes share nothing but the filesystem and git. No shared memory, no messages between them, one report per lifetime. This is the most expensive coordination regime there is, and every finding below follows from it. ## The application under test A small internal web app — an organisation's "roles", each with systems, people, an AI assistant with toggleable skills, and a monthly fee. Five surfaces: ``` index.html role list + role detail system-detail.html one system's page cue-detail.html assistant config, push-review flow, skill toggles team.html roster + person detail ``` Plus `app-ds.css` (design system), `data.js` (fixture + helpers), `shell.js` (routing, storage, shared components), `journeys.py` (browser-driven acceptance suite), `seams.py` (cross-surface suite). Plain files, no build step. Each surface is 200-450 lines with inline CSS and JS. **This size matters** — conclusions about lane counts are relative to a 4-file app. ## What "done" means for a lane Every lane brief required the same things, and this is load-bearing for the results: 1. Build the unit. 2. Run the acceptance suite green. 3. Screenshot at 1440x900 and 390x844 **and read the pixels** — not just check for overflow. 4. **Mutation-test one assertion**: break the thing it checks, watch that exact row go red, restore, watch it go green. An assertion never driven red proves nothing. 5. Commit. Uncommitted work does not exist. 6. Report what it had to work out that the docs did not cover. That last item is the highest-value measurement in the whole programme. It is the direct readout of what your shared documentation fails to transfer. --- # PART 2 — THE ARCHITECTURE THAT WORKS This is the recipe. Every element is here because something broke without it. ## The shape ``` ROOT (alone, first) │ produces: contract, digest, examples, skeletons, │ worktrees, id allocations, seam suite ▼ ┌──────┼──────┬──────┐ L1 L2 L3 SEAM ← all concurrent, one FILE each └──────┴──────┴──────┘ ▼ MERGE → suite + seams green ``` ## The root's six deliverables ### 1. A CONTRACT that freezes POLICIES, not just names A contract listing helper names and file ownership is not enough. Lanes will re-implement nothing and still diverge — on everything the contract leaves silent. **Measured:** three lanes off a symbols-only contract produced **three different output-escaping policies** (one used none, so its page executed script from its URL), **two different numbers for the same audience count** one click apart (12 vs 14), and a **re-invented copy of the shared page-head component**. A code reviewer verified symbol-by-symbol that no lane had re-implemented anything. They diverged purely in the gaps. So the contract states explicitly: - **Output escaping** — the one helper every lane must call - **Every shared number** — its exact definition, which field, whom it counts. Especially any count that appears on more than one surface. - **Which component answers which shape** — so nobody re-invents one that exists - **Empty/error vocabulary** — the words for zero, for missing, for failed - **Id and selector grammar** — and the ID ranges (see 4) ### 2. A DIGEST — what lanes would otherwise each rediscover **Measured:** three lanes on one root returned the *identical* six-item trap list and near-identical ten-file read lists. One shared prologue, executed three times, serially, inside the lanes. The digest is whatever cost the root a wrong turn: harness quirks, viewport traps, fixture sharp edges. Lanes read the digest **instead of** the sources. **Result after adding it:** residual "had to work it out" items dropped from 2-4 per lane to roughly 1, and the survivors changed class — from fixture knowledge to test methodology. ### 3. An EXAMPLE PACK — the single highest-value artifact This was the biggest measured improvement in the programme. **Every residual gap across two waves was the same shape: the docs described a helper and the agent could not tell how to CALL it.** Real cases, each found only after an agent's code silently did nothing: - `attrs()` does not auto-prefix `data-` — `{role: x}` emits `role="x"`, not `data-role="x"` - a toggle's `` is `opacity:0; 0x0` — genuinely unclickable, Playwright included; the real target is the wrapping `

# Performance playbook — diagnosis first, then the right lever class

Speed work fails two ways: optimizing before measuring (three rounds of plausible fixes that
move nothing — measured in a real build), and optimizing the wrong LAYER (execution tuning
when the cost is transport; craft redesign when the cost is a request storm). This playbook
is the ordered method: measure → classify the bottleneck → apply that class's levers → verify
with the same instrument. The goal for an app over a live source of truth is NEAR-REALTIME:
reads that feel instant AND reflect the store's current state.

Figures marked [measured] were taken in a real build on this estate (cold, live host, stated
instrument); figures marked [sourced] cite the reference at the bottom. Everything else is a
design judgment — argue with it.

---

## 1. The diagnosis ladder (in order — each step decides whether the next is needed)

1. **Measure what the user actually waits on** — boot-to-usable, route entry, the specific
   interaction complained about. Instrument the app itself (a server-side timing endpoint +
   client marks); numbers from a dev machine are a ceiling, not the user's number.
2. **Decompose per read, cold AND warm separately.** A mean hides the cold path; "warm is
   80ms" is irrelevant to the user who arrives cold every morning ([measured]: 1.95s cold /
   0.08s warm on the same route; a boot warm of 12 reads costing 7.5s).
3. **Bound the FLOOR: a no-op probe over the same path.** `SELECT 1`-class query, same
   client, same route. If the no-op costs what the real read costs, the trip is the cost and
   ALL execution-side tuning is worthless ([measured]: no-op 1451–2119ms = full-catalogue
   read 1267–1613ms, with `cacheHit: true, totalBytesProcessed: 0` — the engine did zero
   work at full latency).
4. **Count requests** — on route entry, on RETURN to a visited route, and after a multi-line
   write. Storms multiply any per-read cost ([measured]: a remount loop at ~1300 mounts/300ms;
   an N-line write firing N refetches via per-mutation invalidation).
5. **State the data's actual size.** Multi-second reads over kilobyte-to-megabyte data indict
   the channel or architecture, never the query ([measured]: an entire operational dataset =
   2.5 MB; the user-visible slice < 40 KB).
6. **Decompose the transport leg by leg** when the floor is the cost: raw HTTPS to the host ·
   the platform API alone · the full connector chain ([measured]: 80–158ms · 333–436ms ·
   1451–2119ms — the connector leg is fixed and size-independent).

## 2. The lever map — bottleneck classes, levers in cost order

| Class (diagnosed by) | Levers, cheapest first |
|---|---|
| **A. Request multiplication** (step 4: storms, waterfalls, remount refetches) | ONE client data layer (RTK Query/TanStack) — no bespoke fetch beside it · independent reads in parallel (R3) · subscription REUSE (a child subscribing to what the parent holds must not force a refetch; audit `refetchOnMountOrArgChange` against remount loops) · writes BATCH invalidations (one user action = one refetch per dirtied tag, never per loop iteration) · stable mounting (a busy-wrapper swap that remounts a subscriber is a storm generator) |
| **B. Transport** (step 3+6: the floor is the cost) | client/connection REUSE — auth/token exchange once per process ([measured]: 140ms, paid once) · regional colocation (app and store in the same region) · the engine's low-latency call mode with its fast-path observable LOGGED per query, never assumed (BigQuery: `jobCreationMode: JOB_CREATION_OPTIONAL` on `jobs.query`; short mode engaged ⇔ `jobReference` ABSENT in the response; eligibility is decided dynamically by the engine [sourced 1,2]) · COALESCE small reads (a boot hydrate of a <5MB working set is ONE round, not twelve) · remove hops: DIRECT least-privilege credentialed access to the store (lever D2) when the platform chain's floor exceeds the budget ([measured]: 249ms median direct short-mode vs 1509ms through the chain — 6×, from a dev machine; in-region should sit lower) · **the ASSET leg (boot-to-usable, not the store read):** a content-hashed filename is immutable by construction and gets `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable` — a short max-age on a hashed file buys nothing and costs a revalidation on every visit, and PERF-4 measures bundle SIZE only, so a bundle inside budget can still be re-fetched on every visit and pass. The `no-cache` rule in `dev-loop.md` is NOT in tension: it scopes to the HTML entry document and to unhashed/query-versioned assets, which must revalidate so a deploy swap is visible. Self-host webfonts or `font-display: swap` them — a render-blocking stylesheet on a third-party origin adds DNS + TLS + a round trip before the first styled pixel |
| **C. Execution** (the no-op is FAST but the real read is slow) | only NOW do clustering, partitioning, materialized views, BI-Engine-class acceleration apply — they speed the engine's work, and buy exactly nothing when step 3 showed the work is already free ([measured]: disproven for a whole build in one probe). Require the floor probe BEFORE any spend here |
| **D. Architecture / read path** (transport optimized and still over budget, or freshness demands push) | D1 **serving projection / CQRS read store** kept current from the canonical store — the standard serving shape over an analytical warehouse [sourced 3] ([measured]: 42ms vs 1416ms). **It is HOMED in a MANAGED low-latency store, NEVER on the app container** (SKILL P1: the container filesystem is not a store): an IN-PROCESS engine — PGLite, SQLite, a JSON tank — is not a projection, it is a second source of truth that the deploy swap wipes, and its refresh runs on the app's own thread ([measured]: a PGLite projection over a warehouse blocked the Node event loop **2.3–3.1s every 30s, at zero traffic** — every request paid it, and the switch-on landed twelve minutes AFTER a different fix had already removed the connector latency it existed to remove). Price: a SECOND COPY, and divergence is a correctness class ([measured]: a projection hid an open counting round from a user while every gate stayed green; a column present in spec and warehouse but absent from the projection took two screens down). Enablement therefore requires a divergence journey that FAILS when a table lies — **and that is a WALL, not a discipline: `guard.sh divergence` (layer 7, in `all`) reads the `divergence` clause of every `Read-path:` row and goes RED on a projection whose check is `none`, missing from disk, timed out, or non-zero.** It does not compare the copies itself — only the app knows how — so it enforces that the comparison exists, runs and passes, and writes `docs/DIVERGENCE.md` as the evidence. Re-derive rather than trust this line, and note the control must come back non-zero or the scan proved nothing: `git grep -in diverg -- ':/skills/nexus-app-builder/references/scripts'` → hits in `guard.sh` and `divergence.mjs`; `node skills/nexus-app-builder/references/scripts/divergence.mjs --self-test` → every arm proved able to fail · D2 **direct credentialed access, one store** — a least-privilege service credential (query grant at project level, data grants scoped to the ONE dataset, key in the app env, never in git), reads direct in low-latency mode, writes free to stay on the platform connector (rare, latency-tolerant, already-proven path) — removes the divergence class entirely at a latency premium ([measured]: ~200ms over the projection) · D3 **freshness by PUSH, not fast polling** — near-realtime means change-driven currency (CDC/webhook/stream into the projection or client), not a shorter poll; a cache TTL is DERIVED from the data's change cadence and the session shape, never shorter than the user's click interval (a TTL below the visit length makes EVERY request cold — the measured worst case) |
| **E. Perceived speed** | owned by the FEED rubric + R2 (skeletons at the latency profile, optimistic UI, progressive hydration) · PREFETCH the statistically-next destination (the adjacent tab, the next month, the hovered row) on hover/focus for pointer surfaces and on idle otherwise — a prefetch is a normal read into the SAME cache entry the click will hit (never a bespoke fetch beside it, class A), so the transition has no loading state at all — perceived-speed work NEVER substitutes for classes A–D when the measured number is over budget |

## 3. The arbitrations (owner calls — each STANDS once made)

- **Projection vs direct access** (D1 vs D2): both cross from "waiting" to "responsive"; the
  projection is faster, direct access has ONE store and therefore no divergence class. On
  data that drives real-world actions, paying ~200ms to delete a correctness-risk class is
  usually the right trade — but it is the OWNER's trade, made with the measured numbers on
  the table, and the un-chosen rung stays built-and-off, not deleted.
- **Platform connector on the read path**: today the chain adds a fixed ~1–2s per read
  ([measured]; a platform ticket tracks reducing it and exposing the engine's low-latency
  mode through the connector) — so the connector is the WRITE and automation path, and a
  read path only where the budget tolerates its floor. Re-probe when the platform ships
  changes; this paragraph states current-state, not permanent truth.
- **A cache and a projection are NOT substitutes** — they move different numbers, and treating
  one as the cheap version of the other is how an app acquires a store it never needed. A cache
  changes the SECOND read and cannot touch the first; a projection changes the FLOOR, cold reads
  included. So step 2's cold/warm split decides, and it decides alone: **cold over budget → the
  floor is the problem, class D** (no TTL, no client cache and no prefetch moves a cold number).
  **Warm over budget while cold is fine → class A**, a storm or a missing cache — never a new
  store. A projection reached for against a warm-path number buys a divergence class for nothing.
- **Sequencing**: a confirmed storm (class A) HOLDS craft redesign of the affected surface —
  redesigning a screen whose real problem is that it hammers the store is thrown-away work.
  And fix A before measuring B–D: a storm multiplies whatever floor exists and corrupts
  every downstream measurement.

## 4. Verification contract

Every lever applied re-measures with the SAME instrument that diagnosed it, cold and warm,
and the number lands in `docs/PERF.md` (guard layer 5) + the route's R7 journey assertion.
A lever "applied" without its re-measured number is open work (PERF-5). The fast-path
observable (e.g. `jobReference` absence) is per-query evidence — log it; dynamic eligibility
means yesterday's fast path is an assumption today.
