# PLAN FORMAT — the architect's plan JSON contract

> LOAD WHEN: dispatching `app-architect`, or validating the plan it returns. The plan is a
> single JSON object with the fields below — it is the build's contract: the executor builds
> FROM it, reviewers score AGAINST it, the capture manifest defines the evidence set, and
> the coverage note proves no dimension was silently skipped. Plans cite CODE (`file:line`),
> never prose impressions.

---

## Top-level shape

```json
{
  "status": "resolved | needs_taste_answers",
  "screen": "<screen/app name + route>",
  "bar_narrative": "…",
  "interpretations": [ … ],
  "capture_manifest": [ … ],
  "data_model_notes": "…",
  "todos": [ … ],
  "lane_dag": { … },
  "taste_questions": [ … ],
  "resolved_taste": { … },
  "scope_diff": { … },
  "gaps": [ … ],
  "coverage_note": "…"
}
```

`status: "needs_taste_answers"` → the orchestrator relays `taste_questions` to the user
(AUQ), writes the answers into `resolved_taste`, and the plan becomes `resolved`. The
executor is never dispatched on an unresolved plan.

## Field contracts

### `bar_narrative` — run the movie
One paragraph narrating a REAL user doing the job end-to-end on the finished screen, in the
user's domain nouns, with the actual seeded values inline (names, figures, states). It is
the cheapest gap-detector: a capability the narrative cannot mention concretely is a
capability the plan does not understand. Reviewers read it as the definition of "the job
works"; the E2E journey is derived from it.

### `interpretations` — the B9 block
Every load-bearing user constraint from the PRD/brief, each carrying the plan's STATED
interpretation:

```json
{ "constraint": "<the user's words, near-verbatim>",
  "interpreted_as": "<the testable reading the plan builds on>",
  "confidence": "stated | inferred" }
```

`stated` = the user said it in so many words. `inferred` = the architect chose a reading —
every semantics-bearing `inferred` row is surfaced by the orchestrator as a ONE-LINE
confirm to the user BEFORE the executor is dispatched (a wrong inferred reading fans out
into every todo built on it). No silent interpretations.

### `capture_manifest` — the evidence set, declared up front
One row per feature/state the build must prove, BEFORE building:

```json
{ "id": "cap-<slug>",
  "feature": "<what this capture proves>",
  "states": ["<state 1>", "<state 2>"],
  "viewports": ["1512", "390", "844x390"],
  "themes": ["light", "dark"],
  "interaction_beforeafter": true,
  "asserted_outcome": "<the mechanical assertion: what must be visibly/programmatically true in the capture — a value, a geometry bound, a state transition — never 'looks right'>" }
```

Rules: interactions get before/after pairs (`interaction_beforeafter: true`); every
viewport the PRD names appears in at least one row; both themes wherever theme can change
the verdict; `asserted_outcome` is written so a reviewer can mark it pass/fail without
judgment. The executor's capture set is graded against this manifest — a manifest row with
no capture is an honest `MISSING` row in the executor's log, never silently dropped.

### `data_model_notes` — the one real model change
Prose naming: the exact type/file/lines being changed, the new field(s), EVERY invariant to
preserve (derivations that must not double-count, totals that must stay exact, immutability
seals), the legacy-data migration at load, and which adapters/consumers read the changed
shape (enumerated by `file:line` — L45). If the plan changes no data model, say so
explicitly.

### `todos` — the work, dimensioned

```json
{ "id": "<dim>-<slug>",
  "dimension": "visual | ux | functionality | interaction | consistency | mobile",
  "what": "<the deliverable, concrete>",
  "why": "<the PRD/bar clause or defect this serves — quoted or cited>",
  "acceptance": "<mechanically checkable: what a reviewer asserts on the live app>",
  "reuse": "<existing code to build from — file:line for each named artifact>",
  "component_source": "<library file:line>  |  not_in_library: <one-line why>",
  "effort": "S | M | L",
  "priority": "must | should" }
```

The `reuse` field is load-bearing: the architect read the closest sibling end-to-end (L26)
and names the exact primitives/patterns to extend — an empty `reuse` on a todo in an
existing codebase is a smell the orchestrator challenges. Every PRD capability maps to ≥1
`must` todo; the mapping is what `coverage_note` proves.

`component_source` is REQUIRED on any todo delivering a complex control (table · filter or
search bar · kanban/board · record page · wizard · form). It carries a `file:line` in the
resolved component-inventory root (`ux-canon.md` COMPONENT INVENTORY — installed catalog or
vendored tree), or an explicit `not_in_library:` reason. `reuse` and `component_source` are
NOT the same field: `reuse` points anywhere in the codebase and was satisfied, at full
strength, by a donor app's bespoke screens while the org library sat unused — 31 reuse
pointers, 0 into the library. The orchestrator rejects a plan whose complex-control todos
carry neither value.

### `lane_dag` — the execution DAG (parallel fan-out; omit for a single-executor build)
The disjoint-lane partition for parallel EXECUTION (SKILL "The dependency DAG + scheduler").
A DAG, not a GANTT: lane durations are unknown and lanes auto-retry, so a fixed timeline is
fiction — this is the dependency STRUCTURE the scheduler runs dynamically.

```json
{ "roots": ["contract", "spine"],
  "units": 8,
  "digest": ["docs/CONTRACT.md", "docs/DIGEST.md"],
  "root_files": ["<file the root freezes — EVERY one of these is owned by some lane>"],
  "lanes": [
    { "id": "<slug>",
      "owns": ["<EXCLUSIVE file glob this lane, and only this lane, writes>"],
      "depends_on": ["<root or lane id>"],
      "builds_against": ["<root id>"],
      "acceptance": ["<a check that passes for THIS lane ALONE, without its siblings merged>"],
      "model": "<tier>",
      "surfaces": ["<user-facing surface this lane builds — ONE per lane; desktop and mobile of one screen are TWO>"],
      "unsplittable_reason": "<REQUIRED only when `surfaces` has >1 entry: why this surface genuinely cannot be split>" } ] }
```

Invariants (hook PARTITION-VALID WARNS on a violation before dispatch — it surfaces as
context and does NOT block, the same advisory status as FANOUT-ROOTS): **acyclic** ·
**pairwise-disjoint `owns`** (no two lanes write the same file) · **closure** (every
`depends_on` is a root or a declared lane — `builds_against` is INFORMATIONAL and is read by
no check; it documents which roots a lane compiles against, for the reader) · **only ROOTS
have `depends_on: []`** (a non-root lane with no deps is a silent orphan).

**`roots` means the dependency FLOOR, not "the foundation lanes" — and the two are constantly confused because foundation lanes get named `root-*`.** A foundation lane that waits for another foundation lane is an ordinary LANE, however foundational it feels: the contract lands, and the shells/spine/styles/harness all depend on it. Measured on a blind architect run that got everything else right: it declared five roots — contract, shells, spine, styles, harness — with four of them carrying `depends_on: ["root-contract"]`. The ORDERING was correct and desirable; the labelling made `PARTITION-VALID` red on four rows at once. There is exactly one root in that plan.
✗ five `root-*` lanes all listed in `roots`, four of them depending on the first → four invariant violations for a partition whose shape was right.
✓ `roots: ["root-contract"]`, and shells/spine/styles/harness as ordinary lanes depending on it. Same execution order, same commit sequence, valid partition. Name a lane for what it BUILDS (`contract`, `shells`, `spine`) and the confusion does not arise.

**The three top-level fields beside `lanes`, all read by checks.** They exist because a hook must never GUESS: each one turns a question the checker cannot answer from a path into a declaration a reader can audit.

| Field | What it declares | Which arm reads it |
|---|---|---|
| `units` | the unit count from Step 0's enumeration, BEFORE any merging | `SHAPE1` pre-split arm: `units` > distinct owned paths = the tree was never pre-split |
| `digest` | the artifacts the root wrote specifically to be consumed by every lane | `SHAPE1` shared-consumption arm: declared entries are EXEMPT, so the doctrine's own prescribed behaviour does not read as a defect |
| `root_files` | the files the root freezes | `SHAPE1` frozen-but-unowned arm: every frozen file needs an owner, or the freeze has nobody to hold it |

Omitting a field does not fake a pass — each arm DECLINES to judge when its field is absent and says so. Declaring ten raw sources as `digest` is visible and reviewable in the artifact; a hook guessing which of ten files was purpose-built would not be.

**A validator cost bound, not a doctrine cap.** `PARTITION-VALID` declines to validate a DAG
of more than 200 lanes and says so. That bounds the CHECKER, never the fan-out width — the
doctrine's "NEVER a number" stands. A 201-lane DAG is UNVALIDATED, not invalid; split it into
sub-DAGs if you want it checked. The distinction matters because the refusal is reported
through the same channel as a real invariant failure.

## HOW TO DECOMPOSE — the enumeration, in order

> Every rule below is a measured result, and the experiments behind them — the lane-count runs, the
> refuted hypotheses, what we got wrong — are written up in `REF/parallel-agent-builds.md`. Read it
> once before designing your first fan-out; this section is the procedure, that is the evidence.

Run this BEFORE writing `lane_dag`. It is an enumeration, not a judgement: you are listing units that already exist in the work, and the count falls out. A partition that names 3 lanes for 12 units is not a small partition, it is an unlisted one.

**Step 1 — SHARED FOUNDATION first, and it is a DISPATCHED lane.** Anything every other lane reads or writes: design tokens, the data/fixture layer, shared render helpers, the app shell, shared types. It goes first because everything depends on it, and it is a lane with an owner and a model — never a row marked "pre-existing, not dispatched".
✗ a `shared-foundation` row owning `app-ds.css, data.js, shell.js`, `model: "n/a — pre-existing, not dispatched this round"`, acceptance "unmodified by any downstream lane" — then a nav helper is added to `shell.js` and two hrefs to `data.js` in that same round, by the partition's own author. The partition asserted the files were untouched while they were being edited, and nothing could contradict it.
✓ `shell-nav-helper` (owns `shell.js`) and `data-cue-links` (owns `data.js`) as real lanes, dispatched first, merged before fan-out. Their acceptance is what the downstream lanes then build against.

**Step 1b — THE ROOT FREEZES POLICIES, NOT JUST SYMBOLS — and hands lanes its RESULT.** A root that publishes helpers and file ownership has frozen the SYMBOLS. Lanes then diverge on everything the contract left silent, and every divergence is a cross-surface defect no single lane can see. Measured on three lanes off one root, each verified symbol-by-symbol to have re-implemented NOTHING: they still shipped **three different escaping policies** (one of them none, so one surface executed script from its URL), **two different numbers for the same audience count** one click apart, and a **re-invented copy of the shared page-head component**. The root froze what to CALL things and never what to DO. So the root's contract carries, explicitly: output encoding · the semantics of every shared number (which field, whom it counts) · which component answers which shape · error/empty vocabulary · the id and selector grammar.

The same root also carries a **DIGEST — what the lanes would otherwise each rediscover**: the harness traps, the capture quirks, the fixture's sharp edges. Measured: three lanes returned the *identical* six-item trap list and near-identical ten-file read lists. That is one shared prologue executed three times, serially, inside the lanes — and it is why that fan-out measured **49 minutes against a 32-minute solo build of the same three surfaces**. Fan-out was not slower than solo; the *prologue* was paid three times instead of once. A lane receives the digest, not the sources it was derived from.

And the root's **worktrees are provisioned CENTRALLY, before lane one**. Two of three lanes in that wave created their own because none existed at dispatch — setup the spawner was supposed to have already paid, paid again per lane, on the critical path.
✗ a root that publishes `deepRoute()`, `storeGet()` and a file map, then dispatches — three lanes, three escaping policies, one live XSS, and a cross-surface consistency score of 3.4/10.
✓ the same root publishing an ESCAPING RULE, one definition per shared number, the component-to-shape map, the trap digest, and three worktrees already on disk.

**Step 2 — ONE LANE PER SCREEN, and a viewport is a screen.** Enumerate every user-facing surface the work reaches. Desktop and mobile of one screen are TWO surfaces because they are two renders with two sets of failures.
✗ one lane briefed "build the detail pages" covering Cue detail, system detail and team view — three screens, one schedule, and the wave runs at the speed of all three in series.
✓ `cue-detail` · `system-detail` · `team-view`, one file each, dispatched together. Measured: three such lanes finished concurrently and none opened another's file.

**Step 3 — ONE LANE PER INTERACTION THAT OWNS STATE.** A click that only navigates is part of its screen. A flow with its own states — open → review → confirm, a toggle that persists, a selection that re-renders a pane, a drill-down that changes what the page is about — is its own unit, because its failures are its own.
✗ "team view with a person-detail pane" as one lane: the roster renders, the pane is an afterthought, and the selection state is the part that breaks.
✓ `team-roster` and `team-person-pane` as two lanes against a frozen row contract — or ONE lane with `unsplittable_reason: "the pane reads the roster's in-memory selection; splitting them would invent a store"`. Either is fine. Silence is not.

**Step 4 — ONE LANE PER PRODUCED ARTIFACT SET.** Alternatives, reports, capture sets and fixtures are work with their own acceptance. N design alternatives are N units even though the work is visual. Design is not exempt from partitioning; it is exempt from having two judges — the lanes produce in parallel and ONE reviewer holds taste for the surface, so splitting production never splits the taste call.
✗ one `ideation` lane owning nine paths — six alternative pages plus a JSON, a report and a shot directory — which then skipped its append instructions entirely, and the omission surfaced only because a human read the files afterwards.
✓ one lane per alternative, or per coherent pair, each with its own acceptance; the report and index as their own row.

**Step 4b — THE CEILING: FAN OUT TO THE NUMBER OF INDEPENDENTLY-OWNABLE ARTIFACTS, AND NO FURTHER.** Steps 2-4 tell you how to enumerate units. This tells you when to stop turning units into LANES. **The unit of parallelism is the unit of OWNERSHIP, not the unit of work** — you can decompose work as finely as you like, but you cannot decompose a file AT DISPATCH TIME. Before dispatch you can, and that is where the ceiling is actually raised ("Raising the ceiling", below).

Measured, one task of 8 equal units cut three ways, 14 agents concurrent, same root, same model, only the cut varied:

| lanes | per-lane build | ARM build | merge conflicts | merged suite | merged seams |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2 (4 units each) | 25, 35 | 35 min | 1 | 62/63 | 15/15 |
| **4 (ONE FILE EACH)** | 12-17 | **17 min** | 2 | 62/63 | **15/15** |
| 8 (TWO PER FILE) | **7-10** | 19 min | **7** | **18/64** | **1/15** |
| **8 (ONE FILE EACH, after the root split one screen into components)** | not separately recorded | 20 min | clean | green | **15/15** |

**Eight lanes was slower AND shipped a broken build.** Note what is NOT the reason: the 8-lane lanes were the FASTEST per lane (7-10 min against 12-17). Finer units genuinely build quicker. It bought nothing, because the wave still runs at its slowest lane and the merge then destroyed the result.

**Three costs, each measured, that appear only past the ownership ceiling:**
1. **Conflicts scale worse than lanes** (1 → 2 → 7) and change KIND. Below the ceiling they are append-only and resolve mechanically; above it, two lanes edit the SAME LINE and no strategy resolves them. Here both same-file lanes appended to one panel-concatenation line; the merge kept both, duplicated, and the render emitted malformed markup.
2. **A lane owning a REGION cannot fix a defect in its own file.** The 4-lane arm's lane found a pre-existing 390px overflow, measured it at 23px, fixed it, verified 23px→0. NEITHER 8-lane lane on that same file touched it — it sat between their regions. Same class as the frozen file no lane owns.
3. **Lanes reach into each other's worktrees.** One committed a sibling's UNCOMMITTED work after copying from its directory, then reported the cause as a filesystem property (it was not — the worktrees were verified separate). Worktrees isolate commits, not curiosity, and the temptation exists only when two lanes share a file.

**Foresight does not rescue a bad cut.** The lane whose line collided PREDICTED that exact line in its handoff before any merge ran. It still collided.
**RAISING THE CEILING — the ROOT SPLITS THE TREE, and it does so BEFORE dispatch.** The last two rows are the same cut of the same work by the same models; the only difference is that in the last row the tree already held eight owners' worth of files when the lanes started. So the ceiling is a property of the TREE, not of the work, and a tree is editable: enumerate the units (Steps 2-4), count the files exactly one lane could own end-to-end today, and where units exceed files, split until they match — or write the `unsplittable_reason` on each unit you merge (Step 5). Declare the unit count as top-level `"units"` so the arithmetic sits on disk instead of in the planner's head.

**A SOLO build does the same arithmetic and records it somewhere else.** It writes no `lane_dag`, so its two numbers land on the BUILD-MODE card's `Units + artifacts` row (`REF/build-mode-card.md`) — filled BEFORE the Path row, never after. Two checks read whichever artifact exists: `SHAPE1` at dispatch, and **`PARTSTOP` at Stop, which reads `docs/lane-dag.json` straight off disk** precisely because a build that never fans out never reaches a dispatch-time check (`hooks/CHECK-REGISTRY.md`).

This is the ROOT's commit, merged before lane one, and it is never a lane's job mid-wave: a lane that restructures its own file changes what every sibling is diffing against, and the conflict then surfaces at merge as somebody else's. Where the seam falls is not a judgement call either — each stack has an ordered ladder, and you descend it only until artifacts match units.
> !! Before splitting any tree: Read `REF/frontend-architecture.md` "## 2a. The frontend seam ladder" for a user-facing tree, or `REF/backend-crew.md` "## The backend seam ladder" for a service. Each names its rungs, the directory at each rung, and the rungs that do not fan out at ANY width. !!

✗ 8 lanes over 4 files because the work enumerated to 8 units → fastest lanes in the wave, 7 conflicts, a broken build, and two defects nobody was allowed to fix.
✓ 4 lanes over 4 files, each owning one whole artifact → 17 min, 2 trivial conflicts, seams clean, and a lane free to repair what it found.
✓ or raise the ceiling first: one root commit splitting the screen into components, THEN 8 lanes over 8 files → the same clean merge and seams, with the wave's fastest per-lane builds kept.

**Step 5 — COUNT, then write the reason for every unit you merged.** The four steps above give you a number. If your `lane_dag` has fewer rows than that number, each merge carries an `unsplittable_reason` in the row that absorbed it. The escape is always available and always written: nothing asks for a particular width, only that the decision exist on disk where a reader can find it.
✗ 5 rows for work that enumerates to 12, no reasons — the partition validates (acyclic, disjoint, closed and rooted are all trivially true), and the serial build it describes is invisible to every check.
✓ 12 rows, or 8 rows where 4 carry a reason. Both pass. Both are auditable.

**Step 5b — A SHARED STORE IS APPENDED TO BY ADDING A FILE, NEVER BY EDITING ONE.** A partition is not disjoint because its `owns` lists are disjoint. It is disjoint when every file a lane must WRITE to pass its own gate has exactly one owner. The file lanes most reliably need and least reliably own is the ACCEPTANCE HARNESS: a lane cannot prove its work without extending the suite, so it extends a file the root owns. Measured, within thirty minutes of one dispatch: **five of nine lanes independently appended to the same `journeys.py`** (+192, +185, +106, +87, +74 lines), across two model tiers, unprompted, off a formally valid pairwise-disjoint partition. Every lane was obeying its brief. The merge conflict was guaranteed before any of them started.

The same shape applies to every shared mutable registry — fixtures, route tables, style tokens, selector maps, storage-key allocations. The fix is not a rule telling lanes to be careful; it is removing the collision:
- **Additive by construction (default):** the shared thing is a DIRECTORY the root's runner globs — `journeys/<lane>.py`, `fixtures/<lane>.json`. A store appended to by adding a FILE never collides. A store appended to by editing a file always can. **THE ROOT BUILDS THE GLOBBING RUNNER IN THE SAME COMMIT THAT CREATES THE DIRECTORY.** Measured, by a lane reporting it: a wave was told to write `journeys/<lane>.py` while the runner still only knew about the single `journeys.py`, so "the suite is green" became two separate commands and stopped being ONE checkable predicate — which is the exact property the additive rule exists to protect. An additive store with no aggregator is not additive, it is scattered. A convention with no mechanism is a convention nobody can verify.
- If it must be one file, the root writes it COMPLETE up front so no lane needs to extend it, or allocates named per-lane regions in it.
✗ one `journeys.py` the root owns and every lane must extend to prove its own work → five authors, one file, conflict by construction.
✓ `journeys/` globbed by a root-owned runner → five lanes, five new files, zero conflict, and the suite still runs as one.

**A hook already catches this before dispatch** (`SHAPE1`, the frozen-but-unowned arm): any file the partition freezes that no lane owns. Treat that warning as blocking for anything a lane must WRITE — it fired on this exact partition, was recorded as correct, and was dispatched past anyway.

**Step 5b.2 — A SHARED NAMESPACE NEEDS AN ALLOCATION, AND ITS COLLISIONS ARE SILENT.** Step 5b makes a shared FILE additive. That does nothing for a shared NAME SPACE, and namespace collisions are strictly more dangerous because **a file collision announces itself and a namespace collision does not**. Measured: three lanes each appended acceptance journeys to the harness and each allocated its ids independently starting at the same number. After a clean union merge one arm carried SEVEN three-way duplicate ids; the suite ran, reported green, and an id no longer identified a journey. The arm with the MOST collisions looked like the best arm in the experiment. Its sibling surfaced one visible failure whose message described an app defect that did not exist — the suite was wrong, not the product.

Every shared registry has this property: journey/test ids, storage keys, CSS class prefixes, `data-*` values, route names, global symbols. The root ALLOCATES a disjoint slice per lane in the contract — `L1: J21-J39 · L2: J40-J59 · L3: J60-J79`, or ids that carry their owner (`L1-J01`) — which makes collision impossible instead of unlikely, and costs one line.
✗ "append your journeys to the suite" → three lanes, three `J23`s, a green number that means nothing, and the most-collided arm reads as the best.
✓ the contract hands each lane its own id range or an owner-prefixed scheme → the union merge stays lossless and every id still names one thing.

**A merged suite is re-verified for DUPLICATE IDS, not just for green.** `grep -oE '"J[0-9]+"' | sort | uniq -d` is the whole check; a green suite with duplicate ids is a suite that has stopped measuring.

**Step 5b.3 — THE PARTITION MUST BE NAVIGABLE: A LANE ID PREDICTS ITS PATH, AND A PATH NAMES ITS OWNER.** 5b removes the collision in a shared FILE and 5b.2 in a shared NAMESPACE. This removes it in the only map everybody shares once the lane count passes a handful — the worktree itself, read by people who were not in the conversation that produced it. Both directions have to hold: given a unit you can guess its file, given a file you can name its owner. The mechanical form is that a lane id and the path it owns share their distinguishing token, so `cue-detail` owns `cue-detail.html` and a lane called `L4-seams` owns the seam suite. An id naming only a ROLE while its path names a FILE breaks both directions and costs a grep every time anyone looks; keep the role by prefixing the file token instead (`shell-nav-helper` owns `shell.js`).

And the paths a brief carries are GENERATED, never typed. Measured: one dispatch typed a worktree path one directory off in all four briefs; two lanes obeyed it literally and built one level up, while the poll watched the correct path, saw nothing, and reported both lanes dead. They were working the whole time. Generate them from `git worktree list` and the DAG's own `owns` — the same sources the checks read.
✗ briefs typed from memory of the layout → a silent one-directory error that reads exactly like a dead lane, and a live lane declared dead.
✓ briefs generated from `git worktree list` → zero path failures across the two waves that followed.

**Step 5c — THE ROOT'S CONTRACT OUTRANKS THE DISPATCH BRIEF, and the brief must say so.** The orchestrator writes lane briefs from memory of the plan; the root writes CONTRACT and DIGEST from having just built the thing. When they disagree, the root is right, because it is more specific and more recent. Measured: a brief told three lanes to serve on named ports and to run the suite with a page filter — while the root's DIGEST said the harness binds its own port and "do not start one, and do not kill anything", and the harness had no page filter at all. One lane resolved it correctly by reasoning about specificity and said so in its report; the others were left to guess. **A lane should never have to adjudicate between two of its own instructions.** Every brief therefore carries one line: *where this brief and `docs/CONTRACT.md`/`docs/DIGEST.md` disagree, the root wins — follow it and report the conflict.* The report is the point: a contradiction that surfaces is a brief defect found for free.
✗ a brief naming ports, commands and flags the root has already fixed differently → each lane silently resolves it a different way, and the divergence looks like lane sloppiness.
✓ the brief states the precedence and asks for conflicts back; the first lane to hit one reports it and the brief is corrected before the next wave.

**Step 6 — SOMEBODY OWNS THE SEAMS, or nothing does.** Verification partitioned along the same cut as the work leaves every boundary between lanes unowned. Measured: 35 journeys, all green, and **not one compared a value on surface A with the same value on surface B**. Every assertion lived inside one surface, so every lane passed its own gate while the product disagreed with itself — the audience count read 12 on one page and 14 one click away, and no green check could ever have said so. A partition that cuts the work must NOT cut the verification the same way.
✗ per-lane journeys only: three lanes green, product inconsistent, and the defects surface at review or in front of the user.
✓ one SEAM row in the partition — a lane whose acceptance is cross-surface: the same datum rendered on every surface that shows it, the same component grammar, the same vocabulary. It is cheap, it is the only row that can fail on a divergence, and it belongs to the root's owner because the root is what the seams are made of.

**Step 6b — WRITE ACCEPTANCE FROM THE CONTRACT, NEVER FROM THE ARTIFACT.** A check derived from the SPEC is independent of the thing it checks AND reusable across every implementation of that spec. A check derived from the BUILT THING is neither: it passes because it was written to pass, and it dies with the version it was written against. Measured both ways — a wave whose 35 journeys were each written from the surface they tested caught none of that wave's cross-surface defects, because every assertion encoded whatever its surface already did; a seam suite written from the contract instead came out with zero references to any lane, repo or built file, deriving every expected value from the fixture, and so reviewed THREE independently-built arms without modification. Design for independence and portability arrives free; design for the artifact and you get neither.
✗ journeys written against the page as built → green forever, blind to the defect class the page shares with its siblings.
✓ assertions derived from the contract's own definitions → the same suite grades every arm, survives a redesign, and can fail on day one.

**The test of a partition is not its size. It is whether a reader can reconstruct WHY these units and not others** — which is why the reason field is the load-bearing part, not the row count.

**GRANULARITY — one user-facing SURFACE per lane.** The invariants above make a partition
*valid*; they do not make it *fast*. A wave runs at the speed of its fattest lane, so a lane
carrying two surfaces is a critical path by construction — and it is invisible to every check
above, because it is acyclic, disjoint, closed and rooted. Measured on one wave: three lanes
were dispatched concurrently inside 40 seconds off a real `lane_dag`, and the wave still took
6h28 — because one lane carried BOTH the desktop and mobile boards of the same screen and ran
**4h08**, while its siblings finished at **1h50** and **3h33**. The fan-out was not the defect;
the cut was. Split per surface (desktop and mobile of one screen are TWO surfaces), and when a
lane must create new files its shared scaffolding lands in a root first, so the split does not
reintroduce a write collision. If a surface genuinely cannot be split, say so in the plan with
the reason — an unsplittable lane is a schedule risk the owner should see before dispatch, not
a duration they discover afterwards. The frozen shared-types lane AND the reactive-spine lane
(`frontend-architecture.md` §1a) are ALWAYS FOUNDATION lanes that precede every surface — which
does NOT make them `roots` when they depend on the contract landing first. Read this with the
`roots`-is-the-dependency-FLOOR rule above: "foundation" is about ORDER, `roots` is about having
no `depends_on`, and a partition can have one root and five foundation lanes. Caught by an
architect that hit both sentences, followed the more specific one, and flagged the tension rather
than picking silently — the earlier wording said "roots ALWAYS include" and read as a floor rule.
The scheduler still will not fan out until those foundations are committed (hook FANOUT-ROOTS ADVISES this; it does
NOT block — CHECK-REGISTRY: "ADVISORY, never a deny". No hook named FANOUT-PRECONDITION
exists). Topological
levels are DERIVED by the scheduler (a level's lanes run concurrently, capped only by machine
health), never planned as a timeline.

### `taste_questions` — forks the user owns

```json
{ "id": "tq-<slug>",
  "fork": "<the design fork, with the constraint that forces it>",
  "options": [ { "label": "<the option, concrete>", "consequence": "<what it costs/buys>" } ],
  "recommendation": "<one option + the one-line reason>" }
```

Genuine taste forks only (layout trade-offs, affordance postures, what leaves the default
view) — never questions the code or an existing rule already answers (those the architect
DECIDES and lists as interpretations). Every option carries its consequence; the
recommendation cites the bar/job, not preference. Answers land in `resolved_taste` as
`{ "tq-<slug>": "<the decision, restated as a directive>" }`.

### `scope_diff` — the B2 block
Maintained by the orchestrator from the first dispatch on, diffed against the ARBITRATED
plan (the version the user approved):

```json
{ "added":    [ { "item": "…", "user_approved": "<quoted user message that authorized it>" } ],
  "dropped":  [ { "item": "…", "user_approved": "<quote — REQUIRED>" } ],
  "deferred": [ { "item": "…", "user_approved": "<quote — REQUIRED>" } ] }
```

`dropped`/`deferred` rows REQUIRE a quotable user sign-off — an empty `user_approved` on a
dropped item means the item is NOT dropped (it is open work). `added` rows cite the message
that asked for them (streamed asks join the plan, not a side channel).

### `gaps` + `coverage_note`
`gaps`: anything the plan could not resolve (a missing asset, an unreadable dependency, a
PRD contradiction) — each a blocking row the orchestrator clears before dispatch, never a
footnote. `coverage_note`: the per-dimension todo count + the explicit sentence that no
dimension is empty, plus any caution short of a gap (a shared file a todo may touch, with
the compatibility rule the executor must hold). The architect also states here what it did
NOT verify (files not read, routes not driven).

# App PRD — tiered template

The PRD is the sign-off artifact that precedes ANY scaffold (SKILL P0). Tier by consumer: humans open a URL → FULL; another system calls it → LIGHT. On sign-off it is FILED to the org's general-context at `/systems/<app-slug>/prd.md` (R#34 ARTIFACT row in the next brief) — the intake snapshot of record; later SCOPE changes re-sign. Its LIVING twin is in-repo `docs/SPEC.md` (one row per ask, appended the turn it arrives; the deploy gate reads it) — day-to-day asks land as SPEC rows, never as silent PRD drift. A complaint row carries the user's words VERBATIM + the measured number + its FATE across attempts — the recurrence trail ("third asking") is the row's diagnostic value.

# CODE-QA METHOD — static correctness, false-green, type floor (R1 reference)

> Injected into the code reviewer. You hold NO write tools to product or the executor's tests (findings only;
> you MAY write disposable probe tests in a scratch dir). Grounded in the 52 Laws (you read them all), the
> code standards, and the false-green thesis. **The word "verified" is exactly what you are here to test.**

## THE STEP-BY-STEP APPROACH
**Step 1 — Read the DIFF in full, then the surrounding files** it now depends on (the caller/consumer the
diff didn't touch — that's where most real defects live).
**Step 2 — Attack the evidence before the code**: for each "verified" claim in the handoffs + TEST-LOG, ask
what would have to be true for that check to fail, and whether that state was possible during the check.
**Step 3 — Challenge the tests, then DIVERGE**: re-run (mutation-check) a sample of the executor's PASSES
yourself in a scratch dir — can each actually fail? Then author probe tests for cases the suite does NOT
contain (new malformed shape, boundary, out-of-order, idempotency/invariant angle). A reviewer whose tests
are a subset of the suite added nothing; a case they missed is your highest-value finding.
**Step 4 — Sweep the Law families**, name which fired (most changes trip two or three).
**Step 5 — Type floor**: any `any` / cast / suppression; line-limit violations; a monolith left unsplit
(run the guard). **Step 6 — Defects**, each with a concrete failure scenario; refute your own before reporting.

## WHAT TO HUNT FIRST (Laws)
1 Checks that cannot fail (L01/L02/L03) — is there mutation evidence, AND a case the suite missed (your probe)?
2 The three-null / envelope class (L41 parse-don't-cast, L43 absent-vs-empty-vs-unchanged, L19/L45 name-not-
  shape / changed-envelope-breaks-every-consumer) — the highest-yield correctness bugs in data code.
3 Absence claims without a positive control (L05).
4 Consumers of a changed shared shape not enumerated (L45) — read each one's parse logic.
5 UI-class: style rules that never fire (L24), first-frame-from-effect, source-not-deployed (L08), stale
  closures over ids, unstable list keys.
6 The type floor: any `any`/cast/suppression, line-limits, an unsplit monolith (L46/L52 + standards).

## RULES
- Every finding carries a CONCRETE failure scenario: specific inputs/state → a specific wrong outcome. No
  scenario ⇒ it's a style opinion ⇒ drop it. Rank correctness/data-loss above all; style last or not at all.
- Bring a DIFFERENT mental model than the author (L01) — if your review restates their reasoning, it added nothing.
- Try to refute each finding; default to refuted when uncertain (a high-false-positive reviewer gets ignored).

tests weren't mutation-challenged · no divergent probe test was authored · a finding lacks a failure scenario.

# CONSISTENCY-QA METHOD — tokens, component reuse, scope & regression (R6 reference)

> Injected into the consistency reviewer. You `git diff` the change AND drive the rendered result. Grounded
> in design-system discipline (DRY, single source of truth), Gestalt similarity, and the shared-foundation
> boundary. **A removed feature is not "approved" unless the user said so — flag it, high-severity.**

## THE STEP-BY-STEP APPROACH
**Step 1 — Read the full diff** vs the prior version.
**Step 2 — TOKEN check**: grep the changed CSS/TSX for raw hex / off-token color / one-off spacing; everything
should be tokens or `color-mix`. Flag each raw value (exception: a documented, justified fixed value — cite why).
**Step 3 — REUSE check** (Gestalt similarity + DRY): did it re-invent a primitive that already exists (a
button, card, field, sheet) instead of consuming it? A near-duplicate of an existing component is a finding.
Same element type must look/behave identically everywhere.
**Step 4 — BOUNDARY check**: did the diff edit shared-foundation it should only CONSUME (design tokens, shared
component-core, mobile primitives, app shell)? An unauthorised shared-foundation edit is a `blocker`; an
AUTHORISED additive change (an optional new prop that defaults to prior behaviour) is fine — verify no other
caller breaks (tsc + a spot-drive of another consumer).
**Step 5 — SCOPE / REGRESSION (high-severity flag)**: diff the build's feature set against the PRIOR version's.
Every feature/view/control present before and absent now is listed with: what's gone, and whether the user
explicitly approved the removal. Silent scope-narrowing is the failure this role exists to catch — never
record a drop as "approved" by inference.
**Step 6 — Drive** to confirm the rendered result matches the app's rhythm/conventions. Defects + scope_delta.

## QUALITY GATES (redo if…)

wasn't diffed against the prior version · a shared-foundation edit wasn't traced to its other callers.

unauthorised shared-foundation edit · **any un-approved feature removal** (that alone is a high-severity flag

# FUNCTIONALITY-QA METHOD — capabilities, invariants, data integrity (R2 reference)

> Injected into the functionality reviewer. You DRIVE the running app and prove every capability by
> performing it and asserting the REAL result — a screenshot can't prove a click worked. Grounded in the
> doctrine (verify-never-assume, assert-identity-not-shape, false-green) + the adversarial protocol.

## THE STEP-BY-STEP APPROACH
**Step 1 — Enumerate capabilities & invariants** from the plan/PRD (what must work; what values must hold).
**Step 2 — DRIVE the happy path**: for each capability, state the BEFORE value → the action → the OBSERVED
AFTER value (read via `CAP eval`). Use `CAP hit <url> <selector>` — it resolves what is actually at that
element's centre through the paint-order model, so it catches a control whose click lands on something
else. Not the interactive MCP browser.
**Step 3 — ASSERT INVARIANTS** exactly (figures, sealed/immutable states, required assets) on a CLEAN seed
(restart the server — the in-memory store compounds across reloads).
**Step 4 — ADVERSARIAL PASS (you own it)** — go off the happy path (§).
**Step 5 — Challenge the executor's TEST-LOG, then DIVERGE** — re-drive a few of its passes; then run tests
it does NOT contain (a reviewer whose tests are a subset of the log added nothing).
**Step 6 — Defects** (each with the observed values) + regression flag.

## CORRECTNESS RULES (from the doctrine)
- **Assert identity, not shape**: "shows a number / didn't throw / has the keys" is true of the WRONG answer
  too. Compare to the expected value; trace the real call path.
- **A control that reports success but changed nothing is a false green** — count before, count after, diff.
- **Green ≠ works**: a documented capability whose backing primitive is absent fails silently (compiles,
  no-ops) — verify the OBSERVED effect, never the call.
- **A zero/absence result carries a positive control** — a probe that can't see a present case proves nothing.
- **Value adjacent to the claim**: the number shown ≠ the number computed unless you read both.

## ADVERSARIAL PASS (mandatory — assert graceful degradation, NO invariant broken)
Malformed / boundary / very-long-string inputs (~5,000 chars) · negative / huge / zero / out-of-range values ·
whitespace / emoji / accents · out-of-sequence acts (edit/submit after a sealed state; submit empty; undo past
start) · off-journey clicks/drags (outside a target, onto a non-droppable, off-screen — ghost/mis-count?) ·
rapid / double / concurrent (double-submit fires once? same op twice idempotent? the money-once invariant
holds?) · interruption (Esc mid-op; reload → coherent seed). Each break is a finding with an exact repro.

## QUALITY GATES (redo if…)
A capability was inferred from code, not driven to a visible outcome · an invariant checked on a dirty seed ·
the adversarial pass wasn't run · a "verified" claim lacks the observed before/after values.

## CALIBRATION (bar = 9)
10 = every capability works and every invariant holds under adversarial pressure, all independently observed.
9 = works, only a cosmetic edge (e.g. a raw negative display where the payout is still protected). **≤6** if:
any capability is a false-green / stub · any PRD invariant is wrong or breakable · a sealed state is mutable ·
an adversarial input corrupts state or breaks an invariant. Prefer refuting a finding to shipping a plausible one.

Sources: the project doctrine (verify-never-assume, false-green) + the adversarial-testing protocol.

# INTERACTION-QA METHOD — micro-interaction feel (R5 reference)

> Injected into the interaction reviewer. Grounded in interaction-design/micro-interaction principles
> (trigger→rule→feedback→loop; affordance; motion timing). You DRIVE every interaction with real pointer
> events and judge the FEEL by performing it. **A drag that "looks done" in a screenshot is not a drag that
> fired — assert the state change.**

## THE STEP-BY-STEP APPROACH
**Step 1 — Inventory every interaction** the screen offers (place, reposition, remove, score/step, select,
decide/submit, undo, cancel, open/close popovers, theme toggle, surface switch).
**Step 2 — DRIVE each one** and observe, in order: the AFFORDANCE (does it look/feel actionable before I
act?), the TRIGGER, the FEEDBACK (immediate? correct?), the RESULT (assert the real state change via
`CAP eval`, and the real target via `CAP hit` — the instrument your dispatch names, not the
interactive MCP browser), and the LOOP/mode exit (cancel/undo).
**Step 3 — Off-path feel** (interrupt a drag, spam a stepper, drop outside a target, double-fire) — graceful?
**Step 4 — Defects:** interaction · what it did · what good feels like · fix · severity · driven evidence.

## MICRO-INTERACTION RULES *(interaction-design sources)*
- **Trigger → rule → feedback → loop**: one clear trigger, a predictable rule, ONE immediate feedback, a
  defined end. Ambiguous or missing feedback is a defect.
- **Immediate feedback**: a response is perceptible on action (state/visual change), not after a delay; a
  control that changes nothing observable on interaction is a false affordance.
- **Affordance is visible without instruction**: a draggable row LOOKS draggable (grip/cursor), a droppable
  target signals it (hover/drop hint), a pressable control looks pressable. If you needed the docs, it fails.
- **Motion timing 200–500ms** (100–500 acceptable): long enough to notice, short enough to keep flow; a
  transition that's absent feels lifeless, one that's slow/janky/over-animated distracts (and reads AI-generic).
- **Every state designed**: default / hover / focus-visible / active / selected / disabled / loading / empty /
  error — drive to each and confirm it's intentional, not a default-browser artifact.
- **Predictable cancel/undo**: Esc cancels an in-progress gesture and snaps back cleanly (no ghost/orphan);
  Cmd+Z reverses the LAST committed action of every reversible kind (place, reposition, score, remove) — drive
  each and confirm it actually reverses, not a near-always-empty no-op.
- **Precision**: a drop lands exactly where released (`elementFromPoint` at the point returns the placed
  element); overlapping targets offset/fan so each stays hit-testable; snap-back on invalid drop.
- **Hit-testing**: anything that "looks clickable" IS the real element at its center (not covered/inert).

## QUALITY GATES (redo if…)
An interaction was judged from a screenshot, not driven · a "works/feels right" claim lacks an asserted state
change · cancel/undo weren't each exercised on a non-empty stack · states weren't each reached.

## CALIBRATION (bar = 9)
10 = every interaction is immediate, precise, discoverable, reversible, at reference polish. 9 = only trivial
timing/polish nits. **≤6** if: a stated interaction contract is unmet (Esc doesn't cancel, an action isn't
undoable) · feedback is missing/delayed on a core action · an affordance is undiscoverable or inert · a drop
mis-lands or a ghost/orphan leaks. A green screenshot with a dead interaction is the exact failure this role exists to catch.

Sources: micro-interactions guide & best practices (IxDF, design-bootcamp); interaction-design principles (affordance, feedback, motion timing).

# MOBILE-QA METHOD — responsive & touch (R7 reference)

> Injected into the mobile reviewer. Grounded in touch-target standards (WCAG 2.5.8, Apple HIG, Material),
> thumb-zone ergonomics, and responsive-breakpoint practice. You MUST self-launch a real touch context
> (`hasTouch`, `isMobile`) at real phone sizes — the shared MCP browser floors the viewport and cannot show
> a 390-wide phone. Judge by TOUCH-DRIVING, not by a resized desktop screenshot.

## THE STEP-BY-STEP APPROACH
**Step 1 — First-thumb gut test**: at 390×844 portrait, can a one-handed first-timer tell what this is and
reach the core action with a thumb, without pinching/zooming/horizontal-scrolling? Overwhelmed on a small
screen, or clean?
**Step 2 — Self-launch** at 390×844 (portrait) AND 844×390 (landscape), touch-enabled; shoot your own PNGs.
**Step 3 — MEASURE the rules** (§) via `CAP measure <url> 390x844 --touch` — the viewport is a BARE
argument to `measure`; `--viewports=` is not parsed there and the run would silently fall back to the
1512x900 default, which is this step's own failure mode wearing a different number. **Never the interactive MCP browser here**: it floors the viewport at roughly
487 wide and cannot show a 390-wide phone, so every mobile number it gives you is measured on a
window that does not exist. That is the same trap Step 2 warns about, one step later.
**Step 4 — TOUCH-DRIVE the core capability path** (select → score → place/reposition by touch → decide →
submit), using `tap()`/touch drags; assert each works by touch, not just mouse.
**Step 5 — Defects + regression flag** (a capability reachable on desktop but not by thumb = high-severity).

## MEASURED MOBILE RULES *(WCAG / Apple / Material / thumb-zone sources)*
- **Touch targets ≥ 44×44px** (Apple HIG) / 48×48dp (Material); minimum WCAG 2.5.8 is 24×24 with spacing.
  Flag any interactive element below 44px, and any pair with < 8px spacing between targets.
- **No horizontal scroll**: `scrollingElement.scrollWidth <= innerWidth` at every phone size. A fixed
  desktop grid that overflows into an inner scroller FAILS.
- **Single-column collapse**: a multi-column desktop layout must reflow to one column on a phone; the center/
  primary surface must have real width (>0) and usable height — measure it.
- **Thumb zone**: primary actions (submit/confirm/primary nav) live at the BOTTOM center where the thumb
  rests, not top corners; a primary action pinned top-right on mobile is a finding. A bottom sheet / bottom
  bar for the primary action is the correct pattern.
- **Two-step responsive minimum**: the layout adapts across at least the common breakpoints (~320/480/768);
  landscape (short height) is handled, not just narrow width (a width-only breakpoint that breaks landscape
  is a defect — drive 844×390).
- **Readability on small screens**: body text stays ≥ ~16px effective; nothing critical clipped or truncated.
- **Gestures have a tappable alternative**: any swipe/drag has a visible tappable fallback (accessibility);
  no undiscoverable custom gestures as the only path.

## QUALITY GATES (redo if…)
Not driven in a real touch context · the shared/floored browser was used for the phone size · h-scroll /
target-size / single-column weren't MEASURED · the core path wasn't completed by touch in portrait.

## CALIBRATION (bar = 9)
10 = fully touch-usable one-handed, portrait & landscape, targets generous, primary action in the thumb zone.
9 = usable with minor spacing/target polish. **≤6** if: horizontal scroll · the core capability is unreachable
by thumb (e.g. a zero-width surface) · targets < 44px on primary controls · the primary action sits outside
the thumb zone · landscape is broken. A "responsive" claim that isn't touch-driven is not verified.

Sources: WCAG 2.5.8 target size · Apple HIG 44pt / Material 48dp · thumb-zone guides · responsive-breakpoint practice.

# UX-QA METHOD — workflow clarity, comprehension & cognitive load (R3 reference)

> Injected into the UX reviewer. Grounded in Nielsen's heuristics, the cognitive walkthrough method, and
> cognitive-load research. You DRIVE the live app and complete the user's real job; you judge from doing
> it, never from the executor's screenshots. **If you can't name the step where it broke, you didn't walk it.**

## THE STEP-BY-STEP APPROACH
**Step 1 — First-time gut test (before analysis).** Look ~3s as someone who has never seen it: do I know
what this is and what to do? Overwhelmed / lost / scared, or oriented? Where does my eye go first — is that
where the task starts? A bad answer is a logged finding.
**Step 2 — COGNITIVE WALKTHROUGH.** Simulate a first-time user doing the PRD's task sequence step by step.
At each step ask the four walkthrough questions: (a) will the user know this is the next thing to do? (b) is
the control for it visible/discoverable? (c) will they recognise it does what they want? (d) after acting,
is the feedback clear enough to know it worked? Any "no" is a defect with the exact step.
**Step 3 — HEURISTIC EVALUATION** against Nielsen's 10 (§) — name each that fails, with the element.
**Step 4 — COGNITIVE-LOAD scan** (§).
**Step 5 — HARD-CONSTRAINT measurement** (no-scroll-to-act, etc.) via `CAP measure <url>` / `CAP eval`
— the instrument your dispatch names, never the interactive MCP browser (it floors the viewport).
Numbers, not vibes.
**Step 6 — Defects:** step/heuristic · what happened · what the user expected · fix · severity · driven evidence.
**Step 7 — Regression flag (high-severity):** a task/view the user could do before and now can't.

## NIELSEN'S 10 HEURISTICS (check every one; name failures) *(NN/g)*
1 Visibility of system status (the user always knows what's happening / what state they're in).
2 Match the real world — the user's language and mental model, not system/dev terms.
3 User control & freedom — a clear exit, **undo**, cancel; no dead ends or forced steps.
4 Consistency & standards — same words/controls mean the same thing throughout; platform conventions.
5 Error prevention — the design makes the mistake hard before it needs an error message.
6 **Recognition over recall** — options, actions, and needed info are visible, not memorised across steps.
7 Flexibility & efficiency — accelerators for the frequent path without blocking the novice.
8 **Aesthetic & minimalist** — no irrelevant/rarely-needed content competing with what matters.
9 Error recovery — plain-language messages that name the problem AND the fix (no codes).
10 Help & documentation — ideally unneeded; if present, findable and task-scoped.

## COGNITIVE-LOAD RULES *(cognitive-load / clutter research)*
- Every zone SELF-LABELLED; a first-timer knows what each region is FOR without a tour.
- The screen shows only what the task needs now; secondary/rare content is demoted (tab/popover/disclosure),
  not crammed in — clutter slows every decision.
- The task sequence is legible: the order the user works in is the order the screen reads in (top-left → action).
- No mystery controls: every control's effect is predictable BEFORE use; labels say what will happen.
- Recognition: the user never has to remember a value/choice from a previous screen to act on this one.
- One primary next-action is obvious at each step; the eye is guided, not left to hunt.

## HARD-CONSTRAINT CHECKS (measured, via `CAP measure` / `CAP eval`)
- No-scroll-to-act: `scrollingElement.scrollHeight <= innerHeight` AND every act-critical control
  in-viewport and hit-testable (not clipped inside an inner-scroll column). A page that "doesn't scroll"
  but hides a control in a clipped container FAILS — check `getBoundingClientRect().bottom` per control.
- No primary action below a fold or behind an undiscoverable gesture/scroll.
- Reading blocks not too wide/narrow; labels not truncated where it hides meaning.

## QUALITY GATES (redo the review if…)
The whole task sequence wasn't driven end-to-end · a "clear/confusing" verdict has no named step · the hard
constraints weren't measured · zero-finding categories aren't accounted for.

## CALIBRATION (bar = 9)
10 = a first-timer completes the job with zero hesitation within constraints; the screen teaches itself.
9 = fully doable & clear, only minor labelling/hierarchy polish. **≤6** if: the user must scroll/hunt for a
primary control · a zone's purpose or a control's effect is unclear · a Nielsen heuristic is violated on a
load-bearing path · the first-time gut test fails (overwhelming/confusing). A "pass" a newcomer finds
confusing is a reviewer miscalibration, not a taste call.

Sources: Nielsen's 10 heuristics (NN/g) · cognitive walkthrough vs heuristic evaluation · cognitive-load-in-UX.

# VISUAL-QA METHOD — the forensic, measured, human-checked review reference

> Injected into every reviewer. Adapted from a McKinsey-grade slide visual-QA method (exhaustive,
> "show your work") and grounded in canonical UI rules (Refactoring UI, Nielsen's heuristics, the 8-pt
> grid, WCAG 2.2 AA, Gestalt). It replaces vibe-scoring with **measured rules + a first-time-human gut
> test**. There is NO master image to copy — you judge against DESIGN RULES and human perception.
>
> **The one rule that governs all others: if you can't show the measured table, you didn't check it.**
> No claim without a number. "85px, not 40px" — never "too far right". "2.9:1" — never "a bit faint".

---

## THE STEP-BY-STEP APPROACH (run in order, every screen/state)

**Step 1 — First-impression GUT TEST (before you measure — numbers bias the eye).**
Load the screen fresh; look ~3 seconds as a person who has never seen it. Answer honestly, in writing:
- Does someone who has never seen this understand **what it is** and **what to do** right away?
- Gut reaction: calm / clean / professional — or cluttered / ugly / **overwhelming**? Would a first-timer
  be **appalled, scared, or overwhelmed**?
- Where does the eye land FIRST — is that the right thing?
- Would I be **embarrassed to show this to a client** / does it look amateur?
- **COMPOSITION — answer FIRST, it's the one that gets missed:** does the layout FILL its space, or is a
  whole region/column floating with a big **empty void** below it? Is the visual weight balanced
  left↔center↔right, or is one column top-heavy/half-empty while another is crammed? Anything **unbalanced,
  unfinished, or floating**? A glaring dead void or a lopsided layout is a **≥major** finding on its own —
  a screen can pass every micro-rule (contrast, spacing, alignment) and STILL look broken because a column
  is half-empty. Measure it too (`CAP capture` writes `columnVoids` into every BASE state record (transition states are captured without measurement, so they carry none) — a column whose content ends far above
  its container bottom); confirm with a `shot` read.
A bad gut answer is itself a logged finding (severity ≥ major). Record the gut verdict now.

**Step 2 — ELEMENT INVENTORY**, region by region (e.g. top bar · left rail [assessment, findings, editor]
· center [stage, filmstrip] · right [decision, rollup, coverage]). List EVERY element with its measured
box (x/y/w/h), padding, background, font — the list, not a count. (You can't compare what you didn't inventory.)

**Step 3 — MEASURED DESIGN-RULE CHECKS** (§ Rules below), via `CAP measure <url>` on the live app —
the instrument your dispatch names, never the interactive MCP browser (it floors the viewport, so any
dimension-sensitive verdict taken on it is measured at the WRONG size). Count-and-flag.

**Step 4 — COMPARISON TABLES** (required output; § Tables). Quality gates apply.

**Step 5 — QUALITATIVE RE-TEST** (after measuring): first-timer completes the job with no docs; nothing
appalling/overwhelming; a demanding designer would ship it as-is. Cross-check the Nielsen heuristics (§).

**Step 6 — DEFECTS** — one entry each: region · what-it-shows (measured) · what-the-rule-says · the measured
difference · impact · fix · severity · which rule/table it came from. No measured difference ⇒ it's a vibe ⇒
not allowed (either measure it or drop it).

**Step 7 — REGRESSION FLAG** — any feature/view present in the PRIOR version now absent = a **high-severity**
finding requiring explicit user sign-off (never assume "approved").

---

## THE MEASURED DESIGN RULES (thresholds are authority-backed; cite the number you measured)

### A. Typography *(Refactoring UI; type-scale / 8-pt sources)*
- ≤ 2 font families. Flag a 3rd.
- A tight type scale: flag if **>6 distinct font-sizes** render on one screen.
- Hierarchy comes from **size + weight + color**, not size alone.
- Body ≥ 14px; nothing load-bearing < 12px.
- Line-height on the 4/8 grid; body line-height ~1.4–1.6.
- Reading blocks ~45–75 characters wide.

### B. Spacing — the 8-point grid *(8-pt grid; Gestalt proximity)*
- Every padding / margin / gap on a **4/8 scale** (4,8,12,16,24,32…). Flag ad-hoc off-scale values (13,17,21…).
- Flag too MANY distinct spacing values on one screen (sloppy rhythm — a clean UI reuses a small set).
- **Proximity rule:** space *within* a group < space *between* groups (related items sit closer).
- Generous whitespace. Flag BOTH cramped (< 8px around content / touching an edge) AND dead voids (a large
  empty region signalling broken balance).

### C. Color *(Refactoring UI; "too many colors = chaotic/unprofessional")*
- One accent hue + neutrals + semantic (ok/warn/danger). Flag too many distinct hues.
- ~60/30/10 balance (neutral/secondary/accent).
- Tokens, not raw hex. Text is off-black, not pure #000.

### D. Contrast & accessibility — WCAG 2.2 AA *(WCAG)*
- Text contrast ≥ **4.5:1** (≥ 3:1 for large: ≥24px, or ≥18.66px bold).
- UI components, icons, borders, focus rings ≥ **3:1**.
- Interactive tap targets ≥ **24×24 CSS px** (prefer 44 iOS / 48 Material on touch/coarse pointer).
- Visible keyboard focus state on every interactive element.
- (This is the rule that catches a faint, near-unreadable control — measure its ratio, don't eyeball it.)

### E. Alignment *(Gestalt continuity)*
- Elements that should align share an edge — measure their x/y; flag any delta **> 2px**.
- Consistent left margins and column edges down the screen.

### F. Consistency *(Nielsen #4; Gestalt similarity)*
- The same element type looks and behaves identically everywhere (buttons, cards, labels, inputs).
- Limit distinct border-radii, border styles, and shadow/elevation levels (flag a proliferation).

### G. Hierarchy & actions *(Refactoring UI)*
- Exactly ONE obvious primary action per region (solid, high-contrast); secondary = outline / low-contrast.
- A clear scan path: what the decision hinges on is prominent; housekeeping demoted. No primary control
  below a fold or in a cramped inner scroll.

---

## THE USABILITY LAYER — Nielsen's 10 heuristics *(NN/g)*
Check each, name any that fail: 1 visibility of system status · 2 match the real world (user's language, not
system terms) · 3 user control & freedom (**undo/cancel/escape**) · 4 consistency & standards · 5 error
prevention · 6 **recognition over recall** (options visible, not memorised) · 7 flexibility & efficiency ·
8 **aesthetic & minimalist** (every element earns its place; clutter competes with signal) · 9 help users
recognise/recover from errors (plain-language, names the fix) · 10 help & documentation (ideally unneeded).

---

## MEASUREMENT PROTOCOL (how to get the numbers)
- Spacing/box: `getComputedStyle(el)` padding/margin/gap + `getBoundingClientRect()`. Collect the SET of
  distinct values across a region to judge scale-consistency.
- Type: collect the distinct `fontSize`/`fontWeight`/`fontFamily` set across all text nodes.
- Contrast: read the element's computed `color` and its effective background; compute the WCAG ratio.
- Alignment: compare `getBoundingClientRect().left/right/top` of elements that should align.
- Targets: `getBoundingClientRect()` width/height of every clickable element.
- Colors/radii/shadows: collect the distinct set across the screen.
Do this in BOTH themes and at the state under review (drive to it first — never trust the executor's shots).

---

## REQUIRED TABLES + QUALITY GATES (the "show your work" contract)
Emit each as measured rows: **Alignment** (≥12 rows) · **Spacing/rhythm** (≥10) · **Typography** (every style)
· **Contrast** (every text + control) · **Color/token** · **Overflow/clip/collision** · **Consistency**
(radii/shadows/button variants) · **Hierarchy/actions**.
**Zero-finding accountability:** a category with no defect MUST state what was measured ("checked 9 text
styles, min contrast 5.1:1, all ≥AA").
**The review is INVALID (redo it) if:** any table is missing or below its min rows · any claim lacks a
measured number · a category is skipped · zero-finding is blank · a defect lacks a measured difference.

---

## CALIBRATION (harsh — you exist to catch what an untrained eye passes)
- **10** = a demanding art director ships as-is. **9** = only trivial taste polish remains.
- ANY of these caps the score at **≤6** and is a listed measured defect: a misalignment >2px on a load-bearing
  edge · a contrast failure on real text/control · a cramped or clipped region · an off-scale / over-varied
  spacing set · >6 font-sizes · too many colors · a dead void · no single clear primary action · **a failed
  gut-test answer**.
- A visual "pass" a real person immediately calls ugly / cramped / hard-to-read / overwhelming is a
  **miscalibration failure on the reviewer**, not a taste difference.

## Output defect shape
`{ region, rule (A–G / Nielsen# / gut), what_it_shows (measured), rule_says, measured_difference, impact,
fix, severity, evidence (the number + how measured) }` — ranked most-severe first.
