## Output Handling & Chaining

Every execution produces output. What you do with the output determines whether the user is informed, confused, or led into an error.

### Summary-first presentation

The user-facing answer leads with:
1. **Status** — "succeeded" / "failed at tool level" / "partial failure" — in that exact language, not "200 OK".
2. **Key identifiers** — message ID, draft ID, row count, URL. Pick the 1–3 fields that matter for this action.
3. **Next action hint** — "Draft is in your Drafts folder. Open it: https://mail.google.com/... — or send it: `nexus external-tool execute ... --action gmail-send-email ...`".

Show JSON only on request. "Show me the full response" gets the `--json` dump; default gets the summary.

### Field extraction for chains

When the output of action A is input to action B, extract the exact field with `jq`:

```bash
# Extract a single field:
EMAIL_ID=$(... --json | jq -r '.result.id')

# Extract from a nested path:
SUBJECT=$(... --json | jq -r '.result.message.subject')

# Extract an array of IDs:
IDS=$(... --json | jq -r '.result.messages[].id')
```

Do NOT chain by eyeballing output in chat, copying a value into your next prompt, and typing it manually. Use `jq`. Shell variable. Next action reads from shell variable. This is testable; copy-paste is not.

### State passing between tools

For chains of arbitrary shape, use `jq -n --arg` to build the next action's input safely:

```bash
DRAFT_INPUT=$(jq -n \
  --arg to "$RECIPIENT" \
  --arg subject "$SUBJECT" \
  --arg body "$BODY" \
  '{to: [$to], subject: $subject, body: $body}')
```

`jq -n --arg` handles multi-line values, quotes, and special characters correctly — string interpolation (`"{... $VAR ...}"`) does not. Multi-line research output from Perplexity will break naive `"$VAR"` interpolation. Always `--arg`.

### Citation

The prompt-chaining shape here is inspired by Anthropic's [Building Effective Agents](https://www.anthropic.com/research/building-effective-agents) — specifically the decomposition of a task into discrete LLM calls with programmatic handoffs. The Nexus adaptation replaces their "LLM call" with "tool execute", but the discipline (one call, one verifiable output, deterministic handoff) is the same. See Pattern 06 for the read-then-write chain recipe.

### WRONG / RIGHT

**WRONG.** The command returns `{success: true, toolId: "...", action: "gmail-create-draft", result: {id: "r5358...", message: {id: "19d98524...", labelIds: ["DRAFT"]}}}`. You paste the entire JSON blob into chat as the reply.
**— Why:** Principle #6. The user needs "Draft created, ID r5358, in your Drafts folder, open it here: ...". Not 200 lines of nested JSON.
**RIGHT.** "Draft created. ID `r5358`. It's in your Drafts folder — [open in Gmail](https://mail.google.com/mail/u/0/#drafts). Want me to send it?" JSON available on request.

**WRONG.** Chain step A output: `{success: true, result: "Belgian telco Proximus launched AI...\n[1] https://techcrunch.com/..."}`. You build step B's input via `"--input '{\"body\":\"$RESEARCH\"}'"` with shell interpolation.
**— Why:** Newlines in `$RESEARCH` break JSON parsing in the shell. Quotes in the content escape wrong. `jq -n --arg` handles this; raw interpolation doesn't.
**RIGHT.** `DRAFT_INPUT=$(jq -n --arg body "$RESEARCH" '{body: $body}')`. Then `nexus external-tool execute <id> --action ... --input "$DRAFT_INPUT" --json`.

## Destructive Action Protocol

This is the skill's load-bearing section. IRREVERSIBLE actions are where tool execution goes catastrophically wrong. The protocol below is the one-and-only path.

### Step-by-step

1. **Classify.** Confirm the action is IRREVERSIBLE via the four-question procedure. If you're unsure, default to IRREVERSIBLE.
2. **Fully resolve parameters.** Every field in `--input` must be a literal value, not a placeholder. `to: ["alice@realco.com"]`, not `to: "<recipient>"`.
3. **Show the resolved preview.** Present the exact JSON (or a table of fields → values) back to the user. Do NOT paraphrase. Do NOT summarize. Show the JSON.
4. **Offer a safer alternative where one exists:**
   - Test recipient (for send-email): "I can send this to `<your-own-address>` first as a dry check, then to the real recipient after you review."
   - Sandbox credential (for Stripe, Twilio test numbers): offer to switch credential.
   - Reversible sibling (for some tools): `gmail-create-draft` instead of `gmail-send-email`. User reviews the draft in Gmail, then sends manually.
5. **Double-confirm.** The user must affirmatively approve the resolved params. A "sounds good" from three turns ago does not count — the approval must be fresh, and it must follow the preview.
6. **Execute.**
7. **Verify upstream success.** Principle #2 — parse `result.os[].k`. If any element is `error`, REPORT FAILURE, do not declare success because the envelope says success.
8. **Summarize and recommend next action.** "Email sent to alice@realco.com. Message ID `19d98524...`. [Open thread in Gmail](...). Reply tracking: off."

### The test-recipient offer (worked example)

Scenario: user wants to send a product update to `team@company.com` (a distribution list with 42 people).

After preview, `AskUserQuestion`:

```
Title: Send test first?
Description: This email will go to 42 recipients. Before sending for real,
I can send a test to you first.

Option A: "Send test to me first"
  value: "test-first"
  description: "I'll send the email to your own address so you can review
  the rendering, links, and formatting. After you confirm it looks right,
  I'll send to the 42 real recipients."

Option B: "Send to 42 recipients now"
  value: "send-now"
  description: "Skip the test — send the reviewed preview directly to
  team@company.com."

Option C: "Cancel"
  value: "cancel"
  description: "Don't send. Leave the draft if you want to review in Gmail."
```

If user picks A: execute with `to: [user's own email]` first, report, then re-ask about sending to the real list.
If user picks B: execute to the real list.
If user picks C: optionally `gmail-create-draft` instead, so the composition isn't lost.

### Create-destruct cycles (REVERSIBLE WRITE only)

For REVERSIBLE WRITE, a "create-then-destruct" cycle validates that tool + credential + schema all work end-to-end, without leaving artifacts:

```bash
# Create a test row
CREATE_RESULT=$(nexus external-tool execute <sheets-id> --action google_sheets-add-single-row \
  --input '{"sheetId":"<id>","worksheetId":"<id>","values":["test"]}' --credential <cred> --json)

ROW_ID=$(echo "$CREATE_RESULT" | jq -r '.result.id')  # or whatever identifies the row

# Destruct immediately (paired undo)
nexus external-tool execute <sheets-id> --action google_sheets-delete-row \
  --input "$(jq -n --arg id "$ROW_ID" '{sheetId: "<id>", rowId: $id}')" --credential <cred> --json
```

If both halves succeed without upstream errors, tool + credential + schema + action-pair are validated. No persistent artifact. Use this to pre-validate a workflow trigger that depends on a row insert, or to pre-validate before attaching the tool to an agent. See Pattern 03.

### WRONG / RIGHT

**WRONG.** User says "send the Q2 update to the team." You immediately run `nexus external-tool execute ... --action gmail-send-email ...` with inferred recipient `team@company.com`.
**— Why:** Skipped step 3 (preview) and step 5 (double-confirm). The user may have meant a different team, a different distribution list, or a draft for review. IRREVERSIBLE actions require explicit preview + approval.
**RIGHT.** Classify as IRREVERSIBLE → resolve params (recipient, subject, body) → preview as JSON → offer test-recipient option → wait for user choice → execute → verify `result.os[].k !== "error"` → summarize.

**WRONG.** You ran the send, got `{success: true, result: {...}}`, reported "Email sent!" to the user. Three minutes later they tell you "I didn't get it."
**— Why:** Principle #2. The envelope said success but `result.os` contained `{k: "error", err: {...Google 400...}}`. You never parsed `os`.
**RIGHT.** After every execute, check `jq -r '.result.os // [] | map(select(.k == "error")) | length'`. If > 0, report failure with the upstream error shown.

**WRONG.** "Delete all rows where status = 'draft'" — you run a mass delete with no preview.
**— Why:** Mass deletes are IRREVERSIBLE and the blast radius is determined by data you can't see at call time. There could be 3 matching rows or 3,000.
**RIGHT.** First run a READ-tier query ("count rows where status = 'draft'") to show the blast radius. Preview: "This will delete 847 rows matching status=draft. Tuesday's 'draft' imports are included. Proceed? (or: I can filter further.)". Only then execute.

## Anti-Patterns

Named so you can call them out in reviews. Each one is a specific shape of failure we have seen or can confidently predict.

### The Shadow Workflow

You build a workflow to "encapsulate" a one-off tool execution because you want a clean artifact. Result: one workflow, one trigger, one node, one output, no reuse, plus publish/unpublish overhead. The workflow is a fossil.

Signal: a workflow with one plugin node and nothing else, last-executed once.
Fix: delete the workflow, document the CLI invocation as a recipe in a runbook, run it there.

### The Credential Blind Spot

You execute with an unspecified credential and hope the "default" was right. In orgs with multiple credentials on the same tool, this succeeds in the wrong mailbox, posts to the wrong Slack workspace, or charges the wrong Stripe account.

Signal: `nexus external-tool execute ... --action gmail-send-email --input ...` (no `--credential`).
Fix: always `--credential <id>`, chosen via `AskUserQuestion` when multiple match. Never omit.

### The Schema Guess

You type parameter names from memory — `spreadsheetId` (Google's term) when Pipedream expects `sheetId`, `recipient` when the schema says `to`, `text` when the schema says `body`. Nexus doesn't validate; the upstream tool rejects with an opaque 400.

Signal: a 400 from the upstream service on parameters that "look right".
Fix: Principle #3. `nexus tool get <toolId>` → read `actions[].parameters` → use the exact names.

### Chain-Without-Rollback

You chain A → B → C. A and B succeed. C fails. A and B's side effects are still present in the world. If they were writes, you've half-committed a process.

Signal: a chain with two or more write steps and no per-step failure plan.
Fix: before running, identify the point of no return, decide abort-vs-continue policy per step, document the rollback procedure for each committed step.

### The Envelope Trap

You treat `{success: true}` as success. You don't parse `result.os`. You confidently tell the user "done" when the upstream tool actually 400-ed.

Signal: success claims in chat followed by "no, actually it didn't go through" from the user.
Fix: Principle #2. Always check `result.os[].k === "error"` before claiming success.

### The Preview-by-Paraphrase

You tell the user "I'll send an email to alice with the summary" instead of showing the resolved JSON. Alice's address is `alice@wrong-company.com` in your inferred input. The user doesn't catch it because they didn't see the exact field.

Signal: confirmations that describe an action in prose instead of showing the JSON/table of fields.
Fix: for IRREVERSIBLE actions, show the resolved input verbatim. Prose descriptions are for summaries after the fact, not for pre-execution previews.

### The Lazy Inferrer

You guess the user's email, the current date, or "the recent spreadsheet" without showing the inference. The user sees "Done" but you acted on a wrong inference.

Signal: no inferred value appears in the preview; no chance for user correction before execute.
Fix: Principle #7. Infer silently is fine only if you show the inferred value in the preview. If the preview skips the field, you skipped the consent.

### The Dry-Run Lie

You tell the user "I'll dry-run this first" and simulate with an LLM. But IRREVERSIBLE tool actions have no dry-run mode — the LLM's simulation is not connected to the tool. The user thinks they've seen the real output; they've seen a hallucination.

Signal: mentions of "dry-run", "simulate", "let me mock it up" in IRREVERSIBLE action contexts.
Fix: there is no AI dry-run for tool executions. Use resolved-parameter preview, test recipients, or reversible siblings. Never simulate an external-system call.

---

## Definition of Done

A tool execution task is complete when all of the following are true. Reading the list before you declare done is the gate.

1. **Action classified.** Tier is one of READ / REVERSIBLE WRITE / SOFT-REVERSIBLE WRITE / IRREVERSIBLE. You can name the tier.
2. **Schema discovered.** Ran `nexus tool get` or equivalent. Saw the action's `parameters[]`. Supplied the required ones with the exact names.
3. **Credential chosen explicitly.** If multiple existed, asked the user. `--credential <id>` was in every invocation.
4. **Preview shown for non-READ actions.** User saw resolved `--input` JSON (or table) and affirmed before execution.
5. **Executed via `nexus external-tool execute`.** Not the raw API, not `nexus tool execute` (which doesn't exist), not a workflow.
6. **Upstream success verified.** Parsed `result.os[].k`. If error present, reported failure and did NOT claim success because of envelope `success: true`.
7. **Summary delivered.** 1–3 line answer with status, key fields, next-action hint. JSON offered on request.
8. **Follow-up decided.** For SOFT-REVERSIBLE, user knows the artifact is there. For IRREVERSIBLE, user knows it's done and where to inspect. For chains, either all steps succeeded or the partial-success cleanup was stated.

If any item is missing, the task is not done. Finish it. Don't leave the user with an ambiguous state.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# 01-read-single-action.sh
#
# PURPOSE: Execute a single READ-tier action end-to-end.
# Demonstrates the Quick Path of nexus-tool-execute:
#   1) Discover tool via search
#   2) Discover action via tool get
#   3) Execute with --json
#   4) Inspect envelope success AND upstream error field
#
# Tier: READ — executing has no side effects, so no confirmation needed.
# Example chosen: gmail-list-labels (zero-argument read).
#
# Run:
#   export NEXUS_API_KEY=nxs_...
#   bash 01-read-single-action.sh [GMAIL_CRED_ID]
#
set -euo pipefail

# ── Required env vars ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
: "${NEXUS_API_KEY:?export NEXUS_API_KEY=nxs_... before running}"

# ── Args ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Gmail credential is optional as an arg; otherwise we discover below.
CRED_ID="${1:-}"

# ── Known tool ID (from live validation, Apr 2026) ───────────────────────────
GMAIL_TOOL_ID="3d49d29e-8c86-5c43-aa24-f4903f577e68"

# ── Step 1: discover credentials if not provided ─────────────────────────────
# Note: multiple Gmail creds often have IDENTICAL names. In real Cue flow
# we'd ask the user via AskUserQuestion — here we auto-pick the newest.
if [[ -z "$CRED_ID" ]]; then
  echo ">> Discovering Gmail credentials..." >&2
  CRED_ID=$(nexus tool credentials "$GMAIL_TOOL_ID" --json \
    | jq -r 'sort_by(.createdAt) | reverse | .[0].id')
  [[ -n "$CRED_ID" && "$CRED_ID" != "null" ]] \
    || { echo "No Gmail credential found. Connect one first." >&2; exit 1; }
  echo ">> Using credential: $CRED_ID" >&2
fi

# ── Step 2: confirm the action exists on the tool ────────────────────────────
# Keeps the script safe if the Gmail tool's actions list ever changes.
echo ">> Verifying gmail-list-labels action exists..." >&2
ACTION_OK=$(nexus tool get "$GMAIL_TOOL_ID" --json \
  | jq '[.actions[]? | select(.key == "gmail-list-labels")] | length')
[[ "$ACTION_OK" == "1" ]] \
  || { echo "gmail-list-labels not found on Gmail tool — has the action key changed?" >&2; exit 1; }

# ── Step 3: execute the READ action ──────────────────────────────────────────
echo ">> Executing gmail-list-labels..." >&2
RESULT=$(nexus external-tool execute "$GMAIL_TOOL_ID" \
  --action gmail-list-labels \
  --credential "$CRED_ID" \
  --input '{}' \
  --json)

# ── Step 4: canonical execute-verify block (envelope + upstream) ─────────────
# success: true alone is NOT enough — upstream errors bubble in result.os[].
ENV_OK=$(echo "$RESULT" | jq -r '.success')
OS_ERR_COUNT=$(echo "$RESULT" | jq -r '[.result.os[]? | select(.k == "error")] | length')

if [[ "$ENV_OK" != "true" || "$OS_ERR_COUNT" != "0" ]]; then
  echo "FAILED — envelope: $ENV_OK, upstream errors: $OS_ERR_COUNT" >&2
  echo "$RESULT" | jq '.result.os[]? | select(.k == "error") | .err' >&2
  exit 1
fi

# ── Step 5: summarize result (summary-first presentation) ────────────────────
# Summary extraction runs after the verify passes.
LABEL_COUNT=$(echo "$RESULT" | jq '.result.labels | length')
echo ">> SUCCESS — $LABEL_COUNT labels visible."
echo "$RESULT" | jq -r '.result.labels[] | "  - \(.name) (\(.id))"' | head -10

# ── Expected output ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
: <<'EOF'
>> Discovering Gmail credentials...
>> Using credential: 776bcbea-5390-4085-99d9-7028d328f207
>> Verifying gmail-list-labels action exists...
>> Executing gmail-list-labels...
>> SUCCESS — 14 labels visible.
  - CHAT (CHAT)
  - SENT (SENT)
  - INBOX (INBOX)
  - IMPORTANT (IMPORTANT)
  - TRASH (TRASH)
  - DRAFT (DRAFT)
  - SPAM (SPAM)
  - CATEGORY_FORUMS (CATEGORY_FORUMS)
  - CATEGORY_UPDATES (CATEGORY_UPDATES)
  - CATEGORY_PERSONAL (CATEGORY_PERSONAL)
EOF

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# 02-reversible-write-cycle.sh
#
# PURPOSE: Demonstrate a SOFT-REVERSIBLE WRITE cycle.
#   - Create a Gmail draft (persists, but not sent)
#   - Verify it lands in the Drafts folder
#   - Explain why this is SOFT-REVERSIBLE (no gmail-delete-draft action exists,
#     so the user must clean up via the Gmail UI if they want it gone)
#
# Tier: SOFT-REVERSIBLE WRITE
#   - Persistent side effect (draft is stored in the user's mailbox)
#   - Not programmatically undoable from Nexus (no paired delete action)
#   - Acceptable to auto-execute with awareness (draft in Drafts = harmless)
#
# Contrast: a REVERSIBLE WRITE like gmail-add-label-to-email is undoable
# via gmail-remove-label-from-email. See 03-irreversible-with-confirm.sh
# for the tier above (IRREVERSIBLE: gmail-send-email).
#
# Run:
#   export NEXUS_API_KEY=nxs_...
#   bash 02-reversible-write-cycle.sh [CRED_ID]
#
set -euo pipefail

: "${NEXUS_API_KEY:?export NEXUS_API_KEY=nxs_... before running}"

CRED_ID="${1:-776bcbea-5390-4085-99d9-7028d328f207}"  # user's validated Gmail cred
GMAIL_TOOL_ID="3d49d29e-8c86-5c43-aa24-f4903f577e68"

# A unique marker so we can find the draft afterwards
STAMP="$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ)"
SUBJECT="[nexus-tool-execute test] draft $STAMP"
TO_ADDR="you+nexus-draft-test@example.com"

# ── Step 1: Build draft input with jq -n --arg (NEVER string interpolation) ──
# body may contain newlines or quotes; only jq guarantees safe JSON.
DRAFT_INPUT=$(jq -n \
  --arg to "$TO_ADDR" \
  --arg subject "$SUBJECT" \
  --arg body "This draft was created by 02-reversible-write-cycle.sh at $STAMP.

It lands in Drafts and is NOT sent." \
  '{to:[$to], subject:$subject, body:$body}')

# ── Step 2: Create the draft — canonical execute-verify block ────────────────
echo ">> Creating Gmail draft (SOFT-REVERSIBLE WRITE)..." >&2
RESULT=$(nexus external-tool execute "$GMAIL_TOOL_ID" \
  --action gmail-create-draft \
  --credential "$CRED_ID" \
  --input "$DRAFT_INPUT" \
  --json)

ENV_OK=$(echo "$RESULT" | jq -r '.success')
OS_ERR_COUNT=$(echo "$RESULT" | jq -r '[.result.os[]? | select(.k == "error")] | length')

if [[ "$ENV_OK" != "true" || "$OS_ERR_COUNT" != "0" ]]; then
  echo "CREATE FAILED — envelope: $ENV_OK, upstream errors: $OS_ERR_COUNT" >&2
  echo "$RESULT" | jq '.result.os[]? | select(.k == "error") | .err' >&2
  exit 1
fi

# Summary extraction runs after the verify passes.
DRAFT_ID=$(echo "$RESULT" | jq -r '.result.id // .result.message.id // empty')
MESSAGE_ID=$(echo "$RESULT" | jq -r '.result.message.id // empty')
echo ">> SUCCESS — draft created (id=$DRAFT_ID, messageId=$MESSAGE_ID)"

# ── Step 3: Verify by searching Drafts — canonical execute-verify block ──────
echo ">> Verifying draft landed in Drafts folder..." >&2
FIND_INPUT=$(jq -n --arg q "subject:\"$SUBJECT\" in:drafts" '{q:$q, maxResults:5}')
RESULT=$(nexus external-tool execute "$GMAIL_TOOL_ID" \
  --action gmail-find-email \
  --credential "$CRED_ID" \
  --input "$FIND_INPUT" --json)

ENV_OK=$(echo "$RESULT" | jq -r '.success')
OS_ERR_COUNT=$(echo "$RESULT" | jq -r '[.result.os[]? | select(.k == "error")] | length')

if [[ "$ENV_OK" != "true" || "$OS_ERR_COUNT" != "0" ]]; then
  echo "VERIFY FAILED — envelope: $ENV_OK, upstream errors: $OS_ERR_COUNT" >&2
  echo "$RESULT" | jq '.result.os[]? | select(.k == "error") | .err' >&2
  exit 1
fi

MATCHES=$(echo "$RESULT" | jq '.result.messages | length // 0')
echo ">> Found $MATCHES matching draft(s) — expected 1"

if [[ "$MATCHES" -ge 1 ]]; then
  echo ">> SOFT-REVERSIBLE cycle complete."
else
  echo "WARNING: draft create claimed success but search found 0 matches." >&2
  echo "The draft may still be indexing — retry search in 5-10s." >&2
fi

# ── Step 4: Tell the user about the cleanup obligation ───────────────────────
cat <<MSG

SOFT-REVERSIBLE CLEANUP NOTE
  This draft persists in your Gmail Drafts folder. The Gmail Pipedream tool
  does NOT expose a gmail-delete-draft action, so Nexus cannot clean it up
  programmatically. To remove it:

    Gmail UI  →  Drafts  →  find subject "$SUBJECT"  →  discard

  Or use the raw Gmail API via any HTTP tool:

    DELETE https://gmail.googleapis.com/gmail/v1/users/me/drafts/$DRAFT_ID

MSG

# ── Expected output ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
: <<'EOF'
>> Creating Gmail draft (SOFT-REVERSIBLE WRITE)...
>> SUCCESS — draft created (id=r5358123456789, messageId=19d98524abcdef)
>> Verifying draft landed in Drafts folder...
>> Found 1 matching draft(s) — expected 1
>> SOFT-REVERSIBLE cycle complete.

SOFT-REVERSIBLE CLEANUP NOTE
  This draft persists in your Gmail Drafts folder. The Gmail Pipedream tool
  does NOT expose a gmail-delete-draft action, so Nexus cannot clean it up
  programmatically. To remove it:

    Gmail UI  →  Drafts  →  find subject "[nexus-tool-execute test] draft 20260416T..."  →  discard
EOF

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# 03-irreversible-with-confirm.sh
#
# PURPOSE: Demonstrate the IRREVERSIBLE-tier protocol for a destructive action.
#   - Resolve full params (recipient, subject, body)
#   - Print a RESOLVED PARAMS PREVIEW
#   - Double-confirm interactively via two separate read -p prompts
#   - Offer a test-recipient override as the first confirm prompt
#   - Execute only on explicit "SEND" word, not a default "y"
#   - Dual success check: envelope + upstream (.result.os[].k=="error")
#
# Tier: IRREVERSIBLE
#   - Execution IS the effect (gmail-send-email delivers bytes to mailboxes)
#   - No paired undo action exists
#   - Nexus does NOT validate required fields server-side — an empty input
#     passes through to Google and Google returns 400 inside .result.os
#
# Run (interactive):
#   export NEXUS_API_KEY=nxs_...
#   bash 03-irreversible-with-confirm.sh [CRED_ID] [REAL_RECIPIENT]
#
set -euo pipefail

: "${NEXUS_API_KEY:?export NEXUS_API_KEY=nxs_... before running}"

CRED_ID="${1:-776bcbea-5390-4085-99d9-7028d328f207}"
REAL_TO="${2:-alice@example.com}"
TEST_TO="${TEST_TO_OVERRIDE:-you+nexus-test@example.com}"

GMAIL_TOOL_ID="3d49d29e-8c86-5c43-aa24-f4903f577e68"

SUBJECT="Project status update"
BODY="Hi — quick note on where we are with the migration. Shipped auth, DB next."

# ── Confirmation #1: offer test recipient override ───────────────────────────
cat <<PREVIEW

=== IRREVERSIBLE ACTION PREVIEW =========================================
Tool       : gmail (id=$GMAIL_TOOL_ID)
Action     : gmail-send-email   (IRREVERSIBLE — cannot be un-sent)
Credential : $CRED_ID

Resolved parameters:
  to      : ["$REAL_TO"]
  subject : "$SUBJECT"
  body    : |
$(echo "$BODY" | sed 's/^/      /')

Send to REAL recipient, or reroute to TEST recipient ($TEST_TO)?
  [R] real  — send to $REAL_TO
  [T] test  — send to $TEST_TO
  [X] abort — cancel
PREVIEW

read -r -p "Choice (R/T/X): " CHOICE
case "${CHOICE:-X}" in
  [Rr]) EFFECTIVE_TO="$REAL_TO";  TARGET_LABEL="REAL" ;;
  [Tt]) EFFECTIVE_TO="$TEST_TO"; TARGET_LABEL="TEST" ;;
  *)    echo "Aborted by user." >&2; exit 1 ;;
esac

# ── Confirmation #2: explicit SEND word (not just y/enter) ───────────────────
cat <<CONFIRM

About to execute on $TARGET_LABEL recipient: $EFFECTIVE_TO
This will DELIVER a real email. It cannot be recalled.

Type the word SEND (uppercase, exact) to proceed.
Any other input aborts.
CONFIRM
read -r -p "Confirm: " CONFIRM_WORD
if [[ "$CONFIRM_WORD" != "SEND" ]]; then
  echo "Aborted — word did not match." >&2
  exit 1
fi

# ── Build input with jq -n --arg (never string-interp user content into JSON) ──
INPUT=$(jq -n \
  --arg to "$EFFECTIVE_TO" \
  --arg subject "$SUBJECT" \
  --arg body "$BODY" \
  '{to:[$to], subject:$subject, body:$body}')

# ── Execute + verify — canonical block (single attempt, no retries on IRREVERSIBLE) ──
echo ">> Sending..." >&2
RESULT=$(nexus external-tool execute "$GMAIL_TOOL_ID" \
  --action gmail-send-email \
  --credential "$CRED_ID" \
  --input "$INPUT" --json)

ENV_OK=$(echo "$RESULT" | jq -r '.success')
OS_ERR_COUNT=$(echo "$RESULT" | jq -r '[.result.os[]? | select(.k == "error")] | length')

if [[ "$ENV_OK" != "true" || "$OS_ERR_COUNT" != "0" ]]; then
  echo "SEND FAILED — envelope: $ENV_OK, upstream errors: $OS_ERR_COUNT" >&2
  echo "$RESULT" | jq '.result.os[]? | select(.k == "error") | .err' >&2
  echo "NOTE: empty --input passes Nexus's schema check and fails at Google (400)." >&2
  exit 1
fi

# ── Summary-first output (summary extraction runs after the verify passes) ───
MSG_ID=$(echo "$RESULT" | jq -r '.result.id // .result.messageId // .result.message.id // "unknown"')
echo ">> SUCCESS — email sent to $EFFECTIVE_TO (message id: $MSG_ID)"
echo ">> $TARGET_LABEL delivery. If TEST, check inbox $EFFECTIVE_TO to confirm."

# ── Expected output (successful TEST path) ───────────────────────────────────
: <<'EOF'

Send to REAL recipient, or reroute to TEST recipient (you+nexus-test@example.com)?

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# 04-two-tool-chain.sh
#
# PURPOSE: Canonical two-tool chain using `jq -n --arg` for safe JSON stitching.
#   Step 1: Perplexity `search`  → raw markdown string
#   Step 2: jq -n --arg           → build Gmail draft input safely
#   Step 3: gmail-create-draft    → SOFT-REVERSIBLE persist of the research
#
# Tier mix: READ (Perplexity) → SOFT-REVERSIBLE WRITE (Gmail draft).
# No send — user reviews the draft before deciding to send.
#
# WHY jq -n --arg AND NOT string interpolation?
#   Perplexity's `.result` is raw markdown. It contains:
#     - double quotes (in quoted references)
#     - newlines (between paragraphs)
#     - backslashes (in escapes)
#   A naive  --input "{\"body\":\"$RESEARCH\"}"  shatters the JSON.
#   jq -n --arg body "$RESEARCH" reads the variable as a single raw string
#   and emits valid JSON regardless of its contents.
#
# Run:
#   export NEXUS_API_KEY=nxs_...
#   bash 04-two-tool-chain.sh "your research question" [GMAIL_CRED_ID]
#
set -euo pipefail

: "${NEXUS_API_KEY:?export NEXUS_API_KEY=nxs_... before running}"

QUESTION="${1:-"latest developments in retrieval-augmented generation, April 2026"}"
GMAIL_CRED_ID="${2:-776bcbea-5390-4085-99d9-7028d328f207}"
DRAFT_TO="${DRAFT_TO:-you+nexus-chain@example.com}"

PERPLEXITY_TOOL_ID="f2fdba30-6b3d-49b2-99a5-12cce5445b11"
GMAIL_TOOL_ID="3d49d29e-8c86-5c43-aa24-f4903f577e68"

# ── Step 1: Perplexity search (READ) — canonical execute-verify block ────────
echo ">> Step 1: Perplexity search..." >&2
PPX_INPUT=$(jq -n --arg q "$QUESTION" '{content: $q}')

RESULT=$(nexus external-tool execute "$PERPLEXITY_TOOL_ID" \
  --action search \
  --input "$PPX_INPUT" --json)

ENV_OK=$(echo "$RESULT" | jq -r '.success')
OS_ERR_COUNT=$(echo "$RESULT" | jq -r '[.result.os[]? | select(.k == "error")] | length')

if [[ "$ENV_OK" != "true" || "$OS_ERR_COUNT" != "0" ]]; then
  echo "Step 1 FAILED — envelope: $ENV_OK, upstream errors: $OS_ERR_COUNT" >&2
  echo "$RESULT" | jq '.result.os[]? | select(.k == "error") | .err' >&2
  exit 1
fi

# Safe to extract — step 1 verified. Perplexity's result is raw markdown STRING.
RESEARCH=$(echo "$RESULT" | jq -r '.result')
RESEARCH_LEN=${#RESEARCH}
echo ">> Step 1 done — got $RESEARCH_LEN chars of research" >&2

# ── Step 2: Build Gmail draft input using jq -n --arg (CANONICAL) ────────────
echo ">> Step 2: Building draft input via jq -n --arg..." >&2
SUBJECT="Research brief: $(echo "$QUESTION" | cut -c1-60)"
DRAFT_INPUT=$(jq -n \
  --arg to "$DRAFT_TO" \
  --arg subject "$SUBJECT" \
  --arg body "$RESEARCH" \
  '{to:[$to], subject:$subject, body:$body}')

# Sanity-check the input is parseable JSON (would have been obvious if not)
echo "$DRAFT_INPUT" | jq . >/dev/null

# ── Step 3: Gmail create-draft (SOFT-REVERSIBLE) — canonical execute-verify block ──
echo ">> Step 3: Creating Gmail draft..." >&2
RESULT=$(nexus external-tool execute "$GMAIL_TOOL_ID" \
  --action gmail-create-draft \
  --credential "$GMAIL_CRED_ID" \
  --input "$DRAFT_INPUT" --json)

ENV_OK=$(echo "$RESULT" | jq -r '.success')
OS_ERR_COUNT=$(echo "$RESULT" | jq -r '[.result.os[]? | select(.k == "error")] | length')

if [[ "$ENV_OK" != "true" || "$OS_ERR_COUNT" != "0" ]]; then
  echo "Step 3 FAILED — envelope: $ENV_OK, upstream errors: $OS_ERR_COUNT" >&2
  echo "NOTE: step 1 succeeded — research is lost unless you saved it." >&2
  echo "$RESULT" | jq '.result.os[]? | select(.k == "error") | .err' >&2
  exit 1
fi

# Summary extraction runs after the verify passes.
DRAFT_ID=$(echo "$RESULT" | jq -r '.result.id // .result.message.id')

echo ">> CHAIN COMPLETE"
echo "   Question : $QUESTION"
echo "   Research : $RESEARCH_LEN chars"
echo "   Draft id : $DRAFT_ID (in Gmail Drafts folder, NOT sent)"
echo "   To       : $DRAFT_TO"
echo
echo "Review the draft in Gmail. Send from the UI when ready."

# ── Expected output ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
: <<'EOF'
>> Step 1: Perplexity search...
>> Step 1 done — got 2847 chars of research
>> Step 2: Building draft input via jq -n --arg...
>> Step 3: Creating Gmail draft...
>> CHAIN COMPLETE
   Question : latest developments in retrieval-augmented generation, April 2026
   Research : 2847 chars
   Draft id : r5358912345 (in Gmail Drafts folder, NOT sent)
   To       : you+nexus-chain@example.com

Review the draft in Gmail. Send from the UI when ready.
EOF

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# 05-cross-skill-seed.sh
#
# PURPOSE: Cross-skill integration — seed data into an external system so a
# nexus-workflow-builder trigger fires, then verify the run via
# nexus-workflow-executions.
#
# Scenario: a published workflow is triggered by `gmail-new-email-received`
# with a subject filter of "[invoice]". To exercise the workflow end-to-end
# without waiting for a real invoice email, we:
#   1) Confirm the workflow is PUBLISHED (DRAFT triggers never fire)
#   2) Send a seed email matching the filter from tool-execute
#   3) Poll `nexus execution list` for the seeded run
#   4) Inspect the run's node results
#   5) Clean-up guidance (SOFT-REVERSIBLE: archive the seeded email)
#
# This is the canonical cross-skill recipe from
# reference/cross-skill-recipes.md §Recipe 1.
#
# Run:
#   export NEXUS_API_KEY=nxs_...
#   bash 05-cross-skill-seed.sh <WORKFLOW_ID> [GMAIL_CRED_ID]
#
set -euo pipefail

: "${NEXUS_API_KEY:?export NEXUS_API_KEY=nxs_... before running}"

WORKFLOW_ID="${1:?usage: 05-cross-skill-seed.sh <WORKFLOW_ID> [GMAIL_CRED_ID]}"
GMAIL_CRED_ID="${2:-776bcbea-5390-4085-99d9-7028d328f207}"

GMAIL_TOOL_ID="3d49d29e-8c86-5c43-aa24-f4903f577e68"
SEED_TO="${SEED_TO:-you+nexus-workflow@example.com}"

# ── Step 1: workflow must be PUBLISHED ──────────────────────────────────────
echo ">> Step 1: Checking workflow is PUBLISHED..." >&2
STATUS=$(nexus workflow get "$WORKFLOW_ID" --json | jq -r '.status')
if [[ "$STATUS" != "PUBLISHED" ]]; then
  echo "Workflow $WORKFLOW_ID is $STATUS, not PUBLISHED." >&2
  echo "DRAFT triggers do not fire — publish first with: nexus workflow publish $WORKFLOW_ID" >&2
  exit 1
fi
echo "   status=$STATUS"

# ── Step 2: build a seed email that matches the trigger filter ──────────────
STAMP=$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ)
SUBJECT="[invoice] seed $STAMP"
SEED_INPUT=$(jq -n \
  --arg to "$SEED_TO" \
  --arg subject "$SUBJECT" \
  --arg body "Seed invoice email to exercise workflow $WORKFLOW_ID at $STAMP." \
  '{to:[$to], subject:$subject, body:$body}')

echo ">> Step 2: Sending seed email..." >&2
RESULT=$(nexus external-tool execute "$GMAIL_TOOL_ID" \
  --action gmail-send-email \
  --credential "$GMAIL_CRED_ID" \
  --input "$SEED_INPUT" --json)

# Canonical execute-verify block — envelope + upstream.
ENV_OK=$(echo "$RESULT" | jq -r '.success')
OS_ERR_COUNT=$(echo "$RESULT" | jq -r '[.result.os[]? | select(.k == "error")] | length')

if [[ "$ENV_OK" != "true" || "$OS_ERR_COUNT" != "0" ]]; then
  echo "SEED FAILED — envelope: $ENV_OK, upstream errors: $OS_ERR_COUNT" >&2
  echo "$RESULT" | jq '.result.os[]? | select(.k == "error") | .err' >&2
  exit 1
fi
echo "   seed delivered, subject=\"$SUBJECT\""

# ── Step 3: poll workflow executions ────────────────────────────────────────
echo ">> Step 3: Polling for the triggered execution (up to ~2 minutes)..." >&2
RUN_ID=""
for attempt in $(seq 1 12); do
  # Look at the latest run; if its createdAt is after STAMP, it's ours.
  LATEST=$(nexus execution list --workflow-id "$WORKFLOW_ID" --limit 1 --json | jq -r '.data[0] // empty')
  if [[ -n "$LATEST" ]]; then
    RUN_ID=$(echo "$LATEST" | jq -r '.id')
    RUN_STATUS=$(echo "$LATEST" | jq -r '.status')
    RUN_TS=$(echo "$LATEST" | jq -r '.createdAt // .startedAt // empty')
    echo "   attempt $attempt: run=$RUN_ID status=$RUN_STATUS ts=$RUN_TS" >&2
    if [[ "$RUN_STATUS" == "SUCCESS" || "$RUN_STATUS" == "FAILED" ]]; then
      break
    fi
  fi
  sleep 10
done

if [[ -z "$RUN_ID" ]]; then
  echo "No execution appeared within 2 minutes." >&2
  echo "Possible causes: trigger filter doesn't match subject, poll cadence is slow," >&2
  echo "or the watched inbox differs from the Gmail credential owner." >&2
  exit 1
fi

# ── Step 4: inspect node-level results (integration w/ nexus-workflow-executions) ──
echo ">> Step 4: Inspecting run $RUN_ID..." >&2
nexus execution get "$RUN_ID" --json | jq '{id, status, triggerPayload: .triggerPayload?}' \
  || echo "(get failed — run may still be RUNNING)"

# ── Step 5: cleanup guidance ────────────────────────────────────────────────
cat <<CLEANUP

>> SEED + EXECUTION COMPLETE
   Workflow : $WORKFLOW_ID
   Run      : $RUN_ID

CLEANUP (SOFT-REVERSIBLE)
   The seed email persists in the inbox $SEED_TO.
   Archive or delete it via Gmail UI so it does not pollute future monitoring.
   Search: subject:"$SUBJECT"

CLEANUP

# ── Expected output ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
: <<'EOF'
>> Step 1: Checking workflow is PUBLISHED...
   status=PUBLISHED
>> Step 2: Sending seed email...
   seed delivered, subject="[invoice] seed 20260416T182342Z"
>> Step 3: Polling for the triggered execution (up to ~2 minutes)...
   attempt 1: run=01JEJ... status=RUNNING ts=2026-04-16T18:23:45Z
   attempt 2: run=01JEJ... status=SUCCESS ts=2026-04-16T18:23:45Z
>> Step 4: Inspecting run 01JEJ...
{
  "id": "01JEJ...",
  "status": "SUCCESS",
  "triggerPayload": { "subject": "[invoice] seed 20260416T182342Z", ... }
}

>> SEED + EXECUTION COMPLETE
   Workflow : wf_xxx
   Run      : 01JEJ...

CLEANUP (SOFT-REVERSIBLE)
   The seed email persists in the inbox you+nexus-workflow@example.com.
   Archive or delete it via Gmail UI so it does not pollute future monitoring.
   Search: subject:"[invoice] seed 20260416T182342Z"
EOF

# Action Taxonomy

Every tool action falls into ONE of four reversibility tiers. Your execution procedure — confirmation depth, credential selection, recovery strategy, user validation — changes based on the tier. Misclassifying an action is how test emails land in prod inboxes, test charges hit real cards, and test rows leak into production sheets.

This document is the authoritative classification reference. SKILL.md has the summary table; this file has the full 40+ example catalog, edge cases, and the procedure for classifying actions you've never seen.

---

## CRITICAL TAXONOMY REQUIREMENTS

**ABSOLUTE RULES — enforce BEFORE executing any tool action:**

- **NEVER** execute a write action without first classifying its tier. "I think it's reversible" is not a classification — discover explicitly.
- **NEVER** treat an action as REVERSIBLE WRITE without confirming the paired undo action exists. A `create-*` action with no matching `delete-*` action is SOFT-REVERSIBLE, not REVERSIBLE.
- **NEVER** collapse tiers to save confirmation steps. IRREVERSIBLE always double-confirms, even when the user seems impatient.
- **ALWAYS** surface the tier in the preview the user sees. The user approves with full knowledge of reversibility.
- **ALWAYS** assume a new tool is IRREVERSIBLE until you discover otherwise. Fail safe.

**STOP conditions:**

- If you cannot classify an action after reading its `nexus tool get` metadata, STOP and ask the user to confirm the tier before executing.
- If the action list for a tool has no obvious paired undo (e.g., `create-draft` with no `delete-draft`), STOP and classify as SOFT-REVERSIBLE.
- If the action name contains `delete`, `remove`, `destroy`, `cancel`, `refund`, `charge`, `send`, `publish`, `archive-permanently` — STOP. Default tier is IRREVERSIBLE. Argue your way DOWN from there, not up to it.

---

## The Four Tiers

| Tier | Side effect visible externally? | Can undo programmatically via Nexus? | Confirmation procedure |
|------|---------------------------------|--------------------------------------|------------------------|
| **READ** | No | N/A — no side effect | Preview plan, auto-execute |
| **REVERSIBLE WRITE** | Yes | Yes — paired undo action exists in same tool | Single confirm with param preview |
| **SOFT-REVERSIBLE WRITE** | Yes | No programmatic undo — manual or out-of-band cleanup required | Single confirm + surface the "artifact left behind" warning |
| **IRREVERSIBLE** | Yes | No — permanent side effect on external system or other humans | Double confirm with FULL resolved params. Offer test recipient / sandbox credential where the tool supports it. |

### What each tier means in practice

**READ** — the tool returns data. No row inserted, no email sent, no record changed. Executing IS the test. You can run it 50 times with no cumulative harm beyond API rate limits. Examples: `gmail-find-email`, `perplexity search`, `google_sheets-get-values`, `hubspot-get-contact`, `slack-list-channels`.

**REVERSIBLE WRITE** — the tool changes external state, but the same tool offers a clean undo. If you insert a row, you can delete that exact row with the row ID returned by the insert. If you add a label, there's a remove-label action that takes the same email ID. The create-destruct cycle is a valid safety pattern for this tier. Examples: `gmail-add-label-to-email` ↔ `gmail-remove-label-from-email`, `google_sheets-add-single-row` ↔ `google_sheets-delete-row`, `hubspot-create-contact` ↔ `hubspot-delete-contact`.

**SOFT-REVERSIBLE WRITE** — the tool changes external state. The state PERSISTS in the user's external account (a draft sits in Drafts, a signature updates the profile, a label shows in the sidebar), but there is no programmatic delete action exposed in the Nexus tool catalog. Reversal requires the user to clean up manually through the vendor's UI, or to use a separate out-of-band tool (e.g., Gmail's web UI to delete a draft). This tier is the trap — agents often assume it's REVERSIBLE because "a draft isn't a sent email, so what could go wrong?" The gotcha is that if you create 50 test drafts to validate a chain, you've dumped 50 drafts into the user's Gmail account with no way to clean them up from Nexus. Examples: `gmail-create-draft` (no `gmail-delete-draft` in Pipedream Gmail action list), `gmail-create-label`, `gmail-update-primary-signature`, `slack-create-channel` (archive exists, but not delete).

**IRREVERSIBLE** — the tool commits a side effect that cannot be undone by any programmatic action. Sending an email puts bytes on a recipient's server — unsendable. Charging a card moves money — chargebacks are a refund, not an undo. Deleting a row in a sheet drops data — if you didn't snapshot first, it's gone. Publishing a blog post is crawled the moment it goes live. Examples: `gmail-send-email`, `stripe-create-charge`, `twilio-send-sms`, `slack-post-message` (to a channel), `salesforce-send-email`, any `delete-*` action on any tool.

---

## How to Classify an Unknown Action

When you encounter a tool action for the first time, run this procedure before executing. It takes 20 seconds and prevents every classification disaster below.

### Step 1 — Read the verb

The action key follows Pipedream convention: `<toolname>-<verb>-<noun>`. Look at the verb.

| Verb | Likely tier (default) |
|------|-----------------------|
| `get`, `find`, `list`, `search`, `read`, `fetch`, `export` | READ |
| `add-label`, `archive`, `move`, `star`, `unstar` | REVERSIBLE WRITE (check for paired action) |
| `create-row`, `insert`, `update-row`, `upsert` | REVERSIBLE WRITE (delete-by-id typically exists) |
| `create-draft`, `create-label`, `create-folder`, `update-signature`, `create-channel` | SOFT-REVERSIBLE WRITE (check for matching delete) |
| `send`, `post`, `publish`, `charge`, `refund`, `sms`, `email`, `delete`, `remove`, `cancel`, `unsubscribe` | IRREVERSIBLE |

The verb is the strongest signal but is not authoritative. `gmail-remove-label-from-email` has `remove` in it but is REVERSIBLE WRITE because `gmail-add-label-to-email` exists as the paired undo. Always cross-check.

### Step 2 — Check for the paired undo

Fetch the tool's full action list and search for the inverse action:

```bash
nexus tool get "$TOOL_ID" --json | jq '.actions[] | {key, name}' | less
```

For each candidate tier decision:

- If tier is **REVERSIBLE WRITE**, verify the paired undo action exists with a matching signature. `add-X-to-Y` implies `remove-X-from-Y`. `create-Z` implies `delete-Z`. If the paired action doesn't exist, demote to SOFT-REVERSIBLE WRITE.
- If tier is **SOFT-REVERSIBLE WRITE**, confirm the state is WRITTEN to the external account (not sent to third parties). A draft is soft-reversible because it stays in the owner's mailbox. A scheduled send is IRREVERSIBLE because the platform commits to delivery.
- If tier is **IRREVERSIBLE**, double-check for a sandbox mode or test-mode parameter (e.g., Stripe `test_mode: true`, Twilio test credentials). Irreversible in prod, safe in sandbox.

### Step 3 — Inspect the parameters for third-party addressing

If the action accepts `to`, `recipient`, `phone_number`, `channel`, `url`, `webhook_url`, or any field pointing to an external human or system, the action almost certainly commits a side effect visible to a third party. Default to IRREVERSIBLE unless you can prove otherwise.

### Step 4 — Check for `test_mode`, `dry_run`, or sandbox affordances

Some Pipedream components expose a `test_mode` or `dry_run` boolean parameter, or a separate sandbox credential type. If present, IRREVERSIBLE actions can be safely exercised against the sandbox. Document the sandbox usage in the execution preview.

### Step 5 — When in doubt, ask the user

If the procedure above is inconclusive, ask:

```
!! AskUserQuestion !!
question: "I'm about to run <action-key>. I can't tell from the tool metadata
          whether it's reversible. Can you confirm: does this action commit a
          visible side effect to anyone besides you?"
options: ["Yes — third parties see it (treat as IRREVERSIBLE)",
          "No — only affects my own account state (treat as SOFT-REVERSIBLE)",
          "I don't know — skip this action"]
```

Never execute a tier-ambiguous action without this check.

---

| `airtable-update-record` | SOFT-REVERSIBLE WRITE | Airtable has revision history but not exposed via Pipedream. |

| `google_calendar-update-event` | SOFT-REVERSIBLE WRITE | Same attendee-notification risk. |

## Edge Cases

### Eventually-consistent actions

Some actions commit a side effect but do not reflect in reads for seconds to minutes (Salesforce object indexing, Google Drive search indexing, Elasticsearch document writes). A create-destruct test cycle that runs the delete immediately after create may fail because the record isn't yet queryable. Not a tier change — still REVERSIBLE WRITE — but the undo procedure must include a wait loop or rely on the ID returned by the create rather than a lookup.

### Partial-failure actions

Batch actions (`google_sheets-add-multiple-rows`, `salesforce-bulk-create`) may succeed for some items and fail for others. A partial failure is harder to undo because you need the list of successfully-created IDs. Classify as REVERSIBLE WRITE only if the response reliably returns per-item status. Otherwise SOFT-REVERSIBLE (you may leak partial records that you can't identify for cleanup).

### Side-effect cascades

Creating a Salesforce lead triggers automation rules (email campaigns, Slack notifications, webhook fires). The lead itself is REVERSIBLE — delete the lead and it's gone. But the cascaded side effects (emails already sent, webhooks already delivered) are IRREVERSIBLE. If the user has automation rules on the object, treat create-style actions as IRREVERSIBLE.

### Rate-limit-triggered retries

If a tool auto-retries on 429, a previously "successful" execution may have committed twice. For IRREVERSIBLE actions, idempotency keys (Stripe `Idempotency-Key` header, HTTP conditional creates) are the only safe guard. Nexus `external-tool execute` does not currently surface idempotency key controls — document this limitation in the execution preview for high-stakes actions.

### Sandbox vs production credentials

Many tools ship with separate sandbox credentials (Stripe test keys, Twilio trial numbers, HubSpot sandbox workspaces). Executing an IRREVERSIBLE action against a sandbox credential is safe. If the tool has both credential types available in the org:

- For IRREVERSIBLE actions, prefer the sandbox credential for testing.
- For production runs, explicitly confirm the credential tier with the user before executing.

See gotchas #13 (Sandbox vs production) and #14 (Credential scoped for specific action).

### Actions with hidden fan-out

`gmail-send-email` with `cc` and `bcc` fans out to every recipient. The IRREVERSIBLE impact scales with recipient count. Always surface the resolved `to + cc + bcc` list in the preview before sending. A typo in `to` that adds 50 wrong recipients is a 50x data leak.

### "Create" that sends notifications by default

`google_calendar-create-event` with attendees defaults to sending invites. `linear-add-comment` fires assignee notifications. `zendesk-create-ticket` with `public_update: true` emails the requester. When the tier would be SOFT-REVERSIBLE (deleting the artifact is possible), but the create commits a third-party-visible notification, PROMOTE to IRREVERSIBLE. The notification is the real side effect.

## Procedure for Classifying a New Tool

When the user asks you to execute a tool you've never seen:

1. Fetch the action list: `nexus tool get "$TOOL_ID" --json | jq '.actions[] | {key, name, description}'`.
2. For the target action, read the `description` field. Note any phrases like "sends notification", "deletes permanently", "cannot be undone", "immediately visible".
3. Classify the verb via the Step 1 table above.
4. Search the action list for the paired undo (Step 2).
5. Inspect the parameters for third-party addressing (Step 3).
6. Check for `test_mode` / `dry_run` / sandbox (Step 4).
7. Assign the tier and record the classification in your working notes for this session.
8. Surface the tier in the execution preview. Use the confirmation procedure for that tier.

**Checklist before executing any write action:**

- [ ] Tier classified and recorded
- [ ] Paired undo action verified (or absence noted)
- [ ] Sandbox credential considered for IRREVERSIBLE actions
- [ ] Third-party recipients counted and surfaced in preview
- [ ] User confirmation obtained at the correct depth (single-confirm for REVERSIBLE/SOFT, double-confirm for IRREVERSIBLE)
- [ ] Rollback plan documented (for chains only — see `TOOL_EXECUTION_GUIDE.md` → Destructive Action Protocol)

If any checkbox is unchecked, STOP and resolve it before executing.

# Cross-Skill Recipes

Recipes for invoking `nexus-tool-execute` from inside the phases of other Nexus skills. Each recipe answers one question: *"I'm in skill X, phase Y — why and how do I run a single external-tool action RIGHT NOW, without spinning up a workflow or an agent?"*

Every recipe uses `nexus external-tool execute` as the unified command for both PIPEDREAM and CUSTOM_MANIFEST tools. Replace `<...>` placeholders with real IDs discovered via `nexus tool search --json`, `nexus tool credentials <toolId> --json`, etc.

**Envelope caveat (applies to every recipe).** The response envelope wraps the upstream tool call:

```json
{ "success": true, "toolId": "<uuid>", "action": "<key>", "result": <object-or-string> }
```

`success: true` means "Nexus's execute endpoint returned 200" — it does NOT mean the upstream API (Gmail, Salesforce, Perplexity, ...) succeeded. Upstream errors surface inside `result.os[]` as entries with `k: "error"`. Every recipe below checks both envelope success AND `result.os[].k === "error"`.

**Canonical chain recipe.** Whenever a recipe passes multi-line output from one tool into another tool's JSON input, it uses:

```bash
PAYLOAD=$(jq -n --arg body "$UPSTREAM_OUTPUT" --arg subject "My subject" \
  '{to:["user@example.com"], subject:$subject, body:$body}')
```

Never `--input "{\"body\":\"$UPSTREAM_OUTPUT\"}"` — newlines and quotes in `$UPSTREAM_OUTPUT` will shred your JSON. Always `jq -n --arg`.

# Tier 1 — Deep Integration (5 recipes)

## Recipe 1: Seed CRM / Gmail data to fire a workflow trigger

**Source skill:** `nexus-workflow-builder`
**Phase:** Phase 2 — test the workflow with real trigger events

**Scenario.** You're building a workflow whose trigger is `gmail-new-email-received` or a Salesforce `new-lead` plugin trigger. The workflow is published, but you can't validate end-to-end until a real trigger fires. Instead of waiting for an organic event, use tool-execute to seed the upstream state: send an email to the watched inbox, create a test lead in the CRM, push a row to the watched sheet. The workflow trigger fires on the seeded event and you can inspect the run in `nexus-workflow-executions`. Same pattern works for schedule-triggered workflows that read external state at run-time — seed the state, then manually invoke.

**Procedure.**
1. Confirm the workflow is PUBLISHED via `nexus workflow get <workflowId> --json` (DRAFT triggers never fire).
2. Identify the external source the trigger watches. Read the trigger node's `data.appName` and `data.triggerKey` from the workflow JSON.
3. Find the matching write action in the same tool: `nexus tool get <toolId> --json | jq '.actions[] | select(.key | test("create|send|insert"))'`.
4. Confirm which credential to use. If more than one exists, ASK the user — don't autopick. Surface `createdAt` so the user can disambiguate identically-named credentials.
5. Build the input payload with realistic but clearly-test values (subject prefixed `[test]`, lead named `Nexus Test <timestamp>`).
6. Execute the seed action. Capture the returned `result.id` for later cleanup.
7. Watch `nexus execution list --workflow-id <workflowId> --limit 5 --json` — the triggered run should appear within 10-60s depending on the integration's polling cadence.
8. Inspect the run: `nexus execution get <runId> --json`. If nodes failed, use `nexus execution node-result <runId> <nodeId> --json` to see what the trigger actually passed in.
9. Clean up seed records so real monitoring isn't polluted (delete lead, archive email, remove row).

**Bash snippet.**
```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

WORKFLOW_ID="$1"
GMAIL_TOOL_ID="3d49d29e-8c86-5c43-aa24-f4903f577e68"
GMAIL_CRED_ID="776bcbea-5390-4085-99d9-7028d328f207"  # user confirmed this one
TEST_INBOX="you+nexus-trigger-test@example.com"

# 1) Verify workflow is published
STATUS=$(nexus workflow get "$WORKFLOW_ID" --json | jq -r '.status')
[[ "$STATUS" == "PUBLISHED" ]] || { echo "Workflow must be PUBLISHED, got $STATUS" >&2; exit 1; }

# 2) Seed an email that matches the trigger filter
SUBJECT="[test] trigger seed $(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ)"
INPUT=$(jq -n --arg subject "$SUBJECT" --arg to "$TEST_INBOX" \
  '{to:[$to], subject:$subject, body:"Seed body for workflow-trigger test."}')

RESP=$(nexus external-tool execute "$GMAIL_TOOL_ID" \
  --action gmail-send-email \
  --credential "$GMAIL_CRED_ID" \
  --input "$INPUT" --json)

echo "$RESP" | jq -e '.success == true' >/dev/null || { echo "envelope fail" >&2; exit 1; }
echo "$RESP" | jq -e '.result.os[]? | select(.k=="error")' >/dev/null \
  && { echo "upstream error, see full response below" >&2; echo "$RESP" | jq .; exit 1; } \
  || echo "seeded email delivered"

# 3) Poll executions for a new run on this workflow
for i in 1 2 3 4 5 6; do
  RUN=$(nexus execution list --workflow-id "$WORKFLOW_ID" --limit 1 --json | jq -r '.data[0]')
  echo "attempt $i: $(echo "$RUN" | jq -r '.id + " " + .status')"
  [[ $(echo "$RUN" | jq -r '.status') == "SUCCESS" ]] && break
  sleep 10
done
```

**Verify success.** Envelope `.success == true`, no `result.os[].k == "error"`, and a new execution with `status: SUCCESS` (or at least `RUNNING`) appears within ~60s. If no execution appears after 2 minutes, the trigger filter doesn't match your seed — check the trigger node's filter config.

**Clean-up (SOFT-REVERSIBLE).** For Gmail: `nexus external-tool execute <toolId> --action gmail-find-email --input '{"q":"subject:\"[test] trigger seed\""}' --credential <id> --json` then archive or delete via Gmail UI. For CRM: delete the seeded lead via the CRM's delete action.

**Related.** `nexus-workflow-executions/SKILL.md` for run inspection, `nexus-tool-execute/reference/patterns/patterns/02-seed-test-data.md` for the full seed-and-verify procedure.

## Recipe 2: Pre-attachment action validation

**Source skill:** `nexus-agent-management`
**Phase:** Attaching a PLUGIN-type tool config to an agent

**Scenario.** You're about to `nexus agent-tool create <agentId> --label … --type PLUGIN --body '{"config":{"toolId":X,"action":Y,"toolCredentialId":Z}}'`. Once attached, the agent will silently call this action on every matching user turn — and if the credential is wrong, the action is misnamed, or the input schema requires a field you haven't mapped, every conversation will fail with a cryptic runtime error. Run the exact action+credential combo once via tool-execute with realistic inputs BEFORE attaching. This validates that the credential's OAuth scopes match the action, the dynamic dropdown options resolve, and the upstream service accepts the payload shape.

**Procedure.**
1. Discover tool + action: `nexus tool search --query "<tool-name>" --json` then `nexus tool get <toolId> --json | jq '.actions[] | select(.key == "<action-key>")'`.
2. Read the action's `parametersSetup` — note which fields are required, which are dynamic dropdowns, which have defaults.
3. Ask the user for any prompt-time values (recipient, channel ID, spreadsheet row). Use `AskUserQuestion`.
4. Pick credential. If multiple exist, ASK — surface `name`, `type`, and `createdAt` so the user can disambiguate.
5. For dynamic dropdown params (e.g., `sheetId`), resolve via `nexus api POST /tools/<toolId>/resolve-options` with the parent params.
6. Execute once with resolved inputs. Inspect both envelope success AND `result.os[].k == "error"`.
7. If execution succeeds and the upstream payload returned what the agent will need, attach with confidence.
8. If execution fails, fix the parameter or credential before attaching — don't propagate the failure into agent runtime.

**Bash snippet.**
```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

AGENT_ID="$1"
TOOL_ID="$2"
ACTION_KEY="$3"
CRED_ID="$4"
INPUT_JSON="$5"   # pre-resolved JSON payload

# 1) Dry-validate the action+credential combo by executing once
RESP=$(nexus external-tool execute "$TOOL_ID" \
  --action "$ACTION_KEY" \
  --credential "$CRED_ID" \
  --input "$INPUT_JSON" --json)

ENV_OK=$(echo "$RESP" | jq -r '.success')
UPSTREAM_ERR=$(echo "$RESP" | jq '[.result.os[]? | select(.k=="error")] | length')

if [[ "$ENV_OK" != "true" || "$UPSTREAM_ERR" != "0" ]]; then
  echo "PRE-ATTACH VALIDATION FAILED — do not attach." >&2
  echo "$RESP" | jq '.result.os[]? | select(.k=="error") | .err' >&2
  exit 1
fi
echo "Pre-attach validation passed. Safe to attach."

# 2) Now attach the plugin tool
# agentId is POSITIONAL. tool/action/credential live inside --body.config,
# they are not flags.
nexus agent-tool create "$AGENT_ID" \
  --label "$ACTION_KEY" \
  --type PLUGIN \
  --body "$(jq -n \
      --arg t "$TOOL_ID" --arg a "$ACTION_KEY" --arg c "$CRED_ID" \
      '{config: {toolId: $t, action: $a, toolCredentialId: $c}}')" \
  --json
```

**Verify success.** No upstream errors, and the returned payload has the field(s) your agent prompt will reference. If your agent reads `result.id` after calling the action, confirm that ID field is present and non-null.

**Clean-up.** Depends on tier. If you test-executed `gmail-send-email`, you've already sent a real email — recipients should be internal test accounts. For REVERSIBLE WRITE actions (add-row, create-lead), delete the seed record once validated.

**Related.** `nexus-tool-execute/reference/patterns/patterns/03-pre-attachment-validation.md`, `nexus-tool-connection/SKILL.md` for credential discovery.

## Recipe 3: External data fetch to populate a knowledge base

**Source skill:** `nexus-knowledge-base`
**Phase:** Data sources — preparing content for collection ingestion

**Scenario.** The user wants a collection built from data that lives in Google Sheets, Airtable, HubSpot, Notion, or any external system exposed through a Pipedream tool. Manual export + upload works, but stales the moment the source changes. Tool-execute fetches current data on demand. You pull rows, transform (optional — via an AI task if the schema needs normalization), write each row as a text document, and attach to the collection. Re-run the fetch + upload anytime to refresh. This is NOT a replacement for a scheduled workflow (that's what you'd build for daily sync) — it's the one-shot bootstrap or ad-hoc refresh.

**Procedure.**
1. Identify source tool + read action: `nexus tool get <toolId> --json | jq '.actions[] | select(.key | test("get-values|list-records|search"))'`.
2. Execute the read. Structured output goes into `result`. Inspect via `| jq '.result'`.
3. Transform each record into `{name, content}` for text-document upload. For heavy normalization, pipe through `nexus task execute <taskId>` with a summarize-or-normalize AI task.
4. Loop rows, calling `nexus document create-text --name <row> --content <markdown>`. Capture document IDs.
5. Attach all IDs to the target collection via `nexus collection attach-documents <collectionId> --document-ids <id1,id2,...>`.

**Bash snippet.**
```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

SHEETS_TOOL_ID="$1"
SHEETS_CRED_ID="$2"
SHEET_ID="$3"
COLLECTION_ID="$4"

# 1) Fetch current rows from Google Sheets
INPUT=$(jq -n --arg sheetId "$SHEET_ID" --arg range "Sheet1!A2:C" \
  '{sheetId:$sheetId, range:$range}')
RESP=$(nexus external-tool execute "$SHEETS_TOOL_ID" \
  --action google_sheets-get-values \
  --credential "$SHEETS_CRED_ID" \
  --input "$INPUT" --json)

echo "$RESP" | jq -e '.success' >/dev/null
echo "$RESP" | jq -e '.result.os[]? | select(.k=="error")' >/dev/null \
  && { echo "fetch failed" >&2; exit 1; }

# result.values is 2D array; iterate
ROWS=$(echo "$RESP" | jq -c '.result.values // []')

DOC_IDS=()
i=0
for row in $(echo "$ROWS" | jq -c '.[]'); do
  NAME=$(echo "$row" | jq -r '.[0]')
  BODY=$(echo "$row" | jq -r '.[1:] | join("\n\n")')
  DOC=$(nexus document create-text --name "$NAME" --content "$BODY" --json)
  DOC_IDS+=("$(echo "$DOC" | jq -r '.id')")
  i=$((i+1))
done
echo "Created $i documents"

# 2) Attach all to the collection
IFS=','; IDS_CSV="${DOC_IDS[*]}"; unset IFS
nexus collection attach-documents "$COLLECTION_ID" --document-ids "$IDS_CSV" --json
```

**Verify success.** `nexus collection documents <collectionId> --json | jq 'length'` matches the row count. Spot-check one document's content via `nexus document get <docId>`.

**Clean-up.** If the fetch-and-upload went wrong, remove docs via `nexus collection remove-document <collectionId> <docId>` (two positionals, no flag) and delete the docs with `nexus document delete <docId>`.

**Related.** `nexus-knowledge-base/SKILL.md` (collection management), `nexus-skills-and-tasks/SKILL.md` (AI task for normalization), `nexus-tool-execute/reference/patterns/patterns/04-knowledge-fetch.md`.

## Recipe 4: Emulator scenario seeding

**Source skill:** `nexus-emulator`
**Phase:** Scenario setup — before `nexus emulator send`

**Scenario.** You're about to test a support agent in the emulator. The agent's job is "when a user mentions ticket #N, look up the ticket in Zendesk and respond." You can send the emulator message easily — but the agent's tool will return 404 because ticket #N doesn't exist. Solution: tool-execute to create the ticket in Zendesk FIRST, then open an emulator session, then send the message. The agent now has real external state to work with. Same pattern applies for any agent whose behavior depends on external state: CRM lookup agents, inventory agents, order-status agents, SaaS usage-tier agents.

**Procedure.**
1. Identify the external state your agent will read. Read the agent's tool configs (`nexus agent-tool list --agent-id <id> --json`) to see which external systems + actions it uses.
2. Use the matching WRITE action in the same tool to seed the state (create-ticket, add-lead, insert-row).
3. Capture the returned ID — you'll need it in the emulator message to reference the seeded state.
4. Create an emulator session: `nexus emulator session create <deploymentId> --json`.
5. Send the emulator message referencing the seeded ID.
6. Inspect debug info in the response — confirm the agent called its tool with the expected ID and got real data back.
7. After the test: delete the seeded state (or tag it so it's obviously a test record).

**Bash snippet.**
```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

DEPLOYMENT_ID="$1"
ZENDESK_TOOL_ID="$2"
ZENDESK_CRED_ID="$3"

# 1) Seed a Zendesk ticket the agent will look up
TICKET_INPUT=$(jq -n \
  '{subject:"[test] seeded for emulator run", comment:{body:"Please check my order"}, priority:"normal"}')
SEED=$(nexus external-tool execute "$ZENDESK_TOOL_ID" \
  --action zendesk-create-ticket \
  --credential "$ZENDESK_CRED_ID" \
  --input "$TICKET_INPUT" --json)

echo "$SEED" | jq -e '.result.os[]? | select(.k=="error")' >/dev/null \
  && { echo "seed failed" >&2; exit 1; }
TICKET_ID=$(echo "$SEED" | jq -r '.result.ticket.id // .result.id')
echo "seeded ticket #$TICKET_ID"

# 2) Spin up emulator session
SESSION=$(nexus emulator session create "$DEPLOYMENT_ID" --json)
SESSION_ID=$(echo "$SESSION" | jq -r '.id')

# 3) Send a message that forces the agent to look up ticket #$TICKET_ID
nexus emulator send "$DEPLOYMENT_ID" "$SESSION_ID" \
  --content "What's the status of ticket #$TICKET_ID?" \
  --json | jq '.debug.toolCalls'
```

**Verify success.** Debug info shows the agent called its Zendesk lookup tool with `id == $TICKET_ID` and got real data. The agent's text reply references the ticket's subject or body.

**Clean-up.** If Zendesk has a delete action, call it. Otherwise tag the ticket `test-seed` so it's filterable out of reporting.

**Related.** `nexus-emulator/SKILL.md`, `nexus-tool-execute/reference/patterns/patterns/02-seed-test-data.md`.

## Recipe 5: CUSTOM_MANIFEST external-tool validation

**Source skill:** `nexus-skills-and-tasks`
**Phase:** External-tool (CUSTOM_MANIFEST) creation — testing actions before exposing to agents

**Scenario.** You've registered a custom OpenAPI tool via `nexus external-tool create --body path/to/manifest.json`. The manifest declares operations (e.g., `searchUsers`, `getOrder`, `createOrder`). Before adding the tool to an agent's skill list — where misconfigured auth, wrong base URL, or a schema mismatch would break every conversation — execute each operation once. `nexus external-tool execute` works identically for CUSTOM_MANIFEST and PIPEDREAM tools; the only difference is `--action` takes an `operationId` instead of a Pipedream action key. Test each operationId in isolation before attaching.

**Procedure.**
1. List your external tools: `nexus external-tool list --json` → find the CUSTOM_MANIFEST entry.
2. Inspect the manifest: `nexus external-tool get <toolId> --json | jq '.manifest.paths'` — enumerate every `operationId`.
3. For each operationId, build a minimal valid input per the OpenAPI schema (read it from `manifest.paths.<path>.<method>.parameters` and `.requestBody.content.*.schema`).
4. Execute: `nexus external-tool execute <toolId> --action <operationId> --input '{...}' --json`. No `--credential` is needed if auth is embedded in the manifest (e.g., API-key header from `updateAuth`); pass `--credential` if the tool uses per-user OAuth.
5. Confirm both envelope success AND absence of `result.os[].k == "error"`.
6. Test both happy-path and one predictable failure path (bad ID, missing required field) to confirm error handling surfaces meaningfully.

**Bash snippet.**
```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

EXTERNAL_TOOL_ID="$1"  # CUSTOM_MANIFEST tool
OPERATION_ID="$2"      # e.g. "getOrder"
INPUT="$3"             # e.g. '{"orderId":"o_123"}'

RESP=$(nexus external-tool execute "$EXTERNAL_TOOL_ID" \
  --action "$OPERATION_ID" \
  --input "$INPUT" --json)

echo "$RESP" | jq -e '.success' >/dev/null || { echo "envelope fail" >&2; exit 1; }
UPSTREAM_ERR=$(echo "$RESP" | jq '[.result.os[]? | select(.k=="error")] | length')
if [[ "$UPSTREAM_ERR" != "0" ]]; then
  echo "Upstream returned error — check manifest auth, base URL, and input schema." >&2
  echo "$RESP" | jq '.result.os[]? | select(.k=="error") | .err' >&2
  exit 1
fi

echo "Validated: $OPERATION_ID on tool $EXTERNAL_TOOL_ID"
echo "$RESP" | jq '.result' | head -40
```

**Verify success.** The shape of `.result` matches the OpenAPI response schema declared in the manifest. If it doesn't, your manifest's response schema is wrong — fix it before agents try to read fields that aren't there.

**Clean-up.** CUSTOM_MANIFEST actions can be any tier. Check the operation's description. If you executed a mutation (createOrder), run the paired delete operation or note the ID for manual cleanup.

**Related.** `nexus-skills-and-tasks/SKILL.md` (external-tool CRUD), `nexus-tool-connection/SKILL.md` (auth setup for CUSTOM_MANIFEST), `nexus-tool-execute/reference/patterns/patterns/01-discover-and-execute.md`.

## Recipe 6: Deployment channel credential verification

**Source skill:** `nexus-deployments`
**Phase:** Channel setup — before publishing a deployment

**Scenario.** You've configured a WhatsApp/Gmail/Slack channel with a credential. Rather than discover a bad credential when your first real customer message fails, send one test message via tool-execute. The same credential the channel uses is testable through the channel's send-message action.

**Bash snippet.**
```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
GMAIL_TOOL_ID="3d49d29e-8c86-5c43-aa24-f4903f577e68"
CRED_ID="$1"
TEST_TO="$2"
INPUT=$(jq -n --arg to "$TEST_TO" \
  '{to:[$to], subject:"[nexus] channel credential check", body:"If you received this, the credential works."}')
RESP=$(nexus external-tool execute "$GMAIL_TOOL_ID" --action gmail-send-email \
  --credential "$CRED_ID" --input "$INPUT" --json)
echo "$RESP" | jq -e '.success and ([.result.os[]? | select(.k=="error")] | length == 0)' >/dev/null
echo "Credential $CRED_ID verified — safe to publish deployment."
```

**Verify success.** Test recipient receives the message. **Clean-up:** delete the test email in the test inbox. **Related:** `nexus-deployments/SKILL.md`.

## Recipe 8: Failed-execution replay via external state recreation

**Source skill:** `nexus-workflow-executions`
**Phase:** Debugging a failed run

**Scenario.** A workflow ran, failed, and the trigger payload referenced external records that have since changed or been deleted. Straight `nexus execution retry` won't reproduce the failure. Tool-execute recreates the exact upstream state (re-insert the deleted row, re-send the email that triggered) so the retry fires against known data.

**Bash snippet.**
```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
RUN_ID="$1"
RUN=$(nexus execution get "$RUN_ID" --json)
# Extract the original trigger payload
TRIGGER_PAYLOAD=$(echo "$RUN" | jq '.triggerPayload')
# Use it to rebuild the upstream state (example: re-insert a sheets row)
ROW=$(echo "$TRIGGER_PAYLOAD" | jq -c '[.name, .email, .note]')
INPUT=$(jq -n --argjson row "$ROW" --arg sheetId "$SHEET_ID" '{sheetId:$sheetId, values:[$row]}')
nexus external-tool execute "$SHEETS_TOOL_ID" --action google_sheets-add-single-row \
  --credential "$CRED_ID" --input "$INPUT" --json
nexus execution retry "$RUN_ID"
```

**Verify success.** New execution status is `SUCCESS` (or fails on the same node as before — in which case the bug is real, not state-dependent). **Related:** `nexus-workflow-executions/SKILL.md`.

## Recipe 11: Standalone vs workflow latency isolation

**Source skill:** `nexus-tracing`
**Phase:** Debugging slow workflow runs

**Scenario.** A workflow node that wraps a plugin takes 8 seconds. Is the plugin itself slow, or is Nexus's workflow execution overhead adding seconds? Execute the same action standalone via tool-execute and measure — if standalone is also slow, the upstream API is the issue (not Nexus).

**Bash snippet.**
```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
T0=$(date +%s)
RESP=$(nexus external-tool execute "$TOOL_ID" --action "$ACTION_KEY" \
  --credential "$CRED_ID" --input "$INPUT" --json)
T1=$(date +%s)
echo "Standalone latency: $((T1-T0))s"
echo "$RESP" | jq '.result' > /dev/null  # force envelope parse
```

**Verify success.** Standalone timing is meaningfully lower than workflow-node timing → problem is in Nexus. Standalone ≈ workflow → problem is upstream. **Related:** `nexus-tracing/SKILL.md`.

- **Real IDs.** Gmail tool: `3d49d29e-8c86-5c43-aa24-f4903f577e68`. Perplexity: `f2fdba30-6b3d-49b2-99a5-12cce5445b11`. Gmail credential (user-validated, Dec 2025): `776bcbea-5390-4085-99d9-7028d328f207`. Every other `<id>` is a placeholder — discover via `nexus tool search` / `nexus tool credentials`.
- **Envelope parsing.** `jq -e '.success and ([.result.os[]? | select(.k=="error")] | length == 0)'` is the one-liner to gate success on both envelope and upstream state.
- **Chaining.** `jq -n --arg body "$UPSTREAM" '{...}'` — never string-interpolate user-controlled or multi-line content into a JSON string.
- **Credential disambiguation.** If `nexus tool credentials <toolId> --json` returns > 1 entry, ALWAYS ask the user via `AskUserQuestion` — show `name` + `createdAt` + `type`.
- **Cleanup obligation.** Every write-tier recipe documents its cleanup path. SOFT-REVERSIBLE actions (drafts, labels, contacts with no delete) put an obligation on the user — say so explicitly in chat so they know an artifact persists.

# Endpoints Reference

Complete CLI + API reference for standalone tool execution. The canonical surface is the CLI — specifically `nexus external-tool execute`. The underlying API endpoint is documented here for completeness, but some raw paths return 404 via `nexus api` (see "Known issues" below). **Prefer the CLI.**

All CLI commands require `NEXUS_API_KEY` in the environment (prefixed `nxs_`). Default base URL: `https://api.nexusgpt.io` (override via `NEXUS_BASE_URL`).

---

## CRITICAL ENDPOINT REQUIREMENTS

**ABSOLUTE RULES:**

- **NEVER** use `nexus tool execute` — the `tool` namespace has no `execute` subcommand. The correct command is `nexus external-tool execute`.
- **NEVER** use `nexus external-tool test` for new work — it's legacy dashboard-side behavior. Use `execute`.
- **NEVER** parse the response using the historical `{status, output, executionTimeMs}` shape. The REAL envelope is `{success, toolId, action, result}` — see Response Envelope below.
- **ALWAYS** pass `--json` when any downstream step parses the output.
- **ALWAYS** validate both the envelope `.success` AND `.result.os[]` for Pipedream errors. Envelope-success lies when the upstream API failed.

---

## 1. `nexus external-tool execute` — The Primary Command

```bash
nexus external-tool execute <toolId> \
  --action <actionKey> \
  --input '<json-object>' \
  [--credential <credentialId>] \
  [--json]
```

### Positional argument

| Arg | Required | Description |
|-----|----------|-------------|
| `toolId` | yes | UUID (e.g., `3d49d29e-8c86-5c43-aa24-f4903f577e68`) or Pipedream slug (`google_sheets`). UUIDs preferred for consistency. |

### Flags

| Flag | Required | Type | Description |
|------|----------|------|-------------|
| `--action <key>` | yes | string | Action key (Pipedream: `gmail-send-email`, `google_sheets-add-single-row`) or operationId (CUSTOM_MANIFEST: `search`, `getUser`). Discover via `nexus tool get <toolId> --json`. |
| `--input <json>` | yes | JSON string | JSON object with the action's parameters. Empty `{}` is valid but typically fails upstream for required-param actions — see gotcha #4. |
| `--credential <id>` | conditionally | UUID | Credential UUID. REQUIRED when multiple credentials exist for the tool. When omitted, CLI auto-resolves the first available — NOT deterministic for writes. Always pass explicitly for non-READ actions. |
| `--json` | no | boolean | Emit structured JSON (for parsing). Default: human-formatted output. **Pass `--json` for any downstream parsing.** |

### Usage patterns

**Minimal READ (single credential):**

```bash
nexus external-tool execute "f2fdba30-6b3d-49b2-99a5-12cce5445b11" \
  --action search \
  --input '{"content":"what is the current population of Tokyo"}' \
  --json
```

**Write with explicit credential (recommended for any non-READ):**

```bash
nexus external-tool execute "3d49d29e-8c86-5c43-aa24-f4903f577e68" \
  --action gmail-send-email \
  --input '{"to":["dev+test@myorg.com"],"subject":"Hello","body":"Body"}' \
  --credential "776bcbea-5390-4085-99d9-7028d328f207" \
  --json
```

**Using jq to build safely-escaped input:**

```bash
INPUT=$(jq -n \
  --argjson to '["alice@example.com"]' \
  --arg subject 'Report' \
  --arg body "$(cat report.md)" \
  '{to: $to, subject: $subject, body: $body}')

nexus external-tool execute "$GMAIL_ID" \
  --action gmail-create-draft \
  --input "$INPUT" \
  --credential "$CRED_ID" \
  --json
```

## 2. Response Envelope — The REAL Shape

Observed across 6+ live executions (Perplexity search, Gmail list-labels/find-email/create-draft/send-email, and the error path). If you see a different shape, you are reading stale docs.

### Success envelope

```json
{
  "success": true,
  "toolId": "3d49d29e-8c86-5c43-aa24-f4903f577e68",
  "action": "gmail-create-draft",
  "result": {
    "id": "r5358...",
    "message": {
      "id": "19d98524...",
      "threadId": "19d98524...",
      "labelIds": ["DRAFT"]
    },
    "os": [
      { "ts": 1776377018637, "k": "info", "msg": "Draft created" }
    ]
  }
}
```

### Fields

| Field | Type | Notes |
|-------|------|-------|
| `success` | boolean | **TRUE means "Nexus execute endpoint returned 200". DOES NOT mean upstream success.** See gotcha #1. |
| `toolId` | string | Echo of the tool ID used. |
| `action` | string | Echo of the action key used. |
| `result` | object OR string OR null | The upstream payload. Object for most tools, markdown string for Perplexity (gotcha #29), null on some failures (inspect `result.os`). |
| `result.os` | array | Pipedream Observability Stream. Present for Pipedream-backed tools. Entries have `{ts, k, msg/err/info/log}`. Missing for CUSTOM_MANIFEST tools. |

**No `executionTimeMs`. No `status`. No `output`. No `data` wrapper.** The historical `{status, output, executionTimeMs}` shape documented in `nexus-tool-connection/reference/endpoints.md:249-296` is **stale** — see gotcha #2.

### Envelope-success with upstream failure

The most important shape to recognize. The envelope is green, but `result.os[]` contains an error entry:

```json
{
  "success": true,
  "toolId": "3d49d29e-8c86-5c43-aa24-f4903f577e68",
  "action": "gmail-send-email",
  "result": {
    "os": [
      {
        "ts": 1776377018637,
        "k": "error",
        "err": {
          "config": {
            "url": "https://gmail.googleapis.com/gmail/v1/users/me/messages/send",
            "method": "POST",
            "headers": { "...": "..." }
          },
          "response": {
            "status": 400,
            "data": { "error": { "code": 400, "message": "Missing required fields" } }
          }
        }
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

**Detection:**

```bash
ENV_OK=$(echo "$RESULT" | jq -r '.success')
OS_ERR=$(echo "$RESULT" | jq '[.result.os[]? | select(.k == "error")] | length')

[ "$ENV_OK" = "true" ] && [ "$OS_ERR" = "0" ] \
  || { echo "Upstream failure" >&2; exit 1; }
```
