- **`available-variables` shows empty children for the loop node** even after testing. The API does not discover array element properties — you must know them from the upstream node's output schema.
- **One iteration failure = entire loop failure.** If any single iteration fails (e.g., an API call errors for item 3 of 10), the whole loop fails. There is no skip-on-error behavior.
- **Inner output node is REQUIRED for result aggregation.** Without it, loop output is `[null, null, null]`.

### Branching Inside a Loop

Loops support branching nodes inside the loop body for "per-item routing" patterns.

**Architecture:**
```
loop → loopStart → [processing] → branching
                                   ├── branch A → [nodes] → outputNode A
                                   └── branch B → [nodes] → outputNode B
```

**Key rules:**
1. **Each branch needs its own `outputNode`** (with `parentId` = loop node ID). The loop aggregates whichever outputNode fires for each iteration.
2. **Only one branch executes per iteration.** The loop result array contains one entry per iteration — from whichever branch was chosen.
3. **All inner nodes** (branching, branch targets, outputNodes) **must have `parentId` set to the loop node ID.**
4. **Wiring:** Each branch edge from the branching node uses `sourceHandle` matching the branch ID (e.g., `"sourceHandle": "br-001"`).
5. **Loop output with branching:** The aggregated array contains mixed results from different branches. Downstream nodes receive the full array.

WRONG: Creating one shared outputNode after the branching, expecting branches to merge.
RIGHT: Creating one outputNode per branch — branches cannot merge inside loops or outside them.

## Variable References

The `iterationsSetup` field only supports `handler: "variable"` — it must reference an array from an upstream node. The `"manual"` and `"prompt"` handlers are not supported for loop iteration sources.

```json
{
  "items": {
    "handler": "variable",
    "variable": "{{UPSTREAM_NODE_UUID.body.items}}"
  }
}
```

Inside the loop body, inner nodes reference the current iteration's properties **directly on the loop node's UUID** (not the loopStart UUID). The loop "flattens" each array element — there is no `.item` prefix and no `.index` accessor.

```
{{LOOP_NODE_UUID.propertyName}}
```

Example: if the upstream array contains objects `{name, email, company}`, inside the loop body you reference:

```
{{LOOP_NODE_UUID.name}}
{{LOOP_NODE_UUID.email}}
{{LOOP_NODE_UUID.company}}
```

```
WRONG: {{LOOP_NODE_UUID.item.name}}   — ".item" does not exist
WRONG: {{LOOP_NODE_UUID.item}}        — ".item" does not exist
WRONG: {{LOOP_NODE_UUID.index}}       — ".index" does not exist

RIGHT: {{LOOP_NODE_UUID.name}}        — direct property access
RIGHT: {{LOOP_NODE_UUID.email}}       — direct property access
```

**Note on `iteratorName`:** The `iteratorName` field (e.g., `"email"`, `"thread"`) is a display label for the UI — it makes the loop element human-readable in the dashboard. For variable references in the CLI/API, use `{{LOOP_NODE_UUID.propertyName}}` (direct property access on the loop UUID). The `iteratorName` does NOT change the variable reference path.

If you set `iteratorName: "email"` and the array items have `{subject, body}`:
- Dashboard shows: `email.subject`, `email.body`
- CLI/API references: `{{LOOP_NODE_UUID.subject}}`, `{{LOOP_NODE_UUID.body}}`

**Output:** Downstream root-level nodes reference the loop's aggregated results:

```
{{LOOP_NODE_UUID}}
{{LOOP_NODE_UUID.results}}
```

The output is an array of results, one per iteration.

### Variable Reference Behavior by Node Type (Inside Loops)

`{{ref}}` interpolation does NOT behave identically across all node types inside a loop. Some node types resolve loop item references, others don't.

| Node Type | `{{LOOP_UUID.field}}` resolves? | Nested paths (`.a.b.c`)? | Handler context |
|---|---|---|---|
| textFormatter | Yes | Yes | Text field directly |
| plugin (`handler: "variable"`) | Yes | Yes | `variable` field |
| plugin (`handler: "manual"`, `value`) | Unreliable inside loops | Unreliable | May pass `{{ref}}` as literal text |
| aiTask (inputSetup) | Yes | Yes | `variable` field |
| customScript | N/A | N/A | Uses function parameters via `inputs` array (node field must use `{{UUID}}`) |
| outputNode (instructions) | Yes | — | `{{nodeUUID}}` for full passthrough |

**When `manual` handler `{{ref}}` doesn't resolve inside a loop**: Use a `textFormatter` node upstream inside the loop to construct the string value. The textFormatter resolves `{{LOOP_UUID.nested.path}}` correctly. Then reference the textFormatter's output in the plugin parameter via `handler: "variable"`.

WRONG: Plugin inside loop with `handler: "manual"`, `value: "{{LOOP_UUID.properties.title}}!A2:F500"`
=> Passes literal text — not interpolated.

RIGHT: textFormatter inside loop with `text: "{{LOOP_UUID.properties.title}}!A2:F500"` → produces `"Industry_Sources!A2:F500"`. Plugin references textFormatter output via `handler: "variable"`.

## Testing Loops

Loop inner nodes CANNOT be meaningfully tested in isolation — they need loop context (the current iteration item).

**Test procedure:**

```bash
# 1. Test the loop node (runs all inner nodes with real iteration data)
nexus workflow node test "$WF_ID" "$LOOP_NODE_ID" --json

# 2. Get the execution
nexus execution poll --json

# 3. Inspect EACH inner node's result
nexus execution node-result "<execId>" "<innerNodeId1>" --json
nexus execution node-result "<execId>" "<innerNodeId2>" --json
# ... for every inner node

# 4. For AI task inner nodes: verify output VALUES, not just field names
```

WRONG: Test loopStart → test inner nodes individually → each has no loop data.
RIGHT: Test the loop node → inspect inner results via `nexus execution node-result`.

The full workflow test (Phase 5) is NOT a substitute for this. The full test may not expose per-inner-node results.

# Sub-Workflow

## Node Type Identifier

`workflow`

## What It Does

Executes another workflow as a sub-workflow within the current workflow. The target workflow must be published. You select a workflow by ID, optionally configure input parameters, and the sub-workflow runs to completion before the parent workflow continues. The output of the sub-workflow node is the output of the executed workflow.

Only workflows with an `agentInputTrigger` can be used as sub-workflows. The sub-workflow's output flows back to the parent workflow exactly like a plugin node — downstream nodes reference it via `{{subWorkflowNodeUUID}}` or `{{subWorkflowNodeUUID.field}}`.

## When to Use

Use a sub-workflow node when you want to **delegate execution to an existing published workflow**. Three reasons to use sub-workflows:

1. **Reuse (DRY):** A specific block of execution is used across multiple workflows OR in multiple places within the same workflow. Extract it once, call it everywhere.
2. **Complexity management:** Avoid overbloating a workflow with too many steps and logic branches. Break complex flows into manageable, independently testable modules.
3. **Debugging isolation:** Separate sub-processes so failures are easier to trace and fix without affecting the parent workflow.

**Minimum threshold:** A sub-workflow should only be created if it has **more than 2 processing steps** (excluding the trigger and output nodes). If it's 1-2 steps, inline them directly — the overhead of a separate workflow isn't justified.

| Signal | Action |
|--------|--------|
| Same 3+ node sequence appears in multiple workflows | Extract to sub-workflow |
| Workflow exceeds ~15 nodes and is hard to reason about | Decompose into sub-workflows |
| A process has well-defined inputs and outputs | Good sub-workflow candidate |
| Process is 1-2 steps | Inline it — don't create a sub-workflow |
| Target workflow is in DRAFT status | Cannot use — must be PUBLISHED first |

**Do NOT use sub-workflow when:**
- The logic is used only once AND is ≤2 processing steps — just inline it
- The target workflow uses a webhook, schedule, or plugin trigger — only `agentInputTrigger` workflows work as sub-workflows

For the full control flow decision tree, see [Control Flow Selection Guide](../../../reference/node-types-overview.md#control-flow-selection-guide).

## Required Fields in `data`

| Field                | Type     | Description                                                  |
| -------------------- | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `selectedWorkflowId` | `string` | The ID of the published workflow to execute as sub-workflow. |

## Optional Fields

| Field             | Type             | Description                            |
| ----------------- | ---------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| `parametersSetup` | `ParameterSetup` | Input parameters for the sub-workflow. Auto-populated by the backend when `selectedWorkflowId` is set. |
| `label`           | `string`         | Display label for the node.            |

## Default Data (set automatically on creation)

```json
{
  "selectedWorkflowId": "",
  "parametersSetup": {},
  "label": "Workflow",
  "instructions": ""
}
```

## Connection Rules

- Can be placed inside a loop: Yes
- Can be masked (skipped): Yes

## Configuration Steps

1. **Create the node** with `nexus workflow node create` using `--type workflow`.
2. **Connect it** to an upstream node.
3. **Select the target workflow** by updating `selectedWorkflowId` via `nexus workflow node update`. Use `nexus workflow list --json` to list available published workflows and get their IDs. The backend auto-populates `parametersSetup` from the target workflow's `agentInputSchema`.
4. **Verify parametersSetup** by fetching the node and checking that entries were created for each input parameter.
5. **Configure parameters** by setting handler type (`manual`, `prompt`, or `variable`) and values for each `parametersSetup` entry via `nexus workflow node update`.

## Example API Calls

### Step 1: Create the sub-workflow node

```bash
nexus workflow node create "$WORKFLOW_ID" --type workflow --json
```

Capture the `nodeId` from the response.

### Step 2: Connect to upstream node

```bash
nexus workflow edge create "$WORKFLOW_ID" --source "$UPSTREAM_NODE_ID" --target "$SUBWORKFLOW_NODE_ID"
```

### Step 3: List available workflows to find the target

```bash
nexus workflow list --json --limit 50
```

Pick a workflow from the list and capture its `id`.

```
WRONG: Using `nexus workflow list` without filtering for published.
  => Returns ALL workflows including unpublished DRAFTs.

RIGHT: Use `nexus workflow list --json` — look for PUBLISHED workflows with their agentInputSchema.
  => Each result includes the input parameter schema you need for parametersSetup.
```

### Step 4: Set the target workflow

```bash
nexus workflow node update "$WORKFLOW_ID" "$SUBWORKFLOW_NODE_ID" --body '{
  "data": {
    "selectedWorkflowId": "'"$TARGET_WORKFLOW_ID"'"
  }
}'
```

```
WRONG: Selecting a DRAFT workflow as the target.
  => configStatus shows "complete" (it only checks non-empty string),
  but execution FAILS because the sub-workflow cannot run an unpublished workflow.

RIGHT: Only select workflows that are PUBLISHED — these are guaranteed to work as sub-workflows.
```

### Step 5: Verify auto-populated parametersSetup

After setting `selectedWorkflowId`, the backend auto-populates `parametersSetup` from the target workflow's `agentInputSchema`. **VERIFY** that `parametersSetup` was populated:

```bash
nexus workflow node get "$WORKFLOW_ID" "$SUBWORKFLOW_NODE_ID" --json
# Check: data.parametersSetup should contain one entry per agentInputSchema field
```

If `parametersSetup` is empty (`{}`), the target workflow's trigger may not have `parameters` defined. Check: `nexus workflow get <targetId> --json` and verify the trigger node has a `parameters` schema.

### Step 6: Configure parameters

Configure each auto-populated `parametersSetup` entry by setting the handler type and value:

```bash
nexus workflow node update "$WORKFLOW_ID" "$SUBWORKFLOW_NODE_ID" --body '{
  "data": {
    "parametersSetup": {
      "customerName": {
        "id": "param-1",
        "type": "string",
        "handler": "variable",
        "value": "",
        "prompt": "",
        "variable": "{{UPSTREAM_NODE_UUID.body.name}}"
      },
      "orderId": {
        "id": "param-2",
        "type": "string",
        "handler": "manual",
        "value": "ORD-12345",
        "prompt": "",
        "variable": ""
      }
    }
  }
}'
```

### Step 7: Connect output to downstream node

```bash
nexus workflow edge create "$WORKFLOW_ID" --source "$SUBWORKFLOW_NODE_ID" --target "$DOWNSTREAM_NODE_ID"
```

## Common Patterns / Tips

- **The target workflow must be PUBLISHED.** You cannot reference a DRAFT workflow. Use `nexus workflow list --json` and filter for published workflows.
- **Use `nexus workflow list --json` to discover workflows.** Look for PUBLISHED workflows with their `agentInputSchema`, which tells you what input parameters the sub-workflow expects.
- **`parametersSetup` maps to the target workflow's `agentInputSchema`** and is auto-populated by the backend when `selectedWorkflowId` is set. Each key corresponds to a property in the target workflow's input schema. You only need to configure the handler/value for each entry.
- **Parameter handlers:** Each parameter in `parametersSetup` supports `handler: "variable"` (reference an upstream node's output), `handler: "manual"` (hardcoded value), or `handler: "prompt"` (AI-generated value).
- **The node's output is the sub-workflow's output.** Downstream nodes can reference the sub-workflow node's output using `{{SUBWORKFLOW_NODE_UUID}}` or `{{SUBWORKFLOW_NODE_UUID.fieldName}}`.
- **Sub-workflows can be nested.** A sub-workflow can itself contain sub-workflow nodes, enabling deep composition of workflows.
- **Works inside loops.** You can place a sub-workflow node inside a loop to execute a workflow for each item in a collection.
- **Config status is "incomplete" until `selectedWorkflowId` is set.** The node will show `missingFields: ["selectedWorkflowId"]` until a valid workflow ID is provided.
- **`parametersSetup` is auto-populated after setting `selectedWorkflowId`** — the backend reads the target workflow's `agentInputSchema` and creates entries automatically. Always verify by fetching the node after the update. If empty, the target workflow's trigger may lack a `parameters` schema.
- **Node test `outputFormat` shows metadata, not the actual result.** After testing the sub-workflow node, `outputFormat` shows `{shouldPause, subWorkflowId, subWorkflowExecutionId}`. This is execution metadata. The actual sub-workflow output only appears in full workflow test execution results — reference the whole node via `{{subWorkflowNodeUUID}}`.
- **Only `agentInputTrigger` workflows can be sub-workflows.** Workflows with webhook, schedule, or plugin triggers cannot be called as sub-workflows.

## Variable References

The `parametersSetup` field supports variable references for dynamic input:

```json
{
  "customerEmail": {
    "handler": "variable",
    "variable": "{{UPSTREAM_NODE_UUID.body.email}}"
  }
}
```

**Output:** Downstream nodes reference the sub-workflow's result:

```
{{SUBWORKFLOW_NODE_UUID}}
{{SUBWORKFLOW_NODE_UUID.result}}
{{SUBWORKFLOW_NODE_UUID.result.fieldName}}
```

The output structure depends on the target workflow's output node configuration.

# Output Node

## Node Type Identifier

`outputNode`

## What It Does

Terminal node that produces the workflow's final output. Supports three modes: "previous" (pass through the upstream node's output as-is), "custom" (AI-formatted output based on instructions), and "text" (templated text output with variable references).

**CRITICAL**: `"custom"` mode invokes an LLM to reformat the output. If you want to pass through upstream data unchanged (e.g., structured JSON from a parallelai or plugin node), use `"previous"` mode — NOT `"custom"`. Using `"custom"` with structured data produces unpredictable AI-generated responses instead of your data.

## Required Fields in `data`

None. The output node has no required fields and is always considered "complete" in terms of config status.

## Optional Fields

| Field          | Type                               | Description                                                                                                                                                                  |
| -------------- | ---------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `outputType`   | `"previous" \| "custom" \| "text"` | How output is determined. Default: `"previous"`.                                                                                                                             |
| `instructions` | `string`                           | For `"custom"` mode: AI instructions. For `"text"` mode: text template with `{{nodeId.path}}` references. For `"previous"` mode: variable reference to upstream node output. |

**IMPORTANT**: The configuration field is `instructions`, NOT `output`. The `output` field name may appear in some API responses or other node GUIDE examples — it is NOT the correct field to set. Always use `instructions`.
| `label`        | `string`                           | Display label for the node.                                                                                                                                                  |

## Default Data (set automatically on creation)

```json
{
  "label": "Output",
  "instructions": "",
  "outputType": "previous"
}
```

## Connection Rules

- Can be placed inside a loop: Yes
- Can be masked (skipped): No

## Configuration Steps

1. **Create the node** with `nexus workflow node create`.
2. **Connect it** to the final processing node in the chain.
3. **Set the output type** via `nexus workflow node update`.
4. **Configure instructions** (if using "custom" or "text" mode) via `nexus workflow node update`.

## Example API Calls

### Step 1: Create the output node

```bash
nexus workflow node create "$WORKFLOW_ID" --type outputNode --json
```

### Step 2: Connect to the last processing node

```bash
nexus workflow edge create "$WORKFLOW_ID" --source "$LAST_PROCESSING_NODE_ID" --target "$OUTPUT_NODE_ID" --json
```

### Mode 1: Previous Node (passthrough)

Pass through the output of a specific upstream node. ALWAYS set `instructions` to an explicit variable reference, even for the immediately connected upstream node.

```bash
nexus workflow node update "$WORKFLOW_ID" "$OUTPUT_NODE_ID" --body '{
  "data": {
    "outputType": "previous",
    "instructions": "{{UPSTREAM_NODE_UUID}}"
  }
}' --json
```

WRONG: Leaving `instructions` empty and relying on implicit passthrough.
```json
{ "outputType": "previous", "instructions": "" }
```
→ Ambiguous — which upstream node's output? Not verifiable via validate-variables.

RIGHT: Explicit reference to the specific upstream node.
```json
{ "outputType": "previous", "instructions": "{{39f2bade-531c-43ca-9e70-b7e382bf0e6b}}" }
```
→ Clear, verifiable, shows up in validate-variables response.

### Passing through structured data (JSON from parallelai, plugin, etc.)

WRONG: Using "custom" mode to pass through structured data.
```json
{ "outputType": "custom", "instructions": "{{39f2bade-531c-43ca-9e70-b7e382bf0e6b.content}}" }
```
→ "custom" invokes an LLM. The LLM receives your JSON and returns an AI-generated response (often generic "How can I help?" or a summary that drops fields).

RIGHT: Using "previous" mode for structured passthrough.
```json
{ "outputType": "previous", "instructions": "{{39f2bade-531c-43ca-9e70-b7e382bf0e6b}}" }
```
→ Passes the full upstream output unchanged. No AI processing. No latency overhead.

### When to use "custom" mode

Only use `"custom"` when you WANT an AI to transform the output — e.g., "Summarize the research into 3 bullet points." If the workflow's consumer (agent or external system) expects structured JSON, always use `"previous"`.

### Mode 2: Custom (AI-formatted)

The AI generates the output based on your instructions and the data from upstream nodes.

```bash
nexus workflow node update "$WORKFLOW_ID" "$OUTPUT_NODE_ID" --body '{
  "data": {
    "outputType": "custom",
    "instructions": "Summarize the processing results from {{PROCESSING_NODE_UUID}} into a concise report with bullet points. Include the total count and any errors found."
  }
}' --json
```

### Mode 3: Text (template)

Output a formatted text string with variable interpolation.

```bash
nexus workflow node update "$WORKFLOW_ID" "$OUTPUT_NODE_ID" --body '{
  "data": {
    "outputType": "text",
    "instructions": "Processing complete.\n\nResults:\n- Items processed: {{PROCESSING_NODE_UUID.count}}\n- Status: {{PROCESSING_NODE_UUID.status}}\n- Output: {{PROCESSING_NODE_UUID.result}}"
  }
}' --json
```

### Verify configuration

```bash
nexus workflow node get "$WORKFLOW_ID" "$OUTPUT_NODE_ID" --json
```

Always returns `configStatus: "complete"` -- the output node has no required fields.

## Common Patterns / Tips

- **"previous" mode passes through a specific upstream node's output.** Always set `instructions` to `{{UPSTREAM_NODE_UUID}}` — even for the immediately connected upstream node. This makes the data flow explicit and verifiable.
- **Use "previous" with `instructions` set to a variable reference** when you want to pass through a specific upstream node's output that is not the immediately connected one. Set `instructions` to `{{upstreamNodeUUID}}`.
- **"custom" mode invokes an AI** to format the output. This adds latency but allows natural language formatting, summarization, or restructuring of the output.
- **"text" mode is a text template** similar to the text formatter node. Use `{{nodeUUID.path}}` references to build a formatted text output.
- **The output node is a terminal node** with 0 max outputs. No edges can originate from it.
- **Every workflow should end with an output node** (or multiple, on different branches). Without it, the workflow may not produce a usable result.
- **Inside a loop**, the output node captures the result of each iteration. The loop then aggregates all iteration outputs.

## Variable References

The `instructions` field supports inline variable references:

For "previous" mode:

```
{{UPSTREAM_NODE_UUID}}
```

For "custom" mode:

```
Create a summary of {{PLUGIN_NODE_UUID.response}} highlighting the key metrics.
```

For "text" mode:

```
Results: {{PROCESSING_NODE_UUID.count}} items processed with status {{PROCESSING_NODE_UUID.status}}
```

**Output:** The output node is terminal -- it does not produce variables for downstream nodes. Its output is the workflow's final result, returned in the workflow execution response.

# Send Message

## Node Type Identifier

`sendMessage`

## What It Does

Sends a message to a user **through an existing deployment channel** (WhatsApp, Slack, Teams, SMS, email-channel, etc.). This is the NATIVE, credential-free way for a workflow to message a person.

A channel the org deploys an agent on is a **deployment**, not a marketplace tool. To message that channel from a workflow, target its deployment with `sendMessage` — do NOT search the marketplace for a messaging plugin (that is the routing mistake; see SKILL.md "Capability Routing" route (a)).

WRONG: workflow needs to send a WhatsApp chase → `tool search whatsapp` → Pipedream messaging plugin + a credential.
RIGHT: `sendMessage` → `selectedDeployment` = the org's WhatsApp deployment. Zero credential, zero marketplace.

## Required Fields in `data`

| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `selectedDeployment` | `string` | The deployment channel ID to send through. The channel must already be deployed (→ `nexus-deployments`). Without it the node is unusable at runtime even when `configStatus` reads complete. |

## Optional Fields

| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `conversationMode` | `"new" \| "existing"` | Start a new conversation or continue an existing one with the recipient. |
| `instructions` | `string` | The message text/instructions. Supports `{{ref}}` interpolation (e.g. `{{<loopUUID>.field}}` inside a loop). |
| `parametersSetup` | `ParameterSetup` | Structured message parameters (handler-typed, per G#3) when the message is built from fields rather than free text. |
| `whatsappTemplate` | `object` | Approved WhatsApp template config — REQUIRED for business-initiated WhatsApp messages (see below). |
| `whatsappTemplateVariables` | `object` | Variables injected into the WhatsApp template. |
| `label` | `string` | Display label (snake_case). |

`runOutput` / `testExecutionId` / `outputFormat` are read-only.

## Deployment prerequisite

`sendMessage` cannot send until `selectedDeployment` points at a live deployment. In credential-deferred builds ("create everything, connect later") you can create + wire the node and set `instructions`, but leave `selectedDeployment` empty and flag it as a user TODO; do NOT mark the node configured or tested.

## WhatsApp 24-hour window

WhatsApp only allows free-text replies inside a 24h customer-service window. A message the workflow INITIATES (e.g. a scheduled daily chase) is business-initiated and falls outside that window — it MUST use an approved `whatsappTemplate` + `whatsappTemplateVariables`, not free `instructions`. Approve the template in WhatsApp Business first (→ `nexus-deployments` whatsapp-template commands).

## Inside a loop

When `sendMessage` is a loop child, reference the current item by the LOOP node UUID, not `iteratorName` (display-only): `{{<loopUUID>.field}}` in `instructions`/`parametersSetup`. See `node-types/logic/loop/GUIDE.md`.

## Configuration Steps

1. Create the node (or via batch scaffold) and wire its incoming edge.
2. Set `selectedDeployment` to the target deployment's ID (`nexus deployment list --json`).
3. Set the message: `instructions` (free text, in-window) OR `whatsappTemplate` + `whatsappTemplateVariables` (business-initiated WhatsApp).
4. Set `conversationMode` if continuing an existing thread.
5. Verify via `nexus workflow node get`; runtime send is only verifiable once the deployment is live.

# AI Node (AI Task)

> Object-typed fields in `jsonInputSchema` / `jsonOutputSchema` must declare `properties` — see CLAUDE.md G#13.

## Node Type Identifier

`aiTask`

(Legacy alias: `gptTask` -- identical behavior.)

## What It Does

Executes a pre-defined AI task from the Nexus task library. Select a task to auto-populate input parameters from the task's JSON input schema, then configure each parameter with values from upstream nodes or manual input.

## When to Use AI Task

**aiTask is the DEFAULT for any step that processes text.** If the step involves natural language and you are debating between aiTask and another node type (especially customScript), choose aiTask unless you can prove the logic is fully deterministic.

### Use Cases (always aiTask)

- **Summarization:** Condensing text while preserving key information
- **Generation:** Writing new text — emails, responses, descriptions, search queries, reports
- **Translation:** Between languages or between registers (formal to casual, technical to plain)
- **Assessment:** Evaluating quality, relevance, urgency, sentiment, completeness
- **Classification:** Categorizing into predefined or emergent categories
- **Reasoning:** Drawing conclusions from multiple data points, identifying patterns
- **Extraction from unstructured text:** Pulling structured data from variable-format input (emails, documents, chat messages, logs)
- **Contextual query building:** Creating search terms based on understanding what information is needed and how to find it
- **Conversation analysis:** Understanding multi-message exchanges — detecting unanswered questions, identifying commitments, assessing tone shifts

### The "aiTask vs customScript" Mental Test

Ask: "Can the logic be expressed as an algorithm that handles EVERY realistic input correctly, with no edge cases that require interpretation?"

- **No** → aiTask. The variability in input formats, meanings, or context means a script will fail on inputs the developer did not anticipate.
- **Yes** → customScript. The script can be complex (100+ lines is fine) as long as the logic is fully deterministic — identical input always produces identical output, no interpretation needed.

WRONG: "I'll use customScript to extract the recipient and subject from the email header and build a search query — it's just string parsing."
=> Mental test: Can a junior dev handle every email format? No. Display names with commas and angle brackets, multiple recipients in CC vs TO, forwarded chains with nested headers, missing subjects, encoded characters, non-Latin text. This is text processing — use aiTask.

RIGHT: "I'll use aiTask to analyze this email and produce a structured output with the recipient, subject keywords, and a targeted search query."
=> The AI handles format variability, understands context ("this is about the Q3 review"), and produces a query that actually finds the right results.

RIGHT: "I'll use customScript to filter this array of threads to only those where the last message was sent by me more than 3 days ago."
=> `threads.filter(t => t.lastSender === myEmail && daysSince(t.lastDate) > 3)` — a junior dev handles this in two lines, no edge cases.

## One Purpose Per AI Task

> **Design-time rule:** Apply this during Phase 1 (Design) when mapping the node graph — NOT during Phase 3 (Configure). If you're reading this for the first time while configuring a node, the task split should have happened earlier. Go back to Phase 1 step 4a.

Each AI task should have ONE purpose. If your task does both analysis AND content generation, split it into two tasks.

| Pattern | Tasks | Why |
|---------|-------|-----|
| Analyze email + decide if follow-up needed | Task 1: `email_followup_classifier` | Outputs boolean + reason. Feeds branching node. |
| Draft the follow-up email | Task 2: `followup_email_drafter` | Runs ONLY on the follow_up branch. Focused prompt = better quality. |

WRONG: One AI task that analyzes, decides, AND drafts.
```json
{ "output": { "shouldFollowUp": "boolean", "reason": "string", "draftEmail": "string" } }
```
=> Drafting runs even when shouldFollowUp is false (wastes tokens). Prompt tries to do two things (reduces quality of both). PA can't optimize each independently.

RIGHT: Two separate tasks, each with one purpose.
```
Task 1 → branching (logic mode: shouldFollowUp equals true)
Task 2 (on follow_up branch ONLY) → generates email text
```

**How to spot multi-purpose tasks:** If the description uses "AND" or has more than one verb (analyze AND draft, classify AND generate), split it.

**One-purpose applies at the OUTPUT FIELD level too.** For every field in the AI task's output schema, ask: "Could this be computed deterministically from the AI's inputs?" If yes, that field belongs in a customScript downstream — NOT in the AI's output. The AI should output only fields that require language interpretation or genuine judgment. Rule-based / threshold-based / lookup-derived fields belong in a downstream customScript. See `WORKFLOW_DESIGN_GUIDE.md` "Output field decomposition" for the decision table + WRONG/RIGHT pairs.

## Required Fields in `data`

| Field          | Type     | Description                                        |
| -------------- | -------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
| `selectedTask` | `string` | The AI task ID. Obtained from `nexus task list --json`. |

## Optional Fields

| Field             | Type             | Description                                                                                                     |
| ----------------- | ---------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `instructions`    | `string`         | Additional instructions for the AI task execution. Supports `{{nodeId.path}}` variable references.              |
| `parametersSetup` | `ParameterSetup` | Auto-populated from the selected task's `jsonInputSchema`. Each schema field becomes a `parametersSetup` entry. |
| `label`           | `string`         | Display label for the node.                                                                                     |
| `masked`          | `boolean`        | When `true`, the node is skipped during execution (pass-through).                                               |

## Default Data (set automatically on creation)

```json
{
  "parametersSetup": {},
  "additionalParameters": {},
  "outputFormat": null,
  "label": "AI task",
  "selectedTask": "",
  "instructions": ""
}
```

## Connection Rules

- Can be placed inside a loop: Yes
- Can be masked (skipped): Yes

## Pre-Integration Testing (MANDATORY for new tasks)

Before selecting a newly created AI task in an aiTask node, verify it works standalone:

```bash
nexus task execute <taskId> --input '<representative JSON matching the schema>' --json
```

Test with data representing EACH expected output path:
- Classifiers: one input per class (e.g., commercial AND non-commercial email)
- Generators: one input per tone/style variant
- Extractors: one input with all fields, one with edge cases

Verify output SEMANTICALLY — is the boolean CORRECT? Is the text APPROPRIATE?

WRONG: Create task → wire into workflow → test via loop → discover misclassification.
RIGHT: Create task → test standalone with 2-3 inputs → verify → wire into workflow.

## Configuration Steps

1. **Create the node** with `nexus workflow node create`.
2. **Connect it** to an upstream node with `nexus workflow edge create`.
3. **Search for an existing task** before creating a new one:

```bash
nexus task list --json
```

Present matching tasks to the user with: **name**, **creation date**, **input format**, **output format**, and **description**. Let the user decide:

| User decision | Action |
|---|---|
| An existing task fits | Use it — go to step 4 |
| No existing task fits, create a new one | Use the **prompt assistant** (`nexus-prompt-assistant` skill in `ai-task` mode) to generate the task. Read `CONVERSATION_GUIDE.md` first. Then go to step 4 with the new task ID. |

> **STOP — PROMPT ASSISTANT GATE**
>
> You MUST use the prompt assistant for every new AI task. No exceptions.
>
> The PA probes for edge cases, anti-patterns, quality criteria, and input/output schema design that manual prompt writing misses. A manual prompt skips all of this.
>
> **Consequences of skipping:** The task runs in production without edge case handling, without anti-patterns, without validation checks, and without worked examples. When the LLM encounters ambiguous input, it guesses instead of following a tested decision framework.
>
> If you are tempted to skip because "it's a simple task" or "I'm building a complex workflow and don't have time" — those are exactly the scenarios where the PA prevents the most damage.

WRONG: Creating a task with `nexus task create` and a hand-written prompt to save time during a complex workflow build.
=> The 10 minutes "saved" costs hours debugging when the task produces unexpected output.

WRONG: "This is a simple classification task, I'll just write the prompt myself."
=> Manual prompts miss edge cases, lack anti-patterns, produce inconsistent output schemas.

WRONG: Creating a new AI task manually without checking if one already exists.
WRONG: Creating a new AI task without using the prompt assistant.
RIGHT: Search existing tasks → present to user → if no match, use prompt assistant to create → then select.

**When using the prompt assistant for workflow AI tasks:**

Launch the prompt assistant as a background sub-agent so it doesn't block the main workflow build:

1. Gather all context: what the task does, input fields, output format, who/what consumes the output
2. Launch: `nexus prompt-assistant chat --mode ai-task --message "<full context>"`
   The CLI auto-polls and returns the assistant's response — no manual polling needed.
3. Continue configuring other workflow nodes while the conversation runs
4. When the task is generated, come back and select it in the aiTask node

The prompt assistant conversation typically takes 8-15 turns and 1-20 minutes for generation.
The CLI handles polling automatically. Start it early in the workflow build, not at the last minute.

4. **Select a task** by updating `selectedTask` with the task ID via `nexus workflow node update`. The backend auto-populates `parametersSetup` from the task's JSON input schema. **VERIFY** that `parametersSetup` was populated:
   ```bash
   nexus workflow node get <wfId> <nodeId> --json
   # Check: data.parametersSetup should contain one entry per input schema field
   ```
   If `parametersSetup` is empty (`{}`), the task's `jsonInputSchema` may not have been set correctly. Check the task: `nexus task get <taskId> --json` — verify `jsonInputSchema` has flat field definitions.

   WRONG: Setting `selectedTask` and moving on without checking `parametersSetup`.
   => AI task runs with EMPTY input. Produces edge-case fallback output that LOOKS correct but masks a data flow failure.
   RIGHT: Set `selectedTask` → verify `parametersSetup` populated → configure each parameter → test → verify input AND output.

5. **Configure each parameter** in `parametersSetup` by setting handler type (`manual`, `prompt`, or `variable`) and the corresponding value.
6. **Optionally set additional instructions** for the AI.

### Shape Data Before AI Tasks

When the upstream node's output schema doesn't match the AI task's input schema, add a `customScript` node between them to map fields.

WRONG: Plugin returns `{title, description, source: {domain}}` → AI task expects `{article_title, article_description, article_source}` → wire directly → AI receives wrong field names → empty data.
RIGHT: Plugin → customScript (maps `title` → `article_title`, `source.domain` → `article_source`) → AI task receives correctly shaped input.

## Example API Calls

### Step 1: Create the AI task node

```bash
nexus workflow node create "$WORKFLOW_ID" --type aiTask --json
```

### Step 2: Connect to upstream node

```bash
nexus workflow edge create "$WORKFLOW_ID" --source "$UPSTREAM_NODE_ID" --target "$AI_NODE_ID"
```

### Step 3: List available tasks

```bash
nexus task list --json
```

### Step 4: Select a task (triggers auto-population of parametersSetup)

```bash
nexus workflow node update "$WORKFLOW_ID" "$AI_NODE_ID" --body '{
  "data": {
    "selectedTask": "task_abc123"
  }
}'
```

After this update, fetch the node again to see the auto-populated `parametersSetup`.

**Schema-priming after batch creation.** When an aiTask node is created via `nexus api POST /workflows/<id>/batch` with `selectedTask` set inline in the node's `data`, the batch path stores `selectedTask` but does NOT populate `parametersSetup` schema (nor the `outputFormat` mirror) from the bound task's input/output schema. A subsequent PATCH on `parametersSetup` with field-keyed values returns 200 but is silently dropped — there's no schema for the values to write into. Workaround: after batch creation, PATCH `selectedTask` AGAIN with the SAME value (no-op write) — that triggers schema population. THEN PATCH `parametersSetup` with the variable references. The schema-prime PATCH is required ONLY for batch-created aiTask nodes; nodes created via `nexus workflow node create` followed by `nexus workflow node update` populate the schema automatically.
WRONG: batch create with `selectedTask` inline → PATCH parametersSetup → re-fetch shows parametersSetup empty (silent drop).
RIGHT: batch create with `selectedTask` inline → PATCH `selectedTask` again (same value) → re-fetch shows parametersSetup populated with default-valued entries → PATCH parametersSetup with variable refs → lands.

**If `parametersSetup` is empty after setting `selectedTask`:** The auto-population depends on the task having a valid `jsonInputSchema`. If the task was created with `inputFormat: "text"` or the schema is missing, `parametersSetup` will not auto-populate. In this case, manually construct entries matching the task's `jsonInputSchema`:

1. Fetch the task: `nexus task get <taskId> --json` → read `jsonInputSchema.properties`.
2. For each property in the schema, create a `parametersSetup` entry:

```json
{
  "propertyName": {
    "id": "param-<unique-id>",
    "type": "<type from schema>",
    "handler": "variable",
    "value": "",
    "prompt": "",
    "variable": "{{UPSTREAM_NODE_UUID.propertyName}}"
  }
}
```

3. Update the node with the manually constructed `parametersSetup` via `nexus workflow node update`.
4. Call `validate-variables` to confirm all references resolve.

Fetch the node:

```bash
nexus workflow node get "$WORKFLOW_ID" "$AI_NODE_ID" --json
```

### Step 5: Configure parameters

**Handler choice for `aiTask` differs from `plugin` nodes** — for `aiTask`, ALL upstream-referenced fields use `variable`, including strings (the unified resolver fetches the value, then constructs the prompt). The plugin-node rule of "string fields → `manual` with inline `{{}}` references" does NOT apply here.

Each parametersSetup entry supports three handler types:

**Manual (static value):**

```json
{
  "paramKey": {
    "id": "auto-generated-uuid",
    "type": "string",
    "handler": "manual",
    "value": "Hello world",
    "prompt": "",
    "variable": ""
  }
}
```

**Variable (reference upstream node output):**

```json
{
  "paramKey": {
    "id": "auto-generated-uuid",
    "type": "string",
    "handler": "variable",
    "value": "",
    "prompt": "",
    "variable": "{{TRIGGER_NODE_UUID.body.customer_name}}"
  }
}
```

**Prompt (let AI decide at runtime):**

```json
{
  "paramKey": {
    "id": "auto-generated-uuid",
    "type": "string",
    "handler": "prompt",
    "value": "",
    "prompt": "Extract the customer name from the input data",
    "variable": ""
  }
}
```

```bash
nexus workflow node update "$WORKFLOW_ID" "$AI_NODE_ID" --body '{
  "data": {
    "parametersSetup": {
      "email_body": {
        "id": "param-uuid-1",
        "type": "string",
        "handler": "variable",
        "value": "",
        "prompt": "",
        "variable": "{{TRIGGER_NODE_UUID.body.email_content}}"
      },
      "tone": {
        "id": "param-uuid-2",
        "type": "string",
        "handler": "manual",
        "value": "professional",
        "prompt": "",
        "variable": ""
      }
    }
  }
}'
```

### Step 6: Set additional instructions

```bash
nexus workflow node update "$WORKFLOW_ID" "$AI_NODE_ID" --body '{
  "data": {
    "instructions": "Focus on extracting action items and summarizing the key points."
  }
}'
```

## Common Patterns / Tips

- **The `selectedTask` is the only required field.** Without it, the node shows `configStatus: "incomplete"` with `missingFields: ["selectedTask"]`.
- **`parametersSetup` is auto-populated** when you set `selectedTask`. You do not need to manually create entries -- just configure the handler/value for each one.
- **Each parametersSetup entry needs all fields:** `id`, `type`, `handler`, `value`, `prompt`, `variable`. Missing fields may cause execution errors even if the node appears "complete".
- **The `instructions` field supports `{{...}}` variable references.** These are translated automatically by the API.
- **Use `gptTask` as an alias** if needed -- it has identical behavior and data shape.

## Variable References

The `instructions` field supports inline variable references:

```
Analyze the following data: {{UPSTREAM_NODE_UUID.body.data}}
```

The `parametersSetup` entries support variable references in the `variable` field (when handler is `"variable"`) and in the `prompt` field (when handler is `"prompt"`):

```
{{UPSTREAM_NODE_UUID.propertyPath}}
```

**Output:** Downstream nodes reference the AI task's response:

```
{{AI_NODE_UUID}}
{{AI_NODE_UUID.summary}}
{{AI_NODE_UUID.action_items}}
```

The output structure depends on the selected task's output schema.

# Custom Script

> Object-typed fields in `outputFormat` must declare `properties` — see CLAUDE.md G#13.

## Node Type Identifier

`customScript`

## What It Does

Executes custom JavaScript or Python code within the workflow. The script receives input from upstream nodes and returns a result that downstream nodes can reference. Useful for data transformation, computation, or any logic that cannot be expressed with other node types.

## When to Use Custom Script

> **Read this BEFORE writing any code.** If you skip this section and jump to the code examples below, you risk building a node that should be an `aiTask`.

Custom script is for **deterministic algorithms** — logic that is rule-based, repeatable, and produces identical output for identical input every single time. It is NOT for text processing.

### Correct Use Cases (customScript)

- **Filtering arrays:** `items.filter(i => i.status === "active" && i.score > 80)`
- **Merging JSON objects:** Combining outputs from multiple upstream nodes into one structure
- **Rule-based decisions:** `if (amount > 1000 && region === "EU") return "high_priority"`
- **Mathematical computation:** Aggregation, percentage calculation, rounding, currency conversion
- **Data format conversion with fixed rules:** Date format transformation, unit conversion, CSV row to JSON object
- **Deduplication:** Removing duplicates by exact field match
- **Array manipulation:** Sorting, grouping, slicing, flattening nested structures
- **Markup payload (HTML email body, etc.):** return the full markup string verbatim with values injected (`` `Hi ${firstName},` ``) — a `textFormatter` would flatten it

### Incorrect Use Cases (use `aiTask` instead)

Never use customScript for operations that involve:
- Processing natural language or understanding context
- Extracting information from unstructured or variable-format text
- Building search queries from text content
- Summarizing, classifying, or assessing text
- Analyzing conversations, emails, or threads
- Any operation where input format varies and a script would need to handle edge cases in human-written text

WRONG: customScript to "parse the email subject and recipient, then build a Gmail search query."
=> Works on test email. Fails in production when subjects contain quotes, are empty, have "Re: Re: Fwd:" chains, or are in non-Latin scripts. Recipients may be in display-name format, CC vs TO, or comma-separated groups. A script needs 15+ edge-case handlers and still misses the 16th.

RIGHT: `aiTask` to analyze the email and produce a structured search query.
=> The AI understands "Re: Re: Fwd: Q3 Budget Review — updated numbers" is about "Q3 Budget Review." It handles format variation, missing fields, and produces queries that actually find the right results.

WRONG: customScript to "determine if this email thread needs a follow-up."
=> Follow-up detection requires understanding tone, commitments, questions asked, and response patterns. This is classification — an AI task.

RIGHT: customScript to "filter threads where the last message was sent more than 3 days ago by us."
=> `threads.filter(t => t.lastMessage.from === myEmail && daysSince(t.lastMessage.date) > 3)` — pure boolean logic on structured fields.

**Decision shortcut:** If the word "extract," "analyze," "determine," "assess," "classify," or "understand" appears in the step description, it is almost certainly an `aiTask`, not a `customScript`.

## Required Fields in `data`

| Field  | Type     | Description                                                                                |
| ------ | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `code` | `string` | The code to execute. Must differ from the default placeholder to be considered "complete". |

## Optional Fields

| Field      | Type               | Description                                                                                                           |
| ---------- | ------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `language` | `"js" \| "python"` | Programming language. Default: `"js"`.                                                                                |
| `inputs`   | `ScriptInput[]`    | Input variables mapped from upstream nodes. Each entry has `id`, `name`, and `node` (a reference to the source node). |
| `label`    | `string`           | Display label for the node.                                                                                           |

!! WARNING: The input mapping field is `inputs` — not `namedInputs`, `input`, or `parameters`. !!
Using any other field name is silently ignored — the function receives `undefined` with no error.

WRONG: `"namedInputs": [{"name": "data", "value": "{{UUID}}"}]` → silently ignored, function gets `undefined`.
RIGHT: `"inputs": [{"id": "i1", "name": "data", "node": "{{UUID}}"}]` → function receives upstream output.
Three differences: field is `inputs` not `namedInputs`, uses `node` not `value`, requires `id`.

## Default Data (set automatically on creation)

```json
{
  "language": "js",
  "label": "Custom script",
  "code": "function func() {\n    //Your JavaScript Code Here\n}",
  "inputs": [],
  "instructions": ""
}
```

The node is "incomplete" while the code matches the default placeholder exactly.

## Connection Rules

- Can be placed inside a loop: Yes
- Can be masked (skipped): Yes

## Configuration Steps

> !! **STOP — If the customScript was created via `nexus api POST /workflows/<id>/batch`, the `data.inputs` you passed into the batch body are NOT wired to the runtime resolver, even though `node get` shows them stored.** Run a separate `nexus workflow node update --body '{"data":{"inputs":[<SAME ARRAY>]}}'` BEFORE testing the node. Detect: per-node test returns `"CustomScript inputs are missing or malformed"` and `input.inputs[0].value` is null at runtime. See `reference/batch-scaffolding.md` for the full workaround. !!

1. **Create the node** with `nexus workflow node create`.
2. **Connect it** to an upstream node with `nexus workflow edge create`.
3. **Set the language** (optional, defaults to `"js"`) via `nexus workflow node update`.
4. **Write the code** via `nexus workflow node update`.
5. **Map input variables** (optional) from upstream nodes via `nexus workflow node update`.

## Example API Calls

### Step 1: Create the custom script node

```bash
nexus workflow node create "$WORKFLOW_ID" --type customScript --json
```

### Step 2: Connect to upstream node

```bash
nexus workflow edge create "$WORKFLOW_ID" --source "$UPSTREAM_NODE_ID" --target "$SCRIPT_NODE_ID"
```

### Step 3: Write JavaScript code

```bash
nexus workflow node update "$WORKFLOW_ID" "$SCRIPT_NODE_ID" --body '{
  "data": {
    "code": "function func(input) {\n  const items = input.data || [];\n  const total = items.reduce((sum, item) => sum + item.price, 0);\n  return {\n    itemCount: items.length,\n    total: total,\n    average: items.length > 0 ? total / items.length : 0\n  };\n}"
  }
}'
```

### Example: Python code

```bash
nexus workflow node update "$WORKFLOW_ID" "$SCRIPT_NODE_ID" --body '{
  "data": {
    "language": "python",
    "code": "def func(input):\n    items = input.get(\"data\", [])\n    total = sum(item[\"price\"] for item in items)\n    return {\"itemCount\": len(items), \"total\": total}"
  }
}'
```

### Step 4: Map named inputs (optional)

```bash
nexus workflow node update "$WORKFLOW_ID" "$SCRIPT_NODE_ID" --body '{
  "data": {
    "inputs": [
      {
        "id": "input1",
        "name": "webhookData",
        "node": "{{$TRIGGER_NODE_UUID}}"
      }
    ]
  }
}'
```

### Step 5: Test the node

```bash
nexus workflow node test "$WORKFLOW_ID" "$SCRIPT_NODE_ID" --json
```

## outputFormat propagation requires per-node test

A customScript's `outputFormat` schema is auto-populated ONLY after `nexus workflow node test <wf> <node>` runs. Full workflow tests (`nexus workflow test ...`) execute the node but DO NOT update its persisted `outputFormat`. Without populated outputFormat, downstream nodes referencing this script's nested fields show as "field doesn't exist" in the dashboard variable resolver — even though runtime resolution works correctly.

| Test path | Populates outputFormat? | Use when |
|---|---|---|
| `nexus workflow node test <wf> <node>` | YES | Always run after configuring a customScript |
| `nexus workflow test <wf>` (full) | NO | End-to-end check after all per-node tests passed |
| Static `node update` with `data.outputFormat` | YES (explicit) | Workaround — only if a per-node test is platform-blocked |

**How to detect:**
- Dashboard shows "1 error(s) detected. <field> doesn't exist." on a downstream branching or aiTask node.
- `nexus workflow node variables <wf> <downstream>` returns the customScript path with `children: []` (no nested paths).
- Runtime executions work fine — the error is dashboard-only static validation.

**Fix:**
```bash
nexus workflow node test "$WF" "$CUSTOMSCRIPT_NODE"
sleep 5
nexus workflow node get "$WF" "$CUSTOMSCRIPT_NODE" --json | jq '.data.outputFormat'  # confirm populated
# Dashboard error clears on refresh
```

WRONG: Run full workflow tests on a customScript many times — execution works each time, but its outputFormat stays null. Branching node references `<customScript>.someField` → dashboard shows "field doesn't exist". Report workflow correct anyway.
RIGHT: After configuring a customScript, immediately run `nexus workflow node test`. Confirm outputFormat populates. THEN downstream references resolve in the dashboard.

## Agent-invocation ≠ `workflow test` — `inputs[]` resolution gap

A customScript's `inputs` (and `{{…}}` templates inside array elements) resolve under `workflow test` but come back EMPTY/null when the SAME workflow is invoked as an agent tool — agent invocation is a different execution context. The node sees missing inputs and the write/transform silently produces nothing.

Fix: for agent-attached workflows, don't carry agent-supplied values through a customScript `inputs` array. Put them where agent-invocation DOES resolve them — a plugin string-param template using `{{trigger.<field>}}` directly (e.g. build the INSERT/SELECT inside a `run-query` string param).

WRONG: `workflow test` green (inputs resolve) → attach as agent tool → agent runs it → row never written, no error.
RIGHT: verify on the AGENT path (emulator / `tools/<id>/test`), not just `workflow test`; build writes via `run-query` with `{{trigger.field}}` in the SQL string.

## Common Patterns / Tips

- **Function signature for JavaScript:** `function func(param_name) { return result; }`. The function MUST be named `func`. The parameter name should match the `name` field in the `inputs` array. If `inputs` has `[{name: "tab_data", node: "UUID"}]`, the function should be `function func(tab_data) { ... }`. Parameter names should be snake_case. The `node` field MUST use `{{UUID}}` wrapping — see the CRITICAL note above.
- **Function signature for Python:** `def func(input):`. Same naming requirement.
- **The code must differ from the default placeholder** for config status to be "complete". The default is `"function func() {\n    //Your JavaScript Code Here\n}"`.
- **Return values become the node's output.** Whatever the function returns is accessible to downstream nodes as variable references.
- **Scripts run in a sandboxed environment.** External network calls, file system access, and module imports are restricted.
- **CRITICAL: Double-escaping in code strings.** The `code` field is a JSON string. JSON parsers interpret `\n` as a literal newline character — which splits your JavaScript across two lines and breaks it. To store the JavaScript string `"\n"` in code (e.g., `lines.join("\n")`), the JSON payload must contain `\\n`.

  | You want in JavaScript | JSON payload must contain | Why |
  |---|---|---|
  | Line break between statements | `\n` | JSON interprets as newline — correct |
  | The string `"\n"` in code (e.g., `join("\n")`) | `\\n` | JSON interprets `\\` as literal `\`, then `n` stays — produces `\n` in stored code |
  | The string `"\t"` in code | `\\t` | Same principle — all escape sequences need double-escaping |
  | A literal backslash `\` in code | `\\\\` | JSON `\\` → `\`, so `\\\\` → `\\` in stored code |

  WRONG (JSON): `"code": "return { text: lines.join(\"\n\") };"` → stored as two lines → Runtime: `Unterminated string literal at line 20`.
  RIGHT (JSON): `"code": "return { text: lines.join(\"\\n\") };"` → stored as `lines.join("\n")` on a single line → works.

  **Detection:** "Unterminated string literal" immediately after a customScript code update = double-escaping issue. Test the node after EVERY code update to catch this instantly.

- **WARNING: customScript default code breaks JSON in shell pipes.** The default placeholder contains newlines that cause parse errors when constructing PATCH bodies via CLI. Safe pattern: write a minimal placeholder first (`function func(input) { return input; }`), verify the PATCH succeeds, then update with the full code in a second PATCH.

> **CRITICAL: The `node` field in `inputs` MUST be wrapped in `{{}}`** — e.g., `"node": "{{upstream-uuid}}"`, NOT `"node": "upstream-uuid"`. Without the `{{}}` wrapping, the function parameter receives `null`. This is consistent with how ALL variable references work in the platform.

### MANDATORY: Use Named Inputs — Never Hardcode Node UUIDs in Code

The `inputs` array maps upstream node UUIDs to readable names. ALWAYS use it. Hardcoding UUIDs in code creates a silent breakage risk: if the upstream node is ever deleted and recreated (common during development), the UUID changes and the script silently receives `undefined`.

WRONG (raw UUID without `{{}}` wrapping):
```javascript
// inputs: [{ "name": "tab_data", "node": "7f010361-..." }]  ← MISSING {{}}
function func(tab_data) {
  // tab_data is NULL — the platform can't resolve a raw UUID string
}
```

WRONG (hardcoded UUID in code):
```javascript
function func(input) {
  const tabData = input["7f010361-..."];
  // Fragile — UUID changes on node recreation
}
```

RIGHT (named input with `{{UUID}}` wrapping):
```javascript
// inputs: [{ "id": "input1", "name": "tab_data", "node": "{{7f010361-...}}" }]  ← WITH {{}}
function func(tab_data) {
  // tab_data contains the upstream node's actual output
  return tab_data.map(row => row.keyword);
}
```

WHY THIS MATTERS: During development, nodes are frequently deleted and recreated. Every recreation generates a new UUID. With hardcoded UUIDs, you must find-and-replace inside the code string — easy to miss, impossible to validate automatically. With named inputs, you update one `node` field in the inputs array — the code is untouched.

## Variable References

The custom script node does not use `{{...}}` variable references in its `code` field. Instead, it receives upstream data through the `input` parameter of the `func` function.

**Output:** Downstream nodes reference the script's return value:

```
{{SCRIPT_NODE_UUID}}
{{SCRIPT_NODE_UUID.itemCount}}
{{SCRIPT_NODE_UUID.total}}
```

If the function returns an object, downstream nodes can access individual properties via dot notation.

# JSON Parse

## Node Type Identifier

`jsonParse`

## What It Does

Parses a JSON string into a structured object. Takes a raw JSON string (which can include variable references to upstream node outputs) and produces a parsed object that downstream nodes can reference by individual keys.

## Required Fields in `data`

| Field        | Type     | Description                                                                                                                  |
| ------------ | -------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `jsonString` | `string` | The JSON string to parse. Can contain `{{nodeId.path}}` variable references. Must be non-empty for config status "complete". |

## Optional Fields

| Field   | Type     | Description                 |
| ------- | -------- | --------------------------- |
| `label` | `string` | Display label for the node. |

## Default Data (set automatically on creation)

```json
{
  "label": "JSON parse",
  "jsonString": "",
  "instructions": ""
}
```

## Connection Rules

- Can be placed inside a loop: Yes
- Can be masked (skipped): Yes

## Configuration Steps

1. **Create the node** with `nexus workflow node create`.
2. **Connect it** to an upstream node with `nexus workflow edge create`.
3. **Set the JSON string** via `nexus workflow node update`. This can be a literal JSON string or a variable reference to an upstream node's string output.

## Example API Calls

### Step 1: Create the JSON parse node

```bash
nexus workflow node create "$WORKFLOW_ID" --type jsonParse --json
```

### Step 2: Connect to upstream node

```bash
nexus workflow edge create "$WORKFLOW_ID" --source "$UPSTREAM_NODE_ID" --target "$JSON_PARSE_NODE_ID"
```

### Step 3a: Set a literal JSON string

```bash
nexus workflow node update "$WORKFLOW_ID" "$JSON_PARSE_NODE_ID" --body '{
  "data": {
    "jsonString": "{\"status\": \"active\", \"count\": 42, \"tags\": [\"important\", \"urgent\"]}"
  }
}'
```

### Step 3b: Set a variable reference (parse upstream node's string output)

```bash
nexus workflow node update "$WORKFLOW_ID" "$JSON_PARSE_NODE_ID" --body '{
  "data": {
    "jsonString": "{{UPSTREAM_NODE_UUID.body.rawJson}}"
  }
}'
```

### Step 4: Verify configuration

```bash
nexus workflow node get "$WORKFLOW_ID" "$JSON_PARSE_NODE_ID" --json
```

Returns `configStatus: "complete"` when `jsonString` is non-empty.

### Step 5: Test the node

```bash
nexus workflow node test "$WORKFLOW_ID" "$JSON_PARSE_NODE_ID" --json
```

## Common Patterns / Tips

- **Use this node when an upstream node produces a JSON string** (e.g., a custom script that returns a string, or a webhook body field that contains serialized JSON). Parsing it lets downstream nodes reference individual fields.
- **Variable references in `jsonString` are resolved before parsing.** The `{{...}}` references are substituted with actual values first, then the resulting string is parsed as JSON.
- **If the upstream output is already an object** (not a string), you do not need jsonParse. Just reference the nested fields directly with `{{nodeUUID.field.nested}}`.
- **Invalid JSON at runtime causes an execution error.** Make sure the resolved string is valid JSON. Test the node after configuration to verify.
- **Config status is based only on `jsonString` being non-empty.** The API does not validate JSON syntax at configuration time -- only at execution time.

## Variable References

The `jsonString` field supports inline variable references:

```
{{UPSTREAM_NODE_UUID.body.serializedData}}
{{UPSTREAM_NODE_UUID}}
```

**Output:** Downstream nodes reference the parsed object's fields:

```
{{JSON_PARSE_NODE_UUID.status}}
{{JSON_PARSE_NODE_UUID.count}}
{{JSON_PARSE_NODE_UUID.tags}}
{{JSON_PARSE_NODE_UUID.tags[0]}}
```

The output structure mirrors whatever JSON was parsed.

# JSONata

## Node Type Identifier

`jsonata`

## What It Does

Evaluates a JSONata expression with named variable bindings from upstream nodes. JSONata is a lightweight query and transformation language for JSON data, useful for complex data transformations, filtering, aggregation, and restructuring that would be cumbersome with simple variable references.

## Required Fields in `data`

| Field        | Type     | Description                                                                                        |
| ------------ | -------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `expression` | `string` | The JSONata expression to evaluate. Must be non-empty (checked at runtime, not for config status). |

## Optional Fields

| Field             | Type                | Description                                                                                            |
| ----------------- | ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `variables`       | `JSONataVariable[]` | Named variable bindings. Each entry has a `value` field that can contain `{{nodeId.path}}` references. |
| `parametersSetup` | `ParameterSetup`    | Alternative variable binding format using the standard parameter setup structure.                      |
| `label`           | `string`            | Display label for the node.                                                                            |

## Default Data (set automatically on creation)

```json
{
  "label": "JSONata",
  "expression": "",
  "variables": [],
  "parametersSetup": {},
  "instructions": ""
}
```

## Connection Rules

- Can be placed inside a loop: Yes
- Can be masked (skipped): Yes

## Configuration Steps

1. **Create the node** with `nexus workflow node create`.
2. **Connect it** to an upstream node with `nexus workflow edge create`.
3. **Write the JSONata expression** via `nexus workflow node update`.
4. **Bind variables** (optional) from upstream nodes via `nexus workflow node update`. Variables are referenced in the expression using `$variableName`.

## Example API Calls

### Step 1: Create the JSONata node

```bash
nexus workflow node create "$WORKFLOW_ID" --type jsonata --json
```

### Step 2: Connect to upstream node

```bash
nexus workflow edge create "$WORKFLOW_ID" --source "$UPSTREAM_NODE_ID" --target "$JSONATA_NODE_ID"
```

### Step 3: Write the expression and bind variables

```bash
nexus workflow node update "$WORKFLOW_ID" "$JSONATA_NODE_ID" --body '{
  "data": {
    "expression": "$data.orders[status = \"active\"].{ \"id\": id, \"total\": price * quantity }",
    "variables": [
      {
        "value": "{{UPSTREAM_NODE_UUID}}"
      }
    ]
  }
}'
```

### Example: Filter and transform an array

```bash
nexus workflow node update "$WORKFLOW_ID" "$JSONATA_NODE_ID" --body '{
  "data": {
    "expression": "$items[price > 100].{ \"name\": name, \"discounted\": price * 0.9 }",
    "variables": [
      {
        "value": "{{PLUGIN_NODE_UUID.response.rows}}"
      }
    ]
  }
}'
```

### Example: Aggregate data

```bash
nexus workflow node update "$WORKFLOW_ID" "$JSONATA_NODE_ID" --body '{
  "data": {
    "expression": "{ \"total\": $sum($data.items.price), \"count\": $count($data.items), \"average\": $average($data.items.price) }",
    "variables": [
      {
        "value": "{{UPSTREAM_NODE_UUID}}"
      }
    ]
  }
}'
```

### Step 4: Test the node

```bash
nexus workflow node test "$WORKFLOW_ID" "$JSONATA_NODE_ID" --json
```

## Common Patterns / Tips

- **JSONata is powerful for complex transformations** that would require multiple nodes or custom scripts otherwise. Use it for filtering arrays, restructuring objects, aggregating values, and conditional transformations.
- **Variables are bound using the `variables` array.** Each entry's `value` field is a `{{nodeId.path}}` reference that gets resolved at runtime. The bound data is accessible in the expression.
- **The `expression` field itself does NOT use `{{...}}` syntax.** Variable references go in the `variables` array entries, not in the expression string. The expression uses standard JSONata syntax.
- **JSONata reference:** See https://jsonata.org for full syntax documentation. Common functions include `$sum()`, `$count()`, `$average()`, `$map()`, `$filter()`, `$string()`, `$number()`.
- **The node has no config-status required fields** in the strict sense (the registry does not explicitly check `expression`). However, an empty expression will fail at execution time.

## Variable References

The `variables` array entries contain `{{...}}` references in their `value` fields:

```json
{
  "variables": [{ "value": "{{NODE_UUID.path}}" }, { "value": "{{ANOTHER_NODE_UUID}}" }]
}
```

The API translates these references bidirectionally (to/from internal HTML mention format).

**Output:** Downstream nodes reference the JSONata result:

```
{{JSONATA_NODE_UUID}}
{{JSONATA_NODE_UUID.total}}
{{JSONATA_NODE_UUID.items}}
```

The output structure depends on what the JSONata expression produces.

# Parallel AI

> **⚠ STOP — Schema Capacity gate (RECURRING failure mode).** Before configuring any `parallelai → <consumer>` chain, count the consumer's required input fields and compare to the capacity of a single `parallelai` at the chosen tier: `nexus task get <consumerId> --json | jq '.jsonInputSchema | keys | length'` and read the Processor Tiers table for your tier's typical capacity. **If consumer-required > single-node-capacity-at-acceptable-tier, single-`parallelai` is BLOCKED — fan-out by theme/dimension is the architecture, not a recommendation.** Bucket by whatever themes make sense for your domain (e.g., firmographics + leadership + domain-signals + per-person deep dives for sales enrichment; or features + benchmarks + reviews + technical-spec for product research) — feeding a `customScript` spread-merge into the consumer. NEVER compress the consumer schema or pad missing fields with prose defaults — that's silent quality failure (see CLAUDE.md Universal Gotcha #19 + #20).
>
> WRONG: consumer requires 50 input fields. Single `parallelai` (chosen tier produces ~15) + `customScript` pads ~35 missing fields with `"Not researched in this run."`. The consumer reads prose padding as real content and produces a confident-looking output on padded fake data.
> RIGHT: pre-check shows consumer-required > single-node-capacity → STOP single-node design → propose N themed parallelai (each at the right tier for ITS theme's complexity, summed to cover the consumer's schema) → `customScript` merges by spread → consumer receives real data for every field.

> Object-typed schema fields in output schemas must declare `properties` — see CLAUDE.md G#13.

## Node Type Identifier

`parallelai`

## What It Does

Executes structured internet research via the Parallel API. Unlike Perplexity (text in/out), Parallel accepts structured JSON input and returns structured JSON output matching a defined schema. Each output field's description acts as a research brief — telling the AI WHERE to search, HOW to infer missing data, and WHAT format to return.

Use Parallel when you need specific data fields about companies, people, or entities — with sources and confidence scores. Use Perplexity (plugin node) for simple text Q&A.

## Required Fields in `data`

| Field | Type | Description |
|-------|------|-------------|
| `action` | `string` | The Parallel action type: `"task"`, `"search"`, `"task_group"`, `"extract"`, `"chat"`, `"find_all"`. Most common: `"task"`. **NOT `selectedAction`** — that's for plugin nodes. |
| `processor` | `string` | Processing tier: `"lite"`, `"base"`, `"core"`, `"core2x"`, `"pro"`, `"ultra"`, `"ultra2x"`, `"ultra4x"`, `"ultra8x"`. See Processor Tiers below. |
| `inputMode` | `string` | `"json"` or `"text"`. Use `"json"` for structured input (recommended). |
| `outputMode` | `string` | `"json"` or `"text"`. Use `"json"` for structured output (recommended). |
| `inputSchema` | `object` | Input fields. Flat object: `{fieldName: {id: "uuid", type: "string"}}`. NOT standard JSON Schema. |
| `outputSchema` | `object` | Output fields. Flat object: `{fieldName: {id: "uuid", type: "string", description: "research brief"}}`. The `description` is the research instruction — this is what makes Parallel powerful. |
| `parametersSetup` | `object` | Maps each input field to upstream variables. Same format as plugin nodes: `{fieldName: {id, type, handler, variable, value, prompt}}`. Also supports `includeDomains` and `excludeDomains` for source policy. |

## Schema Format (CRITICAL — Different from JSON Schema)

Parallelai uses a FLAT field format, NOT standard JSON Schema (`{type: "object", properties: {...}}`).

WRONG (standard JSON Schema — will fail):
```json
{
  "outputSchema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "employee_count": {"type": "string", "description": "..."}
    }
  }
}
```

RIGHT (flat field format with per-field id):
```json
{
  "outputSchema": {
    "employee_count": {
      "id": "field-emp-001",
      "type": "string",
      "description": "VALUE ONLY — Total global headcount..."
    },
    "employee_count_reasoning": {
      "id": "field-emp-r-002",
      "type": "string",
      "description": "Source, date, method, confidence..."
    }
  }
}
```

Each field has: `id` (unique string), `type` (string/number/array/object), `description` (the research brief).

## Output Structure

Parallel returns a structured object with:

```json
{
  "type": "json",
  "content": {
    "employee_count": "10890",
    "headquarters_location": "Brussels, Belgium",
    "employee_count_reasoning": "10890 employees per LinkedIn. Date: 2026-03. Confidence: HIGH.",
    "headquarters_reasoning": "HQ listed as Brussels, Belgium on company website. Confidence: HIGH."
  },
  "basis": [
    {
      "field": "employee_count",
      "citations": [
        {"url": "https://linkedin.com/company/nexus", "title": "Nexus", "excerpts": ["10,890 employees"]}
      ],
      "reasoning": "LinkedIn company page lists 10,890 employees.",
      "confidence": "high"
    }
  ]
}
```

**Variable references for downstream nodes:**
- `{{nodeId.content.employee_count}}` — the value
- `{{nodeId.content.headquarters_location}}` — another value
- `{{nodeId.basis}}` — full citations array
- `{{nodeId.type}}` — "json"

## Processor Tiers

Choose the LIGHTEST processor that handles your field count. ALWAYS ask the user before selecting `pro` or above.

| Processor | Latency | Max Fields | $/1K requests | Use For |
|-----------|---------|-----------|---------------|---------|
| lite | 10s-60s | ~2 | $5 | Basic metadata, quick lookups |
| base | 15s-100s | ~5 | $10 | Standard enrichments (HQ, revenue, industry, employee count) |
| core | 60s-5min | ~10 | $25 | Cross-referenced, moderately complex |
| core2x | 60s-10min | ~10 | $50 | High complexity cross-referenced |
| pro | 2min-10min | ~20 | $100 | Exploratory web research |
| ultra | 5min-25min | ~20 | $300 | Advanced multi-source deep research |
| ultra2x | 5min-50min | ~25 | $600 | Difficult deep research |
| ultra4x | 5min-90min | ~25 | $1,200 | Very difficult deep research |
| ultra8x | 5min-2hr | ~25 | $2,400 | The most difficult deep research |

WRONG: Defaulting to `pro` ($100/1K) for 4 fields. `base` ($10/1K) handles it fine — 10x cheaper.
RIGHT: ≤2 fields → lite, ≤5 → base, ≤10 → core, ≤20 → pro, 20+ → ultra. ALWAYS ask user for pro+.

## Output Schema — The Key to Quality

The `description` field is NOT a label — it's a detailed research brief. Read `reference/parallel-output-schema-guidelines.md` for the full 6-component structure.

WRONG:
```json
"revenue": {"id": "f1", "type": "string", "description": "The company's annual revenue"}
```

RIGHT:
```json
"annual_revenue_usd": {
  "id": "f1",
  "type": "string",
  "description": "VALUE ONLY — Annual revenue in US dollars as a single integer. Always convert non-USD using fiscal year average exchange rate. SEARCH: SEC 10-K/10-Q, earnings calls, investor relations, Crunchbase/PitchBook, press releases, local registries (Companies House UK, Bundesanzeiger Germany). INFERENCE IF NOT FOUND: (a) employee count × industry benchmark/employee, (b) funding × valuation multiple by stage, (c) customer count × estimated ACV. FORMAT: Integer only. e.g. '5700000000'. No '$', no 'M/B', no ranges."
}
```

### Value + Reasoning Field Pattern

For every value field, add a `{field}_reasoning` companion:
- `employee_count` → `employee_count_reasoning`
- `headquarters_location` → `headquarters_reasoning`
- The reasoning field captures source, method, date, and confidence level

### Source Policy via parametersSetup

Control which domains to search/avoid using `includeDomains` and `excludeDomains` in parametersSetup:

```json
"includeDomains": {
  "id": "ps-include",
  "type": "string",
  "handler": "manual",
  "value": "linkedin.com,crunchbase.com,sec.gov",
  "variable": "",
  "prompt": ""
},
"excludeDomains": {
  "id": "ps-exclude",
  "type": "string",
  "handler": "manual",
  "value": "reddit.com,quora.com",
  "variable": "",
  "prompt": ""
}
```

**GOTCHA — Schema mutation on save**: When you configure `includeDomains`/`excludeDomains` as `type: "string"` with comma-separated values, the API may silently convert them to `type: "array"` with empty `items[]`, effectively dropping your domain list. After configuring source policy, always verify the saved values:

```bash
nexus workflow node get "$WF_ID" "$PAR_ID" --json | jq '.data.parametersSetup.includeDomains'
```

If the domains were dropped, you may need to use array format instead:
```json
"includeDomains": {
  "id": "ps-include",
  "type": "array",
  "handler": "manual",
  "items": ["linkedin.com", "crunchbase.com", "sec.gov"],
  "value": "",
  "variable": "",
  "prompt": "",
  "itemsSchema": {"id": "item-schema", "type": "string"}
}
```

## Complete Configuration Example (CLI Only)

This example creates a workflow that researches a company given its name and website.

```bash
# 1. Create workflow
WF_ID=$(nexus workflow create --name "Company Research" --description "Parallel AI company enrichment" --json | jq -r '.id')

# 2. Set agent input trigger with parameters
TRIGGER_ID=$(nexus workflow trigger "$WF_ID" --type agentInputTrigger --json | jq -r '.node.id // .id')

nexus workflow node update "$WF_ID" "$TRIGGER_ID" --body '{
  "data": {
    "parameters": {
      "name": {"id": "p-name", "type": "string"},
      "website": {"id": "p-website", "type": "string"}
    },
    "runOutput": {
      "name": "Nexus",
      "website": "agent.nexus"
    }
  }
}'

# 3. Create parallelai node
PAR_ID=$(nexus workflow node create "$WF_ID" --type parallelai --json | jq -r '.id')

# 4. Configure parallelai — action, processor, schemas, parametersSetup
nexus workflow node update "$WF_ID" "$PAR_ID" --body "{
  \"data\": {
    \"action\": \"task\",
    \"processor\": \"base\",
    \"inputMode\": \"json\",
    \"outputMode\": \"json\",
    \"inputSchema\": {
      \"name\": {\"id\": \"in-name\", \"type\": \"string\"},
      \"website\": {\"id\": \"in-website\", \"type\": \"string\"}
    },
    \"outputSchema\": {
      \"employee_count\": {
        \"id\": \"out-emp\",
        \"type\": \"string\",
        \"description\": \"VALUE ONLY — Total headcount as integer. SEARCH: LinkedIn, About page, Crunchbase. FORMAT: Integer e.g. 10890.\"
      },
      \"headquarters_location\": {
        \"id\": \"out-hq\",
        \"type\": \"string\",
        \"description\": \"VALUE ONLY — City and country. SEARCH: Company website, LinkedIn, Wikipedia. FORMAT: City, Country e.g. Brussels, Belgium.\"
      },
      \"employee_count_reasoning\": {
        \"id\": \"out-emp-r\",
        \"type\": \"string\",
        \"description\": \"Source, date, confidence. Template: [X] per [source]. Date: [YYYY-MM]. Confidence: [HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW].\"
      },
      \"headquarters_reasoning\": {
        \"id\": \"out-hq-r\",
        \"type\": \"string\",
        \"description\": \"Source and confidence. Template: HQ listed as [loc] on [source]. Confidence: [HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW].\"
      }
    },
    \"parametersSetup\": {
      \"name\": {
        \"id\": \"ps-name\", \"type\": \"string\", \"handler\": \"variable\",
        \"variable\": \"{{$TRIGGER_ID.name}}\", \"value\": \"\", \"prompt\": \"\"
```
