#!/bin/zsh
# deploy_watch.sh <public-url> <content-marker> [timeout-s=600] [poll-s=20] [profile] [appId]
# 1) polls `nexus vibe audit list` until a terminal deploy event; 2) until-loops a
# cache-busted content grep of <public-url> for <content-marker> (HEALTHY precedes swap).
# Exit 0 = marker served; 2 = deploy FAILED event; 3 = timeout; 4 = ACCESS blocked (401/403).
# Pass [appId] to SCOPE the audit poll to your app — an org-wide poll can be satisfied by a
# DIFFERENT app's deploy. Read-only.
URL=$1; MARKER=$2; TIMEOUT=${3:-600}; POLL=${4:-20}; PROF=${5:+--profile $5}; APPF=${6:+--app $6}; T0=$(date +%s)
# ALWAYS pass the profile on shared machines — the ambient active profile can flap mid-run (R#25/org rules)
[ -z "$URL" ] || [ -z "$MARKER" ] && { sed -n '2,6p' "$0"; exit 2; }
URL=${URL%/}   # tolerate a trailing slash so "$URL/?cb=" cannot become "//?cb="
while :; do
  # decide on the NEWEST terminal event only — stale FAILED rows lower in the feed must not poison the verdict.
  # NOTE: the SUCCESS names are verified live (DEPLOYMENT_HEALTHY); the FAILURE names are NOT — no failure was
  # induced when this was re-derived, and the audit --type enum omits every terminal type. Match a family, not
  # one guessed literal, and treat an unmatched terminal state as a timeout rather than a false PASS.
  LATEST=$(nexus vibe audit list ${=PROF} ${=APPF} 2>&1 \
           | grep -m1 -oE "DEPLOYMENT_HEALTHY|DEPLOYMENT_FAILED|DEPLOYMENT_BUILD_FAILED|BUILD_JOB_FAILED")
  case "$LATEST" in
    DEPLOYMENT_FAILED|DEPLOYMENT_BUILD_FAILED|BUILD_JOB_FAILED)
      echo "deploy FAILED (newest audit event: $LATEST)"; echo "DEPLOY_WATCH: FAILED_EVENT"; exit 2;;
    DEPLOYMENT_HEALTHY) break;;
  esac
  [ $(( $(date +%s) - T0 )) -ge "$TIMEOUT" ] && { echo "timeout waiting for terminal event"; echo "DEPLOY_WATCH: EVENT_TIMEOUT"; exit 3; }
  sleep "$POLL"
done
# The marker check reads the STATUS too: a PRIVATE app (the creation default) answers 401 to any plain
# HTTP client, so a marker grep alone returns 0 hits FOREVER on a perfectly healthy deploy. That is an
# ACCESS verdict, not a swap verdict, and no timeout can fix it (deploy-guide.md "Visibility gates the
# marker check").
BODY=$(mktemp); ACCESS_T0=""
# A 401/403 is only conclusive once it PERSISTS: a visibility flip takes ~11s to propagate at the
# edge (measured), so the first 401 after `visibility public` is transient. Wait out a grace window
# before declaring ACCESS_BLOCKED, and reset it the moment any other status appears.
ACCESS_GRACE=${ACCESS_GRACE:-45}
while :; do
  CODE=$(curl -s -o "$BODY" -w '%{http_code}' -m 20 "$URL/?cb=$(date +%s)" 2>&1)
  grep -q "$MARKER" "$BODY" && break
  case "$CODE" in
    401|403)
      [ -z "$ACCESS_T0" ] && ACCESS_T0=$(date +%s)
      if [ $(( $(date +%s) - ACCESS_T0 )) -ge "$ACCESS_GRACE" ]; then
        echo "HEALTHY but the app is not publicly reachable (HTTP $CODE for ${ACCESS_GRACE}s+) — this is an ACCESS state, not swap lag."
        echo "Verify the swap via: nexus vibe app list ${=PROF} --json | jq '.apps[]|select(.publicUrl==\"$URL\")|{servingDeployment,edgeReachability}'"
        echo "Then either make it public (nexus vibe app visibility <appId> public) or fetch with the app's edge token."
        echo "DEPLOY_WATCH: ACCESS_BLOCKED"; rm -f "$BODY"; exit 4
      fi;;
    *) ACCESS_T0="";;
  esac
  [ $(( $(date +%s) - T0 )) -ge "$TIMEOUT" ] && { echo "HEALTHY, HTTP $CODE, marker never served within ${TIMEOUT}s (swap lag or wrong content shipped)"; echo "DEPLOY_WATCH: MARKER_MISS"; rm -f "$BODY"; exit 3; }
  sleep "$POLL"
done
rm -f "$BODY"
echo "deploy verified: marker served (HTTP $CODE)"
# machine-parseable terminal token (W19: the posttool H4 check keys on these, never on prose)
echo "DEPLOY_WATCH: SERVED"

#!/usr/bin/env python3 """fastpack — the deterministic Tier-0 read layer for Nexus retrieval (W15). Zero model tokens: it turns "gather the grounding for task class X" into parallel file operations. Measured 2026-07-13: 15 files / ~116KB in 0.6s. The retrieval hot lane runs this, then a THIN verdict pass over the pack; the model spends tokens on verdicts, never on re-typing content (that is the whole speed win — wall time is model output tokens, not transport). Candidate paths come from (a) a named recipe in fastpack-recipes.md, (b) a keyword grep over the LIVE workspace INDEX's [[links]], (c) explicit --paths. Every signed URL is org-id verified against the first (wrong-org reads look plausible — scratch/ fork orgs hold stale copies); bodies are error-sniffed (a NoSuchKey/XML error body is NEVER packed as OK); a candidate that misses retries the folder form, then lands as MISSING and the process exits non-zero (a pack is never silently partial). Usage: fastpack.py --profile --workspace \ [--recipe ] [--keywords ] [--paths ] \ [--recipes-file ] [--index-cache ] --out Exit: 0 = every candidate packed OK; 1 = at least one MISSING/ERROR row (or a fatal org-id mismatch / no candidates). The manifest table always lists every candidate with its status, so a non-zero exit is diagnosable from the pack alone. CLI-only for resolution (`nexus api …`); stdlib-only otherwise (no third-party deps). """ import argparse import concurrent.futures as cf import json import os import re import subprocess import sys import time import urllib.error import urllib.request LINK_RE = re.compile(r"\[\[([a-z0-9/_.\-]+)\]\]", re.I) ORG_RE = re.compile(r"orgs/(org_[A-Za-z0-9]+)/") ERR_SNIFF = re.compile(rb"NoSuchKey|<\?xml||AccessDenied|SignatureDoesNotMatch") def _run(args, timeout=40): return subprocess.run(args, capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=timeout) def resolve_url(profile, workspace, path): """Ask the platform for a signed URL for one workspace file. Returns URL or ''.""" r = _run(["nexus", "api", "GET", "/workspaces/%s/file?path=%s" % (workspace, path), "--profile", profile, "--json"]) out = r.stdout or "" i = out.find("{") if i < 0: return "" try: d = json.loads(out[i:]) except Exception: return "" return (d.get("data", {}) or {}).get("url") or d.get("url") or "" def fetch(url): """Fetch a signed URL. Returns (body_bytes, err_str). err_str set on HTTP/transport error OR a content-level error body (a 200 wrapping NoSuchKey/XML is NOT success).""" try: body = urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=40).read() except urllib.error.HTTPError as e: return b"", "HTTP %s" % e.code except Exception as e: return b"", type(e).__name__ if ERR_SNIFF.search(body[:400]): return b"", "ERROR_BODY" return body, "" def candidates_for(path): """Path normalisation: a bare INDEX link is tried as

.md then

/README.md (the flat-file-vs-folder ambiguity is the known trap).""" if path.endswith((".md", ".html", ".txt", ".json")): return [path] return [path + ".md", path + "/README.md"] def acquire_one(profile, workspace, path, expect_org): """Resolve + fetch one logical path across ALL its candidate forms before failing (a 404/error-body on `

.md` falls through to `

/README.md` — the flat-vs-folder trap). Returns {path, resolved, body, status, org}; status ∈ OK | MISSING | ERROR:* | ORGMISMATCH. An ORG mismatch aborts immediately (a wrong-org read is never salvageable).""" last_err = None for cand in candidates_for(path): url = resolve_url(profile, workspace, cand) if not url: continue m = ORG_RE.search(url) org = m.group(1) if m else None if expect_org and org and org != expect_org: return {"path": cand, "resolved": url, "body": b"", "status": "ORGMISMATCH", "org": org} body, err = fetch(url) if err: last_err = err # try the next candidate form before giving up continue return {"path": cand, "resolved": url, "body": body, "status": "OK", "org": org} status = ("ERROR:" + last_err) if last_err else "MISSING" return {"path": path, "resolved": "", "body": b"", "status": status, "org": None} def load_recipe(recipes_file, name): """Recipe rows live as data in fastpack-recipes.md: a fenced block ```recipe \n\n\n``` — one path per line, '#' comments ignored.""" if not name or not recipes_file or not os.path.exists(recipes_file): return [] text = open(recipes_file, encoding="utf-8", errors="replace").read() m = re.search(r"```recipe\s+%s\s*\n(.*?)```" % re.escape(name), text, re.S) if not m: return [] rows = [] for ln in m.group(1).splitlines(): ln = ln.split("#", 1)[0].strip() if ln: rows.append(ln) return rows def index_links(profile, workspace, index_cache, keywords): """Grep the LIVE workspace INDEX for the keyword net. W18 recall fix: keywords match ROW TEXT (display names, outcomes), not only [[link]] path tokens — a matching LINE contributes its [[links]] AND its backticked path tokens (a display-name hit whose path token doesn't carry the keyword was the measured miss class). Fetch fresh unless --index-cache points at a fetched file.""" if not keywords: return [] text = "" if index_cache and os.path.exists(index_cache): text = open(index_cache, encoding="utf-8", errors="replace").read() else: url = resolve_url(profile, workspace, "INDEX.md") if url: body, err = fetch(url) if not err: text = body.decode("utf-8", errors="replace") if not text: return [] kw = re.compile(keywords, re.I) hits = {p for p in LINK_RE.findall(text) if kw.search(p)} for ln in text.splitlines(): if kw.search(ln): hits.update(LINK_RE.findall(ln)) hits.update(t.rstrip("/") for t in re.findall(r"`([\w][\w/.-]{2,80})`", ln) if "/" in t.rstrip("/")) return sorted(h.rstrip("/") for h in hits) def active_profile(): """W18: resolve the active CLI profile when --profile is omitted — the reflex must work at reflex speed. `nexus auth status` is the authority; unparseable → None (the caller errors with the pass---profile instruction).""" try: out = subprocess.run(["nexus", "auth", "status"], capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=15).stdout or "" except Exception: return None m = re.search(r"[Pp]rofile[^\w]{0,4}([\w-]+)", out) if m and m.group(1).lower() not in ("override",): return m.group(1) return None def main(): ap = argparse.ArgumentParser() ap.add_argument("--profile", default=None, help="CLI profile; omitted → the active profile (auth status)") ap.add_argument("--workspace", required=True) ap.add_argument("--recipe") ap.add_argument("--keywords") ap.add_argument("--paths", help="file with one path per line") ap.add_argument("--recipes-file", default=os.path.join(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)), "..", "..", "nexus-workspaces", "reference", "fastpack-recipes.md")) ap.add_argument("--index-cache") ap.add_argument("--out", required=True) ap.add_argument("--workers", type=int, default=12) a = ap.parse_args() if not a.profile: a.profile = active_profile() if not a.profile: print(json.dumps({"error": "no --profile and the active profile could not be " "resolved (auth status) — pass --profile "})) sys.exit(2) print("profile: %s (active)" % a.profile, file=sys.stderr) t0 = time.time() cand = list(load_recipe(a.recipes_file, a.recipe)) cand += index_links(a.profile, a.workspace, a.index_cache, a.keywords) if a.paths and os.path.exists(a.paths): cand += [ln.strip() for ln in open(a.paths) if ln.strip()] # de-dup preserving order seen, paths = set(), [] for p in cand: if p not in seen: seen.add(p) paths.append(p) if not paths: sys.stderr.write("fastpack: no candidate paths (recipe/keywords/paths all empty)\n") return 1 # First resolve one path to pin the expected org id, then the rest verify against it. first = acquire_one(a.profile, a.workspace, paths[0], None) expect_org = first.get("org") results = [first] if len(paths) > 1: with cf.ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=a.workers) as ex: results += list(ex.map( lambda p: acquire_one(a.profile, a.workspace, p, expect_org), paths[1:])) ok = [r for r in results if r["status"] == "OK"] bad = [r for r in results if r["status"] != "OK"] wall = time.time() - t0 lines = ["# FASTPACK — org=%s profile=%s workspace=%s" % (expect_org, a.profile, a.workspace), "", "| path | bytes | status |", "|---|---|---|"] for r in results: lines.append("| %s | %d | %s |" % (r["path"], len(r["body"]), r["status"])) lines.append("") lines.append("packed: %d ok, %d failed, wall %.1fs" % (len(ok), len(bad), wall)) for r in ok: lines.append("\n===== %s =====\n" % r["path"] + r["body"].decode("utf-8", errors="replace")) with open(a.out, "w", encoding="utf-8") as fh: fh.write("\n".join(lines)) sys.stderr.write("fastpack: %d ok, %d failed, wall %.1fs → %s\n" % (len(ok), len(bad), wall, a.out)) for r in bad: sys.stderr.write(" %s %s\n" % (r["status"], r["path"])) return 1 if bad else 0 if __name__ == "__main__": sys.exit(main())

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# mirror-sync.sh — the ONE canonical way to sync `.claude/` to the public mirror repo.
#
# Why this file exists: the sync was run three times as a hand-typed `rsync --delete`, and the
# third time the exclude list was retyped without `.git/` and deleted the destination's git
# directory. A list that lives in a file cannot be retyped wrong. Every guard below is a
# measured incident, not a precaution:
#
#   · `--check` is the DEFAULT. Deleting requires `--apply`, typed deliberately.
#   · The destination must be a git repo whose remote matches the expected mirror, so a
#     mistyped path cannot be mistaken for the mirror and emptied.
#   · The delete set is COUNTED AND PRINTED before anything is removed.
#   · `hooks/tests/` never ships (local-only test artifacts), and neither do observe markers,
#     local settings, worktrees, or caches.
#
# Layout note: in the source, doctrine lives under `.claude/`; in the mirror those same
# contents sit at the REPO ROOT. That mapping is the reason a naive directory sync gets it
# wrong, so it is encoded here once.
#
# Usage:
#   mirror-sync.sh --check                 # default: show what WOULD change (no writes)
#   mirror-sync.sh --apply                 # perform the sync
#   mirror-sync.sh --check --src <dir> --dst <dir>
set -euo pipefail

SRC_DEFAULT="/Users/assem/Documents/Doc-Assem/Claude Code/nexus/.claude"
DST_DEFAULT="/Users/assem/Documents/GitHub/claude-code-skills-nexus"
EXPECT_REMOTE="claude-code-skills-nexus"

MODE=check
SRC="$SRC_DEFAULT"
DST="$DST_DEFAULT"
while [ $# -gt 0 ]; do
  case "$1" in
    --check) MODE=check; shift ;;
    --apply) MODE=apply; shift ;;
    --src)   SRC="${2:?--src needs a path}"; shift 2 ;;
    --dst)   DST="${2:?--dst needs a path}"; shift 2 ;;
    -h|--help) sed -n '2,24p' "$0"; exit 0 ;;
    *) echo "unknown argument: $1 (see --help)" >&2; exit 2 ;;
  esac
done

# THE exclude list. Single source of truth — never inline these at a call site.
EXCLUDES=(
  ".git/"                 # the incident: a retyped list omitted this and removed the mirror's history
  ".github/"              # mirror-owned CI, not ours to overwrite
  ".gitignore"            # mirror-owned
  "hooks/tests/"          # local-only: tests never ship to the shared repo
  "skills/cue-retro/"     # local-only: the retro / improvement-cycle skill stays on the source machine
  "skills/cue-retro*"     # W48: the line above excludes the DIRECTORY. A `skills/cue-retro.zip`
                          # sitting beside it matched nothing and shipped the whole local-only
                          # skill to the mirror twice in one session. An exclude scoped to a
                          # directory does not cover an archive of that directory — the same
                          # narrower-than-the-class mistake the `*bak` note below records.
  "skills/hook-development/"  # local-only: the hook-improvement skill stays on the source machine
  "hooks/.*-observe"      # rollout markers are per-machine state
  "__pycache__/"
  ".DS_Store"
  "settings.local.json"
  "worktrees/"
  "*.pyc"
  # W28 — `settings.json` itself DOES ship, deliberately: it carries zero machine paths and 17
  # `$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR` references, so a clone gets identical hook behaviour wherever the
  # person puts their `.claude`. Verified by driving the firewall from a relocated copy, not by
  # counting paths. What must NOT ship is everything below — leftovers, not wiring:
  "*bak"                  # stale copies. Measured on the mirror: two old `settings.json`
                          # backups AND a `nexus-pretool.py.w20bak` — a clone got three files it
                          # could not tell from the live ones. Deliberately `*bak`, not
                          # `settings.json.*bak`: the first version of this line was scoped to
                          # settings and missed the HOOK backup sitting beside it, which is the
                          # narrower-than-the-class mistake this log keeps recording.
  "*.lock"                # live runtime state, plus the OS's " 2" duplicates of it
  "hooks/HANDOFF-*.md"    # a session handoff is process narrative for THIS machine — it cites
                          # transcript paths under the owner's home and names in-flight audit
                          # lanes. The shared repo carries what a USING agent needs, never how
                          # one cycle happened to be run.
)

[ -d "$SRC" ] || { echo "source is not a directory: $SRC" >&2; exit 1; }
[ -d "$DST" ] || { echo "destination is not a directory: $DST" >&2; exit 1; }

# GUARD: the destination must be the mirror, proven by its remote — not by its path looking right.
if ! git -C "$DST" rev-parse --git-dir >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "REFUSED: destination is not a git repository: $DST" >&2
  exit 1
fi
REMOTE="$(git -C "$DST" remote get-url origin 2>&1 || echo none)"
case "$REMOTE" in
  *"$EXPECT_REMOTE"*) : ;;
  *) echo "REFUSED: destination remote does not look like the mirror." >&2
     echo "  expected to contain: $EXPECT_REMOTE" >&2
     echo "  found:               $(printf '%s' "$REMOTE" | sed -E 's#https://[^@]*@#https://***@#g')" >&2
     exit 1 ;;
esac

RSYNC_ARGS=(-a --delete)
for e in "${EXCLUDES[@]}"; do RSYNC_ARGS+=(--exclude "$e"); done

echo "source:      $SRC/"
echo "destination: $DST/   (remote OK)"
echo "excludes:    ${EXCLUDES[*]}"
echo

# Always dry-run FIRST and show the delete set with its count, whatever the mode.
DRY="$(rsync "${RSYNC_ARGS[@]}" --dry-run --itemize-changes "$SRC/" "$DST/")"
DELETES="$(printf '%s\n' "$DRY" | grep '^\*deleting' || true)"
NDEL="$(printf '%s' "$DELETES" | grep -c . || true)"
# `printf '%s\n' ""` emits ONE EMPTY LINE, which `grep -vc` counts as 1 — so this reported
# "would change: 1" on a perfectly synced tree and could never say 0. Caught at a cycle
# close-out, which is precisely when the number is load-bearing: the check exists to prove
# the two surfaces are identical, and it was structurally incapable of saying so. Same class
# as a hook that never logs a clean verdict — correct and quiet is indistinguishable from
# broken. `grep -c .` requires a non-empty line before it counts one.
NCHG="$(printf '%s\n' "$DRY" | grep -v '^\*deleting' | grep -c . || true)"

echo "would change: $NCHG path(s)"
echo "would DELETE: $NDEL path(s)"
if [ "$NDEL" -gt 0 ]; then printf '%s\n' "$DELETES" | sed 's/^/  /'; fi

if [ "$MODE" = check ]; then
  echo
  echo "check mode (default) — nothing was written. Re-run with --apply to perform it."
  exit 0
fi

echo
echo "applying…"
rsync "${RSYNC_ARGS[@]}" "$SRC/" "$DST/"

# Post-condition: the destination is STILL a git repo. If this ever fails, the exclude list
# regressed and the incident repeated.
if ! git -C "$DST" rev-parse --git-dir >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "FATAL: destination lost its .git after sync — the exclude list regressed." >&2
  exit 1
fi
echo "done. destination git intact; review with: git -C \"$DST\" status --short"

# Hook change log

Every change to a check, with the issue that triggered it, the reason this fix and not
another, the test that pins it, and — the field that matters most — **the class sweep**.

**Why the class-sweep field exists.** Twice in one cycle a fix was applied to the instance
that was reported and not to its siblings: `PROT-ROOT` was scoped precisely while `WSW` kept
scanning the whole command, and `vite`/`serve` were anchored while `npm run dev`, `next dev`
and `http.server` were left on the old anchor. Both were found later by an adversarial audit,
not by the person who made the fix. A change that does not name its siblings is whack-a-mole
with extra steps.

**How to use this file.** Before changing a check, read its previous entries: a check that
has been "fixed" repeatedly is telling you the defect is one level up. Before closing a
change, fill in the class sweep honestly — "none, this is genuinely a one-off" is a valid
answer, but it must be a considered one.

Entry format:

    ### <id> — <one-line change>
    **Issue** — what was observed, with a reproduction.
    **Evidence** — the measurement, first-hand.
    **Change** — what was altered, exactly.
    **Why this fix** — why this and not the alternatives.
    **Class sweep** — the siblings checked, and what was found. NEVER "n/a" without a reason.
    **Pinned by** — the test that fails if this regresses.

---

# W28 · 2026-07-28/29

## Wave 0 — store and schema

### session_cache — store roots resolve per call
**Issue** — the test suite wrote permanent directories into the real state store: 401 project
directories, 391 of them litter, 108 created in a single day.
**Evidence** — counted directly: 242 `flag_kbcheck_microsoft-outlook`, 125 `flag_kbcheck_x`,
14 uuid-named, 12 empty. Exactly one directory held real state.
**Change** — `_ROOT`/`_PROOT` module constants became `_root()`/`_proot()`, resolved per call;
`_dir`/`_pdir` gained `create=True`; all seven read paths pass `create=False`;
`tests/test_grounding_checks.py` sandboxes `HOME`.
**Why this fix** — resolving at import made `HOME` redirection impossible for in-process tests,
and `makedirs` on a pure read meant looking at state manufactured it. Both are root causes,
not symptoms.
**Class sweep** — checked BOTH stores (session and project) and all read/write paths, not only
the project one that leaked. Found the same `makedirs`-on-read in `_dir` and fixed it too.
**Pinned by** — `test_w28_store_isolation.py` (12 checks; staged red proved the read arms
passed falsely before the roots were fixed).

### log_decision — a timestamp column
**Issue** — the log exists "so warns can later be promoted to denies on data" and had no time
axis, so a check noisy since day one could not be told from one that started misfiring last week.
**Change** — column 4 is the decision epoch, appended (never prepended: readers index 0/1/2).
**Why this fix** — one column at write time; any external reconstruction is a proxy that
degrades exactly where it matters.
**Class sweep** — the project store has NO decision telemetry at all; recorded as a known gap
rather than silently extended.
**Pinned by** — `test_w28_decision_schema.py`.

### flip_marker — marker rows leave the decision log
**Issue** — 7 of 8,380 rows carried a 4th free-text column, violating the 3-column contract
documented 20 lines away in `nexus-conformance.py`. Two were written by the session that found it.
**Change** — flips write to their own `markers` feed.
**Why this fix** — the alternative (pad markers to the contract) keeps two shapes in one file
and would collide with the new timestamp column.
**Class sweep** — scanned every writer of `decisions`; `flip_marker` was the only one off-contract.
**Pinned by** — `test_w28_decision_schema.py`, plus `test_w27_small_arms.py` updated to assert
the new location AND that nothing marker-shaped leaks back.

### pclear — the missing removal path
**Issue** — `consolidation_hold` could be set in code and never unset in code: 1,094
suppressions, zero emissions, nine days, origin unknown.
**Change** — `pclear(project, key)`, idempotent (clearing an absent flag returns True).
**Class sweep** — audited the whole flag family for other set-without-clear pairs.
**Pinned by** — `test_w28_decision_schema.py`.

## Wave 1 — scope and coverage

### R34-HOLD — a durable hold expires
**Issue** — an instruction-class hold bound every later conversation, with no record of who set
it. Same class W21 retired for `app_build` ("one sprint's flag bled … into every later session").
**Change** — a project-scoped hold is honoured while fresh and cleared once older than
`HOLD_MAX_AGE_S` (24h), with an `R34-HOLD` row recording the expiry.
**Why this fix** — clearing rather than ignoring keeps the disk state matching the behaviour;
the mismatch is what made the original untraceable. 24h sits an order of magnitude below the
measured nine-day failure while surviving an overnight sprint. **This parameter is mine, not
the owner's** — flagged for override.
**Class sweep** — this binds FLAGS, never GATES: `.rm1`/`.rm1b` interlocks untouched, asserted
in the suite. Other durable flags audited for the same unbounded lifetime.
**Pinned by** — `test_w28_hold_scope.py` (17 checks, control arm included).

### STOP-WAKE — a second arm, keyed on work
**Issue** — the check gated on the board holding a PENDING row, so an empty board or one holding
only in-progress rows could not wake the turn however much work was open. Measured: a 3h06m dead
stop with work open, inside a 4h07m uncoverable window.
**Change** — arm 2 fires when the board names nothing and tool calls have happened since the
last board write.
**Why this fix** — `board_state` already returned `in_progress` and nothing read it. The once-key
is a bucket of the WORK counter, never a task-op epoch: keying on compliance is precisely how
TASK1 went permanently silent when tracking stopped.
**Class sweep** — audited every once-key in the lifecycle adapter for the same
compliance-keyed pattern.
**Pinned by** — `test_w28_wake.py` (23 checks).

### exit (c) — a claim that can be observed
**Issue** — the third exit was prose the predicate could not see, so complying re-fired the
identical block. Measured: 3 immediate re-fires at 4.0s, 6.1s, 29.5s.
**Change** — `lane-owes:<task id>` writes a feed row, scoped to that task, expiring after 90 min.
**Why this fix** — a claim in prose is wording; hooks key on state. Scoping to a task id stops
the exit becoming a global mute.
**Pinned by** — `test_w28_wake.py`.

### H2-TURN — a push nothing verified
**Issue** — a session that pushes ONCE and ends was never warned. H2 only fires on a SECOND push.
**Evidence** — probed live before changing anything: push 1 silent (correctly — no previous
deploy exists to have verified), push 2 without verification fires, push-once-and-stop silent forever.
**Change** — a new Stop-event check with its own id.
**Why this fix** — the approved plan proposed dropping H2's first-push guard. Measured, that
would emit "re-pushing without having driven the PREVIOUS deploy" on a first push: a false
positive carrying false wording. The hole was elsewhere and needed a different check.
**Class sweep** — `H2` and `H2-TURN` are separate ids by design; a shared prefix already caused
one mis-attribution of 10 rows.
**Pinned by** — `test_w28_push_unverified.py` (11 checks).

### A6 — every tagged emission records
**Issue** — 58 emit sites against 24 log calls. The firewall's shared `emit()` recorded nothing,
so all 11 of its denies were invisible — which is why two false-positive DENY classes ran
undetected until a blind agent tripped over one.
**Change** — `emit()` takes a check id from the CALL SITE (never derived from message text) and
logs it; the 7 tagged posttool/awareness checks log too.
**Class sweep** — classified EVERY emission by whether it carries a check id. Corrected the
plan's framing: `nexus-lifecycle._emit` is a CONTEXT injector, not a verdict path, so the real
surface was 8 sites and not 60.
**Pinned by** — `test_w28_emission_observable.py` (structural: binds future checks too) and
`test_w28_firewall_observable.py`.

## Wave 2 — the adversarial audit (E01, E04, E05)

### PROT-ROOT — target scoping, then the regression it caused
**Issue (original)** — the guard scanned every path token in the whole command, so
`ls /tmp && rm -rf /tmp/scratch` was denied because of the `ls`. Reproduced three times,
once by a blind agent doing ordinary work.
**Issue (the regression I then shipped)** — the precise parser recognised FEWER shapes than the
broad set it replaced, and a miss did not fall through to a prompt: it reached the scope check
and emitted **`allow`**. Verified: `rm -rf /tmp` denies; `set -e\nrm -rf /tmp` was **allowed**.
15 shapes, 11 of them regressions.
**Change** — `rm_targets` returns **None**, not an empty list, for any shape it cannot resolve;
the caller then uses the broad set. Newline added to both the boundary and the terminator;
prefix words (`command env nohup time exec eval builtin sudo xargs`) absorbed; heredoc-stripped
input; `comments=True`; globs resolved to the directory they empty; `//` normalised.
**Why this fix** — returning None is the load-bearing property: every recognition gap,
**including ones nobody has thought of yet**, degrades to noisy-but-safe instead of to
auto-approval. A wider regex would only move the boundary.
**Class sweep** — E01 found the SAME whole-command-scan defect still live in `WSW` (10 false
positives) and in `RM1`/`RM1B` (three signals matched anywhere in the string). **OPEN — see
below.** This is the sweep I failed to do the first time.
**Pinned by** — `test_w28_guard_scope.py` (63 checks; every one of E04's 21 misses and 4 false
positives is an assertion).

### is_recursive_force_rm — flags are read, not pattern-matched
**Issue** — `RM_RF_RE` matched a lowercase `r` and two flag orders. `rm -Rf /tmp` and
`rm -f -r /tmp` were **allowed**.
**Change** — a function that reads the flags of a real `rm` invocation: `-rf` `-fr` `-Rf` `-fR`
`-r -f` in any order, `--recursive --force`, any mixture.
**Why this fix** — a regex over flag ARRANGEMENT cannot be exhaustive; reading the flags is.
**Class sweep** — all three call sites converted (PROT-ROOT, RM1, RM1B).
**Pinned by** — `test_w28_guard_scope.py`.

### the empty-candidate fall-through — allow became defer
**Issue** — when no path token parsed out, the scope loop never ran and the hook emitted
`allow`, actively suppressing the native prompt. Verified: `bash -c "rm -rf /"`,
`rm -rf "$(pwd)"`, `T=/; rm -rf "$T"`, a heredoc'd `csrutil disable` — all auto-approved.
**Change** — an empty candidate set exits without a verdict.
**Why this fix** — an empty set means "I cannot tell what this touches". That must never become
permission. One line, and it converts every row in that class from auto-approved to prompted.
**Pinned by** — `test_w28_guard_scope.py`.

### MUT_RE — `sed` was documented as covered and was absent
**Issue** — the WSW docstring names `sed -i` as covered; `sed` was in neither mutation regex, so
`sed -i` on a mount — the exact FUSE failure mode R#39 names — passed through.
**Class sweep** — E01 also names `tar`, `unzip` and `git clone` writing INTO a mount as
uncovered. **NOT added**: they would widen a scan that is itself the biggest false-positive
source. Sequencing recorded below rather than making the FP problem worse.
**Pinned by** — `test_w28_guard_scope.py`.

### G19 — every arm anchored, not the two that were reported
**Issue** — W28 anchored `vite` and `serve` to a real command position and left the siblings on
the old anchor; `http.server` had none at all. Verified: `grep -rn http.server .`,
`cat notes/http.server.md`, and `pkill -f npm run dev` — the remediation the gate's own message
implies — all DENIED.
**Change** — all five arms behind `CMDPOS`; `CMDPOS` widened with newline, `bunx`, and
`nohup|sudo|command|env|timeout` prefixes.
**Why this fix** — `B` reads like a command boundary and is a TOKEN boundary; it matches any
space-preceded word. Renaming it was not enough — the arms had to move.
**Class sweep** — this IS the sweep that was missed the first time. Every arm of the gate
checked, both directions.
**Pinned by** — `test_w28_ladder_scope.py` (41 checks).

### the `-h` blanket bypass
**Issue** — `-h` matched anywhere exempted EVERY deny gate. Verified:
`nexus workflow publish abc && df -h` → ALLOW, `ls -h && vite` → ALLOW.
**Change** — `--help` exempts anywhere; `-h` only when the whole command is a single
`nexus … -h` invocation.
**Why this fix** — `df -h`, `du -h`, `ls -h`, `sort -h` are ordinary. This was `--help` intent
leaking onto the short form, not a designed override.
**Pinned by** — `test_w28_ladder_scope.py`.

### wrapper-shell payloads are execution
**Issue** — `sh -c 'npm run dev'` and `bash -c 'nexus workflow publish abc'` were ALLOWED: the
quote stripper removed the payload.
**Change** — wrapper payloads are extracted before stripping and re-appended at a command position.
**Why this fix** — the stripper exists so a MENTION cannot fire. `sh -c '...'` is an EXECUTION.
The distinction is the fix; removing the stripper would reintroduce every mention false positive.
**Pinned by** — `test_w28_ladder_scope.py`.

### the quote stripper is escape-aware
**Issue** — found by the guard denying MY OWN ordinary commands, repeatedly, during this cycle:
`python3 -c "... \" ..."` and `git commit -m "don't run \"csrutil disable\""` leaked their
contents into the keyword view, because `'[^']*'|"[^"]*"` is not shell-aware.
**Change** — a scanner that tracks quote state and honours backslash escapes inside double
quotes.
**Why this fix** — a regex cannot express "escaped quote does not close the span". The user does
not perceive a quoting bug; they perceive a guard firing while they write a commit message,
which is how a guard earns being ignored.
**Class sweep** — the firewall has its OWN `unquote` with the same regex. **OPEN — see below.**
**Pinned by** — `test_w28_ladder_scope.py`.

### `NEXUS_GATE_ACK=1` read from the stripped command
**Issue** — matched against the raw command, so writing documentation ABOUT the override
disabled the gate.
**Pinned by** — `test_w28_ladder_scope.py`.

### `_met` — a shadowed import killed a gate's precision
**Issue** — a function-local `import os` in the `file` branch made `os` local to the whole
function, so the earlier `shape` branch raised `UnboundLocalError` into its own bare `except`.
G8's per-vendor scoping was dead: a shape-read for one vendor satisfied an execute against another.
**Change** — one line deleted; the module already imports `os` at the top.
**Follow-on the suite caught** — with per-vendor matching restored, G8 became UNSATISFIABLE by
its own remedy: `nexus tool get <uuid>` carries no vendor, so the feed records `*`. `*` now
satisfies any vendor. A gate whose own remedy does not clear it is worse than one too broad.
**Class sweep** — grepped every adapter for function-local imports shadowing module-level ones.
**Pinned by** — `test_w28_ladder_scope.py`, `test_w24_g8.py`.

## Wave 3 — closing the class, not the instance (O4)

### strip_quoted_spans — ONE canonical stripper, used by both adapters
**Issue** — the ladder's stripper was fixed in Wave 2; the firewall carried the SAME
non-escape-aware regex as a lambda (`nexus-fs-firewall.py:282`). Leaving it is the exact
whack-a-mole pattern this file exists to stop, so it was closed immediately rather than
queued.
**Change** — the canonical escape-aware scanner now lives in `hook_core.strip_quoted_spans`.
The firewall imports it; the ladder delegates to it with a lazy import (preserving its stated
no-side-effects-on-import property) and falls back to the UNSTRIPPED string, which can only
make a gate more likely to fire, never less.
**Why one implementation** — it had already diverged once. A shared helper is only shared
until someone re-inlines it, so the test exercises BOTH consumers, not just the library.
**Three properties, each learned from a failure while building it:**
1. `\"` inside double quotes does not close the span.
2. `'\''` is **four** characters — close, backslash, literal quote, RE-OPEN. The first draft
   skipped three, landed on the re-opening quote, and leaked the remainder. Caught by the
   firewall probe, not by reasoning.
3. An UNTERMINATED quote emits its remainder **verbatim**. The first draft stripped to
   end-of-string, which hid whatever followed and made the guard MORE permissive on malformed
   input — it turned the "unparseable command still denies" assertion red. A guard must fail
   closed; that assertion is why the regression lasted one run.
**Class sweep** — grepped every adapter for further quote-stripping regexes: none remain.
**Pinned by** — `test_w28_quote_stripper.py` (22 checks: the scanner, plus both consumers in
both directions).

## Wave 4 — the cold source review (E08)

### SEC1 — the credential-leak check was unreachable where it mattered most
**Issue** — `resp` is narrowed to a string near the top of `main()`, but ONLY when the response
dict carries `stdout`; and a later branch re-bound `resp` to the raw dict for its own use.
SEC1's guard is `isinstance(resp, str)`, so it silently stopped running (a) for any response
dict without `stdout` — a credential in `output` or `stderr` was never scanned — and (b) for
every command matching the general-context branch, which are **workspace reads: the commands
most likely to carry an API key inside a URL**.
**Evidence** — 3 of 13 fixture cases red before the fix, including "a general-context read,
dict response".
**Change** — a shape-independent `_resp_text(resp)` gathers every text-bearing field
(`stdout stderr output error result text`); SEC1 guards and searches on that; the
general-context branch uses a LOCAL name instead of clobbering `resp`.
**Why this fix** — narrowing a shared variable for one consumer's convenience is the root
cause; removing the dependency on the narrowed form removes the whole class rather than the
two known instances.
**Class sweep** — E08's own AST pass across all 11 modules confirms the `_met` `os` shadow was
the ONLY remaining shadowed-global instance, and a `symtable` pass found no other names
referenced but never bound. Independently checked for other consumers of the narrowed `resp`:
`_extract_json` legitimately wants the stdout form and is unchanged.
**Severity note** — this is the third check this cycle that read as SATISFIED while being
unreachable (the two swallowed `NameError`s were the others). A check that is documented,
present, and dead is worse than one that is absent, because nobody goes looking for it.
**Pinned by** — `test_w28_sec1.py` (13 checks: four response shapes, the general-context
branch in both shapes, three credential patterns, four no-false-positive controls including
a bare git SHA).

## Wave 5 — the corruption audit (E09, 490 cases)

### dsub() — a nested container is a dict only if it IS one
**Issue** — **LIVE, HIGH-FREQUENCY, SILENT.** `nexus <resource> list --json` crashed the
PostToolUse adapter: `'list' object has no attribute 'get'`. Nine sites wrote
`(x.get("data") or {}).get(...)`, checking the OUTER object and assuming the NESTED one was a
dict too. Every `*-list` returns the flat-list envelope `{data: [...], meta: {...}}`.
**Evidence** — reproduced against the live adapter, exit 1, on `agent/workflow/task/collection/
deployment/model list --json`. R#16's platform-first table is almost entirely `list` calls.
**Blast radius** — a PostToolUse crash is non-blocking, so the command survives and EVERY hint
that adapter exists to inject is lost **invisibly**: the `result.os[]` error surfacing, the
dashboard link, the silent-acceptance reminders. The layer was committing the exact error
CLAUDE.md's own envelope section warns about ("a first-parse crash … = the probe was skipped").
**Change** — `hook_core.dsub(obj, key)` returns the nested value only when it is a dict; all
nine sites rewritten, including two inline `json.loads(...)` variants.
**Class sweep** — grepped the whole tree for the pattern; zero residual sites.
**Pinned by** — `test_w28_resilience.py`.

### fail-open is a SHAPE invariant, not a parse guard
**Issue** — eight of nine adapters crashed on a VALID-JSON non-object (`[1,2,3]`, `"x"`, `42`,
`true`, `null`): `json.load` succeeds, then `.get` raises OUTSIDE the try. And a non-string
`command` (a dict from a misbehaving MCP server, or a harness payload change) took down the
**fs-firewall** — the destructive-command guard — on the first regex.
**Why it matters even though it is latent** — a crashed adapter is a guard BYPASS. The firewall
not running for a call is indistinguishable from the firewall approving it.
**Change** — `if not isinstance(data, dict): sys.exit(0)` in all nine adapters; a non-string
`command` is coerced to empty so the native permission layer decides.
**Pinned by** — `test_w28_resilience.py` (every adapter x five payload shapes).

### _mounts() — the read was guarded, the shape was not
**Issue** — `workspace-mounts.json` parsing to a LIST, or to a dict with string values,
crashed the awareness adapter on **every Read, every Skill load and every prompt**. It was the
only crash in 84 state-corruption cases, and that file is written by external mount tooling —
the state most likely to drift across versions.
**Change** — shape-filtered in both `nexus-awareness._mounts` and `fs-firewall._mount_roots`.
**Class sweep** — both readers of that file fixed together, not just the crashing one.
**Pinned by** — `test_w28_resilience.py` (four malformed shapes).

### What the audit CONFIRMED as sound — do not regress it
490 cases produced **no spurious block**. `rm -rf /` was denied 11/11 with `HOME` unset,
read-only, nonexistent or empty; with an unwritable store; with `CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR` missing;
with `PATH` unset and a broken locale. The destructive guard depends on none of its state,
which is the correct design and is now measured. 83 of 84 state-corruption cases and 58 of 60
transcript-corruption cases exit clean; `session_cache._safe()` neutralises path traversal in
`session_id`.

### read_tail_lines — a tail that is actually a tail
**Issue** — seven sites did `open(path).readlines()[-N:]`. The `N` reads like a bound and is
not: the whole file loads before the slice. Measured on this machine's REAL transcripts, paid
at EVERY turn end — 590 MB → 4.36 s and 731 MB RSS; 204 MB → 2.68 s. Five transcripts on this
box exceed 150 MB, and the cost grows with session length, so it is worst exactly when a
session matters most. `/dev/zero` never returned at all.
**Change** — `hook_core.read_tail_lines(path, n, window)` seeks to the end and reads a BOUNDED
window; all seven sites converted (six in `hook_core`, one ledger tail in `nexus-lifecycle`).
**Why byte-bounded and not merely seek-based** — an endless character device reports size 0, so
a size-guarded seek still reads forever. Capping the READ makes cost O(window) for every input,
including ones that never end.
**Measured after, same 590 MB transcript:** Stop hook **4.36 s → 0.15 s**, peak RSS
**731 MB → 128 MB**. On a synthetic 111 MB file the tail is 19x faster than the slurp and
returns byte-identical lines.
**Class sweep** — the residual check is an AST pass for `readlines()[...]` subscripts, not a
text grep: a text scan matched this fix's own docstring, and would equally miss a call split
across lines — the same failure mode that made a grep report the firewall clean while
multi-line calls were still unguarded.
**Pinned by** — `test_w28_tail_read.py` (14 checks: correctness vs the slurp, no-trailing-
newline, invalid UTF-8, missing file, directory, empty file, the O(window) bound, `/dev/zero`,
and the AST residual scan).

## Wave 6 — the "flaky test" was a live gate denying its own remedy (E03)

### BLD2 — the roster anchor advances only on a COMPLETE push
**Issue** — logged for a release as "a flaky test" (`test_w22_hooks`, 4% idle / 43% under
load). It was not. `sc.log(sid, "bld2-push", …)` ran UNCONDITIONALLY, before the verdict, so a
push WARNED for "no judging seat" still moved the roster window past the executor that built
the wave. Firing a judging seat and re-pushing — **exactly what the warning instructs** — then
landed on the wrong side of the gate. **The gate punished obedience to its own instruction.**
**Evidence** — a predictor of `int(t_executor_dispatch) < int(t_push1)` matched pass/fail with
**zero mismatches across 160 instrumented runs**. The failure rate is a pure function of
machine load, because the race window is the milliseconds between two hook processes calling
`time.time()`. Above one second the failure is CERTAIN: 6/6 at a 2 s gap — an ordinary
interval in a real build.
**Why it read as flaky rather than broken** — the fixture's four subprocess hook calls usually
landed inside one wall-clock second, so the tie `E_x == P_1` passed. The suite was measuring
sub-second luck, and that is how a deterministic defect on a `git push` gate survived a release.
**Change** — one line moved INSIDE the passing branch. "Since the last push" was always meant
to ask: has the roster been complete since it last WAS complete? Only a passing push answers that.
**Why not the other candidate fix** — E03 also offered sub-second epochs (`%.3f` in the
dispatch feed) and flagged, correctly, that it is NOT self-contained: two readers parse with
`int(e)` inside a `try/except ValueError` that degrades to 0, so every row would read as epoch
0 and ROSTER1 would silently never fire again. Shipped the primary alone.
**Fixture lesson, recorded because it cost three red runs** — isolating a gate means satisfying
every gate that PRECEDES it. My first fixtures denied on `ACCESS1` and on a missing BUILD-MODE
card, so I was testing the wrong check twice; and a `Task` payload without the worktree in its
prompt does not populate `app-executor-repos`, so the gate reasons about a repo it was never
told the lane owned. The timing is now EXPLICIT (1.2 s sleeps) rather than lucky.
**Class sweep** — `bld2-push` has exactly one writer and one reader, both in `nexus-pretool`;
`nexus-lifecycle` uses the last judging dispatch as its own anchor and is unaffected. Checked
every other feed written before its verdict: none.
**Pinned by** — `test_w28_bld2_window.py` (8 checks) + `test_w22_hooks` now 8/8 consecutive clean.

## Wave 7 — the battery had a recency blind spot, measured by mutation (E17)

### The measurement that drove this wave
**Issue** — a mutation audit introduced 39 realistic single-line defects and re-ran the whole
battery. **16 survived: 41%.** The pattern was not risk, it was RECENCY. Everything authored in
the current cycle — wake arms, guard scoping, push verification, board reconciliation — was
caught, often by several suites at once. Everything older survived: the ladder DENY matrix,
the firewall's deny family, and `C1`, the FIRST row of the blocking tier, which had **no test
at all** — the literal `2>/dev/null` appeared in ZERO test files, so the check could have been
deleted in silence. Three of the five ladder DENY gates could be removed from the gate matrix
with the battery fully green.
**Why it happened** — the battery grows a strong shell around each cycle's new work and never
goes back. That is the exact failure mode of building "non-destructively": additions are safe,
so nothing forces a second look at what was already there.
**A second-order finding, recorded because it changes how the number is read** — four mutations
*appeared* caught and were not. Their only red suite was the one carrying the BLD2 assertion
that flaked 4 in 10 (wave 6). **A flaky assertion inside a scored suite does not merely add
noise — it MANUFACTURES coverage that does not exist.** The 41% is trustworthy only because
that flake was fixed first.

### C1 — one literal spelling became the whole stderr-suppression family
**Issue** — `_c1_devnull` tested `"2>/dev/null" in s`. Every other spelling of the same act
walked past the first row of the blocking tier.
**Evidence** — measured on the live predicate before the change: of nine shapes, **four were
missed** — `2> /dev/null` (one space), `&>/dev/null`, `2>>/dev/null`, `>/dev/null 2>&1`.
A gate with a whitespace-sized bypass is not a gate.
**Change** — split by CERTAINTY, per the standing deny-only-when-100%-sure rule.
`C1` DENIES where stderr goes to null AS THE ACT: `2>`, `2>>`, `&>`, `&>>`, `2>&-`.
A new `C1B` WARNS on `>/dev/null 2>&1`, whose primary act is discarding STDOUT and which is
the standard capability-probe idiom (`command -v x >/dev/null 2>&1`) where the exit code is
the only signal wanted. Blocking that would be a false positive by construction.
**Why not deny the whole family** — because the certainty differs, and the rule that governs
this layer keys on certainty, not on effect. Denying the probe idiom would make the gate a
thing to route around, which is how a guard stops being believed.
**Order is semantic and the patterns respect it** — `2>&1 >/dev/null` leaves stderr on the
ORIGINAL stdout and suppresses nothing; firing on it would be a false positive. Verified silent.
`(?<!\d)` keeps tokens that merely END in 2 (`-p port22>/dev/null`) out of the fd-2 arm.
**Class sweep** — every other check matching a redirection or an operator by bare substring:
`DISK_RE`'s `mkfs` was the one sibling with the same defect and is fixed in this same wave
(below). `RM_RF_RE`, `MUT_RE` and the ladder's `CMDPOS` family were checked and already
anchored. The deny MESSAGE was also updated: it named one spelling, so a `&>/dev/null` denial
would have quoted a form the operator did not write.
**Pinned by** — `test_w28_mutation_survivors.py`, 14 C1 checks including every silent case.

### DISKWRITE — `mkfs` denied READING about `mkfs` (closes O2)
**Issue** — `\bmkfs\b` was a bare keyword, so `man mkfs`, `which mkfs`, `ls /usr/sbin | grep
mkfs`, `cat notes-about-mkfs.md` and — worst — `grep -n mkfs scripts/format.sh`, which is
someone AUDITING a script for the dangerous call, all denied. No override exists on this tier.
**Evidence** — eight false positives and eight true positives driven through the live regex
before and after. Old: 8/8 true, 8/8 false ALSO denied. New: 8/8 true kept, 0/8 false.
**Change** — anchored to COMMAND POSITION with the wrapper prefix (`sudo`, `env`, `xargs`, an
absolute path, `&&` chains). In every false positive `mkfs` is an ARGUMENT; in every true
positive it is the command.
**Why not require a `/dev/` argument** — that was the obvious alternative and it fails OPEN on
`mkfs.ext4 $DEV`, where the target is a variable. Command position needs no target resolution,
so the guard does not depend on the one thing it cannot know statically.
**Class sweep** — this is the third instance of one class this cycle (`PROT-ROOT` scanning
every path, `G19`'s bare `vite`, now `mkfs`): **a trigger that names a SUBSTRING rather than
the ACT.** Swept the remaining bare-keyword triggers in the firewall: `FORKBOMB` and `SIP` are
both pattern-anchored already. O1 (`WSW`) and O3 (`RM1`) are the same class and stay OPEN —
each needs its own test-first cycle, not a fourth same-day patch.
**Pinned by** — `test_w28_mutation_survivors.py`, 13 DISKWRITE checks.

### The suite itself was mutation-tested, and two of its own assertions were hollow
**Why this is in the change log** — writing a suite to close a coverage measurement and then
NOT measuring the new suite is how the original gap formed. Every check here was driven
against the real defect it claims to catch.
**First run — two survivors inside my own new suite.** `PROT-ROOT drops trailing-slash
normalisation` and `PROT-ROOT stops reading the rm target` both stayed GREEN under mutation:
every fixture happened to be written without a trailing slash, and nothing asserted the
false-positive case the W28 scoping fix exists to prevent. Both are now covered
(`rm -rf /tmp/`, `rm -rf //`, and `ls /tmp && rm -rf <proj>/src/build` staying silent).
**A harness bug worth recording** — the first mutation run reported `mkfs` as surviving. It had
not been tested: the patch replaced the FIRST occurrence of the string, which is in the module
DOCSTRING, and never touched the regex. Same self-matching class as the residual grep that
reported clean while multi-line calls were unguarded. Mutations now target the last occurrence.
**The fail-CLOSED invariant is asserted directly.** `rm_targets` returning `None` versus `[]`
reads alike and behaves OPPOSITELY — `None` routes to the broad candidate set, `[]` routes to
an empty loop and therefore to `allow`. That exact confusion made 11 of 15 destructive commands
stop being denied earlier in this cycle. The adapter tests cover the verdicts; seven new checks
cover the DISTINCTION, because the distinction is what regressed.
**Final state** — 21 mutations applied against the real code (both C1 arms and each of its
sub-arms, all four PROT-ROOT properties, all three `rm_targets` fail-closed returns, all three
DISKWRITE alternations plus the bare-keyword revert, four gate deletions, the G3 prereq, and
the `--help` carve-out widened past DENY): **21 caught, 0 survivors.** Battery 62/62 green.

## Wave 8 — the 20-lane explorer fleet, iteration 1 consumed (E02, E06, E07, E12, E13)

Twenty lanes each drove the LIVE hooks under a throwaway HOME and wrote a report. Every report
below was read first-hand by the main loop and its load-bearing measurements re-derived; no
lane's summary of its own work was taken on trust. `[LIVE]` marks a measurement taken on real
transcripts or the real store rather than a constructed fixture.

### STOP-WAKE — a mention of the exit token is not a claim (E02 S6/S7)
**Issue** — `lane-owes:` was matched anywhere in the raw final message. A fenced block
EXPLAINING the hook — prefixed "I have not actually delegated anything" — registered a real
claim and muted that task for 90 minutes.
**Why this is the sharp one** — it is self-referential. Any turn that discusses this hook,
quotes its own block message back, or pastes an audit of it could silence itself. The block
message itself contains the literal `` `lane-owes:<task id>` ``, and was safe only by
accident: `<` is not in `[\w-]`. Substitute a real id into that echo and the model mutes the
very task it was being asked about.
**Change** — `hc._strip_code` blanks fenced blocks AND inline backtick spans before the match,
preserving line structure. What survives is prose, which is where a real claim lives: "the
retriever owes me this. lane-owes:1" is a claim; the same token in backticks is a mention.
An unterminated fence swallows the rest deliberately — failing toward "no claim" is failing
toward the check still firing. `None`/empty ids are refused: rows are keyed `str(r.get("id"))`,
so `lane-owes:None` muted every id-less row on the board at once.
**Why not a whole-line anchor** — that was the first cut and it broke the legitimate case. The
real distinction is code-span vs prose, not position.
**Class sweep** — every other check reading a CLAIM out of model-authored text. `scan_leak` is
the only sibling and it is deliberately the inverse (it WANTS to catch echoed hook codes, so
stripping would defeat it). No other predicate parses the final message for a token.
**Pinned by** — `test_w28_iter1_fixes.py`, 7 unit + 3 end-to-end through the real hook.

### Two whole-hook crashes, both one line (E02 F1, E13 Q5)
**Issue** — a non-string `last_assistant_message` crashed the entire Stop hook: exit 1,
traceback, and NO hook logic ran that turn. Measured: dict, list and int all crashed; only
null was safe. `list` is the one that matters — `[{"type":"text","text":…}]` is the natural
content shape, so a harness that ever passes the content array takes the whole layer down.
Separately, `"  ".join(spend)` in the awareness adapter sat outside any `try`: ONE non-string
queue element raised TypeError out of `main()`, so the AW4 orientation, the verbatim INDEX
injection and the PC-CANON re-read obligation were all lost with it — and since the clear
never ran, it repeated **every turn for the life of the session**.
**Why these are guard bypasses, not cosmetic** — a crashed adapter is the firewall not running
for that call. The tree already learned this once (the non-dict payload guard, W28/E09); this
is the same lesson one field deeper.
**Change** — coerce `last_assistant_message` at the payload BOUNDARY, so all five consumers
inherit the guard instead of the one that happened to crash; a content array is flattened to
its text rather than stringified into noise. The whisper join coerces with `str()` inside the
guard — coercion, not rescue: swallowing the error keeps the hook alive and drops the good
advisories with the bad.
**Class sweep** — audited every other adapter for a regex/join over a payload field with no
type guard: the non-dict payload check already covers the top level, and no other adapter
consumes a free-form payload string. `or ""` is NOT a guard and was the false comfort here — a
dict is truthy.
**Pinned by** — five payload shapes driven through the real Stop hook; the whisper case asserts
the VALID entries still arrive.

### The advisory channel lost its messages at the front door (E13 L1)
**Issue** — the STOP-WAKE block path printed its decision and `sys.exit(0)` **above** the
queueing block, so a blocked turn DESTROYED every advisory it had accumulated. Permanently:
each check had already burned its `sc.once` key, so re-firing the Stop with the block bypassed
queued nothing.
**Evidence** — one fixture, the only difference being whether STOP-WAKE armed: `queued=4`
became `queued=NOTHING`.
**Why it matters more than the count suggests** — the correlation runs exactly the wrong way.
The busier and more error-prone the turn, the more likely its advisories were thrown away, and
nobody was told: no decision row, no user-visible trace, no way to reconstruct the loss.
**Change** — the queueing is now `_queue_pending()`, called BEFORE the block exit.
**A hollow assertion caught in the writing** — the first version of the test compared source
TEXT POSITIONS, and could never fail: `_queue_pending(sid, msgs)` also occurs inside
`def _queue_pending(sid, msgs):` at the top of the file, so `find()` always returned a tiny
index. Deleting the call from the block path left it green. Replaced with a driven Stop that
actually blocks with an advisory armed.
**Class sweep** — every other `sys.exit` on the Stop path: the observe-mode arm falls through
to the queue correctly, and the `except` fail-open path reaches it too. This was the only
early exit above the queue.

### The decision log could be forged, and half its stamps were in the future (E06)
**Issue** — the format has zero escaping, so a newline in any of the three fields produced a
syntactically perfect EXTRA row attributed to a hook that never ran (11 calls → 14 rows, 7 not
4 columns). And `"%.0f" % t` ROUNDS, so ~half of all rows carried a stamp up to 0.5 s in the
FUTURE of the write — making any "row epoch ≤ artifact mtime" check flaky by construction,
which is the shape of the gate flake that cost a release (wave 6).
**Change** — `_field()` at the boundary; `int()` instead of `%.0f`.
**On the forgery being latent** — all 31 call sites pass literals today, so this is one
careless `f"{tool_name}"` from live, and no test could have caught it because the tests write
their own clean ids. Fixing the FORMAT rather than auditing the callers is the difference
between a property and a promise.
**Class sweep** — `flip_marker`'s `why` is the sibling (free text from `argv[4]`, and a newline
in it forged a MARKER row for a DIFFERENT marker, defeating the function's own reason for
existing). Same `_field`. `log()` itself takes pre-formatted lines from ~70 sites and is not
column-structured, so it is out of scope by design.

### flip_marker could truncate or delete any file (E06 2b)
**Issue** — `name` went straight into `os.path.join` with NO validation, and the `on` branch
opens `"w"`, which TRUNCATES. Measured: `("../outside.txt", True)` zeroed a file outside the
tree; `("nexus-pretool.py", True)` zeroed a LIVE HOOK; `False` deleted either outright.
**Reachability** — `name` comes from `argv[2]` of the module's own CLI, so a typo or an unset
shell variable was one keystroke from destroying a hook. This is the only destructive path in
the library.
**Change** — a marker is a dotfile directly inside the hooks dir and nothing else; anything
else is refused. The right answer to a caller bug is a refusal, not a truncated file.
**Pinned by** — five hostile names, plus assertions that the victim files still hold their
contents and that a legitimate flip still works both ways.

### The store lost data under fan-out (E12)
**Issue** — two independent races, both measured on the real library:
- `drop`/`pdrop` read a whole feed and reopened it `"w"`, so every append landing in the
  window was DESTROYED: **33–43% of concurrent appends lost** (626/1600, 1361/3200,
  2106/6400 at 8/16/32 appenders vs 2 droppers).
- `put()` truncated before writing, so **~50% of concurrent reads were false misses**
  (240/480, 453/960, 929/1920).
**Blast radius** — `pdrop` operates on PROJECT-scoped feeds (`id-cache`, `lifecycle`,
`agent-lifecycle`) that every session and every subagent lane shares by construction, so one
`nexus agent delete` while lanes ran silently ate other lanes' rows. The `put` race fails safe
but `stop-pending` is a read-modify-write: a torn read made the list empty and **silently
dropped queued Stop advisories** — the same loss as the block-path defect above, by a
different road.
**Change** — `put` writes a pid-suffixed temp and `os.replace`s it (atomic on POSIX).
`drop`/`pdrop` hold an exclusive `flock` across read+rewrite, and `log`/`plog` take the same
lock on append — **both sides must participate or the lock buys nothing**, which is why the
append path changed even though `O_APPEND` was already atomic against other appenders.
**Cost, measured** — +0.108 ms per `log()` call (0.108 → 0.216 ms). The battery's wall-clock
tripled in the same window, but that was load average **241** on the machine, not the lock;
re-timing one suite twice under that load gave 43.6 s and 41.9 s.
**Fails open in every direction** — no `fcntl`, or an unlockable filesystem, and every
operation proceeds exactly as before.
**Class sweep** — every read-modify-write in the module: `put`/`get` and `drop`/`pdrop` are the
complete set; `once` is `O_CREAT|O_EXCL` and was already correct under 32-way contention
(20 keys, 20 winners, every time).

### The hold clock could run backwards, and "expired" could be a lie (E07)
**Issue** — the age comes from the flag file's mtime, and a FUTURE-dated mtime (clock skew, a
restore that does not preserve times) produced a negative age, which fails `> MAX` forever: an
**immortal hold**, recreating precisely the silent nine-day suppression the expiry was written
to end. Separately, `pclear` returns False when the flag cannot be removed (measured: a
DIRECTORY-shaped flag) and the caller logged `expired-stale-project-hold` regardless — so the
log claimed the hold was cleared **every session forever** while the directory sat there.
Measured: 3 sessions, 3 rows, 0 removals.
**Change** — negative age counts as stale; the caller branches on `pclear`'s result and logs
`expired-uncleared` when removal failed. Suppression still lifts either way (fail-open is the
safe direction); what must not happen is the record disagreeing with the disk, which is the
exact failure the expiry was meant to remove.
**Not taken this wave** — E07's larger recommendation (store the set-epoch in the flag BODY so
`touch`, `cp` and git-checkout cannot resurrect a hold, and provenance comes back) is a better
fix and is recorded as OPEN rather than half-done.
**Class sweep** — every other age-from-mtime read: `pflag_age_s` has one caller and one key.

### The suite was mutation-tested, and four of its own assertions were hollow
**Why this is in the log** — writing tests to close a coverage measurement and then not
measuring them is how the original gap formed. First run: **8 of 13 mutations caught.** The
five survivors were not code gaps but test gaps, and each is a distinct way to write a test
that cannot fail:
1. **Asserted source-text positions** rather than behaviour — and the string occurred in the
   function's own `def` line, so the ordering check was arithmetically incapable of failing.
2. **Re-implemented the predicate in the test** (`_age < 0 or _age > MAX`), proving only that
   the test can write the condition; the hook stayed reverted and green.
3. **Unit-tested a helper nobody was asserted to call** — `_strip_code` was verified directly
   while the hook read the raw message; a defect fixed in an uncalled helper is not fixed.
4. **A vacuous sample** — the concurrency probe's forked children printed their verdicts and
   `os._exit(0)` skipped the stdio flush, so the run scored 0 hits / 0 misses and "zero
   misses" passed as a statement about nothing.
Plus one harness bug of my own: a mutation that disabled only ONE clause of a multi-clause
guard, which the remaining clauses still caught — reported as a survivor, was not.
**After the rewrite: 17/17 mutations caught**, 54 checks.
**The rule this wave earns** — a test asserts behaviour driven through the real entrypoint. A
test that reads source text, re-implements the predicate, or calls the helper directly is
measuring itself.

## Wave 9 — the adversarial re-verify found a safety regression I shipped (F01)

Iteration 2's first lane was pointed at waves 7 and 8 with one instruction: assume they contain
mistakes. They did. Every claim below was re-derived first-hand before I acted on it.

### The heredoc stripper was defeated by the very form this layer prescribes
**Issue** — `_HEREDOC_RE` required the delimiter to be IMMEDIATELY followed by a newline. Any
trailing token on the opener line — a redirect, a pipe, `&&` — meant the heredoc was not
stripped at all, and its entire body was scanned as command text by the DENY tier. `<<-`, whose
only reason for existing is a tab-indented terminator, was 100% broken for the same reason.
**Evidence [LIVE]** — of 5,675 real heredoc commands, **796 (14%) leaked their body**, and
**716 of those 796 (90%) were the opener followed by `2>&1`**.
**Why that number is the finding** — this layer's own standing rule is "never `2>/dev/null`; use
`2>&1`". So the PRESCRIBED form was the form that disabled the mention-stripper. Writing a
runbook, a postmortem or a test fixture that merely NAMES a dangerous command was denied for
documenting it. The audit lane's own first tool call was denied through exactly this door.
**Worse, wave 7 amplified it**: the new `mkfs` anchor treats a line start as a command position,
and a documentation line beginning `mkfs.ext4 …` inside a leaked body is a line start.
**Change** — `<<-?\s*(['\"]?)(\w+)\1[^\n]*\n.*?\n[ \t]*\2\b`: trailing content allowed on the
opener, indented terminator allowed.
**Why not special-case `2>&1`** — the cause is not `2>&1`; it is that the pattern modelled a
narrower grammar than the shell's. 80 of the 796 leaks are pipes, `&&` and `<<-`. Special-casing
the observed token is the substring-not-act mistake in a new place.

### Three copies of that pattern existed, and one silently overrode the others
**Issue** — `lib/hook_core.py` defined `_HEREDOC_RE` twice, at line 48 and again at line 2076.
Python binds module globals in file order, so **the later definition won every call**: `_strip()`
— the view the whole DENY tier matches on — used the second pattern, not the documented one
beside it 2,000 lines up. A fix applied to the canonical copy would have had no effect at all.
A third copy lived in `nexus-fs-firewall.py`.
**Change** — one canonical `_HEREDOC_RE`; the body-extraction use renamed to
`_HEREDOC_BODY_RE` (two different jobs were sharing one name — stripping needs no groups,
extraction needs the body captured); the firewall now imports the canonical one.
**Class sweep** — this is the "duplication that will drift" class, and it had already been
called out once: wave 3 centralised the quote stripper because *"it had ALREADY diverged once. A
shared helper is only shared until someone re-inlines it."* Three copies is what that looks
like when nobody checks for shadowing.

### `_strip` still carried the quote regex wave 3 declared eliminated
**Issue** — wave 3's class sweep concluded "none remain". It searched the ADAPTERS. The copy is
in the LIBRARY, and it is the view every `classify_bash_reliability` check runs on, plus 14 call
sites in the pretool adapter.
**Evidence** — the two strippers disagree on 41 of 20,007 real commands. Measured example:
`git commit -m "he said \"use 2>/dev/null\" once"` — a pure mention — DENIED under the local
non-escape-aware regex; correctly ignored by the canonical one.
**Change** — `_strip` now calls `strip_quoted_spans`; `_QUOTE_RE` deleted.
**The lesson about sweeps** — a class sweep scoped to "the adapters" cannot find a library copy.
Scope the sweep to the CLASS (every quote-stripping regex in the tree), not to the directory
where the instance happened to be found.

### My wave-7 `mkfs` fix was a safety regression — 6 of 7 real invocations stopped denying
**Issue** — wave 7's entry claimed the command-position anchoring "costs no true positive" and
reported "8/8 true kept". Both were measured against eight invocations that all happened to fall
inside my own hard-coded wrapper list. Outside it the anchor fails OPEN.
**Evidence, verified first-hand before acting** — old `\bmkfs\b` vs the shipped `DISK_RE`:

    old=DENY  new=MISS   env PATH=/sbin mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdb
    old=DENY  new=MISS   DEV=/dev/sdb mkfs.ext4 $DEV
    old=DENY  new=MISS   sudo timeout 60 mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdb
    old=DENY  new=MISS   \mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdb
    old=DENY  new=MISS   sudo nice -n 5 mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdb
    old=DENY  new=MISS   $(which mkfs.ext4) /dev/sdb
    regressions: 6/7

Three shapes broke it, none exotic: `env` was ON the list but the pattern allowed only FLAGS
after it, while `VAR=VAL` is what `env` is FOR; the wrapper list is a closed enumeration and
`timeout`/`nice`/`ionice`/`stdbuf`/`setsid`/`script`/`chroot`/`ssh` all take a command argument;
and `\mkfs` is the standard alias-bypass form.
**The real lesson — which SIDE an allowlist may sit on.** The set of programs that can INVOKE
`mkfs` is unbounded and grows. The set of verbs that merely READ ABOUT it is small, closed, and
is exactly the eight false positives wave 7 enumerated. An allowlist over the small closed set
fails toward DENYING; an allowlist over the unbounded set fails toward ALLOWING. They are not
symmetric, and I picked the one that fails open on the catastrophic tier.
**Change** — match `mkfs` broadly again, and EXCLUDE by reader verb (`_DISK_READ`). Plus two
edges the audit surfaced: a reader verb inside a command substitution is not reading
(`$(which mkfs.ext4) /dev/sdb` formats a disk), and `mkfs.<suffix>` names a filesystem, so a
document extension is a filename — excluded as a small denylist of doc suffixes, never an
allowlist of filesystem names, because a new filesystem must keep denying.
**The terminator** — `\b` matched before `-` and `.`, so `mkfs-report --dry-run` and `mkfs.md`
denied. That was the FOURTH instance of the substring-not-act class, and it is worth naming as a
mechanism: wave 7 changed WHERE the substring had to appear and left it a substring.

## Wave 10 — the blind review found a live auto-approve of a recursive root delete (F18)

### PROT-ROOT was keyed on the FLAG COMBINATION, not on the act
**Issue** — the guard armed on `is_recursive_force_rm`, which requires `-r` **and** `-f`. `-f`
suppresses PROMPTS and missing-file errors; it has nothing to do with how much gets deleted. So a
recursive delete without `-f` skipped the guard entirely, fell through to the scope check,
matched a work dir, and was emitted as **`allow`**.
**Why `allow` is worse than a miss** — silence defers to the native permission flow. `allow`
REMOVES the prompt the user would otherwise have seen. With `defaultMode: acceptEdits`, that
prompt was the last line of defence, and the hook was taking it away.
**Evidence, verified first-hand on the live adapter before acting**:

    deny    rm -rf /tmp
    allow   rm -r /tmp                  <- recursive delete of a work root, AUTO-APPROVED
    allow   rm -R /tmp
    allow   rm --recursive /tmp
    allow   rm -r <project root>

The single most destructive command a session can issue was the one spelling the guard granted.
**Change** — a separate `is_recursive_rm` predicate; PROT-ROOT arms on either.
**Why a separate predicate and not a loosening of the existing one** — `is_recursive_force_rm` is
also consumed by `RM1`/`RM1B`, whose "delete everything except a keep-list" semantics genuinely
do want the forced form. Widening it there would fire those denies on ordinary interactive
`rm -r`, trading one false negative for a class of false positives.
**Verified after** — all seven recursive spellings deny, `/` and the project root deny, and the
three controls are untouched: a non-recursive delete, a recursive delete of an in-scope CHILD,
and a protected path merely READ beside a safe delete. 3/3 mutations caught.
**Test status before the fix** — UNCOVERED and proven so: `test_w28_guard_scope.py` asserts
`rm --recursive --force /` and never a recursive-only delete. Every firewall fixture in the tree
had `-f` in it.

### What this one says about the process
This defect was NOT introduced by any recent wave — it predates the cycle. It took a lane that
was explicitly told to **read the code cold and form its own view before reading `CHANGELOG.md`**
to find it. Every other lane was anchored on the known-issue list and looked where the list
pointed. The blind lane is the only one that could have found a guard nobody had thought to
question, and it is the single highest-yield lane of the twenty.

**A measurement note, recorded because it changes how the finding count should be read.** F18
reviewed a tree that three other lanes were editing underneath it — `lib/hook_core.py` changed
twice mid-review. It pinned sha256 hashes, then RE-DROVE its five highest-severity findings
against the newer tree and reported that all five still reproduced. A concurrent audit that does
not pin and re-verify is reporting on a tree that no longer exists.

## Wave 11 — STOP-WAKE reads the authoritative board (F02) · closes O5 and O14

### The evidence I had recorded was wrong, and a later lane refuted it on the same data
**What I had banked** — E16: "`taskId 45` appears zero times in any project transcript, therefore
a teammate's TaskUpdate never reaches the main transcript and forward-reconciliation is
structurally starved." I wrote that into the OPEN table and into the task record as established.
**Checked first-hand when F02 disputed it** — it appears **4 times in this session's own
transcript**, twice carrying `completed`, across 4 project files. Reconciliation was not starved.
**Why I record this rather than quietly correcting it** — I accepted a lane's headline claim
without re-deriving the one fact the whole diagnosis rested on, and it survived into two durable
artifacts. The cost was low only because a second lane happened to work the same ground.

### The actual defect, narrower and provable
`board_state`'s forward pass only scans for `status in (completed, deleted)`. So it cannot repair
a `pending -> in_progress` transition, and it can NEVER see a task **created after the snapshot** —
that task is not in `rows` at all, so nothing can add it.
**Evidence** — reproduced on the unmodified adapter: a block naming a task the authoritative board
already had `in_progress`, written 7.6 min after the snapshot. Across 90 transcripts: 17 of 25
boards resolve against the store, **3 of 17 disagree, 1 of 17 flips the verdict**. The raw snapshot
drifts hard on this session (994 task-minutes of contradiction, longest window 199.8 min) though
reconciliation repairs all of it *here* — which is why the reverted staleness guard never fired.

### The fix
Read the harness's own task store (`~/.claude/tasks/session-<owner>/<id>.json`, verified
first-hand: 121 dirs, schema as described). Resolution is by FINGERPRINT because there is no key:
0 of 24 team `leadSessionId`s have a transcript, and this session's `session_id` names no store
dir while its board lives under another. The reminder's `(id, subject)` pairs are invariant under
status changes, so they are the key.
**Two conditions, both strict**: the winner contains EVERY pair, and no other dir shares a single
pair. Resolved path cached per session.
**The trap that was one decision from shipping** — the earlier proposal used a
`max(2, len(fp)//2)` floor. F02 CONSTRUCTED the collision: with the true store gone, a stranger
dir sharing two generic subjects ("Fix the bug", "Write tests") wins outright and the check then
names **another session's task** to this one. Ids carry almost no entropy — an id-only match
picked the wrong dir for 6 of 8 unresolvable sessions. Full coverage + zero runner-up resolves
17/25 instead of 15/25 AND rejects the collision.
**Degradation** — every failure path returns exactly today's snapshot behaviour: no store on the
machine, no resolution, an ambiguous store, a corrupt task file, an unreadable dir. A harness
layout change costs the accuracy and never the check.
**O14 closed with it** — `_board is None` killed BOTH arms, though arm 2 exists for "no board +
work happened". What that guard actually bought was the board-USING restriction, now stated
explicitly as `(_board is not None) or _store or _ops`.
**One verdict implementation** — `board_from_rows` is SPLIT OUT of `board_state`, not
re-derived. F02's own first patch re-implemented the unblocked rule and would have silently
dropped the stuck/ghost-cycle handling added the same morning.

### Two more hollow-assertion catches, both in the incoming test
Mutation-tested the new suite: 3 of 5 caught on the first pass.
- **The ambiguous-store case gave both candidate dirs an IDENTICAL board**, so adopting either
  produced the same output — the assertion could not tell resolution from a coin toss, and
  dropping the runner-up guard left it green. Rewritten so the two candidates DISAGREE.
- The `board_from_rows` mutation is owned by the wave-8 suite, not this one; verified there
  rather than duplicated.
After both: 5/5 caught.

### A fixture with a two-hour shelf life, mistaken for a flake
The O14 case passed on arrival and failed 5/5 two hours later, in isolation, with identical code.
Not load: the fixture hard-coded transcript timestamps at `09:0N` while writing its `task-op`
marker as `time.time() - 600`. Those are different clocks — the marker moves, the transcript does
not — and `tools_since_last_task_op` counts only entries after the marker. It worked while it was
being written and expired at 09:20. **Every timestamp in that fixture is now relative to `now`.**
This is the third member of the load-or-clock-sensitive test family (`test_w22_hooks` BLD2,
`test_ledger_checkpoint`, this) and the only one whose cause is fully understood.

**Battery** — 64/64 green, 1024 assertions.
