## Wave 12 — the false-positive census (F20): 37 of 39 firewall denies were false

A corpus of **19,333 unique real Bash commands from 90 transcripts**, plus 222 fixtures labelled
BEFORE anything was run, driven through the real firewall → pretool → ladder chain.

**The number that governs the rest**: in one continuous session, **2.8% of every Bash command a
user issues is hard-blocked**, and 98 of 1,000 turns carry an advisory. The DENY tier barely
de-duplicates — `C1`, `G19` and `G2` have no once-gate by design. That is the volume the false
positives live in. Also worth stating plainly: **38,666 adapter invocations, 0 crashes, 0
unparseable output.** The fail-open shape holds under a large adversarial real-world distribution.

### `WSW-RET` — 33 of 33 live denies false, at DENY tier, with no override
**Issue** — it scanned the RAW command, so any OCCURRENCE of the workspace-write vector anywhere
in the string hard-denied: inside an `echo`, a commit message, a `grep` pattern, a runbook
heredoc documenting the correct route.
**Evidence [LIVE]** — 33 of the 39 firewall denies in the corpus are this check, and all 33 are
false. The slugs named in those denies include `<slug>` (a commit-message placeholder), `$2` (a
shell positional) and `s`: **the message named a workspace that does not exist**. Two of the 33
were the owner auditing this layer.
**Why the raw scan was there** — deliberately, and half-right: the URL carrying the slug is
quoted, so the keyword view would have stripped it and broken the check outright.
**Change** — TWO views, which is what `aw5` in the pretool adapter already does 1,400 lines away:
require the ACT (`curl` + `-X PUT`) on the stripped view, read the OPERAND (the slug) from the
raw text, heredoc bodies stripped first.
**Verified** — real writes still deny (including a `for … do curl … done` loop); all four mention
carriers now defer.

### `SHELL-PORT`'s `sed -i` arm — 32 fires, 32 false, 0 true
**Issue** — the row must tell `sed -i ''` (correct on BSD) from `sed -i` (GNU-only). It was fed
the stripped view, which replaces every quoted span with a space — deleting the `''` that IS the
discriminator. So it fired on both forms, and its advice was a verbatim restatement of what the
user had already typed.
**Evidence [LIVE]** — 45 corpus commands contain `sed -i`; 32 are the correct form; the check
fired on all 32 and on **zero** genuine defects.
**Why it costs more than its own noise** — `SHELL-PORT` is `once()`-gated per session and carries
five CORRECT rules (`grep -P`, `readlink -f`, `date -d`, `find -printf`, `timeout N`). A false
fire consumes the gate, so the one genuine miss in the corpus is likely suppressed by a false
positive earlier in the same session. The rational reader response is to stop reading the check,
and the five good rules go with it.
**Change** — that row alone evaluates the RAW command, anchored to a command position. Raw ALONE
is not enough: it makes `echo "use sed -i on linux"` a new false positive, measured. Command
position is what makes raw-operand reading safe.
**Class sweep** — checked the other five rows: all key on a FLAG whose presence survives
quote-stripping. `sed -i` is the only operand-sensitive row of the six.

### `G19` read the BINARY, not the SUBCOMMAND
**Issue** — `vite` at a command position denied regardless of what vite was asked to do.
**Evidence [LIVE]** — **55 of 115 `G19` denies (48%) are `vite build`** — how an app actually
ships. Also blocked: `vite --version`, `vite -v`, and any npm script whose name merely BEGINS
with `dev`/`start` (`dev:types`, `start:prod`), because `\b` matches before `:`.
**Why it matters** — the message names a "localhost server" that does not exist, on a DENY with
no per-call override. That is the fastest way to teach a reader the gate is noise.
**Change** — `vite` denies only on the SERVING subcommands (bare / dev / serve / preview);
the npm boundary tightens to `(dev|start)(?![\w:.-])`.
**Why not "require a `--port` signal"** — that fails open on `npm run dev`, where the port comes
from `vite.config` and never appears in the command. That is the gate's primary case. The
subcommand is in the text; the port is not.
**Verified** — 12 serving forms still deny; 9 build/version/script forms now pass.

### The mechanism under six of the eight findings
F20's own recommendation, and it is right: the missing thing is not a check but a PRIMITIVE —
`command_positions(cmd) -> set[int]`, built from the scanner `strip_quoted_spans` already walks
(it computes the spans and discards the offsets). Every trigger that names a command then asks
one question — *does my match start at a command position?* — and reads its operands from the
raw text. **Three checks discovered that formulation independently (`aw5` by hand, `DISKWRITE`
and `G19` with `CMDPOS`); four more did not.** Making it a named, tested primitive is what stops
instance #9. Recorded as O25; the three fixes above are the instances, not the mechanism.

### A FIFTH way a test cannot fail
`tests/test_wsw_firewall.py` carries an assertion named "false-positive guard" for `WSW-RET`
mentions — and drives **the pretool adapter only**, while the check that hard-denies lives in the
FIREWALL. The guard was green for years while the behaviour it names was false at DENY tier in
the other adapter. It is also partial for pretool: it covers one carrier of the six that fire.
**The list of ways a test can be hollow is now: source-text assertions · re-implemented
predicates · unit-testing an uncalled helper · an empty sample · driving a different adapter than
the one that enforces.** The fix is a shared `chain(payload)` helper that runs firewall THEN
pretool and returns both, with a rule that every FP guard asserts on the chain.

## Wave 13 — the mechanism, not another instance: `command_positions`

**Why this entry exists at all.** Asked whether this loop was converging or playing whack-a-mole,
the honest answer was: converging on defects, NOT on defect-generating mechanisms. The evidence
was the substring-not-act class reaching **instance #8** while every fix stayed per-check. The
pattern that keeps it alive is visible in the fixes themselves — three checks each solved the
underlying question PRIVATELY (`aw5` by hand at `nexus-pretool.py:1435`, then `DISKWRITE` and
`G19` with their own `CMDPOS` constants) and four never solved it at all. The four that did not
produced most of the measured false positives, including 33 of 39 firewall denies.

**The shared question, named once.** `hc.command_positions(cmd) -> set[int]` — the offsets where
a shell would begin reading a command. A check then asks `at_command_position(cmd, match)` and
reads its OPERANDS from the raw text. Both halves matter: a stripped view protects against
mentions and DESTROYS quoted operands — that is precisely how `SHELL-PORT` lost the `''` that
separates a correct `sed -i ''` from a broken `sed -i`.

**Built on the existing scanner, not a fifth quote regex.** `strip_quoted_spans` already walks
quote state and discards the offsets; this reuses it. A command name inside a string is
therefore never a command position, which is the mention case, for free.

**Shipped with a consumer, deliberately.** A primitive with no caller is dead code. `PROFSW` is
the first: it scanned the RAW command and reported the org name as `other-org"),` — punctuation
lifted out of a python literal in a heredoc that was WRITING a fixture file. Measured live: 3
fires during one audit, all mentions, and 487 fires corpus-wide. That advisory is worse than
noise, because it asserts a FACT about session state ("active org → X") that is false and tells
the reader to remount a folder that does not exist. Now: the act must sit at a command position,
the capture is `[A-Za-z0-9_-]+` on all three regexes, and five mention carriers are silent.

**Where the scan cannot resolve a prefix** (`sudo -u nobody rm`) it stops early and yields an
EXTRA position — erring toward treating something as a command, i.e. toward the guard FIRING.
On a deny tier that is the correct direction to be wrong in, and it is stated rather than left
to be discovered.

**Two defects found by its own test, in the primitive rather than the test.** A bare leading
assignment (`D=/tmp rm -rf x`) put the position on the assignment instead of the verb, because
the prefix group required a wrapper word; and empty input reported a phantom position at offset
0. Both fixed in the function.

**Still open**: `WSW-RET`'s pretool twin, `CW1` and `KR1` read the same `/api/dav/` surface off
the raw command and should move to this primitive (O25). The three DENY-tier instances are
already closed by wave 12; these are warn-tier and can migrate incrementally now that the
primitive exists and is tested.

## Wave 15 — a crashed adapter is a guard that did not run (F13) · registry closed

### The E09 shape check was applied at depth 0 only
**Issue** — W28/E09 added `if not isinstance(data, dict): sys.exit(0)` to every adapter with the
comment *"shape is part of the contract, not just parseability"*. It stops at the TOP LEVEL.
Every nested read is `(data.get("tool_input") or {}).get("file_path", "")`, and `or {}` guards
`None` and nothing else — so a non-string one level down propagates into `os.path`,
`str.startswith`, `str.replace` or a `set` lookup and kills the process.
**Evidence** — verified first-hand before acting: five adapters exit **1** on shapes as ordinary
as `file_path` being a list. Exit 1 is NOT the deny code (these adapters deny with exit 2), so
exit 1 means the hook errored. `nexus-fs-firewall.py` was among them — the adapter holding
`rm -rf` of a protected root, raw-disk writes, the fork bomb and SIP. **A payload shape that
makes it exit 1 is a payload shape for which none of those denies exist.**
**Reachability, stated rather than glossed** — across 33,430 real tool-use blocks there were
ZERO non-string `file_path`/`command`/`content` and zero non-dict `tool_input`. A DEFENSIVE gap,
not an observed incident. Fixed anyway because the fields most at risk — `tool_input` for
`mcp__*` tools — are shaped by third-party servers rather than by the harness's own schemas, and
this layer's own contract already claims shape is part of it.
**Change** — two coercion helpers in `hook_core` (`s()` for a field that must be a string, `d()`
for one that must be a mapping), called at each entry point. 12 call sites across 6 adapters.
**Why NOT a blanket `try/except: sys.exit(0)`** — that converts a crash into a SILENT skip: the
guard still does not run, and now nothing says so. Coercion keeps the guard running on the
fields that ARE well-formed, which is almost always all of them. It is also **the only version
that can be asserted** — a deny on a coerced field is observable, a swallowed exception is not.
Two checks in the new suite exist solely to pin that difference: `rm -rf /` must still DENY when
a sibling field is malformed. Under the blanket catch it would not.
**A second pass was needed** — the first sweep left `tname`/`caller` unguarded in pretool and
posttool, caught by the re-run, not by inspection. `agent_type` as a list reached a `set`
membership test (`unhashable type: 'list'`), which is why the fix had to be at the READ rather
than a `str()` at the use.

## Wave 16 — the delete must be FOUND before it can be judged (F10)

Wave 10 fixed WHICH deletes count as recursive. This is the layer beneath it, and it was worse:
three ordinary sweep idioms were not recognised as an `rm` **at all**.

**Evidence, verified first-hand on the live adapter before acting:**

    allow   find <project> -maxdepth 1 -exec rm -rf {} +
    allow   timeout 60 rm -rf <project>
    allow   parallel rm -rf ::: <project>
    deny    rm -rf <project>          <- the only shape it saw

**`allow`, not `defer`, is the sharp part.** It does not merely miss — it REMOVES the native
permission prompt. The firewall was actively auto-approving emptying the project directory.
And one unrecognised prefix silences **three guards at once**: `PROT-ROOT`, `RM1` and `RM1B` all
key on the same segmenter.

**Three separate causes, found by probing the chain rather than guessing:**
1. **The wrapper list was short.** `timeout`, `parallel`, `nice`, `ionice`, `stdbuf`, `setsid`,
   `script`, `chroot`, `doas`, `su` all take a command argument and none was listed.
2. **`-exec` was not a boundary.** `find` does not WRAP `rm`; it starts a new command at
   `-exec`. Added to the boundary set, not the wrapper set — and to BOTH scanners. Fixing only
   one left `find … -exec rm -rf {} +` recognised as a delete *with no flags*, i.e. not
   recursive, i.e. still silently allowed. The two regexes decide different halves of the same
   question and had been kept in step by convention; that is now written down beside them.
3. **`{}` was treated as a path.** With the first two fixed, targets came back as `['{}', '+']`,
   neither matched a protected root, and the guard fell through to `allow`. `{}` is find's
   placeholder for *whatever it matched* — unknowable statically, which is exactly the
   not-confident case that must route to the broad candidate set. `+` and `;` terminate the
   clause and are not paths either.

**Why widening the wrapper floor is safe here when an allowlist over mkfs invokers was not:** an
unrecognised prefix makes `rm_targets` return `None`, which routes to the BROAD set — toward
denying. The mkfs allowlist failed the other way. Same shape, opposite direction, and the
direction is what decides whether a floor is acceptable.
**Verified after** — 6 evasions deny (including `-execdir` and `nice`); 3 legitimate cases
untouched (`rm -rf <project>/src/build`, `ls /tmp && rm -r /tmp/scratch`,
`find … -name '*.tmp' -exec rm -f {} +`). 3/3 mutations caught.

**Still open from this lane, recorded rather than half-fixed** — F10 asks a design question
bigger than the fix: *should the firewall ever return `allow` for a recursive delete at all,*
given the native prompt is the last line of defence? Every miss in this class became an
auto-approval precisely because `allow` is the terminal verdict for anything in a work dir.
Also open: `RM1`/`RM1B` miss ~60% of real keep-list idioms (`while read`, `find`, `xargs`,
`comm`, extglob), and their `NEXUS_RM_ACK` override is a raw substring — mentioning it in a
comment or a heredoc disarms both guards. **That last one is the substring-not-act class running

class sweep looked only at `if <pattern>: deny` and never at `if <pattern>: skip the deny`.

## Wave 17 — WSW was wrong 95% of the time, and blocked the session's own boundary check (F09)

**Issue** — `WSW` scanned every path token in the whole command whenever any mutating verb
appeared anywhere in it. A mount path merely MENTIONED was a hard deny. This is O1; the lane
quantified it against real traffic and found it far worse than the "10 false positives" recorded.

**Evidence [LIVE]** — every `[WSW]` deny across this machine's transcripts, paired back to the
command that caused it, with shell variables resolved: **118 deny events / 99 unique commands.
40 true positives, 78 false. Of the 22 unique true positives, 18 are `Write`/`Edit` (a different
branch) — so the Bash arm scores 4 true against 77 false. A 95% false-positive rate.**

Verified first-hand before acting; all five shapes below denied, all five are reads:

    GC="<mount>/general-context"; python3 -c "print(1)"      a bare variable assignment
    perl -e 'alarm 8; exec @ARGV' cat "<mount>/INDEX.md"     THE BOUNDARY CHECK ITSELF
    cp "<mount>/tools/x.md" ~/Downloads/                     exporting a file for the owner
    rm -f "$SCRATCH/test.md"; SRC="<mount>/…"                deleting a SCRATCH file
    cd "<mount>/systems"; mkdir -p /private/tmp/…/staging    mkdir in /tmp

**Why the boundary case is the damning one.** `perl -e 'alarm N; exec @ARGV'` is the estate's
bounded-timeout idiom, because macOS has no `timeout(1)` — and `perl` was in the mutating-verb
list. So **every bounded mount probe in the estate denied**, and that probe is the first thing a
session does. The deny then instructed the reader to `curl -X PUT`, a remedy that makes no sense
for a `cat`, while `emit()` appended "The corrected form can run immediately in this turn" —
promising a fix that does not exist. The transcripts show what that trains: agents retrying with
`gtimeout`, then `python3`, then abandoning the mount for REST.

**Change** — `write_targets(cmd, cwd)`, built to the same contract as `rm_targets`, replacing
THREE token scans (the `MUT_NONNET_RE` loop, the `NET_RE` output-flag loop, and the standalone
redirect scan) with one target-based check. Per-verb destination semantics: last-operand verbs
(`cp`/`mv`/`rsync`/`ln`), all-operand verbs (`mkdir`/`rm`/`tee`/`touch`), `dd of=`, `unzip -d`,
`tar -xC`, `git clone <dir>`, curl/wget output flags, and file redirects. Interpreters are read
for a WRITE PRIMITIVE — absence of every one of them is the only thing that licenses "this code
writes nothing".

**The contract is the whole safety argument, and it is mutation-proven.** `None` means "cannot
tell" and routes to the broad every-token set — today's behaviour. `[]` is a positive claim.
So the guard can only become QUIETER, never weaker. Proven by replacing every `return None` in
`write_targets` with `return []`: **two of four real mount writes flip from deny to allow.**
That is exactly the regression `rm_targets` shipped once and then fixed, reproduced on demand.

**Why not the obvious alternative** — narrowing `MUT_NONNET_RE` (drop the interpreters, or
require the mount path to be the last operand) moves the boundary without changing the mechanism:
it still asks "does a path appear near a verb" instead of "what does this command write". And the
gate condition could then be dropped from `MUT_RE or REDIR_RE` to simply "are there mounts",
which is what finally lets `unzip -d`, `tar -xC` and `git clone <dir>` be covered at all —
widening the OLD scan to those verbs was declined precisely because it would have worsened the
false positives.

**Verified after** — 6 read shapes pass (including the boundary probe), 6 write shapes still
deny (`sed -i`, `cp` into, redirect into, a python `open(...,'w')`, `mkdir`, `tee`).

**An ordering bug in the test file, twice now** — two blocks referenced `fwmod` before the later
definition ran. It reads as a missing import and costs a run each time. The loader is hoisted to
the top beside the other modules, so no future block can reference it too early.

## Wave 19 — the five adapters nobody had ever audited (F19)

The largest single wave of the cycle: thirteen findings across `posttool`, `postfail`,
`precompact-rearm`, `conformance` and `awareness`. Every one verified first-hand before
it was touched — and that verification changed three of them.

### The credential guard was blind to our own key
`SEC1` exists to catch a printed credential. Its Nexus pattern was
`\bnxs_[A-Za-z0-9]{16,}` — **and a real key is `nxs_<1 char>_<32>`**, so the class hits the
SECOND underscore after one character and never reaches the bound. Measured against the
live config: every key shares the `3_1_32` skeleton, and the pattern matched **none of
them**. The three patterns that DID fire — `ghp_`, `xox`, `AKIA` — are all third-party.
**The one credential this layer most exists to protect was the one it could not see**, and
this repo's own documented workspace-write recipe prints it (`curl -u "$KEY:" …`).

Widened the CLASS, not the bound: shortening `{16,}` would start matching prose like
`nxs_key_here`, while `[A-Za-z0-9_]` covers every underscore-segmented variant at once.

**Same check, second hole: it only ever scanned the RESPONSE.** A credential typed INTO a
command is in the transcript exactly as much as one printed by it, and
`git remote set-url origin https://u:TOKEN@…` — the standard way a push credential gets
configured — is a *command*. Now scans both, under the same id and the same once-key,
deliberately not a second check (a second id would double-fire when a command echoes its
own credential).

### The one destructive write in the estate fired on a mention
`pdrop` on `id-cache`, `lifecycle` and `agent-lifecycle` — the R#27 completion gate's
memory — matched the RAW command and never asked whether the delete SUCCEEDED. Measured,
all four erasing rows they should not have:

    nexus agent delete <id>        with {"success":false,"error":{"code":"NOT_FOUND"}}
    echo 'cleanup: nexus agent delete <id>'
    cat <<'EOF' > /tmp/note.md … nexus agent delete <id> … EOF
    nexus agent delete <id> --dry-run

A handover note quoting the cleanup commands, or a 404'd delete that gets retried, and
from that point the agent that still exists — unpublished, unevaluated — is invisible to
the gate. `pdrop` rewrites in place, so it is irreversible.

**The success gate exposed a gap in the shared helper.** `response_failed` did not
recognise `{"success": false}` — the platform's OWN envelope failure marker — nor
`NOT_FOUND`, because its prose alternative is `not found` with a SPACE while the error
CODE carries an underscore. Fixed in the helper rather than at the call site: every feed
using it now credits LESS, which is the direction it already fails in.

### Every failing Bash command was diagnosed as a Nexus platform error
`nexus-postfail.py` gated on the tool being `Bash` and nothing else, then handed the text
to a classifier whose verdicts are all Nexus-specific. Measured LIVE, **3 of 4 non-Nexus
failures got Nexus advice**:

| the command | what it was told |
|---|---|
| a shell script printing `500 rows processed` | "500 = server bug → file a ticket" |
| any program printing `usage:` | "run `nexus <subcommand> --help`" |
| `psql` returning `relation NOT_FOUND` | "the id/key is wrong — re-resolve it" |

The middle row is the tell: **the placeholder is un-substituted**, because there was no
`nexus` in the command to extract one from. The check knew it was out of scope and said so
in its own output. Filing a bogus platform ticket is a named failure in the doctrine this
layer enforces. Now scoped to an actual `nexus` invocation, and `is_interrupt` is honoured
— a command stopped with ESC failed because it was stopped, not because it was wrong.

### Four more, each a guard naming a substring rather than an act
`MAN1` on the raw command (false "you dropped shipped features" on a commit message that
merely mentions pushing), and blind to `cd <repo> && git push` from elsewhere — the case
it was built for. `DG1-LEDGER` firing on `git merge-base` (a read-only query used
constantly during rebases) and on `git merge --abort`, which lands nothing. The
general-context grounding log satisfied by `mkdir -p /tmp/general-context/` and by a
directory LISTING — `files?path=` returns filenames, not content, and it silenced the
R#47 gate.

### The compaction re-read obligation almost never arrives
`PC-CANON` was keyed once per SESSION rather than per compaction epoch, while `pc_epoch`
exists for exactly this and is already used that way one file over. In a long session —
the sessions that compact most — the R#13 obligation was **guaranteed absent after the
first compaction**. Live: **7 sessions hold compaction archives, 39 archives between
them, and only 2 ever wrote the pending file at all.**

A second, separate cause remains open (O27): the re-arm hook renames the very `read-log`
that lifecycle reads to BUILD the obligation, and both are concurrent hooks in the same
PreCompact group. Fixing the key was a one-line correction; fixing the race is a move of
ownership between two files, and it is not a thing to do at the end of a long wave.

### A fresh install got no orientation, ever
`AW4` consumed its once-flag at the TOP of the branch, before any variant was chosen. With
no `~/.nexus-mcp/workspace-mounts.json` — **the state of every new install**, since that
file is created by `nexus workspace mount` — it emitted nothing and could never emit
again. Mounting later bought silence. The flag now guards the emission.

### The conformance checker graded the wrong tree
`CF1` matched the written path by SUBSTRING but always ran the checker with
`--root <this .claude>`. Editing ANY other checkout carrying `skills/nexus-app-builder/`
reported the source tree's violations as "RED after this write" — and the live case is
this repo's own public mirror.

### The guard against all of this could never fire
The sharpest finding. `CHECK 3` in the feed-contract suite is the structural check written
to stop the substring class. **Its subject-capture character class included `)`.** On the
universal call form `re.search(r"…", cmd)` it captured `cmd)`, which is not in its
blacklist, so it matched nothing. It could only ever flag `re.search(r"…", cmd, re.I)` —
a form no call site uses. **It was scanning the file that contained the live MAN1 defect
and reported clean.**

Rewritten three ways: the paren dropped from the class; the blacklist INVERTED to an
allowlist of stripped views, so an unfamiliar subject fails toward being flagged rather
than passing by default; and the scope widened from `git push` to every act verb. Law 1
has two halves — match the ACT on a stripped view, read the OPERANDS from the raw text —
so genuine raw reads declare `# raw-read: <reason>`, which makes the exception visible in
review instead of invisible in an allowlist.

**Running it found seven more live instances**, three of which were real act-decisions
feeding prerequisite gates and are now fixed. That is the check doing, on its first honest
run, what it was written for two waves ago.

### Two of my own fixes were wrong, and the drives caught both
Recorded because the lesson is the method, not the code. The `postfail` scope gate used
`re` in a module that does not import it — **a NameError, so the adapter exited 1, and a
crashed adapter is a guard that does not run**: the exact defect class being fixed one
file over. And `MAN1`'s repo resolution called `resolve_repo` as if it returned a string,
when it returns `(rdir, how)`; the tuple flowed into `os.path.join`, threw, and the whole
block went silent inside its own `try`. Both were invisible in the source and obvious the
moment the hook was driven. Reading a helper's contract is not optional because the helper
is familiar.

## Wave 20 — concurrency: the guard layer went quiet together, and the fix was unpinned (F14)

O13 has said "no concurrency fixture" since it was opened. It is now closed, and closing it
immediately caught a regression this same wave had just introduced.

### Why this is live and not theoretical
**A subagent's hook payload carries the PARENT's `session_id`, verbatim.** Proven two ways: a
marker file read from inside a lane landed in the parent's `read-log`, and there has never been
a single `agent-`prefixed session directory on this machine. So one session's twenty lanes all
share one store, and `PreToolUse`/`PostToolUse` fire for **every subagent tool call**.

The module docstring says *"Session-scoped … so two concurrent Cue sessions never collide"*.
That is true, and it is why nobody looked: it answers a different question than the one that
matters.

### 102 checks failed CLOSED on a single store error
`once()` collapsed *"this already happened"* and *"I could not find out"* into the same `False`.
Every caller is written `if sc.once(...): emit`. So one permissions change, one full disk, one
fd limit reached while twenty lanes each open files — and **the entire guard layer returns exit
0 and does nothing**, for the rest of the session, with no decision row and no trace.

Driven: the same payload against a store directory at mode `0500` produced a different set of
advisories, one check silently swapped for another.

A guard must not fail closed. `once` now returns **True** on a store failure — fire, do not
silence. The worst case is a repeated advisory; the worst case of the old behaviour is a layer
that speaks in none of the cases it should, precisely when concurrency makes those transient
errors likeliest. Not a tri-state (`True`/`False`/`None`): that needs all 102 call sites edited,
and any one missed keeps today's behaviour while looking fixed.

Where a repeat is genuinely expensive — AW4b injects the whole `INDEX.md` verbatim — the caller
uses the new `once_strict`, so the conservative direction is a **visible decision at one call
site** instead of a silent global default at 102.

### The class sweep stopped at the module boundary
W28/E12 closed every read-modify-write *inside* the store and declared the class closed. The
pairs that matter are `get`→mutate→`put` in the **adapters**, and both were unprotected. `put`
being atomic prevents a torn read; it does nothing about a **lost update**.

| lanes | `ws-sizes` entries lost |
|---|---|
| 2 | 0% |
| 8 | 77.5% |
| 20 | **79.0%** |

A step function in lane count — invisible at the concurrency the tests used, severe at the
concurrency the system runs at. The queued turn-end advisories lost 74.5% at 8 queuers. Both
now route through a new locked `sc.update()`.

The lock is a **sidecar**, never the JSON file: `put` replaces that file via `os.replace`, so a
lock held on the old inode is released the instant the rename lands and gives no mutual
exclusion at all.

### Readers were never enrolled, and a dead writer left the feed corrupt
`drop` rewrote in place — `seek(0)` → `writelines` → `truncate` — so between the last two steps
the file is `kept rows + stale tail`. Measured at natural timing: **1 corrupt snapshot in
12,000 reads.** Widened deliberately, one snapshot held **3,669 duplicated rows** and a line
sliced mid-token. If the writer dies in that window the flock is released by process death and
the feed **stays that way**, with no recovery path.

That matters because `has`/`lines` are the completion gate's and AW5's inputs: a short read
makes `has` answer False for a row that IS present — so AW5 fires on a skill that was read, or
the completion gate forgets an obligation. The layer's two worst failure classes, produced by an
ordinary `nexus agent delete` while lanes run. Readers now take a shared lock, and the rewrite
writes a sibling and renames.

### The new fixture caught this wave's own regression on its first run
Moving the rewrite to write-temp-and-rename **broke the E12 fix**: the rewriter locked the
sidecar while the appender still locked the data file, so the two stopped excluding each other
and the appender held the old inode while the rename landed. **124 of 640 appends vanished.**

A lock on a file that `os.replace` swaps out is not a lock. Every writer now contends on the
same sidecar — and there is a deterministic invariant asserting exactly that, because the
behavioural checks are races: they prove the guarantee holds, but as *detectors* they are
probabilistic and a broken build passed one run in three.

### Why the fixture uses processes and not threads
`flock` is per-open-file-description. Two threads in one process sharing a file object do not
contend, so a threaded version of this suite would pass against completely unlocked code — a
test that cannot fail, and the fifth instance of that class in this estate, arriving through a
new door. The children are real `subprocess.Popen` interpreters, because real hooks are.

**Already closed before this report was consumed** — F14-4 (the unbounded `flock`, which would
hang every hook behind a wedged holder) was fixed by the F01 wave's bounded acquire. Recorded,
not re-fixed. F14-3's crash half and F14-4 both remain low-probability by the lane's own honest
measurement (5 of 6 natural kill trials landed in the harmless read phase).

**Battery** — 68 suites, **1423 assertions**, all green. New suite
`tests/test_w28_concurrency.py`: 12 checks, **7 mutations, 7 caught, 0 escaped** — after the
first two runs escaped and showed that my mutation anchor was hitting `plog` instead of `log`
(their bodies are byte-identical and `rfind` takes the last), which is the same
wrong-occurrence error the `mkfs` docstring anchor produced in an earlier wave.

Two of my own changes broke other suites and were caught by the full battery, not by review:
the feed-contract guard did not know `once_strict`/`update` were writers and reported two live
feeds as orphaned, and the AW4 composure test stubbed `once` to open a branch whose guard is now
`is_set` — it had been writing to the real store, so it passed once and would have failed
forever after.

## Wave 21 — one hook wrote one file to the wrong directory, and nine checks went wrong (F12)

The app-build gates had been firing on ordinary hook and doctrine work for a whole cycle. The
cause was not nine predicates. It was one write.

### `nexus vibe app create` provisions no directory, and the hook marked one anyway
`BLDF` dropped the `.nexus-app` app-context marker into `data["cwd"]` on a successful
`nexus vibe app create` — a command that creates an app **on the platform** and provisions no
repo. The skill's own cheatsheet says so in as many words: *"app ONLY — NO repo is
provisioned."*

So the marker landed wherever Cue happened to be standing, and permanently converted that
directory into an app repo for **every future session**. Measured live: a 0-byte `.nexus-app`
at this project's root, dated 2026-07-27, while the real app repo is two levels down at
`vibe/horaire`. From there, `H1`, `SPEC1`, `DL1`, `BLD1` and `BLD3` all fire on hook and
CLAUDE.md edits. The marker is a dot-file of zero bytes and no command removes it.

**And the one arm that would have put it in the right place was dead.** The clone arm matched
`git\.nexus[\w.-]*[:/]` — a literal `git.nexus` host. Every real Nexus org is
`git.<org>.gpt.nexus`; the live remote is `https://…@git.dao.gpt.nexus/vibe/<slug>-preview.git`,
which does not match. So the correct writer never ran, and the incorrect one was the only one
that did.

Fixed both: the create arm writes no marker (the honest artifact at create time is the
`app-repos` registry row, which the same block already wrote and `resolve_repo` already
consumes), and the clone arm now matches the real host shape. **The registry write was lifted
out of the marker guard first** — it had been nested inside it, so removing the wrong write
would have silently taken the correct one with it.

**A test was defending the defect.** `test_w23_hooks.py` asserted *"BLDF drops .nexus-app in
cwd on vibe app create"* — pinning the exact wrong behaviour. A test that asserts a defect is
worse than no test: it argues against the repair. Replaced with the three real contract cases
(no marker at create · the registry row still lands · the clone arm marks a real cloned repo).

### `H1` named a location, not a surface
It gated on "a marker exists somewhere up the tree" and counted **every** Write/Edit, including
`.md` and `docs/`. Its two siblings both exclude docs; H1 was the odd one out. So 25 edits to
`CLAUDE.md` asked for a localhost preview.

The new arm asks whether there is anything to **render** — a `package.json` declaring
`dev`/`start`/`preview`/`serve`. Probed against every real directory here it separates the
three real app builds from the two real non-app cases with no near miss, where the obvious
alternative (a git remote pointing at the vibe host) fails on 2 of 3, because the remote is
wired at `provision-repo`, later than the first source write. The non-Node trade is stated in
the code rather than hidden: a Python or Go app would go silent, and a missed heartbeat costs
far less than the measured cost of an unearned one.

### Three smaller ones, all measured
- **`BAS1` called the platform's own git host a foreign donor forge.** The check that exists to
  flag *"you are building on someone else's foundation"* greeted you on your own hosted app

  adopt-vs-fresh decision it polices.
- **`MIGR1` missed `prisma/schema.prisma`**, the commonest schema file in the Node ecosystem

- **`ACCESS1` rejected the markdown forms its own template invites.** The PRD template presents

The whole point of F12-9 is that `H1`'s false-positive class was invisible to every suite —

                             decisions log: G2  (the loss is invisible)
    TURN 2  guide read, deny obeyed, same command re-issued
                             KB2 emitted: False   ← gone for the rest of the session

`KB2` exists to catch *"first workflow build this session with no community-KB consumption on
record"*. It was **unreachable by construction on its own trigger**. `AW5` went the same way.
And because warn rows are logged after the deny exit, neither appears in `decisions`, so the
volume audit could not see the loss either.

This is the deploy-gate defect from an earlier wave, one level up: there a gate punished
obedience to its own instruction; here a gate consumed its siblings' single shot, and obeying
it destroyed them. The ladder decision now runs **above** the warn block. After:

    TURN 1  decision: deny   flags burned: NONE
    TURN 2  KB2 emitted: True

**Not applied to the other four in-block deny sites**, and the reason is measured, not
cautious: `engine_entry_gate` reads `solo-ack` and `fleet_retrieve_gate` reads `fleetr_<cid>`,
and **the warn block above them writes both**. Hoisting those changes what they see. Same class,
own cycle — O35 carries the dependency map so the next wave does not have to re-derive it.

### The most-invoked adapter paid for an import it uses once a session
`nexus-awareness.py` is wired to four events, so every file the assistant reads pays its cost
twice. It imported `urllib.request` at module scope for a call site reachable **at most once per
session**, inside the boundary-inject branch — and the mount path is tried first, so the REST
fallback often never runs at all.

Measured interleaved: the bare interpreter is 29.3 ms; with the import, 58.1 ms. End-to-end A/B
against the pre-fix file, outputs byte-identical: **53.0 ms → 35.3 ms**. The lane, on a machine
at load 373, measured 2.22x on the adapter and **0.9 s of hook wall-time per realistic turn**.

This refutes the OPEN list's conclusion that the cost is *"mostly interpreter startup, which no
code change removes"*. It was one line. The class sweep found no second instance: every other
module-level import in the five hot adapters measured inside noise, because `site` pre-imports
them.

### A 32 KB command stalled the tool call with nothing to attribute it to
`_envelope_sig`'s `[a-z-]+` before `[^|]*` backtracks catastrophically, and it runs twice per
Bash event. Measured: 4 KB 0.025 s · 8 KB 0.096 s · **16 KB 0.392 s** · 32 KB seconds — and the
lane measured **7.2 s end-to-end** at 16 KB under load. There is no timeout anywhere in the
adapter, so the user sees a hang with no output.

Bounded the class to `{1,40}` (a Nexus resource or action never has a 40-character token) plus an
8 KB short-circuit. 16 KB: **0.392 s → 0.0019 s**, and it still matches a real command. Not
"anchor before `--json`" — `[^|]*` would still scan to end-of-string on the **no-match** path,
which is exactly the path that blows up.

### The litter fix that the earlier sweep missed, and that W28 made worse
`drop`/`pdrop` are no-ops on a feed that does not exist, but both called `_dir`/`_pdir` with
`create=True` — so dropping from a feed never written **manufactured the directory**. That is the
exact "looking at state must not manufacture it" rule the earlier sweep established for the seven
read paths; these two were missed because they look like writes while behaving like reads.
Measured live: **188 of 1081 store directories (17%) are empty.**

**And wave 20 made it worse.** The sidecar lock meant the no-op also left a `.lock` file behind —
so the directory was no longer empty, and the empty-directory count stopped detecting it. Fixing
one defect hid another for two waves.

### What the report refuted, which is as useful as what it found
- **O20** (`P25A`/`KB2` scan the whole read-log) — mechanism confirmed, **live exposure
  refuted**. The largest read-log in the real store is 2,596 lines; at that size the scan is not
  measurable. The filed 2.74 s came from a 100k-line synthetic, 38x past anything observed. The
  read-log is also archived at every compaction, which caps it in exactly the long sessions that
  would otherwise reach 10k lines.
- **O20's proposed fix is unsafe, and this is the most dangerous thing in the report.** Hoisting
  `once()` above the read-log scan makes `P25A` **permanently silent after a compaction** —
  proven by driving both trees through write → real PreCompact → write:

      ORIGINAL  pre-fire=False  flag_spent_pre=False  POST-fire=True
      HOISTED   pre-fire=False  flag_spent_pre=True   POST-fire=False

  `once()` mutates, and the condition above it is **not monotone**: the re-arm hook renames the
  read-log. The change would ship as a performance tweak, remove a doctrine guard invisibly, and
  leave the whole battery green — `P25A` has no compaction fixture. **O20 is closed as
  WONTFIX-AS-FILED**, with the safe alternative (a streaming helper, no `once()` movement)
  recorded. The generalised rule: `once()` may only be hoisted above conditions that are monotone
  for the whole session.
- **O12** (per-Bash floor 264 ms) — overstated: **118 ms** in the window measured.
- **O13's flock** — correct and worth its cost. Same-window A/B: zero rows lost locked, total
  loss unlocked. The unbounded-`LOCK_EX` hazard it names was already closed by the F01 wave.
- **Retention** — the filed projection is **7x low**: 147 dirs on 2026-07-28, 128 by mid-morning
  the next day, against a filed 20-53/day. But growth costs **nothing** at runtime (APFS hashes
  directory entries; measured flat at 940, 10k and 70k siblings), and nothing in the layer ever
  enumerates the store. Not fixed here, and any retention pitch claiming a speed-up would be
  wrong. O36 carries the design, including the trap: a naive 7-day mtime sweep would today delete
  the state of **12 live sessions**, because an ordinary Bash call makes zero store writes.

**Battery** — 68 suites, **1448 assertions**, green. **6 mutations, 6 caught** — after one
escaped because my timing threshold (0.5 s) sat *above* the 16 KB cost (0.39 s) instead of
between the two behaviours. Moved to 32 KB, where the separation is 500x and no machine load
closes it. A timing assertion whose threshold does not separate the cases is a test that cannot
fail.

## Wave 23 — a mention is not an act, and a fourth copy of one pattern (F08)

### Seven checks fired on the contents of files being written
The pretool nudge checks matched the **raw** command, so a heredoc that WRITES a file fired on
the file's contents. Driven: a probe script containing `nexus auth switch`, a recursive grep and
a fetch loop drew `CP1`, `FP1` and `KR1` — three advisories about work that is not happening.

The audit lane hit this live while measuring it, and so did I: the hook fired against my own
probe command mid-measurement. One live incident named an org that **does not exist**, because
the regex group carried a closing quote and comma out of a python list literal (`acme_prod",`).

Writing a fixture, a probe, or a doc that quotes CLI examples is ordinary work in this repo.

This is the "guard names a substring rather than an act" mechanism in its **other** form. The
earlier instances were *anchoring* failures inside one view; this is a **view-selection**
failure — the right view exists and the call site passes the wrong one. Cheaper to fix, easier
to regress, because nothing structurally forces the choice. `CHECK 3` in the feed-contract suite
is what now forces it.

### The first fix was wrong, and driving it is what showed that
Routing the seven through `hc._strip` — the quote-AND-heredoc view — silenced the heredoc case
**and silenced `CP1` and `FP1` on a real command.** Their evidence lives *inside* the quotes: a
workspace URL in `nexus api GET "..."`, a grep pattern, a profile name. Stripping quotes deleted
the very text they match on, trading a false positive for a false negative — the worse direction
for a guard.

The right view is the heredoc-only one, and it already existed with a docstring saying exactly
why: *"Quoted URLs are KEPT (a real curl's URL is quoted)."* Both halves are now pinned — the
real command must still fire all four ids, and every heredoc shape must fire none.

### A fourth private copy of the heredoc pattern, still the pre-fix one
`nexus-pretool.py` carried its own `_HEREDOC_RE`, still requiring a newline immediately after the
delimiter. So it stripped `cat <<'EOF'` but **not** `cat <<'EOF' > file`, `cat <<'EOF' | tee`, or
an indented terminator:

| shape | pretool's copy | canonical |
|---|---|---|
| `cat <<'EOF'` ⏎ body ⏎ `EOF` | strips | strips |
| `cat <<'EOF' > /tmp/x.md` | **leaks** | strips |
| `cat <<'EOF' \| tee /tmp/x` | **leaks** | strips |
| `cat <<-'EOF'` … indented `EOF` | **leaks** | strips |

Redirecting a heredoc into a file is how this repo writes fixtures — and the hook that
*instructs* the model to do that was blind to the shape. The wave that canonicalised this pattern
found three copies and swept them; this one lived in an adapter under a different name and
survived. It now delegates: `_HEREDOC_RE = hc._HEREDOC_RE`. One definition.

### The readability fix had reached one emitter of four
An earlier wave changed the turn-end whisper to one advisory per line. The two PreToolUse
emitters and the PostToolUse emitter still joined with spaces — and those carry **every deny and
every warn** (2,283 `C1` + 859 `TE5` + the rest), while the one that got the fix carries a single
block per turn. The readability improvement was applied to the smallest surface.

Measured before: two advisories arrived as one 748-character run-on paragraph. After: N
advisories, N lines. It costs nothing — a newline replaces two spaces. Nothing pinned any
separator, so the earlier change was itself unprotected; all four emitters are pinned now.

### Verified already-closed, and one deliberately not taken
- **`hook_core._strip`'s escaped-quote leak** (the lane's #1, a `C1` DENY on an ordinary
  `git commit -m "fix \\"the 2>/dev/null note\\""`) — already closed by the F01 wave, which
  recorded the same evidence. Driven to confirm: both commit-message shapes silent, a real
  `ls foo 2>/dev/null` still denied.
- **Emptying the firewall's `allow` reason** — measured cost is real (36 chars on ~43% of every
  Bash call), but it rests on **two unverified assumptions**: that the harness accepts an empty
  `permissionDecisionReason`, and that the model receives an allow-reason at all. The lane could
  not settle the first and said so. That decision is load-bearing — it suppresses the native
  permission prompt — so if an empty reason invalidates it, every in-scope operation falls
  through to a prompt. Not changed on a guess. O37 records both probes.
- **The `C1` widening bought 0 new denies on 96,190 real commands** and added 815 warns. Recorded
  as measurement, not a defect: closing a whitespace-sized bypass is right whether or not anyone
  has walked through it. The terse-later-fires design (a −64% measured saving across the whole
  log) is O38 — it is a cross-cutting emission-shape change, not a fix.

**Battery** — 68 suites, **1456 assertions**, green. **5 mutations, 5 caught, 0 escaped** — and
verified honestly: my first mutation table's detail column was matching the word "FAILED" inside
a check *name*, which made a green baseline look like it was reporting failures. Re-ran one
mutation cleanly and confirmed it reddens exactly the three intended checks. A mutation table
whose "caught" column cannot distinguish a real catch from a broken copy proves nothing.

## Wave 24 — reading the verification script counted as running it (F03)

The push-verification pair had eight defects. The worst is that **the check could be
discharged by reading about it**, and the whole path was untested — proven by a mutation.

### The clearing predicate credited a mention
`render_watch_feed` logged "a deploy was verified" whenever the raw command **contained**
`deploy_watch.sh` anywhere — in quotes, a heredoc, a comment, or as the argument to
`cat`/`ls`/`grep`/`vim`. It ran at PreToolUse, so it recorded *intent*, never a run, and never
read the exit token.

Measured on this session's own store: the feed held **59 rows**; 18 commands contained the
string; **exactly one** invoked it. Corpus-wide the lane measured 77 of 85 occurrences (91%) as
`ls`/`cat`/`grep`/`echo`. Every one of those rows silenced a real obligation for the rest of the
session.

This is the "guard names a substring rather than an act" class in its most dangerous form: the
substring **disarms** a check instead of arming it. And the check's own message *provoked* the
disarming — following it meant opening the script to learn what `<marker>` was, and
`cat …/deploy_watch.sh` cleared the obligation. **The message was a mechanism for silencing
itself.**

The credit now lives at PostToolUse and requires `DEPLOY_WATCH: SERVED`. The exit token is the
only signal in the system that distinguishes *ran* from *typed*, and it already existed.

### The proof this was never tested
The lane's decisive experiment: replace the clearing predicate with `if True:` — every command
in the session counting as a deploy verification, the most complete possible destruction of the
check — and **every suite stayed green.** The existing tests seeded the feed with a direct
`sc.log`, so the predicate that decides what "verified" *means* was completely uncovered. That is
how a 91% false-clear rate sat in the tree under a green battery.

That mutation now goes red, along with six others. It took two rounds: my first pinning pass let
it through, because my new assertion exercised the *pretool* path while the mutation lived in
*posttool*.

### Four of five terminal states cleared the obligation, three of them silently
`H4` read exactly one of the four failure tokens. So `DEPLOY_WATCH: FAILED_EVENT` — the script
saying **the deploy failed** — ended the session with every push-verification check green.

| token | before: H4 spoke | before: obligation | now |
|---|---|---|---|
| `SERVED` | no | cleared | cleared — correct |
| `FAILED_EVENT` | **no** | **cleared** | H4 speaks, calls it a rollback decision, obligation stays open |
| `EVENT_TIMEOUT` | **no** | **cleared** | H4 speaks, obligation stays open |
| `MARKER_MISS` | yes | **cleared** | unchanged text, obligation now stays open |
| `ACCESS_BLOCKED` | **no** | **cleared** | H4 speaks (access answer, not swap answer) |

### `git -C <repo> push` was not a push
The predicate needed `git` and `push` **adjacent**, so the standard out-of-tree spelling matched
nothing: no feed row, no obligation, and no push evidence for any other reader. **27 real
occurrences in the corpus** — and `git -C` is exactly what an agent writes when it is not sitting
in the repo, which the corpus says is the normal case (640 of 645 real pushes carried an explicit
`cd`). A lane that pushed an app that way shipped with zero verification pressure and no record
it happened at all.

Replaced with `push_acts()`, which finds the act **and** its repo in one parse — deliberately,
because a second regex that finds the act without the target is how the wrong-repo class keeps
recurring.

**And it needs two views, which is the lesson from one wave earlier:** the ACT test needs quotes
gone (else `echo 'git push'` is a push), while the `-C` path needs them intact (a real path is
quoted exactly when it contains a space). Matching both on one view loses one of them — measured:
`git -C "/a b/app" push` resolved to no repo at all.

### Both arms answered about the wrong directory
`H2` asked about the payload cwd and `H2-TURN` named the Stop cwd, while 99% of pushes name
their repo in the command. Over 645 real pushes the two answers disagreed on **63 of the 323
resolvable ones (19.5%)** — 46 fires where the pushed repo is not an app, 17 silences where it
is.

**The wrong name is worse than silence:** "you pushed `appB` and nothing has verified it" sends
the reader to check an app they never touched, and when that comes back clean, the real
unverified deploy reads as *confirmed fine* in the transcript.

Rows now carry the repo (`push-log-v3`), and `H2-TURN` reads it. Two pushes to two repos are two
obligations, enumerated by name — before, `max(pushes)` made one obligation per session, so
verifying the last repo silenced all of them. `push-ts` and the once-key are scoped per repo too:
a single push to A followed by a single push to B used to tell the reader they were "re-pushing"
an app pushed exactly once.

**`push-log-v2` keeps being written unchanged and the legacy path is kept:** other readers index
it, rewriting a live feed under fan-out is the data-loss class this estate has already measured,
and a session that began before v3 existed would otherwise go silent for its whole length. Rows
with no repo fall back to the old behaviour — driven and pinned.

### Non-deploying pushes armed a deploy obligation
The response was never read, so a `[rejected]` push, a network failure, an `Everything
up-to-date` no-op, a `--dry-run`, a `--delete` and a tags-only push all created a full obligation
to verify a deploy that was never triggered. A rejected push is followed by a pull-rebase-push
cycle, arming again each time — these are the false positives that cluster exactly where the
reader is already frustrated.

A deny-list of unambiguous non-deploy signatures, not an allow-list of success shapes: a quiet
successful push prints to stderr and its shape is not guaranteed, so the check stays biased
toward firing.

### The instruction pointed at a file that does not exist
Both messages said `run skills/shared/scripts/deploy_watch.sh <url> <marker>`. That relative path
resolves **only** when the cwd is exactly `<project>/.claude` — never from an app repo, which is
the one place these messages are ever emitted. Verified: it is a "No such file or directory" from
any app build.

The absolute path is computable at import (`hooks/` and `skills/` are siblings). The message now
also names `<appId>`, which the script's own header calls out — it is positional argument #6, and
without it the audit poll is org-wide, so **another app's deploy satisfies it**.

**One fixture was encoding the old contract:** the push test's response said `"Everything
up-to-date"`, which means *nothing was pushed*. Arbitrary while the response was never read;
wrong the moment it is.

**Battery** — 68 suites, **1470 assertions**, green. **7 mutations, 7 caught, 0 escaped** — after
a first round where 2 escaped, including the one that matters most.

**Recorded, not fixed:** a Stop-queued nudge is delivered on the *next* prompt, so if the user
reads "pushed, done" and closes the session it is never delivered — and its once-key is already
burned, so it cannot re-queue. That is precisely the shipped-and-walked-away shape this pair
exists for. O39.

## Wave 25 — the rollout safety net could not answer its own question (F05)

The estate's stated safety net for a verdict-bearing check is: **marker present = record
only, marker absent = enforcing.** It could not be trusted to answer "is this check enforcing
right now?", on four independent grounds.

### The measurement window was the only mode throwing the sample away
`ACCESS1` and `BLD2` rate-limited themselves to **one row per session per repo — on the
observe branch only.** Enforce had no limiter at all. Driven, 30 identical violations in one
session:

    ACCESS1  ENFORCE  N=30  rows={'deny': 30}
    ACCESS1  OBSERVE  N=30  rows={'warn': 1}

That is the exact inversion. The window that exists to MEASURE a check was the one mode
discarding 29 of 30 observations — and non-uniformly, once per session x repo, so a heavy
user is undercounted more than a light one. A window that discards most of its sample is
worse than no window: it produces a number that looks like data, and a promotion decision
reads exactly that number. The limiter is defensible in enforce (nobody wants a nag loop);
in observe it destroys the thing being collected. Noise during a rollout window is what the
window is for.

### The log could not separate the two states for 6 of 9 markers
Three distortions, in three different directions:

| | distortion |
|---|---|
| `ACCESS1` / `BLD2` | observe undercounts **30:1** (the limiter above) |
| `RM1` / `RM1B` | enforce **overcounts 2:1** — the arm logged, then `emit()` logged again, so one event wrote two rows in enforce and one in observe |
| `BLD2` | its would-deny row and its ordinary card-present advisory were **byte-identical** — the live store's single `BLD2 warn` row cannot say which branch produced it |

Fixed: one event, one row, whichever mode is on; and the observe row gets its own id
(`BLD2-OBS`).

### One id, two checks, two classes, both wired
`WSW-RET` was the firewall's **DENY** on a dav PUT *and* the pretool's **advisory warn**, and
both adapters are wired to `PreToolUse:Bash`, so both run on the same command. The registry
lists `WSW-RET` in the blocking tier only — so an analyst reading the live store's three
`WSW-RET warn` rows concludes the blocking check was downgraded to observe. **It never was.**
This estate already treats a *prefix* overlap as a defect class (it cost one mis-attribution
of 10 rows); an exact collision across two classes is worse. The advisory is now `WSW-RETN`.

### Three markers had no test at all, and one adapter attributed its rows to the wrong session
`.lp1-observe`, `.pw1-observe` and `.conformance-observe` appear in no test file. Proven by
mutation: inverting LP1's observe semantics left every suite naming LP1 green, against a red
control on RM1. So a refactor of the marker read was free to invert them and the suite would
certify the result.

`nexus-conformance.py` was the only adapter keying its rows on `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID`
rather than the payload, while every sibling reads `data["session_id"]`. With the variable
unset, every row pools into a session literally named `unknown` — a valid directory name, so
an entire observe window becomes unattributable and **fails silently**. Latent today, one
harness change from live.

### The corollary the design was hiding
**A warn-class check has no meaningful observe state.** There is no enforcement to withhold,
so "observe" can only be a no-op or a silencing — and silencing a warning is not observing
it, it is disabling it. Measured: for LP1 and PW1 the observe flag's *entire* effect was
appending ` [observe]` to identical text. They have been fully live the whole time; the marker
was a label that misdescribed the check's state.

The honest resolution is not to pick a semantic for them. It is that warn-class checks do not
get markers — their rollout gate is the promotion **to** deny, at which point a marker means
something for the first time.

### The new suite is table-driven off source, deliberately
`tests/test_w28_observe_markers.py` enumerates every `.<name>-observe` literal the adapters
reference and requires each to be either driven there or listed in `WARN_CLASS` **with its
reason**. A tenth marker cannot be added without one or the other — proven: adding one to
the source goes red immediately. A per-check test cannot give that property.

**Battery** — 69 suites, **1494 assertions**, green. **6 mutations, 6 caught, 0 escaped.**

## Wave 26 — the layer disagreed with the doctrine it enforces (F15)

An audit of hook-vs-doctrine agreement. Two divergences were live and costly.

### `WSW` denied exactly what R#39 blesses — and the skill said it didn't
The mount-write arm denied **every** `Write`/`Edit` under a mount root. Its own message
justifies the deny with **bulk** ("bulk mount writes wedge and phantom-fail"), and three
doctrine locations bless the case it was blocking:

- CLAUDE.md R#39: *"Mount = **single interactive edits** + READS"*
- the workspaces SKILL: *"the mount is for READS + **a single interactive edit only**"*
- the same file, naming WSW's scope: *"never **loop** … over `mountPath`; the WSW firewall denies it"*

So a reader who consulted the governing doc was told the operation is both correct and
permitted, and was then denied. Fixing one typo in one general-context file — the most
ordinary workspace operation there is — was blocked.

**And the redirect made it more dangerous, not less.** It pushed a low-risk anchored edit
onto `curl -X PUT --data-binary @file`: a **whole-file replace**, the exact primitive
R#35 #4 exists to prevent, on the org's most confidential store.

This is the recurring class in its third form. The earlier instances named a substring
instead of an act; this one names a **LOCATION** (under a mount root) instead of the act it
cares about (a bulk write loop).

A single `Write`/`Edit` tool call is by construction not a loop — the loop lives in Bash,
which the Bash arm still denies. So the arm now **counts**: edits 1-2 pass with the
REST-verify reminder (`WSW-EDIT`), the batch denies from the third, and the Bash loop is
untouched. The wedge is a bulk-I/O phenomenon, so a counter is the honest predicate. Driven:

    edit #1 -> warn      edit #3 -> deny
    edit #2 -> warn      edit #4 -> deny      Bash loop -> deny

Not "fix the docs to say no mount writes at all": the docs describe a real, verified
property. Rewriting three doctrine locations to match a guard broader than the hazard trades
a correct rule for a convenient one — and would route every single-file correction through
an unguarded whole-file PUT.

### The leak backstop covered 9 ids of about 100
`scan_leak` is the deterministic backstop for *"never emit hook codes to the user"*. It
enumerated bracketed ids **literally**, and the list never grew with the layer:

- **13 of its 20 alternatives named ids no adapter can emit** — the decommissioned judge
  layer, never pruned when it went.
- It was blind to **every DENY-class id**, which are precisely the messages a model relays:
  a deny stops the turn, so the user is owed an explanation. `[STOP-WAKE]` was invisible —
  and that one is *literally a block reason the model is being asked to answer*.
- Suffix-blind: `[C1B]` and the whole `[R34-DUE]` / `[R34-LEDGER]` family missed.

It fired on the three ids a meta-session mentions and stayed silent on the ninety it exists
for — which reads, from the log, as a working backstop.

Replaced with a **shape**: a line-leading bracketed SCREAMING-KEBAB token. Still a pure
identifier match, no wording judgment, and **closed under new ids** — which is the property
that failed. The line-leading anchor keeps the narrowness promise: an inline `R#47` in a
doctrine discussion still does not match. Driven: 13 of 13 ids caught, 4 of 4 ordinary
sentences silent.

Not "add the 91 missing ids": that re-creates the maintenance debt that produced this, and
it has already failed twice here — once in this alphabet and once in the registry. A list
must be edited whenever a check is added; a shape need not be.

### R#18's gate was two commands short, and both matter
The rule names five command classes verbatim; `deployment create` and `version publish` were
backed by nothing. `deployment create` is the command that puts an agent on a **live customer
channel** — WhatsApp, Slack, a phone number — and the deployments skill holds the per-channel
body shapes. And `version publish` was unguarded **the moment its eval prereq was satisfied**,
so one eval anywhere in the session unlocked publishing any version with no skill loaded.

Writing the test surfaced that second half precisely: on a virgin store the ladder denies
`version publish` before any warn runs (correct, and a consequence of the wave-22 hoist), so
the gap only appears once the prereq is met — which is exactly what the report describes.

### Three record-level corrections
- The registry listed `RM1`/`RM1B` as gated by `.rm1-observe` / `.rm1b-observe`, i.e.
  record-only. **Neither marker exists** — not on disk, not in git — so by the registry's own
  rule both are ENFORCING. The table described a state that does not exist.
- A comment in the lifecycle adapter described an **abandoned first cut** ("it must be the
  whole final line"), contradicted by the code twelve lines below and by the CHANGELOG entry

- A cross-doc citation quoted `"## Resident mode"` where the heading is

## Wave 27 — the layer over a long session, end to end (F16)

Three full sessions simulated against the real adapters — 593 events, 831 adapter
invocations. The verdict is worth stating before the defects: **zero crashes, zero
tracebacks, zero unparseable output in 831 invocations**, and only 4.5–21% of invocations
inject anything at all. This is not a chatty layer, and the resilience work holds.

The problem is concentrated. **Two checks produced most of the layer's authority, and both
were structurally wrong** — 4 of the 5 denies in one session came from a single misfiring
check, and 23 of 28 turn-ends were blocked, 8 of them carrying byte-identical text.

### An app-deploy gate denied a push that deploys nothing
`ACCESS1`, `BLD2` and `H2-TURN` all trigger on *"a `git push` from a repo carrying
`docs/PRD.md`"*. Their sibling `H2` excludes public-forge remotes — an exclusion added
because of a measured false fire — and **the sweep never reached the other three**, one of
which sits twelve lines away.

Measured: **4 of 4 pushes in one session denied, 2,744 characters, the same message each
time.** A user's app repo very often has a GitHub origin as well as a vibe remote, and a
library or skills repo that happens to carry a PRD has *only* the GitHub one. Pushing source
to GitHub is not deploying a hosted app, so *"Every hosted app is PRIVATE by default"* and
*"nothing has verified what is now SERVED"* are factually wrong about what just happened.

And it is a DENY, so the push stops and the documented escape is an override flag. **That is
how a deny gate becomes a prefix people type without reading** — at which point the gates
that are right stop being read too.

Same class as the rest of this cycle, in its location-not-act form: the guard named *"a repo
with a PRD, and `git push` appears"* rather than *"this push reaches the platform that hosts
the app"*. `app_repo_ctx` already answers "is this an app repo", correctly; the missing
predicate is a property of the **remote**. Fail direction is preserved: an unreadable remote
keeps the gate armed, so this can only remove a false deny on a remote positively identified
as a forge.

### `NT1` asserted the opposite of the response it was handed
The node-test flag was set on every `workflow node test` and cleared **only** by a later
`execution node-result`. The node test's own response carries
`{"executionId":…,"status":"COMPLETED"}` — and was never read. So the documented-correct loop
(test a node, read COMPLETED, test the next) warned **from the second node onward, forever**,
on the single most common thing a user does here.

Measured: 8 node tests in one session produced 6 warns; an isolated 3-call probe produced 2.
Every response said `COMPLETED`. **It fired into this audit's own transcript while the defect
was being reproduced.**

The race it names is real, so the check stays — the defect was that it ignored the one signal
that settles it. Fail direction: an unparseable or absent status leaves the flag set, so a
genuinely open async test still warns. Driven: three `COMPLETED` tests are silent, a
`RUNNING` one still warns on the next.

### Everything the final Stop produced was computed and then dropped
Stop advisories are queued and delivered at the **next** `UserPromptSubmit`. A session whose
last event is a Stop — **every session that ends** — loses them. Measured: one session ended
with 2 advisories and 655 characters undelivered, and the dropped one was `H2-TURN` on the
**last push of the session**. That check exists precisely for *"a session that pushes ONCE
and ends"*; its delivery channel dropped it at the only moment it is uniquely valuable.

Now: when the turn is being blocked anyway, the queued advisories ride out on the block
reason — it costs nothing, the text is already in hand. When nothing blocks, a **narrow
class** surfaces via `systemMessage`.

Deliberately narrow. Routing every advisory there would put an `R#34` housekeeping self-check
in front of the user at every single turn end — trading a dropped warning for constant noise,
which is how a channel stops being read. Only the shipped-something-unverified class
surfaces, because that is where the user owns the consequence and the session may be over.

### The worst moment was a compaction, and most of it was noise
At a compaction the layer injected **5,164 characters in one turn** — 27% of a whole
session's volume — at the exact moment the model's context has just been destroyed. Of that,
**4,551 characters were a map of every skill in the repo**, alphabetical, several rows
truncated mid-word.

The load-bearing fact was one string: *re-read `nexus-app-builder`*. `PC-CANON`, twelve lines
earlier, had already named it exactly. The map's own framing concedes the redundancy — *"the
gates will force the re-read — this tells you WHICH"* — so its entire value is telling you
which, and it answered that by listing all of them.

Now filtered to what the session actually loaded: **4,551 characters → 477** for a one-skill
session, and **nothing at all** when no skill was loaded.

**Battery** — 69 suites, **1530 assertions**, green. **9 mutations, 9 caught, 0 escaped.**

### Four of my own errors, all caught by driving rather than reading
1. **`subprocess` was not imported in the library**, so my new forge check hit its own
   `except` and returned "deploying" for every input — including GitHub. The fail-open
   direction hid the bug perfectly: every case looked plausible.
2. **I patched the wrong function.** The gate emitting `BLD2` was `engine_entry_gate`, not
   the `deploy_gate` I had scoped; the forge push still denied until I looked at which
   function actually spoke.
3. **The compaction map was computed after the read-log was archived** — the map is now
   filtered *by* that log, so it would have silently produced the empty set, and the empty
   set means "print nothing". Order matters when a fix reads state the same function
   destroys.
4. **An empty set is falsy.** Conflating "no skills loaded" with "unknown history" made a
   session that loaded nothing fall through to the full 21-skill map — the exact case that
   should print nothing. That is the None-means-broad versus `[]`-is-a-positive-claim
   distinction this estate already pays for elsewhere.

And two testing errors of the same shape as earlier waves: a mutation battery that reported
**7 catches against a red baseline** (the copy has no sibling `skills/` tree, so the map was
empty for a reason unrelated to the filter — rewritten to run in-process against a fabricated
tree), and a **source-text assertion** that stayed true when the branch it described was
mutated to `if False:`. A source-text check cannot see a disabled branch.

**Verified already closed:** `CF1`'s session attribution (wave 25) — the report's S5. And the
report confirms an earlier fix held: 72 doctrine edits across three sessions produced **zero**
app-gate fires, so the "any repo containing `.claude/` is an app build" defect stays closed.

**Recorded, not fixed:** `STOP-WAKE` arm 2's only exit is a claim the predicate cannot
observe — the adapter's own comment concedes it, and arm 1 got a writable token while arm 2
shipped without one (O46). Twelve check ids emit with no decision row, and the ladder writes
comma-joined ids into a field the registry says must be matched exactly (O47).

## Wave 28 — the layer as read by someone who did not write it (F17)

The final report of the cycle judged the MESSAGES, not the predicates: 143 of them, scored as
a competent engineer would read them with no rule book open and nothing to look up mid-task.

Its headline measurement is the one that matters: **mean DENY message 226 characters, mean
advisory 212.** The layer did not scale message length to consequence — a catastrophic block
and a "you might want to check the KB" nudge were the same size.

### The four catastrophic denies were the four shortest messages in the estate
`FORKBOMB` (26 chars), `DISKWRITE` (30), `SIP` (42), `PROT-ROOT` (50). Three defects each:

- **They carried no check id.** The only four messages in the layer without one — and the id
  is the sole handle into the registry and the decision log, so the log and what the reader
  saw could not be correlated by anyone holding either.
- **Every one promised a corrected form.** `emit()` appended *"The corrected form can run
  immediately in this turn"* unconditionally. For these there **is** no corrected form: the
  act is refused, not its spelling. A reader taking that at face value hunts for a variant
  that passes — which for a raw disk write means **trying variants of a raw disk write.**
- **Brevity taught the wrong thing.** These are the highest-stakes verdicts the layer issues,
  transmitted in fewer characters than a routine dashboard-link annotation. Short reads as
  unimportant, so the reader skims and re-tries — precisely what a catastrophic guard must
  not train.

All four now open with their id, state what matched and why there is no variant, and name a
real alternative (`xargs -P` for parallel work, Disk Utility for imaging, `xattr -d` for one
quarantined file, the specific subdirectory for a delete). `emit()` takes `recoverable`;
recoverable denies keep the clause, because the bug was that it was unconditional, not that
it existed. `PROT-ROOT`'s missing sentence terminator — which ran the interpolated path into
the next sentence, so a reader copying it got `…tmp.QMpSMjGJtR The` — is fixed with it.

### One message's recovery instruction was a data hazard
`WSW` told the reader to write server-side and take the *"key from `~/.nexus-mcp/config.json`"*.
**That file holds nine profiles, each with its own `apiKey`, plus an `activeProfile` field.**
The obvious reading — a first-match grep — returns whichever profile is lexically first, not
the active one. And the act being redirected to is a **workspace overwrite**.

So following the recovery path literally performs a cross-org write with the wrong org's
credentials. That failure is on this project's record already. **A deny whose recovery
instruction causes harm is worse than a deny with none.** The message now indexes by
`activeProfile`, says in the same breath that a grep picks a different org's key, and adds
the relative-path requirement that six messages teach and none of them stated.

### The only turn-blocking check had an undocumented kill switch
`NEXUS_WAKE_ACK=1` disables `STOP-WAKE` entirely, and it appeared in **exactly one file in
the repository — the adapter that reads it.** No message named it, no doc listed it. Compare
`NEXUS_RM_ACK` (2 files) and `NEXUS_GATE_ACK` (5).

A guard whose escape is undiscoverable is a guard people route around, and the route they
find is not "disable this check" — it is **deleting the hook from `settings.json`**. The
three exits the message did offer are all *compliance* exits; there was no disclosed way to
say "this check is wrong here".

Unlike the other four ACKs this is read from the hook **process environment**, not the
command text, so a turn cannot set it — the honest route is the `env` block in
`.claude/settings.json`, and the message and README now say so.

Exit (c) had a second defect: it said *"name it as `lane-owes:<id>`"* without saying **where**.
The code reads the outgoing reply. The one exit that needed a specific place was the one that
did not name it.

### Five DENY gates were silently overridable and none said so
`NEXUS_GATE_ACK=1` downgrades every ladder deny to a nudge. Two *other* checks honouring the
same variable tell the reader; these five did not.

The asymmetry is worse than either uniform choice. A reader who learns the override from one
gate correctly assumes it generalises; a reader who never meets that gate believes the ladder
is absolute and restructures work around something a colleague waves through. **Two people,
same layer, incompatible mental models** — and the decision log cannot tell them apart,
because a downgraded gate logs as a nudge.

**Battery** — 69 suites, **1560 assertions**, green. **7 mutations, 7 caught, 0 escaped.**

**Three fixtures were encoding the old wording** and each is worth naming, because two were
proxies that stopped being valid rather than assertions that were wrong:
- one asserted the false recovery sentence was present;
- one asserted the exact phrase "Three legal exits";
- one detected prompt injection by asserting **no newline anywhere in the block** — a fair
  proxy while the message was a single line, and broken the moment the message deliberately
  became four. It now asserts the real property: an injected subject cannot **start a line of
  its own**, which is what a forged `[SYSTEM] …` directive needs to read as the hook's own
  output.

**My own error, twice in one edit:** a scripted sweep that appended the override clause to
five messages by slicing "from this row to the next row start" put one clause **inside a
comment** and missed `G14` entirely, because the row it sliced ran past a comment block. The
count said 5. Verified by driving all five gates and counting occurrences, which is how both
were found.

**Verified already closed:** `G19`'s bare-environment-assignment bypass (`PORT=3000 npm run
dev`) — fixed in wave 18; all five shapes deny. And the report's own "fourth instance of the
substring/act class" in the pretool nudges — fixed in wave 23.

**Recorded, not fixed:** six citations name paths that do not resolve from the project root

ids each mean two or three different things, so the telemetry that exists "to promote warns
to denies on data" is aggregating unrelated events (O49). And 56 of 143 messages cite `R#nn`
