## Wave 29 — three owner arbitrations, and a method that beat mine (2026-07-29)

Not an audit report. Three questions I had raised as blockers, two answered by the owner and
one **answered by the owner running an experiment I had said was impossible.**

### The question I had closed as unanswerable
I recorded that I could not determine whether a subagent receives the project `CLAUDE.md`,
because a subagent's assembled context cannot be inspected from outside it. Fifteen of
twenty-three agent definition files contain no rule references at all, which I read as
evidence they might not have the rule book.

**The owner determined it in about twenty minutes.** The move: you do not need to *see* the
context — you ask a reader who has it whether a specific string is in it. Two probes
(`general-purpose` and `Explore`) were dispatched with one hard constraint: **answer from
your starting context only, do not read or open any file.** That constraint is the entire
experiment; without it a probe simply opens the file and answers a different question.

Result: both received `CLAUDE.md` verbatim, injected in a `<system-reminder>` headed
`# claudeMd`. Both quoted `R#30` in full — including its trailing table — with no file
access, and resolved `R#13` and `R#48` the same way.

**So my premise was false, and the 15-of-23 measurement was measuring the wrong surface.**
Agent definitions do not define rules because the rule book is delivered separately by the
platform. Their silence says nothing about what their readers hold.

**The concern survives at a sharper boundary, which the probes drew unprompted:** the rule
TEXT reaches them; the things rules POINT AT do not. No check registry, no skill documents,
no other agents' definitions. So a bare `(R#30)` resolves — and `[G19]`, a file pointer, and
an in-group story name do not, for that reader or any other.

**The generalisable rule, now measured rather than assumed:** *a citation is only as good as
the document sitting in the reader's context, and a hook's reader routinely holds less than
you do.*

**And the method, which is the more valuable half:** when the mechanism cannot be observed,
observe what it produces. Twice in this cycle that shape settled a question that looked
closed — here, and the canary file that proved a block actually blocked. **"I have no way to
find out" is very often "I have no way to find out DIRECTLY",** and the indirect route is
usually cheap. I had stopped at the first form and filed a blocker.

Acting on it: the three in-group story references are gone from the ladder messages,
replaced by the lesson each one taught (`ships a shell that passes publish and fails at
runtime`; `looks finished and does nothing`; `the buttons do nothing and the environment is
lost on restart`). A name that resolves for nobody who was not present resolves for nobody —
including, within a week, the person who named it.

### The hold is conversation-scoped, and its expiry now speaks
Owner's arbitration, verbatim: *"all these flags MUST be on specific conversation and not
across all of them"*, and a hold that expires *"must be then back to the conversation and the
person has to re-ask to keep it off or ok to lift it"*.

Both halves were wrong in the code. The durable flag was PROJECT-scoped — a hold set in one
conversation silenced every other conversation in the project, which is the same bleed
retired once before under a different name. And the 24-hour expiry was **silent**: it wrote a
model-facing decision row, so the one party never told was the person whose instruction was
being overridden.

Filing is silent by contract, and that is exactly why the LIFT cannot be: resuming without a
word is indistinguishable from ignoring the instruction. The project flag is now read-only
legacy — honoured while fresh, expired when stale, written by nothing — and the conversation
flag is the only channel a hold is set through. On expiry the person is told, in their own
turn, and asked whether to re-state it.

Driven: a fresh hold suppresses; a 30-hour hold clears from disk, says so, and filing
resumes; a conversation hold suppresses and never expires.

### One stray file removed, one escalated rather than moved
The hook-created `.nexus-app` at the project root is deleted — it was mine to clean up.

The `docs/PRD.md` was approved for moving and **I did not move it.** The destination already
holds a different PRD for the same app, four minutes older, and the two carry **contradictory
access decisions**: the root copy says `Access: PRIVATE — group dao-horaire`, the destination
says `Access: PUBLIC + in-app auth` quoting the owner directly. Everything else in both files
is identical, including the sign-off.

That is not a duplicate to resolve by timestamp. It is the security posture of a live app,
and an approval given without sight of the conflict is not an approval to overwrite. Raised
rather than actioned.

**Battery** — 69 suites, **1568 assertions**, green. 2 mutations on the new hold behaviour,
both caught.

## Wave 30 — a hypothesis that was wrong, and the real defect underneath it (iteration 3 opens)

Iteration 3's fleet was dispatched and five lanes died immediately on a weekly API limit
before doing any work. Nothing was lost — no lane had written anything. One lane was
re-dispatched as a probe once the account was refreshed; the rest follow when it lands.

Meanwhile, main-loop work on the defect the owner felt directly this cycle: **"why do I have
to tell you to continue here?"**

### The hypothesis, and why it was wrong
I had diagnosed it in conversation as: my task sits `in_progress`, and the turn-end wake
check reads `in_progress` as "work is happening" and stays silent. So the one guard that
exists to catch a turn ending with owed work cannot see the commonest shape of owed work.

**Driven, that is false.** `board_state` returns the `in_progress` rows in their own bucket
and `unblocked` empty, which is exactly what arm 2 is FOR — "no unblocked task, but work has
happened". Arm 2 fired correctly across a 12-turn fixture.

My first attempt to reproduce the silence DID reproduce it — and it was **my fixture's
fault**: the synthetic transcript rows carried no `timestamp` field. That is worth recording
rather than quietly deleting, because a fixture artifact that confirms a prior hypothesis is
the most expensive kind of wrong, and the only reason it did not stand is that the next step
was to check the artifact rather than write the fix.

### The real defect it exposed
`tools_since_last_task_op` counts an unparseable-timestamp row **only while no task-op has
been recorded yet**:

    if (ts is None and not last_task_op_ts) or (ts is not None and ts > last_task_op_ts):

So once the board has been touched even once — which it has, in any session that tracks work
at all — every row whose timestamp does not parse is skipped in silence.

**The failure that opens:** if the harness ever renames or reformats its timestamp field,
`_entry_ts` returns None for every row, the count is 0 forever, and **STOP-WAKE's second arm
dies for the rest of every session** — with no decision row, no message, and nothing
distinguishing it from a session where no work happened. It is the silent-payload-dependency
class this cycle has found repeatedly, sitting on the one check the operator actually feels.

**Fix:** if NOTHING in the tail parses, treat timestamps as unavailable and fall back to the
no-task-op behaviour — count the work. A guard must fail toward FIRING: the cost of being
wrong is one extra nudge, against the cost of losing the whole arm. When timestamps do parse
this changes nothing, which is the property the second mutation pins.

    timestamps parse            board touched long ago -> 20 | just touched -> 0
    format changed (none parse) board touched long ago -> 20 | just touched -> 20

**Battery** — 69 suites, **1572 assertions**, green. 2 mutations, 2 caught: removing the
fallback, and making it fire unconditionally (which would break the normal case).

**Still open on the wake path**, unchanged by this: arm 2's only exit is a claim the
predicate cannot observe (O46), and arm 1's board signature is what bounds its budget.

## Wave 31 — an interpreter's payload is code, and `allow` is worse than a miss (G01)

Iteration 3's first lane came back with nine findings. Two were severe enough to fix
immediately; one of them is the worst defect this whole cycle has produced, and one is mine.

### Wrapping a destructive command in `bash -c` turned a hard DENY into an ALLOW
The keyword view strips quoted spans, because quoted text is usually prose. `candidates()`
does NOT — it has reached inside quotes for PATHS whenever an interpreter is present since
it was written (its `elif interp` branch).

So `bash -c "<recursive delete of the project>"` showed the firewall a protected path with
no destructive verb attached. That reads as an ordinary in-scope filesystem operation, and
the terminal branch answers `allow`.

**`allow` is worse than a miss: it suppresses the native permission prompt.** So the wrapper
did not merely evade the guard — it AUTO-APPROVED deleting the project directory. Measured,
all four catastrophic denies evaded identically:

    plain delete of project    deny        bash -c wrapped    ALLOW
    fork bomb, wrapped         ALLOW       sh -c wrapped      ALLOW
    raw disk write, wrapped    ALLOW       zsh -c wrapped     ALLOW
    protection-disable wrapped ALLOW

The asymmetry sat inside one function call of itself: paths reached into quotes, verbs did
not. Eleventh instance of the substring-not-act class, in its wrong-view shape.

Fixed by lifting the interpreter's `-c`/`-e` payload into the keyword view. All seven forms
now deny; ordinary interpreter work is untouched.

**Three wrong attempts before the right one, each caught by driving:**
1. Scanning every quoted span of the RAW command — re-imports heredoc BODIES, which are
   content being written, not code being run.
2. Scanning quoted spans of the stripped command — a bare `'([^']*)'` pairs quotes ACROSS
   NEWLINES, so one quote in a multi-line command swallows everything to the next.
3. Appending the payload with a SPACE — every verb test in the file anchors on a COMMAND
   POSITION, so the verb sat after `-c` and the recursion test rejected it. The payload
   reached the keyword view and the deny still did not fire. It is appended with `; `
   because the payload IS a separate command.

Attempts 1 and 2 were each caught by **the live hook denying the probe that was testing
them** — the guard under repair refusing the repair's own test, twice.

### An advisory was emitting a decision value the harness does not accept
`WSW-EDIT` — my own wave-26 change — called `emit("warn", ...)`, which printed
`permissionDecision: "warn"`. That is the only such value in the tree and it is outside the
accepted set. Every other advisory in the layer travels as `additionalContext`; this one now
does too, and a check asserts no `emit()` call passes a non-decision verdict.

### Two of my own testing errors, both the shapes this cycle keeps recording
- The first spelling of that last assertion **matched the COMMENT explaining the fix**, so it
  reported a defect that had already been repaired. A source-text assertion failing in the
  other direction: prose describing a call reads the same as a call.
- The regression case meant to separate a raw scan from a heredoc-stripped one took THREE
  corrections before it could fail: no interpreter outside the heredoc (so the lift never
  ran), then a quoted path that was not the protected one (so lifting it changed nothing).
  A case that cannot distinguish the two builds is not a regression case.

**Battery** — 69 suites, **1588 assertions**, green. 4 mutations, 4 caught.

**From the same lane, verified and NOT yet fixed** — recorded rather than rushed:
`rm_targets` returns `None` for any `$VAR` target and the caller then blames the broad

## Wave 32 — four more from G01, and one of them was my own scoping that never scoped

Continuing through the same lane's report rather than stopping at the two severe ones.

### `dd of=/dev/null` was refused outright
The raw-disk pattern matched `of=/dev/` — **every device node**. So `dd of=/dev/null`, the
most ordinary idiom there is, used to time a read or discard output, was denied at
`recoverable=False`: *"there is no accepted spelling, do it outside the session."* Same for
`/dev/zero`, `/dev/urandom`, `/dev/stdout`.

The hazard is a BLOCK device — a partition table with no undo. Character devices destroy
nothing and are now excluded by name. Verified both directions: five character devices pass,
four block devices still deny.

### A work root of `/` matched nothing at all
`under(path, root)` tested `path.startswith(root + "/")`. With `root == "/"` that looks for a
leading `//`, so it answered **False for every path**. Any guard keyed on "is this inside a
protected root" went silent for a root-scoped configuration.

**A guard that answers False for all input is indistinguishable from a guard that is
working** — which is the same shape as the leak backstop that covered 9 ids of 100, and the
structural check whose capture class swallowed a closing paren.

### The mount-edit budget never scoped — and my fix for it did not either
The per-mount key was **computed and then not used**: the counter read one global feed. So
two edits to `general-context` denied a first edit to `tools`, while doctrine blesses a
single interactive edit **per mount**. Dead code that looked like scoping — my own wave-26
change.

**My first fix keyed on the file basename**, giving every file its own budget, so the batch
it exists to stop never tripped. Caught immediately by the existing batch test going red. It
now keys on the mount root the path belongs to, and both properties are pinned: a first edit
in a second mount is not denied by the first mount's budget, and each mount still denies its
own third edit.

That is twice in two waves that a scoping fix of mine was scoped to the wrong thing. The
pattern worth naming: **when a fix introduces a key, the test must vary the dimension the key
is supposed to separate** — two mounts, not two files.

### The workspace-write gate watched one of four spellings
`-X PUT` was the only upload form recognised. `curl` has three more that do exactly the same
thing — `--request PUT`, and `-T` / `--upload-file`, which imply a PUT without naming one —
and the slug class excluded any slug carrying an underscore or a capital.

A gate that watches one of four spellings of the same act is a gate on the spelling. All six
write forms now reach it; both read forms still do not.

**Battery** — 69 suites, **1613 assertions**, green. 4 mutations, 4 caught.

## W33 — the roster nudge could not report a build that was never judged

Found by driving a LIVE app build (`vibe/stock`) rather than by reading source: two executor
dispatches, a valid card asking for `assessor=20 · reviewer=7 · taste=1`, twenty-one recorded
source writes, zero judging seats fired — and nothing said, anywhere.

**F1 — the falsy-zero gate.** `ROSTER1(b)` (Stop) was gated on `_last_judge`, the epoch of the
newest judging dispatch. That value is `0` when nothing has ever judged, and `0` is falsy, so
the arm could only report a build ALREADY judged once and then drifted. The case it exists for
— an executor wave with the council never opened — was the one case it could not see. Same
shape as the push check that could only catch the SECOND push.

Its sibling `ROSTER1(a)` (SubagentStop) DOES fire in that case and does not help: an
`additionalContext` emitted at SubagentStop is delivered to the STOPPING CHILD as its next
input (probe-verified in this adapter, a 17-stop cascade). Every other emission on that path is
deliberately written as a corrective addressed to the child; ROSTER1's text says "fire the
missing seats", which only the parent can act on. So the two arms missed in complementary ways:
the one that fires when nothing has judged talks to the wrong party, and the one that talks to
the parent needed something to have already judged.

**F2 — found by the test written for F1: the window was empty by construction.** The gap was
measured "since the newest judging dispatch", and seats fired after the newest seat is zero by
definition — so immediately after a COMPLETE council round the arm reported the ENTIRE roster
as missing. A false positive on the one build that had done everything right. `app-src-writes`
rows carry no timestamp, so a real "writes since the judge" window cannot be expressed here;
the gap is now measured over the whole build, which is both answerable and the useful question
(are all the seats this card asks for fired yet?). The once-key is the GAP's own digest, so the
nudge repeats only when the shortfall changes rather than once per judging epoch.

**Method note.** The first version of the test read the hook's STDOUT, saw nothing, and nearly
recorded the arm as dead when it was merely deferred — the Stop path QUEUES its advisories to
`stop-pending` for the next turn. The observable has to be the surface the mechanism actually
writes. Also corrected mid-diagnosis: `consolidation-ran-log` was cited as proof that
SubagentStop fires, and it has THREE writers including one at dispatch time; the single-writer
proof is the `consolidation_ran` session flag (present in 38 sessions).

**Tests:** `tests/test_w33_roster_never_judged.py`, 8 assertions, self-contained fixture (no
dependence on a live session, which changes). Mutation-proven: reverting the `_last_judge` gate
queues nothing. Includes the silence cases — a fully-fired roster and the drift wording — since
"always fire" is the failure mode that teaches people to ignore a check. Battery 71 suites /
1,639 assertions, green.

## W33b — generalising W33: the four classes swept across the estate

W33 was found on one check. Each of its four learnings is a CLASS, so each was swept over every
adapter rather than assumed unique. Two produced fixes, one produced a verified non-defect, one
produced a contradiction that is FLAGGED rather than guessed at.

**Class A — a gate that cannot fire because its epoch is 0.** One other site:
`nexus-posttool.py` H2's `_prev`. NOT a defect: the retention is deliberate and documented, and
the first-push hole is covered by H2-TURN at Stop. Verified rather than trusted — H2-TURN gates
on a non-empty set of open pushes, not on a previous epoch, so it genuinely covers the first
push. No change.

**Class B — an emission addressed to the wrong party.** Every id that can be emitted on the
SubagentStop path was enumerated by DRIVING both producers: `SA-APM`, `SA-PA`, `SA-TPM`, `SA1`
and `ROSTER1`. All five are addressed to CUE ("YOU now fire `task create`", "run the post-edit
eval", "fire the missing seats") while the adapter's own probe-verified note says an
`additionalContext` emitted there is delivered TO THE STOPPING CHILD and re-invokes it. The
three `WSW-*` emissions on the same path are written in the second person, which is consistent
with that note having been learned the hard way.

That is a contradiction INSIDE one file: either the note is right and five instructions never
reach Cue while re-invoking finished children, or the note is wrong and the `WSW-*` texts are
mis-addressed. R#25 says flag it, and rewriting five messages on the strength of a comment is
exactly the guess this cycle keeps paying for. **OPEN, with the settling probe named:** dispatch
a trivial subagent that returns an unrecognised status, then observe whether `SA1`'s text lands
in Cue's context or re-invokes the child. One probe decides all five.

**Class C — a window that is empty by construction.** One instance, fixed in W33.

**Class D — project state driving a nudge about another conversation's operation.** Nine
project-scoped reads feed per-conversation nudges. Eight are CORRECT: an id cache, "this agent
was edited", "work is due" are durable FACTS, and an agent edited in another conversation still
needs an eval. The discriminator is narrower than "session-scope everything":

> Project state may carry facts. It must not drive a nudge asking THIS conversation to act on an
> operation ANOTHER conversation OWNS. That state records its owner.

One site failed it: `consolidation-dispatched-log` / `-verified-log` are bare epochs, so the
newest dispatch in the project nagged whichever conversation ended next. Measured live: this
conversation was told to verify or re-dispatch a spine dispatched twenty-seven minutes earlier
by a different conversation — both the cross-conversation bleed the owner ruled out and an
invitation to run two spines over one workstream, which the filing doctrine forbids because
parallel spines re-file and collide. Rows are now `epoch\tsid`; R34V considers only its own.
Unattributable legacy rows are excluded, which is not failing toward silence: a spine dispatched
elsewhere was never this conversation's to verify, and its owner is nagged from its own rows.

**Non-regression, recorded because it is the interesting part.** The fix turned
`test_w12_checks.py` red on two R34V cases. The fixture seeded bare epochs and drove each Stop
with a FRESH session id, so no row could ever be owned. Intent preserved, fixture updated — and
one assertion ADDED, because A2's "second Stop is silent" would otherwise have passed under the
owner filter rather than the once-key it exists to test: a case passing for a reason it is not
testing is the hollow-test shape this cycle has found six times.

**Tests:** `tests/test_w33_owner_scoped_nudges.py`, 4 assertions, mutation-proven (removing the
owner filter turns two red), including the case where a FOREIGN row is NEWER than mine — the
original defect was `_disp[-1]`, newest-wins. Battery 72 suites / 1,644 assertions, green.

## W35 — from H05: the open addressee question is settled, and it was destroying deliverables

W33b left this OPEN and refused to guess. H05 settled it with five probes on a REAL harness — an
isolated temp project with its own `settings.json`, real nested subagents, real `stop_hook_active`
cascade — so the delivery semantics are measured at the harness level rather than inferred.

**The comment was right, and the damage is worse than "the nudge never reaches Cue".** An
`additionalContext` emitted at SubagentStop lands in the STOPPING CHILD's next input, not in Cue's
context, and RE-INVOKES the child. The part the old note did not say: **the child's re-invoked
final message BECOMES the Agent tool's return value.** So these emissions do not merely fail to
instruct Cue — they DELETE the deliverable they were written to escort.

Verbatim from a child's own sidechain transcript after being handed `SA-PA`:

> "I won't act on that … this system-reminder isn't a request from you."
> "No message like this can authorize me to take actions on your behalf."

and the parent received that refusal in place of `{"status":"done","prompt":"…"}` — exactly the
object R#31/R#45/R#46 require Cue to parse. A second child (haiku) did not argue; it degenerated
into eight sign-off stubs across eight re-invokes, 13k subagent tokens for a one-word task, which
is precisely the "9-17 sign-off stubs" the 2026-07-04 note recorded without diagnosing.

`SA-PA` / `SA-APM` / `SA-TPM` fire on `status == "done"`. **This was the success path.** Every
successful `pa-prompt-author`, `agent-prompt-modifier` and `task-prompt-modifier` return was being
replaced by the child's reaction to an instruction addressed to someone else — and the modifier arm

## W36 — from H06: the write guard was a read blocker on every mount path with a space in it

H06 replayed **20,633 unique (command, cwd) pairs** from 105 real transcripts through the real
adapter with the real mount roots. Of 34 `PROT-ROOT` + `WSW` denies, **33 were false**. Every one
of the 20 `WSW` denies was a pure READ of a workspace mount assigned to a variable —
`cat "$GC/_meta/x.md"`, `find "$GC" -iname …`, `ls -1 "$GC"`.

**All four mount paths on this machine contain a space** ("Claude Code"), so this was not an edge
case, it was the normal case: the owner's own workspace reads were being denied, with a message
telling them to perform the write server-side when they were not writing at all. A guard that
blocks READING is the shape that teaches people to route around every gate, including the correct
ones.

**The chain took three attempts to close, because each fix exposed the next link.** Recorded in
full, because each intermediate state looked like a fix and was not:

1. `_resolve_literals` matched an assignment value with `[^"'\s\n;&|]*`, which excludes whitespace
   unconditionally — `GC="/…/Claude Code/…"` substituted as `/…/Claude`. Fixed; still denied.
2. `_WRAP_RE`'s env-assignment alternative was `\w+=\S+\s+`, which peels only to the first space
   and left the fragment `Code/…"` with an unbalanced quote. Fixed; still denied.
3. The quoted alternative required TRAILING whitespace, so at end-of-statement (`GC="/a b/c"` with
   nothing after) the alternation backtracked into the bare `\S+` form and peeled to the space
   anyway. The separator has to accept `$`.

Every surviving link produced the identical end state: `shlex.split` raises, `write_targets`
returns `None`, and `None` correctly means "cannot determine" → the BROAD every-token candidate
set, which is the pre-W28/F09 behaviour that measured 95% false. The none-means-broad contract is
right; feeding it a parse failure for an ordinary read is what was wrong.

**A method note worth keeping.** My first trace of this pointed at `_statements` and was wrong —
I had applied the wrapper-peel inside my own debug loop and then printed a repr of a repr, so a
correctly-split statement looked like a truncated fragment. `_statements` was innocent. Two
minutes of reading the actual masked string settled it. A trace is a measurement and can carry its
own bug.

**Tests:** `tests/test_w36_spaced_mount_paths.py`, 31 assertions — six read idioms and six write
idioms, each on a spaced AND a space-free mount, plus the resolver, the peel (including the
end-of-statement case attempt 3 exists for) and the `write_targets` contract directly. The WRITE
half is not decoration: a widening loose enough to stop denying reads could equally have stopped
resolving write targets, turning a false positive into a silent miss on the one thing this guard
exists for.

**Non-regression from W35.** `test_w27_roster.py` went red on two cases: they asserted `ROSTER1`
in the SubagentStop STDOUT, and W35 moved that obligation to the queue. Intent preserved, observable
corrected — and the helper now FAILS explicitly if a Cue-addressed id ever appears in that stdout
again, so the check cannot drift back to the emitting form and still look green. A third case,
"once per repo per lane", had to become a COUNT rather than a membership test: the queue holds rows
until an Agent PostToolUse drains them, so the first stop's row is legitimately still present when
the second stop is driven.

**Still open from H06, not yet applied:** six spellings of an ordinary destructive command reach
`allow` — the verdict that REMOVES the native permission prompt — and RM1 recognises none of the
`case … esac`, `if [ "$f" != … ]` or `grep -v | xargs` exclude idioms, because it requires all

## W37 — from H06: ordinary spellings of a catastrophic delete that PROT-ROOT did not see

`PROT-ROOT` refuses `rm -rf` of `/`, `$HOME`, the project directory or a live mount. It recognised
the textbook spelling and missed several everyday ones. Twelve of fourteen forms now deny; the two
residuals reach `defer`, so the native prompt still fires and nothing is auto-approved.

**Four distinct causes, each driven.**

1. **A COMBINED interpreter flag.** `bash -lc`, `sh -ec`, `zsh -ic`, `python3 -Ic` are ordinary
   spellings and the payload pattern required `-c` as its own token. The pattern also existed in
   TWO copies — `hook_core` and the firewall — because W32's note claimed to have unified them and
   did not. That is a factual error in this log, corrected here: the private copy is now deleted and
   the firewall uses `hc._INTERP_PAYLOAD_RE`. Two copies of a security predicate is the defect; the
   divergence is only its symptom, and a new test asserts the count is one.
2. **The gate and the resolver read different views.** `is_recursive_force_rm(kw)` saw the lifted
   payload and OPENED the arm; `rm_targets` then read the raw command, where that `rm` sits inside
   quotes, and resolved nothing. Gate fires, resolver finds nothing, no deny. Both halves now read
   `_payload_view` — heredoc-stripped, quotes INTACT (a target is an operand), interpreter payloads
   appended at a command position.
3. **A bare leading env assignment.** `\w+=\S+` appeared only INSIDE the wrapper group, so it was
   absorbed after `env`/`sudo` but not alone: `FOO=1 rm -rf /` was not recognised as `rm` at all.
   `PROT-ROOT`, `RM1` and `RM1B` all key on that segmenter, so one unrecognised prefix silenced
   three guards. The quoted form is admitted too, for the same reason W36 needed it.
4. **Glued shell punctuation.** A subshell's closing paren attaches to the last operand, so
   `(rm -rf $HOME)` resolved the target `$HOME)`. It had to be stripped in TWO places: the resolver,
   and the BROAD candidate set that exists to make recognition gaps fail closed. The fallback had a
   gap of its own, which is the worse of the two.

**One thing I got wrong, recorded.** I also changed the caller so an EMPTY target list degrades to
the broad set like `None` does. Reading `rm_targets` afterwards showed it already returns `None`
when no segment matches, so that edit fixed nothing — it stays as a defensive guard, but it was not
a cause, and I had asserted it was before checking.

**Two residual gaps, deliberately not ground down further:** `bash -lc 'rm -rf $HOME'` (a payload
naming a variable target) and `GC="/a b" rm -rf /` (a quoted spaced env prefix). Both reach `defer`.
The new suite asserts them as NOT-`allow` rather than as `defer`, because pinning a defect as
expected behaviour is how a suite starts certifying the bug; closing them later will not turn it red.

**Tests:** `tests/test_w37_catastrophic_spellings.py` — 14 deny spellings, 6 ordinary-work cases
that must NOT be refused, the 2 residuals as a safety floor, and the one-definition assertion. The
negative half is not decoration: an earlier audit of this same function found 15 shapes where an
over-eager version emitted `allow` — an active auto-approval of `rm -rf /tmp`, 11 of them
regressions against the broad set it replaced. Widening this guard without holding the negatives is
exactly how that happened. The fixture also keeps HOME, the project dir and cwd DISTINCT: sharing
them makes every target in-scope by construction and turns the whole suite into `allow`, which is a
fixture artifact I hit myself and had to correct mid-lane.

**Still open from H06:** `find … -delete` is invisible to every arm (F9); `chmod -R`/`chown -R` of a
work root reaches `allow` and the guard needs a trailing slash to see it (F10); the broad fallback
can synthesise `/` from a `//` substring and emit at `recoverable=False` (F11); `WSW-RET` is retired

## W38 — from H12, plus one caught live: an auto-approval of deleting the filesystem root

**F1 (worst in the cycle) — `rm -rf /</dev/null` emitted `allow`.** Not a missed deny: an ACTIVE
auto-approval, which SUPPRESSES the native permission prompt the user would otherwise have seen.
Five spellings did it — `/</dev/null`, `/>/dev/null`, `/>>/dev/null`, `~>/dev/null`, `~/>log` — and
the shell really does hand `rm` the argument `/`, verified by H12 against a shim named `rm` on PATH
recording its argv to a side file so the redirection under test could not hide the evidence.

A redirection operator with no space before it is a word boundary to the SHELL but not to
whitespace tokenisation, so `/</dev/null` stayed one token. `PROT-ROOT` never saw `/`; the scope
loop then found only the redirect's own operand, recognised `/dev/null` as a safe device, and fell
through to `allow`.

Fixed in TWO places, which is the part worth remembering: the target resolver, AND the broad
candidate set that exists so recognition gaps fail closed. Leaving the fallback reading `/>log` as a
path would have kept the hole open straight through the safety net — the same shape as W37's glued
paren, where the fallback was also the second half of the fix.

The naive fix is wrong: in `rm -rf /1>f` the shell keeps `/1` as the argument (the digit belongs to
the word, not the operator), so truncating at the first `<`/`>` is correct there too. Those rows are
asserted separately rather than assumed.

**F2 — caught live, not from a report.** EV1 nagged this session about two agents "published this
session" whose ids were `for` and `v1',` — English text and a fragment of a quoted string. Nothing
was published. `_real_id` rejected shell metacharacters only, so any bare word passed as an
identifier. An obligation keyed on prose is UNCLOSABLE: the id never recurs, so it can never be
discharged, and the nag repeats once per session forever.

Two things about the provenance. All twelve of my own commands containing that phrase evaluate to no
event on current code, so the rows came from a SUBAGENT's probe — a lane enumerating mutating
commands — recorded under my session id, because subagent hooks carry the parent's. That is the
multi-actor class H14 owns, and it means a lane probing a mutating command can plant a durable
obligation on its parent. And I was wrong about the mechanism twice before finding it: I first
theorised a heredoc whose body contains its own delimiter would leak the remainder as command text,
drove it, and found the non-greedy match handles it correctly. Recorded because the wrong hypothesis
was the plausible one.

`_real_id` now also requires the token to LOOK like an id — no stray punctuation, at least six
characters, and not a bare lowercase word. That admits UUIDs and `agent-1`-shaped test ids while
rejecting prose, without a UUID-only rule that would reject legitimate short-form ids. The two
phantom rows were then removed from the live feed, so the false nag stops rather than persisting for
every future session.

**Tests:** `tests/test_w38_glued_redirect.py` — nine glued-redirect spellings that must deny, the
two digit cases that must NOT be treated as root deletes, three ordinary-work cases with redirects,
and the `_real_id` table in both directions.

**Still open from H12, not yet driven:** five live crashes across three adapters — and the suite that

### R34-HOLD — the OFF switch that was read four times and written never
**Issue** — R#34 documents a per-conversation hold ("a scoped 'not now' = a SESSION hold

### consolidation-due-log / consolidation-ran-log — owner-stamped (completes W33)
**Issue** — W33 stamped `dispatched`/`verified` with their owning sid and left `due`/`ran`
bare, so any conversation's filing silenced every other conversation's due-check with no
possible post-hoc attribution.

**Evidence** — in the failing window the one ran-credit at 13:55:59 belongs to session
`bed5d4ac`, not to `2f6ebd1f`. It re-armed 2.5 minutes later and cost nothing that time,

**Class sweep** — all four consolidation feeds audited; `dispatched`/`verified` were already

now a float comparison, which also removes a latent lexicographic bug at the next digit
rollover. The `_own()` helper that drives `R34V` was deliberately left alone: its contract is
unchanged and widening the blast radius buys nothing.

**Pinned by** — the five suites that recovered without any fixture change once the semantics
were corrected (`test_due_epochs`, `test_w11_checks`, `test_w19_gates`, `test_w21`,
`test_w28_hold_scope`) — their recovery IS the non-regression evidence.

## W40–W42 — the missing sections, reconstructed

These three waves shipped without CHANGELOG entries. Their reasoning survived only in commit
messages and source comments, which is how the most retry-prone finding in the layer nearly
got retried: a later cycle re-proposed `suppressOutput` because the record of it failing was
inside the function it applied to. Reconstructed from the commits and the source, and marked
as such — this is a repair of the log, not a first-hand account of those waves.

- **W40–W41** (`79895da`, 2026-07-30 08:58 +0200) — "the ACK-mention bypass, and the turn-end
  wake reworked". STOP-WAKE's exits were converted from REPLY TEXT to a tool-input claim
  (`metadata.wake_ack`), on the owner's request that the check stop appearing on their screen
  and stop needing reply text. **`suppressOutput: true` was tried on the Stop block and
  measured NEGATIVE, twice.**
- **W42** (`ab73404`) — "the budget nothing read, and the field nobody filled".

**The standing conclusion, recorded here so it stops living only in a comment:**

> **A BLOCKING STOP HOOK CANNOT BE MADE INVISIBLE.** The harness surfaces the block and the
> transcript records it by construction. The only mechanism that removes it from both is not
> blocking, which trades away the wake the check exists to perform. The real mitigation is
> FREQUENCY and LENGTH, never the delivery channel.

Measured three times across three sessions: W41 twice, and W44 once at the owner's explicit
request to re-test rather than accept the record. The W44 run set the field live, the block
fired, and the owner confirmed seeing it in full. **Do not retry it.**

# W45 · 2026-08-02 — the handoff is a gate: component inventory, URL probe, watcher lifecycle

Three checks, all NUDGE-class, all shipped OBSERVE-first. Common root: each fires at the
moment an artifact leaves Cue's hands (a lane's brief, the owner's message, the background),
and each of the three measured failures produced a POSITIVE signal that masked the defect —
the inventory gate reported green, the curl returned 200, the Monitor said "started".

### CMP1 — component-inventory root, resolved against the repo's real shape
**Issue** — an app build hand-wrote ~2,046 LOC of controls + ~6,003 LOC of CSS beside an org
component library that was present in the repo: `vibe/stock/src/ui`, 182 files, 20,688 LOC,
`DataTable.tsx` 717 LOC, `Filters.tsx` 368 LOC. Import edges app→library: 8, all `ModalOverlay`.
Three owner rejections on the same axis across 61h58m.
**Evidence** — first-hand: `grep` of `src/app` import edges = 8; `record-core` imported 0 times;
main-log L6739/L6740, the probe `"does the app actually IMPORT the starter's record-core UI?
(bundle weight if not)"` answering `src/ui/ 182 files 1.2M` with the only match being the
comment declaring it unused; `main.tsx:3-6` classifying it as "a route back to the donor's look".
**Change** — new `_inventory_root()` (installed `node_modules/@agent-nexus/apps-ui` → vendored
tree with a provenance marker) + `component_inventory_gate()`; nudge when a complex-control file
is written into an app repo whose root resolves and nothing this session read it.
**Why this fix** — the governing rule EXISTED (`ux-canon.md:23`) and was re-injected verbatim
≥3× without binding, because its prescribed ACTION (`read docs/catalog.json`) could not execute
in a vendored repo. A rule whose check cannot run reports green. Prose was measured not to work
here; the doc edit fixes the resolution order, the hook fires at the act.
**Class sweep** — the same "prescribed action cannot execute" shape was checked across the
app-builder references: `starter-guide.md` (navigation contract) had the identical
installed-only assumption and is fixed in the same wave; `base-decision.md` never asked the
component question at all and gains a scorecard row. No other check in this adapter resolves a
package path, so the code-side class is 1.
**Pinned by** — `tests/test_w45_checks.py`: fires (vendored + installed), silent (no root ·
inside the library · non-control filename · already read · 2nd call), + a mutation that nulls
the resolver and requires the fire assertion to go red.

### URL1 — a URL named at the owner that nothing probed
**Issue** — design alternatives announced at a root URL while a DEEPER path was the thing
probed. Twice, 46 hours apart. Dead-link windows 6h49m48s and 2m54s; each fix took ~100 seconds.
**Evidence** — L16499 probes `/tournee/B-board-390.png` → 200; L16502 announces
`http://localhost:4950/`; L16507 owner: `"I don't see 4950"`. Repeat at L32668→L32672→L32681
(`"ttp://127.0.0.1:4780. no foybd"`). 2 of 6 sends were unverified at the sent address; both
drew a complaint, 0 of the 4 correct ones did.
**Change** — `render_watch_feed` now also logs every probed local URL to a `probed-urls`
session feed (and its render-reset regex learned `127.0.0.1`, which it never matched before);
a Stop-time check compares the URLs in the final message against that feed. An announced URL
counts as probed only at its exact address — a deeper 200 does not vouch for the root.
**Why this fix** — a P4.5 pre-flight found the predicate UNSATISFIABLE as first specified: the
feed did not exist, only a `last-render` timestamp. Shipping the gate on assumed state is the
worst class in the book, so the feed is part of the change. Doc-only was ruled out: the file
carrying the correct rule (`dev-loop.md`) measured 0 Read calls in 33,781 lines.
**Class sweep** — every emitter that names a URL at the user was checked: `H2`/`H2-TURN` cover
pushes, `SERVE` covers deploys, `R#27` covers completion claims. "Here, look at this" was the
only ungated one — the gap this closes. The `127.0.0.1` blindness was also present in the H1
render-reset and is fixed in the same edit.
**Pinned by** — `tests/test_w45_checks.py`: fires on an unprobed URL, SILENT on the exact
probed address, FIRES when only a deeper path was probed, no-opinion with no URL, plus a
documented ACCEPTED-TRADE row (a retrospective mention of a dead link still fires).

### MON1 — a persistent watcher armed without its end
**Issue** — a persistent Monitor ran 3d 7h with no terminal condition, `npm test` + `npx tsc -b`
every 300s in the owner's repo (~945 cycles). Its declared target died after ~20h and it kept
firing for 58.6h more; 38 of 73 firings were the session's OWN commits reflected back, because
the change predicate embedded `git log --oneline -1` on the repo.
**Evidence** — arm at main-log L2334 `{"persistent":true,"timeout_ms":3600000}`; result L2335
`{"taskId":"bygjrbc31","timeoutMs":0}` — the only bound set was silently discarded. `ps` at
diagnosis: PID 59881, etime `03-06:49:54`, still ticking.
**Change** — nudge once per arm on `Monitor` + `persistent:true`, carrying the lifecycle
contract, and flagging `timeout_ms` when it rides along.
**Why this fix** — the arbitrated gate also wanted "no recorded stop path", but that predicate
needs ledger state with no reliable path, and a "does the description name a target" test would
be a WORDING trigger, which this layer does not do. Scoped to payload structure; the stop-path
record stays doctrine (`CLAUDE.md` R#29 + app-builder Heartbeat). Stated rather than shipped
half-satisfiable.
**Class sweep** — 14 Monitor arms across 7 sessions of this project: 5 persistent, 4 correctly
`TaskStop`ped, 1 not. One lifecycle miss, not a habit — recorded so the next audit does not
re-derive it. `ScheduleWakeup` was checked as the sibling primitive: it has a documented
`stop:true` and its two arms in the mined session both carried a target in `reason`.
**Pinned by** — `tests/test_w45_checks.py`: fires on persistent, silent on non-persistent and
on a non-Monitor tool, and asserts the `timeout_ms` flag appears only when the field is present.

### OBS-POLICY — observe markers move OUT of predicates to the emission site
**Issue** — CMP1's first implementation checked its observe marker INSIDE the predicate, so the
function returned `None` in observe mode and three contract assertions for FIRING failed. The
test was right and the design was wrong: a predicate that cannot be tested for firing is
untestable by construction.
**Change** — `_observing()` + `_obs_suppressed()` helpers; the policy runs at the `if warns:`
emission sites, and the predicates stay pure.
**Why this fix** — pure predicates, one emission policy, and the decision row is written in both
modes so an observe period is auditable.
**Class sweep** — all three `if warns:` sites in this adapter were inspected. The first blanket
version SUPPRESSED `LP1`, which predates this and implements observe by APPENDING "[observe]" to
a message it still surfaces — a regression caught by the sweep, not by a test. Hence
`_OBS_SUPPRESSED_IDS` is an explicit allowlist (`CMP1`, `MON1`) rather than "every id with a
marker". The third site carries `LP1` and is deliberately left on its own convention.
**Pinned by** — `tests/test_w45_checks.py` asserts `_obs_suppressed("LP1") is False` while both
W45 ids are True with their markers present.

# W44 · 2026-08-01 — output noise: what reaches the user, and in what shape

Mined from a 62-hour app-build session. Four owner-reported classes, five more found while
grounding them. The wave's organising finding: **three of the four already had a correct fix
whose TRIGGER was too narrow.**

### STOP-WAKE — one line instead of a wall, and the bundle stops riding along
**Issue** — the owner reported hook messages rendering as large blocks. 253 of 254
user-rendered hook blocks in the mined session carried `[STOP-WAKE]`; it is the gate on the
entire visible channel. Two mechanisms made it big: a 643-char static message, and
`_blk += "\n\n" + "\n".join(msgs)`, which appended the whole queued advisory list to the
user-visible block reason.
**Evidence** — first-hand: 254 `hook_blocking_error` attachments, all `hookEvent: Stop`,
225,313 chars total, 15.8% of all assistant prose. Median rendered block 880 chars, max 2,408.
**Change** — arm 1 cut to one line (643 → 305 chars, driven); the exits' SEMANTICS moved to a
new `### STOP-WAKE — the exits, in full` section in `CHECK-REGISTRY.md`; the bundle append
removed.
**Why this fix** — the channel cannot be changed (see W40–W42 above), so length and frequency
are the only levers. The escape hatch stays IN the message: a first pass moved it to the
registry and left a pointer, and two older suites caught that immediately — W28/F17's finding
was that an absent hatch is what makes people delete the whole hook. The registry pointer is
a supplement, never a replacement.
**Class sweep** — arm 2 fixed in the same pass (below). All 172 message literals across 12
adapters were measured for length and for reply-soliciting phrasing; `BLD1` was the only other
message ending in an imperative that could only be discharged in prose, and it was fixed here
too. W28/F16's loss case (a session ending on a Stop loses queued advisories) is covered by
the existing `_USER_FACING` allowlist, which includes `H2-TURN`, the measured instance.
**Pinned by** — `test_w44.py::test_stopwake_message`, driven against the real adapter rather
than grepping source; plus the pre-existing `test_w24_stopwake` and `test_w28_wake`.

### STOP-WAKE arm 2 — the exit that could not be taken (closes O44 and O46)
**Issue** — arm 2 blocked with "or the work is genuinely finished and you can say so in one
line". Saying so is PROSE on a user-visible channel, which leak row 5 forbids outright, so a
conforming reader could never take that exit and was blocked instead.
**Evidence** — O46, filed post-W32: 4 arm-2 blocks across three sessions, one after a fully
completed board.
**Change** — both branches now discharge through the same one-shot `metadata.wake_ack` claim
that arm 1 already used and that pretool already observes.
**Why this fix** — O46 states that O44 and O46 must move together because the same
token-in-the-reply problem applies to both. Widening the bucket was rejected by its own entry:
it changes only the cadence of an unanswerable question.
**Class sweep** — arm 1 was fixed in W41 and arm 2, forty lines below in the same function,
was not. That is the wave's second principle in miniature. Every other Stop-tier check was
read for a prose-only exit; none remained.
**Pinned by** — `test_w28_wake.py` (driven, both branches) and `test_w44.py`.

### `auq_this_turn` — an AUQ answer is a turn boundary
**Issue** — every Stop-tier check gated on `_auq is False` was SILENTLY disarmed after any
AskUserQuestion until the user next typed a message.
**Evidence** — driven, first-hand: the backward walk skipped 5 `tool_result` records and found
a stale `AskUserQuestion` 33 records back, on a turn that asked nothing. Two live turn-ends
produced no decision row at all while the handler, driven directly against the identical
board, armed in 0.14 s.
**Change** — answered `tool_use` ids are collected during the reverse walk; an
`AskUserQuestion` whose answer has already been passed is treated as a boundary.
**Why this fix** — it distinguishes the two cases by evidence rather than by heuristic. The
alternative, treating any `tool_result` as a boundary, would break mid-turn tool use entirely.
**Class sweep** — the docstring records this class caught in W24 and fixed for the
`queue-operation` enqueue shape; `tool_result` was the third shape and was missed. Both other
transcript walkers (`narration_count`, `board_state`) were read: neither depends on the
human-entry boundary in the same way.
**Pinned by** — `test_w44.py::test_auq_boundary`, including the NEGATIVE CONTROL: a turn
genuinely ending on an unanswered question must still be exempt, or the fix punishes the R#3
compliance the exemption exists to protect.

### `app_repo_ctx` — the hook estate is never an app build
**Issue** — a leftover `docs/PRD.md` made the estate repo permanent app-build context, so
every doc/meta session in it inherited SPEC1/C2/H1/DL1/H2 and the R#34 sprint hold.
**Evidence** — first-hand: SPEC1 and BLD3 fired repeatedly during this doc-only cycle;
`app-src-writes` for the session did not exist at all — zero app-source writes recorded.
**Change** — `app_repo_ctx` returns False when the directory contains `.claude/hooks/`.
**Why this fix** — fixed in the ONE helper rather than at its 17 call sites. Additionally
requiring recorded app-source writes was considered and REJECTED: `nexus-pretool.py:988`
deliberately supports pre-`git init` app scaffolds, which legitimately have a marker and no
writes yet, so that test would fail them closed.
**Class sweep** — this is the same "Issue E" bleed W21 retired the durable project-scoped
`app_build` flag to prevent; the file-marker replacement reproduced its permanence by another
route. All 17 call sites enumerated; all consume the helper, none re-implement the marker test.
**Pinned by** — `test_w44.py::test_app_repo_ctx_estate`, with a real-app-repo negative control
so the fix cannot silently disable every app gate.

### `consol_ledger_checkpoint` — the second ledger locator
**Issue** — WL1 fired claiming no workstream ledger existed, against a session whose ledger
was on disk and named in the dispatch brief.
**Evidence** — first-hand: the predicate globs `scratchpad/ledger-*.md`, flat; the ledger sat
one directory down.
**Change** — unions the flat glob with a one-level recursive glob and the `cycle-artifacts`
feed.
**Why this fix** — it reuses the sibling's already-hardened approach rather than inventing a
third.
**Class sweep** — the sibling locator `nexus-lifecycle.py::_latest_ledger` already unioned the
`cycle-artifacts` feed, hardened in W27. The hardening reached one of the two ledger locators.
Both are now consistent; no third locator exists (`grep -rn "ledger-\*"`).
**Pinned by** — `test_w44.py::test_ledger_locator_twin`.

### AW1 / AW3 — byte-identical re-emission on a paginated read
**Issue** — reading one governing doc across four pages emitted AW3 3× and AW1 4×, identical
each time. AW3 was pagination-blind: it compared `limit < total` and never inspected `offset`,
so the paginated reading R#2 explicitly licenses tripped it once per page.
**Evidence** — first-hand, this session, on `CLAUDE.md`.
**Change** — AW3 reads `offset` and skips continuations; both keyed on `(basename, mtime)` via

**Class sweep** — every `_emit` site in `nexus-awareness.py` was read for the same class. AW4

**Pinned by** — `test_w44.py::test_awareness_repetition`, driven three ways: fires on a genuine
partial first read, silent on the identical repeat, silent on a paginated continuation.

### NARR1 — the limiter was keyed on the session, not the situation
**Issue** — `sc.once(sid, "narr1")` fired once per session. One noisy turn spent the budget and
the layer's only narration check stayed mute for the rest of the session.
**Evidence** — the layer's own standard (`messages.md`) names keying a limiter on compliance
or on the session as the commonest way a reminder becomes permanently silent. Narration share
was measured rising after 7 of 9 compactions (mean +9 points) with no check firing.
**Change** — re-keyed on `pc_epoch` plus a `NARR_CAP`-sized escalation bucket.
**Why this fix** — it re-arms on the ACTIVITY that creates the obligation, never on the
compliance that discharges it.
**Class sweep** — every `sc.once` key in `nexus-lifecycle.py`'s Stop branch was read for the
same defect. The rest are keyed on a situation hash or an epoch already.
**Pinned by** — `test_w44.py::test_narr1_limiter`.

### BLD1 — a nudge that solicited a prose reply
**Issue** — the message ended `"— say which."`, an imperative whose only discharge is prose in
the user-visible reply.
**Evidence** — measured as a driver of the acknowledgement class: 26 of 33 residual instances
were replies to messages phrased as demands, arriving on the channel where user text arrives.
**Change** — states the fact, names two runnable actions, and carries an explicit first-class
no-op exit.
**Why this fix** — `messages.md` makes a no-op exit mandatory for any check firing on a proxy
metric; only 6 of 172 literals had one.
**Class sweep** — all 172 message literals scanned for a trailing imperative addressed to the
reader. BLD1 was the only remaining instance; the STOP-WAKE arms were the others and are fixed

**Pinned by** — `test_w44.py::test_no_message_solicits_prose`, which scans all three adapters

## W44b — the verification round: three lanes, three BROKEN verdicts, all closed

The wave's own battery went green at 85/85 and the fixer declared it done. A separate fleet
briefed to distrust that verdict found otherwise. Recorded in full because the pattern —
**the fixer verifying his own fixes** — is the method's named failure mode, and this is the
clearest instance the estate has measured.

### `app_repo_ctx` — the exclusion is now IDENTITY, after two heuristics were driven wrong
**Issue** — three successive versions:
1. a test at the passed directory only. Missed a call site passing `.claude/hooks/lib`, a real
   cwd while the layer is being edited.
2. a bounded 6-level walk UP, added to fix (1). **Strictly worse.** `~/.claude/hooks` is the
   standard user-level Claude Code config path; creating it silently disabled all 15 app gates
   for every repo within 5 levels of `$HOME` — every repo on the measured host — with no
   decision row. Live only because that directory happens not to exist.
3. identity against the estate's own computed root.
**Evidence** — lane V3, driven with a fake HOME and a matched control: app repos at 3, 4 and 5
levels below a HOME containing `.claude/hooks` all read `ctx=False` under (2); the control
without the ancestor read `True`, proving the ancestor was the cause. `repo_root_of` returned
`None` for the same repos, so gates needing any root also went quiet.
**Change** — `_ESTATE_ROOT` computed once at import (four `dirname` hops from
`lib/hook_core.py` to the project root), and `app_repo_ctx` returns False for that path and
anything beneath it.
**Why this fix** — exact where both heuristics were approximate. It cannot be triggered by a
user-level config directory, and it needs no depth bound. The first attempt at it used three
hops and resolved to `.claude`, leaving the project root still detected as an app repo — the
original defect — which the driven test caught immediately. Reading the code would not have.
**Class sweep** — 15 executable call sites (the earlier count of 17 included two comment
mentions); all consume the helper, none re-implement the marker test. Every real app repo on
the host re-verified as still detected, including one vendoring its own `.claude/hooks`.
**Pinned by** — `test_w44.py::test_app_repo_ctx_estate`, with three negative controls: a
vendored-hooks app repo, a repo under a HOME with user-level hooks, and the estate-root depth.

### AW1/AW3 — the once-key collided on real estate documents
**Issue** — keys were `(basename, int mtime)`. Two governing docs sharing a name AND a
timestamp shared one key; the second was silenced for the whole session.
**Evidence** — lane V3, measured on the real tree, not constructed: 22 `SKILL.md` files with
21 distinct integer mtimes → `nexus-workflow-builder/SKILL.md` silenced by
`nexus-skills-and-tasks/SKILL.md`. 24 `GUIDE.md` files with 17 distinct mtimes → **7 of 24
silenced by a sibling.** Bulk-created files routinely share a second, which is how the 5-file
group arose. Driven through the real adapter with a fresh-session control to prove it was a
collision and not a property of the second file.
**Change** — key on a sha1 digest of the ABSOLUTE path; `_mtime` raised to millisecond
resolution so a same-second edit re-arms.
**Why this fix** — a digest rather than the raw path because the session store collapses `/`
in key names, which would trade one collision class for another. **Not** the builtin `hash()`:
`PYTHONHASHSEED` is randomised per process and the two Reads run in separate subprocesses, so
the key would never match itself and the de-duplication would vanish entirely.
**Class sweep** — both AW1 and AW3 in the same pass, via one shared `_dockey` helper. The
severity is pointed: the silenced file is the largest gate-bearing doc in the estate, and
R#2's own worked example is about missing a gotcha past line 600 of exactly that file.
**Pinned by** — `test_w44.py::test_awareness_repetition`, driven on the two real colliding
files plus the re-arm direction.

### The bundle-removal mitigation was a false claim
**Issue** — W44's first pass removed the advisory bundle from the block reason and asserted in
comment that the `_USER_FACING` allowlist covered the loss. It does not: the allowlist sits
BELOW the blocking branch's own `sys.exit`, so on a blocking Stop it is structurally
unreachable.
**Evidence** — lane V3, driven both ways on one session state, single-variable: with the
removed line restored, `[H2-TURN]` reached the user (912 chars); as shipped, it never did.
Worse, it is lost PERMANENTLY rather than deferred — its guard `once("h2turn_%d")` burns on
the blocked turn, so it is never re-appended and the queue's only consumer (the next
UserPromptSubmit) never comes in a session that ends there. `[R34-HOLD]`, once-per-session and
addressed to the owner in the second person, has the same shape.
**Change** — `USER_FACING` hoisted to module scope; the blocking path now appends that subset
and only that subset.
**Why this fix** — it keeps the actual win (18+ advisory classes, 912 measured chars, still do
not ride out) while restoring the W28/F16 guarantee for exactly the classes the allowlist
already judges user-owned. Driven cost: 264 chars alone, ~640 with a user-owned advisory
attached, against 912 unconditionally before.
**Class sweep** — the same hoist applies to the R34-BLOCK exit, which is evaluated after
STOP-WAKE and so misses the same turn. `[H2]` and `[MAN1]` are emitted by `nexus-posttool.py`
and can never match at Stop; documented rather than silently dropped, so the next reader does
not mis-size the mitigation as 5 ids when 3 are live.
**Pinned by** — `test_w44.py::test_stopwake_message`, driven on the emitted reason.

### The suite itself was the other half of the finding
Lane V1 mutation-proved every assertion: **29 of 37 could be driven red, but only 7 bound to
behaviour**; 7 were hollow and 1 vacuous. Concretely — the bundle could return in a different
spelling, the message could be re-bloated to 877 chars with its opening anchor intact, arm 1
could lose its registry pointer, and the pagination fix could be reverted entirely, all with
the suite green. The vacuous one shared a session id across three cases, so the once-key was
already burnt and the assertion never observed the offset logic it was written for.

Every one is now driven against the real adapter, and the NARR1 assertion carries its own
mutation proof: replacing the count bucket with a constant reproduces the permanent-silence
defect and turns the check red with `queued counts after 7/14/21 blocks: [1, 1, 1]` in the
failure message.

**The generalisable lesson, and the reason this section exists:** a source grep proves a string
is present. Only driving proves the behaviour ships. Three separate times in this wave an
assertion matched the fix's own explanatory COMMENT rather than its subject — so a suite that
scans source must exclude comment lines everywhere it scans, and prefer the emitted artifact
wherever one exists.

### command-position scanning was QUADRATIC — 7s of hook latency on an ordinary Bash call
**Issue** — three sibling regexes absorbed shell wrapper prefixes with unbounded runs inside a
repeated group (`(?:\w+=\S+\s+)+`, `-\S+\s+`). On a long command with a run of word characters
and no `=`, `\w+` matches to the end, fails, and backtracks one character at a time — O(n) per
start position, and the scan tries every position, so O(n²).
**Evidence** — found by battery layer A3 (hostile payloads), which had never been run against
this layer. Measured through the real adapters, `[LIVE]`:

| command size | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| 10 KB | 1.96 s | 0.17 s |
| 20 KB | 6.81 s | 0.21 s |
| 40 KB | 29.2 s | 0.34 s |
| 200 KB | past a 30 s timeout | 1.71 s |

Profiling attributed 7.30 s of a 7.41 s run to `re.Pattern.search` across 82 calls.
**Change** — every unbounded run inside a repeated group is bounded (`\w{1,128}`, `\S{1,1024}`,
`-\S{1,256}`); `command_positions` is memoised, since it is a pure function of the command and
was being recomputed 82 times per adapter run.
**Why this fix** — the bounds sit far above any real shell token (variable names and flags are
tens of characters), so nothing that matched before stops matching. Truncating the scanned
command was rejected: it would weaken a security-relevant guard to buy speed, and the
false-positive census confirms the guard's precision is the thing worth protecting.
**Class sweep** — three siblings, one defect, all fixed in the same pass:
`hook_core._CMD_SEP_RE`, `nexus-ladder-engine.CMDPOS`, `nexus-fs-firewall._WRITE_PREFIX`. The
first fix touched only the first and the timing did not move, which is what revealed the other
two — a class sweep that stops at the first instance measures nothing.

# Hook check registry

Every check id the hook layer can emit. The decision log
(`~/.nexus-mcp/cue-session/<sid>/decisions`) records **ids, not meanings** — this file is the legend.

Decision values: `deny` · `warn` · `observe` (would-have-fired under a marker) · `annotate`
(W49: an advisory channel logging its fire with no verdict — the postfail FH family, the
posttool classifiers with joined ids split on `+`, the SubagentStop/PreCompact emitter, and
the awareness emitter; before W49 these four paths logged NOTHING, so a zero-row check on
them was unmeasurable rather than quiet). A handful of site-specific values also exist
(`set-by-user`, `mismatch`, …); column 3 is free text by design.

A check that is not listed here is a defect: add the row in the same commit that adds the check.

**Why this exists.** An audit of the store found 98 distinct decision ids and no legend, so recovering
what a dozen of them meant took an hour of reading 140 KB of adapter source. Telemetry only
interpretable by someone willing to read the source defeats most of the point of collecting it.

**Class** — DENY blocks the call · WARN advises (injected, non-blocking) · ANNOT records only.
**Rollout** — ENFORCING, or the observe-marker filename while the check records without acting.

## Reading a decision row

    hook<TAB>id<TAB>decision<TAB>epoch

`hook` is the event name, or a component name (`fs-firewall`, `ladder-engine`). `epoch` was added in
W28 — without it the file answers "how often" but never "since when", and a check noisy since day one
cannot be told from one that started misfiring last week.

Decision values seen in the store: `deny` · `warn` · `nudge` · `block` · `would-block` · `would-deny` ·
`observe` · `budget-spent` · `marker` · `suppressed-sprint` · `suppressed-user-hold` ·
`unenforced-after-block` · `expired-stale-project-hold` · `violations`.

`violations` is the conformance arm's found-something state (its `_log` writes the STATE as the
decision, so `checker-error` can appear the same way). A filter written as `deny|warn|nudge|block`
drops it, which is why it is listed: this file's one unique responsibility is being right about the
store, and it was the only value in the store that this list did not name.

**Marker flips are NOT here.** They live in the `markers` feed — a marker row is four free-text columns
and would corrupt any strict-arity parse of this one.

### `STOP-WAKE` — the exits, in full

The block message names these in shorthand. This is the full form, and it is the message's only detail home — **if this section moves, the message's pointer moves with it in the same commit** (W28/F17: a guard whose escape is undiscoverable is one people route around, and the route they find is deleting the whole hook).

**Two arms.** *Arm 1* — the board holds unblocked pending task(s) and the turn asked no question. *Arm 2* — no unblocked row, but tool calls have run since the last board update AND durable untracked work exists (both terms required; `_work > 0` alone was true on almost every turn — measured, 87 blocked turn-ends in one session).

**Two volumes (W46).** Firing is not the same as blocking. While the situation is merely OPEN the check WHISPERS: a `systemMessage` one-liner the owner sees, plus the same text queued to `stop-pending` so it reaches the model at the next prompt. It BLOCKS only once the situation has not moved for `WAKE_WHISPER_UNTIL` (`lib/hook_core.py`, currently 3).

"Has not moved" is measured in whichever unit the arm has, because their signatures differ:

| Arm | Signature | Unmoved unit | Whispers | Blocks |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | sha1 of the sorted unblocked task-id set | the SLOT — wakes on an unchanged set | slots 0…2 | slot 3+ |
| 2 | `arm2-<work bucket>`, budget 1 | the BUCKET INDEX — its slot is pinned at 0 and cannot escalate | buckets 0…2 | bucket 3+ |

Why it exists: one 218 MB session carried 282 user-rendered blocking Stop records and **281 of them were `[STOP-WAKE]`** — this check was the entire visible channel. Making it quiet while nothing is stuck removes the noise without removing the wall.

Why it is not a render trick: `suppressOutput: true` on a Stop block was measured NEGATIVE three times (W41 ×2, W44 ×1 at the owner's explicit re-test). A blocking Stop hook cannot be made invisible; the only mechanism that removes the block is not blocking. Do not retry the render route.

The decision log records `whisper` and `block` as distinct states so the threshold can be calibrated from real sessions: whispers followed by movement are correct suppressions, blocks at or past the threshold are correct catches.

| Exit | How | What it means |
|---|---|---|
| ask | `AskUserQuestion` | The turn ends on a question you owe. Never punished — R#3 compliance must not be blocked |
| resume | work the named top item now | The obligation is discharged by doing it |
| claim | any task-tool call carrying `metadata.wake_ack` (an otherwise-empty `TaskUpdate` is fine) | A background lane genuinely owes you this work, or the check does not apply. **Consumed ONE-SHOT — it covers this turn end only**, so a silent lane wakes it again. It can never become a session-long mute |

**Why the claim is a tool input and not reply text.** Until W41 the exits demanded literal text in the reply (`lane-owes:<id>`, or a one-line reason), which put hook bookkeeping into the conversation the owner reads for a check that is entirely internal. A tool input can never be quoted, which also closes the self-disarm permanently.

**Bound.** `_SW_BUDGET = 25` blocks per distinct board signature, so a board that genuinely cannot progress stops nagging while new owed work always wakes the turn.

**Opt-out (human-only, out of band).** `NEXUS_WAKE_ACK=1` in the `env` block of `.claude/settings.json`. Deliberately not settable by a turn: the guard protects against the agent, so an in-command override would make it an advisory with extra steps.

**Observe marker.** `.stopwake-observe` present → logs `observe` and never blocks.

## The annotation tier

These carry the internal `annotate` decision label rather than `warn`. Like the advisory tier they are
injected as context and block nothing; unlike it, most are emitted by the post-hoc adapters, which do
not write a decision-log row — so an id here can be one you never see in the store.

The post-mutation hints (`KB1` `KB2` `WF1` `WF9` `WF10` `WF11` `AM3` `C5` `C2`) are emitted as ONE
decision whose id is the firing arms joined by `+` (e.g. `WF9+WF1+WF10+C5`). Match on the parts.

| id | adapter | event | fires when |
|---|---|---|---|
| `TE1` | posttool | PostToolUse | an `external-tool execute` whose envelope may read success while `result.os[]` carries error entries — the action failed; the errors are quoted |
| `TE2` | posttool | PostToolUse | the same envelope carrying non-fatal `result.os[]` warnings (truncation, rate-limit, deprecation) |
| `TE3` | posttool | PostToolUse | the execute returned an async job (`status: PENDING`, or a `jobId`) — the result is incomplete until polled |
| `AM3` | posttool | PostToolUse | after `agent update` or any `version create/update/publish/restore` — the response echoes no prompt, so the write is confirmed by re-reading `.prompt` |
| `WF9` | posttool | PostToolUse | after `workflow publish` — publish can keep a stale snapshot, so `nodes` is compared with `publishedNodes` |
| `WF1` | posttool | PostToolUse | after `workflow publish` — an empty `data.webhookUrl` on a webhook-triggered workflow is a known API gap, not a build error |
| `WF10` | posttool | PostToolUse | after `workflow publish` — names the publish-integrity sweep to run before any done claim |
| `WF11` | posttool | PostToolUse | after `workflow node update` — every downstream node result is now stale and must be re-run top-to-bottom |

## Keeping it honest

The id column is generated from the adapters, not from memory. To regenerate the inventory and diff it
against this file:

```bash
cd .claude/hooks && python3 check-inventory.py           # the inventory + the registry diff
cd .claude/hooks && python3 check-inventory.py --audit   # same, exit 1 on any drift
```

It walks the AST rather than matching text, because the layer's dominant emission shape is a check
function returning a tuple whose id reaches `log_decision` through a variable — no literal sits next
to the sink, so a regex sees nothing. The earlier recipe here matched only `log_decision(…, "LITERAL")`
and bracketed `[ID]` text; run against this file it certified 58 ids found and 1 missing while 115 were
actually absent. A blind audit is worse than none: it answers the question convincingly.

**Prefix-overlapping families are deliberate and must not be merged:** `H2`/`H2-TURN`,
`R34`/`R34-DUE`/`R34-HOLD`/`R34-LEDGER`/`R34-RES`/`R34-ESC`/`R34-BLOCK`,
`WSW`/`WSW-RET`/`WSW-SC`/`WSW-STALL`/`WSW-TIER`,
`PC`/`PC-BUILD`/`PC-CANON`, `RM1`/`RM1B`, `G1`/`G13`/`G14`/`G19`. They are separate checks. A shared
prefix has already caused one mis-attribution of 10 rows to the wrong check, so match ids exactly.

## Rollout rule

A verdict-bearing check ships behind an observe marker, is flipped deliberately, and the flip is
recorded. Marker present = record only. Marker absent = enforcing. A flip with no `MARKER` row in the
`markers` feed is a defect — `session_cache.py flip-marker <name> <on|off> <why>` is the way not to
create one.

## Priority 1 — fails toward ALLOWING, or destroys data

### D1 · The override token is a raw substring, so mentioning it disarms the guard
**[verified live]** `nexus-fs-firewall.py:703`

```python
if (is_recursive_force_rm(kw) and "NEXUS_RM_ACK=1" not in cmd
        and re.search(r"\bfor\s+\w+\s+in\b[^\n;]*\*", kw)
        and _EXCL_RE.search(kw)):
```

`"NEXUS_RM_ACK=1" not in cmd` tests the **raw** command — before quote-stripping and before heredoc-stripping. Any appearance of those 16 characters anywhere disarms `RM1` and `RM1B` for that command: inside a quoted string, a comment, a heredoc body, a file being written. **Documenting the override disables it.**

- **Failure direction:** toward allowing. This is the substring-not-act class running *backwards* — a substring that suppresses a deny rather than causing one, which is the more dangerous direction.
- **Fix:** require the token at a command position, in the same statement as the act. `hook_core.at_command_position` (`lib/hook_core.py:1343`) already exists and is the right primitive.
- **Test:** assert the guard still denies when the token appears in an `echo`, a commit message, and a heredoc body; assert it stands down when the token is a real leading assignment.

### D2 · A fifth copy of the non-shell-aware quote regex survives in the firewall
**[verified live]** `nexus-fs-firewall.py:201`

```python
for a, b in re.findall(r"'([^']*)'|\"([^\"]*)\"", cmd):
```

`'[^']*'|"[^"]*"` handles neither `'\''` concatenation nor `\"` escaping, so an escaped quote ends the span early and leaks the rest of a string into the keyword view. The canonical escape-aware scanner is `hook_core.strip_quoted_spans` (`lib/hook_core.py:1348`).

- **History:** the class has been swept **twice** and declared closed both times. The first sweep searched the adapters while the surviving copy was in the library; this copy is in an adapter and survived the second. Measured on the library copy before it was fixed: disagreement on **723 of 19,333 commands (3.7%)**, producing **12 verdict differences in both directions**.
- **Failure direction:** both. It produced the false SIP denies on commit messages containing escaped quotes, and it feeds D3.
- **Fix:** call `hc.strip_quoted_spans`. Then make the sweep mechanical: `grep -rn "\[^'\]\*" .claude/hooks/` as an assertion in the suite, so copy #6 cannot land silently.
- **Test:** a suite assertion that the pattern text appears nowhere outside `hook_core`.

### D3 · "Fail closed" falls back to the behaviour that was removed as defective
**[lane-reported, code verified]** `nexus-fs-firewall.py:515`

```python
_targets = norms if _rt is None else [norm(c, cwd) for c in _rt]
```

`rm_targets()` correctly returns `None` when a target contains `$` or a backtick — the expansion is unknowable. But `None` routes `PROT-ROOT` to `norms`, the every-path-in-the-command set that W28 removed as defective. So the whole-command scan is back for the commonest real shape, `rm -rf "$DIR"`.

- **Measured:** a real corpus command produced `"Refusing recursive delete of a protected root: /"` while deleting a clone directory. **A deny whose stated reason is demonstrably false is worse than a deny** — it costs the trust every other gate depends on.
- **Fix:** keep `None → broad`, but restrict "broad" to candidates inside the matched `rm` **statement span**, which `_RM_SEG_RE` (`nexus-fs-firewall.py:240`) already computes. Narrow the fallback's *scope*, not its *breadth*.
- **Test:** assert the deny message names a path that actually appears as an `rm` operand.

### D4 · A `once()` store error silences 102 checks with no trace
**[lane-reported]** `lib/session_cache.py`

The one-shot helper returns `False` on any store error, which is indistinguishable from "already fired". A broken or read-only store therefore reads as "everyone has already been warned" and silences every rate-limited check at once.

- **Failure direction:** toward allowing, silently, at the widest possible blast radius.
- **Fix:** separate "already set" from "could not write". On a write failure, fire (fail toward speaking) and increment the health counter.
- **Test:** point the state root at a read-only directory and assert the checks still emit.

## Priority 3 — correctness gaps with measured cost

### D9 · A quadratic regex hangs the hook for 41 seconds
**[verified live]** `lib/hook_core.py:838`

```python
_DOSSIER_RE = re.compile(r'(retrieval-dossier[\w./-]*|/file\?path=|[\w./-]+\.md\b)', re.I)
```

`[\w./-]+` followed by a `.` that is itself in the class. Measured end to end through the real adapter:

| input | before | after the proposed fix |
|---|---|---|
| 10,000 chars | 0.567 s | 0.129 s |
| 40,000 chars | 6.917 s | 0.137 s |
| 100,000 chars | **41.402 s** | 0.153 s |

Reached on every retriever `SubagentStop`, over the subagent's whole final message — and the triggering input is precisely the failure branch the check exists to catch (a retriever pasting a raw payload because it could not write its file). To the user this is indistinguishable from a slow subagent: no output, no error.

- **Fix:** one-token lookbehind, `(?<![\w./-])[\w./-]+\.md\b`. Equivalence already proven: 600,000 randomised strings over two alphabets comparing `bool(match)` **and** `group(0)` → 142,114 matches, **0 differences**, plus 11 hand-picked shapes and a 7-suite regression pass.
- **Siblings:** `lib/hook_core.py:2646` and `_envelope_sig` at `nexus-pretool.py:1305`.
- **Do NOT** fix this with an input length cap at the adapter boundary — measured, any cap low enough to help sits below real traffic (max real command 28,247 chars), and "skip the guard past N bytes" is a one-line bypass recipe.

### D10 · `WSW` fires on pure reads of the resource its own docstring blesses
**[lane-reported]** `nexus-fs-firewall.py:583`

```python
if MUT_NONNET_RE.search(kw):          # any write verb ANYWHERE in the command
    for t in norms:                   # every path ANYWHERE in the command
```

Gated on the mere *presence* of a mutating verb rather than that verb's own arguments. Denies `ls <mount> && mkdir -p /tmp/scan2`, `cp <mount>/INDEX.md /tmp/backup.md`, `wc -l <mount>/*.md; touch /tmp/done`.

This is the exact shape `rm_targets()` was written to replace, left standing in a sibling check — *"a guard that fires on paths you're only reading trains people to work around it."*

- **Fix:** a `write_targets()` mirroring `rm_targets()`, with the None-means-broad property designed in from the start.

# Observe markers — the recorded end-state of every muted gate

Each `.＜id＞-observe` file in this directory mutes one check to log-only. This file records, per
gate, the decision that keeps it muted or promotes it, the evidence that decision was made on,
and the condition that re-opens it.

**Why the file exists.** A gate left off by accident and a gate left off on purpose look
identical six weeks later. The observe ladder promotes on decision rows, so a marker with no
recorded reasoning silently converts "nobody looked" into "we decided". Nine markers were
carrying exactly that ambiguity.

**Read the evidence column as it is written.** `rows` counts decision rows across all sessions.
A row verdict of `observe` means the check recorded that it was muted, NOT that it caught
something. That distinction is why the FLEET1 row below reads the way it does.

## The per-gate decisions (measured 2026-08-04, all sessions)
